What this is. A plain-English handbook for explaining every project, technology and number on the resume Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf, in depth and in your own words. Study plans

If you have one evening. Read 01 (intros), 02 (numbers), and the one-minute version plus the "Say this / don't say this" box of chapters 03–07.

If you have three days. - Day 1: 01, 02, 03, 04. Practise the IA whiteboard scripts out loud. - Day 2: 05, 06, 07, 08. Practise each one-minute version. - Day 3: 11 (pick 6 stories and rehearse), skim 09 and 10 for anything unfamiliar, then do the practice drills at the end of each project chapter without looking.

If you have a week. Add one deep-dive doc per day from prep/ (listed below) and do every practice drill twice, once out loud.

How to answer any question (the shape that works)

  1. Direct answer first, in one sentence.
  2. Context: what the system was and why it mattered.
  3. What I did: the design, with one concrete detail.
  4. Result: one or two numbers, said the way chapter 2 shows.
  5. What I learned or would change.

Keep it to about 60–90 seconds, then stop and let them pick the next thread.

The honesty rules (they protect you)

• Uber work was via EPAM. ANZ is historical Uber Mobility work. Menu 98% is offline evaluation.
• 80% is a CI promotion gate, not live accuracy for all tenants. 73% and 74% come from a separate 200-case benchmark.
• 15.5× is query time. The 170 GB OOM is load time. They're not cause and effect.
• 344k is rows per second, not requests per second. The 4.09B copy was in flight.
• Partition rollback means drop the partition and recopy, not an atomic swap.
• At Impact Analytics there's no Kafka, Flink, CDC, Kubernetes operations, Milvus or human review queue. Cluster Copilot and Hindsight are verbal-only depth. LangSmith is Ask Iris only.
• "Led 3" is Uber FRM. "Mentored 2" is Masters India. Don't merge them.
• Kubernetes, Terraform, Spark: study-only / literacy. Never "I operated clusters".
• Never share cluster hosts, passwords or .env values. Don't offer to open-source the copier.

01. Introductions and career story

How to use this page

  • It covers the first five minutes of almost every interview: "tell me about yourself", "walk me through your resume", "why are you looking", "why did you move", and "what are you most proud of".
  • Read it the night before any screen. Say the 30-second and 90-second intros out loud three times each until they feel like your own words.
  • Memorise the numbers in the intros and the one-line reason for each career move. Everything else you can paraphrase.
  • For the stories behind these answers, go to STAR stories. For how each number was derived, go to Numbers explained.

Tags used on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind the number. ESTIMATED means it is arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and resumes. TARGET means it was a design goal, so I say "targeting". If a number has no tag here, it is a resume number and the derivation lives in Numbers explained.

1. The career at a glance

In plain words: I have spent five years building backend and data systems. I started on a consumer education product, moved to a regulated tax-compliance product, then worked inside Uber through the consulting firm EPAM, and I now work at Impact Analytics on a retail planning product with an AI layer. Each move added one new layer of difficulty: first reliability, then scale and correctness under deadlines, then finance-grade auditability and leading people, and now data platforms plus applied AI.

2. Words you may need to explain in an intro

You will not define these in the intro itself. But interviewers often interrupt with "what does that mean?", so have one sentence ready.

  • Backend. The server-side code that stores data, applies business rules and answers requests from apps and websites. Think of the kitchen of a restaurant, not the dining room.
  • Microservices. Splitting one big application into small services that each own one job and can be deployed separately. Like a food court instead of one giant kitchen.
  • p95 latency. The response time that 95 out of 100 requests beat. It tells you how slow the bad-but-normal requests are, not just the average.
  • RPS (requests per second). How many API calls the system answers each second.
  • ClickHouse. A database built for analytics. It stores data by column, so summing one column over hundreds of millions of rows is fast. Postgres is a filing cabinet of complete records. ClickHouse is a stack of ledgers, one per column.
  • Pivot. A planner's summary table, for example "sales by store by week for this season". On raw data it means grouping hundreds of millions of rows.
  • Reconciliation. Checking that two sets of numbers that should match actually match, for example the finance system against the filed quarterly report.
  • Materiality. The dollar size above which an error in the financial statements would matter to a reader. At Uber's Q4 2025 close it was $340M.
  • Strangler pattern. Replacing an old system piece by piece behind the same front door, so the old one keeps serving whatever has not moved yet. Like renovating a house one room at a time while you still live in it.
  • LLM (large language model). A model like GPT, Gemini or Claude that reads and writes text.
  • Eval gate. An automatic test in CI (continuous integration, the pipeline that runs on every code change) that scores the AI on a fixed set of cases and blocks a release if the score is too low.
  • Via EPAM. EPAM Systems is a global engineering services company. I was employed by EPAM and embedded full-time in Uber teams, working in Uber's codebase. Always say "Uber via EPAM".

3. The three introductions

All three use only resume numbers. Speaking pace is about 150 words a minute, so the word counts below match the times.

3.1 The 30-second intro (about 90 words)

Use this for a recruiter screen, a panel where five people introduce themselves, or when someone says "quickly, tell me about yourself".

I'm Tarun Mittal, a senior software engineer with five years in Java, Python and Go backends and data platforms. At Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a retail planning product. I own a Go platform that peaks at 10,000 requests per second, and I built a ClickHouse layer that took planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds. Before that, at Uber via EPAM, I owned a Finance risk-scoping backend that cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days. I'm looking for a senior role with bigger scope and a strong design-review culture.

Why this shape. One sentence of identity, two proofs from the current job, one proof from the previous job, one sentence of what I want. Then stop. If they want more they will ask.

3.2 The 90-second intro (about 230 words)

Use this as the default for a hiring manager or the start of a technical round.

I'm Tarun Mittal, a senior software engineer with five years building backend and data systems in Java, Python and Go.

I joined Impact Analytics in May 2026. I work on AssortSmart, which helps retailers decide which products to keep, drop or add each season. On the platform side I own a multi-tenant Go service that handles 10,000 requests per second at peak, and I built a ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer that took a planner pivot from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250-million-row test. On the AI side I built a decision engine that scores 348,000 article-seasons by blending fixed KPI math with LLM judgement, and I shipped Ask Iris, a chat copilot for planners. Every model change has to pass an 80% accuracy gate in CI before it is promoted.

Before that I spent almost two years at Uber via EPAM. I owned the backend of the Finance risk-scoping platform, which cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days, and I led three engineers on its ORM migration. I also worked on Uber Eats menu ingestion, which took restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours.

Earlier, at Masters India, I led a PHP-to-Spring Boot migration that cut p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and I started my career at GeeksforGeeks on Django.

I'm looking for a senior role with bigger scope and a strong design-review bar.

If they cut you off at 30 seconds, stop after the ClickHouse sentence and the Uber sentence. Do not keep listing companies.

3.3 The 3-minute intro (about 450 words)

Use this only when they explicitly say "take your time" or "walk me through your background". It is chronological and it explains why each move made sense. This is also your answer to "walk me through your resume" (section 5).

I'm Tarun Mittal. I've been a backend engineer for five years, in Java, Python and Go, and over time my work has moved from product APIs towards data platforms and applied AI.

I started at GeeksforGeeks in 2021, straight out of IET Lucknow. I migrated the doubt-support forum from PHP to Django so it could handle 10,000-plus daily queries and the 10x traffic spikes during live coding contests. I also built an influencer earnings dashboard and scheduled background jobs. That job taught me production basics: caching, hot rows, and how to migrate a product people are using every day.

After about a year and a quarter I moved to Masters India, a GST e-invoicing company, because I wanted to own a regulated product and a real migration, not just features. I led the move from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices for 1,500-plus enterprise clients. p95 latency dropped from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and the bulk pipeline handled over a million government submissions a day. I also mentored two engineers. The big lesson there was that sequencing a migration matters more than the target architecture.

Then I joined Uber via EPAM, because I wanted a higher engineering bar and work that sat close to Finance and audit. I owned the backend of the FRM risk-scoping platform: 36 endpoints, an 8-table MySQL schema, and a move off Google Sheets that cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days against a $340 million materiality threshold. I led three engineers on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that took the module to 100% statement coverage. I also worked on Uber Eats menu ingestion, which cut restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saved about $600K a year. Uber taught me what audit-grade correctness feels like.

In May 2026 I joined Impact Analytics to go deep on data platforms and AI. I own AssortSmart's Go platform at 10,000 requests per second at peak. I moved planner pivots onto ClickHouse rollups, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, and I fixed a 170 GB out-of-memory failure in the weekly builds by processing one fiscal week at a time. On the AI side I built the keep-or-drop decision engine over 348,000 article-seasons, with an 80% accuracy gate in CI before any change is promoted, and I shipped Ask Iris, a planner copilot.

The thread through all of it is that I own a system end to end and I decide with measurements. Next I want a senior role with bigger scope and a stronger design-review bar, where I can do that for several years.

Pacing tip. Pause for one breath after each company. If the interviewer's face says "enough", jump to the last paragraph.

4. The career arc: why each move made sense

Interviewers ask "why did you leave X?" for every job. They are testing two things: whether you move towards something (good) or run away from something (worrying), and whether you learned anything. Each answer below is under 45 seconds, positive, and ends with what I learned.

4.1 Starting at GeeksforGeeks (Aug 2021 to Nov 2022)

What the job was. GeeksforGeeks is a large learning platform for programmers. I worked on the courses platform: the doubt-support forum where students post questions about courses and articles, and an analytics and earnings dashboard for influencer partners who sell courses.

What I did. I migrated the doubt-support backend from PHP to Django, page by page behind the same URLs. I built REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads on MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch. It handled 10K+ daily queries and 10x spikes during live coding contests. The growth team attributed a 20% lift in premium subscriptions (relative) to the features. I also built the influencer analytics dashboard and asynchronous scheduled workflows for video processing, reminders and data cleanup. The business team attributed a 30% lift in course sales and a 70% gain in operations efficiency. All of these are HISTORICAL. The honest framing is: "I owned the engineering, and the business team attributed the lift."

What I learned. How to keep a live product reliable while changing it underneath. Practical things like a unique database constraint for vote idempotency (a user voting twice still counts once), counters in Redis to avoid one hot database row, and reconciling counts back to MySQL.

4.2 GeeksforGeeks to Masters India

Why the move made sense.

At GeeksforGeeks I was shipping features on a consumer content platform. Masters India offered ownership of a regulated financial product and a real platform migration. I wanted to grow from feature delivery into owning a service cutover and mentoring people. That's exactly what happened: I led the PHP-to-Spring Boot migration and mentored two engineers.

What the job was. Masters India sells GST compliance and e-invoicing software to Indian enterprises. Clients send invoices to our APIs. We validate them and register them with the government's IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number) and a signed QR code. Without that registration a business-to-business invoice is not valid. So correctness matters more than speed, and filing-deadline days bring big spikes.

What I did. I led the strangler migration from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, one route at a time with canaries. p95 latency went from 1.2s to 300ms (75% lower) across 1,500+ enterprise clients, and throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute. I built the bulk e-invoicing pipeline on Kafka with PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, idempotent processing for 100K+ concurrent imports, dead-letter queues and bounded retries. It carried 1M+ government submissions a day. I added ELK and New Relic tracing plus a Redis cache-aside layer, which cut incident triage by 70% and database read load by 30%. Test coverage went from 35% to 82%, with 98% deployment success. All HISTORICAL.

What I learned. Three things. Sequencing is the real risk tool in a migration. Idempotency is not optional when the other side (a government portal) cannot undo a duplicate. And mentoring is mostly setting conventions and reviewing early, then stepping back.

4.3 Masters India to Uber via EPAM

Why the move made sense.

I had taken the GST platform through its migration and scale-up. Uber via EPAM was a jump in engineering bar, product surface and systems complexity. I wanted Bazel monorepo discipline, Uber-scale practices, and work that sat next to Finance and audit. That's where I owned the FRM scoping backend and the reconciliation migration.

What "via EPAM" means, if asked. I was an EPAM employee embedded in Uber teams. I worked in Uber's monorepo, under Uber's review process, on Uber products. On FRM I was the tech lead of an EPAM pod of three engineers, not a people manager.

What I did. Three products:

  1. FRM (Financial Risk Management) Scoping Platform for Uber Finance. Every quarter, Finance decides which financial line items and legal entities are "in scope" for audit testing. It used to live in Google Sheets. I owned the backend: 36 Spring Boot endpoints, a migration of 19M raw general-ledger rows off Sheets into MySQL, a nested 4-level FSLI (Financial Statement Line Item) hierarchy, and an 8-table normalized schema on SOADB (Uber's standard for service-owned MySQL). Quarterly reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days (70%) against a $340M materiality threshold. I led three engineers on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that removed latent column-aliasing bugs and took module statement coverage to 100%.
  2. Uber Eats menu ingestion. Turning restaurant menus (often messy multilingual PDFs) into Uber's strict catalog format. Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours, saving about $600K a year across 30K+ menus a month, with 98% field fidelity on an offline evaluation. Extraction success reached 95%+ after hardening the scraper fleet, with Kafka and Apache Flink for ingestion.
  3. Uber Mobility ANZ document compliance. Automated driver and vehicle document checks against local rules: 99.9% regulatory compliance and 20 hours a week of manual work removed. HISTORICAL.

What I learned. What audit-grade correctness feels like: every number traceable, every change reviewed, stacked PRs so nothing big lands at once. I also learned to call my own mistakes quickly and turn them into team process (see the refactor story in STAR stories).

4.4 Uber via EPAM to Impact Analytics

Why the move made sense.

I wanted deeper ownership of a data platform and agentic AI systems, not only service APIs, and I wanted to own them directly at a product company. Impact Analytics offered a senior charter on AssortSmart: the Go platform, the ClickHouse analytics path, and the AI decision layer. That matched where I want to go deep.

What the job is. AssortSmart is retail merchandise planning software. Planners at retailers decide which articles (products) to keep, drop or add each season, and the system needs fast analytics over billions of rows plus AI-assisted recommendations.

What I do. Two areas:

  1. Core infrastructure. A multi-tenant Go/Gin platform at 10k peak RPS with Google Wire dependency injection, native HTTP/2 cleartext (h2c) and Datadog tracing. A ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer that made planner pivots 15.5x faster (189s to 12s on a 250M-row test). Weekly rollup builds that used to hit a 170 GB out-of-memory failure, fixed by slicing work into one fiscal week per insert. A custom Go data pump that copies rollups between ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 344k rows per second.
  2. Agentic AI. A decision engine (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style) that evaluates 348k article-seasons, 88k items per pass, across 7 AI "lenses". The LLM never queries the 2.11B-row database directly. It gets prepared JSON context. A 300-case evaluation harness with an 80% accuracy CI gate decides what gets promoted. And Ask Iris, a secure chat copilot for planners built on LangGraph.

What I am learning. Measure first, then choose the tool. Shrink the unit of work before you buy more memory. And with AI, put a deterministic contract around the probabilistic part, and freeze a change when the data says it is not better yet.

5. "Walk me through your resume"

This is different from "tell me about yourself". They want the order of events and a quick sense of scope for each role, so they can choose what to dig into. Go oldest to newest, two or three sentences per role, then hand control back.

Say this (about 2 minutes)

Sure, I'll go in order and you can stop me anywhere.

GeeksforGeeks, 2021 to 2022: my first job. I migrated the doubt-support forum from PHP to Django to handle 10,000-plus daily queries and 10x contest spikes, and built an influencer dashboard and background jobs.

Masters India, end of 2022 to mid 2024: GST e-invoicing. I led a strangler migration from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices for 1,500-plus clients, with p95 going from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and built a Kafka pipeline doing over a million government submissions a day. I mentored two engineers.

Uber via EPAM, mid 2024 to May 2026: I owned the Finance risk-scoping backend, which cut reconciliation from 14 days to 3, and I led three engineers on its ORM migration. I also worked on Uber Eats menu ingestion, 24 hours to 2 hours for onboarding, and earlier on driver document compliance for Australia and New Zealand.

Impact Analytics, since May 2026: I own AssortSmart's Go platform and ClickHouse analytics layer, 189 seconds to 12 for pivots, and the AI decision engine and the Ask Iris copilot.

Which of those would be most useful to go deeper on?

Why end with a question. It turns a monologue into a conversation, and it lets them pick the project they care about instead of you guessing.

6. "Why are you looking?" (the short-tenure question)

What they are testing. Flight risk. I joined Impact Analytics in May 2026, so looking now is early. They want to know whether I will leave them in five months too, and whether I am running from a problem I caused.

The rule. Acknowledge "early" in the first sentence. People who dodge the word "soon" sound like they are hiding something. Then say what I am moving towards. Never criticise an employer, a manager or a team.

Say this

It's early, and I won't pretend otherwise. I joined Impact Analytics in May 2026 and the work is real: the ClickHouse path, the decision engine and Ask Iris are all in production, and I'm proud of them. I'm not leaving because something went wrong.

What I want next is a senior role with bigger scope and a stronger design-review bar: a larger production surface, written design reviews before code, and peers who push back hard on designs. That's the environment where I do my best work.

I'm being selective. I'm talking to a few companies carefully, including yours, because I want my next move to be a multi-year run. And I'll do a proper handover on my current work, whatever my notice period says.

Follow-up they may ask: "Four companies in five years. Why should we believe you'll stay?"

Each move added a layer: product features at GeeksforGeeks, a regulated SaaS migration and mentoring at Masters India, Uber-scale finance and data work via EPAM, and data platforms plus AI at Impact Analytics. The tenures before this one were about a year and a quarter, a year and a half, and almost two years. The short one is the current role, and I'm being open about why. I stay when the scope keeps growing, and that's what I'm optimising for now.

Follow-up: "Does your manager know?"

Not yet. I don't start that conversation before I have a decision. And I won't accept an offer and then leave my current team stuck.

Follow-up: "When can you join?"

I'll confirm the exact notice period from my contract and tell you in writing before we agree a date. I'd rather give you a real date than a guess.

Say this / don't say this

Say Do not say
"It's early, and I won't pretend otherwise." "The role isn't what I was promised."
"I want bigger scope and a stronger design-review bar." Anything about chaos, a bad manager, a boring stack, or being underpaid.
"I'll do a proper handover." "My current job doesn't really count."
"I'm being selective this time." "I'm always exploring."
Mention money only if they ask, and ask for their band first. Lead with compensation.

7. "What are you most proud of?"

Pick one, say it in under 90 seconds, and connect it to a lesson. My strongest answer is the ClickHouse decision because it shows technical depth, influence without authority, and measuring before arguing. The backup is the Uber column-aliasing fix, if they want a correctness or debugging angle.

Primary answer: turning a database argument into an evidence-based decision

The thing I'm proudest of is how we chose ClickHouse at Impact Analytics. Planner pivots on Postgres were taking up to 189 seconds on 250 million rows, and the org was split. One group had audited the old system and concluded "no ClickHouse". Senior experts wanted it everywhere. Both sides had real evidence.

I didn't pick a side. I accepted every measured fact from the audit, and showed that their "no" came from the old system doing in-place updates, which ClickHouse is bad at, not from analytical reads, which it's great at. I proposed a staged path with measurable gates and ran a row-identical proof of concept on the same 250 million rows. The pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, and the org committed to ClickHouse for planning analytics. Postgres kept roles and transactional data.

What I'm proud of isn't the speed-up. It's that nobody "lost". The decision was made on numbers both camps trusted.

The full story, with follow-ups, is Story 3 in STAR stories.

Backup answer: the bug that pointed edits at the wrong line

At Uber, the Finance risk-scoping tool read joined SQL results into maps keyed by column name. Two joined tables both had a column called uuid, and the map silently kept the wrong one. Edits and comments could land on a different financial line than the one on screen. I moved the reads to Spring Data JPA queries with an explicit alias on every column, so names can't collide, and ran the new reconciliation path in parallel with the old one before cutting over. In a tool that feeds audit evidence, a silent wrong answer is the worst kind of bug. Making that class of bug impossible is the work I'm proudest of at Uber.

Full version: Story 6 in STAR stories.

8. A simple framework for answering any question

Most weak interview answers bury the answer at the end. Use this five-step shape for behavioural questions, project questions and even many technical "why" questions.

flowchart LR A["1. Direct answer, one sentence"] --> B["2. Context, two sentences"] B --> C["3. What I did, three or four steps"] C --> D["4. Result, with a number and its tag"] D --> E["5. What I learned, one sentence"]

What to notice: the answer comes first. If they cut you off after step 1, they still got the answer.

  1. Direct answer. Answer the actual question in one sentence. "Yes, I disagreed with a team standard at Uber and we ended up documenting an exception."
  2. Context. Just enough for the answer to make sense. Who, what system, why it mattered. Two sentences, not a history lesson.
  3. What I did. Use "I", not "we", for your part. Three or four concrete actions. Credit others by name of role ("the data pipeline team", "my two mentees").
  4. Result. A number if you have one, and say how solid it is ("measured on a 250-million-row harness", "estimated"). If there is no number, say the qualitative outcome honestly.
  5. What I learned. One sentence that would change how you act next time.

Worked example: "Tell me about a time you made a mistake."

(Answer) Yes. At Uber I slipped a behaviour change into what was supposed to be a pure refactor, and a test caught it. (Context) It was the second of three stacked PRs, consolidating constants across 31 files, on the Finance scoping service. (What I did) When a downstream test failed, I diffed my own PR line by line, found a small helper I'd added that changed the selection strategy, removed it, and then added "pure refactor means zero test diff" to the team's stacked-PR checklist. (Result) It shipped as a true refactor, and the checklist caught a similar issue for a teammate a few weeks later. (Learned) Call your own fouls fast and turn them into process.

Three more rules that make any answer better

  • Stop after the number. The urge to keep talking after a good result weakens it.
  • If the question is unclear, ask. "Do you want the technical deep dive or the leadership side?"
  • If you have not done the thing, say so. "I haven't owned that exact case. Here's how I'd approach it, using a related example." Never invent.

9. Tailoring the intro to the role

Keep the same skeleton (who I am, two current proofs, one past proof, what I want). Swap which proofs you lead with.

9.1 Backend / platform engineering roles

Lead with: the Go platform, FRM ownership, the Masters latency win, idempotency.

I'm Tarun Mittal, a senior backend engineer with five years in Java, Python and Go microservices. At Impact Analytics I own AssortSmart's multi-tenant Go/Gin platform. It peaks at 10,000 requests per second, uses compile-time dependency injection with Google Wire, and protects itself at the HTTP edge with nested timeouts, with Datadog tracing throughout. I also built the tenant isolation and access control across Postgres and ClickHouse. At Uber via EPAM I owned the Finance risk-scoping backend: 36 Spring Boot endpoints on an 8-table MySQL schema, with optimistic locking and deterministic keys so quarterly audit trails never duplicate, and reconciliation went from 14 days to 3. At Masters India I led a strangler migration from PHP to Spring Boot that took p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and built idempotent bulk processing for a million-plus government submissions a day. I'm looking for a senior backend role with bigger scope and a strong design-review bar.

Have ready: why no reverse proxy in front of the Go service, how optimistic locking works, how the idempotency key was built (client + file hash + batch index). See IA core platform, Uber FRM, Masters India.

9.2 Data / infrastructure roles

Lead with: ClickHouse rollups, the 170 GB out-of-memory fix, the Go data pump, Kafka at Masters, Kafka and Flink on Uber Menu.

I'm Tarun Mittal, a senior engineer with five years on backends and data platforms. At Impact Analytics I moved planner analytics onto ClickHouse. Six pre-aggregated rollup tables took a pivot from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250-million-row harness. The weekly rollup build was failing with about 170 GB of memory needed for a full season, so I sliced it into one fiscal week per insert with memory and disk-spill caps. I also wrote a Go data pump over ClickHouse's native TLS protocol to copy rollups between Cloud clusters at about 344,000 rows per second, on partitions up to 4.09 billion rows, because IP allowlists blocked a direct cluster-to-cluster copy. Before that, on Uber Eats I worked on a Kafka and Flink ingestion pipeline with keyed deduplication and idempotent catalog upserts, and at Masters India I built a Kafka e-invoicing pipeline doing over a million submissions a day on Postgres sharded by tax quarter. I'm looking for a senior data platform role with bigger scope.

Say this carefully. 344k is rows per second of copy throughput, not requests per second. The 4.09B-row copy was measured while it was in flight. Do not say the cutover finished. The 15.5x speed-up is query time and the 170 GB fix is load time, so one did not cause the other. Kafka and Flink belong to Uber Menu, never Impact Analytics.

Have ready: why week-sized chunks, what double-buffered batches means, why "atomic partition rollback" is really drop the partition then recopy. See IA core platform and Uber Menu and ANZ.

9.3 AI / agents roles

Lead with: the decision engine, isolating the LLM from the database, Ask Iris, the eval gate, Uber Menu RAG.

I'm Tarun Mittal, a senior engineer with five years in Java, Python and Go, and a growing part of my work is production AI. At Impact Analytics I built AssortSmart's merchandise decision engine. It scores 348,000 article-seasons by blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM calls across seven "lenses". The LLM never touches our 2.11-billion-row ClickHouse table. It gets prepared JSON context, and if the model times out we fall back to the deterministic score. Runs have hard timeouts, circuit breakers and checkpoints, and every output row is stamped with a config hash so we can reproduce it. I also shipped Ask Iris, a LangGraph supervisor copilot for planners, with a three-attempt evaluator loop, LangSmith tracing, and tenant scope frozen when the WebSocket opens. Nothing gets promoted unless it passes an 80% accuracy gate on a 300-case harness. Before that, on Uber Eats, I used Gemini 2.5 Pro with LangChain RAG over Milvus to turn multilingual PDF menus into catalog data at 98% field fidelity on an offline evaluation. I'm looking for a senior role building AI systems that are measured and safe in production.

Say this carefully. 80% is a CI promotion gate, not live accuracy for every tenant. The 73% lower cost and the 74% deterministic baseline come from a separate 200-case gold benchmark, not the 300-case file. When the blended LLM score came in below the deterministic baseline, we froze the blend weights instead of retuning them. Ask Iris is a shipped capability with no usage or SLA numbers. Menu's 98% is an offline evaluation. LangSmith is on Ask Iris only.

Have ready: why not let the LLM write SQL, why a three-attempt cap, how the blend works (final score = 0.4 x deterministic + 0.6 x agent, keep if 0.55 or higher). See IA agentic AI.

10. Other questions that come up in the first five minutes

"What's your biggest weakness?"

I over-invest in written artifacts: decision docs, playbooks, comparisons. They're useful, but a 20-page analysis nobody reads is its own failure. So I now time-box them and lead with a one-page summary that says the decision and the evidence, with the detail underneath for whoever needs it.

"Why should we hire you?" (30 seconds)

You get someone who owns a system end to end and can defend every number. At Uber via EPAM I owned a finance-grade backend that cut reconciliation from 14 days to 3. At Masters India I scaled e-invoicing to over a million submissions a day. At Impact Analytics I run a Go platform at 10,000 requests per second, made pivots 15.5 times faster with ClickHouse, and shipped AI behind real evaluation gates. And I'm honest about what a number means. An 80% CI gate is a gate, not a claim that every customer sees 80%.

"What are you looking for in your next role?"

A senior role where I own a meaningful system for several years. Written design reviews before code, measurement as the default, and a team that argues about designs on evidence. Over three to five years I want to grow into a staff-level engineer or tech lead who owns a domain. Mentoring matters more to me than a management title.

"What do you do outside work?" Only answer if asked. Do not add hobbies to the intro.

11. Say this / don't say this (honesty box)

Say this carefully.

  • Always "Uber via EPAM". On FRM I was tech lead of an EPAM pod of three, not a people manager.
  • "Led 3 engineers" is Uber FRM. "Mentored 2 engineers" is Masters India. Never merge them into "led 5".
  • FRM's 70% (14 days to 3 days) is on the resume as the outcome. Do not walk it back unprompted. If pressed: "the technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what the platform delivered for the close."
  • The HFM data load into MySQL was a shared pipeline responsibility, and the real-time collaboration and Slack notification service was a separate team's. Do not claim them.
  • Menu's 98% is an offline evaluation. ANZ's 99.9% is historical, and it was Mobility, not Eats.
  • At Impact Analytics: no Kafka, Flink, CDC, Milvus or Kubernetes operations. The Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight are verbal only, not resume bullets.
  • The 4.09B-row copy was measured in flight, not a finished cutover. 15.5x (query time) and 170 GB (load time) are separate wins.
  • Never criticise a past or current employer.

12. Practice drill

Say each answer out loud, then check it against the section in brackets.

  1. Give your 30-second intro. Did you stop after "design-review culture"? (3.1)
  2. Give your 90-second intro to a hiring manager for a backend role. (3.2 and 9.1)
  3. Why did you leave GeeksforGeeks? (4.2)
  4. What does "via EPAM" mean? Were you an Uber employee? (4.3)
  5. Why did you leave Uber? (4.4)
  6. You joined in May. Why are you already looking? (6)
  7. Four companies in five years. Why will you stay with us? (6)
  8. What are you most proud of? (7)
  9. Walk me through your resume in two minutes. (5)
  10. Give the data/infra version of your intro. Did you say "rows per second", not "requests per second", for 344k? (9.2)
  11. Give the AI version of your intro. Did you call 80% a gate? (9.3)
  12. What's your biggest weakness? (10)
  13. Answer "tell me about a mistake" using the five-step framework. Did the direct answer come first? (8)

Chapter 2 — Every resume number, explained

How to use this chapter
• Each number has five parts: what it measures, where it comes from (arithmetic or source), why it mattered, how to say it, and what not to say.
• Interviewers love to ask "how did you measure that?". If you can explain the source in one sentence, the number becomes believable.
• Read the "trap pairs" in section 7 last. Those are the numbers people mix up.

Tags used below. - MEASURED: there is a log, benchmark, document or code that shows it. - ESTIMATED: arithmetic you can show on a whiteboard. Say "roughly" and show the math. - HISTORICAL: from your past work records at an earlier company. Say it plainly, and attribute business outcomes to the team that measured them. - OFF-PDF: true, but not printed on the resume. Use it only when it helps an answer.

1. Summary line

Number Meaning How to say it
5 years Aug 2021 (GeeksforGeeks) to now: GFG ~1.3 yrs, Masters India ~1.5 yrs, Uber via EPAM ~1.9 yrs, Impact Analytics since May 2026 "Five years building backend and data systems, the last two-plus on AI-assisted systems."

2. Impact Analytics — AssortSmart (May 2026 to Present)

Agentic

348k article-seasons · MEASURED - What: How many product-in-a-season items the Keep/Drop engine scores. - Source: The scored volume from the Keep/Drop runs. - Why it mattered: It's far more than planners can review by hand, which is why automation plus explanations is valuable. - Say: "It evaluates about 348 thousand article-seasons." - Don't: Confuse it with the 1.6M catalog (all product × season combinations, OFF-PDF).

88k items per pass · MEASURED - What: The batch size of one scoring run. - Why: Sized to fit memory and LLM provider rate limits. Also the unit that checkpoints and circuit breakers protect. - Say: "About 88 thousand items per pass." - OFF-PDF: about $100 per pass in token spend.

7 AI lenses · MEASURED - What: Seven active LLM "questions" (colour cannibalisation, size curve, channel divergence, multi-season consistency, trend velocity, discount dependency, margin resilience). - Say: "Seven structured lenses, each only run when the article has data for it."

2.11B-row ClickHouse master · MEASURED - What: The size of the main fact table the agents' context comes from. - Why: At that size, letting an LLM query it is dangerous and expensive. That's why it gets JSON. - Don't: Mix it with 4.09B (a rollup table in the copier story).

3 attempts (Ask Iris evaluator) · MEASURED (code constant MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3) - Why: Enough to recover from a bad first answer, low enough to cap cost and stop loops.

300 cases / 80% gate · MEASURED (config gold_min_accuracy: 0.8, cases file) - What: A 300-case proxy evaluation set. CI blocks promotion of a config that scores below 80%. - Say: "Promotion is gated at 80% on a 300-case proxy set in CI." - Don't: "80% accuracy in production for all tenants."

73% lower cost at 100% coverage · MEASURED (gold-200 benchmark) - What: On a separate 200-case benchmark, the chosen model cost 73% less than the previous mini model and completed all 200 cases (100% coverage = no pending rows). - Why: Running across all clients every season, cost is what decides whether it's viable. - Don't: Say the 300-case set measured 73%.

Chapter 3 — Impact Analytics: AssortSmart Core Infrastructure & Pipeline

How to use this chapter
• Read sections 1–4 once to understand the product and the big picture. Then study one bullet (C1–C5) per sitting.
• Memorise the one-minute version and the "Say this / don't say this" box.
• Practise the 3-minute whiteboard script at the end out loud, drawing as you talk.
• Companion chapters: Chapter 4 (Agentic AI), Chapter 2 (numbers), Chapter 10 (concepts).

Role: Senior Software Engineer, Impact Analytics, May 2026 to Present. Project title on the resume: AssortSmart — Senior Software Engineer (Platform & AI). The resume has two sub-sections for this job. This chapter is the second one, Core Infrastructure & Pipeline: the Go platform, the formula engine, security and tenancy, the ClickHouse speed-up, and the cluster-to-cluster data copy.

1. The one-minute version (say this out loud)

"At Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a planning product that retailers use to decide which products to carry each season. On the platform side I own the Go and Gin API layer. It is multi-tenant, peaks at about 10,000 requests per second, uses Google Wire for compile-time dependency injection, and protects itself with nested timeouts and Datadog tracing instead of relying on a reverse proxy. I built a formula engine so business users can define KPIs without a code release; it compiles their formulas into safe, parameterised ClickHouse SQL. I made planner pivot screens 15.5 times faster, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250-million-row test, by pre-aggregating data into six ClickHouse rollup tables, and I fixed a 170 GB out-of-memory crash in how those rollups are built. Finally, I wrote a Go data pump that copies those rollups between ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 344,000 rows per second, with ledgers and partition rollbacks so a crash never leaves half-copied data that looks complete."

2. The business in plain English

Who uses it. Merchandise planners at retail companies. A planner is the person who decides, for example, "next autumn we will sell these 400 women's tops in these 120 stores, and we will stop selling these 60."

What they do in the product. They open big pivot grids. Rows might be product categories, columns might be weeks, cells are numbers like units sold, revenue, margin, sell-through (the share of stock that actually sold) and rate of sale (units sold per store per week). They slice by product, by store, by product attribute (colour, size, fabric) and by season or week. They also define their own KPIs ("my margin after discount").

What hurt before. 1. Slow screens. The raw data is at the grain of "one product in one store on one day". Adding that up live for every screen was slow. On a 250-million-row test, a typical pivot took 189 seconds on the old PostgreSQL path. Nobody waits three minutes for a grid. 2. Every new KPI needed a code release. If a client wanted a new formula, an engineer had to write it. 3. Many clients on one platform. Each retailer (tenant) must only ever see its own data, and inside a retailer each planner should only see the part of the product hierarchy they are allowed to see. 4. Data had to move between clusters. Rollup tables needed to be copied between ClickHouse Cloud clusters, and the normal cluster-to-cluster copy was blocked by network allowlists.

Why the company paid for it. Fast screens mean planners actually use the tool during planning season. Self-serve KPIs mean fewer engineering tickets per client. Strong isolation is a contract requirement for enterprise retail clients.

3. Words you need

Term Plain meaning (with analogy)
Tenant One customer company on a shared platform. Like flats in one building: shared plumbing, separate locked doors.
Article / article-season An article is one product. An article-season is that product in one selling season. "Blue linen shirt, Summer 2026" is one article-season.
Go / Gin Go is a compiled language built for network servers. Gin is a lightweight Go web framework (routing, middleware, JSON).
RPS Requests per second that the API serves.
Dependency injection (DI) Instead of a component creating its own database client, logger, etc., someone hands them in. Like a restaurant kitchen where ingredients are delivered to each station instead of every cook going shopping.
Google Wire A Go tool that writes the "hand everything in" code for you at build time. If something is missing, the build fails, not production.
Reverse proxy A server in front of your app (Nginx, Envoy) that forwards traffic, often adding timeouts, TLS, rate limits.
h2c HTTP/2 over plain TCP (no TLS on that hop). HTTP/2 lets many requests share one connection.
Nested timeouts Several time limits inside each other: the whole request gets, say, 30 s; the database call inside it gets less; the server itself also limits slow clients.
Distributed tracing Following one request across services, with a timeline of each step. Like a parcel tracking page. Datadog is the tool.
ClickHouse A columnar analytics database. It stores each column separately and compresses it, so "sum revenue over 250M rows" is fast.
OLTP vs OLAP OLTP = many small reads and writes (PostgreSQL, MySQL). OLAP = big scans and aggregations (ClickHouse, BigQuery).
MergeTree ClickHouse's main table engine. Data is written in sorted chunks ("parts") that are merged in the background.
Partition A slice of a table you can manage as a unit, here one season (PARTITION BY season_code). You can drop or replace one partition without touching others.
Rollup / pre-aggregation Adding numbers up ahead of time and storing the totals, so screens read totals instead of raw rows. Like keeping a monthly bank summary instead of re-adding every transaction.
OOM Out of memory. The query tried to use more RAM than allowed and was killed.
Spill to disk When an aggregation gets too big for RAM, ClickHouse writes partial results to disk and continues, slower but alive.
UAM User Access Management: which user may see which part of the data.
OIDC / JWT / Firebase Admin Ways to prove who a user is. A JWT is a signed token. OIDC is a standard for logging in with an identity provider (here Google). Firebase Admin is Google's server SDK to verify Firebase-issued login tokens.
Constant-time comparison Comparing two secrets in a way that always takes the same time, so an attacker can't guess the key one character at a time by measuring response speed.
Native protocol / port 9440 ClickHouse's own binary protocol (faster than HTTP). 9440 is its TLS-encrypted port.
Double buffering Using two buffers so you can fill one while the other is being sent. Like two buckets in a bucket brigade.

4. Architecture

flowchart LR UI["Planner UI"] --> EDGE["Go / Gin API edge
Wire DI, h2c, nested timeouts"] EDGE --> AUTH["Auth waterfall
Redis cache, Firebase Admin, JWT / Google OIDC, API keys"] AUTH --> PG["PostgreSQL
users, roles, UAM hierarchy scopes, metadata"] EDGE --> KPI["KPI configurator
tokenizer + parser"] KPI --> SQL["Parameterised ClickHouse SQL
ifNotFinite guard"] SQL --> CH["ClickHouse
six rollup tables"] RAW["Daily facts
product x store x day"] --> LOAD["Weekly / season loaders
one fiscal week per INSERT"] LOAD --> CH CH --> PUMP["Go native-TLS pump
500k-row double-buffered batches"] PUMP --> CH2["Target ClickHouse Cloud cluster"] EDGE -.-> DD["Datadog traces"]

What to notice: reads come from rollups, not raw facts; the write side (loaders, pump) is separate from the request side; auth and tenant scope are decided once at the edge and carried into every query.

Box by box. - Planner UI sends HTTP requests: "give me this pivot", "save this KPI". - Go/Gin edge is the single entry point. Routing, JSON, auth middleware, timeouts and tracing all live in this one Go process. Wire assembled its dependencies at build time. - Auth waterfall answers "who is this?" cheaply. Redis first (cached verified identity), then the slower verifiers. PostgreSQL answers "what may they see?" (roles and hierarchy scopes). - KPI configurator turns a formula a business user typed into a safe SQL fragment. - ClickHouse rollups are six pre-aggregated tables that make screens fast. - Loaders build those rollups from raw daily facts, one fiscal week at a time so they never run out of memory. - Go pump copies rollup partitions to another ClickHouse Cloud cluster.

5. One request, step by step

Example: a planner at tenant "Retailer A" opens a pivot "Women > Tops, revenue and sell-through by week, Season 7".

sequenceDiagram participant U as Planner UI participant G as Go/Gin edge participant R as Redis participant P as PostgreSQL participant K as KPI compiler participant C as ClickHouse U->>G: GET /pivot (Bearer token) G->>R: cached identity for token hash? R-->>G: hit: user 42, tenant A G->>P: roles + hierarchy scope for user 42 P-->>G: may see Women > Tops only G->>K: compile "sell_through" formula K-->>G: SQL fragment + parameters G->>C: SELECT ... FROM product_weekly WHERE tenant scope AND season 7 (with query timeout) C-->>G: about 30 weeks x a few hundred rows G-->>U: JSON grid (trace id in Datadog)
  1. The request arrives with a token. The server has a request deadline (for example 30 seconds; the exact values are configuration, keep them qualitative if asked).
  2. The auth middleware hashes the token and checks Redis. A hit means "already verified recently". A miss means verifying with Firebase Admin, or as a JWT / Google OIDC token, then caching the result.
  3. PostgreSQL returns the user's role and hierarchy scope: Retailer A, Women > Tops.
  4. The KPI compiler turns "sell-through" into SQL with parameters and a divide-by-zero guard.
  5. The query hits product_weekly, a rollup table, with partition pruning on Season 7 and a filter for the user's scope. It is bounded by its own timeout, shorter than the request deadline.
  6. JSON goes back. Datadog has a trace showing auth time, compile time and ClickHouse time.

6. Each resume bullet decoded

C1 — Go/Gin platform, 10k peak RPS, Wire, no reverse proxy, h2c, nested timeouts, Datadog

Resume: Architected a multi-tenant Go/Gin platform scaling to 10k peak RPS, utilizing Google Wire for compile-time DI. Deployed as a self-protecting HTTP edge without a reverse proxy, guaranteeing high availability through native h2c, nested timeouts, and Datadog distributed tracing.

In plain words. I designed the main API server. It serves many retail clients, handles about 10,000 requests per second at peak, is assembled safely at compile time, and protects itself (timeouts, HTTP/2 handling, tracing) instead of depending on a separate proxy server in front of it.

How it works.

Wire, compile-time DI. You declare "providers" (functions that build things) and Wire generates the wiring code.

// wire.go (illustrative)
func InitServer(cfg Config) (*Server, error) {
    wire.Build(NewRedis, NewPostgres, NewClickHouse, NewAuth, NewKPIService, NewRouter, NewServer)
    return nil, nil
}

If NewKPIService needs a *ClickHouse and no provider returns one, wire fails at build time. Runtime DI libraries (Uber Fx, Dig) use reflection and would fail when the app starts or, worse, on a code path.

Self-protecting edge. Without Nginx or Envoy in front, the Go process must enforce its own limits. Go's http.Server has them built in:

srv := &http.Server{
    Handler:           h2c.NewHandler(router, &http2.Server{}), // HTTP/2 without TLS on this hop
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,  // slow-loris protection
    ReadTimeout:       15 * time.Second,
    WriteTimeout:      30 * time.Second,
    IdleTimeout:       120 * time.Second,
}
// per request: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 30*time.Second)
// per ClickHouse call: a shorter context deadline derived from ctx

(The numbers above are illustrative. In an interview say "server-level timeouts, a per-request deadline, and shorter per-dependency deadlines inside it".)

Nested timeouts mean the inner call always gives up before the outer one, so the server can still return a clean error instead of hanging. Example: request deadline 30 s, ClickHouse 25 s, Redis 100 ms.

h2c lets one TCP connection carry many concurrent requests (HTTP/2 multiplexing), which cuts connection overhead at high RPS. TLS is handled before traffic reaches this hop. If asked exactly where, describe it at that level and don't invent a specific load balancer.

Datadog tracing. Each request gets a trace ID. Spans for auth, compile and ClickHouse show where time went. This is how you find "pivots are slow because of query X for tenant Y".

Why this design. One less hop means less latency and one less thing to operate. The process owns its own timeouts, so behaviour is the same in every environment. Compile-time DI catches wiring mistakes before deploy.

Alternatives and why not. - Nginx/Envoy in front: a perfectly good choice, and many teams do it. We didn't need its features enough to justify another component to configure and monitor. - Fx/Dig runtime DI: more flexible, but errors show up at runtime and reflection makes code harder to follow.

The numbers. - 10k peak RPS: peak requests per second the platform serves. It is on the resume as a peak, not an average and not an SLA. If asked how you know, name the actual source you saw (for example a Datadog request-rate graph or a load test). Only say the one that is true for you. Don't invent an uptime percentage.

Questions they will ask. - "Why Gin and not the standard library?" Gin gives fast routing, middleware chaining and JSON binding with very little overhead. The standard library is fine too; Gin saves boilerplate across many routes. - "How do you stop one slow tenant from hurting others?" Per-request deadlines and per-query timeouts, so a heavy pivot can't hold a connection forever. Rollups make the heavy work cheap in the first place. - "What happens if ClickHouse is slow?" The inner deadline fires, we return a clear error to the UI, the trace shows the slow span, and the server keeps serving other requests.

C2 — Dynamic KPI configurator and formula parser

Resume: Eliminated deployment bottlenecks by architecting a dynamic KPI configurator and custom formula parser. Engineered a real-time compilation layer that tokenizes operator-authored math into parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragments with native division-by-zero protection, decoupling business logic from code releases.

In plain words. Business users can type a KPI formula. My code checks it, converts it into a safe SQL snippet, and the next request uses it. No engineer, no release.

How it works, with an example.

The user types: margin_pct = (revenue - cost) / revenue * 100

  1. Tokenize: split into pieces: (, revenue, -, cost, ), /, revenue, *, 100.
  2. Parse: build a tree that respects operator precedence (multiply and divide before add and subtract, brackets first).
  3. Resolve names: revenue and cost are logical names. A catalog maps them to physical columns such as sum(revenue) and sum(cost). Unknown names are rejected.
  4. Allowlist functions: only approved functions (for example sum, min, max, if-style helpers) are allowed. Anything else fails.
  5. Emit SQL, wrapped in a guard:
ifNotFinite(toFloat64((sum(revenue) - sum(cost)) / sum(revenue) * 100), 0) AS margin_pct
  1. Parameters: any literal values (thresholds, dates) are sent as query parameters, never pasted into the SQL string.

ifNotFinite(x, 0) returns 0 when x is infinity or NaN (not-a-number). In ClickHouse, dividing by zero gives inf or nan, not an error. Without the guard, a store with zero revenue would put inf into the JSON and break the planner's grid. That is the "native division-by-zero protection" on the resume.

Why this design. Formulas change often and differ per client. Hard-coding them meant a release for every change. Compiling them keeps the logic data-driven but still safe.

Alternatives and why not. - Let users write raw SQL: SQL injection risk and they could scan any table. No. - Evaluate formulas in Go after fetching rows: you'd pull millions of rows out of ClickHouse to compute in Go. Pushing the math into SQL lets ClickHouse do it where the data lives. - A general expression library: possible, but we needed tight control over allowed names and functions and the exact SQL produced.

Questions they will ask. - "How do you prevent SQL injection?" We never concatenate user text into SQL. Every token must parse. Identifiers must exist in the catalog. Functions must be on the allowlist. Literals become parameters. Unknown input fails closed. - "What if the formula is valid but slow?" It only references rollup columns, so the cost is bounded by the rollup's size, not the raw facts. - "Is it a prepared statement?" Not in the generic sense. The guard is parse plus allowlist plus parameters plus ifNotFinite. Say that precisely.

C3 — Multi-tenant isolation and hierarchy access control

Resume: Guaranteed strict multi-tenant data isolation and UAM-scoped hierarchy access control across PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. Redis-fronted Firebase Admin to JWT/Google OIDC waterfall, constant-time API keys, Postgres-backed role resolution.

In plain words. Every request is tied to one tenant and one user scope, and every query to PostgreSQL or ClickHouse is filtered by that scope. Login checks are fast because verified identities are cached in Redis.

How it works.

The waterfall is an ordered list of ways to verify a caller:

func identify(ctx context.Context, token string) (Identity, error) {
    if id, ok := cache.Get(ctx, hash(token)); ok {
        return id, nil                        // fast path: verified recently
    }
    if id, err := firebaseVerify(ctx, token); err == nil {
        cache.Set(ctx, hash(token), id, ttl); return id, nil
    }
    if id, err := jwtOrGoogleOIDCVerify(ctx, token); err == nil {
        cache.Set(ctx, hash(token), id, ttl); return id, nil
    }
    return Identity{}, ErrUnauthorized          // fails closed, never open
}

Constant-time API keys. Service callers use API keys. Ordinary string comparison stops at the first wrong character, so a wrong first character returns slightly faster than a wrong tenth character. Over many tries an attacker can learn the key. subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(a, b) always takes the same time.

Role resolution. After identity, PostgreSQL returns the user's role and hierarchy scope, for example "Retailer A, Women > Tops". That scope is attached to the request context and added to every query as a filter.

Why this design. Verifying a token with an external provider on every call is slow and costly. Caching verified results in Redis keeps auth cheap at high RPS. If Redis misses, we fall through to real verification. We never "fail open".

Important honesty line. Isolation is not encryption. Say "tenant isolation and access control", not "we encrypted each tenant's data".

Questions they will ask. - "What if a user's role changes?" Cached entries have a TTL (time to live). Role data comes from PostgreSQL, so changes apply when the cache entry expires or is cleared. - "How do you test isolation?" Tests that call endpoints as user A and assert no rows from tenant B come back, plus scope filters applied in one shared query-building layer so no endpoint forgets them.

C4 — 15.5× faster pivots with rollups, and the 170 GB OOM fix

Resume: Reduced planner pivot latency by 15.5× (189s to 12s on 250M-row operations) by building a ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer for season and weekly rollups. Prevented 170GB OOM crashes by slicing batch inserts into temporal chunks and enforcing strict distributed memory and disk-spill caps.

This bullet has two separate stories. Keep them apart.

Story 1: query time, 189 s to 12 s

In plain words. Instead of adding up raw daily rows on every screen, we pre-compute totals into six tables and the screens read those.

The six tables (all ClickHouse MergeTree, PARTITION BY season_code):

Grain Product (per SKU) Store (per store, no SKU) Attribute (per colour, size, etc.)
Season product_season store_season attr_season
Weekly product_weekly store_weekly attr_weekly

Example rows, so it feels real:

product_weekly: season 7 | week 2026-W14 | article 123 (blue linen shirt) | units 1,240 | revenue 37,200 | margin 14,900 | closing stock 3,100
store_weekly:   season 7 | week 2026-W14 | store 55 | units 9,870 | revenue 288,000 ...
attr_weekly:    season 7 | week 2026-W14 | attr colour = blue | units 22,400 ...

The attribute table is an "unpivot": one product row becomes several rows, one per attribute. That is why attr_weekly is about five times bigger than product_weekly.

The number. On a 250-million-row harness, the same pivot took 189 seconds on the old PostgreSQL path and 12.3 seconds on ClickHouse rollups (the resume rounds to 12). The harness reported the speed-up as about 15.5× (plain division gives 189 ÷ 12.3 ≈ 15.4, so if someone checks, "about 15 times" is the safe spoken version). Say it as "from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, about 15.5 times faster, on a 250-million-row test". It is a benchmark harness result, not a promise that every screen is 12 seconds, and not "sub-second".

Why ClickHouse. Pivots read a few columns over many rows. A columnar database reads only those columns, compressed, using many cores. PostgreSQL reads whole rows and is built for transactions. PostgreSQL still keeps the small, transactional stuff: users, roles, metadata.

Alternatives. BigQuery (we have it on the tech line, but per-query slot variance makes interactive latency unpredictable), PostgreSQL materialized views (still row storage, refresh is heavy), Apache Druid or Pinot (another system to run). ClickHouse fit both the speed need and the team's skills.

Story 2: load time, the 170 GB out-of-memory crash

What broke. Building the weekly rollups with one INSERT ... SELECT ... GROUP BY for a whole season needed about 170 GB of RAM for the aggregation state (each group keeps around 110 any() values plus argMax / argMin over wide strings). The query was killed with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. It failed even when we tried caps of 80 GB and 200 GB. The replica has roughly 59 cores and about 236 GiB of RAM.

How we found the real unit of work. We measured memory per slice. One fiscal week of the product table peaked at about 11 GB. One week of the attribute table peaked at over 40 GB. So the problem was the size of the unit, not the size of the machine.

The fix. 1. Temporal chunks. One INSERT per fiscal week instead of per season. 2. Caps. Per query: memory cap about 55 GB, spill to disk after about 16 GB of GROUP BY state, 8 threads, at most 4 weeks in flight.

INSERT INTO product_weekly
SELECT season_code, fiscal_year_week, article, sum(units), sum(revenue), any(colour), argMax(price, ts) ...
FROM daily_facts
WHERE season_code = 7 AND fiscal_year_week = '2026-W14'      -- one week only
GROUP BY season_code, fiscal_year_week, article
SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 55000000000,                    -- about 55 GB hard cap
         max_bytes_before_external_group_by = 16000000000,  -- spill after about 16 GB
         max_threads = 8;

max_memory_usage is the hard limit. max_bytes_before_external_group_by tells ClickHouse to write partial GROUP BY results to disk once they get that big, instead of dying.

Trap to avoid. "So fixing the OOM made pivots 15.5× faster?" No. The OOM was about building the tables. The 15.5× is about reading them. Say this before they ask.

Questions they will ask. - "Why not just buy more RAM?" It failed at 200 GB too. And bigger boxes only delay the problem as data grows. Smaller units scale. - "How do you keep store totals equal to the sum of product rows?" Two-pass weighted sums, then validation that product, store and attribute totals match at the same filters. - "Why not query daily facts with FINAL?" FINAL forces merge-on-read, which is slow and skips projections. Pay once at load, read cheaply.

C5 — Cross-cluster migration with a Go native-TLS pump

Resume: Migrated ClickHouse rollups across Cloud clusters at ~344k rows/s by writing a custom Go native-TLS data pump to bypass strict cross-cluster IP allowlist restrictions. Processed partitions up to 4.09B rows using 500k-row double-buffered batches, and eliminated partial-commit ghost rows using TSV ledgers and atomic partition rollbacks.

In plain words. We needed to copy big tables from one ClickHouse Cloud cluster to another. The built-in way (one cluster pulling from the other) was blocked because each cluster only accepts connections from approved IP addresses. My machine's IP was approved on both. So I wrote a Go program that reads from one and writes to the other, fast and safely.

flowchart LR S["Source ClickHouse Cloud"] -->|native TLS SELECT stream| P["Go pump
buffer A and buffer B"] P -->|native TLS INSERT Send| T["Target ClickHouse Cloud"] P --> L["Checkpoint ledger
migrate-checkpoints/table.done"]

How it works. 1. Unit of work = one season partition of one table. 2. Batches of 500,000 rows, held as columns ([]int64, []string...) rather than row objects, so there's no per-row reflection cost. 3. Double buffering. While batch A is being sent to the target, the next 500,000 rows are read into batch B. Then they swap. Reading and writing overlap. This also fixed a real error: when the read stream sat idle during a long insert, the source connection dropped with "unexpected EOF".

// illustrative shape
for {
    next := readBatch(src, 500_000)        // fill buffer B
    if err := <-sendDone; err != nil { return err } // wait for A's Send()
    go func(b Batch) { sendDone <- b.Send() }(next) // send B, then refill A
    if next.Len() == 0 { break }
}
  1. Workers. -workers N copies N seasons in parallel, each with its own connections. Thread and memory caps are per process.
  2. Ledger and rollback. When a season finishes, a checkpoint is written (migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done). On restart, an unfinished season that already has rows in the target gets DROP PARTITION, then is copied again from scratch. Ctrl-C finishes the in-flight batch but does not mark that season done.

What "ghost rows" means. A failed ClickHouse INSERT can still have committed some blocks. So "the partition has rows, skip it" is a lie. We once saw a half-loaded partition of 64.1 million rows pass that check in the loader (the weekly build job, a different program). That's why the loader keeps a TSV ledger of finished (kind, season) pairs, and the copier keeps .done files. Only the ledger, never "row count > 0", decides what is complete.

The numbers. - ~344k rows/s: combined ingest rate of two season streams of about 150k–190k rows/s each, measured at a live snapshot. It is rows per second, not requests per second. If someone says "344k TPS" or "344k RPS", correct them politely. - 4.09B rows: the largest object, the attribute weekly table for two seasons (2,779,317,472 + 1,311,108,195). The copy of that set was measured in flight. Don't say the cutover finished. Rough arithmetic if asked how long it takes: 4.09 billion ÷ 344,000 ≈ 11,900 seconds, a bit over 3 hours at that rate (ESTIMATED). - 500k-row batches: the batch size, chosen to keep about 0.3–0.4 sends per second per worker. Big enough to be efficient, small enough to fit in memory.

"Atomic partition rollbacks" — say it precisely. It means: if a season's copy didn't finish, drop that whole partition and copy it again, so you never keep a half season. It is not an atomic swap that live readers never notice. During a recopy, readers of the target can see a partial season. A swap-based design (REPLACE PARTITION from scratch tables) was written but not executed. Don't claim it ran.

Why not the alternatives. - remoteSecure / cluster-to-cluster INSERT SELECT: blocked by IP allowlists. The best option if networking allows it. - Export to object storage and re-import: valid, more moving parts and storage cost for a one-off move. - Kafka or CDC: wrong tool for a one-off bulk copy, and not part of this project.

Rules you must keep. Never paste cluster hosts, passwords or .env values anywhere. Don't offer to open-source the copier. Whiteboard it instead.

Questions they will ask. - "How did you get 344k rows/s?" Native protocol instead of HTTP, columnar batches with no per-row reflection, 500k-row batches, overlap of read and write through double buffering, and two seasons in parallel. - "What's the biggest risk?" No atomic swap. A crash leaves a truncated season until it's dropped and recopied. For production I'd prefer a network path that allows server-side copy, or an object-storage freeze. - "Why a laptop?" Its IP was on both allowlists. That was a pragmatic workaround, and I say so openly.

8. Hard problems and failure stories

  1. The 170 GB OOM (best "hardest technical problem" story). Symptom: weekly rollup builds killed. Investigation: memory per grain (product week ~11 GB, attr week >40 GB). Fix: one week per INSERT plus memory and spill caps. Lesson: shrink the unit of work before you buy a bigger machine.
  2. Ghost rows from failed inserts. Symptom: a half-loaded 64.1M-row partition looked "done". Fix: ledgers decide completeness, and DROP PARTITION before retry. Lesson: never use "row count > 0" as proof of success.
  3. "Unexpected EOF" in the copier. Symptom: source connection dropped during long inserts. Fix: double buffering kept the read stream active. Lesson: overlapping read and write is both faster and more stable.
  4. Inf / NaN breaking grids. Fix: ifNotFinite wrapper in the formula compiler. Lesson: make bad values impossible at the source, not in every screen.

9. Say this / don't say this

Say: "from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250-million-row test" · "344k rows per second, combined, two streams" · "measured on a 4.09-billion-row set while the copy was in flight" · "partition rollback means drop the partition and recopy it" · "isolation and access control".

Don't say: sub-second ClickHouse · the OOM fix caused the 15.5× · 344k TPS / RPS · the 4.09B cutover finished · atomic swap with no reader impact · Kafka, Flink, CDC or Kubernetes operations at Impact Analytics · that you built the CDC pipeline (a colleague did) · encryption when you mean isolation · that you'll open-source the copier · any host, password or .env value.

Off-PDF but true (fine to say if relevant): 100% Go statement coverage with race detection across 1,200+ tests (that's on LinkedIn), 1.6M article-seasons in the catalog, the 55 GB / 16 GB / one-week knobs.

10. Practice drill

  1. What does AssortSmart do? It helps retail planners decide which products to carry each season, using pivots, KPIs and AI recommendations.
  2. Why Go for the API? Fast, low memory, simple concurrency, single binary. It fits a 10k-peak-RPS edge.
  3. What is Wire and why compile-time? It generates dependency wiring code. Missing dependencies fail the build, not production.
  4. Why no reverse proxy? One less hop and one less component. Go's server handles timeouts and HTTP/2 itself.
  5. What are nested timeouts? A request deadline with shorter deadlines for each dependency inside it, so inner calls fail first and the server still answers cleanly.
  6. How does the formula engine stay safe? Tokenize, parse, map names through a catalog, allowlist functions, parameterise literals, fail closed.
  7. What does ifNotFinite do? It turns infinity or NaN (for example from dividing by zero) into 0.
  8. How is tenant isolation enforced? Identity and scope are resolved once at the edge and attached as filters to every PostgreSQL and ClickHouse query.
  9. Why constant-time comparison? Normal comparison leaks timing information that can reveal a key character by character.
  10. Why rollups? Screens read pre-computed totals instead of adding up hundreds of millions of raw rows each time.
  11. Name the six tables. Product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain.
  12. Why did weekly builds OOM? A whole-season weekly GROUP BY needed about 170 GB of state. One week needs ~11 GB (product) to >40 GB (attribute).
  13. What is 344k? Combined rows per second of the copier across two season streams. Not requests per second.
  14. What is a ghost row? Data left behind by a failed insert that makes a partition look complete.
  15. What would you improve? A swap-based publish so readers never see partial seasons, and a server-side copy path once networking allows it.

11. 3-minute whiteboard script

  1. Draw the request path (45 s). UI → Go/Gin edge → auth (Redis, then Firebase/JWT/OIDC) → PostgreSQL for roles → ClickHouse rollups. Say: "Everything a request needs to be safe is decided once at the edge."
  2. Draw the six-table grid (45 s). Product, store, attr × season, weekly, partitioned by season. Say: "Pay once at load, read cheap. This took a 250M-row pivot from 189 s to 12 s."
  3. Draw the loader (40 s). Daily facts → one fiscal week per INSERT → weekly tables, with "55 GB cap, 16 GB spill" written next to it. Say: "A whole season needed 170 GB and died. A week fits."
  4. Draw the pump (40 s). Source cluster → Go pump with buffers A and B → target cluster, ledger file on the side. Say: "344k rows per second combined. Ledgers decide what's done. Unfinished seasons are dropped and recopied."
  5. Close (10 s). "If I did it again, I'd add a swap-based publish so readers never see a partial season."

Chapter 4 — Impact Analytics: AssortSmart Agentic Flows & Orchestration

How to use this chapter
• Sections 1–5 give you the mental model: what the AI decides, how a score is made, and where the LLM is and isn't allowed to act.
• Then study one bullet (A1–A5) per sitting. A5 (the evaluation numbers) is the one interviewers try to trip you on. Learn the split table by heart.
• Practise the worked score example in section 5 until you can do it on a whiteboard.
• Companion chapters: Chapter 3 (Core platform), Chapter 2 (numbers), Chapter 10 (concepts: circuit breakers, checkpoints, RAG, evals).

Role: Senior Software Engineer, Impact Analytics, May 2026 to Present (AssortSmart — Platform & AI). This is the first IA sub-section on the resume: Agentic Flows & Orchestration. The agent plane is Python (FastAPI, LangGraph). The platform APIs it sits next to are Go/Gin (see Chapter 3).

1. The one-minute version

"On the AI side of AssortSmart I built a decision engine that tells retail planners which products to keep or drop each season, plus two sister pipelines, Missed Opportunities and Top Style. It evaluates 348,000 article-seasons, about 88,000 items per pass. The important design choice is that the money math is deterministic Python and the LLM only does qualitative judgement through seven structured 'lenses'. The model never queries our 2.11-billion-row ClickHouse table. It gets prepared JSON. If the model times out, the article falls back to its deterministic score, so a run always finishes. All three pipelines share an orchestration registry with timeouts, circuit breakers, checkpoints and per-row config hashes. I also shipped Ask Iris, a secure chat copilot for planners built on a LangGraph supervisor with a three-attempt evaluator loop, where the user's data scope is frozen when the socket connects. Nothing gets promoted unless it passes an 80% accuracy gate on a 300-case evaluation set in CI. A separate 200-case benchmark let us pick a model that cut live cost by 73% at full coverage, and when the LLM blend lost to our 74% deterministic baseline, we froze the weights instead of shipping it."

2. The business in plain English

The decision. Every season a retailer must decide, for each product (article), whether to keep it in the range or drop it. Keep a bad product and you're stuck with unsold stock and markdowns. Drop a good one and you lose sales. A large retailer has hundreds of thousands of article-seasons to look at. Planners can't review them all by hand.

The three pipelines (named on the resume). - Keep/Drop: a keep or drop recommendation per article-season, with a short explanation a planner can read. - Missed Opportunities and Top Style: sister pipelines on the same framework that surface opportunities and top-performing styles for planners. If an interviewer asks for their exact logic, describe them at the level you personally built and know. Keep/Drop is the one to go deep on.

Why AI at all? Simple rules ("drop if sell-through below 40%") miss context: a product may sell slowly because it launched late, because it's cannibalised by its own other colours, or because it only sells when discounted. Those patterns are qualitative. An LLM is good at weighing several pieces of evidence and explaining its reasoning in words. But LLMs are bad at arithmetic and can be confidently wrong. So the design uses each for what it's good at.

Why the company cares. Better range decisions directly affect stock, markdowns and sales. Explanations make planners trust and adopt the recommendation. Cost and reliability controls make it affordable to run on every client every season.

3. Words you need

Term Plain meaning (with analogy)
LLM Large language model (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude). Reads text, writes text.
Token A chunk of text, roughly ¾ of a word. LLM providers charge per token in and out.
Structured output / structured invoke Asking the LLM to reply in a strict JSON shape (schema), and rejecting replies that don't fit. Like a form with fixed boxes instead of a blank letter.
Deterministic Same input always gives the same output. Normal code is deterministic; LLM calls aren't.
Sell-through Share of available stock that sold. Sold 80 of 100 units = 80%.
Rate of sale Units sold per store per week. A speed measure.
s_det The deterministic score (0 to 1) from KPI rules like sell-through and rate of sale.
Lens One focused LLM question about an article, like "Is this product cannibalised by its other colours?" Each lens returns a score, a confidence and reason codes.
Decider An LLM step that picks which lenses matter for this article and how to weight them.
s_agent The combined score from the lenses.
Blend / s_final s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent. Keep if s_final ≥ 0.55.
Payload The prepared JSON data the LLM receives.
ReplacingMergeTree (RMT) A ClickHouse table type that keeps only the newest version of each key. Like a notebook where you never erase; you write the new value below and a cleaner later crosses out old lines.
Eventually consistent For a short time you may see an old and a new version. Soon, only the newest remains.
Circuit breaker After too many failures in a row, stop calling the failing service for a while. Like a home fuse that trips to protect the wiring.
Checkpoint Saved progress so a job can resume where it stopped. Like a video game save point.
config_hash A SHA-256 fingerprint of all the settings and prompts used in a run, stamped on every output row.
Telemetry Data the system records about itself: tokens, cost, time, fallbacks.
WebSocket A connection that stays open so the server and browser can send messages both ways, which suits chat.
JWT handshake When the WebSocket opens, the client sends a signed token. The server verifies it once at that moment.
LangGraph A Python library for building LLM workflows as a graph of steps with state, loops and limits.
Supervisor pattern One coordinator node that decides which worker handles each step. Like a dispatcher.
Evaluator loop A check step that grades an answer and asks for a retry if it's not good enough, here at most 3 attempts.
LangSmith A tracing tool for LLM apps: shows each prompt, tool call, tokens and timing.
Gold set Test cases with known correct answers, used to grade the system.
CI gate An automated check in the build pipeline that blocks promotion if a score is below a threshold.
Coverage (eval sense) Share of articles that received a complete score. 100% = no article left pending.

4. Architecture

flowchart TB CH["ClickHouse master
2.11B rows"] --> FEAT["Feature SQL + KPI math
deterministic Python"] FEAT --> DET["s_det per article"] FEAT --> PAY["Compact JSON payload per batch"] subgraph REG["Shared orchestration registry: timeouts, circuit breaker, checkpoints, telemetry"] PAY --> PEER["Peer benchmark context"] PEER --> DEC["Decider: which lenses, what weights"] DEC --> LENS["7 lenses in parallel
structured JSON out"] LENS --> AG["s_agent"] end DET --> BL["Blend: 0.4 s_det + 0.6 s_agent"] AG --> BL BL --> EXP["Explanation for planner"] EXP --> OUT["Output rows + config_hash
written via ReplacingMergeTree"] AG -.->|timeout or error| FB["Fallback: deterministic score"] FB --> OUT

What to notice: the LLM only ever sees JSON; the database reads and writes are done by our code; every failure path still produces a row.
