                        .content("{\"conclusion_scope\":\"In Scope\",\"group_status\":\"Closed\",\"version\":7}"))
           .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
        verifyNoInteractions(service);
    }
}

What to notice: @WebMvcTest starts only the web layer, @MockBean swaps the real service for a Mockito mock, and verifyNoInteractions proves the request never reached business logic. For repository queries themselves, a common practice is a @DataJpaTest against a throwaway MySQL started by Testcontainers. Describe that as general practice if asked, not as a number from this project.

Stacked Bazel PRs and zero downtime. Each package has a Bazel test target, and CI runs the targets layer by layer: entities, DTOs, repositories, services, controllers. All must pass before merge. Work was split into a chain of small PRs in that same order, so a reviewer read one layer at a time and each PR was safe to deploy on its own. Changes were additive: new code paths appeared next to old ones (as with recon v2 next to v1), and the switch happened only after verification. Nothing had to go down.

Reporting SQL allowlists. User input never becomes raw SQL. Only approved values are accepted for things like page names, statuses, filter levels and statement types (fsli_type is bs or is), and reporting queries are built from approved, parameterized shapes. Two concrete examples in the code: GET /scoping_questions only accepts allowlisted page names, and status updates only accept Draft, Review, ReOpen or Closed (enforced by the ReviewStatus enum).

private static final Set<String> ALLOWED_PAGES =
        Set.of("group_scoping", "component_scoping", "residual_risk");   // illustrative names

public List<QuestionDto> getQuestions(String pageName) {
    if (!ALLOWED_PAGES.contains(pageName)) {
        throw new BadRequestException("unknown page");
    }
    return questions.findByPageNameAndIsActive(pageName, "true");    // bound parameter, never string concat
}

FSM gates with 50% delta-variance. Each reviewable line is in one state: Draft, Review, ReOpen or Closed. The gate is a check that blocks moving a scoping item forward, for example to Closed, when the line's quarter-over-quarter change is more than 50% and it has not been reviewed.

static double deltaVariance(BigDecimal current, BigDecimal prior) {
    if (prior.signum() == 0) {
        return Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
    }
    return current.subtract(prior).abs()
            .divide(prior.abs(), MathContext.DECIMAL64)
            .doubleValue();
}

static void checkCanClose(ScopingLine line, boolean reviewed) {
    if (deltaVariance(line.getCurrentAmount(), line.getPriorAmount()) > 0.50 && !reviewed) {
        throw new GateViolationException("variance above 50 percent needs review before Closed");
    }
}

Sketch with illustrative names, to explain the mechanism. Worked example: a line was $400M last quarter and is $650M now. The change is 250 / 400 = 62.5%, above 50%, so the move to Closed is blocked until the line has been reviewed. A line that went from $1,000M to $1,200M (20%) passes. Keep it at this mechanism level. Do not invent extra rules.

Do not confuse this 50% with the residual-risk flag, which checks whether residual balance is above 50% of materiality ($170M on Q4 2025). They are separate checks.

Leading 3 engineers. I was tech lead of the EPAM pod, not a people manager. Concretely: - Task split by layer. Work was cut along the controller, service, repository and entity boundary, so two people could build the same feature without merge collisions. One person took the request DTOs and controller, another took the repository and entities. - Conventions. Thin controllers. Services own the logic, the tree building and the @Transactional boundary. Repositories own every query, with an explicit alias on every projected column. Every write records updated_by from the identity header. No catch block that swallows an exception. These came out of our backend team syncs, and the uniformity across the codebase is the evidence they were enforced. - Review gate. Every PR had to add or update tests in the matching test folder and pass the Bazel targets.

Why this design

  • Aliases on every column because the bug was silent. A crash you notice. A wrong ID you do not.
  • 100% on the module because this code produces audit evidence. Untested lines in a SOX-relevant path are a liability.
  • Stacked PRs because a 1,000-line PR in a finance service is unreviewable, and reviewers miss bugs in big diffs.
  • Allowlists because reporting endpoints take user-chosen filters. An allowlist is the simplest way to guarantee no SQL injection and no surprise query shapes.
  • A state-machine gate because SOX is about enforced process. A big unexplained movement must not slip through to Closed.

Alternatives and why not

  • Patch each raw query by hand. Fixes today's bug, leaves the pattern for the next person. Rejected in favour of the Spring Data JPA migration.
  • Lower coverage target with integration tests only. Slower, flakier, and leaves branches unexercised.
  • One big migration PR with a feature flag. Possible, but review quality drops and rollback is all-or-nothing.
  • Free-form SQL for reporting with escaping. Escaping is easy to get wrong. Rejected.
  • A purely manual variance review. Humans forget under deadline pressure. The gate makes it impossible to forget.

Trade-off. Strict aliasing and allowlists add boilerplate to every new query and filter. What I'd do differently: add a static-analysis rule that fails CI when a repository builds rows into a Map by column name or uses a native SELECT without an explicit alias on every column, so the old pattern cannot creep back in.

The numbers

3 engineers. - What it measures: the size of the EPAM pod I led as tech lead. - How to say it: "I led a pod of 3 engineers." - What not to say: do not call it people management, and do not merge it with "mentored 2 engineers" at Masters India. Those are different jobs.

100% statement coverage. - What it measures: statement coverage of the module touched by the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration. - How to say it: "We raised module statement coverage to 100%." - What not to say: do not claim 100% of the whole monorepo or the whole service. Do not borrow the 82% coverage number from Masters India.

50% delta-variance. - What it measures: the threshold for period-over-period change that triggers the gate. - How derived: |current − prior| / |prior| > 0.5. - How to say it: "A state-machine gate blocks closing a line if it moved more than 50% quarter over quarter without review."

Questions they will ask

"Tell me about the column-aliasing bug." The legacy code ran raw SQL and built each row into a map keyed by column label. We joined a fact table to the hierarchy table, and both had a column called uuid. The result had two uuid columns, and putting the second one into the map replaced the first, so every row silently carried the hierarchy's uuid instead of the line's own uuid. Edits and comments landed on the wrong line. I fixed it by moving to a Spring Data JPA query with an explicit, unique alias on every column, like fsliId versus levelMappingUuid, mapped into a typed projection. Then we made that pattern the standard in the migration so it could not come back.

Follow-up they may ask: "How would you catch that class of bug earlier?" A test that asserts the uuid on each returned row exists in the fact table, and a static-analysis rule that forbids building rows into maps by column name in repositories.

"Why did a JPA migration fix it, and not just better SQL?" Better SQL would have fixed that one query. The migration fixed the pattern. With entities and typed projections, each value lands in a named, typed field chosen by alias, so there is no shared map for two columns to collide in. And because every repository now looks the same, reviewers can spot a missing alias at a glance.

"What does leading 3 engineers actually mean for you?" I was the tech lead of the pod, not their manager. I sliced work by layer so people could work in parallel, set the conventions everyone followed, reviewed PRs, and held the gate that every PR comes with tests and passes Bazel. The recon migration is a good example: 18 files cleanly split across layers.

"How do stacked PRs give you zero downtime?" Each PR is small and additive, and deployable on its own. New code lives alongside old code until it is verified. For the recon migration, the v2 endpoints existed next to v1, and the UI switched only after staging matched. At no point did we have to take the service down or break the old path.

"What is the 50% check for?" SOX wants evidence that big movements were looked at. If a line moved more than 50% since the prior quarter, the state machine refuses to move it to Closed until someone has reviewed it. It turns a "please remember to check" into a rule the system enforces.

8. Tech used in this project and why

Tech What it is Why here Alternative considered
Java Statically typed language on the JVM The service's language. Static types and BigDecimal suit financial math None, it was the team's standard
Spring Boot Java framework for REST services, with dependency injection Thin @RestController classes, @RestControllerAdvice error mapping, Bean Validation on request DTOs Plain Spring MVC wired by hand, more setup for the same result
Spring Data JPA Repository layer that generates queries from interfaces One-line repositories, derived queries, JPQL with named parameters and aliased projections Hand-written JDBC SQL, which caused the bug
Hibernate The JPA implementation that generates SQL and tracks changes @Entity mapping, dirty checking, @Version optimistic locking MyBatis or jOOQ, more SQL control but no built-in version checks
MySQL on SOADB Relational database under Uber's service-owned standard ACID transactions for concurrent edits, platform standard PostgreSQL, a columnar warehouse
JUnit Java test framework (JUnit 5), used with Mockito and MockMvc Layer-by-layer unit tests with mocks, no database needed, 100% module coverage Integration-only tests, slower and flakier
Bazel Monorepo build and test system Uber's monorepo, per-layer test targets gate every merge None, it is the environment
Docker Container packaging Reproducible local and CI runs Running on a bare local JVM

9. Hard problems and failure stories

1. The column-aliasing bug. - What broke: joined queries returned duplicate column names, and the row map kept the last one. Rows carried the wrong uuid. - How found: an edit to one recon line appeared to change a different line. - How fixed: Spring Data JPA queries with an explicit, unique alias on every column, mapped into typed projections, then made that the standard in the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration. - What I learned: silent bugs are worse than crashes. Any code that maps rows by column name must guarantee unique names.

2. Keeping v1 and v2 reconciliation identical during a live close. - What broke (risk): any difference between the Sheets and MySQL paths would put wrong numbers in front of Finance. - How handled: parallel endpoints, side-by-side QA for the same period, invariant checks (parent equals sum of children, empty period returns an empty list, v1 shape unchanged), and v1 kept as fallback. - What I learned: during a deadline, the ability to fall back is worth more than a clean cutover.

3. Lines silently disappearing (active-flag drift). - What can break: joins require both is_active and is_level_active to be true. If the ETL loads a row with the wrong flag, the line vanishes from the tree with no error. - How handled: I call it out as a known risk and check totals against expected parents. - What I'd add: a reconciliation alert that compares row counts and totals per period after each load.

4. Malformed currency strings. - What can break: some amounts arrive as display strings. A malformed string can parse to zero silently. - What I'd add: strict parsing into BigDecimal that fails loudly, plus validation on load.

5. Hardcoded FSLI order. - Risk: if Finance renames a line, it falls to the bottom instead of its proper place. - Why acceptable: it degrades safely (nothing is dropped), but it can look out of order. A config table would fix it.

10. Say this / don't say this

Say this carefully

  • Always say "Uber via EPAM". I was an EPAM employee working on Uber's platform.
  • 70%: state it as the outcome, "from 14 days to 3 days". If pressed: "The technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what the platform delivered for the close." Do not walk it back unprompted.
  • 36 Spring Boot endpoints: if asked for the breakdown, about 31 functional routes in the scoping service plus the collaboration-service comment and notification APIs. I did not build the collaboration service.
  • 19M: "raw GL rows migrated off Sheets." Per-quarter extracts were tens of thousands of rows. The value was correctness, hierarchy and auditability, not throughput. Do not invent a further breakdown.
  • $340M: materiality on the Q4 2025 close. Residual threshold $170M. Not permanent constants.
  • 8 tables vs 11 entities: 8 is the normalized core on the PDF. 11 JPA entities in the service code is verbal depth.
  • ETL: shared pipeline. "The service consumes HFM-loaded tables."
  • Real-time collaboration and Slack-style notifications: a separate service I did not build.
  • Led 3: tech lead of an EPAM pod, not a people manager. Never merge with "mentored 2" at Masters India.
  • 100%: module statement coverage, not the whole codebase. 1,100+ tests is verbal depth.
  • 50% gate: describe the mechanism only. Do not invent extra rules or transitions.
  • Quarter-annualization: describe the generic YTD × 4 / n idea. The exact formula is per FSLI.

Don't say: "I built the HFM ETL." "I built the comments and notifications service." "This is a big-data system." "We had Redis caching" (there was no server-side response cache). Any latency number for this platform (none was measured). "I was an Uber employee."

11. Practice drill

1. What is a quarterly close? It is the few weeks after each quarter where Finance finalises the books, reconciles numbers across systems and produces the financial statements that get filed with the SEC in the 10-Q. My platform supported the scoping step inside that close.

2. What is scoping? Deciding which line items and which entities are significant enough to be tested by the auditors. Too narrow misses risk, too broad wastes audit hours.

3. Explain FSLI and the L1 to L4 hierarchy. An FSLI is one line on the financial statements, like Accounts Receivable. They nest four levels deep, from broad headings like Assets down to detailed lines. Parents are the sum of their children, so one duplicated leaf corrupts every parent above it.

4. What does the $340M mean? It was group materiality on the Q4 2025 close, the size of error that would matter to a reader of the financials. Any line above it is quantitatively material.

5. Group vs component scoping? Group scoping asks whether an FSLI matters for Uber as a whole. Component scoping then decides which entities under that FSLI get tested, using the 5% revenue or assets rule.

6. What is residual risk? What is left uncovered after the in-scope components. Residual balance divided by materiality gives a multiple. If the residual is above half of materiality, $170M on that close, the line is flagged.

7. Why does PwC care about this platform? Scoping is a SOX control, and PwC uses the output in its work papers. They need evidence that the process is reliable: stable IDs, who changed what, enforced reviews. Sheets could not provide that.

8. How did you prevent two managers overwriting each other? Optimistic locking with a JPA @Version field. Hibernate only updates the row if the version still matches what the user read. Otherwise zero rows change, Hibernate throws an optimistic-locking exception, the API returns 409 and the user reloads.

9. How did you stop duplicates across quarterly reloads? Deterministic SHA-256 natural keys, computed with Java's MessageDigest. The question's ID is a hash of its text and normalized page, so re-sending the same question updates the existing row instead of inserting a new one.

10. What does atomic cross-table sync mean in your system? Writes that span two tables happen in one @Transactional service method. Saving an assessment answer and updating the line's qualitative flag either both commit or both roll back.

11. Tell me the column-aliasing bug in 30 seconds. Raw SQL joined two tables that both had a uuid column. We built each row into a map keyed by column name, and the second uuid replaced the first, so rows carried the wrong uuid and edits hit the wrong line. I fixed it with Spring Data JPA queries that give every column an explicit, unique alias, mapped into a typed projection.

12. How did you release without downtime? Small stacked Bazel PRs, each additive and safe to deploy on its own, with new paths running next to old ones until verified, like recon v2 next to v1.

13. What is the 50% delta-variance gate? A state-machine rule that refuses to move a line to Closed if its amount changed more than 50% quarter over quarter without review. Example: $400M to $650M is 62.5%, so it is blocked.

14. Why MySQL and not Postgres? Uber's service standard is MySQL on SOADB, and it gives the transactional guarantees concurrent edits need. We did not need recursive SQL because the ETL flattens the hierarchy into stable IDs.

15. What is the difference between JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA? JPA is the Java standard that says how objects map to tables. Hibernate is the library that implements it and actually writes the SQL. Spring Data JPA sits on top and generates repository code from interfaces, so a one-line JpaRepository gives you findById and save.

16. What would you do differently? An automated nightly parity diff between old and new paths during migrations, a static-analysis rule that bans building rows into maps by column name in repositories, and loud validation on currency parsing instead of silent zeros.

12. 3-minute whiteboard script

First, draw the business (30 seconds). Draw a box "HFM" on the left, an arrow to "MySQL", and a box "PwC" on the right. Say: "Every quarter Uber Finance decides which line items and entities the auditors test. That used to be a Google Sheets workbook. I owned the backend that replaced it, through EPAM."

Second, draw the service layers (60 seconds). Draw a vertical stack between the screens and MySQL: "Controller", "Service", "Repository". Say: "Spring Boot controllers only do HTTP, identity and Bean Validation. Services hold the finance rules: materiality at $340M, the 5% component rule, residual risk, the L1 to L4 tree and quarter-annualization, and they own the @Transactional boundaries. Repositories are Spring Data JPA interfaces over Hibernate entities. 36 Spring Boot endpoints in total. That layering let my pod of 3 engineers work in parallel and test every layer with Mockito mocks, without a database."

Third, draw the schema spine (45 seconds). Draw level_mapping in the middle with balance_sheet, income_statement and component_entity pointing at it. Write uuid, level_id, version. Say: "An 8-table normalized schema on SOADB. The hierarchy lives once. Every reviewable row uses the same Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed status enum. Writes use optimistic locking through a JPA @Version field, which turns a stale save into a 409. Cross-table writes are one transaction, and reference data uses SHA-256 natural keys so quarterly reloads never duplicate."

Fourth, tell the migration and the bug (45 seconds). Draw "v1 Sheets" and "v2 MySQL" side by side under reconciliation. Say: "I ran v1 and v2 in parallel and compared them before switching. Along the way we found that joined raw SQL had two columns named uuid, and building each row into a map by column name kept the wrong one. The Spring Data JPA and Hibernate migration, with an explicit alias on every column, removed that class of bug, and we got the module to 100% statement coverage. We shipped in stacked Bazel PRs with SQL allowlists and a state-machine gate that blocks closing a line that moved more than 50% without review."

Close with the outcome (15 seconds). Write "14 days → 3 days" and "19M GL rows". Say: "Reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days, about 70%, and 19 million raw GL rows now live in a system with stable IDs and an audit trail instead of a spreadsheet."

Chapter 6. Uber Eats Menu Ingestion and Uber Mobility ANZ Document Compliance (Uber via EPAM)

1. How to use this chapter

How to use this chapter

  • What it covers: two separate Uber projects I worked on through EPAM. The main one is Uber Eats Menu Ingestion & Automation: scraping restaurant menus, streaming them through Kafka and Flink, and using RAG with Gemini 2.5 Pro over Milvus to turn messy multilingual PDFs into clean catalog data. The second is a smaller Uber Mobility project in Australia and New Zealand (ANZ) that automated driver and vehicle document checks.
  • When to read it: before any interview that touches streaming (Kafka, Flink), scraping, RAG or LLM systems, data pipelines, idempotency, or "tell me about an AI system you shipped".
  • What to memorise: the one-minute version (section 2), the numbers 24h to 2h, $600K, 30K+, 98%, 95%+, 99.9% and 20 hours a week with their derivations (section 7), the honest "exactly-once" answer, and the whiteboard script (section 12).

Tags used in this chapter. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind it. TARGET means a design goal, so you say "targeting". ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. Menu outcomes and both ANZ numbers are HISTORICAL. The 98% is an offline evaluation number.

Related chapters: Start here · Numbers explained · Uber FRM · Tech glossary · Core concepts · STAR stories. Older source material: Menu deep dive and Uber interview packs. Those older pages also discuss Spark and Pinot. Neither is on the current resume, so treat them as study-only.

2. The one-minute version

"At Uber Eats, through EPAM, I worked on menu ingestion: getting a new restaurant's menu into Uber's catalog so it can start taking orders. Menus arrive as JavaScript-heavy websites, PDFs and images, in many languages. I architected an automated pipeline: a Selenium scraping fleet that I hardened with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries, which took extraction success from an estimated 60 to 65% up to 95% plus. Scraped content flows through Kafka into an Apache Flink job that deduplicates per vendor using a content hash, normalizes everything to one schema and does idempotent catalog upserts. For unstructured PDFs we used RAG: we retrieve similar, already-labelled menus from Milvus and give them to Gemini 2.5 Pro, which outputs structured JSON that must pass schema validation. That reached 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation. Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours at more than 30,000 menus a month, and replacing a roughly $2-per-menu manual and third-party cost saved about $600K a year. Separately, on Uber Mobility in ANZ, I automated driver and vehicle document checks with a deterministic validation backend, which reached 99.9% compliance and removed about 20 hours a week of manual review."

If you only get 20 seconds: "Through EPAM at Uber Eats, I built menu ingestion: Selenium, Kafka and Flink, plus a Gemini RAG path over Milvus for messy PDFs. Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours at 30K+ menus a month, saving about $600K a year."

3. The business in plain English

Restaurant onboarding

When a restaurant signs up for Uber Eats, it cannot take orders until its menu is in Uber's catalog: every dish, description, price, size option and add-on, in a strict format the app understands. Getting that menu in is called onboarding. Until it is done, the restaurant earns nothing and Uber earns nothing. Every hour of delay is lost orders and an unhappy new partner.

Why menus are hard

  • Websites are built with JavaScript. Many restaurant or partner pages only show the menu after scripts run in a browser. A simple download of the page HTML misses the items and prices.
  • PDFs and images. A lot of menus are scanned PDFs or photos. There is no clean text structure, just layout: columns, boxes, prices floating next to names.
  • Many languages and formats. A menu can be in Portuguese, Japanese or Arabic, with prices like "8,50 €" or "¥1,200", and sizes written as "Grande" or "L".
  • Anti-bot defences. Sites block automated traffic with IP bans, CAPTCHAs and soft errors.
  • Duplicates and retries. The same menu gets scraped more than once. If you are careless, you create duplicate dishes.

What hurt before

Onboarding a menu took around 24 hours, and Uber paid roughly $2 per menu for manual and third-party processing. At more than 30,000 menus a month, that is slow and expensive.

Why Uber paid for this

Faster onboarding means restaurants go live the same day, and cutting the per-menu cost at this volume is real money: about $600K a year by the conservative figure on the resume.

The ANZ project, in plain English

Uber Mobility is the rides business, not Eats. In Australia and New Zealand, local authorities set rules for who may drive for a ride-hailing platform and which vehicles may be used. Drivers must provide documents (generic examples: a driver licence, a vehicle registration), and those documents must be valid, of the right type, not expired, and must match the driver and vehicle on record. Checking this by hand is slow and error-prone, and a miss is a regulatory problem. I automated those checks with a deterministic validation backend.

Do not mix the two projects. ANZ is Mobility, not Eats. It does not use the Selenium, Kafka, Flink or RAG stack.

4. Words you need

Catalog and catalog schema. The catalog is Uber Eats' structured store of what each restaurant sells. The schema is the strict shape every menu must fit: item name, description, price, currency, modifiers, availability. Analogy: a form with fixed boxes. Free-form menus have to be poured into those boxes.

Selenium. A tool that drives a real web browser from code. It clicks, scrolls and waits for JavaScript like a human would, so you see the page as a person sees it. A headless browser is one that runs without a visible window.

Proxy and proxy pool. A proxy is a middleman server that makes your request on your behalf, so the website sees the proxy's IP address, not yours. A proxy pool is a set of proxies you rotate through. A dynamic pool adds healthy proxies and removes banned or slow ones automatically. Analogy: a team of couriers. If one courier gets turned away at a door, you send a different one.

Adaptive retries, backoff and jitter. When a request fails, you try again, but wait longer each time (exponential backoff: 1 second, 2, 4, 8), add a random extra delay (jitter) so many workers do not retry in lockstep, and adapt to the kind of failure: a ban means switch proxy, a timeout means wait, a broken page means stop. A retry budget caps how many retries one source can consume so one hostile site does not burn the whole fleet.

Kafka. A distributed, durable log of messages. Producers append messages, and consumers read them at their own pace. Analogy: a conveyor belt that records everything that went past it, so you can rewind and watch again.

  • Topic: a named stream of messages, like "raw menu scrapes".
  • Partition: a topic is split into partitions so it can be read in parallel. Order is guaranteed only within one partition.
  • Key: each message has a key. Messages with the same key always go to the same partition, so they stay in order. We keyed by vendor_id, so all events for one restaurant stay in order.
  • Offset: the position of a message in a partition, like a line number.
  • Consumer group: a set of workers sharing the reading of a topic. Each partition is read by exactly one worker in the group. Different groups read the same topic independently.
  • Replay: because Kafka keeps messages for a while, a consumer can rewind its offset and reprocess, for example after a buggy parser was deployed.

Apache Flink. A stream processing engine. It reads events continuously and processes them one by one, with memory. Analogy: an assembly line worker who also keeps a notebook about each customer.

  • Keyed state: Flink can group events by a key (here vendor_id) and keep a small piece of memory per key, for example "the last menu hash I saw for this vendor". Flink can store large state on local disk with RocksDB.
  • Event time vs processing time: event time is when something actually happened (when the page was scraped). Processing time is when Flink happens to see it. Events can arrive late or out of order, so serious pipelines reason in event time.
  • Watermark: Flink's running statement that "I believe I have now seen all events up to time T". It lets the job decide when it is safe to finalise, while tolerating a bounded amount of lateness.
  • Checkpoint: a periodic consistent snapshot of all state plus the Kafka offsets read so far. After a crash, Flink restores the last checkpoint and rewinds Kafka to the matching offsets.

Deduplication (dedup) and content hash. A content hash is a fingerprint of the menu's content (for example SHA-256 of the normalized menu). Same content, same hash. Dedup means dropping an event whose hash we have already processed for that vendor.

Schema normalization. Converting many input shapes into one standard shape. "8,50 €", "EUR 8.50" and "8.5" all become {"price_amount": 8.50, "currency": "EUR"}.

Upsert and idempotency. An upsert inserts a row if it does not exist and updates it if it does. An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. An idempotent upsert keyed by a stable ID means replays and retries cannot create duplicates.

At-least-once vs exactly-once. At-least-once means every message is processed, but some may be processed more than once after a failure. Exactly-once means each message affects the result exactly one time. In practice, across systems you do not control, you get exactly-once effects by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). Before asking a large language model (LLM) to do a task, you first retrieve relevant examples or facts and put them in the prompt. Analogy: an open-book exam. The model answers better because it can look at worked examples.

Embedding. A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so similar texts get nearby vectors. "Margherita pizza 12" and "Pizza margarita 12,00" end up close together.

Vector database and Milvus. A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the nearest ones to a query vector (vector similarity search). Milvus is an open-source vector database. We used it to store embeddings of already-labelled menus.

LangChain. A Python framework for wiring LLM steps together: load a document, split it, retrieve from a vector store, build a prompt, call the model, parse the output.

Gemini 2.5 Pro. Google's large language model. It reads long, multilingual and visual inputs and can be asked to return structured JSON.

JSON Schema validation. A machine-checkable description of the exact JSON shape you expect (required fields, types, allowed values). Output that does not match is rejected.

Offline evaluation. Measuring a system on a fixed, labelled test set in a controlled run, not on live production traffic.

Field fidelity. Of all the individual fields the system extracted (each item's name, price, description, modifiers), the share that exactly match the human-labelled correct answer.

Deterministic validation backend (ANZ). A rules engine where the same input always gives the same answer. No machine learning and no guessing, just explicit rules like "the expiry date must be in the future".

5. Architecture

Menu pipeline

flowchart LR SRC["Partner sites, PDFs, images"] --> SEL["Selenium fleet on GCP with proxy pools and adaptive retries"] SEL --> RAW["Object storage for raw files"] SEL --> K["Kafka topic keyed by vendor_id"] K --> F["Flink job: keyed dedup, normalize, route"] F -->|"structured"| CAT["Idempotent catalog upsert"] F -->|"unstructured PDF or image"| RAG["LangChain RAG extractor"] RAG --> MV["Milvus: similar labelled menus"] MV --> RAG RAG --> GEM["Gemini 2.5 Pro returns JSON"] GEM --> VAL["JSON Schema validation gate"] VAL -->|"valid"| CAT VAL -->|"invalid or low confidence"| HR["Human review"] CAT --> APP["Uber Eats catalog, restaurant goes live"]

What to notice: acquisition (Selenium), transport (Kafka), processing (Flink) and AI extraction (RAG) are separate stages. Nothing reaches the catalog without either passing Flink's normalization or the schema gate.

Walking through it box by box:

  1. Partner sites, PDFs, images. The sources of menus.
  2. Selenium fleet on GCP. Browser workers, packaged with Docker, load each source like a person would. They route traffic through a dynamic proxy pool and retry adaptively. Each scrape emits an event and stores the raw file (HTML, PDF or image) in object storage, so the event can point at it instead of carrying a large payload.
  3. Kafka, keyed by vendor_id. Scrapers write and move on. They never wait for the catalog. The key keeps each restaurant's events in order on one partition. Kafka retains events so we can replay them.
  4. Flink job. Reads Kafka continuously. Per vendor, it compares the content hash with the last one seen and drops duplicates, normalizes fields to the catalog schema, and routes: structured content goes straight to the catalog, unstructured PDFs and images go to the RAG extractor.
  5. LangChain RAG extractor. Splits the document into chunks, embeds them, and asks Milvus for the most similar already-labelled menus.
  6. Milvus. Stores embeddings of labelled menu chunks with metadata such as vendor, locale and source.
  7. Gemini 2.5 Pro. Gets the target chunk, the retrieved examples and the required schema, and returns structured JSON.
  8. JSON Schema validation gate. Valid output goes to the catalog. Invalid or low-confidence output goes to human review instead of becoming bad data.
  9. Idempotent catalog upsert. Writes keyed by stable IDs, so a retry or replay cannot duplicate items.
  10. Uber Eats catalog. The restaurant can go live.

ANZ document compliance (separate project)

flowchart LR DOC["Driver or vehicle document submitted"] --> RULES["Deterministic validation backend"] REC["Driver and vehicle records"] --> RULES REQ["Local authority requirements as rules"] --> RULES RULES -->|"all rules pass"| OK["Compliant"] RULES -->|"a rule fails"| FAIL["Not compliant, with the failing reason"]

What to notice: the same document always gets the same verdict, and every verdict carries the rule that decided it. That is what makes it auditable.

6. One job, step by step: a Portuguese PDF menu from a Lisbon café

Sample data (illustrative): vendor v_48213, a café in Lisbon, uploads its menu as a scanned PDF in Portuguese.

sequenceDiagram participant SEL as Selenium worker participant K as Kafka participant F as Flink job participant RAG as RAG extractor participant MV as Milvus participant G as Gemini 2.5 Pro participant CAT as Catalog SEL->>K: scrape event, vendor v_48213, hash 9f2c, type pdf K->>F: deliver event on the vendor partition F->>F: hash 9f2c not seen for this vendor, keep it F->>RAG: unstructured, send for extraction RAG->>MV: search with chunk embeddings MV-->>RAG: 3 similar labelled Portuguese cafe menus RAG->>G: chunk, examples and catalog schema G-->>RAG: JSON items RAG->>RAG: validate against JSON Schema RAG->>CAT: upsert keyed by vendor and menu version CAT-->>RAG: written SEL->>K: same PDF scraped again, hash 9f2c K->>F: deliver duplicate F->>F: hash 9f2c already seen, drop it

What to notice: the second scrape of the same PDF never reaches the LLM or the catalog, because Flink's per-vendor state already holds that hash.

The same flow in numbered steps:

  1. Scrape. A Selenium worker downloads the PDF through a proxy. It stores the file and publishes an event:
{
  "event_id": "e7b1...",
  "event_time": "2025-03-04T10:15:02Z",
  "vendor_id": "v_48213",
  "content_type": "pdf",
  "content_hash": "9f2c...",
  "object_uri": "gs://menus-raw/v_48213/9f2c.pdf",
  "locale": "pt",
  "scrape_attempt": 1,
  "status": "ok"
}
  1. Kafka. The event lands on the partition for v_48213.
  2. Flink dedup. Flink looks up the state for v_48213. The last hash was different, so this is a new menu version. It updates the state to 9f2c and continues.
  3. Route. The content type is PDF, so it goes to the RAG extractor.
  4. Retrieve. The extractor splits the PDF into chunks, embeds them, and asks Milvus for the nearest labelled examples. It gets back three Portuguese café menus that humans had already mapped to the catalog schema.
  5. Generate. Gemini 2.5 Pro receives the chunk ("Tosta mista ..... 4,50 €", "Galão ..... 1,80 €"), the examples and the schema, and returns:
{
  "vendor_id": "v_48213",
  "menu_version": "9f2c...",
  "items": [
    {"name": "Tosta mista", "description": "Ham and cheese toastie",
     "price_amount": 4.50, "currency": "EUR", "modifiers": [], "availability": true},
    {"name": "Galão", "description": "Milky coffee",
     "price_amount": 1.80, "currency": "EUR", "modifiers": [], "availability": true}
  ]
}
  1. Validate. The JSON is checked against the schema: required fields present, price is a number, currency is a valid code. It passes.
  2. Upsert. The catalog write is keyed by vendor_id plus menu_version, and each item by a stable item key, so a retry cannot double-insert.
  3. Duplicate arrives. Ten minutes later the same PDF is scraped again. Same hash. Flink drops it. No LLM cost, no catalog write.

7. Each resume bullet decoded

Bullet 1: onboarding 24h to 2h, $600K, 30K+ menus, 98% field fidelity with Gemini, LangChain RAG and Milvus

"Accelerated restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saved $600K annually by architecting an automated ingestion pipeline processing 30K+ menus monthly. Converted unstructured, multilingual PDFs into a strict catalog schema at 98% field fidelity utilizing a Gemini 2.5 Pro and LangChain RAG pipeline over Milvus vector embeddings."

In plain words

I architected the automated pipeline that gets restaurant menus into Uber Eats. It handles more than 30,000 menus a month, cut onboarding from a day to two hours, and removed about $600K a year of per-menu cost. For the hardest inputs, messy PDFs in many languages, we used an LLM with retrieval of similar examples, and in offline evaluation it got 98% of fields right.

How it works

The RAG extraction path, from zero.

  1. Parse and chunk. The PDF or image is turned into text chunks, roughly one menu section per chunk, so each prompt is focused.
  2. Embed. Each chunk becomes an embedding vector.
  3. Retrieve. Milvus returns the most similar chunks from menus that humans already labelled in the catalog schema. A Portuguese café menu tends to retrieve other Portuguese café menus, with their layout quirks and price formats.
  4. Generate. LangChain builds a prompt: the target chunk, the retrieved labelled examples, and the exact JSON schema. Gemini 2.5 Pro returns JSON.
  5. Validate. JSON Schema validation is a hard gate. Anything malformed, or flagged as low confidence, goes to human review instead of the catalog.
def extract_menu(chunk_text: str, locale: str) -> dict:
    examples = milvus_search(embed(chunk_text), top_k=3, filter={"locale": locale})
    prompt = build_prompt(chunk=chunk_text, examples=examples, schema=CATALOG_SCHEMA)
    raw = gemini_generate(prompt)          # Gemini 2.5 Pro, asked for JSON only
    menu = json.loads(raw)
    jsonschema.validate(menu, CATALOG_SCHEMA)   # raises if the shape is wrong
    return menu

Simplified sketch of the flow. Function names and the top_k value are illustrative.

What Milvus stores per labelled chunk (logical fields): the embedding vector, menu and vendor IDs, locale, the chunk text, label tags and the source location.

Why retrieval helps. Without examples, an LLM guesses at layout conventions, might invent an item, or might drift from the schema. With two or three labelled examples of similar menus, it copies the right patterns: which number is the price, how sizes become modifiers, how the currency is written.

Why this design

  • An LLM because regex rules and fixed templates break on every new layout and language. Menus are too varied.
  • RAG rather than a bare prompt because grounding on similar labelled menus keeps output on-schema and reduces invented items.
  • A hard schema gate because the catalog is strict. A malformed menu is worse than a delayed one.
  • Human review for low-confidence output because protecting catalog quality matters more than squeezing out the last few percent of automation.

Alternatives and why not

  • Regex or template parsers per layout. Cheap per call, but an endless maintenance treadmill across thousands of layouts and many languages.
  • OCR plus hand-written rules. Gets the text, but not the structure (which number belongs to which dish).
  • A prompt with no retrieval. Simpler, but less consistent across cuisines and languages.
  • Training a custom model. Needs a large labelled set and retraining whenever the schema changes. With retrieval, a newly labelled menu helps the very next extraction.
  • Other vector stores (pgvector, managed services). Workable. Milvus is what we used, and it is built for vector similarity search at scale.

Trade-off. LLM calls cost money and add latency, and offline evaluation is not the same as live monitoring. What I'd do differently: add continuous sampling of live extractions against human spot checks, so we track fidelity in production, not only offline.

The numbers

From 24 hours to 2 hours. - What it measures: restaurant onboarding cycle time, from the menu being available to it being live in the catalog (HISTORICAL). - How derived: (24 − 2) / 24 ≈ 92%, so "roughly a 90% cut". - Why it mattered: restaurants start earning the same day instead of the next. - How to say it: "Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours." - What not to say: do not present it as a per-request latency.

$600K a year. - What it measures: annual cost removed by replacing manual and third-party menu processing. - How derived: about $2 per menu × 30,000 menus a month × 12 months = $720,000 list. The resume floors it to $600K to be conservative. Monthly that is about $60K. - Why it mattered: direct cost saving at a volume that keeps growing. - How to say it: "About $2 a menu at 30K menus a month is $720K a year. I quote $600K to be conservative." - What not to say: do not claim $720K as the saving, and do not invent a breakdown by vendor.

30K+ menus a month. - What it measures: menus processed by the pipeline per month (HISTORICAL). - How derived: 30,000 / 30 days ≈ 1,000 menus a day. - How to say it: "More than 30,000 menus a month, roughly a thousand a day." - What not to say: do not call it "hundreds of millions of transactions". If someone asks for peak event rate, a rough prep-only estimate is about 200 to 500 events per second during fleet runs, because each menu produces many item, retry and health events in bursts. It is ESTIMATED. Only say it if asked, and say "order-of-magnitude estimate".

98% field fidelity (offline evaluation). - What it measures: the share of extracted fields that exactly match human labels on an offline test set. - How derived: example: a test menu has 50 items with 4 fields each (name, price, description, modifiers), so 200 fields. If 196 match the labels, fidelity is 196 / 200 = 98%. The real evaluation aggregates this across the labelled set. - Why it mattered: it showed the RAG path was accurate enough to trust automatically, with the gate and human review catching the rest. - How to say it: "98% field fidelity in offline evaluation." - What not to say: never call it a live production accuracy or an SLA. If asked how big the test set was, keep it qualitative. Older prep also mentioned "100% schema consistency". It is not on the current PDF. If you bring it up, explain it simply follows from the gate: nothing malformed is written.

Questions they will ask

"How does RAG help Gemini here?" Before asking Gemini to extract a menu, we search Milvus for the most similar menus that humans already labelled, and put two or three of them in the prompt. That shows the model exactly how this kind of menu maps to our schema: which number is the price, how sizes become modifiers. It keeps output on-schema across languages and cuts down invented items. Then a JSON Schema check acts as a hard gate before anything is written.

"Is 98% a production number?" No, it is offline evaluation on a labelled set. Field fidelity means the share of individual fields, like each item's price or name, that exactly match the human label. In production the protection is the schema gate plus human review for low-confidence output.

Follow-up they may ask: "How would you monitor it live?" Sample a small percentage of live extractions for human spot checks, and alert on spikes in schema-gate rejections.

"How did you get to $600K?" About $2 per menu for the manual and third-party processing we replaced, times 30,000 menus a month, times 12. That is $720K. I quote $600K as a conservative floor.

"What stops the LLM from inventing a dish?" Three layers. Retrieval grounds it on real labelled examples. The schema gate rejects anything malformed. Low-confidence output goes to a human instead of the catalog.

Bullet 2: 95%+ extraction success, Selenium hardening, Kafka and Flink, keyed dedup, normalization, exactly-once upserts

"Scaled menu extraction success to 95%+ by hardening a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries. Designed a large-scale data ingestion and processing pipeline using Kafka and Apache Flink, with stateful keyed deduplication and schema normalization to guarantee exactly-once catalog upserts."

In plain words

Scrapers were failing about a third of the time because sites blocked them. I made the fleet resilient, and success went to 95% plus. Then I designed the pipeline behind the scrapers: Kafka as a durable buffer, and Flink to drop duplicates per restaurant, clean up the data into one format, and write to the catalog in a way that can never double-write.

How it works

Hardening the Selenium fleet.

  • Dynamic proxy pools. Each worker takes a proxy from a pool. Proxies that start getting banned or slow are evicted and replaced, so the pool heals itself.
  • IP rotation. Requests spread across many egress addresses, so no single address hammers one site.
  • Adaptive retries. The retry decision depends on the failure type, with exponential backoff, jitter and a per-source retry budget.
def scrape_with_retries(url, source, max_attempts=4):
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        proxy = proxy_pool.get_healthy(source)
        try:
            page = selenium_fetch(url, proxy=proxy)
            if looks_blocked(page):            # CAPTCHA wall or soft 403
                proxy_pool.mark_banned(proxy)
                continue                       # switch proxy immediately
            if item_count(page) == 0:
                raise EmptyMenuError(url)      # do not green-light an empty menu
            return page
        except TimeoutError:
            if not retry_budget.allow(source):
                break                          # protect the fleet from one hostile site
            time.sleep(min(2 ** attempt, 30) + random.uniform(0, 1))
    raise ScrapeFailed(url)

Simplified sketch. Thresholds and helper names are illustrative.

Kafka as the ingest bus. Scrape events go to a topic keyed by vendor_id. Separate streams carry retries and scrape-health signals. Because the key decides the partition, every event for one restaurant is processed in order. Consumers in a group share partitions, so we can scale Flink's parallelism roughly to the partition count. When a parser bug ships, we rewind offsets to before the bad deploy and replay.

Flink keyed deduplication, with an example. The Flink job keys the stream by vendor_id and keeps one value of state per vendor: the last processed content hash, which identifies the vendor's menu version.

class DedupByMenuVersion(KeyedProcessFunction):     # keyed by vendor_id
    def open(self, ctx):
        self.last_hash = ctx.get_state(ValueStateDescriptor("last_hash", Types.STRING()))

    def process_element(self, event, ctx):
        if self.last_hash.value() == event["content_hash"]:
            return                                  # same menu version, drop
        self.last_hash.update(event["content_hash"])
        yield normalize(event)

Python-style pseudocode of the pattern, not a claim about which Flink API language the job used.

Example timeline for vendor v_48213:

Event time Content hash State before Result
10:15 9f2c empty keep, state becomes 9f2c
10:25 9f2c 9f2c drop, duplicate scrape
next day 09:00 a71d 9f2c keep, the restaurant changed its menu

A time-to-live on this state stops it growing forever as vendors come and go.

Event time and watermarks. Scrapes can arrive late, for example after retries. Flink uses the scrape timestamp as event time and a watermark with bounded lateness (for example a few minutes, illustrative), so a late page from an older version does not overwrite a newer one.

Checkpoints. Flink periodically snapshots its state together with the Kafka offsets. If a worker dies, the job restores the last checkpoint and Kafka rewinds to those offsets. Some events get processed again. That is fine, because the sink is idempotent.

Schema normalization. Every source becomes one shape. Examples (illustrative): "8,50 €" becomes 8.50 and EUR, item names are trimmed and whitespace-normalized, size words like "Grande" or "Large" become modifiers, and each item gets a stable key built from vendor, normalized name and size.

Exactly-once catalog upserts, the honest version. The resume says "guarantee exactly-once catalog upserts". What that means in practice: delivery through Selenium, Kafka and Flink is at-least-once (after a failure, some events are processed again), and the catalog write is an idempotent upsert keyed by vendor, menu version and item key. Replaying the same event produces the same final row. So the catalog sees exactly-once effects. It is not a two-phase commit across Gemini, partner sites and the catalog.

INSERT INTO catalog_items (vendor_id, item_key, menu_version, name, price_amount, currency)
VALUES ('v_48213', 'v_48213|tosta mista|regular', '9f2c', 'Tosta mista', 4.50, 'EUR')
ON CONFLICT (vendor_id, item_key) DO UPDATE
SET name = EXCLUDED.name,
    price_amount = EXCLUDED.price_amount,
    menu_version = EXCLUDED.menu_version;

Generic SQL-style illustration of the contract. The real catalog is an internal Uber service, so describe the idempotency contract, not its storage engine.

Why this design

  • Selenium because many partner pages only render menus after JavaScript runs.
  • Kafka between scrapers and processing because scrapers must never block on a slow catalog, we need replay after parser bugs, and several consumers (processing, health monitoring) can share one log.
  • Flink because we needed per-vendor state for dedup, event-time handling for late pages, and continuous low-latency processing to hit a 2-hour onboarding cycle.
  • Idempotent upserts because at-least-once delivery is the realistic guarantee, and idempotency turns it into correct results.

Alternatives and why not

  • Plain HTTP fetches instead of Selenium. Miss JavaScript-rendered items and prices.
  • Scrapers calling the catalog directly. No buffer, no replay, and a slow catalog would stall the fleet.
  • Spark for the hot path. Spark is excellent for batch, but micro-batches add delay and per-key state is less natural. Spark is not on the resume. If asked, it is a reasonable option for large historical backfills, and that is study-level talk, not a claim.
  • Kafka Streams. A lighter option that could work at this event rate. Flink gave richer event-time support and larger keyed state.
  • True end-to-end exactly-once with transactions. Impossible across third-party sites and an LLM. Idempotency is the practical answer.

Trade-off. Kafka plus Flink is more infrastructure than a simple queue and worker, at a volume of about 1,000 menus a day. The justification is the shape of the load (bursts, retries, replay, per-vendor state), not raw throughput. What I'd do differently: add scrape-health dashboards earlier, such as item count per vendor over time, to catch silent DOM changes faster.

The numbers

95%+ extraction success (from an estimated 60 to 65%). - What it measures: the share of scrape jobs that return a complete, usable menu. - How derived: the 95%+ endpoint is HISTORICAL. The 60 to 65% starting point is ESTIMATED. - Why it mattered: every failed scrape meant manual work or a delayed restaurant. - How to say it: "Extraction success went to 95% plus, from roughly 60 to 65% before the hardening." - What not to say: do not present the 60 to 65% baseline as measured. Say "estimated".

Questions they will ask

"Is 30K menus a month really enough to need Kafka and Flink?" On average volume alone, no. The reasons are the shape of the load. Scrapes come in bursts with lots of retries, the same menu gets scraped repeatedly so we need per-vendor dedup state, pages arrive late so we need event time, and when a parser bug ships we need to replay. Kafka gives buffering and replay, Flink gives keyed state and event time. A simple worker queue could cover part of that, but we would end up rebuilding those features by hand.

"Do you really have exactly-once?" We have exactly-once effects in the catalog, not exactly-once delivery end to end. Delivery is at-least-once, so after a failure Flink can reprocess some events. The catalog upsert is keyed by vendor, menu version and item key, so reprocessing writes the same row again instead of a new one. There is no two-phase commit across Gemini or partner sites, and I would not claim zero message loss.

"What is your dedup key?" The stream is keyed by vendor_id, and the state holds the last content hash, the fingerprint of the menu version. Same vendor plus same hash means the event is dropped. A new hash means the restaurant changed its menu, so it goes through.

"What happens when a Flink checkpoint fails mid-run?" The job restores from the last successful checkpoint, Kafka offsets rewind to match it, and events since then are reprocessed. The idempotent upserts mean no duplicates. Consumer lag goes up and alerts until the job catches up.

"How do you know a scraper broke silently?" The dangerous failure is a page that loads fine but has no menu, because the site changed its layout or showed a CAPTCHA. We treat an empty or suspiciously small item count as a failure, not a success, and watch per-vendor item counts and success rates.

Bullet 3: ANZ document compliance (Uber Mobility)

"Achieved 99.9% regulatory compliance for Uber Mobility ANZ by automating driver and vehicle document verification workflows against local authority requirements. Eliminated 20 hours of manual operational overhead per week by replacing manual review queues with a deterministic validation backend."

In plain words

In Australia and New Zealand, drivers and vehicles must meet local authority rules. People used to check submitted documents by hand from review queues. I replaced that with a rules-based backend that checks every document the same way every time, which reached 99.9% compliance and freed about 20 hours a week of manual work. This is a HISTORICAL project from my past work records.

How it works

A deterministic validation backend is a rules engine. For each submitted document it runs explicit checks and returns pass or fail with the reason. The same input always produces the same verdict. Generic examples of the kinds of rules (do not present these as the exact production rule list):

  • Expiry: the document's expiry date is after today.
  • Document type: the document is the type the authority requires for this role or vehicle.
  • Record match: the name or ID on the document matches the driver record, and the vehicle details match the vehicle record.
  • Local authority requirements: the required set of documents for that region is complete.
def validate(doc, driver, vehicle, region_rules, today):
    failures = []
    if doc.expiry_date <= today:
        failures.append("expired")
    if doc.doc_type not in region_rules.required_types:
        failures.append("wrong document type")
    if doc.holder_id != driver.id:
        failures.append("does not match driver record")
    if doc.vehicle_id and doc.vehicle_id != vehicle.id:
        failures.append("does not match vehicle record")
    return ("compliant", []) if not failures else ("non_compliant", failures)

Generic illustrative sketch of what "deterministic validation" means, not the production code.

Why this design

  • Deterministic rules, not ML, because regulatory compliance needs explainable, repeatable decisions. "Rejected because it expired on 3 March" is auditable. A probability score is not.
  • Automated checks instead of manual queues because humans get tired and inconsistent, and queues add delay.

Alternatives and why not

  • Keep manual review. Slow and error-prone, costing about 20 hours a week.
  • An ML classifier. Harder to explain to a regulator, and unnecessary when the rules are explicit.

Trade-off. Rules must be updated whenever the authorities change requirements. What I'd do differently: keep the rules in versioned configuration so a rule change is reviewed and auditable without a code deploy. Say this as an idea, not as something I claim shipped.

The numbers

99.9% regulatory compliance. - What it measures: the compliance rate for driver and vehicle documents after automation (HISTORICAL). - How derived: from my past work records. If asked about the exact denominator, keep it qualitative. - How to say it: "We reached 99.9% compliance." - What not to say: do not invent counts of drivers or documents.

20 hours a week. - What it measures: manual verification effort removed (HISTORICAL). - How to say it: "It removed about 20 hours a week of manual review." - What not to say: do not claim it was re-measured from logs, and do not invent a team size behind it.

Questions they will ask

"Is this part of Uber Eats?" No. It was Uber Mobility, the rides side, for drivers in Australia and New Zealand. Same employer arrangement, Uber via EPAM, but a separate project from the menu pipeline.

"What does deterministic mean here?" The same document always gets the same answer, because the decision is a set of explicit rules, not a model. Every rejection carries the rule that failed, like "expired" or "does not match the vehicle record", which is what makes it auditable.

"What tech did you use?" My past work records describe it as Python automation behind a validation backend. I keep it at that level and do not claim the menu stack for it. If pressed on specifics I do not remember precisely, I say so and explain the design instead.

9. Hard problems and failure stories

1. Silent empty menus. - What broke: a site changed its layout or showed a CAPTCHA, the page loaded "successfully", and the scraper returned zero items, which looked like success. - How found: per-vendor item counts dropped suddenly. - How fixed: treat an empty or suspiciously small menu as a failure, and route it to retry or review. - What I learned: in scraping, "HTTP 200" means nothing. Validate the content.

2. Proxy bans and pool exhaustion. - What broke: hostile sites banned proxies, and naive retries burned through the pool, dragging down every other source. - How fixed: a dynamic pool that evicts banned proxies, failure-aware retries, and per-source retry budgets. - What I learned: isolate the blast radius. One bad site must not take the fleet down.

3. A bad parser deploy. - What can break: a normalization bug writes wrong prices for an hour. - How handled: fix the parser, rewind Kafka offsets to before the bad deploy, and replay. Idempotent upserts overwrite the bad rows with correct ones without duplicates. - What I learned: replayability is a feature you design for on day one, not after the incident.

4. The LLM inventing items. - Risk: without grounding, a model can add a plausible dish that is not on the menu. - How handled: retrieval of similar labelled menus, a strict schema gate, and human review for low-confidence output.

5. Flink state growth. - Risk: per-vendor state grows as vendors come and go, and idle partitions can stall watermarks. - How handled: a time-to-live on dedup state, and watching watermark progress and consumer lag.

10. Say this / don't say this

Say this carefully

  • Always say "Uber via EPAM".
  • 98% is offline evaluation. Field fidelity on a labelled set, not a live SLA.
  • "Exactly-once" means exactly-once effects: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts. No two-phase commit across Gemini or partner sites. Never claim zero message loss.
  • 60 to 65% baseline is ESTIMATED. The 95%+ endpoint is HISTORICAL.
  • $600K: about $2 × 30K × 12 = $720K, floored to $600K.
  • Peak 200 to 500 events per second is a prep-only ESTIMATE. Only if asked.
  • Spark is not on the resume. Mention only as a possible backfill tool if asked. Pinot is not on the resume either.
  • No ClickHouse on Menu. ClickHouse belongs to the Impact Analytics chapter.
  • Milvus is Menu only. Do not attach it to any other project, and do not name Pinecone or another vector vendor.
  • Do not claim fine-tuning (SFT). It is not on the current resume.
  • ANZ is Uber Mobility, not Eats, and HISTORICAL. Do not invent Selenium, RAG or Kafka for it, and do not invent counts behind 99.9% or 20 hours a week.
  • Masters India Kafka is a different product. Do not merge the two Kafka stories.

Don't say: "I owned all of Uber Eats' catalog platform." "98% accuracy in production." "We guaranteed no message is ever lost." "We used Spark Streaming." "ANZ used the menu pipeline."

11. Practice drill

1. Why is menu onboarding hard? Menus come as JavaScript-heavy sites, scanned PDFs and photos in many languages, and sites block bots. All of it has to fit a strict catalog schema before the restaurant can sell.

2. Why Selenium? Many menu pages only show items after JavaScript runs. Selenium drives a real browser, so we see what a customer sees.

3. How did you get extraction success to 95% plus? Dynamic proxy pools that evict banned proxies, IP rotation, and adaptive retries with backoff, jitter and per-source budgets. That took success from an estimated 60 to 65% to 95% plus.

4. What does Kafka do in this pipeline? It is the buffer between scrapers and processing. Scrapers write and move on, events for one vendor stay in order because we key by vendor_id, and we can replay after a bad deploy.

5. What is a consumer group? A set of workers sharing a topic. Each partition goes to exactly one worker in the group, which is how we scale processing.

6. What does Flink do? It reads Kafka continuously, keeps per-vendor state to drop duplicate menu versions, normalizes data to the catalog schema, and routes structured content to the catalog and unstructured content to the RAG extractor.

7. Explain watermarks. A watermark is Flink saying "I've probably seen everything up to time T". It lets the job handle late events within a bounded delay without waiting forever.

8. What happens on a crash? Flink restores the last checkpoint, Kafka rewinds to the matching offsets, some events are reprocessed, and idempotent upserts prevent duplicates.

9. Is it really exactly-once? Exactly-once effects. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts keyed by vendor, menu version and item key.

10. Explain RAG in this project. For a messy PDF we embed its chunks, find similar labelled menus in Milvus, and give those examples plus the schema to Gemini 2.5 Pro, which returns JSON. A JSON Schema check gates the write.

11. What is field fidelity? The share of extracted fields that exactly match human labels. If 196 of 200 fields match, that is 98%. Ours was 98% in offline evaluation.

12. Derive the $600K. About $2 per menu × 30,000 a month × 12 = $720K. I quote $600K to be conservative.

13. What is 30K a month per day? Roughly 1,000 menus a day.

14. What was the ANZ project? Uber Mobility in Australia and New Zealand. A deterministic validation backend checked driver and vehicle documents against local authority rules, reaching 99.9% compliance and removing about 20 hours a week of manual review.

15. Why deterministic rules for ANZ instead of ML? Regulators need explainable, repeatable decisions. A rule like "expired on this date" is auditable. A model score is not, and the rules were explicit anyway.

12. 3-minute whiteboard script

First, the problem (30 seconds). Draw three source icons on the left: "website", "PDF", "photo". Say: "A restaurant can't sell on Uber Eats until its menu is in the catalog. Menus are JavaScript sites, scanned PDFs and photos in many languages. Onboarding took about 24 hours and cost about $2 a menu."

Second, acquisition (30 seconds). Draw a box "Selenium fleet" with a small "proxy pool" box beside it. Say: "Selenium drives a real browser. I hardened it with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries, so extraction success went from an estimated 60 to 65% to 95% plus. Empty pages count as failures, not successes."

Third, the stream (60 seconds). Draw "Kafka, key = vendor_id" and then "Flink". Inside Flink write "state: last content hash per vendor". Say: "Scrapers publish to Kafka keyed by vendor, so each restaurant's events stay in order and we can replay. Flink drops duplicate menu versions using a content hash per vendor, normalizes prices and sizes to one schema, and routes. Structured content goes straight to an idempotent catalog upsert. The resume says exactly-once. Honestly that's at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts, so replays never duplicate."

Fourth, the AI path (45 seconds). Draw a branch from Flink to "RAG", with "Milvus" and "Gemini 2.5 Pro" beside it and a "schema gate" before the catalog. Say: "For messy PDFs we retrieve similar labelled menus from Milvus and give them plus the schema to Gemini 2.5 Pro, which returns JSON. A JSON Schema gate blocks anything malformed, and low-confidence output goes to a human. Offline evaluation showed 98% field fidelity."

Close with outcomes (15 seconds). Write "24h → 2h", "30K+/month", "$600K/yr". Say: "Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours at more than 30,000 menus a month. About $2 times 30K times 12 is $720K, and I quote $600K conservatively."

If there is time, ANZ (15 seconds). Draw a separate small box far from the menu diagram: "ANZ docs, rules engine". Say: "Separately, on Uber Mobility in ANZ, a deterministic validation backend checked driver and vehicle documents against local authority rules. It reached 99.9% compliance and removed about 20 hours a week of manual review."

07. Masters India: GST Compliance & E-Invoicing Platform

How to use this chapter

  • What it covers: my SDE 2 role at Masters India (Noida, December 2022 to June 2024). The product is a GST e-invoicing platform. The chapter covers the PHP-to-Spring Boot migration, the Kafka bulk pipeline, PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, idempotency, retries and dead-letter queues, Redis caching, ELK and New Relic, and test coverage.
  • When to read it: before any interview that may ask about "a migration you led", "a high-throughput pipeline", "idempotency", "Kafka vs a queue", "how you made an API faster" or "how you use Spring Boot in production".
  • What to memorise: p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds (75% lower), 1,500+ enterprise clients, 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, 1M+ government submissions a day, 100K+ invoices processed concurrently in bulk imports, triage 70% faster, database reads 30% lower, coverage from 35% to 82%, 98% deploy success, mentored 2 engineers.
  • Tags used here: HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and resume. ESTIMATED means it is arithmetic I can show on a whiteboard. If an illustration uses made-up sample numbers or sample code, I say "illustrative" next to it.

Related pages: Start here · Every number explained · Tech glossary · Core concepts · STAR stories · Next chapter: GeeksforGeeks. Older source packs: Masters and GFG interview packs, Masters and GFG deep dive, tables and why each tech, schemas and APIs.

Resume stack for this role (Java + Python + Go track, Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf): Java, Spring Boot, Hibernate, Kafka, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, ELK, New Relic, AWS.

2. The one-minute version

Say this out loud, roughly as written:

"At Masters India I worked on a GST e-invoicing platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise clients. Indian businesses must register every B2B invoice with a government portal, which gives back an official invoice number and a signed QR code. Our job was to validate their invoices and register them safely, at volume.

I led the migration of a legacy PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices. We did it gradually, one route at a time behind the gateway, with a small canary percentage first and rollback by a config change. That cut p95 latency by 75%, from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute. I also mentored two engineers through it.

I designed the bulk e-invoicing pipeline: a Kafka event bus, PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, and idempotency keys so a retry can never register the same invoice twice with the government. It handled 1M+ submissions a day. Failed batches went to dead-letter queues with bounded retries, because the government portal is often slow or down near filing deadlines.

On the operations side, ELK logging and New Relic tracing with one request ID cut incident triage time by about 70%. A Redis cache cut database reads by 30%. I also pushed test coverage from 35% to 82%, which got us to a 98% deployment success rate."

3. The business in plain English

What GST is

GST (Goods and Services Tax) is India's main indirect tax, introduced in July 2017. It replaced a long list of separate central and state taxes with one system. Every registered business gets a GSTIN (GST Identification Number), a 15-character ID such as 29ABCDE1234F1Z5. The first two digits are the state code. The middle ten are the business's PAN (tax ID). The last characters are an entity number and a checksum.

When a business sells to another business, the invoice shows the tax. Within one state the tax splits into CGST (central) and SGST (state). Across states it is IGST (integrated). The buyer later claims an input tax credit: "I already paid ₹18,000 of tax to my supplier, so subtract it from what I owe." That credit is why invoice accuracy matters to both sides. A wrong or missing invoice costs the buyer money, not only the seller.

Businesses file periodic returns (statements of their sales and tax) on fixed monthly or quarterly due dates. Reconciliation and audits look at a tax period, so the data naturally groups by period.

What an e-invoice is

An e-invoice does not mean "a PDF sent by email". It means the invoice is registered with the government before it is legally valid for B2B use. Since 2020 India has required this for businesses above a turnover threshold, and the threshold has been lowered in phases, so more and more businesses fall under it.

The government runs the IRP (Invoice Registration Portal). The flow is:

  1. The seller's ERP (accounting software, like SAP or Tally) creates the invoice.
  2. The invoice JSON is sent to the IRP.
  3. The IRP validates it and returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number). This is a unique 64-character hash that identifies the invoice in the government's records.
  4. The IRP also returns a digitally signed QR code. The QR carries the key invoice details plus the government's signature, so anyone can scan it and verify the invoice is genuine.
  5. The seller prints the QR on the invoice and sends it to the buyer.

Think of the IRP like a notary office. You bring a document, the notary checks it, stamps it with a unique serial number and signs it. After that it is an official record.

Where Masters India fits

Most enterprises do not want to talk to the government API directly. It has strict schemas, authentication tokens that expire, rate limits and bad days. Masters India sat in between. Clients sent invoices to us (one at a time from their ERP, or as bulk files with thousands of rows). We validated them, registered them with the IRP, stored the IRN and signed QR, and returned them to the client by API response or webhook. On top of that the product did bulk imports, reconciliation against GST returns, and audit trails. We served 1,500+ enterprise clients (HISTORICAL).

Why double registration is unrecoverable

This is the single most important constraint, and it is why idempotency appears everywhere in this chapter.

Once the IRP issues an IRN, that invoice is a legal record at the government. You cannot edit it. Under the GST rules as I worked with them, cancellation is allowed only in full and only within a short window (24 hours). After that, correcting a mistake needs credit notes and adjustments through returns, which is slow, manual and visible to auditors. If a retry bug registered the same sale twice (say, with a regenerated document number), the client would have two legal invoices for one sale. The buyer's tax credit and the seller's returns would no longer match. That shows up as a compliance problem for our client, and it is not something an engineer can "roll back".

So the design rule was: retries must be safe. Any step that talks to the IRP must be able to run twice and still produce exactly one registration.

Say this carefully. The 24-hour cancellation window and the "cannot edit" rule are general GST rules, not something I built. If an interviewer is a GST expert, keep it at "cancellation is narrow and time-limited, so a double registration becomes a compliance problem for the client". Don't argue tax law.

Filing-deadline spikes

Businesses tend to do tax work close to due dates. On the days before a return deadline, many clients upload a whole month or quarter of invoices at once. Load on those days is many times the normal average, and the IRP itself is under load too, so it gets slower and returns more errors at exactly the same moment. Normal days are easy. The system has to be built for the deadline day.

What hurt before, and why the company paid for this

Before the work in this chapter, the backend was a PHP (Laravel) monolith:

  • It was synchronous. A request that called the IRP held a PHP worker for the whole round trip. When the IRP was slow, workers ran out and every other request queued behind them, even ones that had nothing to do with the IRP.
  • Deploys were all-or-nothing. A change to reconciliation meant redeploying e-invoice submit too.
  • Scaling meant scaling everything. You could not add capacity just for the bulk import path.
  • Debugging meant SSH into boxes and grep logs, with no way to follow one request across components.

For a compliance product, a timeout on a filing day loses client trust fast. The company paid for the migration and the pipeline because faster, safer registration on deadline days is the product.

4. Words you need

General terms

Term Plain meaning
Monolith One big application that holds every feature and deploys as one unit. Like a single restaurant kitchen where one cook does starters, mains and dessert. If he is stuck on one dish, everything waits.
Microservices Many small services, each owning one job (auth, submit, bulk import, reconciliation), deployed separately. Like separate kitchen stations.
Strangler fig pattern A way to replace an old system gradually. You put new code next to the old one and move traffic route by route until the old system has nothing left. Named after a fig vine that slowly grows around a tree and replaces it.
Gateway The front door every request passes through. Here it was Nginx. It decides which backend gets each request.
Canary release Sending a small slice of traffic (for example 5% or 10%) to new code first and watching errors and latency before sending more. From "canary in a coal mine": a small early warning.
Non-blocking (async) IO A style where a thread starts a slow network call and is free to do other work while waiting, then resumes when the answer arrives. Like a waiter who takes the next table's order while the kitchen cooks, instead of standing at the kitchen door.
Connection pooling Keeping a set of open database connections and reusing them, instead of opening a new one for every request. Like keeping a phone line open instead of redialling for every sentence.
N+1 query A bug where code runs 1 query to fetch a list, then 1 more query per item. Fetching 50 invoices and their lines this way is 51 queries instead of 2.
p95 latency The response time that 95% of requests are at or below. Explained with an example in section 7.
Throughput How many requests the system completes per unit of time (here, per minute).
Kafka A durable, ordered log of messages. Producers append messages. Consumers read at their own pace and remember their position. Messages stay for a retention period, so you can re-read them.
Topic, partition, offset A topic is a named stream (like irp.completed). It is split into partitions for parallelism. Order is guaranteed only within one partition. The offset is a consumer's bookmark in a partition.
Partition key The value used to choose a partition. Messages with the same key always go to the same partition, so they stay in order.
Consumer group A team of consumers that share a topic's partitions. Different groups each get their own full copy of the stream.
Replay Moving a consumer group's offset back so it reprocesses old messages, for example after fixing a bug.
Sharding Splitting one large dataset into separate pieces (shards) by some rule, so each piece is smaller and can be managed on its own.
Idempotency An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Pressing a lift button five times still calls one lift.
Idempotency key A unique ID attached to a piece of work so the system can recognise "I have already done this one".
Dead-letter queue (DLQ) A side queue where messages that keep failing are parked, so they stop blocking the main flow and can be inspected and replayed later. Like a "problem parcels" shelf in a post office.
Exponential backoff with jitter Waiting longer after each failed retry (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s), plus a random amount, so thousands of clients don't all retry at the same instant.
Redis An in-memory key-value store, very fast. Used here as a cache.
Cache-aside The app checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with an expiry (TTL), then returns it.
Cache stampede When a popular cache key expires and hundreds of requests all miss at once and hammer the database together.
ELK Elasticsearch (stores and searches logs), Logstash (collects and parses logs), Kibana (the search and dashboard UI).
New Relic An APM (Application Performance Monitoring) product. It shows how long each request takes, broken down into database calls, external calls and code.
