9. Hard problems and failure stories

Story 1: the canary timeout mismatch

  • What broke: on an early canary of the submit route, some requests that worked on PHP failed on the Spring Boot service.
  • How we found it: the canary error-rate dashboard went up for the new service only, while only a small slice of traffic was on it.
  • Root cause: PHP had a 60-second timeout. We had set 10 seconds on the new service. Some IRP calls legitimately took longer than 10 seconds, especially on busy days.
  • Fix: instead of just raising the timeout, we moved the IRP call fully off the request path. The API returned 202 Accepted with an invoice ID, and the client polled or got a webhook.
  • What I learned: the old system's quirks are part of its contract, so contract tests should cover timeouts and slow paths, not just payloads. And canaries earn their keep. A small slice found this before every client did.

Story 2: N+1 queries hiding in the monolith

  • What we found: while rewriting list endpoints, several fetched a page of invoices and then queried lines or status per invoice.
  • Fix: batch fetching in Hibernate (one extra query for all lines on the page), composite indexes on (client_id, invoice_date), and pagination.
  • What I learned: a rewrite is a good moment to profile every query. A lot of the p95 gain came from fixes like this, not from the new framework. It also taught the team to switch on Hibernate's SQL logging in tests, because lazy loading hides N+1 queries very well.

Story 3: the same lookup on every row of a bulk import

  • What we saw: a 100K-row import read the same client config and many of the same GSTIN masters over and over.
  • Fix: Redis cache-aside with TTL jitter, a setIfAbsent stampede lock, and invalidation on write.
  • Result: database read load down 30% (HISTORICAL).

Design risks I planned around (not incident stories)

  • Wrong-quarter writes. If routing derived the wrong quarter, an invoice would land in the wrong shard. We derived the quarter at the API from invoice_date and rejected mismatches.
  • Poison batches. One bad batch must not block a partition. Bounded retries plus DLQ.
  • Unknown IRP outcome after a timeout. Retry through the same idempotency key, and the IRP's own duplicate check is a backstop.

Present these as design decisions, not as dated incidents.

10. Say this / don't say this

Say this

  • "1,500+ enterprise clients."
  • "PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices."
  • "p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, a 75% cut."
  • "700 to 4,000 requests per minute, roughly 12 to 67 per second."
  • "1M+ government submissions a day, about 12 per second on average. Peaks around 8 to 10 times that, which is my estimate."
  • "At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, so the effect is exactly once."
  • "I mentored two engineers."
  • "Triage about 70% faster, roughly 30 minutes down to under 10. The baseline is my estimate."
  • "The migration was gradual, route by route, behind the gateway. People call it the strangler pattern."

Don't say this

  • "2,500+ clients" (older resume, not on the current PDF).
  • "Support tickets down 35%" (older resume, not on the current PDF).
  • "Zero message loss" or "true exactly-once delivery to the government".
  • "I led a team" at Masters India. Mentored 2 is Masters. Led 3 is Uber FRM.
  • Flink at Masters India. Flink belongs to the Uber Menu pipeline, which is a different Kafka system.
  • "Payments" or "money movement". This is tax compliance and invoice registration.
  • A circuit breaker as a measured result. It is a design idea to discuss.
  • TPS or RPS as if they are on the PDF. They are arithmetic I can show.
  • "100,000 separate files uploaded at once." Say "100K+ invoices in flight across concurrent bulk imports".
  • Exact partition counts, chunk sizes, retry counts, pool sizes, thread counts or TTLs as remembered facts. The ones in this chapter are illustrative.
  • The Java snippets as copied production code. They show how the mechanism works.

11. Practice drill

  1. What does Masters India do? It's a GST compliance and e-invoicing SaaS for Indian enterprises. Clients send us invoices, we validate them and register them with the government's Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an IRN and a signed QR code. We return those to the client by API or webhook.

  2. What is an IRN and why does it matter? The IRN is the unique reference number the government portal assigns when it registers an invoice. Together with the signed QR, it makes a B2B invoice legally valid. Without it the buyer can't safely claim tax credit.

  3. Why is a double registration so bad? Once registered, the invoice is a legal record. Cancellation is narrow and time-limited, and after that you need manual corrections through returns. Two registrations for one sale create a compliance mismatch for the client, so every retry had to be idempotent.

  4. Explain p95 with an example. Take 100 requests and sort them by time. The 95th one is the p95. If it's 300 milliseconds, 95% of requests finished in 300 milliseconds or less. Ours went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds.

  5. Where did the latency win come from? Mostly from taking slow IRP calls off the request path into Kafka consumers, plus HikariCP connection pooling and query fixes like composite indexes and removing N+1 queries. Redis cut repeated reads, which helped the typical request more than the slow tail.

  6. How did the canary rollout work? Nginx sent a small percentage of one route's traffic to the new Spring Boot service. We watched error rate and latency, then ramped up or rolled back. Rollback was a config change and reload, not a redeploy.

  7. Why not dual writes during the migration? Two sources of truth in a tax product cause reconciliation nightmares. We kept one shared database during the traffic move and split tables only after a route was fully migrated.

  8. Why is the partition key the GSTIN? So every message for one taxpayer lands on the same partition and is processed in order: submit, result, webhook. Different taxpayers still run in parallel. The risk is one giant client creating a hot partition.

  9. Kafka vs SQS, one sentence each. Kafka keeps an ordered, replayable log that many consumer groups can read independently. SQS is a simpler managed queue that deletes messages on acknowledgement, so there's no cheap replay, and its FIFO mode caps throughput per group.

  10. What is your idempotency key? Client plus fileHash plus batchIndex for bulk work, and the client's invoice reference for single invoices. A unique constraint means a redelivered message finds the existing key and skips the IRP call.

  11. Why backoff with jitter, and how is it wired in Spring? Backoff gives a struggling portal room to recover. Jitter spreads retries out so thousands of workers don't retry at the same second and knock it over again. In Spring Kafka it's a DefaultErrorHandler with an exponential back-off and an attempt limit, plus a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer for the DLQ.

  12. What is a DLQ and why use one? A side queue for messages that keep failing. It stops one poison batch from blocking the rest of the import. An operator can inspect it, fix the cause and replay it safely through the same idempotency keys.

  13. Why shard by quarter? Writes go almost entirely to the current quarter, while older quarters are read for audits. Quarter shards keep the hot table small and make archiving a whole quarter clean. The cost is routing in the data-access layer.

  14. How did ELK and New Relic cut triage time? Every log line, HTTP header, Kafka message and background task carried one request ID, set by a servlet filter and kept in the logging MDC. One Kibana search showed a request's whole path, and New Relic showed where the time went. That took triage from roughly 30 minutes to under 10.

  15. What did the 35% to 82% coverage focus on? Money paths first: registration, reconciliation and imports, written as JUnit 5 and Mockito tests, including contract tests that pinned the old PHP responses. JaCoCo enforced coverage as a CI gate, which together with canaries helped us reach 98% deploy success.

12. 3-minute whiteboard script

First (about 45 seconds): the business and the constraint. Draw three boxes in a row: "Client ERP", "Masters India", "Government IRP". Arrow from client to us, from us to IRP, and back with "IRN + signed QR". Say: "Indian businesses must register every B2B invoice with the government. We sat in the middle for 1,500+ enterprise clients. The one rule that shaped everything: a double registration can't be undone, so every retry must be idempotent. And load spikes hard before filing deadlines."

Second (about 60 seconds): the migration. Inside "Masters India", draw an "Nginx gateway" box splitting to "PHP monolith" and "Spring Boot services", both pointing to one "Shared DB". Write "10% canary" on one arrow. Say: "The PHP monolith was synchronous. A slow IRP call pinned a worker. I led a gradual migration to Spring Boot, route by route, with canaries and rollback by config. The win came from moving IRP calls off the request path into async consumers, HikariCP connection pooling and query fixes, with Redis for repeated reads. p95 went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests a minute. I mentored two engineers through it."

Third (about 60 seconds): the bulk pipeline. Draw "S3 file" to "Spring Batch validation" to "Kafka (key = GSTIN)" to "IRP consumers" to "IRP". Branch from consumers to "DLQ". Branch from Kafka to "Postgres by quarter" and "Mongo snapshots" and "webhooks". Write the key client + fileHash + batchIndex next to the consumers. Say: "Bulk files land in S3 and the client gets a 202 right away. A Spring Batch job validates the file in restartable chunks. Kafka carries each stage, keyed by GSTIN for per-taxpayer order, and it lets us replay after a bug. Consumers check the idempotency key before every IRP call, retry with exponential backoff, and park poison batches in a DLQ. Invoices land in PostgreSQL tables split by tax quarter. That's 1M+ submissions a day, about 12 a second on average and around 100 at deadline peaks, which is my estimate."

Close (about 15 seconds): operations. Write "request ID" along the bottom, touching every box. Say: "One request ID through every service, queue and background task, in ELK and New Relic, cut triage about 70%. Redis cache-aside cut database reads 30%. Coverage went from 35% to 82% with JUnit and a JaCoCo gate, and deploys succeeded 98% of the time."

08. GeeksforGeeks: Courses Platform and Influencer Dashboard

How to use this chapter

  • What it covers: my first role, Software Development Engineer at GeeksforGeeks (Noida, August 2021 to November 2022). The work covers the doubt-support platform migration from PHP to Django, the voting, pinning and locking APIs, why MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch were each used, the influencer analytics and earnings dashboard, and the scheduled background workflows.
  • When to read it: before interviews that ask about early-career ownership, "a migration", "designing a voting or like system", "hot rows", "cron reliability", or "Django vs Spring Boot".
  • What to memorise: 10K+ daily queries, 10x spikes during live coding contests, a 20% lift in premium subscriptions (relative, attributed by the growth team), course sales up 30% (business attribution), engineering operational efficiency up 70%.
  • Tags used here: HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and resume. ESTIMATED means it is arithmetic I can show. "Illustrative" means made-up sample data to explain a mechanism, not a remembered figure.

Related pages: Start here · Every number explained · Tech glossary · Core concepts · STAR stories · Previous chapter: Masters India. Older source packs: Masters and GFG interview packs, Masters and GFG deep dive, tables and why each tech, schemas and APIs.

2. The one-minute version

"My first job was at GeeksforGeeks, the computer-science learning platform. I worked on the courses platform. The doubt-support system, where learners post questions on courses and articles, ran on a fragile PHP backend. It struggled with 10K+ daily queries and with traffic that jumped about ten times during live coding contests. I migrated that backend to Django and built the REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads, using MySQL as the source of truth, Redis for hot counters, MongoDB for flexible content and Elasticsearch for search. The growth team tied those features to a 20% lift in premium subscriptions.

I also built an analytics and earnings dashboard for influencers who promote our courses with affiliate coupon codes, which the business team credited with a 30% rise in course sales. And I designed scheduled background jobs for video processing, user reminders and data cleanup, which cut manual operations work by about 70%.

It's where I learned the basics I used later: unique constraints for idempotency, keeping hot counters off the database, and making scheduled jobs safe to re-run."

3. The business in plain English

GeeksforGeeks (GFG) is one of the biggest computer-science learning sites in India. It has free articles, practice problems, live coding contests and paid courses. Premium subscriptions and course sales are a large part of how it makes money.

Who the users are:

  • Learners, who read articles, take courses and post doubts (questions) when they're stuck.
  • People who answer doubts, plus moderators who keep threads tidy.
  • Influencers, creators who promote GFG courses to their audience with their own affiliate coupon codes and earn from the sales.
  • The ops and course teams, who handle course videos, reminders and housekeeping.

What the doubt-support platform does: a learner on a course or article page asks "Why does my DFS give a stack overflow on this input?" Others reply. Good answers get upvoted so they rise. A moderator or instructor can pin the best thread to the top, and lock a thread to stop new replies, for example once it is resolved or off-topic.

What hurt before:

  • The backend was legacy PHP. It was hard to change safely and lacked clean transactions and request validation.
  • During live coding contests traffic jumped about 10 times, and the doubt pages became slow and unreliable exactly when learners needed them most.
  • Popular doubts got many votes at once, and updating one counter row in the database for every vote caused lock contention, the "hot row" problem explained below.
  • Ops staff did repetitive work by hand: moving videos through processing, sending reminders, cleaning up old recordings and data.
  • Influencers had no clear view of how their coupon codes were converting or what they had earned.

Why the company paid for this: a reliable doubt system is a selling point of premium plans, so if it breaks during a contest, learners have a reason not to pay. A good influencer dashboard keeps partners motivated to promote courses. And automating ops work frees people for higher-value tasks.

4. Words you need

Term Plain meaning
Doubt GFG's word for a learner's question on a course or article. A "doubt thread" is the question plus its replies.
PHP An older web scripting language. The legacy doubt backend was written in it.
Django A "batteries included" Python web framework. It comes with an ORM, admin panel, authentication, forms and migrations. Like buying a furnished flat instead of an empty one.
DRF (Django REST Framework) An add-on to Django for building REST APIs: serializers (validate input, shape output), viewsets and permissions.
ORM Object-Relational Mapper. Lets you work with database rows as Python objects (Vote.objects.filter(...)) instead of writing raw SQL every time.
REST API A web API where URLs name things (/api/v1/votes) and HTTP verbs act on them (POST to create, DELETE to remove).
MySQL A popular relational database with tables, rows, joins and transactions. Used here as the source of truth.
MongoDB A document database. It stores JSON-like documents whose fields can vary from one document to the next.
Redis An in-memory key-value store. Very fast. Used for counters and caches.
Elasticsearch A search engine. It builds an inverted index (word to list of documents) so full-text search is fast. Like the index at the back of a textbook.
Unique constraint A database rule that a combination of columns can appear only once. A second insert with the same values is rejected.
Idempotent Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Pressing "upvote" twice should not count two votes.
Hot row One database row that many requests try to update at the same moment. Each update takes a lock on the row, so they queue up. Like one checkout counter with a hundred people.
Reconcile Periodically recompute the true value from the source of truth and fix any drift in the fast copy.
Cron A scheduler that runs a job at fixed times, for example "every night at 2 AM".
Lock or lease (for jobs) A short-lived "I'm running this" marker, so two servers don't run the same scheduled job at once. A lease expires on its own if the holder crashes.
Idempotent job key A unique ID for one run of one job, such as reminder:course_42:2022-06-10, so a re-run can see "already done" and skip.
Affiliate coupon A discount code tied to a specific influencer. A purchase using that code is credited to them, and they earn a share.
Conversion A visitor actually buying. A "coupon conversion" is a purchase that used the code.
Attribution Deciding which cause gets credit for a business result. Here the growth and business teams did the attribution, not me.

5. Architecture

flowchart LR U["Learners, moderators, influencers"] --> DJ["Django and DRF APIs: doubts, votes, pins, locks, dashboard"] DJ --> MY["MySQL: users, threads, votes, pins, locks, subscriptions, earnings"] DJ --> RD["Redis: vote counters, unread badges, contest hot keys"] DJ --> MO["MongoDB: flexible doubt bodies and content payloads"] DJ --> ES["Elasticsearch: search over doubts and content"] RC["Reconcile job"] --> RD RC --> MY CR["Scheduled jobs with lock and job key"] --> MY CR --> MO CR --> V["Video processing, reminders, data cleanup"]

What to notice: MySQL is the single source of truth. Redis holds fast, possibly slightly stale copies that the reconcile job corrects. The scheduled jobs are separate from the request path.

Walking through it box by box:

  • Learners, moderators, influencers. They use the website and app. All requests go to Django.
  • Django and DRF APIs. These replaced the PHP backend. Serializers validate every request. Writes run inside database transactions.
  • MySQL. Relational data where correctness matters: users, doubt threads and replies, votes with a unique (user_id, content_id) rule, pins, locks, subscriptions, and influencer transactions and earnings.
  • Redis. Fast counters that change constantly: vote totals for display, unread badges, and hot keys that get hammered during contests.
  • MongoDB. Content whose shape varies, such as doubt bodies with code blocks or attachments, and other semi-structured payloads.
  • Elasticsearch. Full-text search, so a learner can search "segmentation fault in recursion" and find existing doubts.
  • Reconcile job. Periodically recomputes vote totals from MySQL and corrects Redis and the stored count.
  • Scheduled jobs. Video processing handoffs, user reminders and data cleanup. Each takes a lock so only one server runs it, and records a job key so a re-run doesn't repeat work.

6. One request, step by step: an upvote during a contest

Sample data (illustrative): learner user_id = 42 upvotes doubt content_id = 123, "Why does my DFS overflow the stack?", during a live contest. Hundreds of others are voting on the same doubt in the same few minutes.

sequenceDiagram participant L as Learner 42 participant D as Django vote API participant M as MySQL participant R as Redis participant J as Reconcile job L->>D: POST /api/v1/votes content_id 123 value +1 D->>M: upsert vote row for user 42 and content 123 M-->>D: old value 0, new value +1 D->>R: INCRBY votes:123 by +1 D-->>L: 200 OK, new count read from Redis L->>D: same POST again after a double click D->>M: upsert finds existing vote with same value M-->>D: no change D-->>L: 200 OK, count unchanged J->>M: every few minutes, SUM votes for content 123 J->>R: overwrite votes:123 with the true total

What to notice: each vote writes its own row (user 42's row for doubt 123), so votes don't fight over one shared row. The shared total lives in Redis. The second click is a no-op because of the unique constraint. The reconcile job is the safety net that keeps Redis honest.

The same flow in words:

  1. Learner 42 clicks upvote. Django validates the request with a DRF serializer.
  2. Django writes the vote into the votes table. A unique constraint on (user_id, content_id) means user 42 can have only one vote row for doubt 123.
  3. If the vote is new or changed, Django adjusts the Redis counter by the difference: +1 for a new upvote, −2 for changing an upvote into a downvote.
  4. The page shows the new count from Redis immediately.
  5. A double click sends the same request again. The row already holds +1, so nothing changes and the count stays right.
  6. Every few minutes the reconcile job sums the real votes in MySQL and overwrites the Redis value and the stored count. Any drift (say Redis was flushed, or an increment was lost) is fixed.

7. Each resume bullet decoded

Bullet 1: the Django migration and the voting, pinning and locking APIs

"Stabilized the doubt-support platform to handle 10K+ daily queries and 10x traffic spikes during live coding contests by migrating the backend to Django. Engineered high-throughput REST APIs for voting, pinning, and locking threads utilizing MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, and Elasticsearch, driving a 20% lift in premium subscriptions."

In plain words

I moved the doubt-support backend from old PHP code to Django, so it stayed reliable on normal days and during contest spikes. I built the APIs that let users vote on answers, let moderators pin and lock threads, and I chose which data store held what. The growth team linked these features to a 20% rise in premium subscriptions.

What the load actually means

  • 10K+ daily queries. 10,000 ÷ 86,400 seconds = about 0.12 per second, roughly one every 9 seconds on average. ESTIMATED arithmetic. That is well under 1 request per second.
  • 10x contest spikes. Even ten times the average is only around 1 per second if spread evenly. But contest traffic is not even. It bunches into short windows, and every posted doubt brings many more reads (page views, vote counts, searches) than writes.

So the honest story is not "massive throughput". The PHP backend was fragile under bursts: no clean transactions, little request validation, slow unindexed paths, and hot rows on popular doubts. The fix was correctness and burst safety, not raw scale.

Say this carefully. "Order of ten thousand daily queries, with roughly ten times that during contests." Don't call it 100K a day (an older resume said that) or 1K a day (an older, narrower metric). Don't compare it to Uber or Impact Analytics scale. The point is reliability under bursts.

How it works: the migration and what Django bought

We migrated page by page behind the same URLs, so users never saw a switch-over day. The same gradual idea came back later at Masters India. Django and DRF helped in four concrete ways:

  1. Transactions. transaction.atomic() wraps a write so it either fully happens or fully doesn't. For example, creating a reply and bumping the unread counter together.
  2. Request validation. DRF serializers reject bad input (missing fields, wrong types, a vote value other than +1 or −1) before it reaches the database.
  3. Read and write separation. Read views (list doubts, show counts) were kept apart from write endpoints, so reads could lean on cache and writes stayed simple and transactional.
  4. Process discipline. Staging, code review and migrations under version control, which the PHP stack lacked.

Caching with Redis took the repeated contest reads (vote counts, unread badges, hot doubt pages) off MySQL. Database constraints made the data correct even under races. A double-submitted vote cannot create two rows.

How it works: voting with a unique constraint and Redis counters

Logical schema (from my notes, LOGICAL and HISTORICAL, not copied from code):

CREATE TABLE votes (
  id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  user_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  content_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  value       TINYINT NOT NULL,          -- +1 or -1
  created_at  DATETIME NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_vote (user_id, content_id)
);

The API upserts the row:

INSERT INTO votes (user_id, content_id, value, created_at)
VALUES (42, 123, 1, NOW())
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE value = VALUES(value);

Illustrative Django view logic:

from django.db import transaction

def cast_vote(user_id: int, content_id: int, value: int) -> int:
    with transaction.atomic():
        vote = (Vote.objects.select_for_update()
                .filter(user_id=user_id, content_id=content_id).first())
        old = vote.value if vote else 0
        if old == value:
            return int(redis.get(f"votes:{content_id}") or 0)   # same vote again: no-op
        Vote.objects.update_or_create(
            user_id=user_id, content_id=content_id, defaults={"value": value})
    return redis.incrby(f"votes:{content_id}", value - old)      # apply only the change

Why this avoids the hot row. The naive design runs UPDATE content SET vote_count = vote_count + 1 WHERE id = 123 on every vote. Every one of those updates locks the same row, so 300 votes in a few minutes on a popular doubt means 300 transactions queuing on one lock. With our design, each vote touches its own (user_id, content_id) row, so there is no contention. The shared total is a Redis INCRBY, which is atomic and takes microseconds.

Worked example (illustrative):

Time Event votes row for (42, 123) Redis votes:123
10:00:01 User 42 upvotes value = +1 87 → 88
10:00:01 Double click, same upvote unchanged 88
10:03:10 User 42 switches to downvote value = −1 88 → 86 (change of −2)
10:05:00 Redis node restarts, key lost unchanged missing
10:05:00 Reconcile runs: SUM(value) = 86 unchanged set to 86

The reconcile query:

SELECT content_id, SUM(value) AS total
FROM votes
WHERE content_id IN (/* doubts with recent activity */)
GROUP BY content_id;

The job writes each total back to content.vote_count in MySQL and to Redis.

How it works: pinning and locking

  • Pinning. A pin record marks a thread as pinned within its context (a course or an article), with an ordering column so pinned threads show in a set order at the top. A unique constraint means pinning the same thread twice is a no-op, which is the same idempotency idea as votes.
  • Locking. A lock record holds content_id, locked_by, reason and an optional expires_at. The "post reply" API checks for an active lock and refuses new replies on a locked thread. Moderation actions sit behind permission checks, so only moderators or instructors can pin or lock.

Logical API surface (from my notes, illustrative):

POST   /api/v1/votes               {content_id, value}   idempotent upsert
DELETE /api/v1/votes/{content_id}                         remove my vote
POST   /api/v1/pins                {content_id}           moderator only
POST   /api/v1/content/{id}/lock   {reason}               moderator only
GET    /api/v1/search?q=...                               Elasticsearch

Why each store: MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch

Store What lived there Why this store
MySQL Users, threads and replies, votes, pins, locks, subscriptions, influencer transactions Relational data that must be correct: unique constraints, joins, transactions. The source of truth.
MongoDB Flexible doubt bodies and content payloads (code blocks, attachments, varying fields) The shape varies from document to document. No schema migration for every new field.
Redis Vote counters, unread badges, contest hot keys Thousands of tiny reads and increments a minute. Memory-speed and atomic INCR.
Elasticsearch Search index over doubts and content Full-text search with relevance ranking. SQL LIKE '%stack overflow%' can't use a normal index and gets slow.

One-liner: "MySQL for truth, Redis for hot counters, MongoDB where the document shape varied, Elasticsearch for search."

The 20% premium lift

  • What it measures: growth in premium subscriptions after these features shipped. Some doubt-support interactions were part of the premium offering.
  • Relative, not absolute: a 20% lift means, for example, 1,000 new premium subscriptions a month becoming 1,200 (illustrative numbers). It does not mean 20% of all users became premium.
  • Who attributed it: the growth team. I owned the APIs and their reliability.
  • How to say it: "The growth team attributed about a 20% relative lift in premium subscriptions to these features. I owned the engineering behind them."

Number conflict to know about. Older prep notes said "15 to 20%". The current resume says 20%. Use 20%, framed as a relative lift attributed by the growth team.

Why this design

  • A unique constraint gives correctness even under races and double clicks, enforced by the database rather than by hopeful app code.
  • Redis plus reconcile removes the hot-row problem without giving up the truth in MySQL.
  • Django fit a 2021 content-and-community product: admin panel, auth, ORM and migrations out of the box, so the team shipped features fast.

Alternatives and why not

Alternative Why not
Update a counter column in MySQL on every vote Hot-row lock contention on popular doubts, worst during contests.
Counters only in Redis, no vote rows Fast but not durable or auditable. You can't stop double votes per user or rebuild after a Redis flush.
Check "has this user voted?" in app code, no constraint Two simultaneous requests can both pass the check. Only a database constraint is race-proof.
Everything in MongoDB Votes, subscriptions and permissions are relational and need constraints and transactions.
Search with SQL LIKE Slow and no relevance ranking.
Stay on PHP The reliability problems were in the code structure, not just the servers.

Trade-off

Displayed counts can be a few minutes stale or slightly off until the reconcile runs. That's fine for a vote badge. It would not be fine for money. Four data stores also mean more to run and keep consistent.

Questions they will ask

"How do you make a vote API idempotent?" With a unique constraint on user ID and content ID in the votes table, so a user can only ever have one vote row per doubt. The API upserts that row. If the value hasn't changed, it's a no-op. A double click or a client retry can never count twice, and the database enforces it even when two requests race.

"How did you avoid hot rows on popular doubts?" We stopped updating a shared counter row on every vote. Each vote writes its own row, keyed by user and content, so there's no contention. The display total lives in Redis and is updated with an atomic increment. A reconcile job sums the real votes from MySQL every few minutes and corrects Redis, so MySQL stays the source of truth. Follow-up they may ask: "What if Redis loses the key?" The next reconcile rebuilds it from the vote rows, and until then the API can fall back to the stored count.

"10K queries a day isn't much. What was hard?" You're right that the average is well under one request per second. What was hard was bursts and fragility. Contest traffic jumped about tenfold in short windows, the PHP code had no clean transactions or validation, and popular doubts created hot rows. The Django migration, Redis counters and database constraints made it hold up during those bursts.

"Why four data stores? Isn't that over-engineering?" Each one did a job the others do badly. MySQL held relational truth with constraints. Redis handled very frequent tiny counters. MongoDB held content whose shape varied. Elasticsearch did full-text search. If I had to cut one today, I'd look hard at whether MongoDB's role could move into MySQL JSON columns.

Bullet 2: the influencer dashboard and scheduled workflows

"Accelerated platform course sales by 30% by launching an influencer analytics and earnings dashboard to dynamically track transactions and affiliate coupon conversions. Increased engineering operational efficiency by 70% by designing asynchronous scheduled workflows for automated video processing, user reminders, and data cleanup."

This bullet has two separate pieces of work. Keep them apart when you talk.

Part A: the influencer analytics and earnings dashboard

In plain words: influencers promote GFG courses with their own coupon codes. I built a dashboard where each influencer could see their transactions, how many purchases used their code, and what they had earned.

How it works:

  • Every course purchase that used a coupon was recorded in MySQL with the coupon code, linked to the influencer account.
  • The dashboard showed transactions, coupon conversions and earnings, with filters and CSV export (from my older resume notes).
  • Near-real-time counters in Redis gave a fresh "today so far" view. Daily rollups by a scheduled job built the historical charts without scanning raw transactions on every page load.

Logical tables (illustrative):

influencer_account (id, name, coupon_code)
earning_txn        (id, influencer_id, order_id, course_id, amount, earning, created_at)
daily_rollup       (influencer_id, day, orders, revenue, earning)

Worked example (illustrative): influencer Priya has coupon PRIYA10. On Monday, 40 course orders use PRIYA10. Each order writes an earning_txn row, and Redis bumps inf:priya:today:orders. Priya opens her dashboard at 3 PM and sees "40 orders today" from Redis. At night the rollup job writes Monday's totals into daily_rollup, and her weekly chart reads from that table. The earning per order follows whatever commission her agreement set. I don't need to quote a rate.

The 30% course sales number:

  • What it measures: growth in course sales after the dashboard launched.
  • Who attributed it: the business team. The likely mechanism is that influencers who can see their conversions and earnings promote more and adjust what works.
  • How to say it: "The business team credited the dashboard with about a 30% rise in course sales. I built the dashboard. They did the attribution."
  • What not to say: "I increased sales by 30%" as if engineering alone caused it.

Part B: asynchronous scheduled workflows

In plain words: jobs that used to need a person, such as moving videos through processing, sending reminders before classes, or deleting old recordings and stale data, now ran automatically on a schedule, safely.

The jobs (from the PDF):

  1. Video processing: hand off newly uploaded course videos to processing and track their status.
  2. User reminders: send reminders to learners, for example before a live class.
  3. Data cleanup: remove expired cloud recordings and stale data.

The two reliability rules:

  • A lock so only one server runs a job. If cron runs on two hosts for redundancy, both wake up at 2 AM. Without a lock, both send the same 5,000 reminder emails. A short-lived lock (a Redis SET NX with expiry, or a MySQL advisory lock) means the second host sees "someone has it" and exits. Because the lock expires, a crashed holder doesn't block the job forever.
  • An idempotent job key so re-runs are safe. Each unit of work gets a key like reminder:{user_id}:{class_id}:{type} or cleanup:{date}. Before doing the work, the job checks whether that key is already marked done. If a job crashes halfway and re-runs, it skips what's already finished.

Illustrative code:

import socket

HOST = socket.gethostname()

def run_once(job_name: str, run_key: str, work) -> None:
    lock = f"cron:lock:{job_name}"
    if not redis.set(lock, HOST, nx=True, ex=3600):    # someone else is running it
        return
    try:
        if JobRun.objects.filter(job_key=run_key, status="done").exists():
            return                                      # already done, safe re-run
        work()
        JobRun.objects.update_or_create(job_key=run_key, defaults={"status": "done"})
    finally:
        redis.delete(lock)

def send_class_reminders(class_id: int) -> None:
    for user_id in enrolled_user_ids(class_id):
        key = f"reminder:{user_id}:{class_id}:1h_before"
        if not SentReminder.objects.filter(key=key).exists():
            send_email(user_id, class_id)
            SentReminder.objects.create(key=key)

Each job also wrote structured success and failure logs, and retried or set aside partial batches instead of failing the whole run.

Worked example (illustrative): the reminder job for class 77 has 2,000 enrolled learners. It crashes after 1,200 emails. On re-run, the first 1,200 keys are already in SentReminder, so it sends only the remaining 800. Nobody gets two emails.

The 70% ops efficiency number:

  • What it measures: time saved on the manual video, reminder and cleanup workflows the team used to do by hand (HISTORICAL).
  • How to picture it (illustrative, not a remembered figure): if those tasks took 10 hours of someone's week, they now take about 3.
  • How to say it: "Automating video handoffs, reminders and cleanup cut the manual effort on those workflows by about 70%."

Why this design

  • The dashboard used Redis for "today" and rollups for history, so the page stayed fast without scanning every transaction each time.
  • Scheduled jobs used locks plus idempotent keys because cron is simple and good enough for daily or hourly work, as long as you make it safe to run twice and impossible to run concurrently.

Alternatives and why not

Alternative Why not
Compute dashboard numbers from raw transactions on every page load Slow, and it gets slower every month as transactions grow.
Plain cron with no lock Two hosts double-run jobs. Duplicate reminder emails.
Plain cron with no job keys A crash halfway means a re-run repeats work or skips it inconsistently.
A full workflow engine Too heavy for a handful of daily and hourly jobs at that stage.

Trade-off

Rollups mean historical charts are up to a day behind. Locks with expiry need the expiry set longer than the job's normal runtime, or a slow run could lose its lock while still working.

Questions they will ask

"How did you stop a cron job from running twice?" Two layers. A short-lived lock in Redis, or a database advisory lock, so only one host runs the job at a time, with an expiry so a crashed host doesn't block it forever. Then an idempotent key per unit of work, like one key per user, class and reminder type, so a re-run after a crash skips what was already done. For example, if the reminder job died after 1,200 of 2,000 emails, the re-run only sent the remaining 800.

"Did your dashboard really increase sales by 30%?" The business team attributed a 30% rise in course sales to the influencer dashboard. I owned building it: tracking transactions and coupon conversions, near-real-time counters in Redis and daily rollups for history. The causal link is their analysis, and the likely mechanism is that influencers who can see what converts promote more and better.

"What made it 'asynchronous'?" None of this work ran inside a user's request. Video handoffs, reminders and cleanup ran as scheduled background jobs, so users never waited on them and a slow job never slowed the site.

8. Tech used in this project and why

Tech What it is in one line Why here Alternative considered
Python General-purpose language Team language. Django ecosystem PHP (the legacy)
Django + DRF Batteries-included web framework plus REST toolkit ORM, admin, auth, migrations, serializers. Fast feature delivery for a content product Staying on PHP, Flask (more assembly needed)
MySQL Relational database Source of truth. Unique constraints and transactions for votes, subscriptions and earnings MongoDB for everything
MongoDB Document database Doubt bodies and content with varying shape MySQL JSON columns
Redis In-memory key-value store Vote counters, unread badges, contest hot keys, dashboard "today" counters, job locks Updating MySQL counters on every event
Elasticsearch Full-text search engine Search over doubts and content with relevance SQL LIKE

Tech line on the PDF: Python, Django, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch. Celery is not on the GFG line, so don't describe the scheduled jobs as Celery here.

Why Django here but Spring Boot later at Masters India? In 2021 this was a content and community product, where Django's admin, auth and ORM saved a lot of time. At Masters India the core problem was a set of long-running enterprise microservices making many calls to a slow government API. Spring Boot fit that job: mature transactions and connection pooling, Kafka integration, and a non-blocking HTTP client so threads don't sit waiting on the portal. Different job, different tool.

9. Hard problems and failure stories

GeeksforGeeks was early career, and my notes describe these as design problems the system was built around, not dated incidents. Tell them that way.

Problem 1: hot rows on popular doubts

  • What hurt: during contests a popular doubt got many votes in minutes. Updating one counter row per vote made those writes queue on a single row lock.
  • How it was seen: vote and doubt pages slowed down during contests.
  • Fix: a vote row per user and content with a unique constraint, a Redis counter for display, and a periodic reconcile from MySQL.
  • What I learned: separate "what is true" (MySQL rows) from "what is fast to show" (Redis), and always have a job that brings them back in line.

Problem 2: counter drift

  • What can go wrong: Redis restarts, an increment is lost, or a bug double-applies a change. The displayed count drifts from reality.
  • Fix: the reconcile job recomputes SUM(value) from the vote rows and overwrites Redis and the stored count.
  • What I learned: a cache you can't rebuild from the source of truth is a liability.

Problem 3: jobs that double-run or half-run

  • What can go wrong: cron on two hosts sends duplicate reminders. A crash midway leaves cleanup half-done.
  • Fix: a lock with expiry so only one host runs a job, an idempotent key per unit of work, and structured success and failure logs.
  • What I learned: every scheduled job should be safe to run twice. I carried this straight into the idempotency design at Masters India.

What I would do differently today

  • Votes as events. Write each vote as an event to a queue and update counters from that stream. Totals become rebuildable by replay, and the reconcile job becomes a check instead of a fix. I learned this pattern later with Kafka at Masters India.
  • Idempotency by default. Give every scheduled job and every reminder an idempotent key from day one, through a shared helper, not as something remembered per job.
  • Contest-day targets. Agree explicit latency targets for contest windows and alert on them, instead of finding out from user complaints.
  • Fewer stores if possible. Re-check whether MongoDB's role could live in MySQL JSON columns, to run one less system.

10. Say this / don't say this

Say this

  • "10K+ daily queries, with roughly 10 times that during live coding contests. That's well under one request per second on average, so the problem was bursts and fragility, not raw scale."
  • "A 20% lift in premium subscriptions, relative, attributed by the growth team. I owned the APIs."
  • "The business team credited the influencer dashboard with a 30% rise in course sales."
  • "Automated video handoffs, reminders and cleanup cut manual ops effort on those workflows by about 70%."
  • "Unique constraint for correctness, Redis for speed, reconcile for truth."

Don't say this

  • "100K daily queries" or "1K daily queries" (older resume figures). Use 10K+.
  • "15 to 20% premium lift" (older prep). The current PDF says 20%.
  • "I increased sales by 30%" as if engineering alone caused it.
  • Celery, Kafka, FastAPI or Spring Boot at GeeksforGeeks. They are not on this role's tech line.
  • Comparing GFG load to Uber or Impact Analytics scale.
  • "SMTP email sends 50% faster" as a resume claim. That was on an older resume and is not on the current PDF. If an interviewer brings it up, explain it as connection reuse (keep one SMTP connection open across a batch instead of a new TCP and TLS handshake per email), framed as an older detail.
  • Unread-count badges as a resume bullet. It's a prep design question (Redis counters with a durable MySQL row), not a PDF bullet.

11. Practice drill

  1. What was the doubt-support platform? The Q&A layer on GeeksforGeeks courses and articles. Learners post doubts, others reply, good answers are upvoted, and moderators can pin or lock threads.

  2. Why migrate from PHP to Django? The PHP backend was fragile under contest bursts. It lacked clean transactions and request validation and was hard to change safely. Django and DRF gave us transactions, serializers for validation, an ORM with migrations, and faster feature work. We migrated page by page behind the same URLs.

  3. What does 10K+ daily queries mean in requests per second? 10,000 divided by 86,400 is about 0.12 per second, so well under one. Contest spikes were about 10 times normal and bunched into short windows, so the challenge was bursts.

  4. How is a vote idempotent? A unique constraint on user ID and content ID means one vote row per user per doubt. The API upserts that row, so a repeat with the same value changes nothing and a changed vote just updates the value.

  5. What's a hot row and how did you avoid it? A single row many requests update at once, so they queue on its lock. We wrote each vote to its own row and kept the shared total in Redis with atomic increments, then reconciled to MySQL periodically.

  6. What if Redis and MySQL disagree? MySQL wins. The reconcile job sums the vote rows and overwrites the Redis value and the stored count. A few minutes of staleness on a vote badge is acceptable.

  7. What's the difference between pinning and locking? Pinning puts a thread at the top of its course or article, in a set order. Locking stops new replies on a thread. Both are moderator-only actions behind permission checks.

  8. Why MongoDB and Elasticsearch as well as MySQL? MongoDB held content whose shape varied, like doubt bodies with code or attachments. Elasticsearch gave fast full-text search with relevance ranking, which SQL LIKE can't do well. MySQL stayed the source of truth.

  9. What did the influencer dashboard show? Each influencer's transactions, coupon conversions and earnings. Redis counters gave a near-real-time "today" view, and daily rollups fed the history charts.

  10. How do you talk about the 30% and 20% numbers? As business results attributed by the business and growth teams. The 20% is a relative lift in premium subscriptions. I owned the engineering and I don't claim the causal analysis.

  11. How did you make scheduled jobs safe? A lock with expiry so only one host runs a job at a time, and an idempotent key per unit of work so a re-run skips finished work. Plus success and failure logs and retries for partial batches.

  12. Why Django here and Spring Boot at Masters India? Django suited a content product that needed admin, auth and ORM quickly. Spring Boot suited Masters India's long-running enterprise microservices, with mature transactions, connection pooling and Kafka integration around calls to a slow government API.

  13. What would you do differently today? I'd put vote events on a queue and build counters from that event stream, so totals are rebuildable by replay rather than by a periodic sum. I'd make idempotent job keys the default for every scheduled job instead of adding them job by job. And I'd set clear latency targets for contest days and alert on them. The Django migration and the vote model were the right call for 2021.

12. 3-minute whiteboard script

First (about 45 seconds): the product and the problem. Draw "Learners" pointing to "Doubt pages". Write "10K+ a day, 10x in contests" beside it. Say: "At GeeksforGeeks, learners post doubts on courses and articles. The backend was legacy PHP. It was fragile under contest spikes of about ten times normal. The daily average is well under one request per second, so the problem was bursts and correctness, not raw scale. I migrated it to Django page by page behind the same URLs."

Second (about 75 seconds): the vote design. Draw "Django API" with arrows to "MySQL", "Redis", "MongoDB" and "Elasticsearch". Under MySQL write votes UNIQUE(user_id, content_id). Under Redis write votes:123 INCRBY. Draw a "Reconcile" box with arrows from MySQL to Redis. Say: "Each vote is its own row with a unique constraint on user and content, so double clicks are idempotent and there's no single hot row. The display total is a Redis counter. A reconcile job sums the real votes and corrects Redis, so MySQL stays the truth. Pinning and locking follow the same pattern: constraint-backed rows behind moderator permissions. MongoDB holds content with varying shapes and Elasticsearch powers search. The growth team tied these features to a 20% relative lift in premium subscriptions."

Third (about 45 seconds): dashboard and jobs. Draw "Influencer dashboard" reading from "Redis today counters" and "Daily rollups". Separately draw "Scheduled jobs" with "lock + job key" written on the arrow to "Video, reminders, cleanup". Say: "I built an influencer dashboard for transactions, coupon conversions and earnings, which the business credited with 30% more course sales. And I built scheduled jobs for video processing, reminders and cleanup, each with a lock so only one host runs it and an idempotent key so re-runs are safe. That cut manual ops effort by about 70%."

Close (about 15 seconds): the lesson. Say: "This is where I learned constraints for idempotency, hot counters off the database, and safe re-runs. I used all three at a much bigger scale at Masters India."

Tech Glossary: every technology on my resume, explained

How to use this page

  • It covers every technology on the Java + Python + Go resume (Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf, Final Java + AI (IA = Py/Go)): the Skills line plus each project's Tech line.
  • Read it the week before interviews, and again the night before a round that names a specific tool in the job description.
  • Memorise three things per entry: the one-line definition, where I used it (or that it is skills-level), and one "why this and not the alternative" sentence.
  • The project stories live in the chapters. This page explains the tools. Jump to IA core platform, IA agentic AI, Uber FRM, Uber Menu and ANZ, Masters India, GeeksforGeeks and numbers explained for the full stories.

How to read the labels

Every entry has a depth label. It tells you how strongly you may claim the technology.

  • Production means the technology appears in a resume bullet or a project Tech line, and I did real work with it in a shipped system. You can go deep.
  • Project means it is on a project Tech line and I used it there, but no bullet is about it. Speak about it confidently but keep claims qualitative. Do not invent numbers.
  • Skills-level means it is on the Skills line as literacy. I can explain how it works and when I would pick it. I do not claim production ownership. If asked "did you run this in production?", the honest answer is "No, here is what I know and where I would use it."

Numbers also carry tags in the project chapters. MEASURED means there is a log, doc or code behind it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal ("targeting"). On this page I only repeat numbers that are already on the resume or in the locked facts.

Code snippets on this page are teaching sketches. They show how the technology works in general. They are not copies of company code. When you speak, describe what we built in words, and use the snippet only to show you understand the mechanism.

1. Languages

Java

Depth: Production. Uber FRM (via EPAM) and Masters India.

What it is. Java is a statically typed, object-oriented language. You compile it to bytecode, and the JVM (Java Virtual Machine) runs that bytecode on any machine. It is the default language for large business backends because the ecosystem (Spring, Hibernate, Kafka clients, monitoring agents) is mature and well tested. Think of a heavy-duty commercial kitchen: it takes a moment to fire up, but once running it serves a huge crowd reliably all day.

How it works (what interviewers probe). - The JVM and JIT. The JVM first interprets bytecode, then the JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler turns hot methods into fast machine code while the app runs. That is why a Java service gets faster after warm-up. - Heap and garbage collection (GC). Objects live on the heap. The garbage collector frees objects nobody references. Most collectors are generational: new objects start in the young generation, most die young and are cleaned cheaply, and survivors move to the old generation. G1 is the default collector in modern Java. ZGC and Shenandoah aim for very short pauses on big heaps. - Threads. A classic Java thread maps to one operating-system thread, which costs memory and context switches. Servlet-based Spring services use one thread per request, so a pool of threads bounds how many requests run at once. - Virtual threads (Java 21). Very light threads managed by the JVM. Blocking code (a JDBC call, an HTTP call) parks the virtual thread instead of holding an OS thread, so you can have many thousands. Same blocking style, much cheaper waiting. - Concurrency tools. ExecutorService pools, CompletableFuture for async composition, and java.util.concurrent locks and atomics. Bounded pools are how you protect a slow downstream system.

// Illustrative sizes. A bounded pool caps calls to a slow external portal.
ExecutorService irpPool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        16, 16, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000),               // bounded queue, no unbounded growth
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());    // back-pressure when full

Future<IrpResponse> f = irpPool.submit(() -> irpClient.register(invoice));
IrpResponse resp = f.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);        // hard timeout per call

// Java 21 virtual threads: one cheap thread per task, same blocking code.
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    exec.submit(() -> irpClient.register(invoice));
}

Where I used it. - Uber FRM (via EPAM): the scoping backend. 36 Spring Boot endpoints on Spring Data JPA, Hibernate and MySQL, tested with JUnit and built with Bazel. - Masters India: the Spring Boot microservices that replaced the PHP monolith, including the Kafka consumers of the bulk e-invoicing pipeline on PostgreSQL.

Why it was chosen there. On FRM, Spring Boot services were the team's standard, and finance logic benefits from strong typing and a mature ORM. At Masters, a long-lived migration off PHP needed a stable, typed platform with first-class Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis and New Relic support.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. Go for a high-traffic edge or a raw-throughput tool, which is why the IA HTTP platform and the ClickHouse data pump are in Go. Python when the work is AI orchestration, because the model and agent libraries are Python-first. Kotlin if a JVM team wants less boilerplate.

Likely interview questions. - "How does garbage collection work in Java?" Objects are allocated on the heap, and the collector frees anything no longer reachable from live references. Modern collectors are generational because most objects die young, so cleaning the young generation is cheap and frequent. G1 is the default and balances throughput with pause targets. If pauses hurt on a large heap I would look at ZGC. I tune from GC logs, not by guessing. - "Platform threads or virtual threads?" Platform threads are OS threads, so you keep them in bounded pools. Virtual threads are cheap JVM-managed threads that park while blocked, which suits services that mostly wait on databases and HTTP calls. They do not make CPU-heavy work faster, and you still need limits on the downstream system, such as the connection pool size. I know them well conceptually and do not claim them on my past projects. - "Why Java for FRM and Masters, but Go and Python at Impact Analytics?" Each service uses what fits its job. FRM and Masters are transactional business services with heavy ORM and messaging work, which is Spring's home ground. The IA edge is plumbing at 10k peak RPS, so Go. The IA agent plane needs LangGraph and model SDKs, so Python. - "How do you find a memory leak in a Java service?" Watch heap usage after full GCs. If the floor keeps rising, take a heap dump and look at what holds the most retained memory. The usual suspects are unbounded caches, static collections, ThreadLocal values in pooled threads and unclosed resources.

Numbers tied to it. None on its own. The Java projects carry the numbers: from 14 days to 3 days reconciliation on FRM, and from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds p95 at Masters.

Python

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics agent plane, Uber Menu and GeeksforGeeks.

What it is. Python is a general-purpose programming language known for readable code and a huge library ecosystem. It is the default language for AI work because almost every model provider and AI framework ships a Python library first. Think of it as a well-stocked kitchen: not the fastest stove, but every ingredient and tool is already on the shelf.

How it works (what interviewers probe). - The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock). Only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time inside one process. That hurts CPU-heavy work but barely matters for I/O-heavy work like calling APIs or databases, because threads release the lock while they wait. For CPU-heavy work you use multiple processes. - asyncio lets one thread juggle thousands of waiting network calls (see asyncio). - Type hints do nothing at runtime by themselves, but tools like Pydantic and FastAPI read them to validate data. - Packaging and environments (virtualenv, pip, lock files) keep dependencies reproducible.

# I/O-bound work: threads or asyncio are fine despite the GIL.
# CPU-bound work: use processes.
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def score(article):            # pure CPU math
    return article["sell_through"] * 0.5 + article["rate_of_sale"] * 0.5

with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    scores = list(pool.map(score, articles))

Where I used it. - Impact Analytics (AssortSmart): the agent plane. Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style batch scoring, and the Ask Iris copilot (FastAPI plus LangGraph). - Uber Eats Menu (via EPAM): the Selenium fleet and the LangChain RAG extraction pipeline. - GeeksforGeeks: the Django backend.

Why it was chosen there. On the AI side, the LLM and agent libraries are Python-first, so fighting that would cost time. Menu extraction lives on LangChain, Gemini and Selenium, which are all strongest in Python. GeeksforGeeks was already a Python shop, and Django was the fastest way off PHP.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. I pick Go when the job is a high-traffic edge or a raw-throughput tool, which is exactly why the IA HTTP platform and the ClickHouse data pump are in Go. I pick Java and Spring Boot for transactional business services with heavy ORM and messaging work, which is what FRM and Masters were.

Likely interview questions. - "Does the GIL make Python bad for backends?" Not for most backends. Most backend time is spent waiting on databases and other services, and threads or asyncio release the GIL while waiting. When I have truly CPU-heavy work I move it to processes or to a compiled language. At Impact Analytics we did both: Python for the agent plane, Go for the high-RPS edge. - "When would you move a Python path to Go?" When the path is hot, latency-sensitive and mostly plumbing, not AI logic. Our 10k peak RPS edge is Go. The LLM orchestration stays in Python because that is where the libraries are.

Numbers tied to it. None on its own. The Python projects carry the numbers (for example from 24 hours to 2 hours onboarding on Menu, 348k article-seasons scored at Impact Analytics, 10K+ daily queries at GeeksforGeeks).

Go

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics.

What it is. Go (also called Golang) is a compiled, statically typed language from Google. It produces a single binary, starts fast, and makes running thousands of tasks at once cheap. Think of it as a lean delivery van: small, quick to start, and able to carry many parcels at the same time.

How it works. - Goroutines are very light threads managed by the Go runtime. You can start tens of thousands of them. - Channels pass data safely between goroutines, so you share memory by communicating. - context.Context carries deadlines and cancellation through every call. This is how "nested timeouts" work: a request deadline is passed down, and each database call gets an even shorter one. - Static binary and garbage collector. Easy to ship in a small container, with predictable latency for most web workloads. - Interfaces are implicit. A type satisfies an interface just by having the methods, which keeps code testable.

// Double buffering: read the next batch while the previous one is being sent.
batches := make(chan [][]any, 1)   // buffer of one = one batch in flight

go func() {                        // reader goroutine
    for b := readNext(500_000); b != nil; b = readNext(500_000) {
        batches <- b               // blocks only if the sender is still busy
    }
    close(batches)
}()

for b := range batches {           // sender loop
    send(ctx, b)                   // INSERT into target cluster
}

Where I used it. All at Impact Analytics: - C1: the multi-tenant Go/Gin platform at 10k peak RPS, with Google Wire, native h2c, nested timeouts and Datadog tracing. - C2: the KPI formula tokenizer and parser that turns operator-written formulas into parameterized ClickHouse SQL. - C5: the custom Go native-TLS data pump that copied ClickHouse rollups between Cloud clusters at about 344k rows per second, in 500k-row double-buffered batches.

Why it was chosen there. The platform edge needs predictable latency under load and cheap concurrency. The data pump needs tight control over memory and buffers. Both are Go's sweet spot.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. Python FastAPI when the work is AI orchestration (that is our agent plane). Java and Spring Boot for ORM-heavy transactional business services, as on FRM and Masters. Rust only if I needed zero garbage-collection pauses, which we did not.

Likely interview questions. - "Why Go for the edge and Python for the agents?" Each language does what it is best at. The edge is plumbing at 10k peak RPS, so I want goroutines and predictable latency. The agent plane needs LangGraph and the model SDKs, which are Python-first. Business rules and authorization stay in one place so the two do not diverge. - "How did you get about 344k rows per second in Go?" Two season streams ran in parallel, each about 150k to 190k rows per second. Each used 500k-row columnar batches and double buffering, so reading the next batch overlapped with sending the previous one. It is ingest rate, not requests per second. - "How do you avoid goroutine leaks?" Every goroutine gets a context it listens to, and every channel has a clear owner who closes it. I also bound concurrency with worker pools instead of starting one goroutine per item.

Numbers tied to it. 10k peak RPS (C1). About 344k rows per second combined, 500k-row batches, partitions up to 4.09B rows (C5). Say "344 thousand rows per second", never "344k RPS".

SQL

Depth: Production. Every project.

What it is. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language you use to ask databases questions and change data. You describe what you want, and the database figures out how to get it. Think of it as ordering at a restaurant: you name the dish, the kitchen decides the steps.

How it works. - Joins combine tables on a key. Duplicate column names across joined tables are a classic trap. - Indexes let the database jump to rows instead of scanning everything. EXPLAIN shows whether an index is used. - Transactions group several changes so they all happen or none happen (atomicity). - GROUP BY and aggregations summarise data. In analytical databases, aggregations are where memory blows up. - Parameterized queries keep user input separate from SQL text, which blocks SQL injection.

-- The FRM column-aliasing trap, and the fix.
-- Bad: both tables have "uuid", the driver may map the wrong one.
SELECT * FROM balance_sheet bs JOIN level_mapping lm ON bs.level_id = lm.uuid;

-- Good: explicit, labelled columns.
SELECT bs.uuid AS line_uuid, lm.uuid AS level_uuid, bs.amount
FROM balance_sheet bs JOIN level_mapping lm ON bs.level_id = lm.uuid;

Where I used it. - Uber FRM: MySQL schema, reporting SQL allowlists, and the column-aliasing bug fix (duplicate column names in joined raw SQL silently mapped rows to the wrong uuid). - Impact Analytics: ClickHouse SQL for six rollup tables, temporal-chunked INSERT SELECT, and the formula parser that emits parameterized SQL fragments. - Masters India: PostgreSQL query and index fixes that were part of the p95 latency win. - GeeksforGeeks: MySQL for users, votes and subscriptions.

Why it matters. Every one of my performance stories ends up in SQL: an index, a rollup, a smaller GROUP BY, or a labelled join.

Alternatives. None really. Even NoSQL and stream tools now offer SQL-like layers. The real choice is which engine runs your SQL.

Likely interview questions. - "Tell me about a SQL bug you fixed." On FRM, joined raw SQL had duplicate column names, so rows were silently mapped to the wrong uuid. Nothing crashed, the numbers were just wrong. We fixed it with aliased selects and explicit labels, and the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration removed that class of bug, because results map to typed entities and DTO projections by name. - "How do you find a slow query?" I run EXPLAIN, check whether the expected index is used, and check how many rows are read versus returned. If an analytical query must scan huge data on every request, I pre-aggregate instead, which is what the ClickHouse rollups do.

Numbers tied to it. 19M raw GL rows migrated off Sheets (FRM). From 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250M-row harness (IA).

C and C++

Depth: Skills-level. Literacy, no production ownership claim.

What it is. C is a low-level language that gives you direct control over memory. C++ adds classes, templates and a large standard library on top. They are what operating systems, databases and game engines are written in. ClickHouse, for example, is written in C++. Think of them as driving a manual car: more control, and more ways to stall.

How it works. - Manual memory. In C you malloc and free yourself. Forgetting free leaks memory. Freeing twice crashes. - Pointers hold memory addresses. Bugs here cause crashes and security holes. - RAII in C++. Objects clean up their resources in their destructor, and smart pointers (std::unique_ptr) automate freeing. - Undefined behaviour. Some mistakes, like reading past an array, have no defined result. The program may seem fine and then fail later.

#include <memory>
#include <vector>
std::unique_ptr<std::vector<int>> v = std::make_unique<std::vector<int>>(1000);
// No delete needed. Memory is freed when v goes out of scope (RAII).

Where I used it. Skills-level only. I list them for systems literacy and data-structures work. I do not claim production C or C++ services.

Why it is on the resume. It signals I understand what Java, Go and Python hide from me: stack versus heap, memory layout, and why garbage collection costs something.

Alternatives. For new systems work I would pick Go (simpler, garbage collected) or Rust (memory safety without garbage collection).

Likely interview questions. - "Have you written production C++?" No. I list C and C++ as systems literacy. My production work is Java, Python and Go. I understand manual memory, pointers and RAII, which helps me reason about things like ClickHouse memory limits. - "Go garbage collection versus C++ manual memory?" Go trades a small, mostly predictable pause cost for safety and speed of development. C++ gives full control, but every allocation is your responsibility.

Numbers tied to it. None.

2. Backend and APIs

The first seven entries are the Java stack of Uber FRM and Masters India. The rest are the Python and Go stack of Impact Analytics, Uber Menu and GeeksforGeeks.

Spring Boot

Depth: Production. Uber FRM F1 and Masters India MI1.

What it is. Spring Boot is a Java framework for building production-ready services quickly. It sits on top of the Spring Framework and makes sensible choices for you: an embedded web server, JSON handling, database connection pooling, health checks and configuration. You add a "starter" dependency and it wires the pieces together. Think of a fully fitted restaurant you can lease: kitchen, tables and fire safety are already installed, and you only bring the menu.

How it works (what interviewers probe). - IoC (Inversion of Control) container and dependency injection. Spring creates your objects ("beans") and hands each one the beans it needs, usually through the constructor. You mark classes with @Service, @Repository or @RestController, or declare them with @Bean. - Auto-configuration and starters. spring-boot-starter-web pulls in Spring MVC, an embedded Tomcat server and Jackson for JSON. Auto-configuration classes switch on only when the right library is on the classpath, and any bean you define yourself wins over the default. - Embedded server, fat jar. The service ships as one jar and starts with java -jar app.jar, which fits Docker images well. - Externalized config and profiles. application.yml, environment variables and @ConfigurationProperties keep settings out of code. Profiles switch config per environment. - Actuator. Built-in health, readiness and metrics endpoints for load balancers and monitoring. - The classic trap. @Transactional and @Async work through proxies. A call from one method to another inside the same class skips the proxy, so the annotation silently does nothing.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/v1/scoping/lines")
public class ScopingLineController {

    private final ScopingService service;               // controller -> service -> repository

    public ScopingLineController(ScopingService service) {
        this.service = service;                          // constructor injection
    }

    @GetMapping("/{lineId}")
    public ScopingLineDto get(@PathVariable String lineId) {
        return service.get(lineId);
    }

    @PatchMapping("/{lineId}/status")
    public ScopingLineDto updateStatus(@PathVariable String lineId,
                                       @Valid @RequestBody StatusUpdate body) {
        return service.updateStatus(lineId, body);       // version checked inside, see Hibernate
    }
}

public record StatusUpdate(@NotNull ReviewStatus status,  // Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed
                           @NotNull Long version) {}      // for optimistic locking

Where I used it. - Uber FRM F1: 36 Spring Boot endpoints automating custom financial math and the nested 4-level FSLI (Financial Statement Line Item) hierarchy, L1 to L4, with dynamic quarter-annualization. The service is layered as controller, service and repository on Spring Data JPA, Hibernate and MySQL on Uber's SOADB. If asked for the split: about 31 functional routes in the scoping service plus the collaboration-service APIs (comments and notifications) from the technical design doc make 36. - Masters India MI1: I led the migration of a legacy PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices using the strangler pattern with a canary per route, and mentored 2 engineers through it. p95 latency went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds across 1,500+ enterprise clients, and throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute.

Why it was chosen there. Finance (FRM) and tax (Masters) data both need typed contracts, real transactions and a mature ORM, which is exactly what the Spring stack gives. At Masters it also had first-class clients for Kafka, PostgreSQL and Redis, and a New Relic Java agent, so the new services were observable from day one.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. Quarkus or Micronaut when startup time and memory matter a lot, for example in serverless functions. Go Gin for a high-RPS edge, which is what the IA platform uses. FastAPI for AI orchestration, which is the IA agent plane. Django when I want an admin panel and the full product toolkit, which is what GeeksforGeeks used.

Likely interview questions. - "How did Spring Boot help bring p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds?" The framework alone did not do it. The biggest win was taking slow government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal) calls off the request thread, using a non-blocking WebClient and Kafka-backed async jobs. Connection pooling with HikariCP, query and index fixes, and Redis for hot reads did the rest. Spring Boot made each of those a configuration choice instead of custom plumbing. - "How do you migrate a PHP monolith without a big bang?" With the strangler pattern. A routing layer sits in front of both systems. We moved one route at a time to Spring Boot, sent a small canary share of traffic to the new route, compared results and errors, then switched fully and retired the PHP route. Rollback was just a routing change. - "How does auto-configuration work?" Spring Boot ships configuration classes guarded by conditions such as "this class is on the classpath" and "no bean of this type exists yet". Adding the Postgres driver and the JPA starter is enough to get a DataSource, a connection pool and an EntityManager. If I define my own bean, the default backs off. - "What is the most common Spring Boot mistake?" Self-invocation. Calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class bypasses the proxy, so there is no transaction. A close second is leaving spring.jpa.open-in-view on, which lets lazy loading fire queries while the response is being written and hides N+1 problems.

Numbers tied to it. 36 endpoints (FRM). From 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds p95 (a 75% cut) across 1,500+ enterprise clients, and from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute (about 12 to about 67 requests per second) at Masters. Mentored 2 engineers at Masters. Do not merge that with "led 3 engineers", which is FRM.

Spring MVC

Depth: On the Skills line. It is the web layer inside the Spring Boot services on FRM and Masters. No bullet is about it on its own.

What it is. Spring MVC is Spring's web framework. It turns HTTP requests into calls on your controller methods and turns the return values back into HTTP responses, usually JSON. Spring Boot uses it whenever you add the web starter. Think of a hotel front desk: every guest walks up to the same desk, and the desk sends each one to the right room.

How it works. - Front controller. One DispatcherServlet receives every request. A handler mapping finds the controller method for the URL and HTTP verb. - Argument binding. @PathVariable, @RequestParam and @RequestBody fill method parameters. Jackson converts JSON to Java objects and back. - Bean Validation. Put @Valid on the request body and constraints like @NotNull, @Size or @Pattern on the DTO (Data Transfer Object) fields. Bad input becomes a 400 response before your code runs. - Central error handling. A @RestControllerAdvice class maps exceptions to status codes in one place. - Thread per request. On the default servlet stack, each request holds one server thread from Tomcat's pool until it finishes. Blocking calls are fine, but they hold that thread while they wait.

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiErrors {

    // A stale @Version on update becomes a clean 409 instead of a 500.
    @ExceptionHandler(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
    public ProblemDetail conflict(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
                "Someone else changed this line. Reload and try again.");
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Invalid request body");
    }
}

Where I used it. Inside every Spring Boot service I built. The 36 FRM endpoints and the Masters routes are Spring MVC controllers, with Bean Validation on request DTOs and central error mapping. I present it as part of the Spring Boot work, not as a separate achievement.

Why it was chosen there. The blocking, thread-per-request model is simple to reason about and matches JDBC and Hibernate, which are blocking too.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. Spring WebFlux, the reactive and non-blocking stack, when a service holds a very large number of slow concurrent connections and its whole call chain is non-blocking. With JDBC and JPA underneath, WebFlux gains little. Java 21 virtual threads give much of the same benefit while keeping plain MVC code.

Likely interview questions. - "Walk me through a request in Spring MVC." Tomcat accepts the connection and hands it to the DispatcherServlet. Filters run first, for example security. The handler mapping picks the controller method, arguments are bound and validated, the method runs, and Jackson writes the return value as JSON. Any exception goes to the @RestControllerAdvice, which turns it into the right status code. - "Spring MVC or WebFlux?" MVC by default, because it is simpler to write, debug and trace. WebFlux only when the service is mostly waiting on many slow streams and every dependency is non-blocking. Mixing a blocking JDBC call into WebFlux defeats the point. - "Where do you validate input?" At the edge, on the DTO with Bean Validation, so bad data never reaches the service layer. Business rules that need the database, like "this line is already Closed", live in the service and return a 409 or 422.

Numbers tied to it. None on its own. It carries the 36 FRM endpoints and the Masters routes.

Spring Security

Depth: Skills-level. On the Skills line. No resume bullet names it.

What it is. Spring Security is the standard framework for authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what are you allowed to do?) in Spring applications. It runs as a chain of filters in front of your controllers. Think of an office building: a security desk at the entrance checks your badge, and badge readers on each floor decide which doors open for you.

How it works. - SecurityFilterChain. An ordered list of servlet filters: CORS, CSRF, authentication, exception translation and authorization. Order matters. - SecurityContext. After authentication, the current user and their roles live in a per-request context that the rest of the code can read. - Two levels of rules. URL rules with authorizeHttpRequests, and method rules with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('REVIEWER')"). - JWT resource server. oauth2ResourceServer().jwt() verifies the token signature against the issuer's public keys (JWKS), and checks expiry and issuer. - Stateless APIs. Token-based APIs set the session policy to stateless and usually turn CSRF protection off, because CSRF attacks target cookie-based sessions.
