LangSmith tells me which step in the Ask Iris graph gave a bad answer and why. - "Why not LangSmith for Keep/Drop?" Keep/Drop is a batch job with checkpoint files and per-row config hashes. Custom JSON telemetry tied to each run was simpler and keeps cost and fallback numbers next to the outputs.

Numbers tied to it. None. Do not claim usage numbers for Ask Iris.

Offline Evaluation

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics A5 and Uber Menu M1.

What it is. Offline evaluation means testing a model or pipeline against a fixed set of labelled cases before it reaches users, and scoring it with clear metrics. Think of a mock exam with an answer key: you only let the student sit the real exam if they pass the mock.

How it works. - Golden set. Cases with known correct answers, kept fixed so scores are comparable over time. - Metrics. Accuracy, field fidelity, coverage (how many cases got a complete answer), cost. - Baselines. Compare against the cheapest reasonable rule. If the model cannot beat it, do not ship it. - CI gate. The pipeline fails if the score drops under a threshold. - Limits. Offline is not live. A proxy set may not match every tenant, and leakage (training on test cases) inflates scores.

{ "suite": "keep_drop_proxy", "cases": 300, "gold_min_accuracy": 0.8 }

If accuracy on the 300 cases is under 0.8, the CI job fails and the change cannot be promoted.

Where I used it. - Impact Analytics A5: a 300-case proxy evaluation harness with an 80% accuracy CI gate (a promotion gate). Separately, a gold-200 benchmark compared models: the chosen model was 73% cheaper in live execution cost at 100% coverage (200 out of 200 complete). The deterministic baseline scored 74% on that set (production threshold 0.65). The blended LLM scored about 63%, under the baseline, so we froze the blend weights instead of retuning them. - Uber Menu M1: 98% field fidelity on offline evaluation of extracted menus.

Why it matters. LLM output is non-deterministic, so the only honest way to know if a change helps is to score it on the same cases every time, and to compare it with a free rule.

Alternatives. Online A/B tests (real users, slower and riskier). LLM-as-judge scoring (scales, but needs its own checks). Offline evaluation is the gate. Online monitoring confirms.

Likely interview questions. - "Does 80% mean the system is 80% accurate for all customers?" No. 80% is the CI promotion gate on a 300-case proxy set. A change cannot be promoted unless it clears it. It is not a live accuracy claim for every tenant. - "Where do 73% and 74% come from?" From a separate gold-200 benchmark, not the 300-case file. 73% is the cost reduction of the chosen model at 100% coverage. 74% is the deterministic baseline on that set. - "What did you do when the LLM lost to the baseline?" We froze the blend weights at 0.4 deterministic and 0.6 agent. We do not retune weights on a small proxy set to make a model look better than a free rule.

Numbers tied to it. 300 cases, 80% gate, 73% lower cost at 100% coverage, 74% baseline, about 63% blended (IA). 98% field fidelity (Menu). Never fuse the 300-case gate with the gold-200 numbers.

5. Data and streaming

Two different data stories. Kafka plus Flink is Uber Menu streaming. ClickHouse plus BigQuery is Impact Analytics analytics. Masters India used Kafka without Flink. Never draw Kafka feeding ClickHouse at Impact Analytics.

Apache Kafka

Depth: Production. Uber Menu M2 and Masters India MI2. Never Impact Analytics.

What it is. Kafka is a distributed, durable, append-only log. Producers write events to topics, and consumers read them at their own pace. Events are kept for a retention period, so consumers can re-read from any point. Think of a conveyor belt with numbered trays that keeps every tray for days: any team can read the belt, and anyone can rewind to tray 4,000 and replay.

How it works. - Topics and partitions. A topic is split into partitions for parallelism. Order is guaranteed only within a partition. - Keys. Events with the same key go to the same partition, so per-key order holds (per vendor menu, per taxpayer). - Consumer groups and offsets. Each group tracks how far it has read. Several groups can read the same topic independently. - Retention and replay. Rewind offsets to reprocess after a bug. - Delivery semantics. In practice you get at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent. Poison messages go to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) after bounded retries.

// Masters-style producer: the taxpayer GSTIN is the key, so one taxpayer's events stay in order.
String idemKey = client + ":" + fileHash + ":" + batchIndex;
kafkaTemplate.send("einvoice.bulk", clientGstin, new BulkBatch(idemKey, invoices));
// Consumer: if idemKey is already registered, skip. After bounded retries, send to the DLQ.

The Java client view (KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener, retries and dead-letter topics) is in Spring Kafka. On Uber Menu, the consumer of the topic is the Flink job.

Where I used it. - Uber Menu M2: the ingestion bus after the Selenium fleet, feeding Apache Flink for stateful keyed deduplication (keyed by vendor and menu, using a content hash), schema normalization and exactly-once catalog upserts. - Masters India MI2: the event bus for a high-concurrency bulk e-invoicing pipeline handling 1M+ daily government submissions, with idempotent processing for 100K+ concurrent imports (idempotency key like client plus file hash plus batch index), dead-letter queues and bounded retries against volatile IRP portals. Producers and consumers were Spring Boot services using Spring Kafka. - Masters Kafka and Menu Kafka are different products at different companies.

Why it was chosen there. - Menu: scrapers are bursty and flaky. Kafka lets a scrape succeed even when the catalog or RAG step is slow, gives replay after a bad parser deploy, keeps per-vendor order, and fans out to several consumers. - Masters: filing deadlines create spikes, a 100K-invoice import cannot be one synchronous request, and double-registering an invoice with the government is not reversible. Kafka absorbs spikes and replays safely with idempotency keys.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. RabbitMQ or SQS for simple job dispatch without replay. A job queue, or Spring @Async and scheduled jobs, for one-off background tasks. Kafka when I need a replayable, partitioned, multi-consumer log with per-key order.

Likely interview questions. - "Do you really get exactly-once?" End to end, exactly-once is mostly a slogan. In practice it is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes. On Menu the catalog upsert is keyed, so a replay overwrites the same row. On Masters the idempotency key with a unique constraint stops a second IRP registration. I never claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across third parties. - "Isn't 30K menus a month too small for Kafka?" The average rate is modest, and I agree. Kafka is there for its properties, not raw volume: replay after a bad parser, decoupling flaky scrapers from slow downstream steps, per-vendor order and fan-out. - "Why no Flink at Masters?" Masters did not need stateful windowing or late-event deduplication. Idempotent consumers and PostgreSQL were enough. Menu needed keyed state for duplicate and late pages.

Numbers tied to it. Masters: 1M+ daily submissions, about 12 TPS average (1,000,000 divided by 86,400), peaks ESTIMATED at 8 to 10 times that around filing deadlines, 100K+ concurrent imports. Menu: 30K+ menus per month. A peak of about 200 to 500 events per second on Menu is an ESTIMATE for prep only, do not volunteer it.

Spring Kafka

Depth: Production. Masters India MI2 (the Java client side of the Masters Kafka pipeline).

What it is. Spring for Apache Kafka (usually called Spring Kafka) is Spring's integration with the Kafka Java client. It gives you KafkaTemplate to publish and @KafkaListener to consume, and it handles the consumer loop, offsets, retries and dead-letter routing for you. Think of a post room for a building: you drop a letter in the outgoing tray or name the mailbox you want to watch, and the post room handles the trucks and the sorting.

How it works. - KafkaTemplate.send(topic, key, value) publishes. The key decides the partition, so the same key keeps its order. - @KafkaListener(topics, groupId) turns a method into a consumer in a consumer group. concurrency sets how many consumer threads run, and more threads than partitions just sit idle. - Acknowledgement mode. Offsets are committed after the listener succeeds, so a crash replays the record. Delivery is at least once, which is why the handler must be idempotent. - DefaultErrorHandler retries a failing record with a back-off, then hands it to a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, which writes it to a dead-letter topic (DLT) so one poison message cannot block the partition. - Serializers (JSON or Avro) turn objects into bytes and back.

@Configuration
class KafkaErrorConfig {
    @Bean
    DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<String, Object> template) {
        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);   // -> einvoice.bulk.DLT
        return new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, new FixedBackOff(2000L, 3L)); // bounded retries
    }
}

@Component
class BulkBatchConsumer {
    @KafkaListener(topics = "einvoice.bulk", groupId = "irp-submitter")
    void onBatch(BulkBatch batch) {
        if (registry.alreadyProcessed(batch.idemKey())) {
            return;                                   // replay or duplicate: do nothing
        }
        irpService.submit(batch);                     // may throw, handled by the error handler
        registry.markProcessed(batch.idemKey());      // unique constraint on idemKey
    }
}

Where I used it. Masters India MI2: the Spring Boot producers and consumers on the Kafka event bus of the bulk e-invoicing pipeline. Idempotency keys (client plus file hash plus batch index) with a unique constraint, dead-letter queues and bounded retries against volatile IRP portals. Uber Menu's Kafka consumers are the Flink job, not Spring Kafka.

Why it was chosen there. The services were already Spring Boot, so Spring Kafka gave consumers, retries and DLQ routing as configuration instead of a hand-written poll loop. It also plugged into the same tracing and logging as the rest of the service.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. The plain Kafka Java client when I need full control of the poll loop. Kafka Streams for stateful stream processing inside the JVM. Flink for heavy stateful processing with event time, which is what Uber Menu used.

Likely interview questions. - "How do you build a dead-letter queue in Spring Kafka?" Configure a DefaultErrorHandler with a bounded back-off and a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer. A failing record is retried a few times, then published to a dead-letter topic with the error in its headers, and the consumer moves on. Someone can inspect and replay the DLT later. - "Why must the consumer be idempotent?" Offsets are committed after processing, so a crash or rebalance between "IRP accepted it" and "offset committed" replays the record. The idempotency key with a unique constraint makes that replay a no-op instead of a second government registration. - "How many consumer threads should you run?" At most the number of partitions in the topic for that group, because each partition is read by one consumer at a time. To scale further you add partitions, and you choose keys so load spreads evenly.

Numbers tied to it. 1M+ daily submissions (about 12 per second on average, peaks ESTIMATED at 8 to 10 times that around filing deadlines) and 100K+ concurrent imports, as for Apache Kafka.

Apache Flink

Depth: Production. Uber Menu M2 only.

What it is. Flink is a stream processor. It reads events continuously (here from Kafka), keeps state per key, and processes each event as it arrives instead of waiting for a nightly batch. Think of a sorting clerk standing at the conveyor belt who remembers every tray he has already seen and throws away duplicates.

How it works. - Keyed streams and keyed state. keyBy(vendor_menu_id) sends all events for one key to the same task, which keeps a small memory (for example "last content hash seen") for that key. - Event time and watermarks. Events can arrive late or out of order. A watermark says "I have probably seen everything up to time T", which bounds how long you wait. - Checkpoints. Flink periodically snapshots all state and Kafka offsets together. After a crash it restores and replays from there. - Exactly-once state, idempotent sink. Checkpoints give exactly-once state. The external write (the catalog) must still be idempotent. - State TTL expires old keys so state does not grow forever.

# Pseudocode for keyed deduplication
class DedupeMenu(KeyedProcessFunction):            # keyed by vendor/menu id
    def process_element(self, event, ctx):
        last = self.last_hash.value()               # per-key state
        if last == event.content_hash:
            return                                  # duplicate page, drop it
        self.last_hash.update(event.content_hash)
        yield normalize_to_catalog_schema(event)    # then idempotent upsert

Where I used it. Uber Menu M2 only: a large-scale ingestion and processing pipeline on Kafka and Apache Flink with stateful keyed deduplication (keyed by vendor and menu, content hash), schema normalization and exactly-once catalog upserts. Not at Masters, not at Impact Analytics.

Why it was chosen there. Scrapes are bursty and retried, so the same menu can arrive several times or late. Flink's keyed state drops duplicates, event time handles late pages, and continuous processing kept catalog freshness in hours instead of a day.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. Plain Kafka consumers for stateless transforms. Spark for big historical backfills (verbal only, not on my resume). Kafka Streams if everything stays inside Kafka and in the JVM.

Likely interview questions. - "Why Flink and not plain consumers?" Plain consumers are fine for fire-and-forget transforms. We needed per-vendor state for deduplication, event time for late pages, and one job that validates, deduplicates and normalizes before the upsert. That is Flink's sweet spot. - "Why not Spark?" Spark Structured Streaming works in micro-batches and is heavier for per-key state on a freshness-sensitive path. I would use Spark for large backfills. It is not on my resume. - "A bad parser shipped. How do you recover?" Stop the job, fix the code, rewind Kafka offsets to before the bad deploy and reprocess. Because the catalog upsert is idempotent, replaying overwrites rows instead of duplicating them.

Numbers tied to it. Extraction success 95%+ (from an estimated 60 to 65%), 30K+ menus per month, onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours. No measured Flink throughput is claimed.

ClickHouse

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics A2, C2, C3, C4, C5. My deepest data technology.

What it is. ClickHouse is a columnar OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) database built for fast aggregations over billions of rows. Normal databases store data row by row. ClickHouse stores each column separately, so summing one column reads only that column, and similar values compress very well. Think of a spreadsheet stored by columns: to total the "revenue" column you lift out one strip of paper instead of reading every row.

How it works (the big ideas). - Columnar storage and compression. Queries read only the columns they touch. - The MergeTree family of table engines (explained below). - Partitions for managing data in big chunks. - Mutations are expensive. ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE rewrites data in the background. ClickHouse prefers inserts over in-place updates. - Aggregation memory. A big GROUP BY holds its state in RAM. Without limits and spill-to-disk, it can run out of memory.

MergeTree

What it is. MergeTree is ClickHouse's main table engine. Each insert writes a sorted, immutable chunk called a part. Background merges combine small parts into bigger ones. Think of a stack of sorted index cards: you drop new sorted bundles on top, and an assistant periodically merges bundles into bigger sorted bundles.

  • ORDER BY sets the sort key, which is also the sparse primary index. It stores one index entry per block of rows (a granule, 8,192 rows by default), so it is tiny and lets ClickHouse skip blocks that cannot match.
  • PARTITION BY groups parts by a value, like season.
  • Big batched inserts are good. Many tiny inserts create too many parts.
CREATE TABLE product_season (
    season_code   UInt16,
    product_id    String,
    store_count   UInt32,
    revenue       Float64,
    units_sold    Float64
) ENGINE = MergeTree
PARTITION BY season_code
ORDER BY (product_id);

ReplacingMergeTree

What it is. ReplacingMergeTree is a MergeTree variant that keeps only the newest version of rows with the same sort key. Duplicates are removed during background merges, not at insert time. Think of a notebook where you never erase: you write the new value below the old one, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines.

  • A version column decides which row wins.
  • Until a merge runs, duplicates can still be visible. Correct reads use argMax(value, version), LIMIT 1 BY key, or FINAL (slower).
  • This makes retries safe: writing the same article twice just leaves the newer version.
CREATE TABLE keep_drop_score (
    article_id String, season_code UInt16,
    s_final Float64, decision String, config_hash String,
    version UInt64
) ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(version)
ORDER BY (season_code, article_id);

-- Read the latest decision per article without waiting for merges
SELECT article_id, argMax(decision, version) AS decision
FROM keep_drop_score WHERE season_code = 7 GROUP BY article_id;

Partitions

What they are. A partition is a big, separately managed slice of a table, chosen by PARTITION BY. You can drop, replace or move a whole partition as one operation, and queries that filter on the partition key skip other partitions entirely. Think of a filing cabinet with one drawer per season: you can empty or refill one drawer without touching the others.

  • Partition pruning. WHERE season_code = 7 reads only drawer 7.
  • ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION 7 removes a season instantly. That is how a half-copied season was cleaned before recopying.
  • Keep the count moderate. Too many partitions means too many parts.

Native protocol

What it is. ClickHouse speaks two protocols. HTTP (port 8123, or 8443 with TLS) is easy to use from anything. The native protocol (port 9000, or 9440 with TLS) is a binary, columnar protocol used by ClickHouse's own client and drivers such as clickhouse-go. It is faster for bulk data because blocks of columns travel as-is. Think of shipping goods in sealed pallets instead of unpacking them into individual parcels.

batch, _ := conn.PrepareBatch(ctx, "INSERT INTO attr_weekly")
for _, row := range rows {          // in practice: columnar appends, 500k rows per batch
    batch.Append(row...)
}
batch.Send()                         // one columnar block over native TLS (port 9440)

Where I used it. All at Impact Analytics: - A2: decoupled AI inference from a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master by serving context as JSON payloads instead of letting the LLM query the database. Writes are eventually consistent through ReplacingMergeTree, with graceful fallback to deterministic baselines on LLM timeouts. - C2: the Go formula parser compiles operator-written KPI formulas into parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragments, with division-by-zero protection by wrapping each expression in ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0). - C3: multi-tenant isolation and UAM-scoped hierarchy access across PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. - C4: planner pivots 15.5 times faster, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250M-row harness, through a pre-aggregation layer of six MergeTree rollup tables (product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain, all PARTITION BY season_code). Separately, prevented 170GB out-of-memory crashes on weekly rollup builds by slicing INSERT SELECT into temporal chunks (one fiscal week per insert) with memory and disk-spill caps. - C5: migrated rollups across ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 344k rows per second with a custom Go native-TLS data pump, because cross-cluster IP allowlists blocked cluster-to-cluster copy. Partitions went up to 4.09B rows, with 500k-row double-buffered batches. Ghost rows were prevented with TSV ledgers (the weekly loader's skip file), copier checkpoint files (migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done) and partition rollbacks (DROP PARTITION, then recopy that season).

-- C2: how one operator formula compiles safely
-- operator writes:   sales / units
-- parser emits:      ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(net_sales) / sum(units_sold)), 0)

-- C4: weekly build, one fiscal week per INSERT, with caps (verbal knobs)
INSERT INTO product_weekly
SELECT ... FROM daily_facts
WHERE season_code = 7 AND fiscal_year_week = 202614
GROUP BY ...
SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 55000000000,                    -- about 55 GB cap
         max_bytes_before_external_group_by = 16000000000,  -- spill after about 16 GB
         max_threads = 8;

Why it was chosen there. Planner pivots were slow on PostgreSQL. Proof-of-concept tests compared Postgres and ClickHouse, and ClickHouse won the large analytical reads. Postgres kept the thin metadata, UAM and roles.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. PostgreSQL for transactional data and small analytics. BigQuery for warehouse-scale batch analytics where per-query latency matters less. Apache Druid or Pinot are other real-time OLAP options.

Likely interview questions. - "Why ReplacingMergeTree instead of plain MergeTree?" Retries and overlapping batches can write the same article twice. ReplacingMergeTree keeps the latest version per key in the background, and we read with argMax so results are correct even before merges finish. That gives eventually consistent, retry-safe writes. - "Why did weekly builds run out of memory?" ClickHouse holds aggregation state in RAM. A whole-season weekly GROUP BY needed about 170GB and failed even at 80GB and 200GB caps. I profiled per grain: a product week was about 11GB and an attribute week over 40GB. So the unit of work became one fiscal week, with a 55GB memory cap, 16GB spill, 8 threads and 4 weeks in flight. - "Did fixing the OOM make pivots 15.5 times faster?" No, they are separate. 15.5 times is query time on a 250M-row harness. The 170GB OOM was load time on weekly builds. Not cause and effect. - "Is 344k rows per second requests per second?" No. It is ingest rate over the native protocol: two season streams of about 150k to 190k rows per second each, combined about 344k. The largest object was 4.09B rows, and that copy was measured in flight, not a finished cutover. - "Is the partition rollback an atomic swap?" No. It is DROP PARTITION, then recopy the season. Readers could see a partial season during that time. A REPLACE PARTITION incremental design was written but not executed.

Numbers tied to it. 2.11B-row master (A2). 15.5 times, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds (12.3 rounded) on 250M rows (C4). 170GB OOM (C4). About 344k rows per second, 4.09B rows (2,779,317,472 plus 1,311,108,195), 500k-row batches (C5). Never say sub-second pivots.

BigQuery

Depth: Project. On the Impact Analytics Tech line. No bullet is about it.

What it is. BigQuery is Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse. You load huge tables and run SQL without managing servers. It is columnar like ClickHouse but tuned for big batch analytics, and you usually pay by bytes scanned. Think of a giant public library where you pay per page you read: perfect for deep research, not for flipping through the same page every few seconds.

How it works. - Serverless. Google allocates compute per query. - Columnar storage, so selecting fewer columns costs less. - Partitioned and clustered tables cut how much data a query scans. - Pricing by bytes scanned (on-demand) or by reserved capacity. - Built for batch analytics, not for low-latency, high-frequency interactive queries.

SELECT season_code, SUM(net_sales) AS revenue
FROM `project.retail.daily_sales`
WHERE sale_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-06-30'   -- partition filter cuts cost
GROUP BY season_code;

Where I used it. Impact Analytics: BigQuery is on the Tech line as the company's upstream historical warehouse, which feeds data toward ClickHouse. ClickHouse is where planners and agents read at runtime.

Why it was chosen. It is the company's existing source of historical truth on GCP.

Alternatives. Snowflake or Redshift on other clouds. ClickHouse when you need predictable latency on repeated interactive queries, which is why planner reads moved there.

Likely interview questions. - "Why not serve planners straight from BigQuery?" BigQuery is excellent for warehouse-scale batch analytics, but interactive pivots that run again and again need predictable latency and a cost model that does not charge per scan. Pre-aggregated ClickHouse rollups fit that better. Keep the answer qualitative, there is no BigQuery latency number on the resume.

Numbers tied to it. None.

ETL Pipelines

Depth: Production. Uber FRM, Uber Menu, Masters India, Impact Analytics.

What it is. ETL means Extract, Transform, Load: pull data from a source, clean and reshape it, and write it to a target. ELT is the same idea but you load first and transform inside the target database. Think of a water treatment plant: take water from the river, filter it, and pipe it to homes.

How it works. - Batch or streaming. Nightly or chunked jobs versus continuous processing (Kafka plus Flink). - Idempotent reruns. Running a step twice must give the same result. Natural keys, upserts and "drop partition then reload" achieve that. - Checkpoints and ledgers. Record which chunks finished so a restart skips them. - Data quality checks. Row counts, sums and schema checks between source and target. - Locking and contention. Loads that update shared tables can block users, so schema and transaction design matter.

FRM example
Extract:   raw GL (general ledger) rows that used to live in Google Sheets
Transform: map accounts to the 4-level FSLI hierarchy (L1-L4), annualize by quarter,
           compute significance against materiality
Load:      upsert into MySQL tables keyed by SHA-256 natural keys, in one transaction

Where I used it. - Uber FRM F1 and F2: the Sheets-to-MySQL migration across 19M raw GL rows, and resolving ETL lock contention during financial close with an 8-table normalized schema, optimistic row-locking and atomic cross-table syncs. The HFM (Oracle Hyperion) extract was a shared pipeline responsibility. - Uber Menu M2: the Kafka plus Flink ingestion and processing pipeline. - Masters India MI2: the bulk e-invoicing import pipeline, with chunked, idempotent batches processed by Spring Boot services. - Impact Analytics C4 and C5: rollup builds with temporal-chunked INSERT SELECT, and the cross-cluster copy with ledgers and checkpoints.

Why it matters. My ETL stories are about correctness and restartability, not just speed: no duplicate audit rows, no ghost rows after a crash, no lock fights during close.

Alternatives. Orchestrators like Airflow or Temporal for scheduling and retries. Spring Batch for chunked, restartable jobs inside a Java service. At Impact Analytics we chose application-native checkpoints because resume logic was tied to ClickHouse inserts and config hashing, so extra infrastructure was not justified.

Likely interview questions. - "How do you make an ETL rerun safe?" Every write is keyed so it can be repeated: SHA-256 natural keys on FRM, idempotency keys at Masters, ReplacingMergeTree and partition reloads at Impact Analytics. A ledger records finished chunks, and an unfinished chunk is cleaned and redone, not appended to. - "What was the FRM lock contention?" During financial close, the ETL load and finance users were touching the same data. Normalizing into 8 tables, using optimistic row-locking (a version check on update) and doing cross-table syncs in one transaction removed the contention.

Numbers tied to it. 19M raw GL rows (FRM). From 14 days to 3 days reconciliation (FRM). 1M+ daily submissions (Masters).

6. Databases and storage

PostgreSQL

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics C3 and Masters India MI2.

What it is. PostgreSQL (Postgres) is an open-source relational database known for correctness, rich SQL and extensions. It is the default choice for transactional data, where every change must be safe and consistent. Think of a meticulous accountant's ledger: every entry balanced, nothing half-written.

How it works. - ACID transactions. Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable. A transaction fully happens or not at all. - MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control). Readers see a snapshot and do not block writers. Old row versions are cleaned by VACUUM. - Indexes. B-tree for equality and ranges, GIN for JSONB and full-text, partial indexes for hot subsets. - Partitioning and sharding. Declarative partitioning splits a table by range or list. Sharding spreads data across separate databases or nodes. - Connection pooling. Postgres uses a process per connection, so an application pool like HikariCP, and sometimes a server-side pooler like PgBouncer, protect it under load.

-- Range partitioning by tax quarter (illustrates the idea behind quarter sharding)
CREATE TABLE invoice_header (
  invoice_id text, client_gstin text, invoice_date date, period_quarter text
) PARTITION BY LIST (period_quarter);

CREATE TABLE invoice_header_2024q1 PARTITION OF invoice_header FOR VALUES IN ('2024Q1');
CREATE TABLE invoice_header_2024q2 PARTITION OF invoice_header FOR VALUES IN ('2024Q2');

Where I used it. - Impact Analytics C3: the thin transactional layer for tenant metadata, UAM and roles. Role resolution in the auth waterfall is Postgres-backed. Planner facts moved to ClickHouse after proof-of-concept tests showed Postgres was too slow for large pivots. - Masters India MI2: PostgreSQL horizontally sharded by tax quarter for the bulk e-invoicing pipeline. Routing derives the quarter from the invoice date. The Spring Boot services reached it through Hibernate and a HikariCP connection pool.

Why it was chosen there. Identity, roles and invoices need real ACID guarantees. GST work is quarter-scoped, so sharding by quarter keeps the hot current-quarter writes separate from cold history.

Alternatives. MySQL (similar role, chosen where it is the company standard, as at Uber). ClickHouse for big analytical reads. MongoDB when the document shape varies a lot.

Likely interview questions. - "Why shard by tax quarter?" GST filings are quarter-scoped, so most reads and writes hit the current quarter. Sharding by quarter isolates hot writes, keeps indexes small, and lets old quarters be archived without touching live traffic. The risk is cross-quarter queries, which become fan-out reads. - "Why keep Postgres at Impact Analytics if ClickHouse is faster?" ClickHouse is fast for aggregations but weak at small transactional updates. Users, tenants, roles and access rules need ACID, so Postgres keeps them and ClickHouse holds the facts. - "How does MVCC work?" Each update writes a new row version. Each transaction sees the versions that were committed when its snapshot started. So readers never block writers, and VACUUM later removes versions nobody can see.

Numbers tied to it. 1M+ daily submissions, 100K+ concurrent imports (Masters). From 189 seconds to 12 seconds once pivots moved off Postgres to ClickHouse rollups (IA, a ClickHouse number).

MySQL and Uber SOADB

Depth: Production. Uber FRM F1, F2, F3 and GeeksforGeeks.

What it is. MySQL is a widely used open-source relational database. Its main storage engine, InnoDB, gives transactions, row-level locks and MVCC. SOADB is Uber's service-owned MySQL standard: each service owns its own MySQL database under a common platform. Think of MySQL as a well-organised shared office, and SOADB as each team getting its own office on the same managed floor.

How it works. - InnoDB row locks. Updates lock only the rows they touch, but long transactions still block others. - Optimistic locking. Instead of locking up front, each row carries a version. An update only succeeds if the version is unchanged. Otherwise the user is told someone else edited first. - Unique constraints and natural keys stop duplicates at the database level. - Transactions across tables keep related changes in sync. - Normalization splits data into tables with one job each, so updates touch less and conflict less.

-- Optimistic row-locking: succeed only if nobody changed the row since I read it
UPDATE scoping_assessments
SET status = 'Review', version = version + 1
WHERE uuid = :uuid AND version = :version_i_read;
-- 0 rows updated means conflict: reload and retry, or tell the user.
-- With Hibernate, a @Version field on the entity generates exactly this WHERE clause.

// Deterministic SHA-256 natural key: the same question on the same page always gets the same id
static String naturalKey(String questionText, String pageName) throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
    MessageDigest sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
    byte[] hash = sha.digest((questionText + normalize(pageName)).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    return HexFormat.of().formatHex(hash);
}

Where I used it. - Uber FRM F1: the Sheets-to-MySQL migration across 19M raw GL rows, behind 36 Spring Boot endpoints. - Uber FRM F2: an 8-table normalized MySQL schema on Uber's SOADB with a polymorphic review-status model (one status model reused across screens: Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed), optimistic row-locking (@Version in Hibernate), atomic cross-table syncs (@Transactional) and SHA-256 natural keys to stop duplicates across quarterly audit trails. - Uber FRM F3: the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration on top of it. - GeeksforGeeks: MySQL as the relational store for users, votes and subscriptions, through Django. - Verbal depth for FRM: there are 11 ORM entity models in the scoping service code, while the PDF's "8-table schema" is the normalized design in F2. If asked, say both clearly.

Why it was chosen there. At Uber, SOADB is the standard store for services, so MySQL was the natural system of record once data moved off Sheets. Optimistic locking fits finance review work, where conflicts are rare but must never silently overwrite.

Alternatives. Pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) in JPA) when conflicts are frequent. PostgreSQL in companies where it is the standard. A warehouse alone was rejected, because finance needed transactional edits and an audit trail.

Likely interview questions. - "Optimistic or pessimistic locking?" Optimistic when conflicts are rare and you do not want users holding locks, which fits finance reviewers working on different lines. Pessimistic when many writers fight over the same row. With optimistic locking, a stale update fails cleanly and the user reloads. - "Why SHA-256 natural keys?" So the same logical record always gets the same id, quarter after quarter. A re-import cannot create a duplicate because the key collides with the unique constraint. Example: uuid equals SHA-256 of the question text plus the normalized page name. - "What is a polymorphic review-status model?" One status table and state machine (Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed) reused across all 8 screens, instead of a separate status column with different rules on every screen.

Numbers tied to it. 8 tables, 19M raw GL rows, $340M materiality threshold, reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days (a 70% cut).

Redis

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics C3, Masters India MI3, GeeksforGeeks.

What it is. Redis is an in-memory key-value store. It is extremely fast because data lives in RAM, and it supports rich types like counters, lists, sets and sorted sets, each with an optional expiry (TTL). Think of sticky notes on your monitor: instant to read, but you would not keep your only copy of a contract there.

How it works. - Cache-aside. The app checks Redis first. On a miss it reads the database, then writes the result to Redis with a TTL. - TTL and invalidation. Expire keys after a time, or delete them when the source changes. - Stampede protection. When a hot key expires, thousands of requests can hit the database at once. A short lock or jittered TTL prevents that. - Atomic operations like INCR make counters safe under concurrency. - Not the source of truth. If Redis is lost, the app must still work from the database.

// Masters-style cache-aside in a Spring Boot service (Spring Data Redis).
public ClientConfig getClientConfig(String gstin) {
    String key = "cfg:" + gstin;
    ClientConfig cached = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
    if (cached != null) {
        return cached;
    }
    ClientConfig cfg = configRepo.findByGstin(gstin).orElseThrow();   // miss: source of truth
    redis.opsForValue().set(key, cfg, Duration.ofMinutes(5));          // cache for 5 minutes
    return cfg;
}

Spring's @Cacheable("clientConfig") on the method does the same thing with less code, and @CacheEvict on the update path removes the stale entry.

Where I used it. - Impact Analytics C3: Redis fronts the auth waterfall so verified identities are not re-checked against Firebase or OIDC on every request. A miss falls through to real verification and Postgres. It never fails open. - Masters India MI3: a Redis cache-aside layer in the Spring Boot services that, together with ELK and New Relic work, lowered database read load by 30%. Redis was also part of the p95 latency win. - GeeksforGeeks: caching and hot counters for the doubt-support platform during contest spikes.

Why it was chosen there. The same data (verified tokens, client config) was read on almost every request. Caching it in memory removed repeated database reads.

Alternatives. An in-process cache (fastest, but each server has its own copy). Memcached (simpler, fewer data types). A CDN for public static content.

Likely interview questions. - "How do you handle cache invalidation?" Short TTLs for data that can be slightly stale, and explicit deletes on write for data that cannot. The database stays the source of truth, so a wrong cache entry expires instead of living forever. - "What if Redis goes down?" Requests fall through to the database. Load goes up, but correctness holds. For auth we never treat a Redis failure as permission. - "What is a cache stampede?" A hot key expires and every request misses at once, hammering the database. Fixes are a lock so only one request refills the key, jittered TTLs, or refreshing before expiry.

Numbers tied to it. Database read load cut by 30% (Masters, together with the tracing work in the same bullet).

MongoDB

Depth: Production. Masters India and GeeksforGeeks (both Tech lines, named in the GFG bullet).

What it is. MongoDB is a document database. Each record is a JSON-like document (stored as BSON), and documents in one collection can have different fields. Think of a drawer of folders where each folder can hold a differently shaped form, instead of a spreadsheet where every row must have the same columns.

How it works. - Documents and collections. Nested objects and arrays are first-class. - Flexible schema. No migration needed to add a field, so you must validate shape in code or with schema validation rules. - Indexes on fields you query, including compound and multikey (array) indexes. - Aggregation pipeline for group, filter and reshape steps. - Replica sets for high availability, sharding for scale.

db.irp_responses.insertOne({
  invoice_id: "INV-88231",
  client_gstin: "29ABCDE1234F1Z5",
  irn: "a1b2c3...",
  signed_qr: "...",
  raw_response: { /* shape varies by portal version */ }
})
db.irp_responses.createIndex({ invoice_id: 1 }, { unique: true })

Where I used it. - Masters India: a document store for flexible or semi-structured payloads, such as snapshots of signed IRP responses and job metadata, next to PostgreSQL as the system of record for invoices. If asked for exact collections, only name ones you can draw. - GeeksforGeeks: flexible documents for community and content shapes that did not fit cleanly in MySQL, alongside MySQL as the relational store.

Why it was chosen there. Government portal responses and community content change shape. Forcing them into rigid relational columns would mean a migration for every new field.

Alternatives. PostgreSQL JSONB columns (one database, transactions, good enough for many cases). DynamoDB for a fully managed key-value workload on AWS.

Likely interview questions. - "MongoDB or Postgres JSONB?" JSONB if the data is mostly relational with a few flexible fields, because you keep joins and transactions in one database. MongoDB when the flexible documents are the main workload and you want document-native indexing and scaling. - "How do you keep a schemaless store clean?" Validate in code, add database-level schema validation rules for required fields, and version the document shape.

Numbers tied to it. None directly.

Elasticsearch

Depth: Production. Masters India (as part of ELK) and GeeksforGeeks (search).

What it is. Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It is excellent at full-text search ("find posts that mention binary search trees") and at searching huge volumes of logs. Think of the index at the back of a book: for every word, a list of the pages where it appears.

How it works. - Inverted index. Maps each term to the documents containing it, which makes text search fast. - Analyzers. Tokenize, lowercase and stem text so "Running" matches "run". - Relevance scoring (BM25 by default) ranks results. - Shards and replicas. Indexes are split into shards across nodes, with replicas for availability. - Near-real-time. New documents become searchable after a refresh, usually about a second.

GET /doubts/_search
{
  "query": { "multi_match": { "query": "binary search tree", "fields": ["title^2", "body"] } },
  "size": 20
}

Where I used it. - Masters India MI3: Elasticsearch as the storage and search layer of the ELK stack for centralized, structured logs with correlation IDs. - GeeksforGeeks G1: full-text search and retrieval over doubts and posts, beyond what SQL LIKE can do.

Why it was chosen there. Searching text and logs at scale is what an inverted index is for. SQL LIKE '%term%' cannot use normal indexes and does not rank by relevance.

Alternatives. OpenSearch (the open-source fork). Postgres full-text search for small datasets. Loki or a cloud log service for logs only.

Likely interview questions. - "Why not just SQL LIKE?" A leading-wildcard LIKE scans every row and cannot rank results. Elasticsearch's inverted index finds matching documents directly, handles word forms through analyzers, and ranks by relevance. - "Would you use Elasticsearch as your primary database?" No. It is a search index. The source of truth stays in MySQL or Postgres, and Elasticsearch is rebuilt from it if needed.

Numbers tied to it. Incident triage cut by 70% at Masters (ELK is part of that, see ELK).

DynamoDB

Depth: Skills-level. Literacy, no production ownership claim.

What it is. DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed key-value and document database. You do not manage servers, it scales almost without limit, and you pay for reads and writes. The price is that you must design around your access patterns up front. Think of a giant coat-check: hand over the ticket number and you get the coat instantly, but you cannot ask "show me all blue coats" unless you planned for it.

How it works. - Partition key and sort key. The partition key decides which storage partition holds an item. The sort key orders items within it. - Access-pattern-first design. Often a single table holds several entity types with carefully designed keys. - Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) support additional query patterns. - Consistency. Reads are eventually consistent by default, strongly consistent on request. - Hot partitions. One very popular key can be throttled, so keys must spread load.

PK = "TENANT#retailer_1"   SK = "PLAN#2025S7"          -> plan metadata
PK = "TENANT#retailer_1"   SK = "PLAN#2025S7#USER#u42"  -> a user's access to that plan
Query: PK = "TENANT#retailer_1" AND begins_with(SK, "PLAN#2025S7")

Where I used it. Skills-level only. Not used in production on any of my projects.

When I'd pick it. For AWS workloads with simple, known access patterns, very high scale and no appetite for running a database, for example sessions, idempotency keys or user profiles. I would not pick it for ad-hoc analytics or complex joins.

Likely interview questions. - "DynamoDB or Postgres?" DynamoDB when access patterns are simple and known, scale is huge, and I want zero operations. Postgres when I need joins, flexible queries and transactions across many entities. - "Have you used DynamoDB in production?" No. It is on my skills line as literacy. My production NoSQL experience is MongoDB at Masters India and GeeksforGeeks.

Numbers tied to it. None.

Amazon S3

Depth: Skills-level on this resume. It is on the Skills line as "Amazon S3". No bullet names it.

What it is. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's object storage. You store files ("objects") of any size in "buckets", addressed by a key, and AWS handles durability and scale. Think of an infinite, very reliable warehouse of labelled boxes. You cannot edit a box in place, you replace it.

How it works. - Buckets and keys. s3://bucket/path/to/file.json. The "folders" are just key prefixes. - Strong read-after-write consistency for new and overwritten objects. - Storage classes and lifecycle rules move old data to cheaper tiers automatically. - Presigned URLs give temporary access without sharing credentials. - Access control through IAM policies and bucket policies. Buckets should be private by default.

s3.put_object(Bucket="raw-payloads", Key=f"menus/{vendor_id}/{content_hash}.pdf", Body=pdf_bytes)
url = s3.generate_presigned_url("get_object",
        Params={"Bucket": "raw-payloads", "Key": key}, ExpiresIn=900)

Where I used it. Skills-level. Masters India ran on AWS, but no resume bullet names Amazon S3, so I do not claim specific S3 usage. The object-storage idea does appear in my Menu design notes (keeping raw scraped payloads so a parser fix can be replayed without re-scraping), but Menu ran on GCP, so that was not S3.

When I'd pick it. For raw files, backups, data lake storage, exports and model artifacts on AWS. On GCP the equivalent is Cloud Storage.

Likely interview questions. - "Why keep raw payloads in object storage?" So you can reprocess after a bug without re-fetching from the source. Object storage is cheap, durable and fits large files. - "How do you secure a bucket?" Block public access, grant least-privilege IAM roles, use presigned URLs for temporary sharing, and turn on encryption and access logging.

Numbers tied to it. None.

7. Cloud, DevOps and testing

GCP (Google Cloud Platform)

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics and Uber Menu (both Tech lines).

What it is. GCP is Google's public cloud: rented compute, storage, databases, networking and managed services such as BigQuery. Think of renting fully equipped workshop space instead of building your own factory.

How it works (what interviewers usually probe). - Projects group resources and billing. - IAM and service accounts. Workloads run as service accounts with least-privilege roles, not as people. - Regions and zones for latency and availability. - Managed services (BigQuery, Cloud Storage, managed databases, container platforms) trade control for less operations work.

gcloud projects list
gcloud iam service-accounts list --project my-project
# Least privilege: give the scraper only the roles it needs

Where I used it. Impact Analytics (the platform and agent plane run on GCP, with BigQuery as the upstream warehouse) and Uber Menu (the scraping and RAG pipeline with Gemini 2.5 Pro). If asked which specific GCP services you ran, only name ones you actually touched.

Why it was chosen. It was where the workloads already lived at each company. It was not my decision to pick a cloud.

Alternatives. AWS (what Masters used) or Azure. The concepts carry over.

Likely interview questions. - "GCP or AWS?" I have worked on both: GCP at Impact Analytics and Uber Menu, AWS at Masters India. The core ideas (IAM, regions, managed databases, object storage) map one to one. The choice is usually driven by where the company already is.

Numbers tied to it. None.

AWS (Amazon Web Services)

Depth: Production. Masters India (Tech line).

What it is. AWS is Amazon's public cloud and the largest one. It offers compute (EC2), object storage (S3), managed databases (RDS, DynamoDB), networking, and hundreds of other services. Same workshop analogy as GCP, a different landlord.

How it works. - Accounts and IAM roles with least privilege. - VPCs (Virtual Private Clouds) isolate networks. - Regions and Availability Zones. Spread across zones for resilience. - Managed services reduce operations work at the cost of some control.

Where I used it. Masters India: the GST compliance and e-invoicing platform ran on AWS. If asked which specific services, only name what you actually touched. Do not invent a list.

Why it was chosen. It was the company's existing cloud.

Alternatives. GCP or Azure.

Likely interview questions. - "What did you run on AWS?" The Masters India Spring Boot microservices and the bulk e-invoicing pipeline with Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, MongoDB and the ELK stack. Keep service names to what you personally operated.

Numbers tied to it. The Masters numbers ran on AWS: from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds p95, from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, 1M+ daily submissions, 98% deployment success.

Docker

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics, Uber FRM, Uber Menu, Masters India (all Tech lines).

What it is. Docker packages an application with everything it needs (runtime, libraries, config) into an image, which runs as an isolated container on any machine. Think of a shipping container: whatever is inside, every crane and ship handles it the same way.

How it works. - Images are layered. Each Dockerfile step adds a cached layer, so ordering steps well makes builds fast. - Containers versus virtual machines. Containers share the host kernel, so they start in seconds and use less memory. - Multi-stage builds compile in one stage and copy only the result into a small runtime image. - Registries store and version images. - Immutable deploys. You ship a new image, not edits to a running server.

FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download                 # cached unless dependencies change
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app ./cmd/server

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

For the Java services the idea is the same: build the Spring Boot fat jar in a JDK stage, then copy only the jar into a smaller JRE image and start it with java -jar.

Where I used it. Every recent project: the IA Go platform and Python agent plane, the FRM Spring Boot scoping service, the Menu scrapers and pipeline workers, and the Masters Spring Boot microservices.

Why it was chosen. Reproducible builds and the same artifact from laptop to production.

Alternatives. Plain virtual machines with configuration management. Buildpacks to skip writing Dockerfiles.

Likely interview questions. - "Container or VM?" A container shares the host kernel, so it is lighter and starts faster. A VM has its own kernel, so isolation is stronger. Most services run in containers, often on VMs underneath. - "How do you keep images small and secure?" Multi-stage builds, a minimal base image, no secrets baked in, and pinned dependency versions.

Numbers tied to it. None directly.

Kubernetes

Depth: Skills-level. Literacy, no cluster operations claim.

What it is. Kubernetes (K8s) is a system that runs and manages containers across many machines. You declare what you want ("3 copies of this service, restart if unhealthy") and Kubernetes keeps reality matching that. Think of a harbour master who keeps the right number of ships at each dock and replaces any that sink.

How it works. - Pods are the smallest unit, usually one container. - Deployments keep N replicas running and roll out new versions gradually. - Services give a stable address in front of changing pods. - Probes. Liveness restarts a stuck container. Readiness keeps traffic away until it is ready. - Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) adds or removes replicas based on load.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry/api:1.4.2
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } }

Where I used it. Skills-level only. I understand how services are deployed and scaled on it, but I do not claim operating Kubernetes clusters, and it is not part of any Impact Analytics bullet.

When I'd pick it. Many services, a platform team to run it, and a need for standard rollouts and autoscaling. For a few services, a managed container platform is often simpler.

Likely interview questions. - "Have you run Kubernetes in production?" I have deployed and debugged containerized services, and I understand pods, deployments, services, probes and autoscaling. I have not operated clusters myself, so I list it as literacy. - "Liveness versus readiness probe?" Liveness answers "should this container be restarted?". Readiness answers "should this container get traffic right now?". Mixing them up causes restart loops during slow startups.

Numbers tied to it. None.

Maven

Depth: Skills-level. On the Skills line. No resume bullet names it. FRM built with Bazel.

What it is. Apache Maven is the standard build and dependency tool for Java projects. One file, pom.xml, declares the project, its dependencies and its plugins, and Maven downloads the libraries, compiles, tests and packages the result. Think of a recipe card plus a pantry service: you list the ingredients and steps, and the pantry delivers the exact versions you asked for.

How it works. - POM (Project Object Model). pom.xml holds coordinates (groupId, artifactId, version), dependencies and plugins. - Lifecycle phases. validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy. Running a phase runs every phase before it. - Dependency scopes. compile, test, provided, runtime. Test libraries such as JUnit stay out of the shipped jar. - Dependency management and BOMs. A BOM (Bill of Materials), such as the Spring Boot parent, pins compatible versions of many libraries at once. - Conflict resolution. When two libraries need different versions of a third, Maven picks the one nearest to your project in the dependency tree. mvn dependency:tree shows what you actually got. - Plugins. Surefire runs unit tests, JaCoCo measures coverage, and the Spring Boot plugin builds the runnable fat jar.

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.3.0</version>                 <!-- the BOM pins compatible versions -->
</parent>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>   <!-- JUnit 5, Mockito, MockMvc -->
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Where I used it. Skills-level. No bullet names it. Uber FRM built and tested with Bazel because of Uber's monorepo. Maven is the default build for standalone Spring Boot services, and I can explain a POM, the lifecycle and dependency conflicts in depth.

When I'd pick it. Any single Java service or library in its own repo. It is predictable, every CI system and IDE understands it, and every Spring guide assumes it.

Alternatives. Gradle, which is faster on large builds and scripted in Kotlin or Groovy. Bazel for large multi-language monorepos with remote caching, which is what FRM used.

Likely interview questions. - "Maven, Gradle or Bazel?" Maven for a standard single-service Java repo, because it is declarative and boring in a good way. Gradle when the build is large and needs custom logic or faster incremental builds. Bazel for a huge monorepo where only affected targets should rebuild, which is Uber's case. - "How do you fix a dependency conflict?" Run mvn dependency:tree to see which version won and why. Then pin the version in dependencyManagement or exclude the transitive dependency that brings the wrong one. Using a BOM avoids most conflicts in the first place.

Numbers tied to it. None.

Bazel

Depth: Production. Uber FRM F3.

What it is. Bazel is Google's open-source build and test system, used for large monorepos. It builds only what changed, caches results, and runs builds in a hermetic (sealed, reproducible) way. Think of a kitchen that remembers every dish it ever cooked from the same ingredients, and only cooks again when an ingredient changes.

How it works. - BUILD files declare targets (libraries, binaries, tests) and their dependencies. - Dependency graph. Bazel knows exactly what depends on what, so it rebuilds and retests only affected targets. - Hermetic builds. Same inputs produce the same outputs, so remote caching works. - Test targets can be run for exactly the code a PR touched.

# BUILD (Starlark)
java_library(
    name = "scoping_repo",
    srcs = glob(["src/main/java/**/repository/*.java"]),
    deps = [":entities", "@maven//:org_springframework_data_spring_data_jpa"],
)
java_test(
    name = "scoping_repo_test",
    srcs = ["src/test/java/ScopingRepositoryTest.java"],
    test_class = "ScopingRepositoryTest",
    deps = [":scoping_repo", "@maven//:org_junit_jupiter_junit_jupiter_api"],
)

Where I used it. Uber FRM F3: zero-downtime releases through stacked Bazel PRs during the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration, with Bazel Java test targets (JUnit) gating merges. The FRM test suite was 1,100+ tests (verbal).

Why it was chosen. It is Uber's monorepo build system, so it was the platform we built on.

Alternatives. Language-native tools (Maven or Gradle for Java, Go modules) for single-language repos. Pants or Buck for other monorepos.

Likely interview questions. - "What are stacked PRs?" A big change split into a chain of small PRs, each building on the previous one. Each is reviewed, tested and merged on its own, so nothing lands as a risky big bang. With Bazel each PR runs only the affected test targets. - "Why is Bazel fast on a huge repo?" It knows the exact dependency graph and caches every result, so a change only rebuilds and retests what depends on it.

Numbers tied to it. 100% module statement coverage on the migrated module (F3).

JUnit 5, Mockito and MockMvc

Depth: Production. Uber FRM F3 (JUnit is on the FRM Tech line) and Masters India MI3.

What it is. JUnit 5 is the standard framework for writing and running Java tests. Mockito creates fake versions ("mocks") of dependencies, so you can test one class on its own. MockMvc sends fake HTTP requests through the real Spring MVC layer without starting a server, so you can test controllers, validation and error mapping. Think of a car inspection: JUnit is the checklist, Mockito is the test dummy in the driver's seat, and MockMvc is the rolling road that lets you test the engine without driving on a real street.

How it works. - JUnit 5 basics. @Test marks a test. @ParameterizedTest runs one test over many inputs, which suits financial math with many edge cases. assertThrows checks failures. - Mockito. @Mock creates a fake, @InjectMocks builds the class under test with those fakes, when(...).thenReturn(...) sets behaviour and verify(...) checks a call happened. - MockMvc with @WebMvcTest. Loads only the web layer. You assert status codes, JSON fields and validation errors. - Slice and integration tests. @DataJpaTest tests repositories against a real database. Testcontainers can start a throwaway MySQL or PostgreSQL in Docker, so tests match production SQL. - Coverage. A tool such as JaCoCo reports statement and branch coverage. Coverage shows what ran, not whether the assertions are meaningful.

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class ThresholdServiceTest {
    @Mock ThresholdRepository repo;
    @InjectMocks ThresholdService service;

    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource({"340000000, 20000000, true", "340000000, 1000000, false"})   // illustrative values
    void flagsSignificantLines(long materiality, long amount, boolean expected) {
        assertEquals(expected, service.isSignificant(amount, materiality));
    }
}

@WebMvcTest(ScopingLineController.class)
class ScopingLineControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockBean ScopingService service;    // @MockitoBean in newer Spring versions

    @Test
    void staleVersionReturns409() throws Exception {
        when(service.updateStatus(eq("abc123"), any()))
            .thenThrow(new ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException(ScopingAssessment.class, "abc123"));

        mvc.perform(patch("/v1/scoping/lines/abc123/status")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"status\":\"REVIEW\",\"version\":7}"))
           .andExpect(status().isConflict());
    }
}

Where I used it. - Uber FRM F3: the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration raised module statement coverage to 100%. JUnit tests ran as Bazel java_test targets that gated every stacked PR. The suite was 1,100+ tests (verbal, off the PDF). - Masters India MI3: test coverage went from 35% to 82%, which hardened the CI/CD release cycle and supported a 98% deployment success rate. The tests were JUnit and Mockito on the Spring Boot services.

Why it was chosen there. JUnit is the default in the Java world and is what Bazel and Maven both run natively. Mockito keeps service tests fast and focused. MockMvc proves the HTTP contract (status codes, validation, the 409 on a stale version) without a deployed environment.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. TestNG, an older alternative with similar features. AssertJ for more readable assertions on top of JUnit. Testcontainers when the behaviour depends on the real database, like locking and constraints. Contract tests (Spring Cloud Contract or Pact) between services.

Likely interview questions. - "How do you get to 100% statement coverage without writing useless tests?" Coverage is the side effect, not the goal. We wrote behaviour tests per repository and service method: happy path, each validation failure, the optimistic lock conflict, and edge cases of the financial math. Parameterized tests covered many inputs cheaply. Anything still uncovered was usually dead code, which we deleted. - "Unit test or integration test?" Both, for different things. Unit tests with Mockito for business logic, because they are fast and pinpoint failures. Integration tests against a real database for queries, constraints and locking, because a mock cannot tell you your SQL is wrong. The column-aliasing bug is exactly the kind of thing only a real query catches. - "How do you test optimistic locking?" At the web layer, mock the service to throw the lock exception and assert a 409 with MockMvc. At the data layer, load the same entity in two transactions, save one, then save the other and assert it fails. - "What did 35% to 82% at Masters change?" Releases became routine. Regressions were caught in CI instead of production, which is what the 98% deployment success rate reflects. If pressed on the exact definition of deployment success, keep it qualitative.

Numbers tied to it. 100% module statement coverage (FRM F3). 1,100+ tests (verbal). 35% to 82% coverage and 98% deployment success (Masters MI3).

CI/CD

Depth: Production. Masters India MI3, Impact Analytics A5, Uber FRM F3.

What it is. CI (Continuous Integration) means every change is automatically built and tested when it is pushed. CD (Continuous Delivery or Deployment) means passing changes are automatically released, often gradually. Think of a factory line with quality checkpoints: a part only moves forward if it passes each inspection.

How it works. - Pipeline stages: lint, unit tests, integration tests, build image, deploy. - Gates stop a release on failed tests, low coverage, or a failed evaluation threshold. - Progressive delivery: canary releases send a small share of traffic to the new version first. - Rollback must be fast and boring. - Coverage is a signal, not a goal on its own. Tests must check behaviour.

# Illustrative CI step: an evaluation gate for an AI pipeline
- name: offline-eval-gate
  run: python run_eval.py --suite cases.json --min-accuracy 0.8
  # fails the job, and blocks promotion, if accuracy on the 300 cases is under 80%

Where I used it. - Masters India MI3: drove test coverage from 35% to 82% and achieved a 98% deployment success rate across the microservices. The PHP-to-Spring Boot migration used a canary per route, and JUnit and Mockito suites gated each release. - Impact Analytics A5: the 80% accuracy CI gate on the 300-case proxy harness, which blocks promotion of a worse model or prompt. - Uber FRM F3: stacked Bazel PRs with test gates, 100% module statement coverage, reporting SQL allowlists and automated FSM (finite state machine) gates with 50% delta-variance checks for SOX compliance.

Why it matters. Each of these is a guardrail: code cannot ship if tests, coverage, evaluation or compliance checks fail.

Alternatives. Manual release checklists (slow and error-prone). The specific CI tool matters less than the gates in it.

Likely interview questions. - "What does 98% deployment success mean?" 98% of deployments across the microservices went out successfully. If pressed on the exact definition or denominator, keep it qualitative and do not invent one. - "How do you gate an AI change in CI?" Run it against a fixed offline set and fail the build under a threshold. Ours was 80% accuracy on a 300-case proxy set. That is a promotion gate, not a live accuracy claim.

Numbers tied to it. 35% to 82% coverage and 98% deployment success (Masters). 80% CI gate on 300 cases (IA). 100% module statement coverage and 50% delta-variance checks (FRM).

8. Observability

Datadog

Depth: Production. Impact Analytics C1.

What it is. Datadog is a monitoring platform as a service. It collects metrics, logs and distributed traces from your services and shows them in dashboards with alerts. Think of a hospital patient monitor for your servers: heart rate, blood pressure and alarms in one screen.

How it works. - Distributed tracing. A trace follows one request across services. Each step is a span with timing, and spans share a trace id passed in headers. - APM (Application Performance Monitoring) shows latency, error rate and throughput per endpoint. - Metrics and monitors for alerting on thresholds. - Logs linked to traces through the trace id.

span, ctx := tracer.StartSpanFromContext(ctx, "clickhouse.pivot",
    tracer.Tag("tenant", tenantID), tracer.Tag("rollup", "product_season"))
defer span.Finish()
rows, err := ch.Query(ctx, sql, args...)

Where I used it. Impact Analytics C1: Datadog distributed tracing on the Go/Gin platform edge.

Why it was chosen. At 10k peak RPS with nested timeouts, you need to see which step of a slow request took the time: auth, Postgres, ClickHouse or the handler.

Alternatives. New Relic (used at Masters), open-source Prometheus, Grafana and Jaeger, or OpenTelemetry as a vendor-neutral layer. LangSmith for the AI steps.

Likely interview questions. - "How do you debug a slow request?" Open the trace, see which span is long, then check that span's tags and linked logs. If it is a ClickHouse span, check the query and whether it hit a rollup or raw facts. - "Datadog or LangSmith?" Datadog for the platform: HTTP latency, errors, database spans. LangSmith for the agent: which graph node produced which answer. Different questions, different tools.

Numbers tied to it. Part of the 10k peak RPS platform.

ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana)

Depth: Production. Masters India MI3.

What it is. ELK is a log stack. Logstash (or a lighter shipper like Beats) collects and parses logs, Elasticsearch stores and indexes them, and Kibana is the UI to search and chart them. Think of a central post office for logs: every service mails its logs in, they are sorted, and you can search any letter instantly.

How it works. - Structured JSON logs with consistent fields (service, level, request id). - Correlation IDs. One id is passed through the API and the Kafka consumers, so a single search shows the whole story of one request. - Index lifecycle keeps recent logs fast and expires old ones. - Kibana queries and dashboards for triage.

{"ts":"2024-03-31T23:58:02Z","service":"irp-consumer","level":"ERROR",
 "request_id":"req-7f3a","client_gstin":"29ABCDE1234F1Z5","msg":"IRP timeout, retry 2 of 5"}

In Kibana, request_id:"req-7f3a" shows the API call, the Kafka hop and every retry in one view.

Where I used it. Masters India MI3: instrumented ELK and New Relic distributed tracing, alongside a Redis caching layer, which cut incident triage time by 70% and database read load by 30%.

Why it was chosen. Before it, triage meant logging into servers and grepping. Central, searchable, correlated logs turned that into one query.

Alternatives. OpenSearch, Grafana Loki, or a cloud logging service.

Likely interview questions. - "How did ELK cut triage time?" By making logs central, structured and correlated. One request id took you from the API call to the consumer and the retries in a single search, instead of hopping between servers. The 70% cut is ESTIMATED, roughly from about 30 minutes to under 10.

Numbers tied to it. Incident triage cut by 70% (ESTIMATED, about 30 minutes to under 10 minutes). Database read load down 30% (shared with the Redis work).

New Relic

Depth: Production. Masters India MI3.

What it is. New Relic is an APM (Application Performance Monitoring) service. Agents inside your services report transaction timing, slow database queries, errors and distributed traces. Think of a fitness tracker for each service: it tells you which step of the workout hurts.

How it works. - Language agents instrument web frameworks, database drivers and HTTP clients automatically. - Transactions and traces show time per endpoint and per downstream call. - Slow query and error analytics point at the worst offenders. - Alerts on latency or error-rate thresholds.

# The Java agent attaches at JVM startup and instruments Spring MVC, JDBC, Kafka and HTTP clients.
java -javaagent:/opt/newrelic/newrelic.jar \
     -Dnewrelic.config.app_name=irp-service \
     -jar irp-service.jar

Where I used it. Masters India MI3: New Relic distributed tracing on the Spring Boot services together with ELK, cutting incident triage time by 70%.

Why it was chosen. It showed where time went (slow IRP calls, slow queries) while ELK showed what happened in detail. Together they made triage fast.

Alternatives. Datadog (what I used at Impact Analytics), or OpenTelemetry with an open-source backend.

Likely interview questions. - "Why both ELK and New Relic?" New Relic answers "which service and which call is slow". ELK answers "what exactly happened in this request". You use the trace to find the problem and the logs to understand it.

Numbers tied to it. Incident triage cut by 70% (ESTIMATED, about 30 minutes to under 10 minutes).

9. Browser automation

Selenium

Depth: Production. Uber Menu M2.

What it is. Selenium automates a real web browser from code: open pages, click, scroll, wait for content and read the result. It is used for testing websites and for collecting data from sites that need a real browser because content loads with JavaScript. Think of robot hands on a keyboard and mouse that do exactly what a person would do, but tirelessly.

How it works. - WebDriver controls Chrome or Firefox, often headless (no visible window). - Explicit waits wait for an element to appear instead of sleeping a fixed time. - Selectors (CSS or XPath) find elements. They break when the site changes. - Proxies and retries. Rotating IPs through proxy pools and retrying with backoff reduce blocking. - Fleet operation. Many browser workers run in parallel, with monitoring for failure rates.

def fetch_menu(url, attempt=0):
    driver = new_driver(proxy=proxy_pool.next())          # dynamic proxy pool
    try:
        driver.get(url)
        WebDriverWait(driver, 20).until(EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, ".menu")))
        return driver.page_source
    except TimeoutException:
        if attempt < 4:
            time.sleep(min(2 ** attempt + random.random(), 30))   # adaptive backoff
            return fetch_menu(url, attempt + 1)
        raise
    finally:
        driver.quit()

Where I used it. Uber Menu M2: scaled menu extraction success to 95%+ (from an estimated 60 to 65%) by hardening a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries. The scraped events then flowed into Kafka and Flink.

Why it was chosen. Many restaurant and partner sites render menus with JavaScript, so a plain HTTP fetch returns an empty page. A real browser sees what a customer sees.

Alternatives. Playwright or Puppeteer (more modern browser automation). Plain HTTP requests when a site serves static HTML or an API. A partner API is always better when it exists.

Likely interview questions. - "How did you get success from about 60 to 65% up to 95%+?" Most failures were blocks and timeouts, not code bugs. Dynamic proxy pools spread requests across IPs, adaptive retries with backoff avoided hammering a site, and explicit waits replaced fixed sleeps. - "How do you detect when a site changes?" Track success rate per site. A sudden drop for one site usually means a layout change, so the selectors get fixed and the failed pages are replayed from Kafka. - "Why not just use APIs?" Where a partner API existed, that is the better path. Many menus were only available on websites or as PDFs, so a browser fleet plus RAG extraction filled the gap.

Numbers tied to it. 95%+ extraction success (from an estimated 60 to 65%). It feeds the 24 hours to 2 hours onboarding and 30K+ menus per month story.

Honesty box for the whole glossary

Say this carefully.

  • Skills-level only: C, C++, gRPC, pgvector, DynamoDB, Amazon S3, Kubernetes, MCP, Tool Calling, Spring Security, Spring Batch, Maven, Celery, and Claude as a provider. Explain how they work. Do not claim production ownership. Spring Batch fits the Masters chunked imports, so describe it at the pattern level.
  • Java is FRM and Masters only. Impact Analytics is Go/Gin plus Python FastAPI and LangGraph. Never say Spring Boot at Impact Analytics. GeeksforGeeks is Django. Java 21 virtual threads are knowledge, not a project claim.
  • Tool design depth (Cluster Recommendation Copilot, 14 tools) is verbal only, not a resume bullet. Hindsight is verbal only too.
  • Milvus is Uber Menu only. LangSmith is Ask Iris only. Kafka and Flink are Uber Menu, and Kafka is also Masters India. None of the three is at Impact Analytics.
  • Kubernetes: no "I operated clusters". Spark is not on the resume.
  • Exactly-once means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes. Never claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across third parties.
  • 80% is a CI promotion gate on 300 cases, not live accuracy for all tenants. 73% and 74% come from the gold-200 bench. 98% on Menu is offline evaluation.
  • 15.5 times is query time. 170GB OOM is load time. They are not cause and effect. Never say sub-second pivots.
  • 344k is rows per second, not requests per second. The 4.09B copy was measured in flight, not a finished cutover. Partition rollback is DROP PARTITION then recopy, not an atomic swap with live readers.
  • Isolation at Impact Analytics is access control and tenant scoping, not encryption.
  • Uber work is always "Uber via EPAM". "Led 3 engineers" is FRM. "Mentored 2 engineers" is Masters India. Do not merge them.
  • Never share cluster hosts, passwords or environment values, and never suggest open-sourcing the ClickHouse copier.

Wrap-up - Concept to project cheat sheet - Say this, not that (honesty box)

Part A. Measuring speed and load

These three ideas come first because almost every number on my resume is either a latency, a throughput or a size. If I mix them up, the interviewer stops trusting the rest.

1. Latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99)

In plain English. Latency is how long one request takes, from the moment it arrives until the response is sent. A percentile tells you how slow the slow requests are. p95 means "95 out of 100 requests finished at or under this time". p50 is the median (the typical request), p95 is the bad-day experience, and p99 is the worst 1 in 100.

Analogy. Think of a coffee shop. The average wait might be 3 minutes, but if 5 customers in every 100 wait 20 minutes, those are the customers who leave angry reviews. p95 is the number that tells you about those 5 customers. The average hides them.

How it works: a 100-request example. Imagine an API served exactly 100 requests in a minute. Here are the response times, grouped:

How many requests Response time each
60 80 ms
30 150 ms
5 300 ms
4 900 ms
1 4,000 ms

Sort all 100 values from fastest to slowest and number them 1 to 100.

  • p50 is the 50th value. Positions 1 to 60 are all 80 ms, so p50 = 80 ms.
  • p95 is the 95th value. Positions 91 to 95 are 300 ms, so p95 = 300 ms.
  • p99 is the 99th value. Positions 96 to 99 are 900 ms, so p99 = 900 ms.
  • Max is the 100th value, 4,000 ms.
  • Average is (60×80 + 30×150 + 5×300 + 4×900 + 1×4,000) / 100 = 18,400 / 100 = 184 ms.

Notice what the average does. It says 184 ms, which is a time that almost no real request took. It is dragged up by one 4-second outlier and still hides the 900 ms tail. That is why teams set goals on p95 or p99, not the mean. (This is the "nearest-rank" method. Monitoring tools often interpolate between neighbours, so their numbers can differ slightly. The idea is the same.)

def percentile(latencies_ms, p):
    s = sorted(latencies_ms)
    rank = max(1, int(round(p / 100 * len(s))))  # nearest-rank
    return s[rank - 1]

data = [80]*60 + [150]*30 + [300]*5 + [900]*4 + [4000]
print(percentile(data, 50), percentile(data, 95), percentile(data, 99))  # 80 300 900

Two more facts interviewers like. First, you cannot average percentiles across servers. If server A has p95 = 200 ms and server B has p95 = 400 ms, the fleet p95 is not 300 ms. You need the raw data or a histogram. Second, tail latency compounds. If one page calls 10 backend services in parallel and waits for all of them, the page is slow whenever any one of them is slow, so each service's p99 matters much more than it looks.

Where it shows up in my work. - Masters India (MI1): "p95 API latency -75% (from 1.2s to 300ms) across 1,500+ enterprise clients." HISTORICAL. The win came from making the slow calls to the government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal) asynchronous in the new Spring Boot services, adding connection pooling (HikariCP for the database), fixing queries and indexes, and putting Redis in front of hot reads. Arithmetic: (1.2 − 0.3) / 1.2 = 0.75, so 75% lower. - IA (C1): the Go/Gin platform is described by 10k peak RPS, which is throughput, not latency. There is no latency SLA on the resume, and I do not invent a p99 for it.
