3.3 About (long), paragraph by paragraph

The current text, quoted from the LinkedIn profile pack:

I am a Senior Software Engineer focused on backend, data, and production AI platforms in Java, Python and Go.

What I am known for:

  • Platform: At Impact Analytics I architected AssortSmart's multi-tenant Go/Gin edge (Wire, h2c, Datadog) to 10k peak RPS. I cut planner pivots from 189s to 12s on 250M rows with six ClickHouse rollup tables (product, store, and attr at season and weekly grains). I keep a 100% statement-coverage CI gate across 1,200+ Go tests.
  • Scale and infrastructure: Weekly grain is built one fiscal week at a time, after a full-season weekly aggregate hit about 170 GB and ran out of memory. I wrote a Go native-TLS pump that copies season partitions between ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 150-190k rows/s per stream, 344k combined. It uses 500k-row columnar batches with double buffering, so the SELECT of the next batch overlaps the INSERT of the last. The largest object I timed is attr weekly at 4.09B rows across two seasons, measured in flight, not a finished cutover. The Kafka and Flink on my profile are Uber Menu, not AssortSmart.
  • Agentic: I built Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, and Top Style over 348k article-seasons (88k items per pass, 7 lenses), reading JSON payloads instead of querying the 2.11B-row ClickHouse master. I shipped Ask Iris, a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot with a LangGraph supervisor, a 3-attempt evaluator, and hierarchy access frozen at the handshake. Promotions are gated on a 300-case proxy harness and an 80% CI gate (a gate, not live accuracy for all tenants). On a separate benchmark we cut live scoring cost 73% at 100% coverage against a 74% deterministic baseline, and froze blend weights when the LLM lost.
  • Uber via EPAM: FRM scoping with 36 Spring Boot endpoints, 19M GL rows, an L1–L4 FSLI hierarchy, an 8-table SOADB schema, and SHA-256 keys. I led 3 engineers to 100% coverage with SOX 50% delta-variance checks. Reconciliation dropped 70%, from 14 days to 3, against $340M materiality. Menu ingestion went from 24 hours to 2 hours, saving $600K/yr on 30K+ menus/month, with 98% offline field fidelity (RAG over Milvus) and Kafka + Flink exactly-once upserts.
  • Masters India: A Spring Boot strangler migration cut p95 75%, from 1.2s to 300ms. A Kafka + PostgreSQL pipeline sharded by tax quarter handles 1M+ submissions/day. Coverage went from 35% to 82% at 98% deploy success. I mentored 2 engineers.

I care about honest metrics (measured vs promotion gate vs historical) and mentoring people to ship safely.

Open to Senior Software Engineer / SDE2+ roles in backend, platform, data infrastructure, and applied-AI systems.

Opening line and "What I am known for"

The opening line tells a search algorithm and a human the same three things: backend, data, AI. "What I am known for" introduces five proof bullets, one per area. Recruiters skim these, so each bullet leads with the area name.

Platform bullet

In plain words. At Impact Analytics you designed the main web service of AssortSmart, a retail planning product. Many retailer customers (tenants) share it. It is written in Go using the Gin web framework and handles up to 10,000 requests per second at peak. You made the slowest screen, the planner pivot table, about 15 times faster by pre-computing summaries in ClickHouse. The Go code base must keep 100% statement coverage to merge.

Phrase Plain meaning
Multi-tenant One running system serves many customer companies, each seeing only its own data. Like an apartment building with separate locked flats
Go/Gin edge The Go service that receives HTTP requests first. Gin is a lightweight Go web framework
Wire Google Wire generates the code that connects Go components at compile time, so a missing dependency fails the build instead of crashing at startup
h2c HTTP/2 without TLS encryption, served directly by Go. You ran it with no reverse proxy (like Nginx) in front
Datadog A monitoring service. Distributed tracing follows one request across every service it touches
Planner pivot The grid screen where merchandise planners slice sales by product, store and week
Rollup table A table of pre-computed totals, so a query reads a few thousand summary rows instead of millions of raw ones. Like keeping monthly bank statements instead of re-adding every receipt
Grain The level of detail of a table, such as per season or per week
Statement coverage The share of code lines that run at least once during tests

If a recruiter asks...

  • "How did you get from 189 seconds to 12?" "Planners were waiting over three minutes for a pivot because every query aggregated raw rows. I built a pre-aggregation layer in ClickHouse: six rollup tables covering product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain. On a 250-million-row benchmark the pivot went from 189 seconds to about 12 seconds, which is roughly 15 and a half times faster."
  • "Why no reverse proxy?" "Fewer moving parts. The Go server handles HTTP/2 directly with h2c and enforces its own nested timeouts, so a slow downstream call cannot hold a connection forever. Datadog tracing shows where time goes."
  • "1,200 tests, really?" "Yes. That is off the PDF, but it is true: 100% statement coverage on the Go code, over 1,200 tests, enforced in CI. Statement coverage proves every line ran under some test. It does not prove every edge case is right, so I treat it as a floor."

Say this carefully. 10k RPS has no SLA attached. Do not claim you operated Kubernetes clusters for this platform.

Scale and infrastructure bullet

In plain words. Two stories. First, building the weekly summary table for a whole season in one go needed about 170 GB of memory and crashed. You fixed it by building one fiscal week at a time with memory limits. Second, you had to copy huge tables between two ClickHouse Cloud clusters that were not allowed to talk to each other directly. So you wrote a Go program that reads from one and writes to the other, at about 344,000 rows per second combined.

Phrase Plain meaning
OOM (out of memory) The database process ran out of RAM and the query was killed
Fiscal week The retailer's accounting week, which may not match the calendar week
Native-TLS pump A Go program that speaks ClickHouse's own binary protocol over an encrypted connection (port 9440), instead of HTTP
Season partition ClickHouse tables are split into partitions by season code, so one season can be copied, dropped or replaced on its own
Columnar batch A block of 500,000 rows sent column by column, which is how ClickHouse stores data
Double buffering While batch N is being written to the target, batch N+1 is already being read from the source. Like one person washing dishes while another dries, instead of one person doing both in turn
Measured in flight The rate was timed while the copy was still running. It is not a report of a finished migration

If a recruiter asks...

  • "Why write your own copier?" "The two ClickHouse Cloud clusters had IP allowlists that blocked a direct cluster-to-cluster copy. So I wrote a Go pump that pulls from one over the native TLS protocol and pushes into the other, in 500,000-row batches with double buffering. Two season streams ran in parallel at about 150 to 190 thousand rows a second each, around 344 thousand combined."
  • "Did the 4-billion-row migration finish?" "I'd say it carefully. I measured the rate on the 4.09-billion-row attribute weekly set while that copy was in flight. I don't claim the full cutover finished. The safety mechanism was checkpoint files per table plus a ledger, and if a partition failed halfway I dropped that partition on the target and recopied the season."
  • "How did you fix the 170 GB problem?" "I sliced the build into one fiscal week per insert and set memory and disk-spill caps. The whole-season build had failed even with 80 GB and 200 GB caps. A single week fit comfortably."

Say this carefully. 344k is rows per second during a copy, never requests per second. The 170 GB fix (load time) did not cause the 189-to-12 win (query time). "Atomic partition rollback" means drop the partition and recopy, not a live atomic swap. Never offer to share the copier code.

Agentic bullet

In plain words. AssortSmart helps retailers decide which products to keep, drop or add each season. You built the AI decision engine that scores 348,000 product-season combinations, 88,000 per batch run. It mixes plain math (sales metrics) with LLM judgements from seven different angles ("lenses"). The LLM never queries the big database. It only sees JSON you prepared. You also shipped Ask Iris, a chat copilot planners use to ask about KPIs and AI decisions. Before any model or prompt ships, it must score at least 80% on a 300-case test set.

Phrase Plain meaning
Article-season One product (article) in one selling season. A t-shirt in Spring 2026 and the same t-shirt in Fall 2026 are two article-seasons
7 lenses Seven separate LLM prompts, each judging the item from one angle. A decider combines them
JSON payloads instead of querying You fetch the facts, package them as JSON and hand them to the model. The model gets no SQL tool
JWT-secured WebSocket A long-lived two-way connection, opened only with a valid signed login token
LangGraph supervisor A LangGraph node that routes each question to the right helper step
3-attempt evaluator A checker that reviews the draft answer and allows at most 3 retries, so the loop cannot run forever
Hierarchy frozen at the handshake The user's allowed scope is read once when the socket opens and cannot change mid-session, which prevents cross-tenant leaks
Proxy harness / CI gate A 300-case test set that runs in CI. A release that scores under 80% is blocked
Deterministic baseline The score from plain math alone, with no LLM
Blend weights The formula final = 0.4 × math score + 0.6 × LLM score. "Frozen" means you stopped tuning it

If a recruiter asks...

  • "Is your model 80% accurate?" "80% is a promotion gate, not a live accuracy claim. A new model or prompt must score at least 80% on our 300-case evaluation harness before it can ship. I don't claim every tenant runs at 80% live."
  • "What does 73% cheaper mean?" "On a separate 200-case gold benchmark we compared models. The one we picked completed all 200 cases at about 73% lower execution cost. On that same benchmark the deterministic baseline scored 74%, and our blended LLM scored lower, so we froze the blend weights instead of tuning them to look better."
  • "Why not let the LLM query the database?" "The master table has 2.11 billion rows. Letting a model write SQL against it risks slow queries, wrong joins and data leaks across tenants. Serving prepared JSON keeps the model's input small and checkable. If the LLM times out, the system falls back to the deterministic score."

Say this carefully. Keep/Drop runs its steps in a fixed order (peer, decider, lenses, blend, explain). No LLM decides what runs next. The supervisor pattern is Ask Iris. LangSmith tracing is on Ask Iris only. There is no human review queue in this system. Ask Iris is a shipped capability with no SLA or usage numbers.

Uber via EPAM bullet

In plain words. You were employed by EPAM Systems and worked on Uber projects. For Uber Finance you owned the backend of the FRM (Financial Risk Management) scoping tool, which replaced spreadsheets for the quarterly close and cut reconciliation from 14 days to 3. For Uber Eats you worked on a pipeline that reads restaurant menu PDFs and turns them into catalog data, cutting onboarding from 24 hours to 2.

Phrase Plain meaning
GL rows General ledger entries, the company's master accounting records. 19M raw rows were migrated off Google Sheets into MySQL
L1–L4 FSLI Financial Statement Line Items grouped four levels deep, from a broad heading down to a specific account group
SOADB Uber's standard service-owned MySQL
SHA-256 keys A stable ID computed from the content itself (for example question text plus page name), so the same item always gets the same ID and duplicates cannot appear
SOX 50% delta-variance SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley) is the US law on financial controls. The tool flags any line whose value moved more than 50% between periods
$340M materiality The threshold above which a misstatement would matter to investors
98% offline field fidelity In offline evaluation (scored against known-correct menus, not live traffic), 98% of extracted menu fields matched the correct value
Exactly-once upserts In practice, at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes, so a replayed message cannot create a duplicate

If a recruiter asks...

  • "Were you an Uber employee?" "I was employed by EPAM Systems and worked on the Uber account, so I say 'Uber via EPAM'. On FRM I was tech lead of an EPAM pod of three engineers."
  • "How did you measure the 70%?" "Quarterly reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days. That was the outcome the platform delivered for the close." If pressed: "The technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what the platform delivered."
  • "How does $600K a year add up?" "Manual or third-party menu entry cost roughly $2 a menu. At 30,000 menus a month over 12 months that is about $720K, and I round it down to $600K to stay conservative."

Say this carefully. 98% is offline evaluation. Milvus is Uber Menu only. Do not claim you built the Slack collaboration and notification service. It was separate.

Masters India bullet

In plain words. Masters India sells GST (Goods and Services Tax) compliance software to Indian companies. Clients send invoices, and the platform validates and registers them with the government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an invoice reference number and a signed QR code. You led the move from an old PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, which made the slowest 5% of requests four times faster, and built the high-volume e-invoicing pipeline.

Phrase Plain meaning
Strangler migration Replace a legacy system one route at a time, with a canary per route, until the old one can be switched off. Like replacing a bridge one lane at a time while traffic keeps flowing
p95 latency 95% of requests finish faster than this number
Sharded by tax quarter The PostgreSQL data is split across databases by tax quarter, so each one stays a manageable size
98% deploy success 98% of deployments went out without a rollback

If a recruiter asks...

  • "What drove the latency win?" "Taking the government portal calls off the request thread with async calls, connection pooling, query and index fixes, and Redis for reads. p95 went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds across more than 1,500 enterprise clients."
  • "1 million a day, how much is that per second?" "About 12 per second on average, since a day has 86,400 seconds. Peaks around filing deadlines are much higher. My estimate is 8 to 10 times the average."

Say this carefully. "Mentored 2" is Masters India. "Led 3" is Uber FRM. Never merge them into "led a team of 5". Flink was never at Masters India.

The closing lines

"I care about honest metrics (measured vs promotion gate vs historical)" is a promise, and interviewers test it. If you say it, you must be the first to say "that was measured in flight" or "that is a CI gate, not live accuracy". "Open to Senior Software Engineer / SDE2+ roles" tells recruiters your target level. Use the same words on the call.

4. Experience entries decoded

The paste-ready blurbs live in the LinkedIn profile pack. This section explains what is in each one and where it differs from the PDF.

4.1 Impact Analytics, Senior Software Engineer (May 2026 to Present)

The entry follows the PDF's two chapters in the PDF's order: Agentic Flows & Orchestration first, then Core Infrastructure & Pipeline. The two Core paragraphs about pivots and the ClickHouse migration are the PDF bullets almost word for word. The Agentic paragraph and the first Core paragraph are shortened summaries of the other PDF bullets.

The entry ends with one paragraph of off-PDF context:

The full catalog holds 1.6M article-seasons. A full scoring pass costs about $100 in LLM tokens. The Go codebase holds a 100% statement-coverage gate across 1,200+ tests, with golangci-lint and SAST/SBOM checks.

Each of those is decoded in the off-PDF table in section 5. The deep technical chapters are IA core platform and IA agentic AI.

Not on LinkedIn and not on the PDF: the Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight. They are still being built. Use them only if an interviewer asks what you are working on next.

4.2 Uber via EPAM, SDE2 (Jul 2024 to May 2026)

Three sub-entries: FRM, Menu (Uber Eats) and ANZ (Uber Mobility). The FRM line names the Java stack (Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate) to match this track's PDF. The ANZ line is HISTORICAL and is Uber Mobility, not Uber Eats. It was a deterministic rules backend, so do not add Selenium or RAG to it. Deep chapters: Uber FRM and Uber Menu and ANZ.

4.3 Masters India, SDE2 (Dec 2022 to Jun 2024)

Same facts as the PDF in a shorter form, including the PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices migration. "700 to 4,000 requests per minute" is roughly 12 to 67 requests per second. "Redis cut database reads 30%" is the cache-aside layer. Deep chapter: Masters India.

4.4 GeeksforGeeks, SDE (Aug 2021 to Nov 2022)

Same facts as the PDF. The 20% premium lift and the 30% course-sales lift are business numbers. Say "I owned the engineering, and the business team attributed the lift." Deep chapter: GeeksforGeeks.

5. Off-PDF facts: what they are and how to say them

These are true and appear on LinkedIn or in your spoken answers, but not on the PDF. A sharp recruiter may notice the difference. The safe move is to own it: "That one isn't on the PDF for space, but yes, it's true."

Fact What it measures Where it appears
100% Go statement coverage, 1,200+ tests Every line of the AssortSmart Go code runs under at least one of 1,200+ tests, enforced in CI About long, IA blurb, cover letter, Application Kit
1.6M article-seasons The size of the full product catalog, counted as product × season IA blurb
$100 per pass LLM token spend for one full scoring pass of about 88k items IA blurb
150k to 190k rows/s per stream Copy rate of each of the two parallel season streams that add up to about 344k About long
golangci-lint, SAST/SBOM Go linting, static security scanning and a software bill of materials in CI IA blurb only
55 GB memory cap, 16 GB spill The limits that made the weekly build fit Application answers

How to talk about each one.

100% Go coverage across 1,200+ tests. Say: "On the Go platform we hold a 100% statement-coverage gate across more than 1,200 tests. It's on LinkedIn rather than the PDF." Do not mix it up with Uber FRM. At Uber the PDF says module statement coverage reached 100% after the ORM migration, and the FRM test count you say out loud is 1,100+. Two different codebases, two different counts.

1.6M article-seasons. This is the catalog. 348k is what the engine actually scores. Say: "The catalog has about 1.6 million article-seasons. The decision engine evaluates 348 thousand of them, 88 thousand per pass." Never say "we score 1.6 million".

$100 per pass. Say: "A full pass of about 88 thousand items costs roughly $100 in tokens. We know because every step logs tokens and USD cost in our JSON telemetry." Do not work backwards from the 73% cost cut to invent a "before" price. Those numbers come from different measurements.

150k to 190k rows/s per stream. Say: "Two season streams ran in parallel at about 150 to 190 thousand rows a second each, around 344 thousand combined." It is a copy rate, not traffic.

golangci-lint and SAST/SBOM. These are on the LinkedIn draft but are not in your locked resume facts. Keep them on the live profile only if you can explain what you configured. Otherwise delete that clause before pasting.

55 GB and 16 GB caps. Verbal depth for the 170 GB story. Use them when the interviewer asks "how did you make it fit?"

6. LinkedIn vs the PDF, and why the differences are fine

Area PDF LinkedIn
Length Two pages, every word fought for About up to roughly 2,600 characters, plus longer experience entries
Voice Achievement bullets tuned for ATS keywords First person, conversational
Off-PDF facts None 100% Go coverage and 1,200+ tests, 1.6M catalog, $100 per pass, per-stream copy rate
Honesty notes Implicit Spelled out ("measured in flight", "a gate, not live accuracy", "Kafka and Flink are Uber Menu")
Stack wording One track per PDF One profile for all tracks. This pack uses the Java + Python + Go wording

The rule. LinkedIn may add true detail. It may never give a different number for the same thing, a different stack for the same project, or a stronger claim than the PDF. "Cut planner pivots from 189s to 12s" on both is fine. "15.5×" on the PDF and "20×" on LinkedIn would not be.

Why this is fine. The PDF is a two-page filter document. LinkedIn is a longer, browsable profile. Recruiters expect LinkedIn to carry more detail. What they punish is inconsistency, not extra truth.

The one real risk: one profile, three PDFs. The live LinkedIn can show only one FRM stack. This pack uses Spring Boot and Spring Data JPA / Hibernate, which matches the Java + Python + Go PDF. Whichever version you put live, keep it consistent with the PDF you send most often. If you send a different track's PDF, expect a recruiter to notice the difference and answer truthfully.

7. Recruiter call script: the first five minutes

The first five minutes decide whether the recruiter sends you on. Your goals are to learn what the role really needs, give a pitch shaped to it, handle logistics cleanly, and leave with a clear next step.

sequenceDiagram participant R as Recruiter participant T as Tarun R->>T: Hi, thanks for making time T->>R: Thanks. Before I share my background, could you tell me about the team? R->>T: Team, stack, level T->>R: 90-second pitch shaped to what you just heard R->>T: Fit questions about stack and scale T->>R: One number per answer R->>T: CTC, notice period, why looking T->>R: Structured answers from section 8 T->>R: What does the process look like, and what is the next step?

What to notice: you ask about the role before you pitch, so your pitch can lead with whatever they care about.

Minute 0 to 0:30. Open and ask first.

"Thanks for reaching out. Before I walk through my background, could you tell me a bit about the team and what this role will own? That way I can focus on what's relevant."

Minute 0:30 to 2:00. The 90-second pitch. Lead with whatever matches what they just said. The default order:

"I'm a Senior Software Engineer with five years in Java, Python and Go backends. Right now at Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a retail planning product. I architected the multi-tenant Go platform that peaks at 10 thousand requests per second, built ClickHouse rollups that took planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, and built an AI decision engine that scores 348 thousand article-seasons, plus a copilot called Ask Iris. Before that I spent almost two years at Uber via EPAM. I owned the Financial Risk Management scoping backend, which cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days, and I led three engineers. I also worked on Uber Eats menu ingestion, which cut restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours. Before that, at Masters India, I led a PHP to Spring Boot migration that cut p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds. I'm looking for a senior backend, platform or applied-AI role where I can own a system end to end."

How to shape it:

  • Data platform or infrastructure role: lead with ClickHouse (189 seconds to 12 seconds, six rollup tables, the Go copier at about 344 thousand rows a second).
  • Applied-AI role: lead with the decision engine, Ask Iris and the 80% CI promotion gate.
  • Backend or fintech role: lead with Uber FRM (14 days to 3 days, 36 endpoints, SOX checks) and Masters India (1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds).

The 30-second and 3-minute versions are in Introductions and career story.

Minute 2:00 to 3:30. Fit questions. Recruiters usually ask "Have you worked with X?" and "What scale?" Answer each with yes or no, then one project, then one number. Keep each answer under 20 seconds.

"Yes, Kafka at two places. At Uber Eats with Flink for menu ingestion, and at Masters India for an e-invoicing pipeline at over a million submissions a day."

If they name something you only know at skills level (Kubernetes, gRPC, DynamoDB, pgvector, C or C++), say so plainly: "I know it at a working level, but I haven't owned it in production. My production depth is in X."

Minute 3:30 to 4:30. Logistics. Use the structures in section 8.

Minute 4:30 to 5:00. Close with questions.

"What level is this role scoped at? What does the interview process look like, and what's the timeline? What's the best next step from here?"

Write down the recruiter's name, the role, the level, the next step and the date they promised. You need them for the follow-up email.

8. Current CTC, notice period and "why are you looking"

These three questions are where candidates most often hurt themselves. Never invent or round a number. The structures below have blanks, and you fill them from your own payslip, offer letter and contract.

8.1 Current CTC

Background checks often verify past pay through payslips or tax documents. An inflated figure can cost you an offer after you have already resigned.

Structure: break it down, state the truth, then move to expectations.

"My current CTC is [fixed amount] fixed plus [variable amount] variable, so [total] in all. [Only if true: There's also [joining bonus / stock] that I can share details on.] For this role I'm looking at [your range], based on the level and the market for this kind of work."

If they push for an expected number before you know the level:

"I'd rather make sure we're aligned on level first. Could you share the band for this role? If it's in the right range, I'm happy to keep moving."

Do not: round up, quote your expected number as your current one, or say "it's confidential" when the form requires it. If the form makes CTC mandatory, enter the true figure.

8.2 Notice period

Structure: contractual number, then what is actually possible.

"My notice period is [N days] as per my contract. [Pick only what is true: I can ask for early release / buyout is possible / I've already resigned and my last day is [date].] Realistically I could join around [date]."

Do not promise an early joining date you cannot get. If you do not know whether early release is possible, say "I'd need to check with my manager, and I'll confirm by [day]."

8.3 "Why are you looking?" (and "why after five months?")

You joined Impact Analytics in May 2026, so a recruiter will notice the short tenure. Answer calmly, positively and briefly. You are not running from the work. You want a bigger stage for it.

Structure: what you built, what you want next, why this company.

  1. What you built (one sentence, positive). "At Impact Analytics I've shipped a lot quickly: the Go platform at 10k peak RPS, the ClickHouse rollups, the AI decision engine and Ask Iris."
  2. What you want next (one sentence, forward-looking). "I want a larger production surface and a harder design-review bar. I'm not running from the work."
  3. Why this company (one sentence, specific). "Your [team or system] is exactly that kind of problem."

If they ask about four companies in five years:

"Each move added a layer. Product features at GeeksforGeeks, a SaaS migration and mentoring at Masters India, Uber-scale platform work via EPAM, and data plus agentic systems at Impact Analytics. I was at Uber via EPAM for almost two years, which shows I stay when the scope compounds. I'm optimising for that again."

Do not: criticise any employer or manager, lead with money, apologise as if you failed, or call the current role "not real". For the full career story, see Introductions and career story.

8.4 Other logistics questions

  • "Are you interviewing elsewhere?" Answer truthfully and briefly: "Yes, a few processes. I'm being selective." Mention an offer only if you actually have one.
  • "Which level are you targeting?" "Senior Software Engineer, or SDE2+ at companies that level differently." These are the same words as your About section.
  • "Were you an Uber employee?" "I was employed by EPAM Systems and worked on the Uber account."

I'm looking at [Company] senior backend / data platform / applied-AI roles. If you are sourcing for [Team], I would love a quick screen. Resume here: [link].

Notes. Use it after a connection is accepted or as an InMail. Replace [Team] with a real team name from the job post.

9.5 Data platform hook

I built six ClickHouse rollup tables for planner reads and a Go pump that copies season partitions at about 344k rows/s combined, measured on a 4.09B-row attr weekly set. Weekly grain is one fiscal week per INSERT after a roughly 170 GB OOM.

Notes. Add it to the cold email for infrastructure roles. Never send the overclaim version, "I stream 4.09 billion rows at 344,000 rows/second". It implies a finished, continuous stream, and the truth is a partition copy timed while running.

Notes. The first line must name something real about their team, such as a blog post, a talk or a line from the job post. A generic compliment reads as a mass message. The last line ("No worries if you are swamped") gives them an easy no, which makes a yes more likely.

9.8 Cover letter

The full text is in Referral asks. Send it only when a form asks. Most engineering recruiters skip cover letters. It names 100% Go coverage across 1,200+ tests, which is off-PDF, so be ready to say so.

10. Follow-up cadence

Most replies come after a follow-up, not the first message. Following up is polite as long as each message is short, adds something, and stops after the third try.

flowchart LR D0["Day 0: send"] --> D4["Day 4 to 5: short bump in the same thread"] D4 --> D10["Day 10 to 12: second bump with one new detail or a redirect ask"] D10 --> D21["Day 21: close the loop politely"] D21 --> STOP["Stop. Re-contact only for a new role"]

What to notice: three touches at most, spaced further apart each time.

10.1 Schedules by situation

Situation When to follow up
Cold email or DM to a recruiter Day 4 to 5, day 10 to 12, close the loop on day 21
Referral ask, no reply One gentle nudge on day 5 to 7, then let it go
Referral ask, they said yes Within 24 hours send the job link, resume and 5-bullet fit summary. Thank them. Update them after each round
Recruiter screen done Same day: thank-you email with a recap of the next steps
Interview round done Within 24 hours: short thank-you to the recruiter
Promised decision date passes One business day later: polite status check
InMail from a recruiter Reply within 24 hours, even if the answer is "not right now"

10.2 Follow-up templates

First bump (same thread):

Hi [Name], bumping this in case it got buried. I'm still keen on [Role] and happy to share anything that helps. Thanks, Tarun

Second bump (add something or redirect):

Hi [Name], one last note on [Role]. If you're not the right person for this, could you point me to who is? Thanks either way.

Close the loop:

Hi [Name], I'll assume the timing isn't right for [Role]. I'd love to stay in touch for future openings on [Team]. Thanks for your time.

Referral said yes: the 5-bullet fit summary. Every line is a PDF fact. Reorder for the role.

Thank you so much! Here is the job link: [link]. My resume is attached. A quick fit summary:

  • Multi-tenant Go/Gin platform at 10k peak RPS at Impact Analytics (AssortSmart).
  • ClickHouse planner pivots from 189s to 12s on 250M-row operations, through six rollup tables.
  • AI decision engine scoring 348k article-seasons, plus the shipped Ask Iris copilot, behind an 80% CI promotion gate.
  • Uber via EPAM, FRM: reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days, 36 Spring Boot endpoints, led 3 engineers.
  • Masters India: p95 latency from 1.2s to 300ms, and a Kafka e-invoicing pipeline at 1M+ submissions/day.

After a recruiter screen:

Hi [Name], thanks for the time today. To recap: [Role], [level], and the next step is [step] by [date]. I've attached my resume again for convenience. Looking forward to it.

Status check after a missed date:

Hi [Name], just checking in on [Role]. I know these things take time. Is there any update on next steps? Thanks, Tarun

11. Say this / don't say this

Say this Not this
"Uber via EPAM" "I worked at Uber" with no qualifier
"344 thousand rows a second during the copy" "344k RPS" or "344k TPS"
"Measured on a 4.09-billion-row set while the copy was in flight" "I migrated 4 billion rows"
"80% is our CI promotion gate" "Our model is 80% accurate in production"
"73% cheaper and the 74% baseline come from a separate 200-case benchmark" "80% vs a 74% baseline" as one comparison
"Kafka and Flink were Uber Eats. Kafka was also Masters India" Any Kafka, Flink, CDC or Kubernetes operations at Impact Analytics
"Led 3 at Uber FRM. Mentored 2 at Masters India" "Led a team of 5"
"98% field fidelity in offline evaluation" "98% accurate in production"
"The catalog is 1.6M. We score 348k" "We score 1.6 million article-seasons"
"100% Go coverage across 1,200+ tests, it's on LinkedIn" Mixing it with the Uber FRM count of 1,100+
"15.5× was query time. The 170 GB fix was load time" "Fixing the OOM made pivots 15× faster"
A structured CTC answer with real numbers Rounded-up or invented CTC figures
"I'm looking for a bigger stage for this kind of work" Criticising your current employer

Also keep these honest: Ask Iris has no SLA or usage numbers. There is no human review queue in the AssortSmart system. LangSmith is on Ask Iris only. The Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight are verbal only. Never offer to share or open-source the ClickHouse copier.

12. Practice drill

  1. "Your LinkedIn says 1,200+ tests but your resume doesn't. Why?" "The PDF is two pages, so it didn't fit. It's true: the AssortSmart Go code holds a 100% statement-coverage gate across more than 1,200 tests, enforced in CI."
  2. "What does '4B-row weekly rollups' mean?" "One table, the attribute-level weekly rollup, holds 4.09 billion rows across two seasons. I timed my Go copier on it while moving it between ClickHouse clusters. Not every table is that big."
  3. "So your system handles 344 thousand requests a second?" "No, that's a copy rate in rows per second, across two parallel season streams. The request number is 10 thousand peak requests per second on the Go/Gin platform."
  4. "How do you use Kafka at Impact Analytics?" "I don't. My Kafka work was at Uber Eats, with Flink, and at Masters India. At Impact Analytics the data layer is ClickHouse, PostgreSQL and BigQuery."
  5. "What's an article-season, and why do you have two numbers, 348k and 1.6M?" "An article-season is one product in one selling season. The catalog has about 1.6 million. The decision engine evaluates 348 thousand of them, 88 thousand per pass."
  6. "What's $100 per pass?" "One full scoring pass of about 88 thousand items costs roughly $100 in LLM tokens. Every step logs tokens and dollar cost in our telemetry, so we know."
  7. "Is your model 80% accurate?" "80% is the CI gate a release must pass on our 300-case harness. It isn't a live accuracy claim for every tenant."
  8. "You worked at Uber?" "Via EPAM. I was employed by EPAM Systems on the Uber account, and I was tech lead of an EPAM pod of three on the FRM platform."
  9. "Why are you looking after only five months?" "I've shipped a lot quickly at Impact Analytics, including the Go platform, the ClickHouse rollups and the AI decision engine. I want a larger production surface and a harder design-review bar. I'm not running from the work, and your [team] is that kind of problem."
  10. "What's your current CTC?" "[Fixed] fixed plus [variable] variable, so [total]. For this role I'm looking at [range], depending on level. Could you share the band?"
  11. "What's your notice period?" "[N days] per my contract. [Only what is true about early release.] Realistically I could join around [date]."
  12. "You led 3 and mentored 2, so a team of 5?" "No, those are two different jobs. I led three engineers at Uber FRM via EPAM, and I mentored two at Masters India."
  13. "How was the 70% reconciliation cut measured?" "Quarterly reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days. That's the outcome the platform delivered for the close." If pressed: "The technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what we delivered."
  14. "Is 98% fidelity in production?" "No, it's an offline evaluation number. We scored the extracted fields against known-correct menus, not live traffic. I don't quote a live production accuracy figure."
  15. "Which roles are you targeting?" "Senior Software Engineer, or SDE2+ where levels differ, in backend, platform, data infrastructure or applied-AI systems."

13. Before every recruiter call: a two-minute checklist

  1. Re-read the job post and pick which pitch order fits (data platform, applied AI, or backend and fintech).
  2. Open your live LinkedIn and check that it matches the PDF you sent.
  3. Have your CTC breakdown, notice period and earliest joining date written down (real numbers, from your own documents).
  4. Pick the two numbers you most want them to remember for this role.
  5. Prepare one question about the team and one about the process.
  6. After the call, send the recap email the same day.

Impact Analytics: AssortSmart, Senior Software Engineer (Platform and AI)

AssortSmart is a retail merchandise planning product. Planners use it to decide which products to keep, drop or add each season. IA platform APIs are Go/Gin. The agent plane is Python (FastAPI, LangGraph).

A2 Decoupled inference from a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master via JSON payloads, ReplacingMergeTree writes, fallback to deterministic baseline on LLM timeouts The model never queries the big database. How to use this page

Tags used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, benchmark output, doc or code behind the number. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal, so say "targeting". HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. A number with no tag is simply the PDF figure.

1. The one-minute version (say this out loud)

"At Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a merchandise planning product that retailers use to decide which products to keep, drop or add each season. My work has two halves. On the AI side, I built a decision engine with three pipelines, Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style. It evaluates 348,000 article-seasons, about 88,000 items per pass, by blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM calls across seven AI lenses. The LLM never touches our 2.11-billion-row ClickHouse table. It gets prepared JSON, and if it times out the item falls back to its deterministic score. I also shipped Ask Iris, a secure chat copilot for planners, and every model change has to pass an 80% accuracy gate on a 300-case evaluation set. On the platform side, I own the multi-tenant Go and Gin API layer, which peaks at 10,000 requests per second. I made planner pivots 15.5 times faster, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, with ClickHouse rollups, fixed a 170 GB out-of-memory crash in how those rollups are built, and wrote a Go data pump that copies them between ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 344,000 rows per second."

If they want only 20 seconds, say: "I own the Go platform and the AI decision engine for a retail planning product. The AI scores 348,000 article-seasons with deterministic math plus seven LLM lenses, behind an 80% CI gate. The platform serves 10,000 peak requests per second, and I cut pivot time from 189 seconds to 12 seconds with ClickHouse rollups."

2. The business in plain English

Who the users are. Merchandise planners at retail companies. A planner decides things like "next autumn we will sell these 400 women's tops in these 120 stores, and we will stop selling these 60." AssortSmart is the SaaS (software as a service) product they do this in. Many retailers share one platform, and each retailer is called a tenant.

What they do in the product. They open large pivot grids of sales, stock, margin, sell-through and rate of sale, sliced by product, store, product attribute and week or season. They define their own KPIs (key performance indicators, the business metrics they track). And every season they decide, product by product, what stays in the range.

What hurt before. 1. Slow screens. Pivots were computed live from raw data on PostgreSQL. On a 250-million-row test, a typical pivot took 189 seconds. 2. Too many decisions to review by hand. A large retailer has hundreds of thousands of article-seasons. Simple rules like "drop if sell-through is below 40%" miss context, for example a product that sells slowly because it launched late or only sells on discount. 3. Every new KPI needed a code release. 4. Strict data separation. Each retailer must see only its own data, and each planner only the part of the product hierarchy they are allowed to see.

Why the company paid for this. Fast screens mean planners actually use the tool in planning season. Good keep and drop decisions reduce unsold stock and markdowns. Explanations make planners trust the AI. Cost and reliability controls make it affordable to run the AI for every client every season.

Words you need

Term Plain meaning
Article-season One product in one selling season. "Blue linen shirt, Summer 2026" is one article-season.
Sell-through / rate of sale Sell-through is the share of stock that sold (80 of 100 units is 80%). Rate of sale is units sold per store per week.
LLM lens One focused question the LLM (large language model) answers about an article, such as "Do other colours of this style steal its sales?" It returns a score, a confidence and reason codes.
Deterministic Same input always gives the same output. Normal code is deterministic. LLM calls are not.
ClickHouse A columnar analytics database. It stores each column separately and compresses it, so summing a column over billions of rows is fast.
Rollup A table of totals computed ahead of time, so screens read totals instead of raw rows. Like a monthly bank summary instead of re-adding every transaction.
ReplacingMergeTree A ClickHouse table type that keeps only the newest version of a row with the same key. Think of a notebook where you never erase: you write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines.
Circuit breaker After too many failures in a row, stop calling a failing service for a while. Like a home fuse that trips to protect the wiring.
Checkpoint Saved progress so a job can resume where it stopped. Like a video game save point.
Google Wire A Go tool that generates the code that wires components together at build time, so a missing dependency fails the build instead of production. This is called compile-time dependency injection (DI).
h2c HTTP/2 over plain TCP without TLS on that hop. HTTP/2 lets many requests share one connection.
UAM User Access Management: which user may see which part of the data.
OOM Out of memory. A query used more RAM than allowed and was killed.
CI gate An automated check in the build pipeline that blocks a change if a score is below a threshold.

What to notice: screens read rollups, never raw facts. The LLM only ever sees JSON, and our code does every database read and write. Every failure path in the AI batch still produces a row.

Walking through it, left to right.

The core platform is the Go side. A planner's browser calls the Go/Gin API edge, a single Go process that handles routing, JSON, auth, timeouts and tracing. There is no reverse proxy (such as Nginx) in front of it, so the edge protects itself with nested timeouts. The auth waterfall answers "who is this?" cheaply: Redis first (a cache of recently verified identities), then the slower verifiers. PostgreSQL answers "what may they see?" through roles and hierarchy scopes. When a screen needs a KPI, the formula parser turns the user's formula into a safe SQL fragment, and the query runs against one of six ClickHouse rollup tables. Separately, on the write side, loaders build those rollups from raw daily facts one fiscal week at a time, and the Go pump copies rollup partitions to another ClickHouse Cloud cluster. Datadog records a trace for every request.

The agent plane is the Python side (FastAPI and LangGraph). Our Python code reads the 2.11-billion-row ClickHouse master, computes KPIs, and produces the deterministic score s_det. It packs only the fields the LLM needs into JSON payloads. The orchestration registry runs the fixed batch order: peer benchmark context, then a decider that picks which lenses matter and how to weight them, then the seven lenses. Their combined score is s_agent. The blend gives the final score, and the result is written as decision rows through ReplacingMergeTree, each stamped with a config_hash. If the LLM times out, the item falls back to s_det and still gets a row. Ask Iris is the chat copilot where planners query KPIs and inspect these decisions, traced in LangSmith.

A tiny worked example of the blend (illustrative numbers, real formula and threshold). A blue linen shirt gets s_det = 0.62 and s_agent = 0.50. The final score is 0.4 × 0.62 + 0.6 × 0.50 = 0.248 + 0.300 = 0.548. The rule is keep if the final score is at least 0.55, so this article is a Drop, with an explanation like "Sell-through is acceptable, but demand is slowing and most units sold on discount." If the LLM had timed out, the shirt would get its deterministic outcome (0.62, so Keep) and the other items in the pass would carry on.

Bullet In plain words How it works Number and what it means
A1 Decision engine The AI tells planners which products to keep or drop each season, plus two sister pipelines for missed opportunities and top styles. Python computes s_det from sell-through and rate of sale. Seven LLM lenses score qualitative evidence, a decider weights them into s_agent, and the blend is 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent. Keep if the final score is at least 0.55. 348k article-seasons are the ones evaluated. 88k is how many items one pass processes. 7 is the number of lenses. Say "348,000 article-seasons, about 88,000 per pass".
A2 LLM never queries the database The model gets a prepared JSON summary, not database access, and a timeout never blocks a run. Python reads ClickHouse and builds trimmed JSON per batch. "Asynchronously" describes how batches run. The LLM has no SQL tool. Results are written through ReplacingMergeTree, so a retry simply writes a newer version of the row. On timeout, the item keeps its deterministic score. 2.11B rows is the size of the ClickHouse master. It shows why we never let a model write queries against it.
A3 Orchestration registry One shared harness that keeps long AI runs alive when the LLM provider fails, and records exactly what each run used. Hard timeouts per call. A circuit breaker trips after about 5 consecutive failures or a high failure fraction. Checkpoint files (det.json, agent_progress.json) let --resume skip work already done. config_hash is a SHA-256 of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog, stamped on every row. JSON telemetry logs tokens, USD cost, step time and fallbacks. 88k articles per batch run, the same pass size as A1.
A4 Ask Iris A chat assistant where planners ask about KPIs and why the AI decided something. JWT (a signed login token) is checked when the WebSocket opens. The user's hierarchy scope (plan_scope) is frozen at that handshake, so it cannot change mid-chat. A LangGraph supervisor routes each step, and an evaluator loop retries a weak answer at most 3 times (MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3). LangSmith traces every step. 3 attempts is the hard loop cap. No usage or SLA (service level agreement) numbers exist, so do not give any.
A5 Evaluation and cost Nothing ships unless it passes a test set, and we picked a cheaper model without losing coverage. A 300-case evaluation file runs in CI. Promotion is blocked below 80% (gold_min_accuracy 0.8 in eval.json). Separately, a 200-case gold benchmark compared models and the deterministic baseline. The blended LLM scored about 63%, below the 74% deterministic baseline, so we froze the blend weights instead of retuning them to look better. 300 cases and 80% gate: the CI promotion bar. 73% lower cost at 100% coverage (200 of 200 complete) and 74% baseline: both from the separate 200-case benchmark. MEASURED.
C1 Go/Gin platform The main API that every planner screen talks to, shared by many retailers. Gin handles routing and middleware. Wire generates the dependency wiring at build time. Go serves h2c directly with no reverse proxy, so the server sets its own nested timeouts (whole request, then each downstream call inside it). Datadog traces each request. 10k peak RPS: requests per second at peak. No SLA number exists, so keep reliability qualitative.
C2 KPI formula parser Business users type a KPI formula and it works on the next request, with no code release. A Go tokenizer and parser read the formula, map logical names to physical columns, allow only approved functions, and emit parameterized SQL. Unknown tokens fail closed. Every expression is wrapped as ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0) so dividing by zero returns 0 instead of infinity. No number on this bullet. The value is speed of change and safety.
C3 Tenancy and access Each retailer sees only its own data, and each planner only their part of the hierarchy. Redis caches verified identities. On a miss, the waterfall tries Firebase Admin, then JWT or Google OIDC. API keys are compared in constant time. PostgreSQL holds roles and UAM scopes, and those scopes filter every PostgreSQL and ClickHouse query. No number. Note: isolation is access control, not encryption.
C4 Faster pivots, and the OOM fix Two separate stories. Pivots got 15.5 times faster through rollups. Separately, the rollup build stopped crashing on memory. Six MergeTree rollup tables (product, store and attribute, each by season and by week), partitioned by season_code. The weekly builds now insert one fiscal week per INSERT SELECT, with memory and disk-spill caps. 15.5× = 189s to 12s on a 250M-row harness (12.3s, rounded). MEASURED. This is query time. 170GB is the out-of-memory crash on weekly builds. This is load time. One did not cause the other.
C5 Cross-cluster copy Copying rollups to another ClickHouse Cloud cluster when the normal cluster-to-cluster copy was blocked by network allowlists. A Go pump speaks ClickHouse's native protocol over TLS (port 9440). It reads the next 500k-row batch while sending the previous one (double buffering). TSV ledgers and checkpoint files record finished work. If a season's copy fails, we DROP that partition and recopy it. ~344k rows/s = combined ingest rate of two season streams, not requests per second. MEASURED in flight. 4.09B = largest partition set copied (attribute weekly, two seasons). 500k rows per batch.

5. Key design decisions (short form)

Each decision has the what, why, alternative and trade-off. The full version is in the handbook chapters.

The LLM never queries the database (A2). What: the model gets JSON prepared by our code. Why: a model writing SQL against 2.11 billion rows could run unbounded scans, break tenant scoping, or invent numbers. Our code computes the math once and the same way every time. Alternative: give the agent a SQL tool. Why not: cost, safety, and tests could no longer check the numbers. Trade-off: the payload must be designed carefully, and the LLM can only reason about what we chose to send. If asked what I'd change, I would keep this boundary.

Deterministic score plus LLM lenses, with fallback (A1, A2). What: money math stays in Python, the LLM only adds qualitative judgement. Why: LLMs are good at weighing evidence and explaining, and bad at arithmetic. Alternative: let the LLM decide alone. Why not: no stable baseline and no safe fallback. Trade-off: two scores to maintain and a blend to justify. The evaluation in A5 is exactly how we kept that honest.

App-native orchestration registry instead of Airflow or Temporal (A3). What: one Python registry shared by all three pipelines. Why: we needed resume logic tied to our own checkpoints, ClickHouse inserts, config hashing and per-run cost JSON. Alternative: Airflow or Temporal, which are strong general workflow engines. Why not: more infrastructure than a batch job with a resume flag needed. Trade-off: we own the retry and resume code ourselves. If the number of pipelines grew a lot, I would revisit a workflow engine.

Rollups, and building them one fiscal week at a time (C4). What: six pre-aggregated tables, loaded week by week. Why: screens read totals instead of raw rows, and one week fits in memory where a whole season did not. Alternative: bigger memory caps. Why not: a whole season failed even at 80 GB and 200 GB caps. Trade-off: many more insert statements to run and track, in exchange for a build that finishes.

A custom Go pump with drop-and-recopy rollback (C5). What: our own native-TLS copier instead of ClickHouse's built-in cross-cluster copy. Why: IP allowlists blocked cluster-to-cluster copy. Trade-off: during a recopy, readers of the target can see a partial season. A swap-based design using REPLACE PARTITION from scratch tables was written but not executed. That is what I would do next.

Honesty box: say this carefully
• 80% is a CI promotion gate, not "every tenant is live at 80% accuracy".
• 73% and 74% come from the separate 200-case gold benchmark, not from the 300-case file. Never fuse the two sets.
• 15.5× is query time and 170 GB is load time. They are two stories. One did not cause the other.
• 344k is rows per second of ingest, not requests per second.
• The 4.09B copy was measured in flight. Say "measured on a 4.09-billion-row copy", not "the cutover finished".
• "Atomic partition rollback" means DROP PARTITION, then recopy that season. It is not an atomic swap that live readers never notice.
• Ask Iris is a shipped capability. There are no SLA or usage numbers. Do not invent any.
• LangSmith is on Ask Iris only, not on the Keep/Drop batch. The batch uses custom JSON telemetry.
• Keep/Drop has no LLM orchestrator. The batch order is fixed: peer, decider, lenses, blend, explain.
• No human review queue. Offline evaluation replaced critic and evaluator agents in Keep/Drop.
• Not at Impact Analytics: Kafka, Flink, CDC (change data capture), Kubernetes operations, Milvus, sub-second ClickHouse claims. Kafka and Flink are Uber Menu. Milvus is Uber Menu. The CDC pipeline from PostgreSQL to ClickHouse was built by a colleague, so do not claim it.
• The platform APIs are Go/Gin. The agent plane is Python (FastAPI, LangGraph). Never say Spring Boot for Impact Analytics.
• Verbal only, not resume bullets: the Cluster Recommendation Copilot design (14 tools) and Hindsight.

Off-PDF but true

These are real and you can say them if an interviewer asks. They are not on the current PDF, so never present them as resume claims.

  • 1.6M article-seasons is the full catalog. It is a different number from the 348k that were scored. Do not mix them.
  • About $100 per pass in LLM token spend.
  • 100% Go statement coverage with 1,200+ Go tests. This is on LinkedIn and in verbal answers.
  • Model names on the 200-case benchmark: gpt-5.6-luna compared against gpt-5.4-mini, 200 of 200 complete.
  • Production deterministic threshold of 0.65 on that 200-case set, and the blended LLM at about 63%.
  • Circuit breaker trips after about 5 consecutive failures, or on a failure fraction.
  • OOM fix knobs: 55 GB memory cap, 16 GB spill, 8 threads, 4 weeks in flight. A product week is about 11 GB and an attribute week is over 40 GB. A whole season failed even at 80 GB and 200 GB caps.
  • 4.09B breakdown: 2,779,317,472 plus 1,311,108,195 rows, attribute weekly, two seasons. Each season stream ran at about 150k to 190k rows per second, about 344k combined.
  • Copy safety files: the weekly loader's TSV skip file and the copier's migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done files.
  • Why ClickHouse: planner pivots were slow on PostgreSQL. Proof-of-concept tests compared PostgreSQL and ClickHouse, ClickHouse won the large analytical reads, and PostgreSQL kept the thin metadata, UAM and roles.

What changed from older prep

Older versions of this page said things the current PDF does not. Use the current wording.

  • Older prep said "335 thousand products". The PDF says 348k article-seasons.
  • Older prep put "1.6M article-seasons" and "2.4 billion weekly rollups" on the PDF. 1.6M is off-PDF (the catalog). 2.4B is not on the PDF or in the current facts, so drop it.
  • Older prep said "88k per pass under $100" as a PDF claim. $100 is off-PDF.
  • Older prep said "physical air-gap" and "two-phase" writes. The PDF says the LLM is decoupled through JSON payloads, with eventually consistent ReplacingMergeTree writes. Don't say "air-gapped".
  • Older prep listed "100% coverage, 1,200+ Go tests, golangci-lint, SAST/SBOM" as a Core bullet. The fifth Core bullet on the PDF is now the cross-cluster migration (C5). Coverage and test count are off-PDF. golangci-lint and SAST/SBOM are not in the current facts, so only mention them if you can describe them from your own work.
  • Older prep put LangSmith in the orchestration registry. LangSmith is Ask Iris only.

6. Practice questions

1. "Walk me through the Keep/Drop decision for one product." I start with deterministic math. Python computes sell-through and rate of sale and turns them into a score called s_det. Then up to seven LLM lenses each answer one focused question, like whether other colours are cannibalising the product, and a decider weights them into s_agent. The final score is 0.4 times s_det plus 0.6 times s_agent, and we keep the product if it is at least 0.55. For example, 0.62 and 0.50 blend to 0.548, so that shirt is a drop, with a written reason the planner can read. Follow-up they may ask: "Why 0.4 and 0.6?" Those weights are frozen configuration. When the LLM underperformed the baseline, we froze them rather than retune them to look good.

2. "Why not let the LLM query ClickHouse directly?" Because the master table has 2.11 billion rows, and a model writing SQL can run unbounded scans, ignore tenant scope, or get the math wrong. Our code reads ClickHouse, computes the KPIs once, and sends the model a trimmed JSON payload. That keeps cost bounded, keeps numbers testable, and means the model can only reason about data we chose to give it. The model never gets a SQL tool.

3. "What happens when the LLM provider goes down mid-run?" The run still finishes. Every call has a hard timeout, and if a call times out the item falls back to its deterministic score and is marked as a fallback. If failures keep coming, about five in a row, the circuit breaker trips and stops hammering the provider. Checkpoint files mean that when we restart with --resume, we skip the deterministic scoring and the batches that already completed.

4. "How do you know which settings produced a given decision?" Every output row carries a config_hash. It is a SHA-256 fingerprint of the guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog used in that run. If a planner questions a decision, I can match it to the exact configuration. We also write JSON telemetry per run with tokens, USD cost, step duration and how many batches fell back.

5. "Your CI gate is 80%. Is the product 80% accurate in production?" No, and I'm careful about that. 80% is the promotion bar on a 300-case evaluation set in CI. A change that scores below it cannot ship. It is a guardrail, not a claim that every tenant sees 80% live. Follow-up they may ask: "Where do 73% and 74% come from?" From a separate 200-case gold benchmark, not the 300-case file.

6. "Tell me about the 73% cost reduction." On a separate 200-case gold benchmark, we compared models and found a cheaper one that completed all 200 cases, so 100% coverage, at 73% lower live execution cost. The same benchmark showed the deterministic baseline at 74%. The blended LLM came in around 63%, below that baseline. So instead of retuning the blend weights until the numbers looked better, we froze them. I'd rather ship an honest system than an overfit one.

7. "How does Ask Iris stop one retailer seeing another's data?" The planner's JWT is verified once when the WebSocket opens, and their hierarchy scope is frozen at that handshake. Later messages in the conversation can't change it. A LangGraph supervisor routes each step, and an evaluator loop retries a weak answer at most three times, so the model can't loop forever. LangSmith gives us a trace of every step. Follow-up they may ask: "What's its latency or usage?" It's a shipped capability. I don't quote usage or SLA numbers.

8. "How did you make pivots 15.5 times faster?" Pivots were adding up raw rows live. I built a pre-aggregation layer in ClickHouse: six rollup tables for product, store and attribute, each by season and by week, partitioned by season. On a 250-million-row test harness, a pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, 12.3 rounded. That is 15.5 times faster. Follow-up they may ask: "Was the 170 GB crash part of that?" No. That was a separate problem in building the rollups, which is load time, not query time.

9. "Tell me about the 170 GB out-of-memory crash." Building the weekly rollups for a whole season in one INSERT SELECT ran out of memory. It failed even with 80 GB and 200 GB caps. I sliced the build into temporal chunks, one fiscal week per insert, and set explicit memory and disk-spill caps so ClickHouse writes partial results to disk instead of dying. Each statement now handles a slice that fits in memory, so the build completes.

10. "Why write your own data pump instead of using ClickHouse's copy?" The normal cluster-to-cluster copy was blocked by IP allowlists between the ClickHouse Cloud clusters. So I wrote a Go pump that reads from one cluster and writes to the other over ClickHouse's native protocol with TLS. It uses 500,000-row double-buffered batches, reading the next batch while sending the previous one, and reached about 344,000 rows per second combined across two season streams. TSV ledgers and checkpoint files record finished work, and if a season's copy fails we drop that partition and copy it again, so we never keep a half season that looks complete. Follow-up they may ask: "Is that rollback atomic for readers?" No. During a recopy readers can see a partial season. A REPLACE PARTITION swap design was written but not executed.

7. Go deeper

  • Chapter 3: IA core platform covers C1 to C5 in full, with a request walk-through, the formula parser example, the auth waterfall and the migration design.
  • Chapter 4: IA agentic AI covers A1 to A5 in full, with all seven lenses, a worked score example, the registry and the evaluation split.

Uber (via EPAM): FRM Scoping Platform (Java + Python + Go track)

Role: Software Development Engineer 2 · July 2024 to May 2026 · Bangalore · always say "Uber via EPAM"
Resume tech line: Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, MySQL, JUnit, Bazel, Docker

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the Financial Risk Management (FRM) Scoping Platform for Uber Finance, explained from the finance basics up to the Spring Boot and Hibernate design, with every resume number and its source.
  • When to read it: before any round that may touch Uber, fintech, Java backends, MySQL data modelling, migrations, concurrency or "tell me about a hard bug".
  • What to memorise: the one-minute version, the five numbers (70%, $340M, 19M, 36, 100%) with how each was derived, the column-aliasing bug story, and the "what not to say" list.

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind it. TARGET means a design goal, so you say "targeting". ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. Numbers printed on the resume are the resume's claims, and you defend them as written.

Longer version of this story: Handbook chapter 5, Uber FRM. Older dense notes: FRM deep dive and Uber interview packs. Older prep said "30+ endpoints, do not say 36" and "do not say 19M" and "70% is only a target". That guidance is obsolete. The current resume prints 36, 19M and 70% as the outcome, and this page follows the resume.

1. The one-minute version

"At Uber, through EPAM, I owned the backend of the FRM Scoping Platform for Uber Finance. Every quarter Finance decides which financial line items and legal entities are important enough for the auditors to test. That used to live in a Google Sheets workbook, and reconciliation alone took about 14 days. I moved it onto a Spring Boot and MySQL service. I migrated 19 million raw general-ledger rows off Sheets into an 8-table normalized schema on Uber's service-owned MySQL standard, and shipped 36 Spring Boot endpoints for the financial math, a four-level line-item hierarchy and quarter-annualization. Reconciliation came down from 14 days to 3 days, a 70% cut, against a $340M materiality threshold. Because several managers edit the same close at once, I used optimistic row-locking, atomic cross-table writes and SHA-256 natural keys. I also led 3 engineers on a Spring Data JPA and Hibernate migration that removed a column-aliasing bug and took the module to 100% statement coverage."

2. The business in plain English

A public company like Uber publishes results every quarter. Before it can, Finance runs the quarterly close, a few intense weeks of finalising and cross-checking numbers. Inside the close, the FRM team runs scoping: deciding which lines and which entities are "in scope" for audit testing. Uber's external auditor, PwC, uses that output as evidence in its work papers.

Before this platform, scoping lived in spreadsheets. A spreadsheet row has no permanent identity, two people can overwrite each other, copies drift apart, and checking internal numbers against the filed numbers was manual. Scoping is a SOX control (Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the US law that makes public companies prove their financial-reporting process is reliable). So Uber needed something faster, repeatable, auditable and safe for many editors at once.

3. Words you need

  • GL (general ledger). The master record of every account balance. Think of it as one giant bank statement for every account at once. A "raw GL row" is one balance for one account, entity and period.
  • Oracle HFM (Hyperion Financial Management). Uber's consolidation system. It combines every entity's books into group numbers. The platform checks HFM amounts against the filed 10-Q (the quarterly SEC report).
  • FSLI (Financial Statement Line Item). One line on the balance sheet or income statement, such as Cash or Accounts Receivable. They nest four levels deep, L1 to L4, like folders. A parent equals the sum of its children.
  • Materiality. The size of mistake that would change a reasonable reader's decision. On the Q4 2025 close it was $340M. Any line above it is quantitatively material.
  • Quarter-annualization. Scaling a part-year income figure to a full-year estimate so it can be compared fairly. Generic form: year-to-date × 4 / number of quarters so far.
  • SOADB. Uber's standard for service-owned MySQL. Each service owns its database on a shared operating model, like every team getting its own locker in one maintained building.
  • JPA, Spring Data JPA and Hibernate. JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is Java's standard for mapping rows to objects. Hibernate is the engine that implements it. Spring Data JPA sits on top and writes the repetitive repository code for you.
  • Optimistic locking. Each row has a version number. A save only succeeds if the version is still the one you read. Like a shared document that says "someone edited this since you opened it, please reload".
  • Natural key. An ID computed from the data itself, so the same content always gets the same ID. Like identifying a book by its ISBN instead of a sticker number.
  • FSM (finite state machine). An item is always in exactly one named state (here Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed), and only some moves are allowed. A gate is a check that can block a move.

4. Architecture

flowchart LR HFM["Oracle HFM"] -->|extracts| ETL["Shared ETL pipeline"] ETL -->|loads rows| DB["MySQL on SOADB"] UI["Finance screens"] -->|REST calls| C["Spring Boot controllers"] C -->|DTOs| S["Services: rules, tree, annualization"] S -->|entities| R["Spring Data JPA repositories"] R -->|Hibernate SQL| DB UI -->|comments| COLLAB["Separate collaboration service"] DB -->|scoping output| PWC["PwC audit evidence"]

What to notice: requests only flow controller, then service, then repository, then MySQL. The ETL and the collaboration service are neighbours I integrate with, not systems I claim to have built.

Box by box. HFM and the shared ETL load quarterly balances into MySQL. That ETL was a shared pipeline responsibility, so I say "the service consumes HFM-loaded tables". Controllers (@RestController) are thin. They read the caller's identity from the x-auth-params-email header that Uber's gateway injects, validate the body with Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotNull), and an @ControllerAdvice maps errors to status codes. Services own the finance rules: materiality, the 5% component rule, residual risk, building the L1 to L4 tree and quarter-annualization. Repositories own every query. The collaboration service for comments and notifications was a separate service that I did not build.

Why layering matters: each layer can be tested with the layer below mocked, and three engineers could work on one feature without merge collisions.

5. Each resume bullet decoded

Bullet 1: ownership, 70%, $340M, 19M rows, 36 endpoints, L1 to L4

In plain words. I owned the backend Finance uses to scope the quarterly audit. I moved the data from Sheets into MySQL and built the API that does the finance math and the four-level tree.

How it works. The ETL gives every line a permanent uuid and stores the L1 to L4 labels once in a level_mapping table. Fact rows only hold a level_id that points at it. I personally owned the reconciliation v1 to v2 migration: the old Sheets-backed endpoints stayed live while new MySQL-backed /v2/ endpoints were added next to them (18 files, about +1,268 lines, MEASURED from the migration write-up). QA compared both for the same period, and the screens switched only after staging matched. v1 stayed as the fallback.

The core rule is two tests joined by OR: a line is Significant if its amount is above materiality or a manager answered a qualitative risk question with yes. Example: Accounts Receivable at $1,200M is above $340M, so it is material. Prepaid expenses at $90M is not, unless flagged.

Why this design, and alternatives. MySQL over Sheets because SOX needs stable IDs, concurrency control and an audit trail. A parallel run instead of a big-bang switch because the close has a hard deadline. PostgreSQL would have worked, but SOADB MySQL is Uber's service standard, and the ETL already flattens the hierarchy so we did not need recursive SQL. A columnar warehouse was rejected because this workload is many small transactional edits. Trade-off: two code paths for a while. What I'd do differently: an automated nightly diff between v1 and v2 instead of relying on QA side-by-side checks.

The numbers.

Number What it measures Where it comes from How to say it
70%, from 14 days to 3 days Quarterly reconciliation time (14 − 3) / 14 is about 79%, stated conservatively as 70%. The technical design doc framed this cut, and the platform delivered it "Reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days, about a 70% cut."
$340M Group materiality on the Q4 2025 close A metric row set by Finance and the auditors (MEASURED). Residual threshold was $170M, half of it "Against a $340M materiality threshold."
19M Raw GL rows migrated off Sheets Resume figure. Each quarterly extract was about 38K to 95K rows, about 1.7K to 1.8K accounts, about 400 entities "19 million raw GL rows moved into MySQL."
36 Spring Boot endpoints About 31 functional routes in the scoping service plus the collaboration-service comment and notification APIs from the design doc "36 endpoints automating the math and the hierarchy."

Why it mattered: reconciliation sits at the front of scoping, so every day saved there gives managers and PwC more review time before the filing deadline.

Bullet 2: 8-table schema, optimistic locking, atomic syncs, SHA-256 keys

In plain words. During close, data loads and managers' edits were fighting over the same data (lock contention: writers queuing on the same database locks). I designed a normalized schema where each fact lives once, gave every reviewable item one shared status model, and added three safety mechanisms.

Optimistic locking in Hibernate. A @Version field makes Hibernate add AND version = ? to every UPDATE and throw an exception when zero rows match.

@Entity
@Table(name = "balance_sheet")
public class BalanceSheetLine {
    @Id private String uuid;
    private String levelId;
    private BigDecimal hfmAmount;
    private BigDecimal priorAmount;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) private ReviewStatus groupStatus;
    private String conclusionScope;
    private String updatedBy;
    @Version private long version;
    // getters and setters omitted
}

public enum ReviewStatus { DRAFT, REVIEW, REOPEN, CLOSED }

Worked example: two managers open the same line at version 7. Manager A saves first and the row becomes version 8. Manager B saves with version 7, Hibernate's UPDATE matches zero rows, and Spring raises ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. The controller advice turns that into HTTP 409 Conflict, and B's screen asks them to reload. Nobody held a lock while thinking, and nobody's work was silently lost.

Polymorphic review-status means one status model reused by different kinds of rows: group lines, component lines, residual lines and threshold rows all move through Draft, Review, ReOpen and Closed. One validator and one state machine serve all eight screens.

Atomic cross-table syncs. Saving a qualitative answer and updating the mapped line's flag happen in one transaction. A runtime exception rolls both back.

@Transactional
public void saveAnswerAndSync(String assessmentId, String answer, String lineId, String user) {
    assessmentRepo.updateAnswer(assessmentId, answer, user);
    int rows = lineRepo.updateQualitative(lineId, "Yes".equals(answer) ? "YES" : "NO", user);
    if (rows == 0) {
        throw new NotFoundException("mapped line not found");   // rolls back both writes
    }
}

SHA-256 natural keys. Scoping questions are reloaded each quarter. The ID is a hash of the question text plus the normalized page name, so a reload updates rows in place instead of duplicating them.

static String questionUuid(String questionText, String pageName) throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
    String page = pageName.strip().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
    byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
            .digest((questionText + page).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest).substring(0, 32);
}

The normalization shown is illustrative. The insert then uses MySQL's ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.

Alternatives. Pessimistic locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) serialise everyone during the busiest weeks. Last-write-wins silently loses work, which is unacceptable for audit evidence. Auto-increment IDs plus "check if exists" is racy and differs between environments. 8 tables vs 11 entities: 8 is the normalized core on the PDF. The service code ends up with 11 mapped entities (verbal depth) because supporting tables arrived as screens landed.

Bullet 3: led 3 engineers, JPA/Hibernate migration, 100% coverage, Bazel, allowlists, 50% gate

The column-aliasing bug. Legacy native SQL joined a fact table to level_mapping, and both have a uuid column. Results were turned into a map keyed by column name, so the two uuid values collapsed into one key and the mapping table's value replaced the fact row's.

String[] keys = {"uuid", "amount", "uuid"};
Object[] row  = {"fact-111", 1200, "map-999"};
Map<String, Object> m = new HashMap<>();
for (int i = 0; i < keys.length; i++) m.put(keys[i], row[i]);
// m is {uuid=map-999, amount=1200}. The fact uuid is gone.

Symptom: rows looked right on screen but carried the wrong ID, so an edit to one recon line appeared to change another. Fix: typed JPQL projections into a record, where every column has its own name.

@Query("""
    select new com.uber.frm.ComponentRow(i.uuid, i.levelId, lm.uuid, lm.level1, i.amount)
    from ComponentEntity i
    join LevelMapping lm on lm.uuid = i.levelId
      and lm.fiscalQuarter = i.fiscalQuarter and lm.fiscalYear = i.fiscalYear
    where i.fiscalQuarter = :q and i.fiscalYear = :y
    """)
List<ComponentRow> findComponents(@Param("q") String q, @Param("y") int y);

public record ComponentRow(String fsliId, String levelId, String levelMappingUuid,
                           String level1, BigDecimal amount) {}

Package and entity names are illustrative. fsliId and levelMappingUuid can never collide.

100% module statement coverage means every statement in the migrated module runs in at least one test. Controller tests use @WebMvcTest and MockMvc with a mocked service, so no database is needed.

@WebMvcTest(GroupScopingController.class)
class GroupScopingControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockBean GroupScopingService service;

    @Test
    void staleVersionReturns409() throws Exception {
        when(service.updateLine(eq("a1f3"), any(), eq("priya@uber.com")))
            .thenThrow(new ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException(BalanceSheetLine.class, "a1f3"));
        mvc.perform(patch("/frm-scoping/group_balance_sheet/a1f3")
                .header("x-auth-params-email", "priya@uber.com")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"groupStatus\":\"CLOSED\",\"version\":7}"))
           .andExpect(status().isConflict());
    }
}

Stacked Bazel PRs are a chain of small, additive pull requests (entities, then repository, then service, then controller), each passing its Bazel test target and safe to deploy alone. That is how releases stayed zero-downtime. Reporting SQL allowlists mean only approved page names, statuses and statement types are accepted, and queries use bound parameters. The FSM gate blocks moving a line to Closed if it moved more than 50% quarter over quarter without review.

static void checkCanClose(BigDecimal current, BigDecimal prior, boolean reviewed) {
    if (reviewed) return;
    if (prior.signum() == 0) throw new IllegalStateException("no prior amount, review needed");
    BigDecimal change = current.subtract(prior).abs().divide(prior.abs(), 4, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    if (change.compareTo(new BigDecimal("0.50")) > 0) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("variance above 50 percent needs review before Closed");
    }
}

Example: $400M to $650M is 250 / 400 = 62.5%, so closing is blocked. $1,000M to $1,200M is 20%, so it passes. Do not confuse this with the residual-risk flag ($170M, half of materiality).

Leading 3 engineers means tech lead of an EPAM pod, not people manager. I split work by layer, set conventions (thin controllers, services own logic, repositories own queries, every write records updated_by), and held the review gate that every PR adds tests and passes Bazel. Across the service there are 1,100+ tests (verbal depth).

6. Tech used and why

Tech One line Why here Alternative
