Java + Spring Boot JVM language plus opinionated framework with embedded server Typed REST services, mature ecosystem, thread-per-request model fits short MySQL calls Python web stack
Spring Data JPA + Hibernate Repository layer plus ORM engine @Version locking, @Transactional, typed projections that killed the aliasing bug Raw JDBC strings, which caused the bug
MySQL on SOADB Relational database under Uber's standard ACID transactions for concurrent edits PostgreSQL, a warehouse
JUnit 5 + Mockito Test framework plus mocking Layer-by-layer tests without a database Integration-only tests
Bazel Monorepo build and test Per-layer test targets gate every merge Not a choice, it is Uber's monorepo
Docker Container packaging Reproducible local and CI runs Bare machines

7. Questions they will ask

"What exactly did you own?"
I owned the scoping service backend: the Spring Boot controllers, the services holding the finance rules, the repositories and the JPA entities. I personally drove the reconciliation migration from Sheets to MySQL. The HFM ETL was a shared pipeline and the comments service belonged to another team. The screens were built by front-end engineers on my APIs.

"19 million rows is not much for MySQL. Why is this hard?"
Agreed, it is not a scale problem. The hard part is correctness. One duplicated leaf silently inflates every parent in a four-level tree, several managers edit at once, and the output becomes audit evidence for an SEC filing. The slow part of the old process was manual mapping and chasing differences, and the platform automated that, which is where the 14 days to 3 days came from.

"Why optimistic locking and not row locks?"
Conflicts are rare and humans are slow. Managers mostly own different lines, so holding a lock for the minutes someone takes to type a conclusion would block everyone and make lock contention worse. With @Version, the second writer gets a clear 409 and reloads.
Follow-up they may ask: "How does Hibernate implement it?" It adds the version to the WHERE clause, increments it on success, and throws when zero rows match.

"Tell me the column-aliasing bug in 30 seconds."
A native query joined two tables that both had uuid. Rows were mapped into a map keyed by column name, so one uuid overwrote the other and edits landed on the wrong line. I moved those reads to typed JPQL projections with a distinct name for every column, and made that the standard in the migration.

"Why SHA-256 for a key?"
I needed a deterministic ID, the same question on the same page giving the same ID in every environment and every quarter. A content hash makes the bulk load idempotent, and the cost is trivial at this volume.

"How did stacked PRs give zero downtime?"
Each PR was small, additive and deployable on its own. New code lived beside old code until verified, like the v2 recon endpoints beside v1.

"Is the 70% measured?"
It is the outcome on the resume, 14 days to 3 days. If pressed: "The technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what the platform delivered for the close."

8. What not to say

  • "I was an Uber employee." Say Uber via EPAM.
  • "I built the HFM ETL" or "I built the comments and notifications service." Both belong to others.
  • "30+ endpoints" or "do not mention 19M". Obsolete. The resume says 36 and 19M.
  • Walking back the 70% unprompted, or claiming a precise time study.
  • "Big-data system" or any latency number for this platform. None was measured.
  • "Redis caching on FRM." There was no server-side response cache.
  • "100% coverage of the whole service." It is the migrated module only.
  • Merging "led 3 engineers" (FRM) with "mentored 2 engineers" (Masters India).
  • Extra FSM rules beyond the 50% delta-variance gate, or a specific annualization formula per line.
  • "55 line items and 14 entities" from an older resume. It is not on the current PDF.

Uber (via EPAM): Menu Ingestion & Automation, Uber Eats

Role: Software Development Engineer 2 · July 2024 to May 2026 · Bangalore · always say "Uber via EPAM"
Resume tech line (exact): Python, Selenium, Kafka, Flink, LangChain, Gemini, RAG, Milvus, GCP, Docker

This project stays Python on every resume track. There is no Spring or Java claim here.

How to use this page

  • What it covers: how restaurant menus get from messy websites and PDFs into the Uber Eats catalog, through a hardened Selenium fleet, Kafka, Apache Flink and a Gemini RAG extractor over Milvus. A short box at the end covers the separate ANZ document-compliance project.
  • When to read it: before questions on streaming, scraping, RAG or LLM systems, deduplication, idempotency or "an AI system you shipped".
  • What to memorise: from 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year and its derivation, 30K+ menus a month, 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation, 95%+ extraction success, and the honest meaning of "exactly-once".

Tags on this page. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. MEASURED means a log or document. The menu outcomes are HISTORICAL, and 98% is an offline evaluation number.

Longer version: Handbook chapter 6, Menu and ANZ. Older notes: Menu deep dive, Menu streaming numbers and Menu, ANZ and Milvus panel. Older notes also mention Spark, Pinot and fine-tuning. None of those is on the current resume, so treat them as study-only.

1. The one-minute version

"At Uber Eats, through EPAM, I worked on menu ingestion, which gets a new restaurant's menu into the catalog so it can take orders. Menus arrive as JavaScript-heavy sites, PDFs and images in many languages. I architected an automated pipeline. A Selenium fleet, which I hardened with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries, took extraction success to 95% plus from an estimated 60 to 65%. Scrapes flow through Kafka into a Flink job that deduplicates per vendor by content hash, normalizes to one schema and does idempotent catalog upserts. For messy PDFs we used RAG: retrieve similar labelled menus from Milvus and give them to Gemini 2.5 Pro, which returns JSON that must pass schema validation. That reached 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation. Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours at 30,000+ menus a month, and replacing a roughly $2 per menu manual and third-party cost saved about $600K a year."

2. The business in plain English

A restaurant on Uber Eats earns nothing until its menu is in the catalog, Uber's strict structured store of dishes, prices, sizes and add-ons. Getting it there is onboarding. Menus are hard because many pages only show items after JavaScript runs, many menus are scanned PDFs or photos, prices look like "8,50 €" or "¥1,200", sites block bots, and the same menu gets scraped repeatedly. Before this work onboarding took about 24 hours and cost about $2 per menu in manual and third-party processing. At 30K+ menus a month, that was slow and expensive.

3. Words you need

  • Selenium. Drives a real browser from code, so you see the page as a person does. Headless means no visible window.
  • Proxy pool. A set of middleman servers you rotate through, so the site sees their IP, not yours. A dynamic pool evicts banned or slow proxies automatically. Like a team of couriers: if one is turned away, send another.
  • Adaptive retries. Retry differently by failure type. A ban means switch proxy, a timeout means wait longer (backoff plus random jitter), a broken page means stop. A retry budget caps how much one hostile site can consume.
  • Kafka. A durable message log. We keyed messages by vendor_id, so each restaurant's events stay in order on one partition and can be replayed.
  • Apache Flink. A stream processor that keeps memory per key (keyed state). A watermark is Flink saying "I believe I have seen everything up to time T". A checkpoint is a consistent snapshot of state plus Kafka offsets, used to recover after a crash.
  • Content hash. A fingerprint (for example SHA-256) of the normalized menu. Same content, same hash.
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). Retrieve relevant examples first and put them in the prompt. Like an open-book exam.
  • Embedding and Milvus. An embedding is a list of numbers that captures meaning, so similar text lands close together. Milvus is an open-source vector database that finds the nearest embeddings fast.
  • Field fidelity. The share of extracted fields (name, price, description, modifiers) that exactly match the human label.
  • Idempotent upsert. Insert if missing, update if present, keyed by a stable ID, so doing it twice changes nothing.

4. Architecture

flowchart LR SRC["Partner sites, PDFs, images"] --> SEL["Selenium fleet on GCP"] SEL -->|raw files| RAW["Object storage"] SEL -->|scrape events| K["Kafka keyed by vendor_id"] K --> F["Flink: keyed dedup, normalize, route"] F -->|structured| CAT["Idempotent catalog upsert"] F -->|PDF or image| RAG["LangChain RAG extractor"] RAG -->|similar menus| MV["Milvus"] RAG -->|prompt| GEM["Gemini 2.5 Pro"] GEM -->|JSON| VAL["JSON Schema gate"] VAL -->|valid| CAT VAL -->|invalid or low confidence| HR["Human review"] CAT --> APP["Uber Eats catalog"]

What to notice: acquisition, transport, processing and AI extraction are separate stages. Nothing reaches the catalog without passing Flink's normalization or the schema gate.

Box by box. The Selenium fleet, packaged with Docker on GCP, loads each source through the proxy pool and stores the raw file, so the event only carries a pointer. Kafka lets scrapers write and move on without waiting for the catalog. Flink drops duplicate menu versions per vendor, normalizes fields, and routes structured content straight to the catalog and unstructured content to RAG. The RAG extractor chunks the document, finds similar labelled menus in Milvus, and asks Gemini 2.5 Pro for JSON. The schema gate blocks anything malformed.

5. One job, step by step

Illustrative data: café v_48213 in Lisbon has a scanned Portuguese PDF menu.

  1. A Selenium worker downloads the PDF, stores it, and publishes {"vendor_id": "v_48213", "content_type": "pdf", "content_hash": "9f2c...", "locale": "pt"}.
  2. Flink sees a hash it has not stored for this vendor, saves 9f2c, and routes the PDF to RAG.
  3. The extractor retrieves three already-labelled Portuguese café menus from Milvus.
  4. Gemini receives the chunk ("Tosta mista ..... 4,50 €"), the examples and the schema, and returns {"name": "Tosta mista", "price_amount": 4.50, "currency": "EUR"}.
  5. The JSON passes schema validation and is upserted keyed by vendor, menu version and item key.
  6. Ten minutes later the same PDF is scraped again. Same hash, so Flink drops it. No LLM cost and no catalog write.

6. Each resume bullet decoded

Bullet 1: 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K, 30K+ menus, 98% fidelity

In plain words. I architected the automated pipeline that gets menus into Uber Eats. For the hardest inputs, messy multilingual PDFs, we used an LLM grounded on similar labelled menus.

How it works.

def extract_menu(chunk_text: str, locale: str) -> dict:
    examples = milvus_search(embed(chunk_text), top_k=3, filter={"locale": locale})
    prompt = build_prompt(chunk=chunk_text, examples=examples, schema=CATALOG_SCHEMA)
    raw = gemini_generate(prompt)                 # Gemini 2.5 Pro, JSON only
    menu = json.loads(raw)
    jsonschema.validate(menu, CATALOG_SCHEMA)     # raises if the shape is wrong
    return menu

Simplified sketch. Function names and top_k are illustrative. Without examples, an LLM guesses at layout, may invent a dish, or drifts from the schema. Two or three labelled examples of similar menus show it which number is the price and how sizes become modifiers.

Why this design, and alternatives. Regex or template parsers break on every new layout and language. OCR plus rules gets the text but not the structure. A bare prompt is less consistent across cuisines. Training a custom model needs a big labelled set and retraining whenever the schema changes, while with retrieval a newly labelled menu helps the very next extraction. pgvector or a managed vector service would also work, and Milvus is what we used. Trade-off: LLM calls cost money, and offline evaluation is not live monitoring. What I'd do differently: sample live extractions for human spot checks to track fidelity in production.

The numbers.

Number What it measures How derived How to say it
24 hours to 2 hours Onboarding cycle time (HISTORICAL) (24 − 2) / 24 is about 92% "Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours."
$600K a year Cost removed About $2 per menu × 30,000 × 12 = $720K list, floored to $600K to be conservative "About $2 a menu at 30K a month is $720K. I quote $600K conservatively."
30K+ a month Menus processed (HISTORICAL) 30,000 / 30 is about 1,000 a day "More than 30,000 menus a month."
98% Field fidelity on an offline labelled set Example: 196 of 200 fields match labels "98% field fidelity in offline evaluation."

Why it mattered: restaurants go live the same day instead of the next, and the per-menu saving grows with volume.

Bullet 2: 95%+ success, Selenium hardening, Kafka and Flink, exactly-once upserts

Hardening the fleet.

def scrape_with_retries(url, source, max_attempts=4):
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        proxy = proxy_pool.get_healthy(source)
        try:
            page = selenium_fetch(url, proxy=proxy)
            if looks_blocked(page):              # CAPTCHA wall or soft 403
                proxy_pool.mark_banned(proxy)
                continue
            if item_count(page) == 0:
                raise EmptyMenuError(url)        # never green-light an empty menu
            return page
        except TimeoutError:
            if not retry_budget.allow(source):
                break
            time.sleep(min(2 ** attempt, 30) + random.uniform(0, 1))
    raise ScrapeFailed(url)

Simplified sketch with illustrative thresholds.

Flink keyed dedup. The stream is keyed by vendor_id, and state holds the last content hash.

Event time Hash State before Result
10:15 9f2c empty keep, state becomes 9f2c
10:25 9f2c 9f2c drop, duplicate scrape
next day a71d 9f2c keep, the menu changed

A time-to-live on state stops it growing forever. Event-time watermarks with bounded lateness stop a late page from an older version overwriting a newer one.

Exactly-once, the honest version. Delivery through Selenium, Kafka and Flink is at-least-once. After a crash, Flink restores the last checkpoint and reprocesses some events. The catalog write is an idempotent upsert keyed by vendor, menu version and item key, so a replay writes the same row again. The catalog sees exactly-once effects. It is not a two-phase commit across Gemini, partner sites and the catalog.

Why Kafka and Flink at about 1,000 menus a day? Not for average volume. For the shape of the load: bursts and retries, repeated scrapes needing per-vendor state, late pages needing event time, and replay after a parser bug. A simple worker queue would mean rebuilding those by hand. Kafka Streams could work at this rate, and Flink gave richer event-time support. Spark is not on the resume. If asked, it is a reasonable batch backfill option, as study-level talk only.

The number. 95%+ extraction success is HISTORICAL. The 60 to 65% starting point is ESTIMATED. Say: "Success went to 95% plus, from roughly 60 to 65% before hardening."

7. Tech used and why

Tech Why here Alternative
Python Scrapers, workers, LLM glue Go, less natural for browser automation and LLM tooling
Selenium JavaScript-rendered pages Plain HTTP, which misses rendered items
Kafka Buffer bursts, per-vendor order, replay Scrapers calling the catalog directly
Flink Keyed dedup state, event time Kafka Streams
LangChain + Gemini 2.5 Pro + RAG Chunk, retrieve, prompt, parse multilingual menus Templates and regex
Milvus Similarity search over labelled menus pgvector, managed services
GCP + Docker Where the fleet ran, packaged repeatably Bare VMs

8. Questions they will ask

"Is 98% a production number?"
No. It is offline evaluation on a labelled set, measuring the share of fields that exactly match the human label. In production the protection is the schema gate plus human review for low-confidence output.
Follow-up they may ask: "How would you monitor it live?" Sample a small share of live extractions for spot checks and alert on spikes in gate rejections.

"Do you really have exactly-once?"
Exactly-once effects, not exactly-once delivery. Delivery is at-least-once, and the upsert keyed by vendor, menu version and item key makes reprocessing harmless. I would not claim zero message loss.

"What stops the LLM inventing a dish?"
Three layers. Retrieval grounds it on real labelled examples, the schema gate rejects malformed output, and low-confidence output goes to a person instead of the catalog.

"How do you know a scraper broke silently?"
The dangerous case is a page that loads fine with no menu, after a layout change or CAPTCHA. We count an empty or suspiciously small menu as a failure and watch per-vendor item counts.

"What happens when a Flink job crashes?"
It restores the last checkpoint, Kafka offsets rewind to match, events since then are reprocessed, and idempotent upserts prevent duplicates. Consumer lag rises and alerts until it catches up.

"How did you get to $600K?"
About $2 per menu, times 30,000 menus a month, times 12, is $720K. I quote $600K as a conservative floor.

9. Related project: ANZ Document Compliance (Uber Mobility)

Keep this separate from Menu. ANZ is Uber Mobility (rides), not Eats, and it is HISTORICAL. I automated driver and vehicle document verification in Australia and New Zealand against local authority rules with a deterministic validation backend, a rules engine where the same document always gets the same verdict with the failing reason (for example "expired" or "does not match the vehicle record"). That reached 99.9% regulatory compliance and removed 20 hours a week of manual review queues. Rules beat ML here because regulators need explainable, repeatable decisions. Do not attach Selenium, Kafka, Flink or RAG to it, and do not invent driver or document counts.

10. What not to say

  • "98% accuracy in production" or "98% SLA". It is offline evaluation.
  • "Zero message loss" or "two-phase commit end to end".
  • The 60 to 65% baseline as measured. It is ESTIMATED.
  • $720K as the saving. The resume says $600K.
  • Spark, Pinot or fine-tuning as resume claims. None is on the PDF.
  • ClickHouse on Menu. ClickHouse belongs to Impact Analytics.
  • Milvus anywhere except Menu.
  • "I owned all of Uber Eats' catalog platform."
  • Peak 200 to 500 events per second unless asked, and then only as an ESTIMATED order of magnitude.
  • Merging the Menu Kafka story with the Masters India Kafka story. They are different products.

Masters India: GST Compliance & E-Invoicing Platform (Java + Python + Go track)

Role: Software Development Engineer 2 · December 2022 to June 2024 · Noida
Resume tech line: Java, Spring Boot, Hibernate, Kafka, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, ELK, New Relic, AWS

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the PHP-to-Spring Boot migration, the Kafka bulk e-invoicing pipeline, PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, idempotency and dead-letter queues, Redis caching, ELK and New Relic, and test coverage.
  • When to read it: before any question on "a migration you led", "a high-throughput pipeline", "idempotency", "Kafka vs a queue" or "how you made an API faster".
  • What to memorise: p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds (75%), 1,500+ clients, 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, 1M+ submissions a day, 100K+ concurrent imports, triage 70% faster, reads 30% lower, coverage 35% to 82%, 98% deploy success, mentored 2 engineers.

Tags on this page. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and the resume. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. MEASURED means a log or document. "Illustrative" marks made-up sample data used to explain a mechanism.

Longer version: Handbook chapter 7, Masters India. Older notes: Masters and GFG deep dive and Masters and GFG interview packs.

1. The one-minute version

"At Masters India I worked on a GST e-invoicing platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise clients. Indian businesses must register every B2B invoice with a government portal, which returns an official invoice number and a signed QR code. We validated their invoices and registered them safely at volume. I led the migration of a legacy PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, one route at a time behind the gateway with canaries. That cut p95 latency by 75%, from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute. I mentored two engineers through it. I designed the bulk pipeline on a Kafka event bus with PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, with idempotency keys so a retry can never register an invoice twice. It handled 1M+ submissions a day, with dead-letter queues and bounded retries because the government portal is unreliable near deadlines. ELK and New Relic with one request ID cut triage time by about 70%, a Redis cache cut database reads by 30%, and coverage went from 35% to 82%, which got us to 98% deployment success."

2. The business in plain English

GST (Goods and Services Tax) is India's main indirect tax. Every registered business has a GSTIN, a 15-character tax ID. For B2B sales above a turnover threshold, an invoice is only legally valid once it is registered with the government's IRP (Invoice Registration Portal). The IRP validates the invoice JSON and returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number) plus a digitally signed QR code. Think of the IRP as a notary that stamps a unique serial number on each document.

Masters India sat between enterprises and the IRP. Clients sent invoices one at a time from their ERP (accounting software) or as bulk files with thousands of rows. We validated them, registered them, stored the IRN and QR, and returned them by API or webhook.

The one constraint that shaped everything: once an IRN is issued, the invoice is a legal record. Cancellation is narrow and time-limited. A retry bug that registered the same sale twice would leave the client with two legal invoices and a compliance mismatch. So every step that talks to the IRP had to be safe to run twice.

What hurt before. The PHP (Laravel) monolith was synchronous. A request that called the IRP held a worker for the whole round trip. When the IRP was slow, workers ran out and unrelated requests queued. Deploys were all-or-nothing, and debugging meant logging into boxes and searching text logs. Load spikes many times above average in the days before filing deadlines, and the IRP is slowest exactly then.

3. Words you need

  • Strangler fig pattern. Replacing an old system gradually by routing traffic, route by route, to new code until the old system has nothing left. Named after a vine that slowly grows around a tree.
  • Canary release. Sending a small slice of traffic to new code first and watching errors and latency before sending more.
  • p95 latency. Sort 100 requests by time and take the 95th. 95% of requests were that fast or faster.
  • Kafka. A durable, ordered log of messages. A topic is a named stream, split into partitions for parallelism. Order holds only within a partition. Messages with the same key go to the same partition. A consumer group shares a topic's partitions, and different groups each read the full stream.
  • Idempotency. Doing something twice has the same effect as once, like pressing a lift button five times. An idempotency key is the ID that lets the system recognise "already done".
  • DLQ (dead-letter queue). A side queue for messages that keep failing, so they stop blocking the main flow. Like a "problem parcels" shelf in a post office.
  • Exponential backoff with jitter. Waiting longer after each failure (1s, 2s, 4s), plus a random amount so thousands of workers do not retry at the same instant.
  • HikariCP. The default database connection pool in Spring Boot. It keeps connections open and reuses them, like keeping a phone line open instead of redialling.
  • Cache-aside. Check Redis first. On a miss, read the database, store the result with an expiry (TTL), then return it.

4. Architecture

flowchart LR ERP["Client ERP or dashboard"] --> GW["Nginx gateway with per-route canary"] GW -->|not yet migrated| PHP["PHP monolith"] GW -->|migrated routes| API["Spring Boot services"] API --> RD["Redis cache"] API --> S3["Amazon S3 bulk files"] API -->|invoice events| KF["Kafka topics keyed by GSTIN"] KF --> W1["IRP submit consumers"] W1 -->|bounded retries| IRP["Government IRP"] W1 -->|failures| DLQ["Dead-letter topic"] KF --> W2["Persistence and webhook consumers"] W2 --> PG["PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter"] W2 --> MG["MongoDB signed responses"] API -->|request ID| OBS["ELK and New Relic"]

What to notice: PHP and Spring Boot sit side by side behind one gateway during the migration. Everything that talks to the IRP sits behind Kafka consumers and retries, never inside a user's request thread.

Box by box. The gateway decides per route whether traffic goes to PHP or a Spring Boot service, and in what percentage. Spring Boot services were split by domain (auth, single submit, bulk import, reconciliation), with Bean Validation on every request. Amazon S3 holds uploaded bulk files so the upload can return fast. Kafka carries stage events. IRP submit consumers call the government with capped concurrency and retries. Persistence consumers write the IRN and status into the right quarter table in PostgreSQL, and keep the variable-shaped signed responses in MongoDB for audits. Background work that did not need a replayable log ran as @Async and @Scheduled jobs, and chunked bulk-import validation fits Spring Batch (a skills-line item, so describe it at that level).

5. One job, step by step

Illustrative data: Acme Steel uploads 12,000 October invoices two days before its deadline. Say batches of 500, so 24 batches.

  1. The bulk service stores the file in S3, computes a SHA-256 fileHash, and returns 202 Accepted with an import_id. The browser does not wait.
  2. Validation runs batch by batch (schema, GSTIN format, duplicates). Each batch gets the key client + fileHash + batchIndex, for example acme:9f2c...e1:7.
  3. Valid invoices go to topic invoice.accepted keyed by GSTIN, so Acme's messages stay in order.
  4. A submit consumer checks the key in PostgreSQL. If already registered, it skips. Otherwise it marks irp_pending and calls the IRP.
  5. The IRN and QR come back. A persistence consumer writes them to the quarter table. An invoice dated 14 October 2023 lands in fy2023_q3.
  6. If one batch keeps failing, it goes to the dead-letter topic after bounded retries. The other 23 carry on.

6. Each resume bullet decoded

Bullet 1: migration, p95 and throughput

In plain words. I led the move from one PHP application to small Spring Boot services, gradually, so clients never saw a switch-over day.

How it works. For each route: record the PHP responses and write contract tests so the new service returns the same fields. Send a small canary percentage through Nginx. Watch error and latency dashboards. Ramp to 100% or roll back with a config reload, not a redeploy. Old and new code shared one database during cutover, on purpose, so there was one source of truth and no dual writes.

Where 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds came from. Caching alone cannot do 75%. Four changes added up:

  1. IRP calls left the request thread. The API returned 202 Accepted and Kafka consumers did the slow call. Where a call stayed synchronous, a non-blocking client (Spring WebClient) with a timeout, or a bounded thread pool, stopped it pinning a worker. This fixed the tail.
  2. Connection pooling with HikariCP instead of a new connection per request.
  3. Query and index fixes. Composite indexes like (client_id, invoice_date), pagination, and removing N+1 queries (1 query for a list plus 1 per item) with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph in Hibernate.
  4. Redis for repeated reads, which sped up the typical request, the body.

Short version: "Async IRP calls, pooling and query fixes moved the tail. Redis moved the body."

Alternatives. A big-bang rewrite risks every route on one day. Tuning PHP worker counts only moves the cliff. Dual writes create two sources of truth in a tax product. A fully reactive WebFlux rewrite was not needed because moving IRP calls to consumers already removed the blocking wait. Trade-off: two stacks to monitor for a while. What I'd do differently: put request-ID logging in place before the first canary.

Mentoring two engineers. Each owned a service extraction. I set the conventions (controller, service, repository layers, validation at the boundary, shared retry and idempotency helpers), reviewed their PRs closely early on, and paired on the first canary. This is mentoring, not people management.

Bullet 2: Kafka pipeline, quarter sharding, idempotency, DLQ

Why shard by tax quarter. Almost all writes land in the current quarter. Older quarters are mostly read for reconciliation and audits. Quarter shards keep the hot table and its indexes small and let a cold quarter be archived as one unit. Routing lived in application code, derived from the invoice date. India's financial year starts on 1 April.

static String taxQuarter(LocalDate d) {
    int fyStart = d.getMonthValue() >= 4 ? d.getYear() : d.getYear() - 1;
    int q = ((d.getMonthValue() - 4 + 12) % 12) / 3 + 1;
    return "fy" + fyStart + "_q" + q;
}
// 2023-10-14 gives fy2023_q3. 2024-02-10 gives fy2023_q4.

A wrong-quarter write is the main risk of this design, so the API rejected requests whose declared filing period did not match the derived quarter. Say this carefully: the PDF says "horizontally sharded by tax quarter". Describe the routing and reasons, and do not claim separate database clusters unless you clearly remember that. Today I would start with native PostgreSQL range partitioning.

Idempotent consumer with bounded retries and a dead-letter topic.

@KafkaListener(topics = "invoice.accepted", groupId = "irp-submit")
public void onBatch(InvoiceBatch batch) {
    String key = batch.idempotencyKey();              // client:fileHash:batchIndex
    if (jobs.isRegistered(key)) return;               // redelivery after success
    jobs.markPending(key, batch.clientId());          // INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    IrpResult result = irpClient.register(batch);     // throws Transient or Permanent IrpException
    jobs.markRegistered(key, result.irn());
}

@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler irpErrorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
    var toDlq = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
            (rec, ex) -> new TopicPartition("irp.submit.dlq", rec.partition()));
    var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);
    backOff.setInitialInterval(500);
    backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
    backOff.setMaxInterval(30_000);
    var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(toDlq, backOff);
    handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(PermanentIrpException.class);
    return handler;
}

Retry counts and delays are illustrative, not remembered production values. Spring Kafka's default backoff has no jitter, so add jitter with a custom BackOff. Because the partition key is the GSTIN, one taxpayer's messages are handled by one consumer at a time. If a worker crashes after the IRP succeeded but before marking it, the redelivery reaches the IRP again, and the IRP's own duplicate-document check is the backstop. A permanent error such as an invalid GSTIN goes straight to the dead-letter topic with no retries.

Exactly-once, the honest version. Kafka and retries give at-least-once delivery. Idempotent processing makes the second arrival a no-op. Together that is an exactly-once effect. The IRP is outside our transaction, so true exactly-once delivery across systems is not possible.

Why Kafka and not SQS or RabbitMQ. We needed per-taxpayer ordering, replay after a bug (move a group's offset back and reprocess), and several independent consumer groups on one stream (persistence, webhooks, audit). SQS deletes on acknowledgement and FIFO caps throughput per group. RabbitMQ could honestly have dispatched tasks at our scale. Replay and multi-reader audit tipped it to Kafka, at the price of more operational work.

The numbers. 1M+ a day is 1,000,000 / 86,400, about 12 per second on average (ESTIMATED). Deadline peaks were roughly 8 to 10 times that, so around 100 per second (ESTIMATED). 100K+ means invoices in flight across concurrent bulk imports, not 100,000 separate files uploaded at one instant.

Bullet 3: observability, caching, coverage

Request ID. A servlet filter stamps one ID on every request and puts it into the logging context (MDC), so every JSON log line, outgoing header and Kafka message header carries it.

@Component
public class RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String rid = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Request-ID"))
                .orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        MDC.put("request_id", rid);
        res.setHeader("X-Request-ID", rid);
        try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.remove("request_id"); }
    }
}

One Kibana search for that ID showed the whole path: accepted, sent to the IRP, timed out three times, parked in the DLQ. New Relic showed where the time went.

Redis cache-aside. In a 100K-row import every row needs the same client config and many repeated GSTIN lookups. Caching them is why total read load fell about 30%.

public ClientConfig clientConfig(String clientId) {
    String key = "client:config:" + clientId;
    String hit = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
    if (hit != null) return json.read(hit, ClientConfig.class);
    ClientConfig cfg = configRepo.load(clientId);
    long ttl = 600 + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(121);    // TTL jitter
    redis.opsForValue().set(key, json.write(cfg), Duration.ofSeconds(ttl));
    return cfg;
}

Config keys were deleted on every write. Slow-changing tax-rate masters were TTL-only. A short Redis lock (SET NX with expiry) lets only one worker rebuild a hot key after it expires, which stops a cache stampede.

Coverage and deploys. JUnit and Mockito suites, money paths first (registration, reconciliation, imports), including the contract tests against PHP responses. Coverage was a CI gate. 35% to 82% is a rise of 47 percentage points.

Number Tag How to say it
75% p95 cut HISTORICAL. (1.2 − 0.3) / 1.2 = 0.75 "From 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds."
700 to 4,000 rpm HISTORICAL. About 12 to 67 per second, about 5.7 times "Roughly 12 to 67 requests a second."
70% triage HISTORICAL. Baseline about 30 minutes to under 10 is ESTIMATED "Roughly half an hour to under ten minutes."
30% fewer reads HISTORICAL. Total database read load "For the same traffic, 100 reads became about 70."
98% deploys HISTORICAL. About 98 of 100 deploys with no failure or rollback "98% deployment success."

7. Questions they will ask

"What actually drove p95 down? Caching can't do 75%."
Agreed. The tail came down because IRP calls stopped pinning request threads. They moved to Kafka consumers and the API returned 202. HikariCP pooling, composite indexes and N+1 fixes did the rest of the tail. Redis cut repeated reads, which helped the typical request.

"How do you guarantee exactly-once?"
Strictly, we did not get exactly-once delivery, because the IRP is outside our transaction. We had at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing keyed by client, fileHash and batchIndex. A redelivered message finds the key already registered and skips the IRP call.

"How do 700 to 4,000 per minute and 1M a day fit together?"
They measure different things. 700 to 4,000 per minute is API requests at the gateway, about 12 to 67 a second. 1M+ a day is government submissions, about 12 a second on average. One bulk request carries many invoices.

"Why shard by quarter and not hash by client?"
Access was time-scoped. Writes go to the current quarter and old quarters are read for audits. Quarter shards keep the hot table small and archive cleanly. The cost was routing in our code, so we validated the quarter at the API.

"What goes into the DLQ and what happens next?"
Batches with a permanent error, or that ran out of retries. They are parked with the reason so the rest of the import continues. An operator fixes the cause and replays through the same idempotency keys, so a replay cannot double-register.

"Why Spring Boot MVC and not WebFlux?"
Once IRP calls moved to consumers, request threads only did short database and cache work, which the servlet model handles well. A reactive rewrite would have added complexity across the whole team for little gain.

8. What not to say

  • "2,500+ clients" or "support tickets down 35%". Older resume figures. Use 1,500+.
  • "I led a team" at Masters India. It is mentored 2. "Led 3" is Uber FRM.
  • Flink at Masters India. Flink is the Uber Menu pipeline, which is a different Kafka system.
  • Celery on this track's Masters story. It is not on this PDF's Masters tech line.
  • Spring Batch as a resume bullet claim. It is a skills-line item that fits chunked imports.
  • "Zero message loss" or "true exactly-once delivery to the government".
  • "Payments" or "money movement". This is tax compliance and invoice registration.
  • A circuit breaker as a measured result. It is a design idea to discuss.
  • Exact partition counts, chunk sizes, retry counts or TTLs as remembered facts.
  • TPS or RPS as if printed on the PDF. They are arithmetic you can show.

GeeksforGeeks: Courses Platform and Influencer Dashboard

Role: Software Development Engineer · August 2021 to November 2022 · Noida · first job after college
Resume tech line (exact): Python, Django, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch

This project is Django on every resume track. Older Java-track notes described it as Spring Boot. That was wrong and has been fixed here.

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the doubt-support platform migration from PHP to Django, the voting, pinning and locking APIs, why each of the four data stores was used, the influencer earnings dashboard, and the scheduled background jobs.
  • When to read it: before questions on early-career ownership, "design a voting system", hot rows, safe cron jobs, or "Django vs FastAPI vs Spring Boot".
  • What to memorise: 10K+ daily queries, 10x contest spikes, 20% relative lift in premium subscriptions (attributed by the growth team), 30% course sales lift (business attribution), 70% operational efficiency gain.

Tags on this page. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and the resume. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. "Illustrative" marks made-up sample data used to explain a mechanism.

Longer version: Handbook chapter 8, GeeksforGeeks. Older notes: Masters and GFG deep dive and MongoDB and Elasticsearch.

1. The one-minute version

"My first job was at GeeksforGeeks, the computer-science learning platform. Learners post doubts, meaning questions, on courses and articles, and that system ran on a fragile PHP backend. It struggled with 10K+ daily queries and with traffic that jumped about ten times during live coding contests. I migrated it to Django and built the REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads, with MySQL as the source of truth, Redis for hot counters, MongoDB for flexible content and Elasticsearch for search. The growth team tied those features to a 20% lift in premium subscriptions. I also built an influencer analytics and earnings dashboard, which the business team credited with 30% more course sales, and scheduled jobs for video processing, reminders and cleanup that cut manual ops work by about 70%. It is where I learned unique constraints for idempotency, keeping hot counters off the database, and making jobs safe to re-run."

2. The business in plain English

GeeksforGeeks (GFG) has free articles, practice problems, live contests and paid courses. Premium subscriptions and course sales are a big part of revenue. On the doubt-support platform a learner asks "Why does my DFS overflow the stack?", others reply, good answers are upvoted, and a moderator can pin the best thread to the top or lock it to stop new replies.

What hurt before: the PHP backend lacked clean transactions and request validation, doubt pages got slow during contest spikes, popular doubts caused database lock queues, influencers could not see how their coupon codes converted, and ops staff did video handoffs, reminders and cleanup by hand. A reliable doubt system is part of what premium users pay for, so breaking during a contest costs money.

3. Words you need

  • Django. A "batteries included" Python web framework with an ORM, admin panel, auth and migrations. Like renting a furnished flat. DRF (Django REST Framework) adds serializers (validate input, shape output) and permissions.
  • Unique constraint. A database rule that a combination of columns can appear only once.
  • Idempotent. Doing it twice has the same effect as once. Clicking upvote twice should count one vote.
  • Hot row. One row that many requests update at once. Each update locks it, so they queue, like a hundred people at one checkout counter.
  • Reconcile. Periodically recompute the true value from the source of truth and fix drift in the fast copy.
  • Cron. A scheduler that runs a job at fixed times.
  • Lease lock. A short-lived "I'm running this" marker that expires on its own if the holder crashes.
  • Affiliate coupon and attribution. A discount code tied to one influencer. Attribution is deciding which cause gets credit for a business result. Here the business and growth teams did it, not me.

4. Architecture

flowchart LR U["Learners, moderators, influencers"] --> DJ["Django and DRF APIs"] DJ -->|source of truth| MY["MySQL"] DJ -->|hot counters| RD["Redis"] DJ -->|flexible content| MO["MongoDB"] DJ -->|full-text search| ES["Elasticsearch"] RC["Reconcile job"] -->|true totals| RD RC -->|sum votes| MY CR["Scheduled jobs: video, reminders, cleanup"] -->|job keys| MY

What to notice: MySQL is the single source of truth. Redis holds fast copies that the reconcile job corrects. Scheduled jobs never run inside a user request.

Box by box. Django and DRF replaced PHP, with serializers validating every request and writes inside transaction.atomic(). MySQL holds data that must be correct: users, threads, votes, pins, locks, subscriptions and influencer transactions. Redis holds vote totals, unread badges and contest hot keys. MongoDB holds doubt bodies whose shape varies (code blocks, attachments). Elasticsearch gives full-text search with relevance ranking, which SQL LIKE '%stack overflow%' cannot do well.

5. One request, step by step: an upvote during a contest

Illustrative data: learner 42 upvotes doubt 123 while hundreds of others vote on it.

  1. Django validates POST /api/v1/votes {content_id: 123, value: +1} with a serializer.
  2. It upserts the vote row. A unique constraint on (user_id, content_id) means one row per user per doubt.
  3. If the value changed, Redis is adjusted by the difference: +1 for a new upvote, −2 when an upvote becomes a downvote.
  4. A double click sends the same request. The row already holds +1, so nothing changes.
  5. Every few minutes the reconcile job sums the vote rows in MySQL and overwrites Redis. If Redis lost the key, it is rebuilt.

6. Each resume bullet decoded

Bullet 1: Django migration, 10K+ queries, 10x spikes, voting, pinning, locking, 20%

What the load really means. 10K a day is 10,000 / 86,400, about 0.12 requests per second on average (ESTIMATED). Even ten times that is around 1 per second if spread evenly. Contest traffic bunches into short windows, and each doubt brings many reads. So the honest story is correctness and burst safety, not raw scale.

How the vote API works.

CREATE TABLE votes (
  id         BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  content_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  value      TINYINT NOT NULL,            -- +1 or -1
  UNIQUE KEY uq_vote (user_id, content_id)
);

from django.db import transaction

def cast_vote(user_id: int, content_id: int, value: int) -> int:
    with transaction.atomic():
        vote = (Vote.objects.select_for_update()
                .filter(user_id=user_id, content_id=content_id).first())
        old = vote.value if vote else 0
        if old == value:
            return int(redis.get(f"votes:{content_id}") or 0)   # repeat click: no-op
        Vote.objects.update_or_create(
            user_id=user_id, content_id=content_id, defaults={"value": value})
    return redis.incrby(f"votes:{content_id}", value - old)

Illustrative. The schema is logical, from my notes. The lock is only on this user's own row, so votes do not queue behind each other.

Why this avoids the hot row. The naive design runs UPDATE content SET vote_count = vote_count + 1 WHERE id = 123 on every vote, so 300 votes in a few minutes means 300 transactions waiting on one lock. Here each vote touches its own row, and the shared total is an atomic Redis INCRBY.

Pinning and locking. A pin row marks a thread as pinned within its course or article, with an ordering column and a unique constraint so pinning twice is a no-op. A lock row holds content_id, locked_by, reason and an optional expiry, and the "post reply" API refuses replies on a locked thread. Both are moderator-only behind permission checks.

Alternatives. A counter column updated on every vote causes the hot row. Counters only in Redis are fast but cannot stop double votes or rebuild after a flush. An app-level "has this user voted?" check races, and only a database constraint is race-proof. Putting everything in MongoDB loses the constraints and transactions that votes and subscriptions need. Trade-off: displayed counts can be a few minutes stale until reconcile, which is fine for a vote badge and would not be fine for money.

The 20%. A relative lift in premium subscriptions after these features shipped, attributed by the growth team (HISTORICAL). Illustratively, 1,000 new premium subscriptions a month becoming 1,200, not 20% of all users becoming premium. Say: "The growth team attributed about a 20% relative lift to these features. I owned the engineering."

Bullet 2: influencer dashboard (30%) and scheduled workflows (70%)

The dashboard. Every coupon purchase was recorded in MySQL linked to the influencer. The dashboard showed transactions, coupon conversions and earnings. Redis counters gave a fresh "today so far" view, and a nightly job built daily rollups for the history charts, so page loads never scanned raw transactions. Illustrative tables: influencer_account(id, coupon_code), earning_txn(influencer_id, order_id, amount, earning, created_at), daily_rollup(influencer_id, day, orders, revenue, earning). The 30% course sales lift was attributed by the business team. The likely mechanism is that influencers who can see what converts promote more.

Scheduled jobs. Video processing handoffs, user reminders and data cleanup. Two reliability rules made them safe:

def run_once(job_name: str, run_key: str, work) -> None:
    lock = f"cron:lock:{job_name}"
    if not redis.set(lock, HOST, nx=True, ex=3600):    # another host has it
        return
    try:
        if JobRun.objects.filter(job_key=run_key, status="done").exists():
            return                                      # safe re-run
        work()
        JobRun.objects.update_or_create(job_key=run_key, defaults={"status": "done"})
    finally:
        redis.delete(lock)

Illustrative. The lock stops two hosts both sending 5,000 reminder emails at 2 AM. A per-unit key like reminder:{user_id}:{class_id}:1h_before means a job that crashed after 1,200 of 2,000 emails sends only the remaining 800 on re-run. The 70% is the drop in manual effort on those workflows (HISTORICAL). Illustratively, 10 hours of someone's week becoming about 3. Celery is not on this role's tech line, so describe these as scheduled jobs, not Celery tasks.

7. Tech used and why

Tech Why here Alternative
Python + Django + DRF ORM, admin, auth, migrations, serializers. Fast delivery for a content product Staying on PHP, Flask
MySQL Unique constraints and transactions for votes, subscriptions, earnings MongoDB for everything
MongoDB Doubt bodies with varying shape MySQL JSON columns
Redis Vote counters, badges, "today" dashboard counters, job locks Updating MySQL counters per event
Elasticsearch Search over doubts with relevance SQL LIKE

Why Django here, but Spring Boot at Masters India? In 2021 this was a content and community product, where Django's admin, auth and ORM saved time. At Masters India the problem was slow calls to a government API at high volume, and Spring Boot services with Kafka consumers fit that. Different job, different tool.

8. Questions they will ask

"How do you make a vote API idempotent?"
A unique constraint on user ID and content ID means one vote row per user per doubt, and the API upserts it. A double click or client retry can never count twice, and the database enforces that even when two requests race.

"How did you avoid hot rows on popular doubts?"
We stopped updating a shared counter on every vote. Each vote writes its own row, the display total lives in Redis with atomic increments, and a reconcile job sums the real votes every few minutes so MySQL stays the truth.
Follow-up they may ask: "What if Redis loses the key?" The next reconcile rebuilds it, and until then the API can fall back to the stored count.

"10K queries a day isn't much. What was hard?"
You're right, the average is well under one request per second. The hard part was bursts and fragility: about tenfold spikes in short contest windows, no clean transactions or validation in PHP, and hot rows on popular doubts.

"Why four data stores?"
Each did a job the others do badly. MySQL for relational truth, Redis for very frequent tiny counters, MongoDB for content whose shape varied, Elasticsearch for search. If I had to cut one today, I would check whether MongoDB's role could move into MySQL JSON columns.

"How did you stop a cron job running twice?"
A lock with expiry so only one host runs it, and an idempotent key per unit of work so a re-run skips finished work.

"Did your dashboard really raise sales 30%?"
The business team attributed it. I built the dashboard: transaction and coupon tracking, Redis counters for today and rollups for history. The causal analysis is theirs.

"What would you do differently?"
Write votes as events to a queue and build counters from that stream, so totals rebuild by replay. Make idempotent job keys the default through a shared helper. Set explicit latency targets for contest days.

9. What not to say

  • "Spring Boot", "Hibernate" or "Java" at GeeksforGeeks. The PDF says Django.
  • "100K daily queries" or "1K daily queries". Older figures. Use 10K+.
  • "15 to 20% premium lift". Older prep. Use 20%, relative, attributed by the growth team.
  • "I increased sales by 30%" as if engineering alone caused it.
  • Celery, Kafka, FastAPI or AWS at GeeksforGeeks. None is on this role's tech line.
  • Comparing GFG load to Uber or Impact Analytics scale.
  • "SMTP sends 50% faster" or unread-count badges as resume bullets. They are older or prep-only details.
