A10. Hard problems and failure stories

1. The canary timeout mismatch. What broke: in the first canary, some requests that worked on PHP failed on the new Spring Boot service. How we found it: the canary dashboards showed a rise in errors on the new route only. Cause: PHP allowed 60 seconds per request and we had set 10 seconds on the new service. Some IRP calls legitimately took longer than 10 seconds. Fix: we moved those IRP calls fully async and returned 202 Accepted with polling, instead of raising the timeout. What I learned: agree a timeout budget per route before the first canary, and treat "slow but legitimate" calls as async work, not as a reason to raise timeouts. This is also a good example of why canaries exist: we caught it at a small percentage, before a full ramp.

2. Retry storms against the portal. Risk: when the IRP slowed down, naive retries would all fire at the same time and make the outage worse. Fix: exponential backoff with full jitter in the Spring Kafka error handler, a cap on parallel calls through listener concurrency, and bounded attempts followed by the dead-letter topic. Lesson: retries are a load source. Always cap them and spread them.

3. Poison batches. Problem: one malformed chunk could block an import if it kept failing. Fix: separate validation errors (fail at once with a reason) from transient errors (retry), and park repeat failures in the DLQ so the other chunks finish. Lesson: isolate failure to the smallest unit you can.

4. Cache stampede on hot keys. Risk: a popular config key expiring during a 100K-row import would send a burst of identical reads to the database. Fix: TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, and a SETNX lock so only one request rebuilds.

A11. Say this / don't say this (Masters India)

Say this

  • "1,500+ enterprise clients", "from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds", "from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute", "mentored two engineers", "PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices".
  • "Kafka for the pipeline stages, Spring Batch for chunked imports, async and scheduled jobs for side tasks."
  • "Exactly-once in effect, meaning at-least-once delivery plus idempotency keys. The IRP is outside our transaction."
  • "About 12 per second on average, roughly derived from 1M divided by 86,400. Peaks were an estimated 8 to 10 times that."
  • "Quarter-scoped tables or schemas, with the quarter derived from the invoice date in application code."
  • "Triage went from roughly 30 minutes to under 10." Say the baseline is an estimate.

Don't say this

  • "2,500+ clients". "Support tickets down 35%" or "audit churn down 15%" as current claims.
  • Flink at Masters India. That was Uber Menu. Do not merge the Masters Kafka with the Uber Menu Kafka.
  • "Led 3 engineers" here. That is Uber FRM. At Masters it is "mentored 2".
  • Zero message loss, two-phase commit with the government, payments or money movement.
  • A formal pager rotation or incident-commander title.
  • That Redis alone produced the p95 drop, or that switching frameworks alone did.
  • Celery at Masters India. Side tasks ran as @Async and scheduled jobs inside the Spring Boot services.

A12. Three-minute whiteboard script (Masters India)

  1. Draw first (30 seconds): client ERP on the left, government IRP on the right. Say: "We sit in the middle. Clients send invoices, we validate and register them with the government, and return the IRN and signed QR."
  2. Draw second (60 seconds): the gateway with two arrows, one to the PHP monolith and one to Spring Boot services. Say: "We migrated route by route with canaries. That plus non-blocking IRP calls, HikariCP pooling and query fixes took p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute."
  3. Draw third (60 seconds): Kafka between the API and the IRP workers, PostgreSQL with quarter drawers, a dead-letter topic box. Say: "Accept fast, queue durably, submit at a bounded pace. Spring Kafka listeners retry with backoff and jitter, then park the record on a dead-letter topic. The idempotency key is client plus file hash plus batch index, so retries are safe. More than a million submissions a day, about 12 per second on average with deadline peaks of roughly 8 to 10 times."
  4. Draw last (30 seconds): Redis next to the API, ELK and New Relic underneath. Say: "Cache-aside cut redundant reads 30%. One request ID across services cut triage 70%. Coverage went from 35% to 82%, with 98% of deploys succeeding."

Part B. GeeksforGeeks (SDE, Noida, Aug 2021 to Nov 2022)

B1. The one-minute version (say this out loud)

"At GeeksforGeeks I worked on the courses platform and the influencer dashboard. The doubt-support platform, where learners ask questions on courses and articles, was struggling under contest-day spikes, so I helped migrate its backend from PHP to Django. It then handled more than 10,000 daily queries and 10x traffic spikes during live coding contests. I built the REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads on MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch, and the growth team attributed a 20% lift in premium subscriptions to that work. I also launched an influencer analytics and earnings dashboard, which the business tied to a 30% rise in course sales, and built scheduled workflows for video processing, reminders and data cleanup that raised engineering operational efficiency by 70%."

B2. The business in plain English

GeeksforGeeks is a large computer-science learning site with articles, paid courses and live coding contests. Learners who get stuck post a doubt (a question) on a course or article, and mentors or other learners answer. Good answers get voted up, the best one can be pinned, and a moderator can lock a thread that is resolved or going off-track. Some of these interactions were premium features, which is how this work connects to subscriptions.

Influencers are creators (YouTubers and educators) who promote GeeksforGeeks courses with affiliate coupon codes and earn a share of sales. They needed a dashboard to see their transactions, coupon conversions and earnings.

What hurt before. The doubt-support backend ran on legacy PHP and wobbled during live contests, when traffic jumped about tenfold within minutes. Influencers had little visibility into their earnings. The ops team did repetitive manual work on video processing, reminders and cleanup.

B3. Words you need (GeeksforGeeks)

  • Django. A "batteries included" Python web framework with an ORM, an admin panel, authentication and migrations built in. Like a fully furnished flat: you move in and start living.
  • DRF (Django REST Framework). A library on top of Django for building REST APIs, with serializers (validate and convert data), viewsets and permissions.
  • ORM (Object Relational Mapper). Code that lets you work with database rows as Python objects instead of writing SQL by hand.
  • REST API. An HTTP interface where URLs name resources (/doubts/123/votes) and HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE) act on them.
  • Hot row. A single database row that many requests try to update at the same moment, for example the vote count on a viral post. Each update waits for the row lock, so they queue up. Like one checkout counter that everybody lines up at.
  • Denormalized counter. Storing a precomputed total (like vote_count) next to the data instead of counting the votes table every time. Fast to read, but it must be kept in sync.
  • Unique constraint. A database rule that a combination of columns, such as (user_id, doubt_id), can appear only once. It makes "vote twice" impossible at the database level.
  • Reconciliation job. A periodic job that recomputes a total from the source of truth and fixes any drift in the fast copy.
  • Cron and scheduled workflows. Cron is the classic Unix scheduler that runs a command at set times ("every night at 2 AM"). "Asynchronous scheduled workflows" on the PDF means jobs that run on a schedule in the background, not inside a user request.
  • Lease or advisory lock. A lock a job takes before running so that if two servers both have the cron entry, only one actually runs. Like a "room booked" sign on a meeting room door.
  • Inverted index. The core idea of Elasticsearch: a map from each word to the list of documents containing it, like the index at the back of a book.
  • Relative lift vs percentage points. A 20% relative lift means the number grew by a fifth of itself (1,000 becomes 1,200). It is not "20 percentage points". These are example numbers only.

B4. Architecture

flowchart LR U["Learners and influencers"] --> DJ["Django and DRF: doubt APIs, votes, pins, locks, dashboard"] DJ --> MY["MySQL: threads, permissions, votes source of truth"] DJ --> RD["Redis: vote counters, badges, unread counts"] DJ --> MG["MongoDB: flexible doubt bodies and attachments"] DJ --> ES["Elasticsearch: doubt and content search"] CR["Scheduled jobs with a lease"] --> VID["Video processing handoffs"] CR --> REM["User reminders"] CR --> CLN["Data cleanup"] CR --> MY RD -.->|"periodic reconcile"| MY

What to notice: MySQL is the source of truth, Redis is the fast copy that gets reconciled back, and the scheduled jobs are separate from the request path.

Walking through it. Learners and influencers call Django and DRF APIs. MySQL holds the relational truth: threads, replies, permissions and individual votes. Redis holds the counters that are read on every page view (vote totals, unread badges) so popular posts do not create hot rows in MySQL. MongoDB holds doubt bodies and attachments whose shape varied. Elasticsearch powers search across doubts and content. Separately, scheduled jobs take a lease, then handle video processing handoffs, reminders and cleanup.

B5. Bullet G1 decoded: Django migration, 10K+ daily queries, 10x spikes, voting, pinning, locking, 20% premium lift

"Stabilized the doubt-support platform to handle 10K+ daily queries and 10x traffic spikes during live coding contests by migrating the backend to Django. Engineered high-throughput REST APIs for voting, pinning, and locking threads utilizing MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, and Elasticsearch, driving a 20% lift in premium subscriptions."

In plain words

The question-and-answer part of the site was fragile on contest days. We rebuilt its backend in Django, page by page behind the same URLs, and it became stable at more than 10,000 queries a day with tenfold contest spikes. I built the APIs that let users vote on answers, pin the best answer and lock threads, using the right store for each job. The growth team linked those features to a 20% lift in premium subscriptions.

How it works: the migration

We migrated incrementally, page by page, behind the same URLs, so users never saw a switch. Reliability came from things the PHP code lacked: ORM-managed transactions (a reply and its counter update succeed or fail together), request validation through DRF serializers, a clean split between read views and write endpoints, plus staging and code review discipline.

How it works: voting without hot rows

# Illustrative Django models
class Vote(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    doubt = models.ForeignKey(Doubt, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    value = models.SmallIntegerField()          # +1 or -1

    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(fields=["user", "doubt"], name="one_vote_per_user"),
        ]

class Doubt(models.Model):
    is_locked = models.BooleanField(default=False)   # moderators lock threads
    pinned_rank = models.IntegerField(null=True)     # ordering within a context

# Illustrative vote endpoint logic
def cast_vote(user, doubt_id, value):
    vote, created = Vote.objects.update_or_create(
        user=user, doubt_id=doubt_id, defaults={"value": value})
    if created:
        redis.incrby(f"votes:{doubt_id}", value)   # fast display counter
    # changed votes adjust the counter by the difference; a reconcile job fixes drift

Why it works. The unique constraint makes a double-submit idempotent: a second click updates the existing vote instead of adding another. The display counter lives in Redis, so a viral doubt does not make thousands of requests queue on one MySQL row. A periodic reconciliation job recomputes counts from MySQL and corrects Redis if they drift. MySQL stays the source of truth.

Pinning and locking. Pinning uses an ordering column per context (for example per course or article), not a free-for-all sort. Locking is a moderation flag: a locked thread rejects new replies at the API.

How the four stores split. MySQL holds relational truth (threads, permissions, votes). Redis holds hot counters, badges and unread counts. MongoDB holds flexible doubt bodies and attachments whose shape varied. Elasticsearch powers full-text search across doubts and content. Details are in 02_mongodb_elasticsearch.md.

Why this design, and the alternatives

What: Django and DRF, with MySQL as truth, Redis counters reconciled back, Mongo for flexible bodies and Elasticsearch for search.

Why Django here: in 2021 this was a CMS-style product with admin, auth and ORM needs, and Django's batteries fit. At Masters India later, the work was a typed, event-driven pipeline with Kafka consumers, chunked bulk imports and strict tax payloads, which suited Spring Boot.

Alternatives: updating MySQL on every vote (simple, but viral posts create hot rows), counting votes on every page view (correct but slow), counter-only in Redis (fast but no durable truth and no protection against double votes), storing everything as JSON in MySQL (search and flexible shapes become awkward).

Trade-off: the Redis count can be briefly off until reconciliation. For a vote badge that is fine.

What I'd do differently: put vote events on a queue and make counters event-sourced, so the count is always rebuildable from the event stream.

The numbers

Number What it measures Tag
10K+ daily Doubt-support queries (questions and interactions) per day HISTORICAL
10x Traffic spikes during live coding contests HISTORICAL
20% Relative lift in premium subscriptions, attributed by the growth team HISTORICAL

Scale arithmetic. 10,000 / 86,400 = about 0.12 per second on average, which is well under 1 per second (ESTIMATED). The engineering problem was the spike, not the average. Contest traffic arrives in a burst at the start of a contest, roughly ten times normal.

Why it mattered. Contests are the moments when the most learners are on the site and judging it. Stable doubt support on those days and premium-gated interactions fed subscriptions.

How to say it. "Order of ten thousand daily queries with tenfold contest spikes. The point was surviving the spike. The growth team attributed a 20% relative lift in premium subscriptions."

What not to say. Do not say 100K daily (older 4-year resume) or 1K (older narrower metric). Do not say "15 to 20%", the current PDF says 20%. Do not claim the 20% was caused by you alone. Do not oversell "high-throughput" as huge scale. Say it was built for the contest spike.

Questions they will ask

"10K queries a day is small. Why does it need engineering?" On average it is small, about 0.12 per second, and I do not pretend otherwise. The problem was the tenfold spike at the start of live contests, when everyone posts and refreshes at once, and the PHP backend was fragile under that. The Django migration gave us transactions, validation and a clean read and write split, and Redis counters kept viral threads from creating hot rows. The win was reliability under bursts, not raw scale.

"How did you make voting idempotent and avoid hot rows?" A unique constraint on user and doubt means a second click updates the existing vote instead of adding one. The visible count lives in Redis, so thousands of votes on a viral post do not queue on one MySQL row. A reconciliation job recomputes from MySQL and fixes drift. MySQL stays the source of truth.

"How do you know the 20% premium lift came from your APIs?" I do not claim sole cause. The growth team measured and attributed the 20% relative lift to the features that gated some interactions behind premium. I owned the engineering: the APIs and their reliability. So I say "attributed by the growth team".

B6. Bullet G2 decoded: influencer dashboard +30% course sales, scheduled workflows +70% ops efficiency

"Accelerated platform course sales by 30% by launching an influencer analytics and earnings dashboard to dynamically track transactions and affiliate coupon conversions. Increased engineering operational efficiency by 70% by designing asynchronous scheduled workflows for automated video processing, user reminders, and data cleanup."

In plain words

Influencers who sell our courses could not see what their coupons were earning, so I built a dashboard showing their transactions, coupon conversions and earnings. With that visibility they promoted more, and the business tied it to a 30% rise in course sales. Separately, I replaced manual ops chores with scheduled background jobs, which saved about 70% of the time spent on those workflows.

How it works: the dashboard

The dashboard aggregated video and course analytics, transactions and affiliate coupon conversions per influencer. Older resumes mention filters and CSV export. Near-real-time counters came from Redis, and daily rollups were computed by scheduled jobs. An illustrative daily rollup:

-- Illustrative nightly rollup of coupon conversions per influencer
INSERT INTO influencer_daily (influencer_id, day, orders, revenue, earnings)
SELECT c.influencer_id, DATE(o.created_at), COUNT(*), SUM(o.amount),
       SUM(o.amount * c.commission_rate)
FROM orders o JOIN coupons c ON c.code = o.coupon_code
WHERE o.created_at >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL 1 DAY AND o.created_at < CURDATE()
GROUP BY c.influencer_id, DATE(o.created_at);

How it works: the scheduled workflows

The jobs covered video processing handoffs, automated user reminders, and data cleanup (older notes include cloud recording deletion and payment processing). Reliability rules:

  1. Take a lease first, so two hosts never run the same job twice.
  2. Use idempotent job keys, so a re-run after a crash does not send a reminder twice.
  3. Log success and failure in a structured way, so someone can see what ran.
  4. Retry partial batches instead of restarting everything.
# Illustrative lease using a MySQL named lock
with connection.cursor() as cur:
    cur.execute("SELECT GET_LOCK('reminder_job', 0)")
    if cur.fetchone()[0] != 1:
        return                      # another host is running it
    try:
        send_due_reminders(run_key=f"reminders:{date.today()}")
    finally:
        cur.execute("SELECT RELEASE_LOCK('reminder_job')")

Older resume detail, not on the current PDF: SMTP connection reuse. Older resumes say email send time dropped about 50% by keeping one SMTP connection open and reusing it across a batch instead of a new TCP and TLS handshake per message. A handshake often costs 100 to 400 milliseconds, so amortising it across a batch roughly halves wall-clock time for reminder and promo sends. Use it as depth only if asked.

Why this design, and the alternatives

Dashboard. Why: Redis for near-real-time numbers and nightly rollups for history keeps the dashboard fast without heavy queries on the orders table. Alternative: querying raw orders on every page load, which is simple but slow and loads the main database.

Scheduled jobs. Why: plain scheduled jobs were enough for the volume, with a lease and idempotent keys for safety. Alternatives: a full workflow tool (heavier than needed) or a task queue like Celery (not on the GeeksforGeeks tech line). What I'd do differently: make idempotency keys the default on every cron job from day one, and set clear latency targets for contest days.

The numbers

Number What it measures Tag
30% Rise in course sales, attributed by the business team to the influencer dashboard HISTORICAL
70% Time saved on the manual video, reminder and cleanup workflows HISTORICAL

How to explain 70%. It is time saved on those specific workflows. An illustrative picture, not a measurement: if ops spent 10 hours a week on those chores and the jobs cut it to 3, that is (10 - 3) / 10 = 70%.

How to say it. "I owned the engineering. The business team attributed a 30% rise in course sales to the dashboard, and the scheduled jobs saved about 70% of the time spent on those manual workflows."

What not to say. Do not mix the two halves. The dashboard drives the 30%. The scheduled jobs drive the 70%. Do not claim sole causality for sales.

Questions they will ask

"How do you keep cron jobs reliable?" Every job takes a lease first, so two hosts never run it twice. Each run has an idempotent key, so a crash and re-run does not double-send a reminder. Results are logged as structured success or failure, and partial batches retry instead of starting over. The 70% figure is time saved on those manual video, reminder and cleanup workflows.

"How did the dashboard drive 30% more course sales?" I built the engineering, and the business team attributed the lift. The dashboard gave influencers clear visibility of their transactions, coupon conversions and earnings, and that visibility encouraged them to promote more. Technically it combined Redis counters for near-real-time numbers with nightly rollups for history.

B7. Say this / don't say this (GeeksforGeeks)

Say this

  • "10K-plus daily queries, order of ten thousand, with tenfold contest spikes."
  • "A 20% lift in premium subscriptions, attributed by the growth team."
  • "I owned the engineering. The business team attributed the 30% sales lift."

Don't say this

  • "100K daily queries" or "15 to 20%".
  • That you single-handedly caused the sales or subscription lift.
  • Celery or Kafka at GeeksforGeeks. They are not on that tech line.
  • The SMTP 50% as a current resume claim. It is an older detail.

B8. Three-minute whiteboard script (GeeksforGeeks)

  1. Draw first: learners on the left, a Django box in the middle. Say: "We moved the doubt backend from PHP to Django, page by page behind the same URLs, to survive tenfold contest spikes at 10K-plus daily queries."
  2. Draw second: MySQL, Redis, MongoDB and Elasticsearch under Django. Say: "MySQL is truth, Redis holds counters to avoid hot rows, Mongo holds flexible bodies, Elasticsearch powers search. A unique constraint makes votes idempotent."
  3. Draw third: a scheduled-jobs box with a lease. Say: "Video handoffs, reminders and cleanup run as leased, idempotent jobs, saving about 70% of ops time. The influencer dashboard drove a 30% sales lift as attributed by the business."

Mock interview: the hardest questions, with speakable answers

Masters India

Interviewer: You were on AWS. Why Kafka instead of RabbitMQ or SQS for e-invoicing?

Candidate: We needed three things together: per-taxpayer ordering, durable replay for compliance, and independent consumer groups. The partition key was the seller's GSTIN, sometimes plus document type, so the submit, the IRN callback and the webhook for one taxpayer stayed in order on one partition. Kafka's log let us reset offsets and reprocess a bad window after a parser bug. SQS deletes messages once they are processed and does not give cheap multi-consumer replay, and SQS FIFO limits throughput per message group. RabbitMQ could have handled task dispatch at our scale, and I am honest about that. We still picked Kafka for replay, for several readers on one topic (IRP workers, audit projector, metrics) without fanout plumbing, and because Spring Kafka gave our Spring Boot services listeners, bounded retries and dead-letter topics out of the box. Ops cost was the trade-off, and correctness plus replay won.

Interviewer: Derive TPS and RPS from your resume numbers. Do they even hang together?

Candidate: Yes. A million daily submissions divided by 86,400 seconds is about 11.6, so roughly 12 per second on average, and that is my arithmetic, not a dashboard number. Filing-deadline spikes are the real sizing problem, and we sized for roughly 8 to 10 times average, so around 100 per second, also an estimate. API throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, which is about 12 to about 67 requests per second. Those are different meters: the daily count is government-registered documents, and the per-minute figure is API capacity. p95 went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds for 1,500-plus clients.

Interviewer: What actually drove p95 from 1.2s to 300ms? Caching alone cannot do that.

Candidate: Right, caching helped the middle of the distribution, and the tail came from removing PHP's synchronous bottleneck. IRP calls no longer held a worker for the full round trip, because the Spring Boot services called the portal through a non-blocking WebClient with a hard timeout, or handed the work to Kafka workers behind a 202. HikariCP connection pooling replaced per-request connection storms. We killed N+1 list queries, including lazy-loading ones in Hibernate, and added composite indexes on client ID and invoice date. Redis cut redundant database reads by 30%, which shortened the body. So off-thread IRP work, pooling and query fixes moved the tail, and the cache moved the body.

Interviewer: Cache-aside specifics: keys, TTLs, invalidation, thundering herd. Make the 30% read cut plausible.

Candidate: It was classic cache-aside: on a miss, read the database and set the value with a TTL. The hot keys were IRP auth tokens with a TTL below the token's lifetime, client config and feature flags, GSTIN master lookups and tax-rate masters. Config and GSTIN entries were deleted in the update path, so admins never saw stale credentials. Masters used TTL-only expiry with jitter so they did not all expire at once. For the thundering herd, one worker takes a SETNX lock and rebuilds while the others wait or serve slightly stale data. The 30% is plausible because every row of a 100K-row import repeated the same config and GSTIN lookups, and caching removed that duplicate read fan-out.

Interviewer: Quarter-based sharding: why shard GST data by financial quarter instead of plain partitioning?

Candidate: Because GST work is period-based and deadline-driven. Writes concentrate in the current quarter, and older quarters are mostly read for reconciliation and audits. Separate quarter tables or schemas let us archive a cold quarter without touching the hot write set, and kept the hot indexes small. Compared with native range partitioning, we owned routing in our data-access layer, which is more moving parts, but it gave us an explicit "archive this quarter" operation and clear runbooks. The footgun is a wrong-quarter write, so we derived the quarter from the invoice date at the API boundary and rejected mismatches.

Interviewer: Sketch the IRP e-invoicing path and where Kafka sits.

Candidate: The client creates the invoice in their ERP and posts JSON to our API. We validate the schema and GSTIN, then register it with a government Invoice Registration Portal, which returns the IRN and a signed QR code. That is what makes a B2B GST e-invoice valid. Kafka carried the async stages: accepted import chunks, IRP submit jobs, persistence of the signed response to MongoDB snapshots, and client webhooks. Idempotency keys plus unique client references stopped double registration, which is not cleanly recoverable with the government. Bulk files go to S3, get chunked and validated, then go to the IRP with bounded concurrency while the dashboard shows progress.

Interviewer: You mentored 2 engineers on a monolith-to-microservices migration. What did "spearheading" mean day to day?

Candidate: I owned the playbook: a strangler migration behind the gateway, not a big bang. I set the conventions, meaning controller, service and repository layers, DTOs with Bean Validation at the boundary, and shared retry and idempotency helpers. Each of the two engineers extracted a service, and I reviewed their early PRs closely and paired on the first canary cutover. The canary was an Nginx percentage route: watch errors and latency, then ramp up or roll back with a config change. We shared the database during the traffic cutover to avoid dual writes, and split tables afterwards.

Interviewer: ELK plus New Relic cut triage 70%. Prove that is not vanity.

Candidate: Before, we had to SSH into boxes and grep, with no way to correlate requests. After, every log was structured JSON with a request ID going into Elasticsearch and Kibana, New Relic APM traced requests across services, and alerts fired on error rate and latency. The real win was one request ID across the API, the Kafka consumer and the IRP worker, so one search showed the whole journey. Roughly 30 minutes down to under 10 is my estimated baseline behind the 70% we reported. Separately, coverage went from 35% to 82% with JUnit 5 and Mockito tests and a JaCoCo CI gate on money paths, and deploys succeeded 98% of the time.

Interviewer: What broke during the migration?

Candidate: The first canary showed a timeout mismatch. PHP allowed 60 seconds and we had set 10, and some IRP calls legitimately took longer. Instead of raising the timeout, we moved those calls fully async and returned 202 with polling. The canary caught it at a small percentage, before any full ramp, which is exactly why we used canaries.

GeeksforGeeks

Interviewer: Doubt support at 10K+ daily queries. Design unread counts without melting MySQL.

Candidate: First the scale: 10K-plus daily interactions is well under one per second on average, with contest-day spikes of about ten times, so this is a burst problem, not a big-data problem. Unread counts lived behind a REST API, with per-user counters in Redis for the badge and durable thread and message rows in MySQL. A new reply increments the counter, and a read receipt clears it. A periodic reconcile from MySQL fixed any drift. The Django migration gave us the transactions, validation and read and write separation the PHP stack was missing.

Interviewer: Voting API idempotency and hot rows. How did MySQL, Redis, MongoDB and Elasticsearch split?

Candidate: The vote table had a unique constraint on user and content, so a double-submit is idempotent at the database. Display counters sat in Redis and reconciled to MySQL asynchronously, which avoided hot-row contention on popular doubts. MySQL stayed the source of truth for threads, permissions and votes. MongoDB held flexible payloads where the doubt body or attachments varied, and Elasticsearch powered search across doubts and content. Pinning was an ordering column per context, and locking was a moderation flag. The 20% premium lift is the growth team's relative attribution.

Interviewer: Cron pipelines claimed +70% ops efficiency. How do you keep crons reliable?

Candidate: The jobs covered video processing handoffs, automated reminders, payment processing and cloud recording cleanup. Each one takes a lock or a database lease first so two hosts do not double-run, uses idempotent job keys, writes structured success and failure logs, and retries partial batches. The 70% is time saved on those manual ops workflows. Course sales up 30% is the business team's attribution for the influencer dashboard, and I own the engineering, not the causality.

Interviewer: You also cut email send time 50% with SMTP changes. Is that real?

Candidate: Yes, it is on older resumes, though not on the current one. We kept one SMTP connection open and reused it across sends instead of a TCP and TLS handshake per message. A handshake often costs 100 to 400 milliseconds, so reusing the connection across reminder and promo batches roughly halves wall-clock send time. It is a GeeksforGeeks detail, not a Masters India claim.

Interviewer: Why Django at GeeksforGeeks but Spring Boot at Masters India?

Candidate: They were different jobs. GeeksforGeeks in 2021 was a CMS-style product that needed admin, auth and an ORM, and Django ships all of that. Masters India was a typed, event-driven compliance pipeline: Kafka consumers with bounded retries and dead-letter topics, chunked bulk imports, and tax payloads where a wrong type means a rejected document. Spring Boot had Spring Kafka, Spring Batch and Bean Validation ready for that, and it was the team standard. I would pick Django again for the first and Spring Boot again for the second.

Interviewer: What would you change today at GeeksforGeeks?

Candidate: I would put vote events on a queue and make counters event-sourced, so they are always rebuildable. I would add idempotency keys to every reminder cron by default. And I would set clear latency targets for contest days. These are the event patterns I later used at Masters India, and I would backport them.

Confidence audit

How sure you can be on each PDF bullet, and what to say if pressed.

Resume bullet Rating Fallback wording if pressed
MI1: PHP to Spring Boot, p95 1.2s to 300ms, 1,500+ clients, 700 to 4,000 req/min, mentored 2 SOLID If they cite older resumes, the band was 1,000 to 1,200 ms down to 300 to 400 ms. Never say 2,500+ clients.
MI2: Kafka plus PostgreSQL by tax quarter, 1M+ daily, 100K+ idempotent imports, DLQ, bounded retries SOLID on pattern and throughput. NEEDS CARE on peak TPS and the word "sharded" Say about 12 TPS average and roughly 100+ at peak as estimates. Describe quarter-scoped tables with app routing. Admit RabbitMQ could work at that scale. Circuit breaker is verbal only.
MI3: ELK and New Relic, triage -70%, Redis -30% reads, coverage 35% to 82%, 98% deploys SOLID on coverage and deploys. NEEDS CARE on the triage baseline Claim alerting, not pager ownership. The 30 minutes to under 10 baseline is an estimate behind the reported 70%. Tickets -35% and audit churn -15% are older details, not current claims.
G1: Django, 10K+ daily, 10x spikes, voting, pinning, locking, 20% premium SOLID on engineering. NEEDS CARE on the 20% "Order of ten thousand daily". "Relative lift attributed by the growth team. I owned the APIs and reliability." Never 100K, never 15 to 20%.
G2: dashboard +30% sales, scheduled workflows +70% ops NEEDS CARE Own the engineering, attribute the sales lift to the business team, and describe 70% as time saved on those workflows.

Uber Menu Ingestion Deep Dive (Kafka, Flink, RAG over Milvus)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the Uber Eats Menu Ingestion and Automation project in depth. It teaches Kafka, Flink, delivery guarantees, RAG, embeddings and Milvus from scratch, then applies them to the project. A short ANZ section and a clearly labelled Spark study section are at the end.
  • When to read it: when you expect a system design or data-engineering round, or when an interviewer is likely to dig into "Kafka and Flink" on the resume. For a quick refresh, read the Menu section of the interview pack (first quick link below) instead.
  • What to memorise: the architecture diagram in section 3, the four Flink ideas (keyed state, event time, watermarks, checkpoints), the sentence "at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upsert gives an exactly-once effect", and the numbers in section 11.

  • ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. Say "roughly, derived from...".
  • HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and resume, not re-measured from logs in this repo.

Resume alignment (current PDF). Menu outcomes: from 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year, 30K+ menus a month, 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation using Gemini 2.5 Pro and LangChain RAG over Milvus, and 95%+ extraction success. The pipeline is Kafka plus Apache Flink with stateful keyed deduplication, schema normalization and exactly-once catalog upserts.

  • ClickHouse belongs to Impact Analytics, not this pipeline.
  • Spark is NOT on the PDF. It appears in section 13 only as a verbal, study-only backfill option. It is not a resume claim.

1. The project in plain English

Uber Eats lists restaurants and their menus. When a restaurant joins, its menu has to become structured catalog data: item names, prices, categories, options, in a fixed schema. Restaurants send this in whatever form they have. Some give a website that builds the menu with JavaScript. Some send a PDF. Some send a photo of a printed menu. Many are not in English.

Before this pipeline, conversion was slow and partly done by a paid third-party tool at about $2 per menu. A restaurant could wait about a day before its menu was ready. I architected the automated pipeline that does this at 30K+ menus a month. It has three parts:

  1. Acquisition: a Python Selenium fleet on GCP that fetches menus reliably, even from sites that block scrapers.
  2. Streaming backbone: Kafka carries every scraped menu event, and Flink deduplicates, normalizes and writes them to the catalog exactly once in effect.
  3. AI extraction for unstructured input: multilingual PDFs go through a LangChain RAG pipeline that retrieves similar labelled menus from Milvus and asks Gemini 2.5 Pro to produce catalog fields, followed by a strict schema check.

2. Words you need

This section teaches the vocabulary. Each term gets a plain definition, an analogy and a tiny example.

2.1 Kafka

Kafka is a distributed, durable, append-only log. Producers write messages to the end. Consumers read from any position. Messages are kept for a configured time even after they are read. Analogy: a post office that keeps a copy of every letter, in order, for a week, so anyone authorised can come back and re-read them.

  • Topic: a named stream of messages. Example: menu.raw holds every scraped menu event.
  • Partition: each topic is split into partitions so it can be read in parallel. Order is guaranteed only within a partition. Analogy: a bank with several tellers. Each teller's line is in order, but the lines move independently.
  • Message key: Kafka hashes the key to pick the partition. Same key, same partition, every time. Example: key v123 (a vendor id) always lands on, say, partition 4, so all of that restaurant's events stay in order.
  • Consumer group: a team of consumers sharing one topic. Each partition is assigned to exactly one member at a time. Add members to scale out, up to the number of partitions. Example: 12 partitions and 4 Flink workers means each worker owns 3 partitions.
  • Offset: the position of a message within a partition, an increasing number. A consumer commits the offset it has finished. Analogy: a bookmark.
  • Replay: reset a consumer group's offsets to an earlier point and re-read. Example: a parser bug shipped at 10:00. Fix it, rewind to 09:55, and reprocess.
  • Consumer lag: how far behind the newest message a consumer is. Rising lag means processing is slower than arrivals. It is the main health alert for a streaming pipeline.
Topic menu.raw (3 partitions shown)

partition 0: [v101 e1][v104 e1][v101 e2][v104 e2] ...
partition 1: [v123 e1][v123 e2][v150 e1] ...        <- all v123 events, in order
partition 2: [v099 e1][v177 e1][v099 e2] ...
                       ^ consumer's committed offset (bookmark)

What to notice: one vendor's events always sit in one partition, in order, so per-vendor processing never sees them shuffled.

2.2 Flink

Apache Flink is a stream-processing engine. It reads events continuously, processes each one as it arrives, and keeps state between events. Analogy: an assembly line where each worker has a notebook and remembers what passed by before.

  • Keyed stream and keyed state: key_by(vendor_id, menu_id) routes all events for one key to the same worker. That worker keeps a small piece of memory per key. Example: for key (v123, m9), remember last_hash = "ab12". Analogy: a clerk with one index card per restaurant.
  • State backend: where keyed state lives. For large state, Flink commonly uses RocksDB, an embedded key-value store on local disk. (General Flink knowledge, useful for interviews.)
  • Event time: the time an event actually happened, for example when the page was scraped. Different from processing time, which is when Flink sees it. Using event time means a late-arriving page is still handled as "older than" a newer one.
  • Watermark: a marker flowing with the data that says "all events up to time T have probably arrived". It lets Flink close windows and decide what counts as late. Example: watermark = newest scrape time minus 2 minutes, which tolerates pages arriving up to 2 minutes out of order. (The 2 minutes is a teaching example, not a project setting.)
  • Checkpoint: Flink periodically takes a consistent snapshot of all state plus the Kafka offsets it has read. After a crash, it restores state from the snapshot and resumes reading from those offsets. Analogy: a save point in a video game. You lose only what happened since the last save.
  • Backpressure: if a downstream step (like the catalog write) slows down, Flink's internal buffers fill and it slows its reading from Kafka. Nothing runs out of memory. Kafka simply holds the messages, and consumer lag rises.

2.3 Delivery guarantees

  • At-most-once: each message is processed zero or one times. Fast, but you can lose data.
  • At-least-once: each message is processed one or more times. No loss, but after a failure a few messages are processed again.
  • Exactly-once: each message's effect happens exactly once. Inside Flink, checkpoints give exactly-once state. To an external system, true exactly-once needs a sink that takes part in transactions.
  • Idempotent upsert: a write that gives the same final result however many times it runs. "Insert this item for (vendor, menu, item), or update it if it is already there."

The key sentence: at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent upsert gives an exactly-once effect. If the same message is processed twice, the second write overwrites the same row with the same data. The catalog cannot tell the difference. That is what "exactly-once catalog upserts" means on the resume.

-- Illustrative only. The real sink was the Uber Eats catalog.
-- The idea: the write is keyed, so repeating it is harmless.
INSERT INTO catalog_items (vendor_id, menu_id, item_key, name, price, content_hash)
VALUES ('v123', 'm9', 'tacos-al-pastor', 'Tacos al Pastor', 3.50, 'ab12')
ON CONFLICT (vendor_id, menu_id, item_key)
DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name,
              price = EXCLUDED.price,
              content_hash = EXCLUDED.content_hash;

2.4 RAG, embeddings and Milvus

  • Embedding: a list of numbers (a vector) that captures the meaning of text. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that are close together. Analogy: GPS coordinates for meaning. Two taqueria menus end up as neighbours, a sushi menu lands far away.
  • Vector database: a database built to store embeddings and quickly find the nearest ones to a query vector.
  • Milvus: the open-source vector database used here. We stored embeddings of already-labelled menus in it.
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): retrieve relevant examples first, put them in the prompt, then ask the LLM. Analogy: before asking a new hire to fill a form, show them three correctly filled forms for similar cases.
  • LangChain: a Python framework that chains the steps: load, split, embed, retrieve, prompt, call the model, parse.
  • Gemini 2.5 Pro: Google's large language model, used to read menu content and return catalog-shaped JSON.
  • Schema validation gate: a strict check (for example a Pydantic model) that every field exists, has the right type, and uses allowed values, before anything is written.
  • Field fidelity: the share of extracted fields that exactly match a hand-labelled answer key.
  • Offline evaluation: measuring on a fixed labelled test set rather than live traffic. Repeatable and comparable between versions, but not a live production SLA.

2.5 Acquisition terms

  • Selenium: drives a real browser from code. Needed because JavaScript-built menus do not exist in the raw HTML.
  • Proxy pool: a set of intermediate servers with different IP addresses that requests go through. Dynamic means proxies that start getting blocked are removed and fresh ones are added automatically.
  • IP rotation: using a different outgoing address for successive requests, so no single address looks like a bot.
  • Adaptive retries: retrying failures with growing waits (exponential backoff) and a retry budget per source, so one hostile site cannot consume the whole fleet.

3. Architecture

flowchart LR Src["Restaurant sites, PDFs, images"] --> Sel["Selenium fleet on GCP: proxy pools, IP rotation, adaptive retries"] Sel --> K["Kafka topic, key = vendor and menu"] K --> F["Flink job: keyed dedupe, normalize, validate, route"] F -->|structured menu| Up["Idempotent catalog upsert"] F -->|unstructured PDF| RAG["LangChain RAG path"] RAG --> MV[("Milvus: embeddings of labelled menus")] MV --> RAG RAG --> GM["Gemini 2.5 Pro: catalog JSON"] GM --> Gate["Schema validation gate"] Gate -->|valid| Up Gate -->|invalid| Retry["Retry or review path"] Up --> Cat["Uber Eats catalog"]

What to notice: Kafka decouples scraping from processing. Flink is the one place where deduplication and normalization happen. The LLM never writes to the catalog directly. Its output must pass the schema gate first.

Walking through it.

  1. The Selenium fleet on GCP fetches menus. It routes requests through a dynamic proxy pool, rotates IPs, and retries with backoff and per-source budgets.
  2. Each fetched menu becomes an event on a Kafka topic, keyed by vendor and menu. Kafka absorbs bursts when the fleet runs, keeps messages for replay, and lets more than one consumer read the same data.
  3. A Flink job consumes the topic. It groups events by key and keeps the last content hash per key. If a new event has the same hash, it is a duplicate and is dropped. Otherwise Flink normalizes fields to the catalog schema and routes the event.
  4. Structured menus go directly to the idempotent catalog upsert.
  5. Unstructured PDFs go to the RAG path. It retrieves similar labelled menus from Milvus, prompts Gemini 2.5 Pro, and passes the output to the schema gate. Valid output is upserted. Invalid output goes to a retry or review path instead of the catalog.

The older plain-text version of this diagram, kept because it shows the role split clearly:

Partner sites / PDF + image menus
        |
        v
Selenium scrapers (GCP) + proxy pools     <- acquire HTML / files
        |
        v
Kafka (keyed by vendor_id)                <- buffer, replay, fan-out
        |
        +--> Flink (event time)           <- normalize, validate, dedupe, route
        |         |
        |         +--> catalog upsert (idempotent)
        |         +--> unstructured -> RAG / Gemini path
        |
        +--> [study only, NOT on PDF] Spark backfill (see section 13)

ANZ compliance is a separate Uber Mobility project. It is not on this path.

What to notice: the Spark branch is drawn only to support a "what would you do for backfills" discussion. It is not something I claim.

4. Why Kafka plus Flink for this project

4.1 Why Menu is the right home for the streaming story

Project Verdict Why
Uber Menu Kafka plus Flink, on the PDF Bursty scraping needs a durable buffer (Kafka) and online per-key dedupe with recovery (Flink).
Masters India Not Flink It already has Kafka plus Spring Boot consumers for bulk GST e-invoicing. Adding Flink there would not be backed by evidence.
Impact Analytics Not Kafka or Flink That work is ClickHouse analytics and Go/Gin APIs, not a stream job.
Skills line only Too weak Data and backend screens want an experience bullet, not just a skills chip.

4.2 The decision in full

What. Selenium publishes menu events to Kafka. A Flink job consumes them, deduplicates by key and content hash, normalizes to the catalog schema, and upserts idempotently.

Why Kafka. - Scrapers must not block on slow catalog writes. Kafka lets them publish and move on. - After a bad parser deploy, we can rewind offsets and replay. - Several consumers can share one log (the Flink job, audits, future consumers). - Keying by vendor keeps one restaurant's events in order.

Why Flink. - Per-key state for deduplication by content hash. - Event-time handling, so a page that arrives late does not overwrite a newer version. - Checkpointed recovery with Kafka offsets, which is the basis of the exactly-once effect. - Low latency per event, so catalog freshness is minutes, not a nightly batch.

How. Topic keyed by vendor and menu. Flink key_by on the same key. ValueState holds the last content hash. A normalize step maps prices, currencies and category names to the schema. The sink is an idempotent upsert.

Alternatives considered. - Scrapers write straight to the catalog over HTTP. Simple, but scrapers stall when the catalog is slow, there is no replay, and duplicate handling is scattered. - A plain Kafka consumer script. Works for stateless transforms. For per-key state, event time and crash recovery you would rebuild what Flink already gives you. - Kafka Streams. A reasonable option for lighter transforms at this event rate, especially if it were the team standard. Flink was chosen for richer event-time support, larger keyed state and a clearer story for a dedicated processing job. - Spark Structured Streaming. Not on the resume. Its micro-batch model adds seconds of latency per batch. See section 13 for how to discuss Spark if asked.

Trade-off. Flink is more to operate than a consumer script: checkpoints, state size, upgrades.

What I'd do differently. Put consumer lag, dedupe drop rate and schema-gate reject rate on one dashboard from day one. Those three numbers tell you almost everything about pipeline health.

5. Kafka in this pipeline, in detail

Topic and key. One topic for raw menu events, keyed by vendor and menu. Same key, same partition, so per-restaurant order holds.

Why key by vendor and menu, not randomly. Random keys spread load perfectly but scramble order. If version 2 of a menu is processed before version 1, the catalog ends up with stale data. Keying by vendor and menu keeps versions in order.

Hot keys. A very large restaurant group can make one partition busier than the others. Options: include menu id in the key (which we did) so a vendor's menus spread out, and add partitions if needed.

Consumer group. The Flink job's Kafka source is one consumer group. Partitions are split across its parallel tasks.

Offsets and replay. Flink stores the Kafka offsets inside its checkpoints rather than relying only on Kafka's committed offsets. On restore it resumes from exactly the checkpointed positions. For a deliberate replay after a bad deploy, start the job from an earlier offset or timestamp.

What an event looks like (illustrative shape):

{
  "vendor_id": "v123",
  "menu_id": "m9",
  "source": "website",
  "scraped_at": "2025-03-14T10:02:11Z",
  "content_hash": "ab12...",
  "payload_uri": "gs://bucket/menus/v123/m9.html",
  "scrape_status": "ok"
}

The payload_uri field shows a general practice worth knowing: large payloads (HTML, PDF) sit in object storage and the event carries a pointer, so Kafka messages stay small and brokers stay fast. If asked exactly how payload size was handled on the project, keep it qualitative.

6. Flink in this pipeline, in detail

Topic What I say
API DataStream API, keyed by vendor and menu
Time Event time from the scrape timestamp. Watermarks with bounded out-of-orderness for late pages.
State Keyed dedupe state (last content hash or menu version), commonly in the RocksDB state backend
Fault tolerance Checkpoint barriers. On a worker loss, restore from the last successful checkpoint.
Delivery Kafka source with checkpointed offsets. The catalog sink is idempotent, so replays are harmless.
Backpressure A slow catalog fills Flink's network buffers, Flink reads Kafka more slowly, and consumer lag rises. Lag is the alert.
Bad deploy Fix the normalizer, rewind Kafka offsets to before the bad deploy, and reprocess. Idempotent upserts make the replay safe.

6.1 Keyed dedupe, worked example

State for key (v123, m9) starts empty.

Event content_hash State before Action State after
e1 ab12 empty new, normalize and upsert ab12
e2 (retry of e1) ab12 ab12 duplicate, drop ab12
e3 (menu changed) cd34 ab12 new, normalize and upsert cd34

An illustrative PyFlink-style implementation:

class DedupeMenu(KeyedProcessFunction):
    def open(self, ctx):
        desc = ValueStateDescriptor("last_hash", Types.STRING())
        self.last_hash = ctx.get_state(desc)

    def process_element(self, event, ctx):
        if self.last_hash.value() == event["content_hash"]:
            return
        self.last_hash.update(event["content_hash"])
        yield normalize(event)

(events
    .key_by(lambda e: (e["vendor_id"], e["menu_id"]))
    .process(DedupeMenu())
    .add_sink(idempotent_catalog_upsert))

6.2 Event time and watermarks, worked example

Two versions of the same menu are scraped at 10:00 and 10:05. Because of a retry, the 10:05 version reaches Flink first and the 10:00 version arrives a minute later. With processing time, the older 10:00 version would be applied last and overwrite the newer one. With event time, Flink compares scrape timestamps and keeps the 10:05 version as the latest. The watermark bounds how long Flink waits for stragglers before it treats an event as late.

sequenceDiagram participant S as Scraper participant K as Kafka participant F as Flink S->>K: version A, scraped 10:00, delayed by retry S->>K: version B, scraped 10:05 K->>F: version B arrives first F->>F: state latest is now 10:05 K->>F: version A arrives late F->>F: 10:00 is older than 10:05, do not overwrite

What to notice: ordering by when the event happened, not when it arrived, is what stops stale menus from winning.

6.3 Checkpoints and recovery, worked example

  1. Flink checkpoints at offset 1,000 on partition 4, with last_hash = ab12 for (v123, m9).
  2. It processes offsets 1,001 to 1,050 and upserts them.
  3. A worker crashes before the next checkpoint.
  4. Flink restores state from the checkpoint and resumes reading at offset 1,001.
  5. Offsets 1,001 to 1,050 are processed again. The upserts are idempotent, so the catalog is unchanged.

That is the whole exactly-once story in five steps.

6.4 Backpressure

Flink uses credit-based flow control between tasks. If the catalog sink slows, its input buffers fill, it stops granting credits upstream, and the Kafka source reads more slowly. Kafka holds the unread messages, and consumer lag rises. Nothing runs out of memory. The fix is to speed up or scale the sink, not to "add pods and hope". This is a Menu concept. Do not tell it as an Impact Analytics story.

7. Exactly-once, honestly

Q: Is it exactly-once end to end? "Not in the strict distributed-transaction sense. Across Selenium, Kafka, Flink and an external catalog, what you really get is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent upsert. Inside Flink, state and Kafka offsets are checkpointed together. After a failure some messages are replayed, and the keyed upsert makes those replays harmless. True end-to-end exactly-once needs a transactional sink that participates in the commit. I don't claim two-phase commit across Gemini or third-party sites, and I never claim zero message loss."

8. The RAG path over Milvus

What. Multilingual PDF and image menus become catalog JSON through LangChain RAG plus Gemini 2.5 Pro, with Milvus as the retrieval store.

Why. PDFs and photos have no stable structure. Rule-based parsers break on every new layout and language. An LLM can read them, and retrieval keeps it grounded in what correct output looks like.

How, step by step.

  1. Parse the PDF and split it into chunks.
  2. Embed the content.
  3. Query Milvus for the nearest labelled menus (similar cuisine, layout or language).
  4. Build the prompt: the catalog schema, the retrieved examples with their correct outputs, and the new menu.
  5. Gemini 2.5 Pro returns JSON.
  6. A Pydantic model validates it. Valid output is upserted. Invalid output is retried or sent for review.
examples = milvus_store.similarity_search(menu_text, k=3)
prompt = build_prompt(schema=CATALOG_SCHEMA, examples=examples, menu=menu_text)
raw = gemini.invoke(prompt)
try:
    menu = CatalogMenu.model_validate_json(raw)
except ValidationError:
    send_to_retry_or_review(menu_id)
else:
    upsert_catalog(menu)

This sketch is illustrative, to show the shape of the flow. It is not Uber code.

Alternatives. - Paid third-party extraction at about $2 per menu. This is what we replaced. - Prompt-only with no retrieval. Cheaper, but more invented fields and inconsistent categories. - Fine-tuning (SFT). Discussed in older prep, removed from the PDF. Treat as verbal only. - Another vector store (Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector). Do not claim any of them for Menu. The vector store was Milvus.

Trade-off. LLM cost per menu, and the labelled examples and test set have to be kept fresh.

What I'd do differently. Sample live outputs weekly against human labels, so there is an online quality signal next to the offline 98%.

Industry parallel (citation, not a personal claim). Delivery platforms commonly combine OCR or LLM structuring with retrieval grounding and a confidence or human gate. Mention the pattern, but defend my own LangChain, Gemini and Milvus work, not any other company's internals.

9. The Selenium fleet and anti-bot hardening

What. A Python Selenium fleet on GCP that fetches restaurant menus.

Why it needed hardening. Sites detect and block scrapers: IP bans, CAPTCHA walls, soft 403 responses, and pages that load but hide the menu.

How. - Dynamic proxy pools: requests go out through many IP addresses, and proxies that start getting blocked are swapped out. - IP rotation and user-agent variation, so traffic does not look like one bot. - Adaptive retries: exponential backoff with a retry budget per source, so one hostile site cannot use up the fleet. - Scrape-health signals in each event, so empty or suspiciously small menus are caught instead of being treated as success.

Result. Extraction success reached 95%+. The starting point was an estimated 60 to 65%.

Trade-off. Proxies cost money and add latency, and the fleet needs monitoring when sites change.

13. Spark: verbal, study-only backfill option (NOT a resume claim)

Read this label first. Spark is not on the PDF, not in the Menu tech line, and not something I claim to have run on this project. This section exists only so I can answer "how would you reprocess history?" or "why Flink and not Spark?" with good judgement. If I mention Spark, I say "as an option I'd consider", never "we ran Spark".

Apache Spark in one paragraph. Spark is a distributed batch-processing engine. It splits a big dataset into partitions, runs the same function on each across a cluster, and shuffles data between machines for joins and group-bys. Analogy: instead of one person counting a warehouse, a hundred people each count one aisle, then the totals are combined. Spark Structured Streaming adds a streaming mode built on small, frequent batches (micro-batches).

When I'd suggest Spark for this design. For a one-off historical reprocess, for example re-normalizing 90 days of menu items after a schema change. That job is batch-shaped: large reads from object storage, big joins, run once. An older prep estimate put a typical 90-day reprocess at about 1 to 2 million item rows. That figure is ESTIMATED and study-only.

Why Flink, not Spark, for the live path. Scrapes are bursty. The live path needs per-key state for dedupe, event-time ordering for late pages, and per-event latency so catalog freshness is minutes. Spark micro-batches add seconds of delay per batch and are a weaker fit for keyed state.

Why Spark, not Flink, for a big backfill (as an option). A one-shot rewrite of history is a large shuffle and SQL-style join. Spark's DataFrame API fits that shape. Standing up large Flink state for a one-time job is the wrong cost curve. In this pipeline, though, Kafka replay plus idempotent upserts already covers short reprocessing windows, so Spark would only matter for history older than Kafka retention.

Study topic What to know
Role in a design like this Backfill, reprocess, large joins. Not the live path.
API Spark SQL and DataFrames over object-storage dumps
Skew A few huge vendors can overload one partition. Salt the keys or isolate the biggest vendors.
AQE Adaptive Query Execution re-plans at runtime to handle skew and merge small partitions.
Structured Streaming A near-real-time option. Do not claim both Flink and Spark for the same live path.

Study questions with speakable answers.

  • "Why not only Spark Structured Streaming?" "Micro-batch latency and weaker keyed-state support make it a worse fit for live catalog freshness under scrape bursts. On my resume the live path is Kafka and Flink. Spark is something I'd consider for a large one-off backfill."
  • "Spark versus ClickHouse?" "Different problems. A Menu backfill would be ETL over scrape history. ClickHouse is my Impact Analytics work, which is interactive analytics on planner data. I keep the two stories separate."
  • "How deep is your Spark?" "Study-level. I know the execution model, shuffles, skew handling and AQE, but Spark is not on my resume and I don't claim production ownership. My production streaming experience is Kafka and Flink on Menu."

Industry reading (for study, not claims): Confluent: Spark Streaming vs Flink, Estuary: Spark vs Flink, Spark cluster overview, Structured Streaming guide.

"An earlier version of your resume said Menu was only Selenium. Which is it?" "Both layers were there. Selenium acquires the pages. Kafka and Flink process them and land catalog data. An earlier one-page version dropped the streaming detail to save space. The current resume matches the fuller story, and that's what I defend. Kafka at Masters India is a separate product, for GST e-invoices."

"Derive 200 to 500 events a second." "30K menus a month is about a thousand a day. Each menu produces many item-level events plus retry and health events during a fleet run, and runs are bunched into windows. That puts the peak in the hundreds per second. Steady state is much lower. It's an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a dashboard screenshot, and it's not on my resume."

"A Flink checkpoint fails mid-run. What happens?" "The job restores from the last successful checkpoint. State goes back to that snapshot and the Kafka offsets rewind to the checkpointed positions. Messages since then are re-read, and the idempotent upserts make that harmless. Consumer lag alerts fire until it catches up. If a whole window was corrupted by a bad deploy, I fix the code and replay from Kafka."

"Isn't Kafka plus Flink overkill at 30K menus a month?" "Volume is moderate, yes. The choice is about the shape of the problem, not just throughput. Scraping is bursty, the same menu shows up more than once, pages arrive out of order, and we need replay after a bad deploy. Kafka gives buffering and replay, and Flink gives keyed state, event time and recovery. A single consumer script could work at this scale, but we'd be rebuilding those guarantees by hand."

"Why not Kafka Streams?" "Kafka Streams is a good fit for lighter transforms, and at this event rate it could have worked if it were the team standard. Flink gave us richer event-time handling, larger keyed state and a clearer story for a dedicated processing job."

"How do you know the dedupe isn't dropping real updates?" "Dedupe is by content hash per vendor and menu, so only byte-identical repeats are dropped. If anything on the menu changes, the hash changes and the event goes through. I'd watch the drop rate. A sudden spike would mean something upstream is re-sending, or the hash input is wrong."

"What happens when the catalog is slow?" "Backpressure. Flink's buffers fill, it reads Kafka more slowly, and consumer lag rises. Nothing is lost because Kafka holds the messages. Lag is the alert, and the fix is to speed up or scale the sink."

"Does Databricks-style Spark depth apply to you?" "I'd be straightforward. Spark is study-level for me and it's not on my resume. My production streaming work is Kafka and Flink on Menu, and my analytics depth is ClickHouse at Impact Analytics."

RECOMMENDATION

Run the pivot as a hybrid, not a swap.

Neither engine wins outright — the workload splits cleanly. ClickHouse owns every read / aggregate / pivot and crushes storage; Postgres owns the interactive single-cell write-back by two orders of magnitude. The right design serves the grid from ClickHouse and keeps cell edits authoritative in Postgres — exactly the split the existing MTP backend already half-implements (BigQuery reads + Postgres OLTP).

The decision rule: if a surface aggregates many rows → ClickHouse. If it mutates a few cells and must read them back instantly → Postgres. The pivot needs both, so it needs both engines. (Headline magnitudes below are raw measurements; an adversarial pass corrected them — see Verification.)

WHO WINS WHAT

Scoreboard

Measured at 250M rows (current Briscoes is ~5M; the recommendation must survive growth). Magnitudes are medians of repeated warm runs — raw figures; the adversarial pass corrects several downward (CH reads ~2–3× typical, PG writes ~14× tuned, storage low-single-digits realistic).

The same query — pivot grid with contribution-% and option-count, joined across hierarchy, cluster, and calendar. Bars are log-scaled wall-clock; ClickHouse stays interactive while Postgres falls off a cliff.

At 250M the Postgres pivot takes 3 minutes 9 seconds and spills 42 GB of sort files to disk. ClickHouse answers the same question in 12 seconds on a 3.3 GB VM. Even the “selective drill” — Postgres’s one early win at 5M — flips to a ClickHouse win (18.5×) once each subclass holds more SKUs.

THE WRITE SPLIT

Why Postgres still owns the keyboard

A planner tabbing through Wp cells does single-row edits and expects the value back instantly. That is the one thing a columnar append-store is built to be bad at — and the one thing a row store is built to be great at.

Postgres is sub-millisecond and flat with scale (indexed point update). ClickHouse is ~70–100 ms because each edit creates a new part + read-modify-write + dedup-on-read.

Inverts the story: ClickHouse append stays flat while Postgres in-place UPDATE scales with row count — CH ends up ~2,500× faster for bulk edits and reloads.

Implication: single-cell edits → Postgres; “apply +10% to a whole subclass”, rollups, and full reloads → ClickHouse. The write side is also a split, not a one-engine answer.

STORAGE & THE MODELING TRAP

Two findings that reframe the question

Storage: ClickHouse is ~50× leaner

Honest caveat (from verification): this synthetic data is wildly compressible — with realistic high-entropy measures, ClickHouse’s ratio collapses from 83.7× to ~1.6–2.6×. Postgres is genuinely not bloated (157.6 B/row = theoretical min). Expect a real-world storage edge of low-single-digits to ~10×, not 50× — still meaningful, not magical.

The 11-second query is mostly a modeling bug

The live Briscoes pivot takes 11.3 s on Postgres — but most of that is the JSONB layout, not Postgres itself. Same logical pivot, same data:

2.06× penalty just from JSONB extraction per row. Flattening the fact is the cheapest win available — independent of any ClickHouse decision.

HOW THIS WAS KEPT HONEST

Methodology & fairness

Fair-model vs fair-model

Row-identical data. Same deterministic row→(choice,cluster,week) mapping in both engines; aggregate fingerprints match exactly (250M float-derived sums agree to 2×10⁻¹²).

Each engine’s best physical model. Postgres: flat, partitioned by week, indexed. ClickHouse: MergeTree sorted on the pivot keys. The slow JSONB layout is reported separately, not as “Postgres”.

Realistic shape. The grid joins fact × hierarchy × cluster × calendar and computes contribution-% windows — not a toy single-table scan (joins are where ClickHouse is supposedly weak).

Postgres got every advantage

Postgres ran native on the host with 48 GB RAM, 12 GB shared buffers, 8 parallel workers, fast local NVMe.

ClickHouse was boxed in a 10-CPU / 3.3 GB Docker VM — and still won every read.

So the read wins are conservative; the Postgres-favorable findings (write-back, point reads) get full credit.

Warm medians over repeated runs; the 250M heavy grid run once (it takes minutes on PG).

Engines provisioned fresh and isolated for this study — the shared ClickHouse (Arhaus / ItemSmart) and read-only Briscoes Postgres were used only as real-world anchors, never as the head-to-head.

WHAT THE CURRENT BACKEND DOES — AND WHAT TO FIX

Reusing the existing pivot

The MTP AssortSmart backend already runs a de-facto hybrid: it aggregates the heavy “hindsight” grid in BigQuery (GROUP BY + window contribution-%) and keeps plan state + write-back in Postgres (in-place keyed UPDATE, JSONB merge, TRUNCATE+COPY syncs). The pivot’s row/column rotation is largely shaped by the GROUP BY + the front-end, not a SQL PIVOT.

Keep

The read/write split is already correct in spirit. Write-back as keyed Postgres UPDATE is the right primitive and matches this benchmark’s winner.

Optimise

(1) Flatten the JSONB fact → 2× immediately. (2) Put the interactive pivot on a ClickHouse MergeTree refreshed from the plan store, instead of paying BigQuery latency/cost per grid. (3) Replace per-row UPDATE loops + full TRUNCATE+COPY with block appends.

RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE

The hybrid pivot, concretely

A working POC of exactly this runs against the live 250M dataset: GET /pivot builds the grid from ClickHouse with contribution-%; POST /cell writes the edit to Postgres (authoritative) and mirrors it to the ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree. The edited cell reads back correctly from both within one request.

The cost of hybrid (don’t gloss over it)

Two stores means a sync path and a freshness window between the Postgres edit and the ClickHouse copy. For a single editor this is invisible; for the grid’s correctness it must read the ClickHouse copy with dedup (argMax/FINAL) or read the just-edited cells from Postgres. This is the one real operational tax of the recommendation.

ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION

We tried to break our own conclusions

Independent skeptics ran counter-tests against the live 250M engines to refute each headline. They confirmed every direction — but caught three overstated magnitudes. The honest, corrected picture:

Net: the recommendation (CH for reads/scale, PG for interactive write-back) holds — but the honest magnitudes are ClickHouse ~2–3× on typical aggregates (up to ~13× when grids include distinct-counts) and Postgres ~14× on tuned single-cell writes (not the eye-popping 90–283× from untuned defaults). The decision is real but less lopsided than raw numbers suggest.

THREE REAL USE CASES AT SCALE

Views 1.1.1 / 1.1.2 / 1.1.3 — where the verdict flips, and when

We built three actual wireframe screens end-to-end (schema, API, row-identical data at 5.76M / 50M / 250M) to test the recommendation on real surfaces. The split is consistent — but the read crossover point depends on the screen.

Full-cluster (cross-subclass) reads are ClickHouse at every scale on both views, widening to 13–15× at 250M. The selective read flips later when its output stays small (1.1.2’s threshold bucketing collapses to ~10 rows → Postgres holds to ~250M; 1.1.1 fetches thousands of rows + joins the growing product dim → flips at 50M).

The honest cross-view read: writes belong to Postgres at every scale (sub-ms, flat). Reads belong to ClickHouse for anything cross-cutting, and for selective screens once they grow — the crossover is 50M (1.1.1) to ~250M (1.1.2), set by output size + joins, not the engine. At Briscoes’ current ~5M, the selective screens still run fine on Postgres; the ClickHouse case is the full-grid views and the road to 50M+. Pick the engine per surface, not per product.

THREATS TO VALIDITY

Where these numbers could mislead

Synthetic data is compression-friendly. The 138× storage ratio at 250M is optimistic; trust the ~47–54× real-world anchor.

ClickHouse single-row write latency can be tuned. async_insert / buffering narrows it — but at the cost of read-after-write immediacy, which is the whole point of write-back. (See adversarial.)

The 5M “present” is small for OLAP. At today’s scale Postgres-only is survivable (4 s grid); the case for ClickHouse is about where Briscoes is heading (50–250M+ multi-tenant), where the grid becomes unusable on Postgres.

Contribution-% / option-count drive the gap. COUNT(DISTINCT) spills hard on Postgres; it’s a real wireframe measure, so it stays — but a pre-aggregated rollup narrows specific grids.

Architecture should be hybrid | HOLDS | The read/write split is real and survives tuning; hybrid stands.
