How to answer any "tell me about this tech" question

Use the same five steps every time. It keeps answers short, concrete and senior.

  1. Where. Name the product and the exact place in the request path. "In AssortSmart, ClickHouse serves the planner grid."
  2. Why. Name the failure it prevents, not "industry standard". "Postgres took 189 seconds on that grid."
  3. Rejected. Name one alternative and why it lost. "We kept Postgres for small edits because it is better at single-row writes."
  4. Number. Give the number with its tag. On Impact Analytics, never invent throughput beyond 10k peak RPS.
  5. Failure. Say what breaks if this piece dies, and what we do then. "If the LLM times out, we fall back to the rule score."

Example, spoken: "In AssortSmart, ClickHouse serves the planner pivot grid. On Postgres that grid took 189 seconds on 250 million rows, which is unusable. We considered tuning Postgres, but it is a row store and the grid aggregates whole columns. On ClickHouse it dropped to about 12 seconds. If ClickHouse is down, the grid is down, so Postgres keeps the small metadata and access tables that login depends on."

Impact Analytics: AssortSmart (Platform and AI)

The business in plain English

AssortSmart is a SaaS product for retail merchandise planners. Every season a planner decides which products (articles) to keep in the range, which to drop, and which they are missing. Planner pivots used to run on PostgreSQL and were too slow to use interactively. AssortSmart gives them fast grids over billions of rows of sales and inventory data, plus AI recommendations they can question in a chat.

Words you need

  • Article-season: one product in one selling season, for example "Blue linen shirt, Spring-Summer 2026".
  • Go / Gin: Go is a compiled language that is good at many concurrent requests. Gin is a small web framework for it.
  • Google Wire: a tool that writes the code connecting your components (database, cache, handlers) at build time. If something is missing, the build fails instead of a live request. Think of it as a checklist checked before the plane takes off.
  • h2c: HTTP/2 without TLS. HTTP/2 lets many requests share one connection. It is used inside a trusted network where TLS is handled elsewhere.
  • Reverse proxy: a server like Nginx that sits in front of your app and handles timeouts, TLS and routing. We chose not to have one, so the Go process does that work itself.
  • ClickHouse: a column-oriented analytics database. It stores each column separately, so "sum sales for all rows" reads only the sales column. Great for big aggregates, poor for single-row edits.
  • MergeTree / ReplacingMergeTree: ClickHouse table types. MergeTree stores sorted data in parts and merges them in the background. ReplacingMergeTree also keeps only the newest version of rows with the same key. Think of a notebook where you never erase: you write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines.
  • LangGraph: a Python library for building LLM workflows as a graph of steps with shared state, loops and limits.
  • LangSmith: a tracing tool for LLM apps. It shows each step, prompt, tool call and token count.
  • OIDC and JWT: OIDC (OpenID Connect) is a standard way to log in with Google or similar. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed token that proves who you are on each request.
  • UAM: User Access Management, the rules for which parts of the product hierarchy each user may see.

User flow, one planner session

  1. A planner signs in. The Go/Gin platform checks the token: first a Redis cache of verified tokens, then Firebase Admin, then JWT or Google OIDC. Their roles come from Postgres.
  2. They open a pivot grid. Gin builds the query, including any operator-authored KPI formulas compiled by the formula parser, and ClickHouse answers from pre-aggregated rollup tables.
  3. In batch runs, the Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style pipelines score each article. Rule math runs first. The LLM gets a JSON summary, never database access.
  4. The planner opens Ask Iris, a chat over WebSocket, and asks "why did we drop this shirt?" Their data scope was frozen when the socket opened, so the answer can only use data they are allowed to see.

Architecture

flowchart LR P["Planner UI"] --> G["Go Gin platform: Wire, h2c, nested timeouts, Datadog"] G --> R["Redis: verified token cache"] G --> PG["PostgreSQL: UAM, roles, metadata"] G --> CH["ClickHouse: 2.11B master and season and weekly rollups"] B["Python batch pipelines: Keep/Drop, Missed Opp, Top Style"] --> CH B --> J["JSON context payloads"] J --> L["LLM: 7 lenses and decider"] L --> W["ReplacingMergeTree results"] W --> CH P --> I["Ask Iris: FastAPI WebSocket"] I --> S["LangGraph supervisor and 3-attempt evaluator"] S --> LS["LangSmith traces"]

What to notice: the LLM boxes never connect directly to ClickHouse. Python code reads the data, packs JSON, and writes results. Go serves the planner. Python runs the AI.

Walking the boxes: the Go/Gin platform is the front door for every planner request and handles about 10k requests per second at peak. Redis keeps recently verified tokens so login checks do not hit Firebase on every call. PostgreSQL holds the small, frequently edited tables: users, roles, access scopes, metadata. ClickHouse holds the big analytical data and the rollup tables that make grids fast. The batch pipelines read features from ClickHouse, compute rule scores, hand JSON to the LLM, blend, and write results. Ask Iris is a separate Python service for chat.

Key design decisions

1. Serve the LLM JSON, never a SQL tool. - What: deterministic Python code reads ClickHouse, computes KPIs and packs a JSON payload per batch. The model scores from that payload. - Why: an LLM writing SQL against a 2.11B-row table can launch runaway scans, exhaust the connection pool, or be steered by prompt injection. - Alternative: give the model a read-only SQL tool. Rejected for the risks above and because math accuracy would then depend on the model. - Trade-off: the payload must contain everything the model needs, so adding a new signal means a code change. - Differently next time: version the payload schema explicitly from day one, so lens prompts and payload fields cannot drift.

2. ClickHouse for planner reads, Postgres for thin metadata. - What: pivots read ClickHouse rollups. Postgres keeps UAM, roles and metadata. - Why: the benchmark showed Postgres at 189 seconds and ClickHouse at about 12 seconds on 250M rows. Postgres won single-cell edits. - Alternative: one database for everything. Rejected because each engine is bad at the other's job. - Trade-off: two engines to run, and data must be kept consistent across them. - Differently next time: build weekly rollups at one-week grain from the start, which would have avoided the 170 GB OOM.

3. Partition rollback for the cluster copy. - What: if a season's copy fails midway, drop that season's partition on the target and recopy it. - Why: a failed insert in ClickHouse can still commit some blocks, leaving "ghost rows". A partial count looks fine but is wrong. - Alternative: an atomic swap with REPLACE PARTITION. I wrote that incremental design, but we did not execute it. - Trade-off: during recopy, that season's partition is briefly incomplete on the target. It is not an atomic swap with live readers. - Differently next time: run the REPLACE PARTITION design I wrote, so readers never see a dropped partition.

Tech on the PDF and why it is there

Tech Where it sits Why it is here Rejected alternative Number
Go, Gin, Wire The HTTP edge for planners Many concurrent requests, compile-time wiring, timeouts in-process A Python public edge 10k peak RPS
ClickHouse Planner grids, master fact table, rollups Columnar engine for big aggregates Postgres for analytics. Snowflake for this UI 189s to 12s on 250M. 2.11B master
KPI formula parser Compiles operator formulas into SQL fragments New KPIs without a code release, divide-by-zero safe via ifNotFinite Hard-coded SQL per KPI none
Firebase, OIDC, Redis, Postgres roles Login and access control Stop one tenant seeing another's data Treating encryption as isolation none
LangGraph Ask Iris supervisor and evaluator Explicit loops with a hard cap A single prompt chain 3 attempts
Offline eval gate CI before promotion A change must beat the bar before it ships Shipping on demo feel 300 cases, 80% gate, 74% baseline
Datadog and LangSmith Go edge tracing and LLM tracing Different questions: "which service was slow" versus "which prompt step failed" One tool for both none

Verbal only: the Cluster Recommendation Copilot (14 tools, 3 gates), Hindsight, 63/8 DDL. See the verbal section of the IA pack.

Uber via EPAM: FRM Scoping Platform

The business in plain English

Every quarter, Uber Finance must decide which financial line items and which entities are big or risky enough to need audit testing. This is "scoping". Analysts used to do it in Google Sheets, copying general ledger data, applying thresholds by hand and emailing status. It took about 14 days. The platform moved it into a proper backend with a database, automated math and a review workflow, and cut it to about 3 days.

Words you need

  • FSLI: Financial Statement Line Item, one line on the balance sheet or income statement, such as Cash or Revenue. Ours were a four-level tree, L1 to L4.
  • Materiality: the dollar amount above which a misstatement would change a reader's decision. Q4 2025 used $340M.
  • GL: General Ledger, the master record of accounting entries.
  • HFM and 10-Q: HFM (Oracle Hyperion Financial Management) is the consolidation system. The 10-Q is the quarterly filing. Reconciliation checks they agree.
  • SOADB: Uber's standard for a MySQL database owned by one service.
  • ORM: Object-Relational Mapper, a library that maps classes to tables. Here it is Hibernate, used through Spring Data JPA: each table is a Java class marked @Entity, and a repository interface gives you queries without hand-written SQL.
  • Optimistic locking: each row has a version number. An update only succeeds if the version has not changed since you read it. Like editing a shared doc and being told "someone changed this, reload". In JPA this is a @Version field on the entity.
  • Natural key: an ID derived from the data itself. We used SHA-256 of fields like question text plus page name, so the same question always gets the same ID.
  • SOX: Sarbanes-Oxley, the US law that requires auditable controls over financial reporting.

User flow

  1. HFM data lands in MySQL through a shared ETL pipeline.
  2. An analyst runs Reconciliation to tie HFM to the 10-Q.
  3. They set Materiality and thresholds, then work through EMI, Group, Component and Residual Risk scoping screens. The backend computes significance automatically.
  4. Each screen's rows move through Draft, Review, ReOpen and Closed. Big swings are flagged at gates.
  5. The output feeds the auditor (PwC) work papers.

Architecture

flowchart LR HFM["HFM data via shared ETL"] --> DB["MySQL on SOADB: 8 normalized tables"] UI["Finance UI: 8 screens"] --> API["Spring Boot scoping service: 36 endpoints"] API --> ORM["Spring Data JPA and Hibernate"] ORM --> DB API --> FSM["Review state machine with 50 percent variance gates"] DB --> OUT["Auditor work papers"]

What to notice: the ETL from HFM was a shared pipeline, and the collaboration and Slack notification service was separate. I owned the scoping service and its schema.

Key design decision: one polymorphic review-status model

  • What: a single status model (Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed) reused by every screen, instead of one status table per screen.
  • Why: eight screens with eight status implementations would drift, and auditors need one consistent trail.
  • Alternative: per-screen status columns. Rejected for duplication and inconsistent audit history.
  • Trade-off: the shared model must be general enough for every screen, so screen-specific rules live in the service code.
  • Differently next time: use JPA entities and queries with explicit column aliases from day one. The column-aliasing bug (duplicate column names in joined raw SQL silently mapped rows to the wrong uuid) came from raw SQL joins.

Tech and numbers

Tech Why here Number on PDF
Java and Spring Boot, with Bean Validation DTOs REST controllers with typed request validation for financial inputs 36 Spring Boot endpoints
Spring Data JPA and Hibernate Entity mappings and aliased queries that removed the aliasing bug class 100% module statement coverage, led 3 engineers
JUnit 5, Mockito and MockMvc Unit and controller tests that proved the migration 100% module statement coverage
MySQL on SOADB Uber's paved road for service-owned data 8-table schema, 19M raw GL rows
Bazel Uber's build system. Stacked PRs shipped small changes with zero downtime none
Outcome Scoping moved off Sheets 70%, from 14 days to 3 days, against $340M materiality

Verbal depth if asked: 8 screens, 11 ORM models, about 55 line items across 14 entities in a sample close, the 18-file reconciliation v2 change.

Uber via EPAM: Menu Ingestion (Uber Eats) and Document Compliance (Mobility ANZ)

The business in plain English

New restaurants on Uber Eats send their menus as PDFs, images or web pages, in many languages. Someone had to turn each into Uber's strict catalog format: items, prices, options. That took about a day per restaurant and cost about $2 per menu with a third-party or manual step. This pipeline automated it, so menus go live in about two hours.

Words you need

  • Selenium: a tool that drives a real browser, used here to scrape restaurant sites.
  • Kafka: a durable log of events that many consumers can read at their own pace. Like a conveyor belt that remembers every box.
  • Apache Flink: a stream processor that keeps state per key. Here it remembers the last content hash per menu, so duplicates are dropped.
  • RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Before asking the LLM to extract a menu, we look up similar, already-labelled menus and include them as examples.
  • Milvus: a vector database that finds "similar" items by comparing embeddings (numeric fingerprints of text).
  • Upsert: insert a row, or update it if the key already exists.

Architecture

flowchart LR SRC["Restaurant sites"] --> SEL["Selenium fleet: proxy pools, adaptive retries"] SEL --> K["Kafka"] K --> F["Flink: keyed dedupe, schema normalization"] F --> C["Idempotent catalog upsert"] PDF["Unstructured multilingual PDFs"] --> X["Gemini 2.5 Pro with LangChain RAG"] M["Milvus: similar labelled menus"] --> X X --> V["Strict catalog schema check"] V --> C

What to notice: there are two paths into one catalog. Scraped menus stream through Kafka and Flink. Unstructured PDFs go through the RAG extraction path and a schema check. "Exactly-once" on the PDF means each menu lands in the catalog once. Under the hood that is at-least-once delivery from Kafka plus idempotent upserts keyed by vendor, menu and content hash.

Key design decision: Flink keyed dedupe before the catalog

  • What: Flink keeps per-menu state and drops events whose content hash it has already seen.
  • Why: scrapers retry and overlap, so the same menu arrives many times. Writing each copy would churn the catalog.
  • Alternative: dedupe in the database at write time. Rejected because every duplicate would still travel the whole pipeline and hit the catalog with a write.
  • Trade-off: Flink state must be checkpointed and sized.
  • Differently next time: measure the extraction success baseline properly before hardening, so "about 60 to 65%" would be a measured number, not an estimate.

Numbers

From 24 hours to 2 hours. $600K a year (about $2 × 30K × 12 = $720K, floored). 30K+ menus a month. 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation. 95%+ extraction success. Spark is not on the PDF.

Document Compliance, Uber Mobility ANZ

A deterministic validation backend checks driver and vehicle documents against local authority rules in Australia and New Zealand, replacing a manual review queue. 99.9% regulatory compliance and 20 hours a week saved. This is historical, and it is Mobility, not Eats. Do not add Selenium or RAG to it.

Masters India: GST E-Invoicing

The business in plain English

Indian businesses above a size threshold must register every invoice with the government's IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number) and a signed QR code. Masters India does this for 1,500+ enterprise clients. Clients upload invoices in bulk, often near filing deadlines, and the government portal is slow and flaky.

Words you need

  • Strangler pattern: replace an old system one route at a time. New routes go to the new service and the old one shrinks until it can be removed.
  • Canary release: send a small share of traffic to the new version first, and widen only if it is healthy.
  • Idempotent: doing an operation twice has the same effect as once. Our key looked like client + fileHash + batchIndex.
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ): where messages go after they fail too many times, so they stop blocking the rest.
  • Sharding: splitting one big table across several databases by a key. Ours was the tax quarter.
  • Cache-aside: the app checks Redis first. On a miss it reads Postgres and fills the cache.
  • ELK and New Relic: ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) for searchable logs, New Relic for request tracing.

Architecture

flowchart LR CL["Enterprise clients"] --> API["Spring Boot microservices, migrated from PHP by route"] API --> RD["Redis cache-aside"] API --> PG["PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter"] API --> K["Kafka event bus"] K --> WK["Spring Boot Kafka consumers with bounded retries"] WK --> IRP["Government IRP portal"] WK --> DLQ["Dead-letter queue"]

What to notice: the client never waits on the government portal. Kafka absorbs bursts, workers retry within limits, and repeat failures go to the DLQ.

Key design decision: Kafka between the API and the government portal

  • What: the API accepts the upload and writes events. Workers submit to the IRP.
  • Why: the IRP is slow and unreliable near deadlines. Calling it inline made p95 latency terrible and caused client timeouts.
  • Alternative: synchronous calls with longer timeouts. Rejected because it ties up connections and still fails under load.
  • Trade-off: as with any queue-based design, the result arrives asynchronously, so each invoice needs a tracked status rather than an instant answer.
  • Differently next time: put tracing in before the migration, so the triage baseline would be measured instead of estimated.

Numbers

p95 down 75%, from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds. 700 to 4,000 requests per minute (about 12 to 67 per second). 1M+ submissions a day (about 12 per second on average). 100K+ concurrent imports. Triage down 70%. DB read load down 30%. Coverage 35% to 82%. 98% deployment success. Mentored two engineers. No Flink here, and this Kafka is a different product from Uber Menu's.

GeeksforGeeks: Courses Platform and Influencer Dashboard

The business in plain English

GeeksforGeeks sells programming courses. Students post doubts (questions) that mentors answer, and traffic spikes about ten times during live coding contests. Influencers promote courses with coupon codes and want to see their earnings.

What I built

  • I moved the doubt-support backend from PHP to Django (a Python web framework with a built-in ORM and admin), with REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads on MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch. It handled 10K+ daily queries and 10x contest spikes. The growth team attributed a 20% lift in premium subscriptions.
  • I built the influencer analytics and earnings dashboard (transactions, coupon conversions), credited with 30% higher course sales, and asynchronous scheduled workflows for video processing, reminders and data cleanup, which made engineering operations about 70% more efficient.

Say it this way: "I owned the engineering. The business team attributed the lift."

Common interview questions: filled answers (your experience)

How to use this page

  • These are the classic HR and hiring-manager questions ("Tell me about yourself", "Greatest weakness", "Tell me about a conflict") with answers built from your real projects.
  • Read it before any behavioural or manager round. Practise each answer out loud. Each one should take 30 to 60 seconds.
  • Every answer follows the same shape: the direct answer first, then the reason, then a project example. Memorise the first sentence of each and the example you attach to it.
  • Start with "Technical terms in plain English" so you can explain any term an interviewer picks up on.

The format follows the "90 toughest interview questions" style: a numbered question, an answer, and sometimes a follow-up. Question 20 must be customised per employer.

Tags used here. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind the number. TARGET means a design goal, so say "targeting". ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. Full rules live in GROUND_TRUTH.md.

HTML: 32_common_interview_qa.html · Hub: ApplicationKit.html

Technical terms in plain English

Behavioural answers still contain technical words, and a good interviewer will pick one and ask "what does that mean?" Each term below has a plain definition, a tiny example, and where it appears in my answers.

p95 latency. The response time that 95% of requests are faster than. If 100 requests take between 100ms and 2s, and the 95th-fastest took 300ms, the p95 is 300ms. It matters more than the average because it shows what slow users feel. In my work: Masters India p95 went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds.

Strangler pattern. A way to replace an old system piece by piece. New services take over one route at a time while the old system keeps serving the rest, until the old one can be switched off. Example: move /invoice/validate to the new service first and leave everything else on PHP. In my work: the Masters India PHP to Spring Boot migration.

Canary release. Sending a small slice of real traffic, say 5%, to the new version first and watching errors before sending everyone. In my work: each migrated route at Masters India went out as a canary.

Idempotency key. A unique ID attached to an operation so that doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Example: if a client retries "register invoice 42" with the same key, the server returns the first result instead of registering it again. In my work: Masters India used client + file hash + batch index as the key.

Dead-letter queue (DLQ). A side queue for messages that keep failing, so they are parked for inspection instead of blocking everything behind them. In my work: Masters India IRP submissions that failed after bounded retries went to a DLQ.

Optimistic locking. Each row carries a version number. You read version 3, and your update only succeeds if the row is still version 3. If someone else saved first, your update fails and you retry with fresh data. In my work: Uber FRM review-status updates, using a @Version field on the JPA entity.

ORM (Object-Relational Mapper). A library that maps database tables to code objects, so you write accountRepository.findById(id) instead of raw SQL. Hibernate is the ORM, and Spring Data JPA generates the repository code on top of it. In my work: the Uber FRM migration to Spring Data JPA / Hibernate.

ReplacingMergeTree. A ClickHouse table type where you never update a row in place. You insert a new version, and a background merge later keeps only the newest one. It is like a notebook where you write corrections below the old line and a cleaner crosses out old lines later. In my work: Impact Analytics AI decision writes.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). Look up relevant reference material first, then hand it to the LLM with the question, so it answers from evidence. It is an open-book exam for the model. In my work: Uber Eats menu extraction with Gemini, LangChain and Milvus.

CI gate. An automatic check in the build pipeline that blocks a change if a score is below a bar. In my work: the 80% accuracy gate on the 300-case harness for AssortSmart AI changes.

SOX and materiality. SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley) is the US law that requires companies to prove their financial reporting controls work. Materiality is the size threshold above which an error would matter to investors. In my work: Uber FRM scoped accounts against a $340M materiality threshold.

1. Tell me about yourself.

Answer: I'm a Senior Software Engineer with about five years building backend and data platforms in Java, Python and Go. Right now at Impact Analytics I own the AssortSmart platform: a Go/Gin service that peaks at 10k requests per second, ClickHouse rollups that cut planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, and an AI decision engine that scores 348k article-seasons, plus a shipped copilot called Ask Iris. Before that, at Uber via EPAM, I owned the Finance risk scoping backend (Spring Boot and MySQL, 36 endpoints) that cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days, and I worked on Uber Eats menu automation that cut restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saves about $600K a year. At Masters India I led a PHP-to-Spring Boot migration for 1,500+ clients that took p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and worked on a Kafka pipeline handling over a million government submissions a day. I started at GeeksforGeeks, moving their doubt-support backend to Django. The common thread is that I own systems end to end and I can defend every number I quote.

Follow-up they may ask: "Which of those are you proudest of?" Pick the one that matches the role (see 08_role_targeting_and_rapid_fire.md).

2. Why should we hire you?

Answer: Because I bring design ownership, production discipline and mentoring, not just ticket delivery. At Uber via EPAM I owned the FRM backend design while leading 3 engineers, and the Eats menu work saves about $600K a year. At Masters India I led the Spring Boot migration that raised throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, and I mentored 2 engineers through it. At Impact Analytics I own a Go/Gin edge at 10k peak RPS, a 15.5x faster pivot path in ClickHouse, and an AI engine that only promotes changes through an 80% CI gate. I'm also careful with claims: I'll tell you which numbers are measured, which are gates, and which are historical. One example of that care: Kafka and Flink on my profile belong to Uber Menu, not Impact Analytics, and I keep those stories separate.

3. What is your greatest strength?

Answer: My greatest strength is turning messy production constraints into a clear system design and shipping it safely. I do my best work where correctness, latency and ownership collide. At Uber Finance, quarterly risk scoping still ran on Google Sheets, with no durable line IDs and no audit trail. I designed a layered Spring Boot and MySQL backend, migrated 19M raw general ledger rows off Sheets, and owned the reconciliation v2 rewrite, an 18-file change that ran in parallel with the old Sheets version until Finance trusted it. I encoded the materiality logic ($340M materiality and $170M residual on the Q4 2025 close, with 5% significance thresholds) and the checks of HFM (Oracle Hyperion) data against the filed 10-Q. The result was reconciliation going from 14 days to 3 days. It shows I can work under audit pressure and think in both product and engineering terms.

Follow-up they may ask: "What was the hardest bug?" The column-aliasing bug: duplicate column names in a joined raw SQL query silently mapped rows to the wrong ID. I fixed it with aliased selects and explicit labels, and the later Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration removed that class of bug.

4. What is your greatest weakness?

Answer: I used to hold on to critical-path work too long instead of delegating early. Earlier in my career I took too many reconciliation and cutover tasks myself to "guarantee quality", and that slowed down mentoring. I changed the habit at Masters India and later at Uber via EPAM. Now I set the API contract, pair with a teammate on the first slice (the first canary or the first reconciliation screen), then step back and let them own it. Leading 3 engineers on the FRM Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration and mentoring 2 on the Spring Boot migration forced me to practise that. Clear expectations and a steady review rhythm work better than doing everything myself.

5. Tell me about a time you failed.

Answer: At Masters India, early in the PHP-to-Spring Boot cutover, I set API timeouts too tight compared with the old PHP path. Some legitimate calls to the government Invoice Registration Portal took longer, so the first canary showed timeouts and put filing-day traffic at risk. I owned the mistake. I moved those calls to a fully asynchronous flow, where the API accepts the job, returns a "202 Accepted" response, and the client polls for progress. I aligned timeouts with how the portal really behaved and added idempotency keys, bounded retries and a dead-letter queue so failed calls could be replayed safely. The lesson stuck: for third-party compliance APIs, design for slow responses and safe retries from day one, not after the first scare.

Follow-up they may ask: "How did you know the timeouts were the problem?" The canary errors were timeouts on the government portal calls, which the old PHP path had tolerated with longer waits. Beyond that, keep the detail qualitative.

6. Describe a time when you had to deal with a difficult team member.

Answer: I dealt with it by finding the cause before escalating. At Uber via EPAM on FRM, a teammate kept missing API contract and test gates, which blocked Finance-facing releases. I set up a one-on-one and learned they were overloaded across UI and backend spikes. We re-split ownership: I kept the schema and the reconciliation v2 critical path, and they owned a bounded set of screens and APIs with a clearer definition of done. I paired with them on the first pull request using our controller, service and repository layering. Delivery stabilised, CI stayed green, and we hit the quarterly release without damaging the relationship.

7. Where do you see yourself in five years?

Answer: I see myself as a senior-to-staff backend or platform engineer who owns a multi-service domain end to end: design, reliability and mentoring. I want to keep deepening distributed systems, data platforms and production AI systems. That direction comes straight from my last few projects, where the hard part was always making something correct and safe at scale, not just making it work. I also want to help others ship safely behind clear contracts and quality gates, like the CI gate on our AI changes. I'm looking for a multi-year build where scope compounds, not a short hop.

8. Why do you want to leave your current job?

Answer: I'm looking for a role whose day-to-day ownership matches a multi-year backend and platform charter. At Impact Analytics I have learned a lot, especially about ClickHouse at billions of rows, LangGraph agents, and how to evaluate AI safely before promoting it. What I want next is deeper production ownership of distributed systems and data platforms at scale, which this role offers. I'm closing my open work professionally and interviewing carefully for fit, not running away from anything.

Follow-up they may ask: "You joined in May 2026. Isn't that short?" Say it honestly: the work has been intense and productive, and I'm being selective. Do not criticise the employer. See 13_behavioral_why_switch.md.

9. How do you handle pressure and stress?

Answer: I treat pressure as a signal to prioritise and communicate, not to panic. I break the work into milestones, protect the critical path, and keep stakeholders updated on risk. During Uber FRM quarterly close windows and Masters India GST filing spikes, I sequenced the reconciliation and portal work so the most important piece shipped first. I relied on observability (ELK logs, New Relic traces and CI gates) so we were not guessing under load. Time-boxing, a clear owner list, and honest status updates keep me calm.

10. What motivates you?

Answer: Hard systems problems with real business or compliance impact motivate me. Examples: fixing a broken financial close, making filing-day government traffic safe, or building an AI engine that cannot silently write bad decisions. On that last one, every AssortSmart output row carries a config_hash, a fingerprint of the exact prompts and settings that produced it, so any decision can be traced. I like designing the trade-off, shipping it, and being able to defend the numbers afterwards. Teamwork matters too: mentoring engineers through a migration is as satisfying as the metric itself.

11. How do you handle constructive criticism?

Answer: I treat it as a free design review. I listen, find the real failure mode, and change the system, not just the slide. At Impact Analytics, reviewers pushed on two things. First, whether the LLM should ever query ClickHouse directly. I agreed it should not, so the model only receives a prepared JSON payload and has no SQL tool. Second, whether our 80% number could be misread as live accuracy. I changed how we describe it: it is a CI promotion gate, not a claim that every tenant runs at 80%. That feedback made both the architecture and our reporting more honest.

12. Tell me about a time you led a team.

Answer: I led a pod of 3 engineers at Uber via EPAM on the FRM scoping backend, as tech lead rather than people manager. I set the layered architecture (controller, service, repository), the API contracts and the design reviews, and I personally owned the reconciliation v2 migration. We delivered 36 endpoints behind 8 Finance screens, and I led the ORM migration to Spring Data JPA / Hibernate, which removed latent column-aliasing bugs and raised module statement coverage to 100%. We shipped with zero downtime using stacked Bazel pull requests, which are small dependent changes reviewed and merged in order. Separately, at Masters India, I mentored 2 engineers through the Spring Boot migration with the same approach: pair first, then hand off.

Follow-up they may ask: "How many tests?" About 1,100+, but that is verbal, not on the PDF.

13. Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision.

Answer: I disagreed with using row-level updates in ClickHouse for planning data at Impact Analytics. ClickHouse mutations (in-place UPDATE or DELETE) rewrite whole data parts in the background and queue up, which makes them slow and unpredictable for interactive work. I pushed for insert-only writes with ReplacingMergeTree, where each change is a new row version and reads resolve the newest one. Planner pivots had been slow on PostgreSQL, and proof-of-concept comparisons showed ClickHouse winning on large analytical reads, while Postgres kept the thin metadata, user access and roles. I backed the design with measurement: a pre-aggregation layer took pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250-million-row benchmark harness. Presenting evidence rather than opinion is what made the decision stick.

14. Tell me about a time you had to decide with incomplete information.

Answer: On Uber Eats menu ingestion, partner sites and anti-bot defences changed without notice, so we could never have a complete list of failure modes. Instead of waiting, I hardened the Selenium scraping fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries, which raised extraction success to 95%+ from an estimated 60-65%. For unstructured PDF menus we kept a LangChain RAG path with Gemini 2.5 Pro over Milvus, with a strict schema check before anything reached the catalog. We decided with partial information by measuring the success rate and offline field fidelity (98% on the evaluation set) rather than freezing delivery. Measurement replaced certainty.

Say this carefully: older prep also cites 100% schema consistency offline. It is not on the PDF, so lead with 98% and always say "offline".

15. What are you most proud of?

Answer: Two things, both about correctness under pressure. First, replacing a fragile Finance close on Google Sheets with a real FRM platform at Uber via EPAM, and owning reconciliation correctness under audit, which cut the cycle from 14 days to 3 days. Second, making bulk GST e-invoicing durable at Masters India with Kafka, PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, and idempotent retries, so a million-plus submissions a day never meant double-registering an invoice with the government. Both combined systems design with real accountability.

16. Tell me about a time you went above and beyond.

Answer: At Uber Finance, reconciliation v2 was not "just another API" to me. I went beyond the ticket and validated HFM extracts against the public 10-Q filings, line by line. I tracked down a silent identity bug where duplicate column names in a joined query mapped rows to the wrong ID, and fixed it with explicit aliases. I also kept v1 running in parallel until Finance trusted v2. That protected the audit work papers and the quarterly close, which mattered more than shipping an endpoint.

17. How do you handle conflict in the workplace?

Answer: I separate the people from the design argument and get everyone to agree on one success metric. At Masters India, the team split between a big-bang rewrite and a gradual cutover to Spring Boot. I framed the debate around filing-day risk: what happens if the new system fails on the busiest day? That led us to a canary per endpoint behind the gateway, a shared database during the traffic move, and instant rollback. We chose the gradual migration, I mentored two engineers on the pattern, and we still took p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds.

18. What is your leadership style?

Answer: Collaborative and standards-driven. I set the architecture and the quality bar (contracts, CI, observability) and then let people own their slices. On FRM I reviewed closely early on and stepped back once ownership stuck. At Masters India I paired on the first canary and then let the engineers I mentored take whole services. I adapt to risk: I stay more hands-on for compliance and audit paths and give more autonomy on well-bounded features.

19. Tell me about a time you had to learn something new quickly.

Answer: When I joined Impact Analytics in May 2026 I had to ramp up fast on ClickHouse at billion-row scale and on LangGraph agents. I read the existing design docs and the Postgres-versus-ClickHouse proof-of-concept results, then learned by building: the six rollup tables that cut pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, and the fix for weekly builds that ran out of memory at 170GB. On the AI side I learned LangGraph by shipping Ask Iris, with a supervisor that routes questions and an evaluator capped at 3 attempts. My method is always the same: read the source of truth, build something small and measurable, then go deep where the measurements point.

Follow-up they may ask: "How did you fix the out-of-memory problem?" I sliced each big INSERT SELECT into one fiscal week at a time and set memory and disk-spill caps. That was a load-time fix, separate from the pivot speedup.

20. What do you know about our company?

Answer: (Customise per employer, keep this skeleton.) Your company is known for [product or platform, and engineering bar]. I respect your focus on [reliability, developer platform, AI or scale], and this role matches where I have shipped: backend platforms, event-driven systems and careful production AI. I'm excited to contribute to [team mission] with the same ownership I brought to Uber FRM, the Masters India e-invoicing pipeline and AssortSmart.

21. How do you handle tight deadlines?

Answer: With ruthless prioritisation and visible risk. I scope the must-have path, cut nice-to-haves, and tell stakeholders about trade-offs early. On Uber FRM reconciliation v2 under quarterly close pressure, I did the identity-correct joins and the HFM-versus-10-Q checks before any polish, kept v1 running in parallel as a safety net, and leaned on CI gates so speed never meant silent breakage. At Masters India during filing spikes, making portal calls asynchronous with a dead-letter queue mattered more than perfect synchronous latency. Deliver the critical path first, and never surprise anyone on the last day.

Quick tips

  • Prefer stories (company, constraint, action, number) over generic soft-skill claims.
  • Uber FRM's 70% (from 14 days to 3 days) is on the PDF as the outcome. Defend it. If pressed, say the technical design doc framed that cut and that is what the platform delivered for the close. (Older prep tagged it TARGET. That guidance is obsolete.)
  • Ask Iris is a shipped capability. Do not invent usage numbers or an SLA. The 80% is a CI gate, not live accuracy.
  • Cluster Recommendation Copilot, its 14 tools, and "63 tables / 8 layers" are verbal design depth, not PDF bullets. Older versions of answers 11, 13 and 19 used them. Do not bring them up unless asked about clustering.
  • No human review queues and no MCP claims on Impact Analytics.
  • Menu 98% is offline evaluation. ANZ 20 hours/week is HISTORICAL.
  • Keep "led 3" (Uber FRM) and "mentored 2" (Masters India) separate.
  • For Q20, read the company's latest product or engineering blog the night before.

Senior screen deep Q&A: scale, production, performance, product, deploy

How to use this page

  • This page covers the senior technical screen: "Have you handled millions of requests?", "Tell me about a production issue", "How do you deploy safely?", plus general computer-science questions like "What is idempotency?"
  • Read it before any senior backend, platform or hiring-manager technical round.
  • Start with the 30-second cheat sheet. For each general concept, learn the plain definition and tiny example first, then the sentence that ties it to your work.
  • Memorise the first sentence of every answer and the number attached to it.

PDF: Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf (Java + Python + Go track).

Stack on this track. Uber FRM is Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate and MySQL. Masters India is Spring Boot microservices with Hibernate. The AssortSmart platform APIs at Impact Analytics are Go/Gin. The AI agent plane is Python (FastAPI, LangGraph). MCP is skills-level, not an Impact Analytics bullet.

Tags used here. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind the number. TARGET means a design goal, so say "targeting". ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. Full rules: GROUND_TRUTH.md.

0. Thirty-second cheat sheet

When a senior screener asks one of these, lead with the story in the second column and the number in the third. The last column reminds you how careful to be.

Question Lead with Number How careful
Millions of requests or rows? Impact Analytics platform, or Masters India IRP pipeline 10k peak RPS; 2.11B-row master; 348k article-seasons; 1M+ submissions/day On the PDF. Masters is past work
Production issue? 170GB weekly-build OOM (Impact Analytics), or Menu anti-bot, or Masters timeout canary 170GB; 95%+ On the PDF. Menu and Masters are past work
Performance? ClickHouse pivots, or Masters p95, or Menu onboarding time from 189s to 12s; from 1.2s to 300ms; from 24 hours to 2 hours MEASURED / HISTORICAL
Core product? AssortSmart, FRM, Eats Menu, GST e-invoicing, GFG See section 1
Complex system? AssortSmart JSON payloads + Ask Iris, or Menu end to end, or FRM schema 2.11B; exactly-once upserts On the PDF
Deploy? 80% AI CI gate, or Masters canary, or FRM stacked Bazel PRs 80% gate; 98% deploy success On the PDF

1. Core products

What this section is for. Screeners open with "Walk me through what you work on." They want the product in plain English, your piece of it, and the scale. Answer in that order.

Q1.1 What is Impact Analytics / AssortSmart, and what do you own?

Answer: AssortSmart is a retail merchandise planning SaaS. It helps retailers decide which articles to keep, drop or add each season. I own two parts of it. The first is the AI layer: an engine with three pipelines (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style) that scores 348k article-seasons, 88k items per pass, by blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM calls across 7 AI lenses, plus Ask Iris, a shipped WebSocket copilot built on LangGraph. The second is the core platform: a multi-tenant Go/Gin service at 10k peak RPS, a KPI formula parser, tenant isolation across PostgreSQL and ClickHouse, ClickHouse rollups that cut pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, and a Go data pump that copies about 344k rows per second between clusters. The AI layer never queries the 2.11B-row ClickHouse master directly. It receives JSON payloads, and nothing is promoted without passing an 80% CI gate on a 300-case harness.

Follow-up they may ask: "What is an article-season?" One product (article) in one selling season. A shirt sold in Spring 2026 and again in Fall 2026 is two article-seasons.

Say this carefully. The 80% gate is a promotion rule, not "every tenant is live at 80%". The 73% cost cut is from a separate 200-case benchmark, not the 300-case file. Do not add TPS or SLA numbers. No Kubernetes operations, Kafka or Flink on this product. Off the PDF but true if asked: 1.6M article-seasons in the catalog (a different number from the 348k scored), $100 token spend per pass, 100% Go statement coverage with 1,200+ tests, and the 55GB memory and 16GB spill caps. Cluster Copilot and Hindsight are verbal only.

Q1.2 What did you do at Uber?

Answer: I worked on three Uber projects through EPAM. The main one was the FRM (Financial Risk Management) scoping backend for Uber Finance, which I owned: 36 Spring Boot endpoints, 19M raw general ledger rows moved off Google Sheets into MySQL, a four-level FSLI (Financial Statement Line Item) hierarchy, and an 8-table schema on SOADB, Uber's standard for service-owned MySQL. It cut quarterly reconciliation by 70%, from 14 days to 3 days, against a $340M materiality threshold, and I led 3 engineers on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that took module coverage to 100%. The second was Uber Eats menu ingestion, which cut restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saves about $600K a year using Gemini 2.5 Pro, LangChain RAG and Milvus at 98% offline field fidelity, with Kafka and Flink for exactly-once catalog upserts. The third, which is historical, was Uber Mobility document compliance in ANZ: 99.9% compliance and about 20 hours a week of manual work removed.

Follow-up they may ask: "Were you an Uber employee?" No, I was at EPAM Systems working on Uber projects. Always say "Uber via EPAM". I did not own any React front end.

Q1.3 What did you do at Masters India?

Answer: Masters India sells GST compliance and e-invoicing software to Indian enterprises. Clients send invoices, and the system validates them and registers them with the government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an invoice number and a signed QR code. I led the migration of a legacy PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices for 1,500+ clients, which cut p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds and raised throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute. I also worked on the bulk pipeline that handled 1M+ government submissions a day on Kafka with PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter. I mentored 2 engineers there.

Q1.4 What did you do at GeeksforGeeks?

Answer: GeeksforGeeks was my first job, on the courses platform. I stabilised the doubt-support platform for 10K+ daily queries and 10x traffic spikes during live coding contests by migrating its backend from PHP to Django, and built REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads. The growth team attributed a 20% lift in premium subscriptions to it. I also built an influencer analytics and earnings dashboard, and the business attributed a 30% course sales lift to it. Asynchronous scheduled workflows for video processing, reminders and data cleanup improved engineering ops efficiency by 70%.

2. Scale: "Have you handled millions of requests or rows?"

The concept in plain words. Scale questions mix up three different rates, and senior screeners notice. RPS (requests per second) counts API calls. TPS (transactions per second) counts business operations such as invoice submissions. Rows per second counts data moved in bulk. Tiny example: one API request that uploads a file of 10,000 invoices is 1 request, 10,000 transactions, and maybe 10,000 rows. Always name which rate you mean.

Q2.1 What is the biggest scale you've handled?

Answer: On API traffic, the AssortSmart Go/Gin platform peaks at 10k requests per second. On data, the ClickHouse master table holds 2.11B rows, and individual rollup partitions reach 4.09B rows. On business transactions, the Masters India pipeline handled 1M+ government submissions a day, about 12 per second on average (1,000,000 divided by 86,400), with estimated peaks of 8 to 10 times that near filing deadlines. For bulk data movement, my Go pump copied about 344k rows per second between ClickHouse Cloud clusters. I keep those four numbers separate because they measure different things.

Follow-up they may ask: "What's 344k in requests?" It is not requests at all. It is rows per second, the combined rate of two season streams of roughly 150k to 190k rows per second each.

3. Complex system: "Describe the most complex system you've built"

The concept in plain words. A system is complex when it has many moving parts that can fail independently, and the hard part is keeping the whole correct when one part misbehaves. Tiny example: an online checkout calls payments, inventory and email. If email is down, checkout should still succeed. Good answers name the failure modes and how the design contains them.

Option A. AssortSmart AI layer (best "platform plus AI" story).

Answer: The most complex system I own is AssortSmart's AI decision layer, because it mixes LLMs, a 2.11B-row database and multiple tenants. The key decision was to decouple the model from the data. The LLM never gets a SQL tool. We build a JSON payload of exactly the context it needs, so cost is predictable and access is controlled by our code. Writes go into ReplacingMergeTree tables as new row versions, and if the model times out the item falls back to its deterministic score, so a pass always completes. A shared registry adds hard timeouts, circuit breakers, durable checkpoints and a config_hash on every row. For Ask Iris, the user's hierarchy access is frozen at the WebSocket handshake, so a conversation can never read another tenant's data.

Option B. Uber Eats Menu end to end.

Answer: Menu ingestion was complex because every stage faced a different enemy. Scraping faced anti-bot defences, so I hardened the Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries and got extraction to 95%+. Streaming faced duplicates and replays, so Kafka and Flink did keyed deduplication by vendor and content hash with idempotent catalog upserts. Extraction faced messy multilingual PDFs, so Gemini 2.5 Pro with LangChain RAG over Milvus produced output that had to pass a strict catalog schema, reaching 98% field fidelity offline. The result was onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours.

Option C. Uber FRM.

Answer: FRM was complex because it was about correctness under audit, not speed. I designed an 8-table normalized MySQL schema with a polymorphic review-status model, meaning one status model (Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed) reused across all screens. Updates use optimistic row-locking, cross-table syncs happen in one transaction, and SHA-256 natural keys stop duplicates across quarterly audit trails. On top of that, finite-state-machine gates with 50% delta-variance checks enforce SOX controls. It moved 19M general ledger rows off Sheets and cut reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days.

Option D. Masters India strangler migration plus Kafka pipeline.

Answer: Masters India was complex because traffic spiked hard around tax filing deadlines and the government portal was unreliable. We migrated the PHP monolith route by route with a canary per route, so any route could roll back instantly. Bulk submissions went through Kafka, with idempotency keys built from client, file hash and batch index so 100K+ concurrent imports could be retried without double-registering invoices. Failures after bounded retries went to dead-letter queues. That combination kept 1M+ submissions a day safe.

4. Production issue: "Tell me about a production problem you fixed"

The concept in plain words. An OOM (out of memory) failure happens when a process asks for more memory than it is allowed, and the system kills it. Tiny example: a query that groups a whole year of data in one go may need 200GB, while grouping one week needs 11GB. Fixes usually make the unit of work smaller, cap memory, or let the work spill to disk. A good production story covers what broke, how you found it, how you fixed it, and what you changed so it would not recur.

Q4.1 Impact Analytics weekly rollup OOM (on the PDF, best default).

Answer: The best one is the 170GB out-of-memory failure on our weekly ClickHouse rollup builds. Building a whole season of weekly rollups in one INSERT SELECT kept failing, even with memory caps of 80GB and 200GB. The cause was the size of the grouping: an attribute-level week alone needed over 40GB, and a whole season multiplied that. I sliced the build into one fiscal week per insert and enforced memory and disk-spill caps, roughly a 55GB memory cap, 16GB spill, 8 threads and 4 weeks in flight. After that the weekly builds stopped running out of memory. This was a load-time fix, separate from the pivot speedup.

Follow-up they may ask: "Is the 170GB why pivots got faster?" No. The 15.5x is query time. The OOM fix is load time. They are not cause and effect.

Q4.2 Uber Eats Menu anti-bot (past work).

Answer: Our Selenium scraping fleet was losing to partner sites' anti-bot defences, and extraction success sat at an estimated 60-65%. I added dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries so blocked requests rotated identity and backed off instead of hammering the site. That raised success to 95%+. Because the downstream Kafka and Flink pipeline was idempotent, retries never created duplicate catalog entries.

Q4.3 Masters India timeout canary (past work).

Answer: Early in the Spring Boot cutover, I set API timeouts tighter than the old PHP path, and legitimate calls to the government portal started timing out on the first canary. Because it was a canary, only a small slice of traffic was affected. I moved those calls to an asynchronous flow that returns "202 Accepted" and lets the client poll, aligned timeouts with real portal behaviour, and added idempotency keys, bounded retries and a dead-letter queue. The lesson was to design for third-party latency and safe retries from day one.

Q4.4 Python connection-leak OOM (a story from older prep, not a PDF bullet).

Say this carefully. Older prep includes a story about an Impact Analytics Python/FastAPI worker that leaked connections or cursors inside a long-lived async loop until it ran out of memory. The fix was context managers, pool limits and backpressure. It is not a PDF bullet, so only use it if asked for "another example", label it as such, and do not claim you operated the Kubernetes cluster.

5. Performance: "How have you made something faster?"

The concept in plain words. Pre-aggregation means computing summaries ahead of time so a query reads a small summary table instead of scanning raw rows. Tiny example: instead of summing 250 million daily sales rows every time a planner opens a screen, keep a table of sales per product per season, which might be a few million rows. p95 latency is the response time 95% of requests beat. It is the right metric for "how slow does it feel for unlucky users".

Q5.1 Your best performance win?

Answer: Planner pivots in AssortSmart, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, a 15.5x speedup, measured on a 250-million-row benchmark harness. Pivots had been slow on PostgreSQL, so we compared Postgres and ClickHouse, and ClickHouse won the large analytical reads. I then built a pre-aggregation layer of six MergeTree rollup tables: product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain, partitioned by season code. The pivot reads the right rollup instead of the raw data. Precisely, 12.3 seconds rounds to 12.

Follow-up they may ask: "Why not sub-second?" I don't claim sub-second. 12 seconds was the measured result, and the next step would be narrower rollups or caching, not a promise I can't back.

Q5.2 An API latency win?

Answer: Masters India, where p95 latency dropped 75%, from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, across 1,500+ enterprise clients during the PHP-to-Spring Boot migration. The gain came from four things: non-blocking calls to the government portal (Spring WebClient and bounded thread pools) so request threads did not sit idle, connection pooling with HikariCP, query and index fixes, and Redis for hot reads. Throughput rose from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute at the same time, roughly 12 to 67 requests per second.

Q5.3 A process-time win?

Answer: Uber Eats restaurant onboarding, from 24 hours to 2 hours. This is end-to-end business time, not API latency. It came from automating menu extraction with RAG and hardening the scraping fleet, so a menu no longer waited for manual entry.

Do not add numbers you cannot defend. The 10k peak RPS is on the PDF. Do not add a p99 or an SLA for the Go platform.

6. Deploy and CI: "How do you ship safely?"

The concept in plain words. CI/CD (continuous integration and delivery) is the automated pipeline that tests every change and deploys it. Statement coverage is the share of code lines that tests execute. A canary sends a small slice of traffic to a new version first. A CI gate blocks promotion if a score is below a bar. Tiny example: a pull request runs 1,000 tests, coverage must stay above a threshold, and only then does it deploy to 5% of traffic.

Q6.1 How do you deploy AI changes safely?

Answer: Through a gate. At Impact Analytics, any change to the AI layer (a model, prompt or parameter) must pass an 80% accuracy CI gate on a 300-case proxy evaluation harness before promotion. We also compare against a deterministic baseline. On a separate 200-case benchmark the baseline scored 74%, and when the blended LLM came in around 63% we froze the blend weights instead of retuning them. Every output row carries a config_hash, so if something goes wrong we know exactly which configuration produced it.

Q6.2 How do you deploy backend changes safely?

Answer: Small, reversible steps with measurement. At Masters India we used a canary per route during the strangler migration, raised test coverage from 35% to 82%, and reached 98% deployment success. At Uber FRM we shipped zero-downtime releases through stacked Bazel pull requests, which are small dependent changes merged in order, and module statement coverage reached 100% on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration. At Impact Analytics the Go codebase has 100% statement coverage with 1,200+ tests, which is verbal and not on the PDF.

Say this carefully: older prep also lists golangci-lint, SAST/SBOM security scans and Bitbucket pipelines for Impact Analytics. Mention them only if you can describe them.

Q6.3 How do you recover from a bad streaming deploy?

Answer: Rewind and replay. In the Uber Menu pipeline, the recovery path for a bad parser deploy is to roll back the code, rewind the Kafka consumer offsets to before the bad change, and reprocess. That is safe because catalog upserts are idempotent, so replaying a message cannot create duplicates.

7. General computer-science questions, tied to my work

Senior screens often switch to "explain this concept". Give the definition, a tiny example, then one sentence on where you used it.

Q7.1 What is idempotency? An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Example: "set balance to 100" is idempotent, but "add 10 to balance" is not. You make writes idempotent with a unique key the server remembers. At Masters India the key was client + file hash + batch index, so 100K+ concurrent imports could be retried without double-registering invoices.

Q7.2 What does "exactly-once" really mean? True exactly-once delivery across systems is very hard. In practice you get at-least-once delivery, where a message may arrive twice, and make the write idempotent so the second arrival changes nothing. Example: a consumer crashes after writing but before committing its offset, so it re-reads the message and writes again, harmlessly. On Uber Menu, "exactly-once catalog upserts" meant exactly that. I don't claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across third parties.

Q7.3 What is a circuit breaker? A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing, so you fail fast instead of piling up slow requests. After a cool-down it lets a test call through. Example: after 5 failed calls in a row, stop calling the model for a short cool-down period. In the AssortSmart registry the breaker trips after about 5 consecutive failures or a high failure fraction, and items fall back to deterministic scores.

Q7.4 What is eventual consistency? Eventual consistency means a write becomes visible everywhere after a short delay rather than instantly. Example: you update your profile photo and a friend sees the old one for a few seconds. ReplacingMergeTree in ClickHouse is eventually consistent: two versions of a row can coexist until a background merge keeps the newest, so reads that need the latest version must resolve it explicitly.

Q7.5 Optimistic versus pessimistic locking? Pessimistic locking locks the row when you read it, so others wait. Optimistic locking does not lock. It checks a version number at update time and fails if someone else changed the row. Example: UPDATE ... SET status='Review', version=4 WHERE id=7 AND version=3 updates zero rows if someone got there first. Optimistic locking suits low-conflict workloads, which is why I used it for Uber FRM review-status updates. In Spring Data JPA, a @Version field on the entity makes Hibernate add that version check to every update and throw an optimistic-lock exception when it fails.

Q7.6 What is sharding? Sharding splits one big table across several databases by a key, so each holds a slice. Example: invoices for tax quarter Q1 live in one shard and Q2 in another. At Masters India, PostgreSQL was sharded by tax quarter, which matched how filings and queries were naturally grouped.

Q7.7 What is cache-aside? In cache-aside, the application checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database and puts the result in the cache for next time. Example: first request for client 42's settings hits Postgres, the next hundred hit Redis. At Masters India a Redis cache-aside layer cut database read load by 30%.

Q7.8 What is dependency injection, and why compile-time? Dependency injection means a component receives its dependencies (database client, config) from outside instead of creating them itself, which makes it easy to test and swap. Compile-time injection, like Google Wire in Go, generates the wiring code at build time, so a missing dependency is a build error rather than a crash at startup. That is how the AssortSmart Go/Gin platform is wired.

Q7.9 What is the strangler pattern? It replaces a legacy system gradually: new services take over one route at a time while the old system serves the rest. Example: route /validate to the new Spring Boot service while /reports stays on PHP. I used it with a canary per route at Masters India.

8. Senior fit: "Why are you senior?"

Answer: I fit senior because I own designs and the gates that protect them, not just tickets. At Impact Analytics I designed the ClickHouse rollup layer and the copy tooling, and I put the AI layer behind a promotion gate that compares against a free deterministic baseline. At Uber FRM I designed the schema and the SOX controls, including the 50% delta-variance checks, and led 3 engineers as tech lead of an EPAM pod. At Masters India I mentored 2 engineers through a production migration. I'm also clear about my limits: I don't claim Kubernetes cluster operations.

9. "How would you debug a misbehaving AI agent?"

Answer: I start with the plumbing, then the agent logic. First I check Datadog traces for timeouts, connection pool exhaustion and slow dependencies, because many "agent bugs" are infrastructure bugs. Then I look at the agent itself in LangSmith: which node the supervisor routed to, whether the evaluator loop hit its 3-attempt cap, and whether the frozen hierarchy scope is what I expect for that user. Finally I check the structured-output guards, the schema validation on what the model returned. For the batch engine, the config_hash and the JSON telemetry (tokens, cost, step duration, fallbacks) tell me which configuration and which batch went wrong.

Say this carefully: LangSmith is on Ask Iris, not the Keep/Drop batch. The batch has its own JSON telemetry.

Why hire Tarun — screening and pitch Q&A

Track: Final Java + AI (IA = Py/Go) · PDF: Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf · Contact: tmittaliet@gmail.com · (+91) 9079727197

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the "sell yourself" questions. Why hire me, why leave, why this company, biggest risk, and the objections recruiters and hiring managers raise.
  • When to read it: the night before a recruiter screen or hiring-manager round, and again 15 minutes before the call.
  • What to memorise: the 30-second "why hire me" (section 1.1), the biggest-risk answer (1.4), and the objection answers (section 5). Read the 90-second versions out loud twice. Do not memorise them word for word.
  • Technical depth lives elsewhere (links below). This page is persuasion plus honesty.

Technical depth: IA pack · Uber packs · Masters and GfG packs · IA bullet defense · STAR stories

What the tags mean. Some numbers carry a tag so you know how strongly you can state them.

  • PDF means the number is printed on the resume. Say it plainly.
  • MEASURED means there is a log, benchmark, doc, or code behind it.
  • ESTIMATED means it is arithmetic I can show. Say "roughly, derived from...".
  • TARGET means it is a design goal. Say "targeting".
  • HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records, not something I can re-run today.
  • Verbal only means it is real interview depth but not on the resume. Use it only if they ask.

Say these carefully. They are the lines interviewers check.

  • The 80% number is a CI promotion gate. It means a change cannot be promoted unless it scores at least 80% on a 300-case test set. It does not mean "every tenant runs at 80% accuracy in production".
  • The 73% cost cut and the 74% baseline both come from a separate 200-case gold benchmark. They do not come from the 300-case file. Never fuse the two.
  • Ask Iris is a shipped capability. I do not have SLA or usage numbers for it, so I do not quote any.
  • On the PDF for Impact Analytics: 10k peak RPS, 2.11B-row master, 348k article-seasons, 88k items per pass, six rollup tables, 170GB OOM, about 344k rows per second, partitions up to 4.09B rows.
  • Off the PDF (verbal only): $100 per pass token spend, the 1.6M-row catalog, the 55 GB and 16 GB memory knobs, 100% Go test coverage.
  • Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight are verbal only. They are not resume bullets.
  • Menu 98% is from offline evaluation. Uber work was via EPAM. ANZ 99.9% is HISTORICAL and belongs to Uber Mobility, not Uber Eats.
  • No Spark, Pinot, Kubernetes operations, or CDC ownership anywhere. Kafka and Flink belong to Uber Menu, not to Impact Analytics.

How to structure any answer on this page

Every answer here follows the same four-step shape. If you lose your place mid-answer, come back to it.

  1. Direct answer first. One sentence that answers the question as asked. "You should hire me because I own systems end to end and I can prove the numbers."
  2. Two or three proof points. Each one is a project, what I did, and at most two or three numbers. More numbers than that and the listener stops hearing them.
  3. Explain any technical word in one clause. "ClickHouse, which is a database built for fast analytical reads, ..." The listener may not be an engineer.
  4. Short close. One sentence that ties it back to their role. Then stop talking.

Two lengths are written for the main questions. The 30-second version is for recruiter screens and the opening of a hiring-manager call. The 90-second version is for when they say "tell me more" or for a dedicated "why you" question.

0. Recruiter blurb (third person)

Paste this into emails or give it to a recruiter who needs to pitch you internally.

Tarun Mittal is a Senior Software Engineer with 5 years of experience building high-throughput, cloud-native distributed systems in Java, Python and Go.

At Impact Analytics he owns the Go/Gin platform behind AssortSmart, a retail merchandise-planning product, serving 10k peak requests per second. He made planner pivot screens 15.5× faster (from 189 seconds to 12 seconds) with a ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer, and he shipped Ask Iris, a LangGraph-based copilot that lets planners ask questions about their KPIs and AI decisions.

At Uber via EPAM he owned the Financial Risk Management scoping backend (36 Spring Boot endpoints), which cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days. He also owned Uber Eats menu ingestion, which cut restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saved about $600K a year.

At Masters India he led a PHP-to-Spring Boot migration that cut p95 API latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and scaled government e-invoicing to 1M+ submissions a day.

He is a Google Code Jam 2021 qualifier (rank 2260 of 37,000+), a Smart India Hackathon 2020 national finalist (top 3), and holds HackerRank Problem Solving and LangChain Academy certificates.

20-second spoken version (first person):

"I'm a senior backend engineer with five years in Java, Python and Go. At Uber via EPAM I owned a finance-grade reconciliation platform and the Uber Eats menu ingestion pipeline. At Masters India I scaled an e-invoicing path to over a million submissions a day. Now at Impact Analytics I own the Go platform and the AI decision engine for a retail planning product. I make decisions with benchmarks, and I can defend every number on my resume."

1. Why should we hire Tarun?

1.1 Why hire you — 30-second version

"Because I own systems end to end, and I measure before I claim. Three examples. At Uber via EPAM I owned the finance risk scoping backend, and quarterly reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days. At Masters India I led the migration off a PHP monolith, and p95 latency went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds. At Impact Analytics I own the Go platform and the AI decision engine, and I put an 80% accuracy gate in CI so no AI change ships without passing a test set. You get someone who builds it, measures it, and is honest about what the numbers mean."

1.2 Why hire you — 90-second version

"The short answer is ownership, evidence, and honesty. Let me give you one example of each.

Ownership. At Uber via EPAM I owned the FRM scoping backend. FRM is Financial Risk Management, the tool Finance uses each quarter to decide which accounts are in scope for audit. I designed the API contracts, built 36 Spring Boot endpoints, and led a pod of 3 engineers. Reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days. On Uber Eats I owned menu ingestion end to end, from the Selenium scrapers through a Kafka and Flink pipeline to the catalog. Kafka is a durable message queue and Flink is a stream processor that cleans and deduplicates events as they arrive.

Evidence. At Impact Analytics, planner pivot screens were slow on PostgreSQL. Instead of arguing about databases, I ran a proof of concept on a 250-million-row test harness. With ClickHouse rollup tables the pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds. The same benchmarks also showed where ClickHouse is the wrong answer, which is small keyed updates to single cells. So we kept those in Postgres.

Honesty. When our AI model scored below a simple rule-based baseline, I froze the blend weights instead of shipping it anyway. I'm also careful with my own numbers. The 80% figure is a CI gate, not live accuracy for every customer. Ask Iris is a shipped capability, and I don't quote usage numbers I don't have.

So you get an engineer who can own a system, prove it works, and tell you plainly where the edges are."

Follow-up they may ask: "What does 'froze the blend weights' mean?" Answer: "Our final score is a weighted mix of a rule-based score and an LLM score. On a 200-case benchmark the rule-based baseline scored 74% and the blended LLM scored lower. So we kept the weights fixed instead of tuning them to favour the LLM."

1.3 Why you over someone with more years?

Direct answer: "Scope, not years. I've already owned systems where mistakes are expensive."

"At Uber via EPAM my platform was the system of record for a $340M materiality threshold. Materiality is the dollar line above which an account must be audited, so a wrong number becomes audit evidence. At Masters India the pipeline I worked on handles over 1 million government submissions a day. At Impact Analytics the platform peaks at 10k requests per second over a 2.11-billion-row ClickHouse table. I've also led 3 engineers at Uber and mentored 2 at Masters.

Here's the boundary, so you hear it from me. I haven't run a 50-person org, and I haven't operated Kubernetes clusters. If the role needs those, I'd ramp on them. If it needs someone who owns hard systems and can defend the design, that's what I already do."

1.4 Why not hire you? What is your biggest risk?

Short version: "The honest risk is that my newest AI work is recent. Ask Iris is shipped, but I don't have long-term usage numbers yet. My longer production record is at Uber and Masters India."

Full version: "Let me separate what's proven from what's new. Ask Iris, the copilot at Impact Analytics, is a shipped capability. I won't invent an SLA or usage stats for it. The 80% figure is a CI gate that blocks bad changes. It isn't a claim that every tenant runs at 80% accuracy. Some AI designs I can talk about, like the Cluster Recommendation Copilot, are design depth and aren't on my resume.

What has run in production for a long time is the Uber menu pipeline, the FRM platform, and the Masters India e-invoicing system. Those are where my track record is strongest, and I'm happy to go as deep as you want on any of them."

1.5 What makes you different?

Direct answer: "Five things: finance-grade correctness, real money saved, scale, benchmark-driven decisions, and AI with guardrails."
