5.1 The 15.5× in depth

  • What it measures. Wall-clock time of the heaviest planner pivot (a grid with contribution percent and option count, joined across hierarchy, cluster and calendar) at 250M rows.
  • How it was derived. On the benchmark, the old PostgreSQL path took 189,408 ms and spilled 42 GB of sort files to disk. ClickHouse took 12,256 ms on the same pivot. 189,408 ÷ 12,256 ≈ 15.45, which rounds to 15.5. The ClickHouse side ran on a small VM (about 10 CPUs and 3.3 GB), while PostgreSQL had a 48 GB host, so the hardware did not favour ClickHouse.
  • Why it mattered. Three minutes per grid refresh makes a planning tool unusable. Twelve seconds is slow but workable for a 250M-row grid.
  • How to say it. "From 189 seconds to about 12 on the 250M-row pivot benchmark, roughly 15.5 times faster."
  • Say this carefully. The 189 s baseline in the benchmark was PostgreSQL, the old path, not a raw-ClickHouse query. If someone asks "189 seconds on what?", say "on the old PostgreSQL path, same 250M-row pivot." The rollups are how that ClickHouse read layer is served to planners in production. The benchmark notes also say lighter, typical aggregates were closer to 2 to 3 times faster. The 15.5× is the heavy grid.
  • What not to say. "Sub-second pivots." "Every query got 15.5× faster." "The OOM fix caused the 15.5×."

5.2 Scale cheat sheet

  • 1.6M article-seasons: product × season catalog (verbal, LinkedIn).
  • Product weekly, seasons 6 and 7: about 839M rows (569.4M + 269.8M).
  • Attr weekly, seasons 6 and 7: 4.09B rows (2,779,317,472 + 1,311,108,195).
  • 2.11B: the agentic fact table from bullet A2. It is a different table.
  • Ratios: weekly grain has roughly 2× the groups of season grain. The attr unpivot is why attr weekly is the largest object, about 5× product weekly on Briscoes seasons 6 and 7.

6. The 170 GB OOM (C4, second half): hero story

Use this for "hardest technical hurdle", "tell me about a failure" and "how do you debug at scale".

6.1 Plain English first

Building the weekly rollup for a whole season in one SQL statement needed more memory than the machine had. We tried giving it more memory and it still died. The fix was not more memory. It was a smaller unit of work: one fiscal week per statement, with hard caps so any single statement stays inside a known budget.

6.2 Why weekly is so heavy

A weekly rollup row carries about 110 any() states, plus argMax() and argMin() over wide string columns. ClickHouse must hold all of that for every group until the GROUP BY finishes. Weekly grain has roughly twice as many groups as season grain, and attr multiplies rows again through the unpivot. For a whole season the estimated aggregator state was around 170 GB. The replica has about 59 cores and 234 to 236 GiB of RAM, shared with everything else.

6.3 STAR

  • Situation. Weekly rollups need about 110 any() states plus argMax and argMin over wide strings. A whole-season weekly INSERT SELECT was estimated at around 170 GB of aggregator state. It failed with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED at an 80 GB cap and again at a 200 GB cap. The replica is about 59 cores and 234 to 236 GiB.
  • Task. Keep weekly grain, because planners need fiscal_year_week, without melting the box.
  • Action. I changed the unit of work from one season to one fiscal week. The generated weekly settings were 8 threads, a 55 GB memory cap, a 16 GB spill threshold, and 4 weeks in flight. I measured per-week peaks: a product week peaked around 11 GB, and a Briscoes attr week peaked above 40 GB, which is why a 40 GB cap was too low. Rule I set: never raise season parallelism and week parallelism together on the same box.
  • Result. Weekly grain builds reliably. The request path stays partition-pruned reads. The 15.5× is a different benchmark (the 250M pivot). Say that unprompted.

Trap: "So you fixed the OOM, and that is why latency is 15.5×." No. The OOM is load time. The 15.5× is query time.

6.4 What one weekly insert looks like (simplified SQL)

INSERT INTO product_weekly
SELECT
    season_code,
    fiscal_year_week,
    product_code,
    any(style)                 AS style,       -- ~110 any() columns in the real build
    argMax(price, sale_date)   AS last_price,
    argMin(price, sale_date)   AS first_price,
    sum(units)                 AS units,
    sum(revenue)               AS revenue
FROM daily_sales
WHERE season_code = {season}
  AND fiscal_year_week = {week}               -- one fiscal week per statement
GROUP BY season_code, fiscal_year_week, product_code
SETTINGS
    max_memory_usage                   = 55000000000,  -- 55 GB hard cap for this query
    max_bytes_before_external_group_by = 16000000000,  -- start spilling to disk at 16 GB
    max_threads                        = 8;

Simplified illustration. Column names are illustrative. The real SQL is generated, and the generated settings are the source of truth. {season} and {week} are filled in by the driver loop.

The three settings, in plain words.

  • max_memory_usage is the hard ceiling for one query. Go over it and ClickHouse kills the query with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED instead of letting it take down the server. It is a circuit breaker for RAM.
  • max_bytes_before_external_group_by is the spill threshold. When the GROUP BY's in-memory state passes it, ClickHouse writes partial aggregates to disk and merges them at the end. Setting it well below the hard cap (16 GB against 55 GB) means a heavy week slows down instead of dying.
  • max_threads limits how many CPU threads the query uses. Each thread keeps its own partial aggregation state, so fewer threads also means less memory.

6.5 The driver loop

sequenceDiagram participant D as Driver loop participant CH as ClickHouse replica participant QL as system.query_log participant T as TSV ledger D->>T: Is this kind and season already finished? T-->>D: No loop Each fiscal week, up to 4 in flight D->>CH: INSERT SELECT for one week with 55 GB cap, 16 GB spill, 8 threads CH-->>D: Response, or a client timeout D->>QL: Did this query_id reach QueryFinish? QL-->>D: Yes or no end D->>T: Append kind and season as finished

What to notice: success is judged by system.query_log, not by whether the HTTP client returned cleanly. The ledger is written only after every week finished.

Sanity-check arithmetic (ESTIMATED). Four weeks in flight at a 55 GB cap each is at most 220 GB, which is under the replica's roughly 234 to 236 GiB. Raising weeks in flight and season parallelism together would blow straight through that. That is the reason for the "never raise both" rule.

6.6 Design decision: shrink the unit of work, don't buy RAM

  • What. One fiscal week per INSERT SELECT, with a memory cap, a spill threshold, a thread cap and bounded weeks in flight.
  • Why. Memory grows with the number of groups in one statement. Cutting the time range cuts the groups. More RAM did not work: it failed at 200 GB too.
  • How. A generated loop over weeks, capped settings per statement, success checked in system.query_log, finished seasons recorded in a TSV ledger.
  • Alternatives an interviewer may suggest, and how I'd answer.
  • "Just use a bigger machine." It failed at a 200 GB cap on a 234 GiB box. There is no headroom left to buy on that replica, and a bigger box just moves the cliff.
  • "Spill everything to disk." Spill alone at season scale would be very slow and still risky. Spill works best as a safety net under a right-sized unit of work.
  • "Slice by store instead of week." It is possible, but week is the natural grain of the target table, so each slice writes complete rows with no later merge step.
  • Trade-off. More statements and more orchestration. Total build time is longer than one giant query would be if it could fit. The ledger and query-log checks are extra code.
  • What I'd do differently. Profile memory per grain on a small sample before the first full-season run, instead of discovering the 170 GB cliff by failing.

7. Partial loads, ghost rows and the TSV ledger (the loader)

7.1 Plain English

A load can fail halfway and still leave rows behind. If the next run only asks "does this partition have rows?", it will wrongly skip a half-loaded season. Those leftover rows are ghost rows: they look like real data but belong to a run that never finished.

7.2 What actually happened

  • A weekly HTTP INSERT failed on the client side, but the server had already committed some blocks.
  • A half-loaded partition with 64.1M rows once passed a "skip if the partition has rows" check. This was in the POC loader, not the copier.
  • Fix 1: a TSV ledger. Weekly resume reads a TSV file listing finished (kind, season_code) pairs. If a pair is missing, the loader runs DROP PARTITION for that season and rebuilds it from scratch.
  • Fix 2: trust the server, not the client. Completion of each HTTP INSERT is checked by its query id reaching QueryFinish in system.query_log, not by the curl exit code.

What the ledger looks like (illustrative):

product_weekly  6
product_weekly  7
store_weekly    6

Each line means "this kind of table, for this season, finished completely". If attr_weekly 7 is not in the file, that season is dropped and rebuilt, no matter how many rows it currently has.

Rule to say out loud: never use count() > 0 as the success test for a weekly build.

8. The Go native-TLS copier (C5)

8.1 Plain English first

We had to move rollup tables from one ClickHouse Cloud cluster to another. Normally you would tell the target cluster to pull directly from the source with remoteSecure. That was blocked: each cluster's IP allowlist did not include the other cluster. The operator machine's IP was allowed on both. So I wrote a Go program that runs on that machine, reads from the source and writes to the target, both over ClickHouse's native protocol with TLS. It is an allowlisted pump, a workaround, not a design goal.

flowchart LR SRC["Source ClickHouse Cloud"] -- "native TLS port 9440, SELECT stream" --> GO["Go copier on allowlisted machine"] GO -- "native TLS port 9440, INSERT Send" --> DST["Target ClickHouse Cloud"] SRC -.->|"remoteSecure blocked by IP allowlist"| DST GO --> CK["migrate-checkpoints table.done files"]

What to notice: the dotted line is the direct path that was blocked. Everything goes through one machine, which is why caps are per process and why it is not a production pattern.

Whiteboard version:

source CH Cloud  --native TLS-->  laptop Go process  --native TLS-->  target CH Cloud
                     SELECT stream                    INSERT Send()
                     500k columnar                    500k columnar
                     buffer A while B sends           checkpoint season_code

8.2 How it gets about 344k rows per second

  • Batch size. batchSize = 500_000 rows per batch.
  • Columnar buffers. Each column is a typed Go slice ([]T). Rows are appended with batch.Column(i).Append(...), then Send() ships the block. There is no per-row reflect. Reflection inspects types at runtime and is slow when done billions of times.
  • Double buffering. Two buffer sets. While batch N is being sent to the target, the reader is already filling batch N+1 from the source.
  • Why double buffering also fixed an error. In an earlier HTTP-based version, the source SELECT sat idle while the INSERT ran, and the idle connection died with "unexpected EOF". Overlapping read and write keeps the read stream busy. Moving to the native protocol helped too.
  • Never retry Send on a spent batch. Once Send() has been called, the batch is consumed. Retrying it either duplicates rows or fails again. The correct recovery is DROP PARTITION and restart that season.

Simplified double-buffering sketch (not the real code):

const batchSize = 500_000

type colBuf struct {
    ids     []uint64
    names   []string
    revenue []float64
}

func (b *colBuf) reset() { b.ids, b.names, b.revenue = b.ids[:0], b.names[:0], b.revenue[:0] }

func copySeason(ctx context.Context, src, dst driver.Conn, season uint16) error {
    rows, err := src.Query(ctx, "SELECT id, name, revenue FROM attr_weekly WHERE season_code = ?", season)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    free := make(chan *colBuf, 2)  // two buffers: one filling, one sending
    full := make(chan *colBuf, 1)
    errc := make(chan error, 1)
    free <- &colBuf{}
    free <- &colBuf{}

    go func() { // writer: sends a full buffer while the reader fills the other one
        for buf := range full {
            batch, err := dst.PrepareBatch(ctx, "INSERT INTO attr_weekly")
            if err != nil {
                errc <- err
                return
            }
            batch.Column(0).Append(buf.ids)
            batch.Column(1).Append(buf.names)
            batch.Column(2).Append(buf.revenue)
            if err := batch.Send(); err != nil { // a spent batch is never retried
                errc <- err
                return
            }
            buf.reset()
            free <- buf
        }
        errc <- nil
    }()

    handOff := func(b *colBuf) error { // give a full buffer to the writer unless it already failed
        select {
        case full <- b:
            return nil
        case err := <-errc:
            return err
        }
    }

    buf := <-free
    for rows.Next() {
        var id uint64
        var name string
        var rev float64
        if err := rows.Scan(&id, &name, &rev); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        buf.ids, buf.names, buf.revenue = append(buf.ids, id), append(buf.names, name), append(buf.revenue, rev)
        if len(buf.ids) == batchSize {
            if err := handOff(buf); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            select {
            case buf = <-free: // waits only if both buffers are busy
            case err := <-errc:
                return err
            }
        }
    }
    if len(buf.ids) > 0 {
        if err := handOff(buf); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    close(full)
    return <-errc
}

What to notice: the channel free holds at most two buffers. The reader blocks only when both are in use, which is exactly when the writer is still sending. That back-pressure keeps memory bounded at two batches per worker. The real copier also handles per-table column lists, connection setup with TLS from environment variables, the per-table lock and checkpoints.

8.3 Workers and resource caps

  • -workers N copies N seasons in parallel. Each worker has its own source and target connections.
  • Caps are per process. Two terminals each running -workers 2 double the total budget, so they can oversubscribe the cluster.
  • The copier assumes the host has about 59 CPUs and 236 GiB. It splits about 48 threads and 180 GiB across workers. Example: with 2 workers, each query gets 24 threads and 90 GiB.

8.4 The 344k number, explained

  • What it measures. Rows per second written to the target, combined across two season streams. It is an ingest rate, not requests or transactions per second.
  • How it was derived. A live snapshot about 34 minutes into a run with two workers and 500k batches. Each stream ran at roughly 150k to 190k rows per second, about 344k combined. Cross-check: each worker committed about 0.3 to 0.4 Send() calls per second. 0.35 × 500,000 ≈ 175,000 rows per second per worker, and two workers give about 350,000, consistent with 344k.
  • Why it mattered. At billions of rows, the copy rate decides whether a migration takes hours or days.
  • How to say it. "About 344 thousand rows per second combined, two season streams on one machine, measured on a 4.09-billion-row table."
  • What not to say. "344k TPS" or "344k RPS". "I migrated 4.09 billion rows." If they hear TPS, correct them.

8.5 Failure handling and idempotency

Plain English. The unit of work is one season (one partition). A season is either recorded as done, or it is treated as dirty and redone from scratch. There is no "resume from the middle of a season".

  1. Ledger. The copier writes migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done, listing finished seasons.
  2. Incomplete season. If the target already has rows for a season not in the ledger, the copier runs DROP PARTITION (or DELETE) for that season and recopies it.
  3. No full wipe. There is no TRUNCATE of the whole table unless the operator passes -reset.
  4. Ctrl+C (SIGINT). The copier finishes the in-flight batch and does not checkpoint that season, so it will be redone next time.
  5. Per-table flock. Two terminals cannot copy the same table at once.
flowchart TD A["Start table copy"] --> B{"Season in table.done?"} B -- "yes" --> S["Skip season"] B -- "no" --> C{"Target already has rows for season?"} C -- "yes" --> D["DROP PARTITION season"] C -- "no" --> E["Copy season in 500k batches"] D --> E E --> F{"Finished cleanly?"} F -- "yes" --> G["Append season to table.done"] F -- "no, crash or Ctrl C" --> H["No checkpoint, redo next run"]

What to notice: the only way a season counts as done is a clean finish followed by a ledger write. That is what "eliminated partial-commit ghost rows" means.

Say this carefully. DROP PARTITION is not an atomic swap. If the copier crashes, the target has a truncated season until it is dropped and retried, and readers of the target can see that partial season meanwhile. The incremental design, which builds into scratch tables and swaps in with REPLACE PARTITION, was written and not executed. Do not claim it ran.

8.6 Checkpoint status at the 8 Sep 2026 snapshot

Say this if they ask "did the 4.09B copy finish?"

Table Status at snapshot
product_season seasons 3 to 7 done
attr_season seasons 3, 6 and 7 done
store_weekly seasons 6 and 7 done
product_weekly empty ledger. Failed mid-copy, partitions dirty
attr_weekly empty ledger. In flight for seasons 6 and 7 (the 4.09B object)
Hindsight three tables season 7 done

So the phrase is "measured on" a 4.09-billion-row set, never "migrated 4.09 billion rows".

The Hindsight tables on this path are tiny (season 7 on source): keep_drop_score 4,150 rows, missed 360, top style 360. Mention only if asked. Hindsight is not a PDF headline.

8.7 Design decision: a laptop pump over native TLS

  • What. A custom Go program on an allowlisted machine, native protocol with TLS on both sides, 500k-row columnar batches, double buffering, per-season checkpoints, DROP PARTITION replay.
  • Why. Cluster-to-cluster pull was not available because of the Cloud IP allowlists. The operator machine was allowed. The PDF does not name the Cloud function that failed.
  • How. Sections 8.2 to 8.5.
  • Alternatives an interviewer may suggest, and how I'd answer.
  • "Use remoteSecure or INSERT SELECT across clusters." That is the right answer when the clusters can reach each other. Here the allowlists blocked it.
  • "Export to object storage and import." Freezing partitions out through object storage is a good production pattern. It is one of the things I would pick for production.
  • "Use the HTTP interface." HTTP is simpler, but the earlier HTTP version hit unexpected EOF when the SELECT sat idle. Native blocks are also more efficient for columnar data.
  • Trade-off. Everything flows through one machine, so it is a single point of failure, and the caps are per process. There is no atomic swap, so target readers can see partial seasons during a redo.
  • What I'd do differently. For production I would get the clusters allowlisted to each other and use INSERT SELECT, or freeze through object storage, rather than copy through a laptop. I would also make REPLACE PARTITION from a scratch table the default, so readers never see a partial season.

9. Failure catalog (say these out loud)

  1. OOM on the weekly GROUP BY. Shrink the unit to one week, and measure attr weeks before raising RAM.
  2. A half-written partition looks complete. Never use count() > 0 as the success test for weekly builds. Use the ledger.
  3. HTTP client timeout after the server already committed. Trust system.query_log, not the client's exit code.
  4. HTTP SELECT dies with EOF during the INSERT. Double buffer, or use the native protocol.
  5. Retrying a spent batch. It causes duplicates or a second failure. DROP PARTITION and restart the unit instead.
  6. Connection reset on native TLS. The copier crashes. Only finished seasons are checkpointed, so the next run redoes the dirty season.
  7. Cluster-to-cluster pull blocked by allowlists. The laptop pump is a workaround, not the ideal design.
  8. Oversubscribed workers. Caps are per process, so two terminals double the load.
  9. Credentials. Never commit Cloud passwords. They come from environment variables only, and the binary does not read .env for you.

10. Interview questions (speakable answers)

1. How did you design the rollup schema, and why not query daily facts on every request?

"We pay once at load time and read cheap. A daily GROUP BY with many any() and argMax() states over wide rows is far too slow for an interactive grid, and FINAL on a ReplacingMergeTree is slower still and skips projections. So there are six MergeTree rollups, product, store and attr at season and weekly grain, all partitioned by season, with bloom filter indexes on product, store and attr keys. Product keeps SKU dimensions. Store and attr drop them and re-weight so store totals match the sum of SKUs. Attr is an unpivot using ARRAY JOIN, which is why attr weekly is about five times product weekly on the Briscoes seasons 6 and 7."

Follow-up they may ask: "How do you know the rollups are right?" Answer: "We compare product, store and attr sums under the same filters. On the earlier season-grain check, product and store revenue matched the weekly spine with zero difference across seasons 1 to 7."

2. Walk through a time you hit severe resource limits. How did you debug and fix the OOM?

"Building weekly rollups for a whole season in one statement needed an estimated 170 GB, and it failed at both 80 and 200 GB caps on a replica with about 236 GiB. The cause was aggregator state: about 110 any() columns plus argMax over wide strings, for every group. I did not raise memory first. I profiled by grain, shrank the unit to one fiscal week, then capped it at 55 GB with a 16 GB spill threshold, 8 threads and four weeks in flight. Product weeks peaked around 11 GB and attr weeks above 40 GB, so attr is the hog, and now it builds reliably."

3. How did you get about 344k rows per second in Go? Was that an HTTP API?

"No, it is a copy rate in rows per second, not requests. Two workers each streamed one season over native TLS at roughly 150 to 190 thousand rows a second, about 344 thousand combined at a live snapshot around 34 minutes in. The speed came from 500k-row columnar batches with typed slices, no per-row reflection, and double buffering, so reading the next batch overlaps sending the previous one. That overlap also fixed an unexpected-EOF problem we had when the SELECT sat idle over HTTP."

Follow-up they may ask: "Why a Go pump at all?" Answer: "Cluster-to-cluster pull was blocked by the Cloud IP allowlists, and the operator machine was allowed on both. It is a workaround, not a shard-to-shard design goal."

4. How did you handle failure and idempotency on billion-row copies?

"The unit is one season partition, and a season is either done or redone from scratch. The copier records finished seasons in a per-table .done checkpoint file. If the target has rows for a season that is not in the file, it drops that partition and recopies. Ctrl+C finishes the in-flight batch but does not checkpoint the season, and a file lock stops two terminals copying the same table. Separately, on the loader side, we once had a 64.1-million-row half-loaded partition pass a 'has rows' check, which is why weekly loads use a TSV ledger and check system.query_log instead of trusting the client."

Say this carefully: "DROP PARTITION then recopy is not an atomic swap. Readers can see a partial season until the redo finishes. The REPLACE PARTITION design was written, not run."

5. What is the scale?

"The largest object I timed is the Briscoes attr weekly table for seasons 6 and 7: 4.09 billion rows in one table, two partitions. Product weekly for the same seasons is about 839 million. Season grain is smaller. The replica is about 59 cores and 234 to 236 GiB. The 15.5× is a separate number, a 250M-row pivot benchmark, and the PDF rounds 12.3 seconds to 12."

6. Why not one INSERT of the whole season at weekly grain?

"Because it needed about 170 GB of aggregator state and failed at both an 80 GB and a 200 GB cap. One week at a time is about 11 GB for product and over 40 GB for attr, which fits under a 55 GB cap with spill as a safety net."

7. How do store totals stay consistent with SKUs?

"Store totals are built in two passes: weighted sums first, then a re-weight so each store's total equals the sum of its SKUs. Then we validate product, store and attr sums at the same filters. On the earlier Briscoes season-grain check, product and store revenue matched the weekly spine with zero difference across seasons 1 to 7."

8. How do ReplacingMergeTree corrections work?

"A correction is a new INSERT with a newer updated_at version, and ReplacingMergeTree keeps the newest version per key during background merges. Rollups are rebuilt at a captured watermark, so a rebuild is repeatable. I avoid FINAL where I want projections to work. One subtlety: the 'dirty' arrival token on the materialized view is not the same clock as the build watermark, so you cannot use one to reason about the other. The incremental pipeline is a design only."

9. What is the biggest production risk in the copier?

"There is no atomic swap. If it crashes, the target has a truncated season until we drop and retry, and readers of the target can see that partial season. For a real production move I would not copy through a laptop. I would allowlist the clusters to each other and use INSERT SELECT, or freeze through object storage, and swap seasons in with REPLACE PARTITION."

10. Whiteboard the Go copier.

"I draw three boxes: source cluster, the Go process on an allowlisted machine, target cluster, both connections native TLS. Inside the Go box I draw two buffers of 500k rows: one filling from the SELECT stream while the other is sent with Send(). Then I add the .done checkpoint per table and the rule that only finished seasons are recorded. Finally I note that -workers N means N seasons in parallel with their own connections, and that caps are per process: about 48 threads and 180 GiB split across workers, so 24 threads and 90 GiB each with two workers."

11. Did the 4.09-billion-row copy finish?

"At the snapshot I am quoting, no, it was in flight. The attr weekly ledger was still empty, with seasons 6 and 7 being copied, and product weekly had failed mid-copy with dirty partitions. Product season, attr season, store weekly and the small Hindsight tables had finished seasons. So I say the rate was measured on a 4.09-billion-row set, not that I migrated 4.09 billion rows."

11. Say this / don't say this

Safe to say Not safe to say
Six rollup tables, partitioned by season "Sub-second pivots"
From 189 seconds to about 12 on a 250M-row pivot benchmark, against the old PostgreSQL path "Every query got 15.5× faster" or "the OOM fix caused the 15.5×"
A whole-season weekly build needed about 170 GB and failed at 80 and 200 GB caps. Fixed with one fiscal week per insert "We just added more RAM"
Go native-TLS pump, about 344k rows per second combined "344k TPS" or "344k requests per second"
Measured on a 4.09B-row attr weekly set "I streamed 4.09 billion rows at 344,000 rows a second" as a finished job
500k batches with double buffering "Atomic DROP PARTITION" or "zero-downtime swap"

Kafka, Flink or CDC on Impact Analytics. Open-sourcing or sharing the copier. Hosts or passwords

LinkedIn and outreach. Safe: six tables, the 170 GB OOM and week slicing, the Go pump, about 344k rows per second combined, 4.09B attr weekly as the largest object timed, 500k batches and double buffering. The CI gate (100% statement coverage, 1,200+ Go tests, SAST and SBOM checks) is fine on LinkedIn. It left the PDF for the copier bullet. SAST is static application security testing. SBOM is a software bill of materials, the list of dependencies.

12. Three-minute whiteboard script

  1. First, draw the daily fact box and the six-table grid (product, store, attr × season, weekly). Say: "Planners can't GROUP BY daily data on every click, so we pay once at load and read small tables partitioned by season."
  2. Second, draw one weekly INSERT SELECT with a loop around it. Say: "Whole-season weekly needed about 170 GB and failed even at 200. One fiscal week per statement, 55 GB cap, 16 GB spill, 8 threads, four weeks in flight. The TSV ledger and query_log decide success, not row counts."
  3. Third, draw source cluster, Go box, target cluster. Say: "The allowlists blocked direct pull, so a Go pump on an allowlisted machine copies seasons over native TLS in 500k double-buffered batches, about 344k rows a second combined. Seasons are checkpointed only when finished. Dirty seasons are dropped and recopied."
  4. Close with the honesty line. "15.5× is query time, 170 GB is load time, and the 4.09-billion-row copy was measured in flight. DROP PARTITION is not an atomic swap. For production I'd use REPLACE PARTITION from a scratch table."

IA bullet defense: Agentic + Core (PDF Sep 2026)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: every Impact Analytics line on Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf, one by one. For each: the exact PDF text, what it means in plain words, how it works, why it was built that way, what each number means, and the questions interviewers ask with answers you can say out loud. It ends with four screening answers (why hire me, a production bug, a complex system, an agentic pipeline).
  • When to read it: after the deep dive (10), when you want to rehearse follow-up questions. Use the interview pack (23a) for the short pitches.
  • What to memorise: the "Split these numbers" box, the first sentence of every answer, and every "Do not say" line.

PDF: Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf · Canonical: docs/ASSORTSMART_TAB_RESUME.md

Every answer here uses real AssortSmart work. None of them import Kafka, Flink, CDC, Kubernetes operations, Milvus, sub-second ClickHouse, or a 70% document-RAG pipeline onto Impact Analytics.

Tags used here. MEASURED means there is a log, benchmark report, config or code behind it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal, so say "targeting". HISTORICAL means from my past work records. VERBAL means true but not printed on the PDF.

Split these numbers. 348k article-seasons is the scored Keep/Drop volume on the PDF. 1.6M is the full catalog (VERBAL). $100 per pass is off the PDF. 300 cases and 80% are the CI gate. "73% cheaper at 100% coverage" is the gold-200 model benchmark (n = 200). 74% is the production deterministic threshold's accuracy on that same 200 set. 55 GB, 16 GB and one fiscal week are VERBAL OOM settings. The PDF says "temporal chunks" and "memory and disk-spill caps". Partition rollback means DROP PARTITION then recopy. It is not a live reader swap. The 4.09B copy was in flight. A gate is not "all tenants live". Ask Iris is a shipped capability with no SLA.

Words you need

  • Article-season. One product in one selling season. The unit we score, like a report card per student per school year.
  • Sell-through. The share of available stock that sold. 84 sold of 100 is 84%.
  • Rate of sale (ROS). Units sold per selling store per week.
  • Lens. One focused question the LLM answers about an article, like one specialist on a panel of doctors.
  • Structured LLM invoke. An LLM call whose output must match a JSON schema. A form with fixed boxes, not a blank page.
  • s_det, s_agent, s_final. The rule score, the LLM score, and the blend 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent. Keep if s_final is at least 0.55.
  • ClickHouse. A columnar analytics database that reads only the columns a query needs.
  • MergeTree and ReplacingMergeTree. MergeTree writes sorted chunks and merges them in the background. ReplacingMergeTree also keeps only the newest version per key, like a notebook where old lines get crossed out later by a cleaner.
  • argMax. A ClickHouse function: argMax(value, time) returns the value from the row with the latest time. It is how a reader gets "the newest line" without waiting for the cleaner.
  • Circuit breaker. Stops calling a failing dependency after too many failures, like the breaker in your fuse box.
  • Checkpoint. Saved progress so a job resumes after a crash. A save point.
  • config_hash. A SHA-256 fingerprint of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog. SHA-256 turns any input into a fixed 64-character fingerprint, and any change gives a totally different one.
  • LangGraph supervisor. The routing node in an LLM graph, like a triage nurse.
  • Evaluator loop. A checker that sends an answer back for another try, capped at 3 attempts.
  • LangSmith. A tracing tool for LLM runs.
  • JWT. A signed token that proves identity without a server call, like a stamped wristband.
  • WebSocket handshake. The first HTTP "upgrade" request that opens a long-lived two-way connection.
  • OIDC. OpenID Connect, the standard behind "Sign in with Google".
  • Constant-time compare. Comparing secrets in a fixed amount of time so timing leaks nothing.
  • Wire. Compile-time dependency injection for Go. It generates the wiring code, so a missing piece fails the build.
  • h2c. HTTP/2 without TLS on that hop. Many requests share one connection.
  • Nested timeouts. Deadlines inside deadlines: server, then request, then each database call. Russian dolls.
  • Rollup. A pre-summed table, like a monthly statement instead of every card swipe.
  • OOM and spill. Out of memory means the query is killed. Spill means writing overflow aggregation state to disk to avoid that.
  • Native protocol. ClickHouse's binary protocol for moving columnar blocks. Port 9440 adds TLS.
  • Double buffering. Fill batch B while batch A is sending. Two kitchen trays.
  • DROP PARTITION. Delete one whole season's data at once, like emptying one drawer.
  • Ghost rows. Leftover rows from a failed partial write that make a table look complete.

SECTION 1: Agentic Flows & Orchestration

A1. Multi-pipeline engine: 348k article-seasons, 88k per pass, 7 lenses

PDF: Architected a multi-pipeline AI merchandise decision engine (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style) evaluating 348k article-seasons. Optimized inference at scale, processing 88k items per pass, by blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM invokes across 7 AI lenses.

In plain words. A batch system with three named pipelines. For every product in every season, code computes the hard numbers, an LLM answers seven focused questions about patterns, and the two are combined into a keep or drop recommendation.

What. Batch scoring across Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style. Deterministic Python owns the KPI math. The LLM sees packed JSON and returns structured lens scores. The seven active lenses are trend_velocity, size_curve, colour_cannibalization, channel_divergence, multi_season_consistency, discount_dependency and margin_resilience.

Why. LLMs are bad at arithmetic. Hardcoded KPI math stays financially correct. Lenses do the qualitative pattern work a planner would otherwise do by eye.

How (with an example). A tee with sell-through 84% and ROS 1.168 gets s_det ≈ 0.65 from code. A cheap gate sees five sizes, two colours and 12 weeks on sale, so size_curve, colour_cannibalization and trend_velocity are eligible. The batch of up to 64 articles goes through peer benchmark, then decider, then lenses, then blend, then explanation, in that fixed order. If s_agent = 0.711, then s_final = 0.4 × 0.65 + 0.6 × 0.711 ≈ 0.687, which is a keep.

Design decisions. Keep the deterministic layer separate from prompt payloads. Use strict JSON schemas. Cap batch size for memory and provider rate limits.

  • Alternative: one big prompt per article. Harder to evaluate and fix. Narrow lenses each have a rubric and can be fixed alone.
  • Alternative: rules only. Coarse and tends to over-keep.
  • Trade-off. More LLM calls per article, kept in check by the gate and batching.
  • What I'd do differently. Get planner-labelled gold data earlier.

The numbers. - 348k is the count of article-seasons the engine has evaluated. Say "348 thousand article-seasons". Don't equate it with the 1.6M catalog. - 88k is the size of one pass. Say "about 88 thousand items per pass". Don't invent how many passes add up to 348k. - 7 is the number of active lenses. An eighth lens exists but is switched off. Not every lens fires on every article. - $100 per pass (VERBAL) is the token spend. Mention only if they ask about cost.

Q: Why not let the LLM calculate KPIs through Python tools? A: "For security, speed and determinism. A scoring agent with a code or SQL tool across 88k items is a latency and injection surface. We pre-compute the KPIs in code and pass JSON, so math accuracy never depends on the model. The model's job is judgement, not arithmetic."

Q: How did you handle rate limits at 88k items? A: "Parallel article batches with a global cap on in-flight LLM calls, hard per-batch timeouts, backoff, and a circuit breaker in the orchestration registry. A throttle doesn't wipe the run. Checkpoints let it resume the LLM phase without recomputing the deterministic scores." Follow-up they may ask: "What's the batch size?" Up to 64 articles per LLM call.

Q: How do you choose which lenses run? A: "A cheap Python gate runs before any LLM call. A lens only runs if the article has the data for it. A single-size product skips size_curve, and a single-colour product skips colour_cannibalization. That saves money and stops a lens from returning a meaningless middle score."

Do not say: 348k is the 1.6M catalog. $100 is on this PDF. It's one giant chatbot.

A2. JSON payloads, ReplacingMergeTree, timeout fallback

PDF: Decoupled AI inference from a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master by asynchronously serving context via JSON payloads rather than direct database querying. Engineered an eventually consistent write pattern via ReplacingMergeTree that guaranteed system availability by gracefully falling back to deterministic baselines during LLM timeouts.

In plain words. The LLM never gets database access. We query, we pack JSON, we send it. Results are written so that duplicates are harmless. If the LLM is slow, the rule score stands and the run keeps going.

What. Scoring LLMs do not query the 2.11B-row master. Context is packed JSON. Writes go through our engine code onto ReplacingMergeTree tables. A timeout means the deterministic score stands and the run continues.

Why. Direct SQL from an LLM against a production analytical table risks runaway queries, connection-pool exhaustion and prompt injection.

How.

{"article": "TEE-0412", "season": 74,
 "kpis": {"sell_thru_eop_pct": 84.0, "ros": 1.168},
 "size_count": 5, "style_color_count": 2,
 "week_series": [{"w": 1, "qty": 210}, {"w": 2, "qty": 238}]}

-- Readers always take the latest version per key
SELECT article, argMax(s_final, computed_at) AS s_final
FROM reco_final_score
WHERE season_code = 74
GROUP BY article;

Design decisions. No database tool on the scoring path. An async batch mapper. A version column on the ReplacingMergeTree so retries do not duplicate articles. On the Keep/Drop path the default output is still CSV first, and publishing to ClickHouse is a separate operator step, so a bad config shows up in a CSV diff before any planner sees it.

  • Alternative: give the agent a SQL tool. Rejected for safety, cost and latency.
  • Alternative: delete then insert on retry. Deletes are heavy mutations in ClickHouse. Append with "latest wins" is cheaper.
  • Trade-off. For a short window two versions of a row can exist, so every reader must ask for the latest.

The numbers. 2.11B is the row count of the ClickHouse master that the agents are kept away from. Say "a 2.11-billion-row master". Don't confuse it with the 4.09B copy set or the 250M benchmark harness.

Q: Why ReplacingMergeTree instead of plain MergeTree? A: "Because retries and overlapping waves can land the same article twice. ReplacingMergeTree keeps the latest version per key during background merges. Readers don't wait for that. They query with argMax or LIMIT 1 BY, so we never need OPTIMIZE FINAL as a runtime requirement."

Q: What happens on an LLM timeout? A: "Every batch has a hard timeout that scales with batch size and has a ceiling. When it fires, the batch is marked as a fallback and the article keeps its precomputed deterministic score. One vendor 504 never blocks the other 88k items." Follow-up they may ask: "Doesn't fallback hide problems?" No, fallbacks are counted in the run telemetry, so a spike is visible.

Q: So the LLM still queries ClickHouse, just asynchronously? A: "No, and that's an important correction. 'Async' describes the batch executor. The model never gets a SQL tool. It's JSON in and engine writes out."

Do not say: "Physical air-gap" as the PDF phrase (that was older wording). "Zero corruption" as if it were a two-phase-commit guarantee. "The LLM issues ClickHouse writes." "I authored CDC" (pg2ch_cdc was Ashvin Sharma).

A3. Registry: timeouts, breakers, checkpoints, config_hash

PDF: Engineered a shared orchestration registry to guarantee 88k-article batch runs survive provider failures by implementing hard timeouts, circuit breakers, and durable checkpoints that bypass redundant deterministic scoring. Ensured full observability by stamping every output row with a frozen config hash and custom JSON telemetry tracking tokens, USD cost, step duration, and batch fallbacks.

In plain words. One shared harness runs all three pipelines. It sets deadlines, stops hammering a dead provider, saves progress so a crash resumes, and records which config produced each row and what the run cost.

What. The harness freezes the config, keeps a claim ledger, runs timed LLM batches, has a circuit breaker, writes resume files, and emits telemetry JSON.

Why. A provider 502 or 504 halfway through 88k items must not force a full deterministic recompute.

How.

Step 1  Deterministic scores for all articles   -> det.json            (saved first)
Step 2  LLM chunks finish one by one            -> agent_progress.json (appended)
Crash
Step 3  Rerun with --resume                     -> reload det.json, skip finished articles,
                                                   continue only the LLM work

The circuit trips after about 5 consecutive failures or once the failure fraction passes a threshold. config_hash is a SHA-256 of the frozen guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog. Because prompt text is in the hash, changing one word of a prompt creates a new hash, so you can always tell which prompts produced a row.

  • Alternative: Airflow or Temporal. See the answer below.
  • Alternative: a run UUID instead of a config hash. A UUID tells you which run, not which configuration.
  • Trade-off. We own the orchestration code and its bugs, and there is no built-in UI.
  • What I'd do differently. Turn the run ledger and cost telemetry on by default.

Q: How do checkpoints work? A: "Deterministic results land first. As LLM chunks complete, we append per-article progress. A restart reloads the deterministic results, skips finished articles and continues the LLM map. That's what 'bypass redundant deterministic scoring' means on the resume."

Q: Why not Airflow or Temporal? A: "This workload needed resume logic tightly coupled to ClickHouse inserts, config hashing and per-run token and USD accounting. We already owned a batch CLI and an HTTP start path. A heavy external orchestrator would have been extra infrastructure without a clear payoff." Follow-up they may ask: "When would you pick Temporal?" When workflows are long-lived, span many services, and need durable timers and signals beyond one batch job.

Q: What does the circuit breaker actually do? A: "It's a deterministic run controller, not an agent. It counts failures. If about five fail in a row, or too large a fraction of calls fail, it stops the step and exits with a clear code instead of burning money on a dead provider."

Do not say: HITL validation queues (not in this system). LangSmith on this bullet (on this PDF, LangSmith belongs to Ask Iris). Netflix Hystrix as the product.

A4. Ask Iris: JWT WebSocket, 3-attempt evaluator, frozen handshake

PDF: Shipped "Ask Iris," a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot enabling planners to interactively query KPIs and inspect AI decisions on a multi-billion-row database. Prevented infinite LLM loops and multi-tenant data leaks by orchestrating a LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator loop, utilizing LangSmith for observability, and strictly freezing hierarchy access on the initial socket handshake.

In plain words. A chat assistant in AssortSmart. Identity and permissions are locked once when the connection opens. A routing node sends each question to the right worker, and a checker can send an answer back at most three times.

What. A FastAPI WebSocket chat. The JWT arrives at the handshake as Authorization: Bearer ... or ?token=. plan_scope is frozen once. The supervisor routes to workers, the evaluator retries up to MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3, and LangSmith traces every run.

Why. Chat is a tenant-bleed and token-loop surface if scope can change mid-session.

How.

sequenceDiagram participant B as Browser participant API as FastAPI WebSocket participant SUP as Supervisor participant EV as Evaluator B->>API: Upgrade request with JWT API->>API: Verify token, freeze plan_scope B->>API: Show sell-through for my tops API->>SUP: Question plus frozen scope SUP->>EV: Worker draft answer EV-->>SUP: Retry, attempt 2 of 3 EV-->>API: Accepted answer API-->>B: Answer

What to notice: scope is set once at the top and never read from chat text.

  • Alternative: re-check permissions per message. Scope could then depend on message content. Freezing at the handshake makes widening scope structurally impossible.
  • Alternative: uncapped loops. Runaway cost and latency.
  • Trade-off. If permissions change mid-session, the user must reconnect to pick them up.

Q: How do you prevent multi-tenant leaks? A: "Tenant, hierarchy and plan scope are bound at the JWT handshake. Every tool call inherits that frozen plan_scope. A later chat message can't pivot into another tenant's hierarchy, because nothing in the message can change the scope."

Q: How do you stop infinite LangGraph loops? A: "The evaluator loop is capped at three attempts, and there's a recursion limit on the supervisor graph as a second guard. When the cap is hit, it fails closed with a graceful answer instead of another tool hop."

Q: How do you debug a bad answer? A: "LangSmith. I open the trace for that run and see which worker the supervisor picked, what the tool calls returned, what the evaluator rejected and how many tokens it took."

Do not say: a tenant-wide SLA, questions per week, "generates dynamic charts" as a PDF claim (it was dropped), or an HITL review queue.

A5. 300-case proxy, 80% CI gate, 73% cost, 74% baseline, frozen weights

PDF: Built a 300-case proxy evaluation harness and an 80% accuracy CI gate to enforce strict deployment guardrails. Reduced live execution costs by 73% at 100% coverage by benchmarking models against a 74% deterministic baseline, strategically freezing final decision weights when the LLM underperformed the baseline.

In plain words. Nothing ships unless it scores at least 80% on a fixed 300-case test set. On a separate 200-case benchmark, I picked a model that cost 73% less while still completing every case. The plain rule scored 74% on that set and the LLM blend scored lower, so I froze the blend weights instead of tuning them to a small sample.

Split (say this unprompted if they fuse the numbers):

Number Source Meaning
300 cases, 80% eval.json (gold_min_accuracy: 0.8) and cases.json CI promotion gate
73% cheaper, 100% coverage gold-200 bench, gpt-5.6-luna vs gpt-5.4-mini, 200 of 200 complete Model pick for live scoring
74% Production deterministic threshold 0.65 on that 200 set The free rule the LLM must beat
Frozen blend weights Same bench: blended LLM about 63%, below the rule's 74% Do not retune 0.4 and 0.6 on a small proxy

How the 300 proxy labels are made. We score season A and label using only season B, which the pipeline never sees. Strong next-season sell-through and rate of sale is a KEEP. Weak is a DROP. The middle band is skipped. The builder avoids circularity (labelling on the pipeline's own inputs) and treatment leakage (an article a planner already dropped sells zero next season by construction).

The numbers. - 80% is a promotion gate, not live accuracy. Say "an 80% accuracy CI gate". - 73% means the chosen model's run cost about 27% of the previous model's run on the same 200 cases. Say "73% lower live execution cost at full coverage". - 74% is the rule baseline on the 200 set. Say "a 74% deterministic baseline". - Model names are not on the PDF. Use them only if asked.

Q: What did you do when the LLM scored below the deterministic baseline? A: "I held the blend weights frozen. We don't ship a 'smarter' model that loses to a free rule on the proxy set. Promotion still requires the 80% CI gate on the 300-case file. The gap told us to improve the lenses and the labels, not to bend the weights."

Q: How did you choose the model? A: "On the gold-200 set, Luna completed 200 out of 200 with full lens coverage and was 73% cheaper than mini. A nano-tier option was slightly cheaper but left pending rows. Completion reliability won. That 73% comes from the 200-case benchmark, not the 300-case suite."

Q: Isn't accuracy alone a weak gate? A: "Yes, and the config knows it. A set that is mostly keeps can clear 80% while missing half the drops. That's why the gate config also supports a drop-recall threshold, and raising it is the lever against over-keeping."

Do not say: "All tenants are live at 80%." "gpt-5.6-luna is on the PDF." "The 73% came from the 300-case file."

SECTION 2: Core Infrastructure & Pipeline

C1. Go/Gin at 10k peak RPS, Wire, h2c, Datadog

PDF: Architected a multi-tenant Go/Gin platform scaling to 10k peak RPS, utilizing Google Wire for compile-time DI. Deployed as a self-protecting HTTP edge without a reverse proxy, guaranteeing high availability through native h2c, nested timeouts, and Datadog distributed tracing.

In plain words. The API the planner UI talks to is a Go service. Nothing sits in front of it, so it protects itself with deadlines, size limits and graceful shutdown.

How.

// Illustrative: h2c plus nested deadlines
srv := &http.Server{
    Handler:           h2c.NewHandler(router, &http2.Server{}),
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,                  // outer
}
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(c.Request.Context(), 20*time.Second) // request
qctx, qcancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 15*time.Second)               // query

Plus a request body cap, a SIGTERM drain so in-flight requests finish during deploys, and Datadog spans across handler, cache and database calls. The values are illustrative.

The numbers. 10k peak RPS is the peak request rate of the Go edge. Say "10k peak requests per second". Don't add an uptime percentage or a tenant count.

Q: Why Wire over Fx or Dig? A: "Wire is compile-time. It generates plain Go, so wiring errors fail the build instead of a request path, and there's zero reflection at runtime. Fx and Dig resolve dependencies at runtime with reflection."

Q: Why no reverse proxy? A: "The process owns h2c, nested context timeouts and traces. That's one less hop and one less ops surface, and all the timeout logic lives in one place. The trade-off is that the service has to protect itself. I don't invent a 99.9% SLA for it." Follow-up they may ask: "When would you add one?" For multi-region routing or if we needed edge features like a WAF.

Q: What are nested timeouts? A: "Deadlines inside deadlines. The server has an outer deadline, each request gets a smaller budget, and each database call inside gets a smaller one again. A slow ClickHouse query fails cleanly before the connection does."

Do not say: Nginx or Envoy as the timeout story. Kubernetes cluster operations.

C2. KPI configurator, tokenizer, division-by-zero protection

PDF: Eliminated deployment bottlenecks by architecting a dynamic KPI configurator and custom formula parser. Engineered a real-time compilation layer that tokenizes operator-authored math into parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragments with native division-by-zero protection, decoupling business logic from code releases.

In plain words. Operators type a KPI formula. A Go parser turns it into safe ClickHouse SQL immediately, so a new KPI no longer needs a code release.

What actually ships. A Go tokenizer and parser, allowlisted functions, logical names mapped to physical columns, and a SELECT wrapped as ifNotFinite(toFloat64(<expr>), 0).

Input:   margin_pct = margin / revenue * 100
Output:  ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(margin) / sum(revenue) * {p1:Float64}), 0)   p1 = 100
Input:   revenue; DROP TABLE x
Output:  rejected: unknown token ";"

ifNotFinite(x, 0) returns 0 if x is Infinity or NaN, so a zero-revenue row gives 0 instead of breaking the planner's JSON.

  • Alternative: let operators paste SQL. Injection risk.
  • Alternative: hardcode every KPI. Safe but needs a release per change, which was the bottleneck.
  • Trade-off. We own a small language, so the grammar must stay small and well tested.

Q: How do you prevent SQL injection? A: "We never concatenate raw operator text into SQL. Tokens must parse, functions must be on an allowlist, identifiers resolve through a catalog, and constants are bound as parameters. Anything unknown fails closed, so the formula is rejected, not guessed at."

Q: How does division by zero work? A: "Compilation wraps the whole expression in ifNotFinite(..., 0), so Infinity and NaN never reach planner JSON. That's the 'native division-by-zero protection' on the resume."

Do not say: "Operators can paste arbitrary SQL." If they press on implementation, don't call it a generic prepared statement around free-form SQL. The guard is parse plus allowlist plus catalog plus ifNotFinite.

C3. Isolation, the OIDC waterfall, constant-time keys

PDF: Guaranteed strict multi-tenant data isolation and UAM-scoped hierarchy access control across PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. Redis-fronted Firebase Admin to JWT/Google OIDC waterfall, constant-time API keys, Postgres-backed role resolution.

In plain words. Each request proves identity through one of several methods tried in order, Redis caches the result, Postgres says what the user may see, and every query on both databases is filtered to that scope.

How. Check Redis for an already-verified token. On a miss, try Firebase Admin, then JWT or Google OIDC verification. API keys are checked with a constant-time compare. Roles and the UAM hierarchy come from Postgres. The same tenant ID filters ClickHouse queries as bound parameters, for example tenant_id = {t:String} AND l1_name IN {l1:Array(String)}.

import "crypto/subtle"
ok := subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(given), []byte(stored)) == 1
  • Alternative: a database per tenant. Strongest isolation, heavy to operate across many tenants.
  • Trade-off. Cached auth means revocation waits for cache expiry, so cache lifetimes stay short.

Q: What does constant-time comparison protect against? A: "A normal == stops at the first mismatched byte. An attacker can time responses and guess the key one character at a time. A constant-time compare takes the same time on any mismatch, so timing reveals nothing."

Q: What about auth latency? A: "Redis fronts verified tokens, so we're not calling Firebase or the OIDC provider on every API call. A miss falls through to real verification and then Postgres. It never degrades open."

Q: Is this encryption? A: "No. It's access control and data isolation. Encryption at rest and in transit is a separate concern."

Do not say: "encryption product", "privacy program", Milvus, or a sub-millisecond SLA. Keep the cache benefit qualitative ("Redis-fronted").

C4. 15.5×, the 170GB OOM, temporal chunks, spill caps

PDF: Reduced planner pivot latency by 15.5× (189s to 12s on 250M-row operations) by building a ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer for season and weekly rollups. Prevented 170GB OOM crashes by slicing batch inserts into temporal chunks and enforcing strict distributed memory and disk-spill caps.

In plain words. Two stories in one bullet. Pivots got much faster by reading pre-summed ClickHouse tables. Separately, building the weekly tables crashed from memory, and I fixed that by building one week at a time with hard limits.

Split. 15.5× is query time, the pivot on a 250M-row harness. 170GB is load time, a whole-season weekly GROUP BY. They are not cause and effect.

The six tables. product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain, all MergeTree with PARTITION BY season_code. Planners read rollups, not raw daily facts.

The numbers. - 15.5× is 189,408 ms divided by 12,256 ms on the 250M harness (Postgres versus ClickHouse on the same heavy pivot, row-identical data). The PDF rounds 12.3 s to 12 s. Say "from 189 seconds to 12 seconds". MEASURED POC. Don't call it sub-second or a production p95. - 170 GB is the estimated aggregation memory for a whole-season weekly insert. It failed at 80 GB and at 200 GB caps. - VERBAL settings (true, off the PDF): one fiscal week per insert, 55 GB memory cap, 16 GB spill, 8 threads, 4 weeks in flight. A product week is about 11 GB. An attribute week is over 40 GB.

Q: Why did it OOM? A: "ClickHouse holds aggregation state in RAM for every group. A whole-season weekly GROUP BY, with lots of any() and argMax states over wide strings, pushed about 170 GB. It failed even at 200 GB, so I sliced the work to one fiscal week per insert and enabled external GROUP BY spill to disk."

Q: What's the rollup shape? A: "Six MergeTree tables partitioned by season: product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain. Planners read rollups, not raw daily facts. Store totals are re-weighted so they match the sum of SKUs."

Q: Was the 12 seconds measured on the rollups? A: "The 189-to-12 figure is from the 250-million-row harness, where ClickHouse ran the same heavy pivot that took Postgres 189 seconds. In production, planners read the rollup tables, which do less work per query. I don't quote a production latency number on top of that."

Q: Was the benchmark fair? A: "It was tilted toward Postgres. Postgres ran on a 48 GB host and ClickHouse on a 10-CPU, 3.3 GB Docker VM. Honestly, most of the gap came from the option-count distinct, which Postgres can't parallelise. Without it, ClickHouse is more like 2 to 3 times faster on typical aggregates."

Do not say: sub-second pivots. "The OOM fix caused the 15.5×." "4.09B is this bullet."

C5. Go native-TLS pump, about 344k rows/s, 4.09B, TSV, partition rollbacks

PDF: Migrated ClickHouse rollups across Cloud clusters at ~344k rows/s by writing a custom Go native-TLS data pump to bypass strict cross-cluster IP allowlist restrictions. Processed partitions up to 4.09B rows using 500k-row double-buffered batches, and eliminated partial-commit ghost rows using TSV ledgers and atomic partition rollbacks.

In plain words. The two ClickHouse clusters couldn't talk directly. An allowlisted machine could reach both, so I wrote a Go program there that reads from one and writes to the other in big columnar batches, with bookkeeping so a crash never leaves fake-complete data.

How. One season per worker. 500k-row columnar buffers. Two buffer sets, so reading the next batch overlaps sending the previous one. A .done checkpoint file per table and season. A per-table file lock. SIGINT finishes the in-flight batch but does not checkpoint that season. An incomplete season gets DROP PARTITION and a full recopy.

season 6:  read A ──► send A
                read B ──► send B        (read and send overlap)
                     read C ──► send C
           all sent ──► write migrate-checkpoints/attr_weekly.done

The numbers. - About 344k rows/s is combined native-protocol ingest from two season streams of roughly 150k to 190k rows/s each, at a live snapshot. Say "about 344 thousand rows per second". It is not RPS or TPS. - 4.09B is 2,779,317,472 plus 1,311,108,195 rows of attribute weekly data across two seasons. Say "measured on a 4.09-billion-row set". The copy was in flight. - 500k is the batch size in rows.

Q: Why not remoteSecure or distributed tables? A: "Cross-cluster IP allowlists blocked the clusters from talking to each other. An operator machine was allowlisted, so a Go pump over native TLS on port 9440 was the workaround. The PDF says 'allowlist', not the name of the function that failed."

Q: How do you avoid ghost rows, and what are the TSV ledger and the rollback? A: "A failed INSERT can still commit some blocks, so count() > 0 is a lie. The weekly loader keeps a TSV ledger of finished chunks and confirms completion in system.query_log. The copier has its own .done files per table. On restart, any season without a checkpoint gets DROP PARTITION and a full recopy. That's the 'atomic partition rollback' on the PDF. It is not an atomic swap with live readers."

Q: Is 344k HTTP requests per second? A: "No. It's combined native-protocol ingest from two season streams, using 500k-row columnar batches and double buffering, where we read the next batch while Send() runs on the previous one. It's not REST traffic."

Q: What's the biggest risk in this design? A: "There's no atomic swap. If it crashes mid-season, the target has a truncated season until we drop and recopy, and readers could see partial data in that window. A REPLACE PARTITION design from scratch tables would fix that. It was written but not executed. For a real production cutover I'd allowlist the clusters to each other or go through object storage."

Do not say: "I finished the 4.09B cutover." "344k TPS." "We open-sourced the copier." "TSV is the copier's ledger."

Full whiteboard: 42_clickhouse_rollup_migration.md.

Why should we hire you? (senior level)

At Uber, through EPAM, I owned the FRM scoping backend. I built 36 Spring Boot endpoints over 19 million GL rows with a four-level L1 to L4 hierarchy and SHA-256 natural keys, and cut quarterly reconciliation by 70%, from 14 days to 3 days, against a $340M materiality threshold, while leading 3 engineers. On Uber Eats I owned menu ingestion with Selenium, Kafka, Flink and exactly-once catalog upserts. At Impact Analytics I own AssortSmart across two chapters. On the agentic side: Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style over 348k article-seasons, 88k items per pass, seven lenses, JSON payloads instead of LLM access to a 2.11-billion-row ClickHouse master, Ask Iris as a JWT WebSocket copilot with a three-attempt LangGraph evaluator, and an 80% CI gate on 300 cases, with a model 73% cheaper at full coverage against a 74% rule baseline and frozen weights. On the platform side: a Go and Gin edge at 10k peak RPS, a KPI parser with ifNotFinite protection, pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on 250 million rows, a 170 GB OOM fixed with temporal chunks and spill caps, and a Go native-TLS pump at about 344k rows per second on partitions up to 4.09 billion rows.

If you need someone who can design independently, debug at scale, and refuse a bad agent with a gate, that's the work I already do."

Do not say Kubernetes as Impact Analytics production work, Kafka on Impact Analytics, or "sub-second ClickHouse".

A production bug you resolved (use the 170 GB OOM)

  • Situation. Weekly ClickHouse rollups feed the planner pivots.
  • Task. Keep weekly grain, because planners need fiscal-week views, without crashing the replica.
  • Crisis. The whole-season weekly INSERT SELECT built about 170 GB of aggregation state and hit MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. It failed even at 80 GB and 200 GB caps.
  • Investigation. I profiled by grain instead of throwing RAM at it. A product week peaked around 11 GB. An attribute week peaked above 40 GB. The unit of work was simply too big.
  • Fix. One fiscal week per INSERT, a 55 GB memory cap, 16 GB spill, and a bounded number of weeks in flight.
  • Prevention. Spill settings are now in the generated SQL, and we never GROUP BY a whole season at weekly grain.

Say it like this: "The build kept dying even at 200 GB, so I stopped adding memory and measured per week. Attribute weeks alone needed over 40 GB. I rebuilt it as one week per insert with a 55 GB cap and 16 GB of spill, and weekly grain finally built reliably."

Alternate (Masters India, people and process): the IRP timeout canary. Timeouts on government portal calls were too aggressive, and we moved to non-blocking calls with idempotency keys. Do not lead with the connection-leak OOM or the Kafka heap-leak story as if it were an Impact Analytics bullet. Those are packet stories, not PDF bullets.

A complex system you developed (AssortSmart, not CDC)

  • Problem. Planner pivots on PostgreSQL were too slow (about 189 seconds on the 250M harness), and agents could not be allowed to run SQL against a 2.11B-row fact table.
  • Architecture. A Go and Gin edge (Wire, h2c, Datadog), then Postgres UAM with the Redis-fronted OIDC waterfall, then six ClickHouse rollup tables for reads, then Python batch agents working only on JSON payloads, and Ask Iris over a WebSocket with a frozen plan scope.
  • Hard part. The weekly-grain OOM, and a cluster copy blocked by allowlists. I solved them with temporal INSERT chunks and a Go native-TLS pump, not with Kafka or CDC.
  • Result. 15.5× on the 250M harness, 348k article-seasons scored by Keep/Drop, Ask Iris shipped, and an 80% CI gate guarding promotions.

Do not draw Kafka to Flink to ClickHouse for Impact Analytics. That picture is Uber Menu.

An agentic pipeline you owned (Keep/Drop and Ask Iris, not document RAG)

  • Business. Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style recommendations for merchandise planners.
  • Stack. Python batch plus LangGraph for Ask Iris. Not Milvus. Milvus is Uber Menu.
  • Loop. Deterministic KPI JSON, then 7 structured lenses, then the blend, then a ReplacingMergeTree insert or a CSV bake. Failures: a timeout falls back to the deterministic score, the circuit breaker stops a dead provider, and checkpoints let the run resume.
  • Interactive path. JWT WebSocket, then the frozen hierarchy, then the supervisor, then the 3-attempt evaluator, with LangSmith tracing.
  • Guardrails. The 300-case proxy set, the 80% CI gate, and frozen weights when the LLM loses to the 74% rule.

Do not tell a 70% invoice-extraction RAG story as this bullet. Menu RAG is a different PDF chapter.
