Deployment and Scale for Every Resume Project

How to use this page

  • Part 1 explains deployment and scaling ideas from zero: canary, rollback, blue-green, autoscaling, rate limiting, circuit breakers, backpressure, caching, sharding and more. Each one ends with where it honestly shows up in my work.
  • Part 2 goes project by project: how each system shipped, how it scaled, how it rolled back, and which numbers I can defend.
  • Read it before system-design rounds and "how did you deploy this / what happens at 10x" questions.
  • Memorise the per-project "deploy story" paragraphs in Part 2 and the honesty lines. They're what you'll actually say.

Tags: MEASURED means there's a benchmark, log or doc behind it. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from past work records, not re-measured. DESIGN means designed but not claimed as running.

The one honesty rule for this page. I have deployed and consumed containerised services (Docker on GCP and AWS). I have not operated Kubernetes clusters, written Terraform, or run multi-region setups. Those are study topics. When an interviewer asks about them, explain how they work and say plainly that I didn't own them.

Part 1: The concepts, from zero

1. Build, image, release

Plain English. Deploying means getting new code running for real users. First you build the code. Then you package it into a container image, a sealed box holding the app and everything it needs. A release starts new copies of that image and stops the old ones.

Analogy. A container image is like a meal-prep box: same ingredients, same recipe, so it tastes the same on any stove.

Where it shows up in my work. Every project shipped as Docker images: Impact Analytics on GCP, Masters India on AWS, Uber Menu on GCP, and Uber FRM through Uber's release process with Bazel builds.

2. Rolling, blue-green and canary deployments

These are three ways to swap old code for new without a big outage.

  • Rolling deploy. Replace copies one at a time. Like changing the tyres on a bus one by one while it's parked at different stops.
  • Blue-green deploy. Run two full environments. "Blue" serves users while "green" gets the new version. When green looks healthy, flip all traffic over in one step. Rollback means flipping back.
  • Canary deploy. Send a small share of real traffic, say 5%, to the new version. Watch errors and latency. If it's healthy, increase step by step to 100%. The name comes from canaries that miners carried to detect gas early.
flowchart LR U["Users"] --> G["Gateway"] G -->|"95 percent"| OLD["Old PHP route"] G -->|"5 percent"| NEW["New Spring Boot route"] NEW --> M["Watch errors and p95"]

What to notice: only a small slice of real users hit the new code first. If the metrics look bad, the gateway sends everyone back to the old route.

Tiny example. Week 1, /invoice/status sends 5% of traffic to the Spring Boot service. Error rate matches PHP, and p95 is lower. Week 2 it's 50%. Week 3 it's 100%, and the PHP route is retired.

Where it shows up in my work. - Masters India: canary per route. This is my real canary experience. During the strangler migration (replacing the monolith one endpoint at a time), each route moved to a Spring Boot service behind the gateway with a canary percentage. Rollback was a traffic flip, not a rebuild. - Blue-green: not claimed. The closest idea in my work is the ClickHouse REPLACE PARTITION design at Impact Analytics, which loads data into a staging table and swaps it in one step. That design was written but not executed. Don't present it as running.

3. Rollback

Plain English. Rollback means returning to the last known good state when a release goes wrong. There are three kinds, and interviewers like it when you separate them.

  1. Code rollback. Run the previous version again. Easy if the deployment is a traffic flip or an image tag change.
  2. Data rollback. Undo or redo data changes. Much harder, because data has already been written.
  3. Schema rollback. Undo a database structure change. The safe pattern is expand and contract: first add the new column (expand), make the code use it, and only later remove the old one (contract). At every step, both the old and the new code still work.

Tiny example of expand and contract. You want to rename amount to amount_usd. Release 1 adds amount_usd and writes to both columns. Release 2 reads from amount_usd. Release 3 drops amount. If release 2 breaks, you roll back to release 1 and nothing is lost.

Where it shows up in my work. - Masters India. Code rollback was flipping the canary traffic back to the PHP route. - Uber FRM. Rollback was the previous service revision plus migration discipline in the expand-and-contract style. Releases went out as stacked Bazel PRs (a chain of small, dependent pull requests), so each step was small enough to revert. - Uber Menu. Data rollback by replay. If a bad parser shipped, we rewound the Kafka consumer offsets to before the bad release and reprocessed events with the fixed parser. - Impact Analytics (data). For the cluster migration, a failed season copy was handled by DROP PARTITION for that season, then recopying it. That's a "drop and redo", not an atomic swap with live readers. - Impact Analytics (AI). Every output row is stamped with a config_hash, a fingerprint of the prompts, parameters, guardrails and catalog used. If a config turns out bad, the hash tells you exactly which rows came from it and need rerunning.

4. Feature flags and config-driven changes

Plain English. A feature flag is an on/off switch in configuration that turns a feature on for some users without a new deployment. Config-driven means behaviour comes from data or config, not hard-coded logic.

Analogy. A light switch versus rewiring the house.

Tiny example. if flags.enabled("new_scoping_screen", user): show_new() lets you turn the screen on for the Finance team first.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics, KPI configurator. Operators change KPI formulas as configuration. A Go parser turns them into safe ClickHouse SQL, so business logic changes without a code release. - Uber FRM. Older notes describe staged rollout and feature flags inside the finance tooling path. Keep it general if asked. - Uber Menu. Proxy pools and IP settings for anti-bot handling were configuration, not code.

5. Zero-downtime deploys, health checks and graceful shutdown

Plain English. Zero-downtime means users never see an error during a release. Three pieces make it work:

  • Health checks. The platform asks each copy "are you ready?" and only sends traffic to copies that say yes.
  • Graceful shutdown. When the platform wants to stop a copy, it sends a signal called SIGTERM. A well-behaved service stops accepting new requests, finishes the ones in flight, then exits. This is called draining.
  • Backward-compatible changes. Old and new versions must both work during the overlap, which is why expand-and-contract matters.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics Go edge. There's no reverse proxy in front, so the Go process itself has to handle slow clients, request-size limits and draining on SIGTERM. That's part of what "self-protecting edge" means. - Uber FRM. Zero-downtime releases via stacked Bazel PRs (on the PDF). - Masters India. Canary per route meant no single release could take the whole system down. We had no outage during deadline windows throughout the migration.

6. Horizontal versus vertical scaling, and statelessness

Plain English. - Vertical scaling means a bigger machine: more CPU and memory. It's simple, but there's a ceiling and it gets expensive. - Horizontal scaling means more machines running copies of the same service, with a load balancer spreading requests across them. - Stateless services keep no user data in memory between requests, so any copy can serve any request. Stateless services are easy to scale horizontally.

Analogy. Vertical is hiring one faster cashier. Horizontal is opening more checkout lanes.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics. The Go/Gin edge is stateless. Auth results are cached in Redis, not in process memory, so it can scale out by adding copies. The 170 GB out-of-memory story is a lesson in not scaling vertically: a bigger memory cap still failed, and slicing the work into one-week chunks fixed it. - Masters India and Uber Menu. Kafka consumers scale horizontally, up to the number of topic partitions.

7. Autoscaling

Plain English. Autoscaling automatically adds copies when load rises and removes them when it falls. It's usually based on a metric like CPU usage, request rate or queue length.

Tiny example. "Keep average CPU around 60%. If it goes above that for 3 minutes, add a copy. Never run fewer than 2 or more than 20." For queue workers a better signal is often queue lag: "if more than 10,000 messages are waiting, add a worker."

Things interviewers like to hear. - Autoscaling reacts with a delay, so you still need headroom for sudden spikes. - Scaling the app without scaling the database just moves the bottleneck. - For queue consumers, you can't usefully run more consumers than there are partitions.

Where it shows up in my work (honestly). I didn't own autoscaling policies on any project. What I did own is designing services so they can scale out: a stateless Go edge, Kafka consumers that scale with partitions, and Menu scrapers and stream consumers that scale as separate jobs. If asked "how was it autoscaled?", say: "The platform team owned scaling policies. My part was making the services stateless and the work partitionable."

8. Load balancers and reverse proxies

Plain English. A load balancer spreads incoming requests across copies of a service. A reverse proxy, like Nginx, sits in front of an app and can also enforce timeouts, size limits and TLS.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics. The Go edge deliberately runs without a reverse proxy, so it handles HTTP/2 and timeouts itself. - Masters India. The canary split happened at the gateway in front of the PHP and Spring Boot services. Older notes say that gateway was Nginx.

9. Rate limiting and quotas

Plain English. Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, so one noisy client can't starve everyone else. Servers usually reply with HTTP 429 "Too Many Requests" when the limit is hit.

How a token bucket works. Each client has a bucket that holds, say, 10 tokens and refills at 5 tokens per second. Each request takes one token. A burst of 10 requests is fine. After that, the client is limited to 5 per second. An empty bucket means a 429.

t=0s   bucket=10  -> 10 requests pass, bucket=0
t=1s   bucket=5   -> 5 pass
t=1s   11th request in that second -> 429 Too Many Requests

Two kinds of limits for AI products. Request limits protect the API. AI systems also need budgets: maximum tokens, maximum cost, maximum tool calls or retries per session. An HTTP 429 doesn't stop an agent that is already looping. You need limits inside the agent too.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics, AI side. The Ask Iris evaluator is capped at 3 attempts, so a chat can't loop forever. The batch engine has hard timeouts and circuit breakers for LLM provider failures, and it logs tokens and USD cost per run as JSON telemetry. - Impact Analytics, API side. The PDF claim is a self-protecting edge with nested timeouts. If asked whether the Go edge has per-tenant request rate limits, keep it qualitative unless you can point to the code. - Masters India. We were on the receiving end of the government portals' limits and instability. Bounded retries with backoff kept us from hammering them. Bulk work went through Kafka instead of the HTTP tier, so the API wasn't the bulk throttle. Background and scheduled work ran inside the Spring Boot services as @Async and @Scheduled jobs on bounded thread pools, with Spring Batch for chunked bulk imports, so the pool size capped how hard we could push the portals. - Uber Menu. Also on the receiving end, from restaurant and aggregator websites blocking bots. We used proxy pools, adaptive retries and per-source retry budgets.

10. Timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers

Plain English. - Timeout. Stop waiting after a set time. Without one, a slow dependency ties up your workers forever. - Nested timeouts. An outer limit on the whole request, inner limits on each call inside it. The inner ones must be shorter. - Retry with exponential backoff. If a call fails, wait and try again, doubling the wait each time (1 s, 2 s, 4 s), usually with some randomness (jitter) so clients don't all retry at once. - Circuit breaker. After several failures in a row, stop calling the failing service for a while and use a fallback. Like a fuse that trips to protect the house.

Tiny example. An LLM call has a 30-second timeout. Five calls in a row time out, so the breaker opens. For the next minute, items get the deterministic score instead of waiting on the LLM. Then the breaker lets one test call through.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics. The orchestration registry has hard timeouts and circuit breakers that trip after about 5 consecutive failures or a high failure fraction. On an LLM timeout the item falls back to the deterministic baseline score, and the batch continues. The Go edge uses nested timeouts. - Masters India. Bounded retries against the government portal, with a dead-letter queue for messages that keep failing. - Uber Menu. Adaptive retries with per-source budgets for scrapers.

11. Queues and backpressure

Plain English. A queue sits between a producer and a consumer, so bursts don't crush the consumer. Backpressure means a slow consumer pushes back, so the producer slows down instead of everything overflowing memory.

Analogy. A restaurant's order rail. If the kitchen is slow, tickets pile up on the rail, and the host stops seating new tables.

flowchart LR S["Scrapers"] --> K["Kafka buffer"] K --> F["Flink job"] F --> C["Catalog sink"] C -.->|"slow sink"| F F -.->|"reads slower"| K

What to notice: when the catalog slows down, Flink reads from Kafka more slowly, and events wait safely in Kafka instead of piling up in memory.

Where it shows up in my work. - Uber Menu. Kafka buffered bursty scrapers. Flink's built-in backpressure slowed consumption when the catalog sink slowed down. - Masters India. Kafka absorbed bulk import spikes around filing deadlines. - Impact Analytics. No Kafka. The batch engine controls its own pace through batch sizes (about 88k items per pass), and the data pump through 500k-row double-buffered batches.

12. Idempotency and dead-letter queues

Plain English. Idempotent means doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once. That matters because retries and message re-delivery always happen eventually. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) holds messages that keep failing, so a human can inspect and replay them instead of the system retrying forever.

Tiny example. Key = client_42:filehash_ab12:batch_3. The first attempt registers the invoice and stores the key. A retry with the same key returns the stored result and doesn't submit to the government again.

Where it shows up in my work. - Masters India. Idempotency keys (client plus file hash plus batch index) across the whole bulk pipeline, plus a DLQ with replay. This is the double-filing near-miss story. - Uber Menu. "Exactly-once catalog upserts" in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts keyed by vendor or menu and content hash. - Impact Analytics. ReplacingMergeTree keeps the newest version of a row with the same key, so a retried batch doesn't leave duplicate decisions.

13. Caching

Plain English. A cache keeps a copy of frequently read data somewhere fast, usually in memory with Redis, so you don't hit the database every time. Cache-aside means the app checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database and fills the cache. The hard part is staleness: deciding how long a cached value may live.

Where it shows up in my work. - Masters India. A Redis cache-aside layer cut database read load by 30%. - Impact Analytics. Redis fronts the auth waterfall, so verified identities don't get re-checked against Firebase or OIDC on every request.

14. Sharding and partitioning

Plain English. Partitioning splits a big table into slices inside one database, often by date. Sharding splits data across separate databases. Both keep each piece small and let queries skip irrelevant data.

Where it shows up in my work. - Masters India. PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter. - Impact Analytics. ClickHouse rollup tables partitioned by season code. Migration and rollback happen one season partition at a time.

15. Pre-aggregation and batching

Plain English. Pre-aggregation means computing totals ahead of time, so queries read small summary tables. Batching means processing many items together to reduce per-item overhead.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics. Six rollup tables took planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250-million-row benchmark. The weekly rollups are built one fiscal week at a time to keep memory bounded.

16. Observability: logs, metrics, traces

Plain English. - Logs are timestamped text records of what happened. - Metrics are numbers over time, like requests per second or error rate. - Traces follow one request across services, showing where the time went. - For LLM apps, LLM tracing records every prompt, tool call and model response.

Where it shows up in my work. - Impact Analytics. Datadog distributed tracing on the Go edge. LangSmith traces for Ask Iris. Custom JSON telemetry for the batch engine, covering tokens, USD cost, step duration and batch fallbacks. - Masters India. ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana, a log search stack) plus New Relic tracing cut incident triage time by about 70%. The baseline is ESTIMATED: from about 30 minutes to under 10.

17. Load testing and capacity planning

Plain English. Load testing sends realistic traffic at a system to find where it breaks before users do. Capacity planning uses those results plus growth estimates to decide how much headroom to keep.

Tiny example. If normal peak is 1,000 requests per second, test at 3,000 and watch p95 latency, error rate, connection pools and memory.

Where it shows up in my work. The connection-leak STAR story (a packet story, not on the PDF) ended with a load test at 3 times peak added to CI. The ClickHouse PoC was a benchmark on 250 million rows, which is a form of capacity test for reads. Don't invent other load-test numbers.

18. Kubernetes (literacy only)

Plain English. Kubernetes runs containers across a cluster of machines. You describe what you want ("3 copies of this image, with this health check") and it keeps reality matching: restarting crashed copies, rolling out new versions and scaling.

Words worth knowing. A pod is one or more containers running together. A Deployment manages rolling updates of pods. A Service gives pods a stable address. Readiness and liveness probes are health checks. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds or removes pods based on metrics.

Where it shows up in my work. Skills-level only. It's on my skills line as literacy. I haven't operated clusters. If asked, explain the concepts above and say: "I've deployed services that ran on container platforms, but I didn't own the cluster operations."

Practice questions

"How did you roll out the Masters migration safely?"

One route at a time, behind the gateway, with a canary share first. We shadowed read routes before moving them, moved bulk Kafka paths before interactive filing, and froze cutovers in deadline weeks. Rollback was flipping a route's traffic back to PHP.

"What happens if the LLM provider goes down mid-batch at Impact Analytics?"

Each call has a hard timeout. After about five failures in a row, a circuit breaker stops calling the provider for a while. Items get the deterministic score instead, so the batch finishes. When the provider recovers, we resume from the checkpoint and skip work that's already done.

"How would you autoscale your Go service?"

It's stateless, with auth cached in Redis, so it scales horizontally. I'd scale on request rate or CPU, keep headroom for spikes, and watch ClickHouse, because scaling the edge just moves load to the database. To be clear, I didn't own the autoscaling policies there.

"How do you roll back bad data?"

It depends on the system. On Uber Menu we rewound Kafka offsets and reprocessed. On the ClickHouse migration we dropped the failed season's partition and recopied it. For AI outputs, every row carries a config hash, so we know exactly which rows came from a bad config and need rerunning.

"Have you used Kubernetes?"

At skills level. I understand pods, deployments, probes and autoscalers, and my services ran in containers. I haven't operated clusters myself.

"What's the difference between a canary and blue-green?"

A canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version and ramps up gradually. Blue-green runs two full environments and flips all traffic at once. Canary limits blast radius. Blue-green makes rollback a single flip. I used canaries per route at Masters India.

This is the Java + Python + Go track. Uber FRM uses Spring Boot with Spring Data JPA and Hibernate. Masters India uses Spring Boot microservices with Kafka consumers for background work. Impact Analytics is a Go/Gin platform with a Python (FastAPI, LangGraph) agent plane. Facts match GROUND_TRUTH.md, not older resume narratives.

What the tags mean on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, doc or code behind it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show, so I say "roughly, derived from...". HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal. "Verbal only" means I can talk about it if asked, but it is not a PDF bullet, so I never lead with it.

How to read the diagrams. The ASCII versions are what I sketch in an interview. The mermaid versions render on the site. Solid arrows are the main path. Dotted arrows are fallback, optional or "not mine" paths.

1. Impact Analytics — AssortSmart (Platform & AI)

The business in plain English

Impact Analytics sells AssortSmart, a merchandise planning SaaS for retailers. Planners use it to decide, for each selling season, which articles (products) to keep, which to drop and which to add. An "article-season" is one product in one selling season. The data is huge, so the platform has two halves: a Go/Gin platform that serves fast analytical pivots and enforces who can see what, and an AI layer that scores Keep/Drop decisions in batches and lets planners ask questions through a chat copilot called Ask Iris.

Words you need

  • Go/Gin: Go is a compiled language that is good at many concurrent requests. Gin is a lightweight Go web framework.
  • Google Wire: a compile-time dependency injection tool. It generates the wiring code, so a missing dependency breaks the build rather than a live request.
  • h2c (HTTP/2 cleartext): HTTP/2 without TLS inside a trusted network, letting one connection carry many requests at once.
  • ClickHouse: a column-oriented analytical database. It reads only the columns a query needs, which makes big aggregations fast. Think of a spreadsheet where you can grab one whole column without touching the rest.
  • MergeTree / ReplacingMergeTree: ClickHouse table types. ReplacingMergeTree keeps only the newest version of a row with the same key, eventually. It is like a notebook where you never erase, you just write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines.
  • Rollup table: a pre-aggregated summary table, like keeping weekly totals so you never re-add daily receipts.
  • LangGraph: a Python framework for building LLM agents as graphs of steps. A supervisor is the node that decides which worker step runs next.
  • LangSmith: a tracing tool for LLM apps. It shows every prompt, tool call and response in a run.
  • UAM (User Access Management): the rules for which user can see which part of the product hierarchy.
  • config_hash: a SHA-256 fingerprint of the guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog used for a run, stamped on every output row so any decision can be traced to the exact setup that produced it.

flowchart LR PL["Planner web UI"] --> GO["Go/Gin API edge"] GO --> AUTH["Auth waterfall"] AUTH --> RD["Redis auth cache"] AUTH --> PG["PostgreSQL UAM and roles"] GO --> KPI["KPI formula parser"] KPI --> CH["ClickHouse master and rollups"] BQ["BigQuery historical"] -->|"ingest"| CH PC["Planner chat"] -->|"JWT WebSocket"| IRIS["Ask Iris LangGraph"] IRIS -->|"scoped reads"| CH IRIS --> LS["LangSmith"] CH -->|"context rows"| BATCH["Keep/Drop batch engine"] BATCH -->|"JSON payloads only"| LLM["LLM provider"] BATCH -->|"ReplacingMergeTree writes"| CH GO --> DD["Datadog"]

Box-by-box walkthrough

  1. Go/Gin API edge. This is the multi-tenant platform that every web request hits, scaling to 10k peak RPS. It exists because planners need fast pivots and strict tenant isolation in one place. It runs as a self-protecting HTTP edge with no reverse proxy in front: it speaks native h2c, wraps every call in nested timeouts (the request deadline contains the database deadline), and sends Datadog distributed traces. Wire builds the dependency graph at compile time. Why not a reverse proxy? The process already owns timeouts, h2c and tracing, so a proxy would add one more hop and one more thing to operate.
  2. Auth waterfall. Each request is authenticated by trying a Redis cache first, then Firebase Admin, then JWT or Google OIDC. API keys are compared in constant time, so an attacker cannot guess a key by timing responses. Roles come from PostgreSQL. Arrow content: a token or API key in, a user identity plus role and hierarchy scope out.
  3. PostgreSQL. It keeps thin metadata, UAM and roles. Background worth knowing: planner pivots were slow on PostgreSQL, POCs compared PostgreSQL with ClickHouse, and ClickHouse won the large analytical reads. PostgreSQL kept the small, relational, frequently updated data.

  4. KPI formula parser. Operators type formulas like sell_through = units_sold / units_received. A Go tokenizer and parser turns that into a parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragment. Only allowlisted functions are accepted, logical names map to physical columns, and unknown tokens fail closed. Division is wrapped so a zero denominator returns 0 instead of infinity. This decouples business formulas from code releases.

    sql -- illustrative output for sell_through ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(units_sold) / sum(units_received)), 0)

  5. ClickHouse. The analytical store, per tenant. It holds a 2.11B-row master and six MergeTree rollup tables (product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain, partitioned by season_code). The rollups are why planner pivots went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250M-row harness (12.3 seconds, rounded), which is 15.5 times faster.

  6. BigQuery. The historical source that is ingested into ClickHouse. Arrow content: historical rows, loaded in batches.
  7. Keep/Drop batch engine. Python batch pipelines (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style) that evaluate 348k article-seasons, about 88k items per pass, using deterministic KPI math blended with structured LLM calls across 7 AI lenses. It reads context from ClickHouse, sends only JSON payloads to the LLM, and writes results back with ReplacingMergeTree, so writes are eventually consistent. It runs through the shared orchestration registry (section 1b).
  8. Ask Iris. A JWT-secured WebSocket copilot that lets planners query KPIs and inspect AI decisions. It is Python FastAPI with a LangGraph supervisor and a 3-attempt evaluator loop, traced in LangSmith (section 1c).

Failure modes and what handles them

What fails What happens Where it is handled
LLM call times out The item uses its deterministic baseline score Batch engine fallback
LLM provider keeps failing Circuit breaker trips after about 5 consecutive failures or a high failure fraction Orchestration registry
Batch process crashes mid-run Restart with --resume, skipping finished deterministic scoring det.json, agent_progress.json
Slow database call Inner timeout fires before the request deadline Go/Gin nested timeouts
Bad operator formula Unknown token is rejected Parser fails closed
Divide by zero in a KPI Returns 0 instead of infinity ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0)
Chat tries to read another tenant Scope was frozen at the handshake, so the request stays in scope Ask Iris plan_scope
Agent keeps retrying forever Stops after 3 attempts and replies gracefully Ask Iris MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

Say this carefully on Impact Analytics. No Kafka, Flink, CDC, Kubernetes operations or Milvus here. The CDC pg2ch tool was authored by a colleague (Ashvin Sharma), so I do not claim it. No "sub-second" ClickHouse claims. No HITL or human review queues: offline evals replaced the critic and evaluator agents in Keep/Drop. LangSmith is on Ask Iris, not on the Keep/Drop batch. Isolation is not encryption. No invented SLA for the Go platform or for Ask Iris.

1b. One Keep/Drop pass, step by step

The batch order is fixed: peer, decider, lenses, blend, explain. There is no LLM orchestrator choosing the next step.

sequenceDiagram participant REG as Orchestration registry participant CH as ClickHouse participant DET as Deterministic scorer participant AG as LLM steps participant OUT as Writer REG->>CH: Read context rows for one pass of about 88k items CH-->>REG: Rows become JSON payloads REG->>DET: Score sell-through and rate of sale DET-->>REG: s_det per item, saved to det.json REG->>AG: Fixed steps peer, decider, 7 lenses with JSON only alt LLM answers in time AG-->>REG: s_agent per item else Timeout or breaker open REG-->>REG: Fall back to deterministic baseline end REG->>OUT: Blend, explain, stamp config_hash OUT->>CH: Insert rows into ReplacingMergeTree

What to notice: progress is checkpointed (det.json, agent_progress.json), so a crash after the deterministic step does not redo it.

Worked example of the blend. The final score is s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent, and an article-season is kept if s_final is at least 0.55. Suppose an article has s_det = 0.50 and s_agent = 0.70.

s_final = 0.4 x 0.50 + 0.6 x 0.70 = 0.20 + 0.42 = 0.62
0.62 >= 0.55, so the decision is KEEP

If the LLM had timed out, the item would fall back to its deterministic baseline instead of waiting.

Why this design. What: LLM context is served as JSON, writes are eventually consistent, LLM failure falls back to deterministic scores. Why: letting an LLM query a 2.11B-row table is slow, expensive and unsafe. Alternatives: give the LLM a SQL tool (rejected: unbounded queries and leakage risk), or use Airflow or Temporal for orchestration (rejected: we needed app-native resume coupled to ClickHouse inserts and config hashing, and the extra infrastructure was not justified). Trade-off: the registry is custom code we maintain. What I'd do differently: revisit a managed workflow engine if the number of pipelines grew a lot.

Evaluation numbers (keep them apart). The 300-case proxy evaluation harness backs an 80% accuracy CI promotion gate. That is a gate, not "every tenant is live at 80%". Separately, a gold-200 benchmark showed 73% lower live execution cost at 100% coverage, against a 74% deterministic baseline. Because the blended score was below the deterministic baseline on that set, the blend weights were frozen, not retuned.

1c. One Ask Iris question, step by step

sequenceDiagram participant P as Planner participant WS as Ask Iris WebSocket participant SUP as LangGraph supervisor participant EV as Evaluator participant DATA as KPI and decision data participant LS as LangSmith P->>WS: Open socket with JWT WS-->>WS: Verify JWT and freeze plan_scope P->>WS: Why was article 1234 dropped this season WS->>SUP: Route question with frozen plan_scope loop Up to 3 attempts SUP->>DATA: Read KPIs and decision rows inside plan_scope DATA-->>SUP: Rows SUP->>EV: Draft answer EV-->>SUP: Accept or ask for retry end SUP-->>WS: Answer or graceful fallback message WS-->>P: Reply WS->>LS: Trace of the whole run

What to notice: the scope is decided once, at the handshake. A later message cannot widen it.

Box by box. The WebSocket keeps one live connection per planner. The JWT is checked once, and the hierarchy access (plan_scope) is frozen for the life of the socket, which prevents cross-tenant leaks. The supervisor routes the question to worker steps. The evaluator checks the draft answer, and the loop stops after 3 attempts (MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3) so the agent cannot loop forever. LangSmith records every step for debugging. Ask Iris is a shipped capability. There are no SLA or usage numbers to quote.

1d. Rollups, the 170GB OOM fix, and the cluster migration pump

flowchart LR BASE["ClickHouse master"] -->|"one fiscal week per INSERT SELECT"| ROLL["Six rollup tables by season_code"] ROLL --> PIV["Planner pivots 189s to 12s"] SRC["Source ClickHouse Cloud cluster"] -->|"native TLS port 9440"| PUMP["Go data pump"] PUMP -->|"500k-row double-buffered batches"| DST["Destination ClickHouse Cloud cluster"] PUMP --> CK["Checkpoint files per table"]

What to notice: the top row is about query time and load time. The bottom row is the migration. They are three separate stories.

Rollups and the OOM. The six rollups made pivots 15.5 times faster, which is query time. Building the weekly rollups for a whole season in one statement ran out of memory, needing around 170GB, which is load time. These are not cause and effect. The fix was to slice each INSERT SELECT into temporal chunks (one fiscal week per insert) and enforce memory and disk-spill caps. If asked for the knobs (verbal): a 55 GB memory cap, 16 GB spill, 8 threads, 4 weeks in flight. A product week was about 11 GB and an attribute week was over 40 GB. A whole season failed even at 80 GB and 200 GB caps.

The migration pump. The rollups had to move between ClickHouse Cloud clusters. Cross-cluster IP allowlists blocked a direct cluster-to-cluster copy, so I wrote a Go data pump that speaks the ClickHouse native protocol over TLS (port 9440). It moves 500k-row batches and is double-buffered, meaning it reads the next batch while sending the previous one. Combined throughput was about 344k rows per second across two season streams of roughly 150k to 190k rows per second each. That is an ingest rate, not requests per second. The largest partitions reached 4.09B rows (attribute weekly, two seasons: 2,779,317,472 plus 1,311,108,195). The 4.09B copy was measured in flight. Do not say the cutover finished.

Ghost rows and rollback. "Ghost rows" are duplicate rows left by a half-finished retry. Two guards stop them: TSV ledgers (the weekly loader's skip file, which records finished weeks) and copier checkpoint files migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done. A "partition rollback" means DROP PARTITION, then recopy that season. It is not an atomic swap with live readers. A REPLACE PARTITION incremental design was written but not executed.

2. Uber FRM — Risk Scoping (Uber via EPAM)

The business in plain English

FRM (Financial Risk Management) is a team inside Uber Finance. Every quarter, during the financial close, they decide which financial line items and which legal entities are "in scope" for risk assessment and audit testing. The output is evidence that PwC, the external auditor, uses in its audit work papers. Before this platform, the work ran on Google Sheets: no stable line IDs, no concurrency control, versions drifting. I owned the scoping backend, which cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days, a 70% cut, against a $340M materiality threshold.

Words you need

  • GL (General Ledger): the master record of every financial transaction. 19M raw GL rows were migrated off Sheets into MySQL.
  • FSLI (Financial Statement Line Item): a line on the balance sheet or income statement, like "Cash" or "Revenue". They form a nested 4-level hierarchy, L1 to L4.
  • Materiality: the size of error that would matter to a reader of the financial statements. On the Q4 2025 close it was $340M, and the residual threshold was $170M.
  • HFM (Oracle Hyperion Financial Management): Uber's consolidation system. Its numbers are reconciled against the filed 10-Q (the quarterly report filed with the SEC).
  • SOADB: Uber's service-owned MySQL standard.
  • Spring Boot: a Java framework for building web services. You write @RestController classes and it handles HTTP, JSON and configuration for you.
  • Spring Data JPA / Hibernate: the database layer. Hibernate maps Java classes (@Entity) to tables. Spring Data JPA generates repository classes so you write a method signature instead of boilerplate SQL code.
  • Optimistic locking: each row has a version number. An update succeeds only if the version has not changed since you read it. It is like editing a shared doc that refuses your save if someone else saved first.
  • FSM (finite state machine): a fixed set of statuses and allowed moves between them.
  • SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley): US law requiring controls over financial reporting.

Box-by-box walkthrough

  1. React UI, 8 screens. Reconciliation, Materiality, EMI Scoping, Group Scoping, Threshold Setup, Component Scoping, Residual Risk and Summary. These are the steps of the quarterly close. Arrow content: REST calls for a quarter, an entity and an FSLI level.
  2. 36 Spring Boot endpoints. If asked for the breakdown: about 31 functional routes in the scoping service controller, plus the collaboration-service APIs (comments and notifications) from the technical design doc, make 36. I did not build the real-time collaboration and Slack notification service itself.
  3. Controllers. @RestController classes validate the request DTO with Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotNull) and call one service method. No business logic here.
  4. Services. Own the financial math: materiality, the 5% significance thresholds, residual risk, the nested L1 to L4 FSLI hierarchy, and dynamic quarter-annualization (turning year-to-date figures into an annual run-rate for the quarter). They also run the review-status FSM.
  5. Repositories (Spring Data JPA / Hibernate). All SQL lives here, as JPA entities, repository methods and JPQL or native queries with explicit aliases. I led 3 engineers on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration, which eliminated latent column-aliasing bugs and raised module statement coverage to 100%.
  6. MySQL on SOADB. An 8-table normalized schema. Moving off Sheets into this schema is what resolved ETL lock contention during the close. The code has 11 ORM models (JPA entities, verbal detail), so say "8-table normalized schema" for the PDF and "11 models in the service code" only if asked.
  7. Oracle HFM and the shared ETL. HFM extracts feed MySQL through a shared pipeline. ETL from HFM was a shared responsibility, not mine alone.
  8. Filed 10-Q. The reconciliation screen compares HFM numbers against the public filing.
  9. PwC work papers. The audited output. This is why correctness and audit trails matter more than throughput.

Quarterly user flow

flowchart LR A["Load HFM"] --> B["Recon vs 10-Q"] B --> C["Set materiality"] C --> D["Group and component scope"] D --> E["Residual risk and EMI flags"] E --> F["Summary"] F --> G["Export for audit"]

What to notice: each box is one screen, and each move between screens is gated by the review status.

Logical ER (say this, do not invent extra tables)

fiscal_period 1--* fslib_fact (BS/IS lines)
entity 1--* component_assessment
fslib_fact *--* scoping_decision (material / qualitative)
emi_investee 1--* emi_assessment
recon_leaf (HFM amt, filed amt, difference, line_id)
metrics_table (materiality, residual threshold)

What to notice: this is a speaking sketch of the main entities, not the exact table list. The PDF number is the 8-table normalized schema. For full table catalogs see 34_er_tables_tech_why.md.

Three mechanisms with tiny examples

Optimistic row-locking.

UPDATE scoping_decision
SET status = 'Review', version = version + 1
WHERE id = :id AND version = :version_read;
-- 0 rows updated means someone else saved first: reload and retry

In JPA this is a @Version field on the entity. Hibernate adds the AND version = ? check to every UPDATE for you, and throws an OptimisticLockException when 0 rows match.

Deterministic SHA-256 natural keys. The same question on the same page always gets the same ID, so quarterly audit trails never duplicate it.

byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
        .digest((questionText + normalize(pageName)).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
String uuid = HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest);

Polymorphic review status with FSM gates. One status model is reused across screens: Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed. Moves between states are automated gates, including 50% delta-variance checks for SOX compliance. Cross-table syncs happen in one transaction (a @Transactional service method), so a status change and its related rows commit together or not at all.

Failure modes

What broke or could break How it was handled
ETL lock contention during the close Normalized 8-table schema on SOADB instead of Sheets
Two managers edit the same row Optimistic locking with a version check
Duplicate rows across quarters SHA-256 natural keys
Joined raw SQL with duplicate column names silently mapped rows to the wrong uuid JPA queries with explicit column aliases mapped into projections
A release breaks the close Zero-downtime releases via stacked Bazel PRs, reporting SQL allowlists
Moving recon from Sheets to MySQL Recon v1 (Sheets) and v2 (MySQL) ran in parallel: 18 files, +1,268 lines of code

The numbers

  • From 14 days to 3 days (70%). Quarterly reconciliation time. Stated as the outcome on the PDF. If pressed: "the technical design doc framed that cut and that's what the platform delivered for the close."
  • 19M raw GL rows. Migrated off Sheets. Individual quarterly GL extracts were about 38K to 95K rows, so the value is correctness, hierarchy and auditability, not big-data throughput.
  • 36 endpoints, 3 engineers led, 100% module statement coverage. Tests are 1,100+ (verbal).

How to draw FRM in 3 minutes

  • Minute 1. Draw the 8 screens as a strip at the top. Say "the quarterly close as a workflow, replacing Google Sheets".
  • Minute 2. Draw three stacked boxes: controller, service, repository. Say "thin Spring Boot controllers, rules in services, SQL in repositories, Spring Data JPA and Hibernate". Then MySQL on SOADB below with "8-table normalized schema".
  • Minute 3. Add HFM and the 10-Q on the left, PwC work papers on the right. Say "from 14 days to 3 days, $340M materiality, optimistic locking and SHA-256 natural keys stop overwrites and duplicates". Draw the collaboration service dotted and say it was separate.

3. Uber Eats Menu + ANZ Mobility (separate projects, Uber via EPAM)

The business in plain English

Uber Eats needs every restaurant's menu in its catalog. Many menus arrive as messy websites, PDFs or photos, often in several languages. Typing them in by hand was slow and costly. The Menu Ingestion pipeline scrapes, cleans and converts them into Uber's strict catalog schema. It cut restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours, handles 30K+ menus a month, and saves about $600K a year.

ANZ (Uber Mobility in Australia and New Zealand) is a different project, about rides, not food. It is shown at the end of this section.

Words you need

  • Selenium: a tool that drives a real browser from code, used to scrape sites that need JavaScript.
  • Proxy pool: a set of IP addresses to rotate through, so a site does not block the scraper.
  • Kafka: a durable event log. Producers append events and consumers read them at their own pace. Think of a conveyor belt that remembers every parcel.
  • Flink: a stream processor that reads events continuously and keeps state per key.
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): before asking the LLM, fetch similar examples and give them as context.
  • Milvus: a vector database that stores embeddings (number lists that capture meaning) and finds the most similar ones quickly. Milvus is a Uber Menu technology only.
  • Field fidelity: the share of extracted fields that match the correct value.

Architecture

 Third-party menu sites (HTML / PDF / image)
        |  Selenium fleet + dynamic proxy pools + adaptive retries
        v
 +-----------------+
 | Kafka ingest bus|  ordered per vendor key . replayable
 +--------+--------+
          v
 +--------------------------+
 | Flink                    |  stateful keyed dedupe (vendor/menu,
 | normalize . dedupe .     |  content hash) . schema normalization
 | route                    |
 +----+--------------+------+
      |              | unstructured
      |              v
      |   +------------------------------+
      |   | LangChain RAG + Gemini 2.5   |
      |   | Pro over Milvus embeddings   |
      |   | schema gate, low confidence  |
      |   | goes to human review         |
      |   +--------------+---------------+
      | structured       |
      v                  v
 +--------------------------------------+
 | Uber Eats catalog idempotent upsert  |
 +--------------------------------------+

What to notice: two branches. Structured menus skip the LLM entirely. Only unstructured ones pay for RAG and Gemini.

flowchart LR SITES["Menu sites HTML PDF image"] --> SEL["Selenium fleet with proxies and retries"] SEL --> KF["Kafka ingest bus"] KF --> FL["Flink keyed dedupe and normalize"] FL -->|"structured"| UP["Idempotent catalog upsert"] FL -->|"unstructured"| RAG["LangChain RAG over Milvus with Gemini 2.5 Pro"] RAG --> GATE["Schema gate"] GATE -->|"pass"| UP GATE -.->|"low confidence"| HR["Human review"] UP --> CAT["Uber Eats catalog"]

Box-by-box walkthrough

  1. Selenium fleet. Scrapes third-party menu pages. Hardening it with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries raised extraction success to 95%+, from an estimated 60 to 65%. Arrow content: raw HTML, PDF or image plus vendor metadata.
  2. Kafka ingest bus. Decouples scraping from processing. Events are keyed by vendor, so one vendor's events stay in order, and the log can be replayed after a bug fix.
  3. Flink. Reads from Kafka and does stateful keyed deduplication (keyed by vendor and menu, using a content hash), then normalizes to the schema and routes each menu to the structured or unstructured branch. Peak load of roughly 200 to 500 events per second is an ESTIMATE for prep only.
  4. RAG branch. For unstructured multilingual PDFs, LangChain retrieves similar labeled menus from Milvus, and Gemini 2.5 Pro generates the structured output. A schema gate validates it. Low-confidence output goes to human review. Field fidelity is 98%, measured in offline evaluation.
  5. Catalog upsert. Writes into the Uber Eats catalog. The PDF says "exactly-once catalog upserts". In practice that is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts. Not ClickHouse.

One menu, step by step

sequenceDiagram participant S as Selenium participant K as Kafka participant F as Flink participant R as RAG and Gemini participant C as Catalog S->>K: Menu PDF for vendor 881, menu 3 K->>F: Event keyed by vendor 881 F-->>F: Hash content and compare with last hash for vendor 881 menu 3 alt Same hash F-->>F: Drop duplicate else New content and unstructured F->>R: Route PDF to RAG branch R-->>F: Structured items that passed the schema gate F->>C: Upsert keyed by vendor and menu end

What to notice: a replay after a crash writes the same row again, which is harmless because the upsert key is stable.

Failure modes

What fails What happens
Site blocks the scraper Proxy pool rotates IPs, adaptive retries back off
Same menu scraped twice Flink drops it on matching content hash
Flink restarts mid-stream Resumes from checkpoint, replays events, idempotent upserts absorb duplicates
LLM output breaks the schema Schema gate rejects it, low confidence goes to human review
Need to reprocess history Kafka replay. Spark is a verbal backfill option only, not on the PDF

The numbers

  • From 24 hours to 2 hours for restaurant onboarding.
  • $600K a year saved. Derived from about $2 per menu in third-party or manual cost × 30K menus × 12 months = $720K, floored to $600K to be conservative. Say "$600K a year", not "$600K-plus".
  • 98% field fidelity is offline evaluation. Always say "offline".
  • 95%+ extraction success, from an estimated 60 to 65%.

ANZ Document Compliance (Uber Mobility, not Eats)

flowchart LR DOC["Driver and vehicle documents"] --> VAL["Deterministic validation backend"] RULES["Local authority rules"] --> VAL VAL --> RES["Pass or fail with reason"]

What to notice: no LLM, no Selenium, no RAG. It is rules applied deterministically.

The backend checks driver and vehicle documents against local authority rules. It reached 99.9% regulatory compliance and eliminated about 20 hours a week of manual effort. Both numbers are HISTORICAL. This is Mobility, not Eats, so never mix it into the Menu story.

How to draw Menu in 3 minutes

  • Minute 1. Draw sites on the left, then Selenium, then Kafka. Say "95%+ extraction success with proxy pools and adaptive retries, Kafka keyed by vendor and replayable".
  • Minute 2. Draw Flink and split into two branches. Say "keyed dedupe by vendor and menu with a content hash, structured goes straight through, unstructured goes to RAG over Milvus with Gemini 2.5 Pro".
  • Minute 3. Draw the schema gate and the catalog. Say "exactly-once upserts means at-least-once plus idempotent writes, 98% field fidelity offline, from 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year". Draw ANZ as a separate small box and say "different project, Mobility".

4. Masters India — GST / E-Invoicing

The business in plain English

Masters India sells GST compliance and e-invoicing SaaS to Indian enterprises. Clients send invoices, and the platform validates them and registers them with the government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number) and a signed QR code. I led the migration of a legacy PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, mentored 2 engineers, and owned the bulk pipeline that handles over 1 million government submissions a day.

Words you need

  • Strangler pattern: replace an old system one route at a time, like a vine slowly replacing a tree, so you never do a risky big-bang cutover.
  • Canary: send a small share of traffic to the new version first and watch it.
  • Sharding: splitting one big database into pieces by a key. Here the key is the tax quarter.
  • Idempotency key: a unique label for an operation so retrying it does not repeat its effect.
  • Spring Kafka consumer: a method in a Spring Boot service (annotated @KafkaListener) that reads messages from a Kafka topic and processes them off the request path.
  • @Async / scheduled jobs: Spring annotations that run a method on a background thread pool, or on a timer, instead of on the request thread.
  • Spring Batch: a Java framework for chunked bulk jobs. It reads, processes and writes N records at a time and remembers which chunk it reached, so a failed job restarts from that chunk.
  • HikariCP: the default database connection pool in Spring Boot. It keeps a set of open connections ready so each request does not pay to open one.
  • DLQ (dead-letter queue): a side queue where repeatedly failing work is parked for an operator.
  • ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana): a stack for collecting and searching logs. New Relic: an APM (application performance monitoring) tool that traces requests.

Architecture

 Client ERP / Dashboard
        |
 +------v----------------------------------+
 | API Gateway  (canary % -> Spring Boot)  |
 |              (fallback -> PHP)          |
 +------+----------------------------------+
        v
 Spring Boot microservices (auth . submit . bulk . recon)
        |
   +----+------------+--------------+--------------+
   v    v            v              v              v
  PG   Redis      Kafka topics    MongoDB         S3
  (by  (cache-    (chunks . IRP   (IRN/QR         (bulk file
  tax  aside,      jobs . hooks)   snapshots)      landing)
  qtr) hot config)
        |
        v
  IRP workers (Spring Kafka consumers)
     --idempotency + retries + DLQ--> Government IRP
        |
   ELK + New Relic (request-id correlation)

What to notice: the gateway is what makes the migration safe. Every route can be sent back to PHP on its own.

flowchart LR ERP["Client ERP or dashboard"] --> GW["API gateway canary per route"] GW -->|"canary share"| API["Spring Boot microservices"] GW -.->|"fallback"| PHP["Legacy PHP monolith"] API --> PG["PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter"] API --> RD["Redis cache-aside"] API --> S3["S3 bulk file landing"] API --> KF["Kafka event bus"] KF --> WK["IRP workers Spring Kafka consumers"] WK -->|"idempotent submit with retries"| IRP["Government IRP"] WK -.->|"poison batches"| DLQ["Dead-letter queue"] WK --> MG["MongoDB IRN and QR snapshots"] API --> OBS["ELK and New Relic"]

Box-by-box walkthrough

  1. API gateway with per-route canary. Sends a percentage of each route's traffic to the Spring Boot services and falls back to PHP. The rule was shared database first, no dual-write source of truth.
  2. Spring Boot microservices. Auth, submit, bulk and recon services. p95 latency fell 75%, from 1.2 seconds to 300 ms, across 1,500+ enterprise clients. The latency win came from non-blocking IRP calls (Spring WebClient) and bounded thread pools, HikariCP connection pooling, query and index fixes, plus Redis for reads.
  3. PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter. Filing work clusters around quarters, so sharding by quarter keeps each shard's working set small.
  4. Redis cache-aside. Holds hot config and master data. Together with ELK and New Relic work, database read load fell 30%.
  5. S3. Bulk files land here before validation (from the Masters deep dive).
  6. Kafka. The event bus carrying chunks, IRP jobs and webhook events between services. This is a different product from the Uber Menu Kafka, and there is no Flink at Masters.
  7. IRP workers. IRP calls, PDF generation, webhooks and email ran off the request path, in Kafka consumers inside the Spring Boot services, with retries and idempotency keys, so request threads never blocked on the government portal. Smaller background work used @Async and scheduled jobs, and chunked bulk imports fit Spring Batch. Keep the exact split between these qualitative if asked.
  8. MongoDB. Stores flexible IRN and QR snapshots and vendor responses. Elasticsearch powered invoice search and the ELK stack.
  9. ELK and New Relic. One request ID across API, Kafka consumer and IRP worker. Incident triage fell about 70% (HISTORICAL, from roughly 30 minutes to under 10, ESTIMATED).

One bulk import, step by step

sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant API as Spring Boot API participant K as Kafka participant W as IRP worker Kafka consumer participant IRP as Government IRP participant DB as PostgreSQL and MongoDB C->>API: Upload invoice file API-->>API: Store in S3 and validate in chunks API->>K: Publish chunk events K->>W: Chunk for batch 7 W-->>W: Check key client plus fileHash plus batchIndex W->>IRP: Submit batch with bounded concurrency alt IRP succeeds IRP-->>W: IRN and signed QR W->>DB: Save status and snapshot else IRP fails repeatedly W-->>W: Backoff retries then park in DLQ end API-->>C: Progress on dashboard or webhook

What to notice: the idempotency check happens before the government call, so a retried message never double-registers an invoice.

Failure modes

What fails What happens
IRP portal is slow or down Exponential backoff with bounded retries, then DLQ for operator replay
Same chunk processed twice Idempotency key client + fileHash + batchIndex returns the earlier result
Filing-deadline spike Roughly 8 to 10 times the average (ESTIMATED), absorbed by Kafka buffering and bounded worker concurrency
New Spring Boot route misbehaves Gateway sends that route back to PHP
Cache stampede on hot keys TTL jitter and SETNX lock (prep pattern)

The numbers

  • 1M+ daily submissions is about 12 per second on average (1,000,000 / 86,400 = 11.6).
  • Throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, which is about 12 to about 67 requests per second.
  • 100K+ concurrent imports handled with exactly-once idempotent processing.
  • Coverage from 35% to 82%, 98% deployment success.

How to draw Masters in 3 minutes

  • Minute 1. Draw the client, then the gateway, with Spring Boot on one side and PHP dotted on the other. Say "strangler with canary per route, p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 ms across 1,500+ clients, mentored 2 engineers".
  • Minute 2. Draw PostgreSQL by tax quarter, Redis, MongoDB and S3 under the Spring Boot services. Then Kafka to the IRP workers (Kafka consumers) to the government IRP.
  • Minute 3. Write the idempotency key on the worker arrow and draw the DLQ dotted. Say "1M+ a day, about 12 per second average, 700 to 4,000 requests per minute". Finish with ELK and New Relic and "triage about 70% faster".

5. GeeksforGeeks

The business in plain English

GeeksforGeeks runs a learning platform with courses and live coding contests. Learners post doubts (questions) during courses and contests, and influencers sell courses with affiliate coupons. I migrated the doubt-support backend from PHP to Django so it could handle 10K+ daily queries and 10x traffic spikes during live contests, and built the influencer analytics and earnings dashboard.

Words you need

  • Django: a Python web framework with an ORM, admin and auth built in.
  • Elasticsearch: a search engine that indexes text for fast full-text search.
  • Asynchronous scheduled workflows: background jobs that run on a schedule, separate from user requests.

Architecture

        v

 +--------+---------+
     +----+----+--------+

Box-by-box walkthrough

  1. Django REST APIs. The voting, pinning and locking APIs for doubt threads, rebuilt from PHP.
  2. MySQL. Source of truth for threads and permissions. The vote table has a unique (user_id, content_id) constraint, so a double-submit is harmless.
  3. Redis. Holds display counters, reconciled asynchronously to MySQL to avoid hot-row contention on popular doubts.
  4. MongoDB. Holds flexible payloads such as doubt bodies or attachments that vary in shape.
  5. Elasticsearch. Powers search across doubts and content.
  6. Async scheduled workflows. Video processing, reminders and data cleanup. These lifted engineering ops efficiency 70%.
  7. Influencer dashboard. Transactions and affiliate coupon conversions. Course sales rose 30%.

Failure modes

What fails What happens
Contest spike, 10x traffic Counters in Redis absorb hot writes, MySQL reconciled asynchronously
User double-clicks vote Unique constraint makes it idempotent
Slow background job Runs outside request path, so users are unaffected

The numbers and how to say them

  • 10K+ daily queries, 10x traffic spikes during live contests.
  • 20% lift in premium subscriptions, relative, attributed by the growth team. Older prep said "15 to 20%". The current resume says 20%.
  • +30% course sales and +70% ops efficiency. Say: "I owned the engineering, the business team attributed the lift."

Reading the tags on this page

Every schema and number here carries a tag so you know how hard you can lean on it.

Tag What it means How to say it
MEASURED There is a log, a document or code behind it (for schemas: the ORM models or a validated DDL file). State it plainly.
MEASURED design A written, validated design document exists, but it has not run under production load. "The design specifies..."
TARGET A design goal. "We were targeting..."
ESTIMATED Arithmetic I can show. "Roughly, derived from..."
HISTORICAL From my past work records, no artifact in this repo. State it, keep it qualitative if pushed for raw data.
LOGICAL The shape of the data as I would draw it on a whiteboard. Not the literal production table names. "Logically, the data looked like..."
ILLUSTRATIVE A teaching example I wrote to explain a mechanism. Column names and sample values are made up. "To illustrate..." Never present it as the production schema.

Words you need on this page

  • ER diagram (entity-relationship diagram). A drawing of the things a system stores (entities, usually tables) and how they connect. Think of a family tree for data: boxes are tables, lines say "one of these has many of those".
  • Primary key (PK). The column that uniquely identifies a row, like a passport number for that row.
  • Natural key. A key built from the real-world content itself (for example a hash of the question text) instead of a random number. The same input always produces the same key, so re-inserting the same thing finds the existing row instead of making a duplicate.
  • Foreign key (FK). A column that points at another table's primary key. Some systems enforce it in the database. Others, like the FRM scoping service, keep it as a "logical join" that the application respects.
  • Index. A sorted lookup structure that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, like the index at the back of a book.
  • OLTP vs OLAP. OLTP (online transaction processing) is many small reads and writes of individual rows, like a bank ledger. OLAP (online analytical processing) is a few huge reads that scan and summarise millions of rows, like a quarterly sales report.
  • Row store vs columnar store. A row store (MySQL, PostgreSQL) keeps each row together on disk, which is great for "fetch or update this one invoice". A columnar store (ClickHouse, BigQuery) keeps each column together, which is great for "sum revenue over 250 million rows" because it only reads the columns it needs.
  • Partition. A physical slice of a table, usually by time (a month, a season, a tax quarter). Queries that filter on the partition key skip every other slice. You can also drop or replace one slice without touching the others.
  • MergeTree. ClickHouse's main table engine. Data is written in sorted chunks ("parts") that a background process merges together, like shuffling small sorted piles of cards into bigger sorted piles.
  • ReplacingMergeTree (RMT). A ClickHouse table type that keeps only the newest version of rows that share the same sort key. Think of a notebook where you never erase. You write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines. Until the cleaner runs, you read with argMax or FINAL to see only the newest line.
  • argMax. A ClickHouse function: "give me the value of column X from the row where column Y is largest". argMax(status, event_seq) returns the latest status.
  • Append-only / insert-only. You never update or delete a row in place. A change is a new row. Current state is computed by a view over the history.
  • Sharding. Splitting one logical dataset across separate physical tables, schemas or databases by a key (tenant, tax quarter). Each shard is smaller and hotter or colder independently.
  • Idempotency. Doing the same operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. A pressed-twice lift button still takes you to one floor.

How to answer schema questions in interviews

  1. Draw the store map first. Boxes for each store (MySQL, ClickHouse, Kafka, Redis) and arrows for who writes and who reads.
  2. Name 2-3 critical tables and say their primary key or natural key out loud.
  3. For each major technology, say one sentence: the problem, why this tech fits the data shape, and what we rejected.
  4. Tag numbers MEASURED, TARGET, ESTIMATED or HISTORICAL as you say them.

1. Impact Analytics: AssortSmart (ClickHouse plus thin PostgreSQL)

In plain English. AssortSmart is a retail merchandise planning product. Planners at a retailer decide which articles (products) to keep, drop or add each season. They look at huge pivot tables of sales, inventory and forecasts, and the AI engine scores every article-season (one product in one selling season) to recommend Keep or Drop. The data problem has two halves. The read side is enormous analytical scans, so it belongs in a columnar database. The control side (users, roles, which hierarchy a user may see) is small and must be transactional, so it belongs in PostgreSQL.

There are two different schema stories at IA. Keep them apart in an interview.

  1. The resume-level stores (what the PDF bullets rest on): the 2.11B-row ClickHouse master that agents never query directly, the six ClickHouse rollup tables that made planner pivots fast, the AI decision outputs written through ReplacingMergeTree with a config_hash on every row, and PostgreSQL for identity, UAM (User Access Management) and roles, fronted by Redis for auth.
  2. The Agentic Cluster Module Phase-1 DDL design (63 tables, 8 layers). This is a validated design document for the Cluster Recommendation Copilot. It is verbal depth only, not a resume bullet, and it has no runtime evidence yet (load test planned at bring-up). Older prep treated it as "the one resume ClickHouse bullet". The current PDF does not, so present it as "a design I wrote and validated", not as production.

The problem we faced

  • Planner pivots were slow on PostgreSQL. We ran proof-of-concept comparisons of PostgreSQL vs ClickHouse. ClickHouse won the large analytical reads. PostgreSQL kept the thin metadata, UAM and roles.
  • Agent probes on shared BigQuery were jittery. The Phase-1 design notes record planner probes on shared BigQuery varying from about 1 second to 20+ seconds, which is too unpredictable for an AI agent tool loop. BigQuery stays the upstream company warehouse, not the runtime store for agents.
  • The incumbent product updates and deletes rows in place. ClickHouse "mutations" (its ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE / DELETE) run asynchronously and rewrite whole data parts, so they degrade under many small updates. ClickHouse is not an OLTP database. We needed a way to correct data without a mutation queue.
  • LLMs must not touch the database. A model that can write SQL against a 2.11B-row table is a runaway-query, connection-pool and prompt-injection risk.

Resume-level store map (draw this first)

erDiagram TENANT ||--o{ APP_USER : "has members" APP_USER ||--o{ ROLE_ASSIGNMENT : "resolved in Postgres" ROLE_ASSIGNMENT }o--|| HIERARCHY_SCOPE : "UAM grants" CH_MASTER ||--o{ ROLLUP_TABLE : "pre-aggregated into six" CH_MASTER ||--o{ JSON_PAYLOAD : "context packed for LLM" JSON_PAYLOAD ||--o{ DECISION_OUTPUT : "scored rows" RUN_CONFIG ||--o{ DECISION_OUTPUT : "config_hash stamped" HIERARCHY_SCOPE ||--o{ ROLLUP_TABLE : "filters reads"

What to notice: PostgreSQL entities (tenant, user, role, hierarchy scope) are small and relational. ClickHouse entities (master, rollups, decision outputs) are huge and append-friendly. The LLM only ever sees JSON_PAYLOAD, never CH_MASTER. Entity names here are logical (ILLUSTRATIVE), not physical table names, except the six rollups below which are real.

Walking through it. The ClickHouse master holds the large fact data (2.11 billion rows, MEASURED). Planner screens never group that table on every request. Instead a load job pre-aggregates it into six rollup tables, and screens read those. The AI batch reads the master once per pass, packs per-article context into JSON payloads, and sends the payloads to the model. Scored rows come back and are inserted into a ReplacingMergeTree table with the frozen config_hash of the run. Every request is first authenticated (Redis cache in front of Firebase Admin, then JWT / Google OIDC), and the user's roles and hierarchy scope are resolved from PostgreSQL. That scope filters what ClickHouse rows the user may see.

The six rollup tables (MEASURED names)

All six are ClickHouse MergeTree tables, all PARTITION BY season_code. The daily source grain is SKU by store by date, which planners cannot group on every chart.

Grain Product (keeps SKU dimensions) Store (no SKU, two-pass totals) Attr (attribute unpivot, about 5x product weekly)
Season product_season store_season attr_season
Weekly product_weekly store_weekly attr_weekly
  • Why partition by season. Planners almost always look at one season. Partition pruning means a season filter skips every other season. A season is also the unit of rebuild and of copy: the Go copier checkpoints per season, and a failed season is fixed by DROP PARTITION then recopy (not an atomic swap with live readers).
  • Why attr weekly is the biggest. "Attr" is an unpivot: each product row becomes one row per attribute pair (via ARRAY JOIN). Attr weekly for two seasons is 4.09B rows (2,779,317,472 + 1,311,108,195). Product weekly for the same two seasons is about 839M.
  • Why store totals still match. Store and attr tables drop SKU-level leftovers and re-weight with two-pass sums, so the store total equals the sum of SKUs. The team validated product vs store vs attr sums at the same filters.

Decision outputs (A2 and A3)

The Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style pipelines write scored rows through the engine's insert path onto a ReplacingMergeTree table. A version column means a retried or overlapping batch that lands twice collapses to one row per article. Reads use argMax or LIMIT 1 BY, not OPTIMIZE FINAL at runtime. Every output row carries the frozen config_hash (SHA-256 of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog), so any number can be traced to the exact configuration that produced it. Say this carefully: Keep/Drop defaults to CSV output first, and the ClickHouse publish is a separate operations step.

Why each tech (resume level)

Tech The problem Why it fits the data shape Alternative and why not
ClickHouse Huge planner pivots and per-pass AI context reads over billions of rows Columnar OLAP. Only reads the columns a pivot needs, compresses well, scans fast. The 250M-row pivot POC went from 189 seconds to 12.3 seconds (PDF rounds to 12s, about 15.5x, MEASURED). PostgreSQL for the heavy grids (it lost the POC on large analytical reads).
Six MergeTree rollups Grouping SKU by store by date on every chart is the wrong cost model Pay once at load time, read cheap at query time. Partition by season matches how planners filter. Querying daily facts with FINAL on every request (FINAL also cannot use projections).
ReplacingMergeTree for AI outputs Retries and overlapping batches can write the same article twice Keeps the newest version per key, so writes are eventually consistent and retry-safe without UPDATEs Plain MergeTree (duplicates). ClickHouse ALTER UPDATE per row (mutation storm).
JSON payloads instead of a SQL tool LLM querying a 2.11B-row master Model gets pre-computed context. Math stays deterministic. No injection or runaway query surface. Giving the agent a database tool.
PostgreSQL (thin) Identity, UAM, roles need real ACID transactions Small, relational, transactional. Exactly what a row store is for. Putting identity in ClickHouse (no transactions, eventual consistency). Putting planner facts in Postgres forever (lost the POC).
Redis Hitting Firebase / OIDC on every API call is slow Caches verified tokens in front of the auth waterfall. A miss falls through to the real check. It does not fail open. Calling the identity provider on every request.
BigQuery Company historical truth Upstream feed into ClickHouse Using BigQuery as the runtime agent store (1 to 20+ second jitter).
Go / Gin Multi-tenant HTTP platform at 10k peak RPS Compiled, cheap goroutines, Wire compile-time dependency injection, native h2c (HTTP/2 without TLS inside the trust boundary) A reverse proxy plus a slower runtime.
Python / FastAPI / LangGraph Agent plane (Ask Iris, batch scoring) Python is where the LLM ecosystem lives. LangGraph gives an explicit state machine for the supervisor and the 3-attempt evaluator. One opaque prompt chain.
Datadog / LangSmith Different debugging questions Datadog for platform traces. LangSmith for Ask Iris agent traces (LangSmith is Ask Iris only on the resume, not the Keep/Drop batch). One tool for everything.

Design decisions, explained

Decision 1: ClickHouse for reads, PostgreSQL for control data. - What: Large analytical facts and rollups live in ClickHouse. Users, roles, hierarchy access and metadata live in PostgreSQL. - Why: The two halves have opposite data shapes. Pivots scan hundreds of millions of rows and touch a few columns. Role checks touch one row and must be transactionally correct. - How: POCs compared both. ClickHouse won large reads. PostgreSQL kept UAM and roles. Redis fronts the auth path. - Alternatives: All-PostgreSQL (lost the pivot POC). All-ClickHouse (no real transactions for permission changes). - Trade-off: Two databases to keep consistent. Tenant isolation has to be enforced across both (C3 on the resume). Isolation is access control, not encryption. - What I'd do differently: Write down the cross-store consistency rules (which side is the source of truth for each entity) on day one instead of discovering them during migration.

Decision 2: Pre-aggregate into six rollups instead of grouping on request. - What: Six MergeTree tables (product, store, attr by season and weekly). - Why: The 250M-row pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds (15.5x, query time). - How: Generated load SQL. Weekly builds are sliced one fiscal week per INSERT SELECT with memory and disk-spill caps, because a whole-season weekly aggregate needed about 170GB of memory and failed even at 80GB and 200GB caps. - Alternatives: Materialized views on every insert (harder to rebuild at a known watermark). Querying raw daily facts (too slow). - Trade-off: Rollups are only as fresh as the last build. Load cost moves from query time to build time. - What I'd do differently: Execute the incremental REPLACE PARTITION design (written, not run) so a rebuild never exposes a half-loaded season to readers.

Say this carefully: 15.5x is query time (pivots). The 170GB OOM fix is load time (weekly builds). One did not cause the other.

Decision 3: AI outputs on ReplacingMergeTree, never UPDATE. - What: Scored rows are inserted. Corrections and retries are new versions. - Why: ClickHouse mutations are slow and asynchronous. Batches can land twice. - How: Version column. Read latest with argMax or LIMIT 1 BY. On an LLM timeout the precomputed deterministic score is written instead, so the run keeps going. - Alternatives: MergeTree plus a dedupe job. A transactional database for outputs (cannot join cheaply with the analytical data). - Trade-off: Until background merges run, raw reads can see two versions, so every reader must use the latest-version pattern. - What I'd do differently: Wrap the latest-version read in a named view from the start so no reader forgets it.

Agentic Cluster Module, Phase-1 DDL design (verbal depth only)

Say this carefully. This 63-table design is for the Cluster Recommendation Copilot, which is verbal depth and not a resume bullet. It is MEASURED design: syntax-validated on ClickHouse 25.12, four adversarial review passes, 58 named SQL operations mapped. It has zero runtime evidence (load test at bring-up). Do not quote production latency from it. The approval and write-back flow in this design is not a shipped human-review queue, and the IA resume makes no HITL (human-in-the-loop) claim. Omit the old "624 columns" figure: it is not on the source page. If someone says "60 tables", the overview abbreviated it; the DDL creates 63 including 7 stage twins.

The one idea: never erase. The incumbent product updates rows in place. This design bans that on the hot path. Facts and cubes arrive as whole-partition swaps (build a "stage twin" table, then REPLACE PARTITION). Decisions arrive as append-only events. Approvals mint immutable snapshots. "Current state" is always a view over history. A stage twin is a copy of a table with the same structure where you build the new version of a partition offline before swapping it in, like rehearsing on a spare stage before moving the set onto the main one.

Inventory (MEASURED design): 63 tables including 7 stage twins, 8 layers, 5 dictionaries (store, hierarchy, fiscal, channel, sister-store, plus dict_user at bring-up), 19 views, 4 roles / 3 profiles / 2 quotas. The agent database profile is readonly=1, so the exploring surface physically cannot write. Service roles are INSERT-only on the tables they own.

The design uses four storage patterns, named P1 to P4 in the notes:

  • P1, partition swap: MergeTree plus stage twin plus REPLACE PARTITION. Used for facts and cubes.
  • P2, ReplacingMergeTree plus dictionaries: used for slowly changing dimensions (stores, hierarchy, fiscal calendar).
  • P3, append-only status events: status is a stream of events, and the latest status is argMax(event_seq) in a view.
  • P4, immutable ledger / snapshot: written once, never changed. Used for watermarks, approvals, outcomes, telemetry.
Layer Pattern What it holds
L0 facts plus ledger P1 partition swap, P4 ledger Ingested facts (sales, inventory, forecast) and sync watermarks
Grounding dimensions P2 RMT plus dictionaries Store, hierarchy, fiscal calendar
L1 cubes plus caches P1 / P2 Planner rollups, significance caches
PostgreSQL mirrors (transitional) EXCHANGE / swap Read models bridging from the incumbent while migrating
Decision plane P2 / P3 / P4 Cluster configs, runs, status events, approvals
Outcome loop P4 / P1 Immutable outcomes
Write-back (transitional) P3 status Wire back to the incumbent product
Telemetry P4 Probe logs 
 tenant_db (one ClickHouse database per retailer)
   |
   +-- fact_* / cube_*   --P1--  stage twin, then REPLACE PARTITION
   +-- dim_* / dict_*    --P2--  ReplacingMergeTree(version), read with FINAL / argMax
   +-- decision_event_*  --P3--  append-only, v_* views = argMax(event_seq)
   +-- approval_snapshot --P4--  immutable
   +-- telemetry_*       --P4--  append-only

   user >--< membership >--< tenant

What to notice: nothing in the ClickHouse half is ever updated in place. Every arrow into a table is an INSERT.

What to notice: the conceptual layers, not physical tables. Use this when asked "how would you model mutable planning data in an append-only engine?"

Industry note (general teaching). ReplacingMergeTree deduplicates rows with the same ORDER BY key during background merges. Correctness at query time needs FINAL or argMax. That matches the "views over history" doctrine (ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree guide).

Why each tech in the Cluster Module design (design reasoning, not shipped claims):

Tech Problem Why chosen Rejected
ClickHouse per tenant Slow, jittery agent reads and huge pivots Columnar OLAP. One database per retailer makes isolation a database boundary. PostgreSQL-only for heavy grids. ClickHouse ALTER UPDATE per cell.
Insert-only plus partition swap Mutations pile up Facts restate by stage twin plus REPLACE PARTITION. Decisions append. Latest via argMax views. Row UPDATE / DELETE on the hot path.
