Dynamic quarter-annualization. /is_components applies YTD (year-to-date) annualization: income-statement amounts are cumulative through the quarter, so to compare a Q2 YTD number against an annual threshold it is scaled to a full year. As a general illustration, a Q2 YTD amount covers two quarters, so it is multiplied by 4 / 2. Balance-sheet amounts are point-in-time and are not annualized.

2.7 Five contracts in full

Request and response bodies below are ILLUSTRATIVE (shaped from the response DTO names and columns above, with made-up values). Request DTOs carry Bean Validation annotations (@Valid on the controller parameter, @NotNull and allowlist checks on fields), so a bad body is rejected with 400 and a validation error body before any service code runs.

A. GET /frm-scoping/v2/recon_balance_sheet?fiscal_quarter=Q4&fiscal_year=2025

Purpose: return the HFM vs 10-Q tie-out as a nested L1-L3 tree from MySQL.

{
  "fiscal_quarter": "Q4",
  "fiscal_year": "2025",
  "data": [
    {
      "level_1": "Assets",
      "children": [
        {
          "level_2": "Current assets",
          "children": [
            { "uuid": "c9e2...", "level_3": "Cash",
              "hfm_amount_in_millions": 812.40,
              "financial_statement_amount_in_millions": 812.40,
              "difference": 0.00 }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Status codes: 200, and 400 with a validation error body if the quarter or year fails validation. Idempotent (read). Auth: edge header. Pagination: none in the notes. The period filter bounds the response (per-quarter extracts were about 38K-95K raw GL rows across about 1.7K-1.8K accounts), so if asked, say the period is the natural page and a cursor would be the next step if it grew.

B. PATCH /frm-scoping/group_balance_sheet/{uuid}

Purpose: change the scope conclusion or review status on one balance-sheet line.

{ "conclusion_scope": "In scope", "group_status": "Review" }

{ "uuid": "7f3c...", "conclusion_scope": "In scope", "group_status": "Review", "updated_by": "analyst@uber.com" }

Status codes: 200. 400 with a validation error body if group_status is not in the allowlist (Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed). 404 for an unknown uuid (ILLUSTRATIVE mapping). Idempotent: it sets explicit values by primary key, so replaying it gives the same state. Auth: x-auth-params-email becomes updated_by.

C. POST /frm-scoping/scoping_questions/bulk

Purpose: seed or refresh the qualitative questions for a screen.

[
  { "question_text": "Is there a new revenue stream this quarter?", "page_name": "Group Scoping", "is_active": "Y" },
  { "question_text": "Any restatement in the prior year?", "page_name": "Group Scoping", "is_active": "Y" }
]

{ "uuids": ["5d0e...", "b871..."] }

Status codes: 200 (upsert), 400 with a validation error body on validation failure. Idempotent by design: the uuid is the SHA-256 natural key, so sending the same list twice updates in place.

D. PATCH /frm-scoping/scoping_assessments/{uuid}

Purpose: save an answer. If the answer changes the line's qualitative materiality, the balance-sheet row is updated in the same database transaction (an atomic cross-table sync, one @Transactional service method), so the answer and the conclusion can never disagree.

{ "answer_text": "Yes, new revenue stream this quarter" }

{ "uuid": "e204...", "line_id": "7f3c...", "answer_text": "Yes, new revenue stream this quarter", "synced_balance_sheet": true }

Status codes: 200, 400 (validation error body), 404. Idempotent (set semantics). If the second write fails, both roll back.

E. GET /frm-scoping/residual_risk?fsli_type=bs&fiscal_quarter=Q4&fiscal_year=2025

Purpose: show, per leaf line, how much uncovered balance is left after in-scope components and whether it still matters.

{
  "fsli_type": "bs",
  "materiality": 340000000,
  "lines": [
    { "uuid": "7f3c...", "level_4": "Cash and equivalents",
      "residual_balances": 150000000.00, "residual_multiples": 0.44,
      "greater_than_50pct_materiality": false }
  ]
}

Status codes: 200, and 400 with a validation error body if fsli_type is not bs or is. Read only.

2.8 Idempotency, auth and pagination summary

  • GET, PATCH and PUT by uuid set explicit values, so they are idempotent.
  • Questions bulk: deterministic uuid, so it upserts.
  • POST /add_scoping_metrics appends a new version (old rows deactivated via is_active). It is not strictly idempotent, which is acceptable because the history is the point.
  • Auth: the edge authenticates. The service trusts x-auth-params-email and writes it to the audit columns. page_name and status values are allowlisted. Reporting SQL uses allowlists (PDF).
  • Concurrency: each write is one committed @Transactional unit keyed by uuid, with rollback on failure. The PDF's optimistic row-locking means "update only if the version you read is still current". In JPA the standard mechanism is a @Version field, which Hibernate checks on every UPDATE and reports as an OptimisticLockException when it is stale. Say this carefully if pressed: the TDD places the version-number check in the separate collaboration service and the frontend, and the scoping service relies on transactional per-uuid writes.
  • Pagination: responses are bounded by the fiscal period. No pagination is recorded in the notes.

2.9 The column-aliasing bug (schema-linked story)

What broke. A raw SQL join of balance_sheet and level_mapping returned two columns both named uuid. The code mapped each result row into a map keyed by column name, and the second uuid silently overwrote the first. A PATCH then targeted the level_mapping id instead of the balance-sheet line id. No error, wrong row.

The fix. Spring Data JPA queries with explicit column aliases, mapped into a typed projection, so the two ids can never collide. This was part of the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration I led with 3 engineers, which raised module statement coverage to 100%.

// ILLUSTRATIVE, shaped like the fix
public interface FsliRow {
    String getFsliId();
    String getLevelMappingUuid();
    BigDecimal getHfmAmountInMillions();
    String getLevel1();
    String getLevel2();
}

@Query(value = """
        SELECT b.uuid AS fsliId, l.uuid AS levelMappingUuid,
               b.hfm_amount_in_millions AS hfmAmountInMillions,
               l.level1 AS level1, l.level2 AS level2
        FROM balance_sheet b
        JOIN level_mapping l ON b.level_id = l.uuid
        WHERE b.fiscal_quarter = :quarter AND b.fiscal_year = :year
        """, nativeQuery = true)
List<FsliRow> findFsliRows(@Param("quarter") String quarter, @Param("year") String year);
// each id has its own alias and getter, so neither can overwrite the other

3. Uber Eats Menu: event, catalog and RAG schemas (LOGICAL)

In plain English. Restaurant menus arrive as websites, PDFs and images in many languages, and must become a strict catalog of items, prices and modifiers. A Selenium fleet scrapes, Kafka buffers events, Apache Flink deduplicates and normalizes, and Gemini 2.5 Pro with LangChain RAG over Milvus extracts structured menus from unstructured files. Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K per year saved, 30K+ menus per month, 98% field fidelity on offline evaluation, and extraction success of 95%+.

There is no production DDL in this repo. Defend the shapes. Do not present these field names as Uber's real table names.

3.1 Kafka scrape event (producer: Selenium)

What it is. One message per scrape attempt. Partitioned by vendor_id, so all events for one restaurant stay in order on one partition.

{
  "event_id": "uuid",
  "event_time": "2024-...Z",
  "vendor_id": "string",
  "menu_id": "string or null",
  "source_url": "https://...",
  "content_type": "html | pdf | image",
  "content_hash": "sha256",
  "object_uri": "gs://.../raw/...",
  "locale": "en | ...",
  "scrape_attempt": 1,
  "proxy_pool": "string",
  "status": "ok | blocked | timeout",
  "http_status": 200
}

Why each field exists. - vendor_id: the partition key, which gives per-vendor ordering. - content_hash: SHA-256 of the raw bytes. Same bytes, same hash, so Flink can drop exact duplicates. - object_uri: the raw file lives in object storage. The event carries a pointer, not the file, which keeps messages small and lets us replay extraction from the raw input when a parser breaks. - scrape_attempt, proxy_pool, status: feed the adaptive retry logic and proxy-pool health (how success rose to 95%+).

3.2 Flink dedupe state and catalog upsert contract

Dedupe state (Flink keyed state). Key (vendor_id, content_hash). If the key was seen recently, drop the event. Late events are handled by event time. Keyed state is per-key memory Flink keeps for you and checkpoints, like a per-restaurant notebook of "menus I have already processed".

Catalog upsert contract.

{
  "vendor_id": "...",
  "menu_version": "content_hash or version",
  "items": [
    {
      "item_key": "vendor_id+normalized_name+size",
      "name": "...",
      "description": "...",
      "price_amount": 12.99,
      "currency": "USD",
      "modifiers": [{ "name": "...", "price_delta": 1.5 }],
      "availability": true,
      "raw_refs": ["object_uri#chunk"]
    }
  ],
  "idempotency_key": "vendor_id+menu_version"
}

Why the keys exist. item_key is a natural key from vendor, normalized name and size, so the same dish maps to the same catalog row on every run. idempotency_key (vendor plus menu version) makes a redelivered message rewrite the same state. That is how the PDF's "exactly-once catalog upserts" works in practice: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts. Do not claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across third parties.

3.3 RAG, Milvus metadata and the schema gate

milvus collection fields (logical):
  embedding vector
  menu_id / vendor_id
  locale
  chunk_text
  label_tags
  source_uri

Gemini output -> JSON Schema validate -> catalog upsert
low confidence -> human review queue (LOGICAL)

What each piece does. An embedding is a list of numbers that captures meaning, so similar menu text sits close together. Milvus is a vector database that finds the nearest embeddings fast. For a new menu, we retrieve similar labeled menu chunks (filtered by locale where useful), give them to Gemini as examples, and ask for JSON in the catalog schema. A JSON Schema check rejects anything malformed before it reaches the catalog.

Offline HISTORICAL numbers: 98% field fidelity and 100% schema consistency on the offline evaluation set. Say "offline evaluation", not a live SLA.

3.4 Processing APIs (LOGICAL operations surface)

POST /internal/scrape/jobs          {vendor_ids[], priority}
GET  /internal/scrape/jobs/{id}     lag / success
POST /internal/catalog/upsert       (from the Flink sink, idempotent)
POST /internal/rag/extract          {object_uri} -> validated menu JSON
GET  /internal/menus/{vendor_id}    latest normalized menu and its onboarding status

Older prep labelled the last endpoint a "freshness SLO (24h to 2h)". The 24 hours to 2 hours number is restaurant onboarding time on the PDF, not a freshness SLO, so it is described that way here.

One contract in full: POST /internal/rag/extract (LOGICAL).

{ "object_uri": "gs://bucket/raw/vendor-881/menu.pdf", "vendor_id": "vendor-881", "locale": "ja" }

{
  "vendor_id": "vendor-881",
  "menu_version": "sha256:4be1...",
  "schema_valid": true,
  "items": [ { "item_key": "vendor-881+tonkotsu ramen+regular", "name": "Tonkotsu Ramen", "price_amount": 1200, "currency": "JPY" } ]
}
  • Status codes (ILLUSTRATIVE): 200 with validated JSON. 422 when the model output fails the schema gate (not written to the catalog). 503 when the model provider is unavailable, so the job is retried with backoff.
  • Idempotency: keyed by content_hash. Re-extracting the same file produces the same menu_version, and the upsert is idempotent.
  • Auth: internal service-to-service only.
  • Pagination: GET /internal/scrape/jobs would page by cursor on job creation time (design suggestion).

Load. 30K+ menus per month on the PDF. Peak around 200-500 events per second is an ESTIMATE, prep-only.

ANZ Mobility (separate product): driver, vehicle, document, compliance_check, authority_rule. A deterministic validation backend, 99.9% regulatory compliance and about 20 hours per week saved (HISTORICAL). Not Eats Kafka topics.

4. Masters India: GST e-invoice schemas and APIs (LOGICAL / HISTORICAL)

In plain English. Indian businesses must register B2B invoices with the government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number) and a signed QR code. Masters India does that for 1,500+ enterprise clients. I led the move from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices (p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute) and built the bulk pipeline: 1M+ daily government submissions, Kafka, PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, idempotent processing for 100K+ concurrent imports, dead-letter queues and bounded retries.

4.1 PostgreSQL tables (sharded by tax quarter)

-- clients
client_id PK, gstin UNIQUE, name, config JSONB, created_at

-- invoice_header_YYYY_QN   (or one schema per quarter)
invoice_id PK
client_id, gstin
invoice_number, invoice_date
supply_type, place_of_supply
taxable_value, cgst, sgst, igst, total_value
status Enum('accepted','irp_pending','registered','failed','cancelled')
idempotency_key UNIQUE   -- client + document reference
period_quarter           -- derived at the API; reject mismatch
INDEX (client_id, invoice_date)

-- invoice_line
line_id PK, invoice_id, hsn, qty, rate, tax_breakup...

-- irp_registration
invoice_id PK/FK
irn, signed_qr, ack_no, ack_date
irp_status, raw_response_ref  -- points to the Mongo snapshot

clients: what it stores. One row per business. gstin (the 15-character GST tax id) is UNIQUE, because one business must never exist twice. config JSONB holds per-client settings, which Redis caches. Sample: client_id = 1042, gstin = '27ABCDE1234F1Z5' (made-up), name = 'Acme Traders'.

invoice_header_YYYY_QN: what it stores. One row per invoice, in the table for its tax quarter. CGST, SGST and IGST are the central, state and integrated GST components. Sample (made-up): invoice_id = 88812, client_id = 1042, invoice_number = 'INV-2024-00931', invoice_date = 2024-02-14, period_quarter = '2023-24 Q4', taxable_value = 10000.00, igst = 1800.00, total_value = 11800.00, status = 'registered'.

Why each key or index exists. - Quarter table: "PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter" on the PDF. The current quarter is the hot shard. The API derives period_quarter from invoice_date and rejects a mismatch, so an invoice can never land in the wrong shard. - idempotency_key UNIQUE: the database itself refuses a second copy of the same client document, which is the last line of defence against double registration. - INDEX (client_id, invoice_date): serves the most common read, "this client's invoices in a date range", and the composite order means a filter on client_id alone can use it too.

invoice_line. The items on an invoice. hsn is the HSN code (the product classification used for GST rates). Serves invoice detail and tax breakup.

irp_registration. At most one row per invoice (primary key equals the invoice id), holding the IRN, signed QR and acknowledgement. The one-to-one key enforces "registered at most once". raw_response_ref points to the full response in MongoDB.

4.2 MongoDB, Redis and Kafka

mongo.invoice_payload_snapshot:
  { invoice_id, request_doc, irp_response, irn, qr, ts }

redis keys:
  irp:token:{env}           TTL shorter than the IRP token lifetime
  client:config:{client_id}
  gstin:master:{gstin}

kafka topics (logical):
  invoice.accepted      key=gstin
  irp.submit            key=gstin
  irp.completed         key=gstin
  client.webhook        key=client_id
  *.dlq
  • MongoDB snapshot: the IRP response shape varies, and we must keep exactly what the government signed. A document store keeps it as-is.
  • Redis: the same GSTIN master data and client config are needed for every row of a bulk file. Cache-aside means: read Redis, on a miss read PostgreSQL and fill Redis. That cut DB read load by 30% (MI3). The IRP auth token is cached with a TTL shorter than its real lifetime, so we never send an expired token.
  • Kafka topics keyed by GSTIN: all events for one business stay in order on one partition. Failed messages go to *.dlq (dead-letter queue) after bounded retries, so one bad invoice never blocks the rest.

4.3 REST and async API contracts

POST /v1/einvoice/submit
  Headers: Authorization, Idempotency-Key
  Body: { gstin, invoice_number, invoice_date, lines[], ... }
  -> 200 { invoice_id, status, irn? }  or  202 { invoice_id, status: irp_pending }

GET  /v1/einvoice/{invoice_id}
POST /v1/bulk/imports          multipart -> S3; returns import_id
GET  /v1/bulk/imports/{id}     progress {chunks_done, failed, irp_ok}
POST /v1/webhooks/irp/callback (if used) / internal consumer from Kafka
GET  /v1/invoices?client_id&from&to   // Elasticsearch-backed search optional

A. POST /v1/einvoice/submit. Purpose: register one invoice.

POST /v1/einvoice/submit
Authorization: <client credential>
Idempotency-Key: 1042-INV-2024-00931

{
  "gstin": "27ABCDE1234F1Z5",
  "invoice_number": "INV-2024-00931",
  "invoice_date": "2024-02-14",
  "lines": [ { "hsn": "8471", "qty": 1, "rate": 10000.00, "igst_rate": 18 } ]
}

{ "invoice_id": 88812, "status": "irp_pending" }
  • Status codes: 200 with the IRN if the IRP answered quickly. 202 Accepted with irp_pending if the IRP call is still in flight (the client polls GET /v1/einvoice/{invoice_id}). 409 if the same Idempotency-Key arrives with a different body. 400 with a validation error body on validation failure (Bean Validation on the request DTO), including an invoice_date that does not match the quarter. 429 when rate limited (ILLUSTRATIVE mapping).
  • Idempotency: a repeat with the same key returns the original invoice_id and status. The IRP is never called twice for one invoice.
  • Auth: per-client credential in Authorization.
  • Why async: the latency win (1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds at p95) came from non-blocking IRP calls (Spring WebClient) and bounded thread pools, HikariCP connection pooling, query and index fixes, and Redis for reads.

B. POST /v1/bulk/imports. Purpose: upload a file of thousands of invoices. The file goes to S3, the server splits it into chunks (the shape a Spring Batch chunked job handles), and each chunk becomes Kafka work for the IRP consumers.

{ "import_id": "imp-5521", "status": "queued", "chunks_total": 40 }
  • Status codes: 202 Accepted (processing is asynchronous). 400 with a validation error body for an unreadable file.
  • Idempotency: each chunk has the key client + fileHash + batchIndex. Re-uploading the same file, or a worker retrying a chunk, finds the existing record and does not resubmit to the IRP. This is what made 100K+ concurrent imports safe.

C. GET /v1/bulk/imports/{id}.

{ "import_id": "imp-5521", "chunks_done": 38, "failed": 1, "irp_ok": 37950 }

Idempotent read. Failed chunks are visible here and sit in the DLQ for replay.

D. GET /v1/invoices?client_id=1042&from=2024-01-01&to=2024-03-31. Purpose: list a client's invoices. Served by the (client_id, invoice_date) index or by Elasticsearch for text search. Pagination (ILLUSTRATIVE): cursor-based, ?limit=100&after=<last invoice_id>, because new invoices arrive constantly and offset pages would shift.

Numbers: p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute (about 12 to about 67 requests per second), 1M+ submissions per day (about 12 TPS on average, 1,000,000 / 86,400, with peaks ESTIMATED at 8-10x around filing deadlines), Redis cut DB read load by 30%.

5. GeeksforGeeks: content, votes and subscriptions (LOGICAL / HISTORICAL)

In plain English. GeeksforGeeks has a doubt-support forum used heavily during live coding contests. I migrated the PHP backend to Django and built REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads on MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch. It was stabilised for 10K+ daily queries and 10x contest spikes, and the growth team attributed a 20% lift in premium subscriptions. I also built the influencer analytics and earnings dashboard (course sales +30%) and asynchronous scheduled workflows (engineering ops efficiency +70%).

5.1 MySQL core

users(id, email, ...)
content(id, type, author_id, title, status, created_at)
votes(
  id PK,
  user_id, content_id,
  value TINYINT,              -- +1 / -1
  UNIQUE(user_id, content_id) -- idempotent cast
)
pins(user_id, content_id, created_at) UNIQUE(user_id, content_id)
locks(content_id, locked_by, reason, expires_at)
subscriptions(user_id, plan, status, started_at, renewed_at)
unread_counters(user_id, thread_id, count)  -- durable; Redis serves the badge hot path

Table by table. - votes: one row per user per piece of content. Sample: (id = 901, user_id = 55, content_id = 3120, value = 1). UNIQUE(user_id, content_id) means a second vote from the same user is an update, not a new row. Serves "score for this doubt" and "has this user voted". - pins: a user pinning a thread. Same unique-pair reasoning. - locks: a moderator locking a thread during a contest. expires_at lets a lock lapse on its own, so a forgotten lock does not block a thread forever. - subscriptions: premium plans. Serves entitlement checks. - unread_counters: the durable count of unread replies. Redis serves the badge number on the hot path. MySQL is the record.

5.2 MongoDB, Elasticsearch and Redis

mongo: flexible article / doubt payloads
elasticsearch: content_id, title, body, tags  (search)
redis: vote_buffer:{content_id}, unread:{user_id}, contest hot keys

Why Redis vote buffers. During a contest spike, thousands of votes land on the same few doubts. Incrementing one MySQL row per vote makes that row a lock hotspot. Instead, Redis increments vote_buffer:{content_id} in memory, and a job reconciles the totals to MySQL asynchronously. The votes table still records each user's vote for correctness.

5.3 REST contracts

POST   /api/v1/votes              {content_id, value}  -> idempotent upsert
DELETE /api/v1/votes/{content_id}
POST   /api/v1/pins               {content_id}
POST   /api/v1/content/{id}/lock
GET    /api/v1/unread/count
POST   /api/v1/subscriptions      ...
GET    /api/v1/search?q=

One contract in full: POST /api/v1/votes (LOGICAL).

{ "content_id": 3120, "value": 1 }

{ "content_id": 3120, "value": 1, "score": 47 }
  • Status codes (ILLUSTRATIVE): 200 (created or updated, since it is an upsert). 401 if not logged in. 403 if the thread is locked. 422 if value is not +1 or -1.
  • Idempotency: the unique (user_id, content_id) pair. Sending the same vote twice leaves one row with the same value.
  • Auth: Django session or token auth for the logged-in user.
  • Pagination: GET /api/v1/search pages results (Elasticsearch size and search_after, general practice).

Numbers (HISTORICAL): 10K+ daily queries, 10x contest spikes, premium subscriptions +20% (relative, attributed by the growth team), course sales +30% (influencer dashboard), engineering ops efficiency +70% (scheduled workflows, a separate bullet). Older prep said "premium +15-20%" and "10K+ daily interactions". The resume says 20% and 10K+ daily queries.

6. One-page whiteboard cheat sheet

Project Draw first API first
IA (resume) ClickHouse master, six rollups by season, decision outputs on ReplacingMergeTree with config_hash, PostgreSQL UAM Ask Iris WebSocket (JWT handshake, frozen plan_scope), KPI compile with ifNotFinite, auth waterfall
IA (verbal design) fact_*, cluster_run plus cluster_run_event, plan_snapshot Read-only tools, then Go POST /v1/runs and approvals
FRM level_mapping, then balance_sheet, then scoping_assessments GET / PATCH /group_balance_sheet and /v2/recon_*
Menu scrape event, Flink keyed state, catalog plus Milvus Idempotent upsert and schema-gated extract
Masters invoice_header by quarter, irp_registration, Kafka by GSTIN Submit with Idempotency-Key, bulk import, progress
GFG content and votes with unique user plus content Vote and pin APIs plus Redis counters

Practice drill

  1. How does a retried AI batch avoid duplicate rows at IA? Outputs go into a ReplacingMergeTree whose sort key is the article identity, with a version column. A duplicate collapses to the newest version, and readers use argMax so they never see both.
  2. What is config_hash and why stamp it on every row? It is the SHA-256 of the frozen guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog for a run. Stamping it makes every decision reproducible and lets me compare runs fairly.
  3. How does Ask Iris prevent cross-tenant leaks? The JWT is verified on the socket handshake and the hierarchy scope is frozen for the whole connection. Every tool inherits that scope, so a later message cannot reach another tenant's data.
  4. How does the KPI compiler stop divide-by-zero? It wraps every compiled expression in ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0), so Infinity and NaN become 0 before they reach planner JSON. Unknown tokens fail closed.
  5. In the Cluster design, how do you claim a job without locks? Each worker appends a claimed event with its own token, then reads the latest-status view. Only the token that wins the argMax proceeds.
  6. FRM: why is uuid on scoping_questions a hash? So re-seeding the same question each quarter upserts instead of duplicating. Same text and page, same key.
  7. FRM: how many endpoints, really? 36 Spring Boot endpoints on the PDF. The scoping controller maps 32 routes (about 31 functional plus health), and the collaboration-service APIs from the TDD make up the rest.
  8. FRM: what is an atomic cross-table sync? Saving an assessment answer updates the balance-sheet line's qualitative fields in the same transaction. Both commit or both roll back.
  9. FRM: what was the aliasing bug? Two joined columns were both named uuid, so the name-keyed row map kept the wrong one and a PATCH hit the wrong row. JPA queries with explicit column aliases mapped into a typed projection removed that class of bug.
  10. Masters: what stops a double IRP registration? The idempotency key on every write (client + fileHash + batchIndex for bulk), a UNIQUE constraint on the invoice table, and a one-to-one irp_registration row per invoice.
  11. Masters: why return 202? The IRP is slow and volatile. Returning 202 with irp_pending frees the client immediately, and the status is polled or pushed later.
  12. Menu: what makes the upsert idempotent? The catalog key is vendor plus normalized item name plus size, and the message key is vendor plus menu version. A redelivered message rewrites the same rows.
  13. GFG: how do votes survive a 10x spike? Redis buffers the counts so no single MySQL row becomes a hotspot. The unique (user_id, content_id) row keeps each user's vote correct.

LLM Agents (OpenAI / Gemini / Claude)

What it is. An "agent" is an LLM used in a loop: it reads the situation, decides what to do, maybe calls a tool, checks the result, and continues until done. Think of a junior analyst with a checklist and a phone, who can call specific people but has to report back after each call. The brackets on the PDF are the provider APIs I am comfortable with.

How it works (what matters in interviews). 1. Each step is one model call with a prompt, some context and, often, a required output schema. 2. Control flow is either fixed in code ("always do A then B") or chosen by the model ("decide which tool next"). Fixed is safer and cheaper. Model-chosen is more flexible. 3. Every loop needs a hard stop: a maximum number of attempts or a recursion limit. 4. Cost and latency grow with the number of calls, so batch work should minimise model-chosen hops.

Where I used it. - Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style (Impact Analytics). The batch order is fixed in code: peer, then decider, then lenses, then blend, then explain. There is no LLM orchestrator. Each step is a structured LLM call over a batch of articles. The final score blends rules and the LLM: s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent, keep if s_final ≥ 0.55. - Ask Iris (Impact Analytics). A LangGraph supervisor routes the planner's question to workers, and an evaluator checks the answer, up to 3 attempts. - Uber Menu. Gemini 2.5 Pro extracts menus into the catalog schema. - Providers. OpenAI models at Impact Analytics (the benchmark compared two of them, names not on the PDF). Gemini at Uber. Claude is provider familiarity: I know its API style, but no PDF bullet names it.

Why there. Keep/Drop needs qualitative judgement (is this trend real, is this item a niche hit?) that pure KPI math misses. But math must stay exact, so rules compute KPIs and the LLM only judges.

Interview question. "Why not let one agent decide everything?" "Because a batch of 88 thousand items cannot afford model-chosen control flow. Every extra hop is cost, latency and another chance to fail. So the order is fixed in code, the rules do the arithmetic, and the model only scores structured lenses. In the chat product, Ask Iris, the model does route, but under a supervisor with a three-attempt cap."

Do not say. "Autonomous agents that write to production." "Seven agents debating." Claude as a production provider on a bullet.

LangGraph

What it is. LangGraph is a Python library for building LLM workflows as a graph. Nodes are steps (call the model, run a tool, check a result). Edges decide what runs next. A shared state object travels through the graph. It is like a flowchart that actually runs, with loop counters built in.

How it works. 1. You define a state (for example: question, scope, draft answer, attempt count). 2. You add nodes and conditional edges ("if the evaluator says fail and attempts < 3, go back to the supervisor"). 3. A recursion limit stops runaway graphs. 4. A ToolNode runs whatever tool the model asked for and feeds the result back.

A tiny example of the Ask Iris shape:

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

def route_after_eval(state):
    if state["verdict"] == "pass":
        return "respond"
    if state["attempts"] >= MAX_ATTEMPTS:
        return "graceful_fallback"
    return "supervisor"

graph.add_node("supervisor", supervisor)
graph.add_node("evaluator", evaluator)
graph.add_conditional_edges("evaluator", route_after_eval)
flowchart LR Q["Planner question over WebSocket"] --> SUP["Supervisor"] SUP --> WK["Worker step with tools"] WK --> EV["Evaluator"] EV -->|"pass"| OUT["Answer"] EV -->|"fail, attempts under 3"| SUP EV -->|"third failure"| FB["Graceful fallback answer"]

What to notice: there is no path that loops forever. The third failure exits.

Where I used it. Ask Iris (PDF bullet A4). In Keep/Drop, a small bounded LangGraph tool loop runs the peer step's tool calls. The Keep/Drop batch itself is plain Python in a fixed order.

Why LangGraph and not a plain chain. Ask Iris needs a loop (evaluate, retry) with a hard cap and shared state. A linear chain cannot express "go back up to twice". Hand-written loops work too, but LangGraph gives the cap, the state and LangSmith tracing for free.

Alternatives. Plain Python control flow (best when the order is fixed, which is why Keep/Drop uses it). Temporal or Airflow for long-running durable workflows (heavier infrastructure).

Interview question. "How do you stop infinite agent loops?" "Two caps. The evaluator gets at most three attempts, and the supervisor graph has a recursion limit. On the third failure we return a graceful answer instead of another tool hop."

Do not say. LangGraph runs the Keep/Drop batch order. It does not.

LangChain

What it is. LangChain is a toolkit of building blocks for LLM apps: document loaders, text splitters, embedding wrappers, retrievers, prompt templates. Think of it as a box of Lego pieces for wiring a RAG pipeline quickly.

How it works. You load documents, split them into chunks, embed the chunks, store them in a vector database, and at query time retrieve the closest chunks and put them into a prompt template.

Where I used it. Uber Menu: LangChain glued the RAG pipeline that fed Gemini 2.5 Pro with similar labelled menus from Milvus (PDF bullet M1). I also hold the LangChain Academy certificate.

Why there. It provides ready-made loaders, retrievers and prompt templates, which keeps the custom work focused on the schema and evaluation.

Alternatives. LlamaIndex (strong for document indexing), or plain SDK calls (fewer abstractions, more code).

Interview question. "LangChain or LangGraph?" "LangChain gives you the pieces: retrievers, templates, loaders. LangGraph gives you control flow with state and loops. At Uber I used LangChain for a retrieval pipeline. At Impact Analytics I used LangGraph where I needed a supervisor and a capped evaluator loop."

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)

What it is. Before asking the LLM a question, you look up relevant reference material and put it in the prompt. It is an open-book exam instead of a closed-book one.

How it works. 1. Index: split reference documents into chunks and turn each chunk into an embedding (a list of numbers that captures meaning). 2. Retrieve: embed the new input and find the nearest chunks. 3. Generate: send the input plus retrieved examples to the LLM with clear instructions and an output schema. 4. Validate: check the output against the schema before using it.

An illustrative walk-through:

New multilingual menu PDF
  -> embed the text
  -> Milvus: find the most similar menus we already labelled
  -> prompt Gemini 2.5 Pro: "Here are labelled examples. Extract this menu into the catalog schema."
  -> validate against strict catalog schema
  -> catalog upsert

Where I used it. Uber Menu, PDF bullet M1. It reached 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation.

Why there. Menus are messy and multilingual. Showing the model similar, correctly labelled menus helps it map odd layouts to our schema.

Alternatives. Fine-tuning a model on labelled menus (more cost and upkeep, and not a PDF claim). Rule-based parsers per template (break on every new layout).

Interview question. "How did you evaluate the RAG pipeline?" "Offline, against labelled menus. We measured field fidelity: did each field, like name, price or modifier, come out right. It was 98% on that set. I always say offline evaluation, because that is what it is."

Do not say. RAG at Impact Analytics. Keep/Drop is not document RAG. It is structured JSON scoring.

Milvus

What it is. Milvus is a vector database. It stores embeddings and quickly finds the nearest ones to a query embedding. Like a librarian who finds books "about the same thing" even when the titles differ.

How it works. It builds an approximate nearest-neighbour index (for example HNSW, a graph of neighbours, or IVF, clustered buckets), so a search does not compare against every vector.

Where I used it. Uber Menu only, as the store for labelled menu embeddings in the RAG pipeline.

Why there. It held the embeddings of labelled menus, so the retriever could find similar examples quickly for each new menu.

Alternatives. pgvector (simpler if you already run Postgres and the set is modest), managed vector services.

Do not say. Milvus at Impact Analytics, or Milvus as a privacy or isolation store.

pgvector

What it is. A Postgres extension that adds a vector column type and similarity search. It lets you keep embeddings next to normal rows in the same database.

Where I used it. Not in production. It is on the skills line as literacy.

When I would pick it. When the vector set is small to moderate, the team already runs Postgres, and you want joins between vectors and normal tables. I would pick Milvus or a managed service at large scale or high query rates.

Interview question. "pgvector or Milvus?" "pgvector if the data is modest and already in Postgres, because you avoid another system. Milvus when the vector set is large or search load is high. At Uber Menu we used Milvus. I have not run pgvector in production."

Tool Calling

What it is. Tool calling (also called function calling) lets an LLM ask your code to run a named function with typed arguments. The model never runs anything itself. It says "please call get_scope_benchmarks with these arguments", your code checks and runs it, and the result goes back to the model. Think of a pilot asking the tower for permission. The tower decides.

How it works. 1. You describe each tool to the model: name, purpose, and a JSON schema for the arguments. 2. The model replies with a tool call instead of text. 3. Your code validates the arguments, runs the function, and returns the result. 4. You cap how many tool calls are allowed per request.

A generic example of a tool contract (teaching example, not copied from the repo):

tools = [{
    "name": "get_article_kpis",
    "description": "Return KPIs for one article within the planner's current scope.",
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"article_id": {"type": "string"}, "season_code": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["article_id", "season_code"],
    },
}]
# The tool reads plan_scope from the frozen session, never from model arguments.
sequenceDiagram participant U as Planner participant A as Ask Iris participant M as LLM participant T as Tool code U->>A: Why did we drop this shirt A->>M: question plus tool list M-->>A: call a KPI lookup tool A->>T: run with frozen plan_scope T-->>A: KPI rows A->>M: tool result M-->>A: answer A-->>U: answer

What to notice: the user's data scope is set by the server at handshake, not by the model's arguments. A prompt cannot widen it. (Illustrative flow. The tool name is generic.)

Where I used it. - Ask Iris. Tool calls inherit the hierarchy scope (plan_scope) frozen at the JWT WebSocket handshake. A later message cannot pivot into another tenant's data. - Keep/Drop peer step. The pipeline doc shows a peer-benchmark step with a budget of 2 tool calls per batch, using allowlisted batch tools (get_sibling_colours_batch, get_scope_benchmarks_batch) that each return data for the whole batch in one query. These are fixed functions we wrote. The model never writes SQL. - Cluster Recommendation Copilot (verbal only, DESIGN). 14 audited tools that only read planning data, with 3 gates before any write-back through the existing product write path. Clustering failure baseline measured at 8.5% (37 of 437), targeting under 2%. It is being built, not shipped.

Why it matters. Tool calling is how you give a model data without giving it a database shell. You control what each tool can read, how many calls it gets, and whose data it sees.

Alternatives. Pre-packing context as JSON with no tools at all. That is what the Keep/Drop lenses do, because it is cheaper and safer at 88k items per pass.

Interview question. "How do you keep tool calls safe in a multi-tenant product?" "The model only picks a tool and fills typed arguments. The server owns identity and scope. In Ask Iris, the hierarchy scope is frozen when the socket opens and every tool reads it from the session, not from the model. Tools are allowlisted functions, not free-form SQL, and calls are capped."

Follow-up they may ask: "Is tool calling on your resume as a bullet?" "It is on my skills line. The bullets describe the systems. If you want, I can walk through how the Ask Iris tools are scoped."

Do not say. "The LLM queries ClickHouse." "The agent writes SQL." Do not present the Copilot's 14 tools as shipped.

MCP (Model Context Protocol)

What it is. MCP is an open protocol for exposing tools and data to LLM applications in a standard way. An MCP server publishes a list of tools with schemas. Any MCP-capable client (an IDE assistant, a chat app, an agent) can discover and call them over a JSON-RPC style connection. Think of it as USB for AI tools: build the tool once, plug it into any compatible client.

How it works. 1. A server declares tools (name, description, input schema) and optionally resources and prompts. 2. A client connects, lists the tools, and passes them to its model. 3. When the model asks for a tool, the client sends the call to the server and returns the result. 4. Auth, scoping and audit still belong to the server. MCP standardises the plumbing, not the permissions.

Where I used it. Skills-level. The Cluster Recommendation Copilot design hosts its audited read-only tools over MCP (verbal only, DESIGN). It is not an Impact Analytics PDF bullet.

Why it is a fit there. If several clients (a copilot UI, internal tools) need the same planning tools, MCP lets them share one audited tool server instead of each re-implementing tools.

Alternatives. Plain in-process tool calling (simplest when one app owns the tools, which is how Ask Iris works). A normal REST API that a tool wrapper calls.

Interview question. "What's the difference between tool calling and MCP?" "Tool calling is the model asking to run a function. MCP is a protocol for how tools are published and called across processes, so any compatible client can use the same tool server. You still need tool calling underneath. MCP just standardises discovery and transport. Permissions and audit stay in the server."

Do not say. "I shipped an MCP server in production at Impact Analytics." Say it is skills-level and part of the Copilot design.

Prompt Engineering

What it is. Designing the instructions, examples, context and output format you give an LLM so it reliably returns what you need. It is writing a very precise brief for a contractor who will do exactly what the brief says.

How it works (the ideas that matter). 1. Structured outputs. Ask for JSON that matches a schema, and validate it. Reject or retry anything that does not parse. 2. Minimal context. Give each prompt only the fields it needs. Less noise, fewer tokens. 3. Separate prompts per task. One prompt per lens, one for the decider, one for explanations, each versioned. 4. Cite the data. Require the model to reference the numbers it was given, so explanations are grounded.

Where I used it. - Impact Analytics Keep/Drop. Separate prompts for base, each lens, the decider, explanations, Top-N taglines and the peer step, managed through a prompt registry. Each lens gets a compact feature set with only the fields it needs (for example only the last 12 weeks for trend lenses). Lenses must cite the computed sales momentum fields. Prompts are part of the frozen config hash, so every output row records which prompt version produced it. - Uber Menu. Schema-shaped extraction prompts with retrieved labelled examples.

Illustrative shape of a structured lens output (the pipeline stores per-lens score, outcome and confidence. The other values here are made up for teaching.)

{
  "article_id": "A-10293",
  "lens": "trend_velocity",
  "score": 0.72,
  "outcome": "keep",
  "confidence": 0.8,
  "evidence": ["sales_momentum.last_4w_vs_prior_4w = +18%"]
}

Interview question. "Prompt engineering or fine-tuning?" "Prompt engineering first, with strict schemas and offline evaluation. It is cheaper to change and every version is tracked in the config hash. I would only consider fine-tuning if a well-evaluated prompt plateaued below the bar. Fine-tuning is not something I claim on this resume."

Do not say. Fine-tuning or SFT as a resume claim.

LangSmith

What it is. LangSmith is a tracing and debugging tool for LLM apps. Every run becomes a tree: which node ran, which prompt, which tool call, how many tokens, how long, and what failed. Like a flight recorder for your agent.

Where I used it. Ask Iris only (PDF bullet A4).

Why there. When a chat answer is wrong, you need to see which step went wrong: supervisor routing, a tool result, or the evaluator. Datadog shows which service was slow. LangSmith shows which prompt step failed.

What Keep/Drop uses instead. Custom JSON telemetry in the orchestration registry: tokens, USD cost, step duration and batch fallbacks per run, plus the frozen config hash on every output row.

Interview question. "Why both Datadog and LangSmith?" "They answer different questions. Datadog traces the Go platform: which service, which request, how long. LangSmith traces the LLM graph in Ask Iris: which step, which prompt, which tool. One tool for both would do neither well."

Do not say. LangSmith on the Keep/Drop batch or on the orchestration registry.

Offline Evaluation

What it is. Testing model behaviour against a labelled set before release, instead of discovering problems in production. It is unit tests for AI: a fixed set of inputs, expected answers, and a pass mark.

How it works. 1. Build a labelled set (gold set). For Keep/Drop, labels are a proxy for real outcomes, because true answers are only known after the season. 2. Run the candidate model or prompt on the set. 3. Compare against a baseline that costs nothing, such as the rule-only score. 4. Block promotion in CI if it misses the bar.

The real gate config looks like this:

{ "gold_min_accuracy": 0.8 }

Where I used it. - Impact Analytics, PDF bullet A5. A 300-case proxy set with an 80% accuracy CI gate. A separate gold-200 benchmark picked a model 73% cheaper at 100% coverage, and showed the rule-only baseline at 74%. The blended LLM scored about 63% there, below 74%, so we froze the blend weights instead of retuning them on a small set. In v2 of the pipeline, offline evals replaced the critic and evaluator agents that used to run inside Keep/Drop. - Uber Menu. 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation.

Why it matters. It lets you say no to a model with evidence. "The new model looks smarter" is not a reason to ship if it loses to a free rule.

Interview question. "What did you do when the LLM did worse than the rules?" "We did not ship a smarter-looking model that lost to a free baseline. On the 200-case benchmark the rules scored 74% and the blend scored lower, so we froze the blend weights. Promotion still needs 80% on the 300-case gate."

Do not say. "80% accuracy in production for all tenants." "The 300 cases showed the 73% saving." Human review queues for low-confidence scores (there are none in this repo).

One-liners to memorise

  • Agents: "Keep/Drop blends rule-based KPI math with structured LLM lenses in a fixed order. Ask Iris is a shipped LangGraph copilot with a supervisor, a three-attempt evaluator and a frozen data scope."
  • Tool calling: "The model picks a tool and fills typed arguments. The server owns scope. No SQL from the model."
  • MCP: "A standard way to publish tools to any LLM client. Skills-level for me, and part of the Copilot design."
  • Offline evaluation: "80% is a CI promotion gate on 300 cases, not live accuracy. The 73% cost cut and 74% baseline are from a separate 200-case benchmark. Menu 98% is offline."
  • Observability: "LangSmith for Ask Iris, custom JSON telemetry for the batch registry, Datadog for the Go edge."

Do not say

  • That MCP or Tool Calling is an Impact Analytics experience bullet. They are on the skills line.
  • That you shipped an MCP server in production.
  • Fine-tuning or SFT as a resume claim.
  • The Cluster Recommendation Copilot or Hindsight as resume bullets, or the Copilot as shipped.
  • pgvector as production. It is literacy.
  • Milvus, RAG, Kafka or Flink at Impact Analytics.
  • LangSmith on the Keep/Drop batch.
  • Human-in-the-loop review queues on Keep/Drop.

Tech depth index

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the map of the tech-depth folder. There is one study page per technology group on my resume. Each page teaches the technology from scratch, shows exactly where I used it, explains the design choices, ties the numbers, and ends with interview questions and speakable answers.
  • When to read it: at the start of a study session, to pick the pages that match the job description. Read the "Where each technology lives" table before any round.
  • What to memorise: the placement table below. Most interview slip-ups are putting a technology on the wrong project.
  • Which resume: these pages match Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf, whose summary says "Expertise in Java, Python and Go microservices". Uber FRM and Masters India are Java and Spring Boot. Impact Analytics is Go/Gin plus a Python agent plane.

Labels used across these pages. MEASURED means we have a log, doc, config or code for it. STATED means printed on the resume from the project's own source with no extra arithmetic in prep. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show ("roughly, derived from..."). HISTORICAL means from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal ("targeting"). Verbal means true but not printed on the resume.

LangGraph, LLM agents, tool calling, MCP, RAG, Milvus, LangSmith and offline evaluation

How to use this page

  • What it covers: every item on the Generative AI skills line, explained from scratch, and mapped to where I actually used it. That means Ask Iris (LangGraph supervisor plus evaluator, LangSmith) and the Keep/Drop decision engine (structured LLM invokes, 7 lenses, offline eval gate) at Impact Analytics, and the menu RAG pipeline (LangChain, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Milvus) at Uber Menu. MCP, tool calling and pgvector are explained honestly as skills-level.
  • When to read it: before any AI engineer, applied ML or "LLM in production" round, and before the IA Agentic deep dive.
  • What to memorise: LangGraph is Ask Iris. Keep/Drop has a fixed step order and no LLM orchestrator. RAG and Milvus are Uber Menu. MCP is skills-level. LangSmith is Ask Iris. 80% is a CI gate on 300 cases, while 73% and 74% come from a separate 200-case benchmark.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc, config or code for it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). Verbal means true but off the resume.

Say these carefully

  • 80% is a CI promotion gate on the 300-case proxy set. It does not mean "every tenant runs at 80% accuracy live".
  • 73% lower cost at 100% coverage, and the 74% baseline, come from the gold-200 benchmark, not the 300-case file. Never fuse them. Model names are not on the resume.
  • Keep/Drop has no LLM orchestrator. Its step order is fixed in code: peer benchmark, then decider, then lenses, then blend, then explanation. Do not call it "seven agents talking to each other".
  • LangGraph and LangSmith are Ask Iris. The Keep/Drop batch uses custom JSON telemetry, not LangSmith.
  • RAG and Milvus are Uber Menu only. Never Impact Analytics. Menu's 98% is offline evaluation.
  • MCP and tool calling are skills-level. The Cluster Recommendation Copilot tool design (14 tools) is verbal depth only, not a resume bullet. Say "building", not "shipped", for the Copilot.
  • No human review queues (HITL) at IA. Offline evals replaced critic and evaluator agents in Keep/Drop.
  • Ask Iris is a shipped capability with no SLA or usage numbers. Do not invent any.
  • No fine-tuning or SFT claims on the resume.

1. LLM agents and structured outputs

1.1 Plain English

A large language model (LLM) predicts text. An LLM agent is a program that uses an LLM to decide steps: which tool to call, what to ask next, when to stop. A plain "chain" always runs the same steps in the same order. An agent chooses its path at runtime. That flexibility is also the danger, because agents can loop, wander, or take actions you did not intend.

A structured LLM invoke is a call where the model must return JSON that matches a schema. Think of a form with fixed boxes instead of a blank page. You validate the answer like any API response.

# Teaching sketch: a structured lens call with Pydantic validation.
class LensScore(BaseModel):
    lens: Literal["trend_velocity", "size_curve", "colour_cannibalization"]
    score: float = Field(ge=0, le=1)
    rationale: str

raw = llm.invoke(prompt, response_format=LensScore.model_json_schema())
result = LensScore.model_validate_json(raw)   # rejects anything off-schema

1.2 Where I used it: the Keep/Drop decision engine (A1, A2, A3)

Architected a multi-pipeline AI merchandise decision engine (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style) evaluating 348k article-seasons. Optimized inference at scale, processing 88k items per pass, by blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM invokes across 7 AI lenses.

In plain words: for each article-season (one product in one selling season), code computes hard KPIs such as sell-through (share of stock that sold) and rate of sale (units per selling store per week). Then the LLM answers up to seven focused questions, the lenses, and the two are blended into a keep-or-drop recommendation.

The seven active lenses are trend_velocity, size_curve, colour_cannibalization, channel_divergence, multi_season_consistency, discount_dependency and margin_resilience. An eighth exists but is switched off. A cheap Python lens gate runs first and skips lenses that make no sense, for example size_curve for a single-size product.

flowchart LR CH["ClickHouse facts"] --> DET["Deterministic KPI math: s_det"] DET --> PAY["JSON payload per article, batches up to 64"] PAY --> PEER["Peer benchmark"] PEER --> DEC["Decider"] DEC --> LENS["Lens calls, structured JSON"] LENS --> BLEND["Blend: s_final = 0.4 x s_det + 0.6 x s_agent"] BLEND --> EXP["Explanation"] EXP --> OUT["Output rows with config_hash"]

What to notice: the order of steps is fixed in code. No LLM decides what runs next.

Worked example (from prep): a tee with sell-through 84% and rate of sale 1.168 gets s_det of about 0.65 from code. The gate sees five sizes, two colours and 12 weeks on sale, so size_curve, colour_cannibalization and trend_velocity are eligible. If s_agent = 0.711, then s_final = 0.4 x 0.65 + 0.6 x 0.711, which is about 0.687. That is at or above 0.55, so it is a keep.

Why the LLM gets JSON, not tools: the master table is 2.11B rows. A scoring model with a SQL or code tool across 88k items is a latency, cost and injection risk. Code computes the KPIs. The model does judgement, not arithmetic. On timeout, the deterministic score stands (A2).

Why the step order is fixed: a batch of 88k items needs predictable cost and behaviour. An LLM choosing the path per item would make cost and evaluation unpredictable.

Numbers: 348k article-seasons evaluated (MEASURED, and not the 1.6M catalog), 88k items per pass (MEASURED), 7 lenses (MEASURED, config). About $100 per pass in tokens is true but off the PDF.

2. LangGraph and Ask Iris

2.1 What LangGraph is

LangGraph is a library from the LangChain team for building LLM applications as a graph of steps with shared state. Each node is a function (call a model, call a worker, check an answer). Edges connect nodes. Conditional edges choose the next node from the current state. Graphs can loop, which is what agents need, and LangGraph adds checkpointing (save state between steps) and a recursion limit (a maximum number of steps per run).

Analogy: a hospital triage desk. The triage nurse (supervisor) looks at the patient and sends them to a specialist (worker). A senior doctor (evaluator) reviews the specialist's note and can send it back. Hospital policy says "no more than three reviews", so nobody circles forever.

2.2 How Ask Iris uses it (A4)

Shipped "Ask Iris," a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot enabling planners to interactively query KPIs and inspect AI decisions on a multi-billion-row database. Prevented infinite LLM loops and multi-tenant data leaks by orchestrating a LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator loop, utilizing LangSmith for observability, and strictly freezing hierarchy access on the initial socket handshake.

sequenceDiagram participant B as Planner browser participant API as FastAPI WebSocket participant SUP as Supervisor node participant W as Worker node participant EV as Evaluator node B->>API: Upgrade request with JWT API->>API: Verify token, freeze plan_scope B->>API: Why was TEE-0412 dropped? API->>SUP: Question plus frozen scope SUP->>W: Route to the right worker W-->>EV: Draft answer EV-->>SUP: Not good enough, attempt 2 of 3 SUP->>W: Retry W-->>EV: Revised answer EV-->>API: Accepted API-->>B: Answer

What to notice: scope is set once at the top. The evaluator can send work back, but never more than three times.

# Teaching sketch of the graph shape. Not production code.
MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

def evaluator(state):
    ok = judge(state["draft"], state["question"])
    if ok or state["attempts"] >= MAX_ATTEMPTS:
        return {"final": state["draft"] if ok else graceful_fallback(state)}
    return {"attempts": state["attempts"] + 1}

g = StateGraph(IrisState)
g.add_node("supervisor", supervisor)
g.add_node("worker", worker)
g.add_node("evaluator", evaluator)
g.add_edge("supervisor", "worker")
g.add_edge("worker", "evaluator")
g.add_conditional_edges("evaluator", lambda s: END if "final" in s else "supervisor")
app = g.compile()
app.invoke(state, config={"recursion_limit": 25})   # illustrative limit

2.3 Design decisions for Ask Iris

  • What: a supervisor graph with a capped evaluator, behind a JWT-verified WebSocket, with scope frozen at handshake, traced in LangSmith.
  • Why: chat is the riskiest LLM surface. Scope that can change mid-session invites tenant bleed, and uncapped self-critique loops burn tokens.
  • Alternatives considered:
  • A plain chain (no graph). Simpler, but it cannot route different question types to different workers or retry.
  • A fully autonomous agent with free tool use. More flexible and much harder to bound or test.
  • Re-check permissions per message. Then scope depends on message content. Freezing at the handshake makes widening scope structurally impossible.
  • Trade-off: if a user's permissions change mid-session, they must reconnect. A capped evaluator sometimes returns a "best effort" answer.
  • What I'd do differently: build an Ask Iris-specific offline eval set from real planner questions early, so routing changes are gated like Keep/Drop changes.

2.4 What not to claim

No SLA, latency target, user count or questions per week. It is a shipped capability.

3. Tool calling and MCP (skills-level)

3.1 Tool calling

Tool calling (also called function calling) lets a model ask the application to run a function. You describe the tools with names and JSON schemas. The model returns "call get_kpis with {article: 'TEE-0412'}". Your code validates the arguments, runs the function and gives the result back to the model. The model never runs anything itself. Your code does.

{"name": "get_article_kpis",
 "description": "Read KPIs for one article within the caller's scope",
 "parameters": {"type": "object",
   "properties": {"article_id": {"type": "string"}, "season": {"type": "integer"}},
   "required": ["article_id", "season"]}}

Rules I follow when designing tools:

  1. Read-only by default. Writes go through normal product APIs with their own checks.
  2. Typed arguments, validated. Reject anything off-schema before it touches data.
  3. Scope comes from the session, not the arguments. The model cannot pass a tenant id.
  4. No free-form SQL tools. Narrow functions with known cost.
  5. Budgets: a cap on tool calls per turn and per-tool timeouts.

Where: IA's Keep/Drop scoring deliberately uses no tools. It is JSON in, structured score out. Ask Iris workers read data within the frozen plan_scope. On the resume, tool calling is a skills-line item, and I present my tool design depth verbally through the Copilot design below.

3.2 MCP (Model Context Protocol)

MCP is an open protocol that standardises how LLM applications connect to tools and data. Think of it as USB-C for AI tools: one plug shape, so any compliant app can use any compliant tool server.

  • An MCP host is the LLM app (an IDE assistant, a chat app).
  • An MCP client inside the host keeps a connection to each server.
  • An MCP server exposes tools (functions the model can call), resources (data the app can read) and prompts (reusable templates).
  • Messages use JSON-RPC, over stdio for local servers or HTTP for remote ones.

Why it matters: without MCP, every app writes custom glue for every tool. With MCP, you write a tool server once.

Where: skills-level. I understand the protocol and how I would expose platform reads as MCP tools. It is not a shipped IA bullet. Older prep said IA had "MCP-hosted tool calling to audited read-only planning tools". That is the Copilot design, verbal only.

Verbal only: Cluster Recommendation Copilot tool design

Use this if an interviewer wants depth on tool design. Say "the design was..." and "building", not "shipped".

  • 14 audited read-only tools over planning data. No free-form SQL.
  • 3 confirm gates in the design before any write-back through product APIs. This is a design flow, not a shipped human review queue.
  • Budgets in the design: tool calls per session, parallel clustering jobs per tenant, token caps, per-tool timeouts.
  • Measured baseline: an 8.5% clustering failure rate (37 out of 437), with a TARGET under 2%. TARGET turnaround from days to under 1 hour.
  • Phase 1 design review passed. Load test pending.

4. Prompt engineering

Prompt engineering is designing the instructions, context and output format you give a model so it behaves reliably. In production that means:

  • One narrow job per prompt. Each lens has its own rubric instead of one giant "decide everything" prompt. Narrow prompts are easier to evaluate and fix.
  • Strict output schemas. JSON with bounded numeric fields.
  • Context as data, not instructions. Facts go in a JSON block, clearly separated from the instructions. That reduces prompt-injection risk from data fields.
  • Versioning. At IA, prompt text is part of the config_hash (SHA-256 of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog) stamped on every output row. Change one word and the hash changes, so you always know which prompt produced a decision.
  • Few-shot examples. At Menu, retrieval supplied similar labelled menus as examples (section 6).

5. Offline evaluation and the CI gate (A5)

Built a 300-case proxy evaluation harness and an 80% accuracy CI gate to enforce strict deployment guardrails. Reduced live execution costs by 73% at 100% coverage by benchmarking models against a 74% deterministic baseline, strategically freezing final decision weights when the LLM underperformed the baseline.

5.1 Plain words

Offline evaluation means testing a model or prompt on a fixed labelled set before it reaches users. A proxy set uses labels that stand in for the truth, because the real "right answer" for Keep/Drop is only known after the season ends. A CI gate is an automated check in the continuous integration pipeline that blocks promotion if a number is too low.

5.2 Two different test sets. Keep them apart.

Set Size What it gave us Tag
Proxy eval harness 300 cases (cases.json) The promotion gate: eval.json has gold_min_accuracy: 0.8. Below 80%, a change cannot be promoted MEASURED (config)
Gold-200 benchmark 200 cases Chosen model about 73% cheaper than the previous one, with 200 out of 200 completed (100% coverage). Deterministic baseline at the production threshold 0.65 scored 74%. Blended LLM scored about 63% MEASURED
flowchart LR CHG["Prompt or model change"] --> P300["300-case proxy eval"] P300 --> G{"At least 80 percent?"} G -->|"no"| BLOCK["Blocked from promotion"] G -->|"yes"| PROMO["Eligible to promote"] G200["Separate gold-200 bench"] --> COST["Model pick: about 73% cheaper, 200 of 200 complete"] G200 --> BASE["Det baseline 74%, blended about 63%"] BASE --> FREEZE["Freeze blend weights, do not retune"]

What to notice: two separate boxes. The 80% gate lives on the 300-case path. The 73% and 74% live on the gold-200 path.

5.3 The judgement call interviewers like

The rule-only baseline scored 74% on gold-200. The blended LLM score came in around 63%, which is lower. Instead of retuning blend weights on a 200-case set (overfitting), we froze the weights. The model has to beat a free rule before it is allowed to move decisions more. That is a senior call: the eval system can, and did, say no to the AI.

5.4 How to say the numbers

  • "Promotion requires at least 80% on a 300-case proxy set. It's a CI gate."
  • "On a separate 200-case benchmark, the model we picked cost about 73% less and still completed all 200 cases."
  • "The rule-only baseline scored 74% on that same 200 set. When the blend came in lower, we froze the weights."

Do NOT say: "80% accuracy in production", "the 300 cases showed 73%", "100% test coverage" for this bullet, or the model names as if they were on the resume.

5.5 Menu's offline evaluation

98% field fidelity on the Menu RAG pipeline was measured offline against labelled menus. Each field (item name, price, description, modifier) is compared with ground truth. Older prep also quoted "100% schema consistency". The current resume does not, so stick to 98%.

6. RAG, embeddings, Milvus and LangChain (Uber Menu)

Accelerated restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saved $600K annually by architecting an automated ingestion pipeline processing 30K+ menus monthly. Converted unstructured, multilingual PDFs into a strict catalog schema at 98% field fidelity utilizing a Gemini 2.5 Pro and LangChain RAG pipeline over Milvus vector embeddings.

6.1 Plain English

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) means: before asking the model, fetch relevant reference material and put it in the prompt. It is an open-book exam instead of a closed-book one.

An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning have vectors that are close together. A vector database such as Milvus stores millions of these vectors and quickly finds the nearest ones to a query. It uses approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes such as HNSW (a layered graph you walk greedily towards the target) or IVF (cluster the vectors, then only search the closest clusters).

LangChain is a Python framework with building blocks for LLM apps: document loaders, text splitters, embedding wrappers, vector store connectors, retrievers and prompt templates. We used it as the glue for the RAG pipeline.

6.2 How the menu pipeline worked

flowchart LR PDF["Multilingual menu PDF or image"] --> SPLIT["Extract text and chunk by section"] SPLIT --> EMB["Embed chunks"] EMB --> MIL["Milvus: find similar labelled menus and schema examples"] MIL --> PROMPT["Prompt: schema, retrieved examples, menu chunk"] PROMPT --> GEM["Gemini 2.5 Pro: structured extraction"] GEM --> VAL["Schema validation"] VAL -->|"valid"| CAT["Idempotent catalog upsert"] VAL -->|"invalid or low confidence"| HOLD["Held back from auto-publish"]

What to notice: retrieval supplies examples of what correct output looks like, and a schema gate sits between the model and the catalog.

  1. A messy PDF menu arrives (multiple languages, columns, images).
  2. The text is extracted and split into chunks such as a section or a block of items.
  3. Each chunk is embedded, and Milvus returns similar, already-labelled menus and schema examples.
  4. The prompt gives Gemini 2.5 Pro the target catalog schema, the retrieved examples and the menu chunk.
  5. Gemini returns structured items: name, price, description, modifiers.
  6. A schema validator checks types, required fields and price formats. Valid output becomes an idempotent catalog upsert. Invalid or low-confidence output is held back from auto-publish (older prep describes a manual review path for these).

6.3 Why this design

  • Why RAG over plain prompting: menus vary wildly. Showing the model similar solved examples makes output more consistent than instructions alone.
  • Why not regex or templates: they break on every new layout and language.
  • Why not fine-tuning: it costs more to iterate and needs a labelled training set per change. Retrieval examples can be updated by adding labelled menus. No fine-tuning is claimed on the resume.
  • Why Milvus: a dedicated, scalable vector database with ANN indexes. pgvector is a reasonable alternative when vectors live next to relational data in Postgres at moderate scale (see 6.5).
  • Trade-off: retrieval quality depends on the labelled corpus. A stale index or poor chunking hurts accuracy quietly.
  • What I'd do differently: track retrieval quality separately from generation quality in the offline eval, so you know which half regressed.

6.4 The numbers

Number Meaning Tag
98% field fidelity Share of extracted fields matching labelled ground truth HISTORICAL, offline evaluation
From 24 hours to 2 hours Restaurant onboarding time, about 92% faster HISTORICAL
30K+ menus a month Volume HISTORICAL
$600K a year About $2 per menu x 30,000 x 12 = $720K list, floored to $600K ESTIMATED on HISTORICAL inputs

Say it: "98% field fidelity on our offline evaluation set." Do NOT say "98% accuracy in production" or "$720K saved".

6.5 pgvector (literacy)

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector column type and nearest-neighbour search (HNSW and IVFFlat indexes). It is great when you want vectors next to your relational data, with one database to operate and SQL joins between vectors and metadata. A dedicated vector database such as Milvus scales further and offers more index options. I have not run pgvector in production. It is skills-level.

7. LangSmith and LLM observability

LangSmith is a tracing and evaluation tool for LLM apps from the LangChain team. Every run becomes a trace tree: each node, model call, prompt, response, token count and latency. You can replay a bad answer, see which step went wrong, and build datasets from real traces.

What Tool Why
Ask Iris graph runs LangSmith See supervisor routing, evaluator retries and tokens per question
Keep/Drop batch runs Custom JSON telemetry (tokens, USD cost, step duration, batch fallbacks) plus config_hash A batch of 88k items needs per-run cost accounting tied to output rows
Go platform HTTP and database calls Datadog Distributed tracing of the edge

Debugging a bad Ask Iris answer, end to end: find the trace in LangSmith, check which worker the supervisor chose, read the evaluator's reasons, see the data the worker had. If the data was wrong, follow the request into Datadog on the Go side.

8. Model providers (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude)

  • OpenAI: the gold-200 benchmark compared OpenAI models for the Keep/Drop lenses. The specific model names are not on the resume. Do not volunteer them.
  • Gemini: Gemini 2.5 Pro powered the Uber Menu extraction.
  • Claude: on the skills line as a provider I can work with. I have no resume project that names it, so keep it at skills level.

What I compare when choosing a model: quality on my offline set, cost per item, completion reliability (does it finish every case, or leave rows pending), latency, context length and structured output support. On gold-200, a third, even cheaper model left rows pending, so completion reliability decided the pick.

9. Failure modes and guards

Failure Guard
Hallucinated or malformed output Strict JSON schemas, Pydantic validation, reject and fall back
Hallucinated tool arguments Typed schemas, scope from session not arguments, read-only tools
Infinite loops and cost blow-ups MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3, recursion limit, circuit breakers, hard timeouts
Provider outage mid-run Circuit breaker, deterministic fallback, checkpoints with --resume
Prompt drift Prompts inside config_hash. Every change re-runs the 300-case gate
Eval leakage (offline does not equal production) Say "offline" every time. Keep proxy and gold sets separate. Monitor fallbacks in telemetry
Stale embeddings or RAG index (Menu) Re-embed when the labelled corpus changes. Track retrieval quality
Prompt injection from data Facts passed as JSON data, not instructions. Model has no SQL or write access

10. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. Why LangGraph instead of a plain chain? Because Ask Iris needs routing and bounded retries, which are a graph with a loop, not a straight line. The supervisor picks a worker per question, and the evaluator can send a draft back. LangGraph gives me explicit state, conditional edges and a recursion limit, so I can cap the evaluator at three attempts. A chain can't loop, and a free-form agent is harder to bound.

Q2. Is Keep/Drop an agent? Not in the "LLM decides the next step" sense, and I'm careful about that. It is a batch pipeline with a fixed order in code: peer benchmark, decider, lenses, blend, explanation. The LLM parts are structured invokes that return JSON scores. I chose that because 88k items per pass needs predictable cost and behaviour, and offline evals replaced critic agents.

Q3. Why not give the scoring model a SQL tool? The master is 2.11 billion rows. A SQL tool across 88k items is a latency, cost and injection surface, and a hallucinated query could scan billions of rows. Code computes the KPIs and packs a JSON payload. The model only judges patterns. On timeout the deterministic score stands, so the run never stalls.

Q4. How do you evaluate an LLM feature before shipping? Offline, on a fixed labelled set, as a CI gate. For Keep/Drop, every prompt or model change has to score at least 80% on a 300-case proxy set to be promoted. Separately, we benchmark models on a 200-case gold set for cost and coverage. That's where the chosen model was about 73% cheaper with all 200 completed. And we always compare with the free deterministic baseline, which scored 74% on that set. Follow-up they may ask: "Is 80% your production accuracy?" No. It's the promotion threshold.

Q5. The LLM scored below the rule baseline. What did you do? We froze the blend weights instead of retuning them on a small set. The blended score was about 63% against the rule's 74% on gold-200. Retuning weights on 200 cases would just fit noise. The principle is that a model must beat a free rule before it gets more say. The eval system saying no is the eval system working.

Q6. Explain RAG and how you used it. RAG means retrieving relevant reference material and putting it in the prompt before generating. At Uber Menu we embedded menu chunks, used Milvus to find similar labelled menus and schema examples, and gave those to Gemini 2.5 Pro with the target catalog schema. Its structured output went through a schema validator before an idempotent catalog upsert. That got 98% field fidelity on our offline evaluation and helped onboarding go from 24 hours to 2 hours.

Q7. What is MCP and have you used it? MCP is an open protocol for connecting LLM apps to tools and data. A host app talks to MCP servers that expose tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC, so a tool server written once works with any compliant app. It's on my skills line at skills level. I haven't shipped an MCP server as a resume bullet. My tool-design depth comes from a copilot design with 14 read-only tools and confirm steps before any write-back. That design is still being built.

Q8. How do you stop prompt injection? Instructions are not the control. Capabilities are. In Keep/Drop, the model has no tools and no database access, and data goes in as a JSON block separated from instructions. Its output is schema-validated before code writes it. In Ask Iris, scope is frozen in code at the handshake, so an injected "show me tenant B" can't widen it. The worst case is a wrong sentence, not a data leak or a write.

Q9. Prompt engineering or fine-tuning? I start with prompt engineering, retrieval and structured outputs, because they are cheap to iterate and easy to evaluate offline. Fine-tuning is for when you have a large labelled set and a stable task where prompting has plateaued. Neither of my production projects claims fine-tuning.

Q10. LangSmith or Datadog? Both, for different layers. LangSmith traces Ask Iris graph runs: routing, evaluator retries, tokens. Datadog traces the Go platform's HTTP and database calls. The Keep/Drop batch uses custom JSON telemetry for tokens, USD cost, step duration and fallbacks, stamped with a config hash, because batch cost accounting per run is what we need there.

Skills on the resume: fundamentals, where I used each, and how strongly to claim it

How to use this page

  • What it covers: every item on the Skills section of Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf (summary line: "Expertise in Java, Python and Go microservices"), plus the extra technologies that appear on project Tech lines. For each item: what it is in one line, the fundamentals an interviewer will probe, where it appears on my resume, and how strongly I can claim it.
  • When to read it: when a job description names a technology and you want to know in 30 seconds what to say, or when an interviewer points at your skills list and says "tell me about X".
  • What to memorise: the claim strength column. "Production" means I can tell a project story. "Skills-level" means I can explain it well but there is no resume bullet. "Literacy" means I know the concepts and must say so plainly. If you cannot place a skill, do not emphasise it.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. STATED means printed on the resume from the project source. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal.

Claim strength key

Strength Meaning How to talk about it
Production I used it in shipped work that is on the resume Tell the project story with numbers
Production (historical) Used in past roles, from work records State the outcome plainly. Some baselines are estimates
Skills-level I can explain and design with it. It is not a resume bullet "I know it well and have designed with it, but it's not one of my shipped bullets"
Literacy I know the concepts "I understand how it works. I haven't owned it in production"

Placement rules that interviewers check

  • Java and Spring Boot: Uber FRM (36 Spring Boot endpoints, Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration, JUnit) and Masters India (PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, Hibernate). Never Spring Boot at Impact Analytics.
  • Go/Gin: Impact Analytics platform. Python with FastAPI and LangGraph: the IA agent plane (Ask Iris, Keep/Drop batch). Python: Uber Menu. Django: GeeksforGeeks.
  • Kafka: Uber Menu and Masters India (two different products). Flink: Uber Menu only. Neither at Impact Analytics.
  • ClickHouse, LangGraph, LangSmith, Datadog: Impact Analytics. LangSmith is Ask Iris only.
  • RAG, Milvus, LangChain, Selenium, Gemini 2.5 Pro: Uber Menu.
  • ELK, New Relic: Masters India.
  • Spring MVC, Spring Security, Spring Batch, Maven, Amazon S3, Celery, asyncio: skills-line items with no bullet naming them. Explain where they fit, don't attach outcomes.
  • MCP, tool calling: skills-level. IA tool design (Cluster Recommendation Copilot, 14 tools) is verbal only.
  • C, C++, pgvector, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, gRPC: literacy. No production ownership claims.

2. Backend and APIs

Spring in one paragraph. Spring is the standard Java framework for backend services. Its container creates your objects (beans) and hands each one its dependencies, which is dependency injection. Spring Boot adds defaults and an embedded web server so a service starts from one main method. The other Spring items below are modules that plug into a Spring Boot service.
