Observability and cloud: Datadog, LangSmith, ELK, New Relic, Docker, GCP, AWS, Kubernetes, Bazel, CI/CD

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the observability tools (logs, metrics, traces, LLM traces) and the cloud and DevOps items on my resume. That means Datadog on the Impact Analytics Go edge, LangSmith on Ask Iris, custom JSON telemetry on the Keep/Drop batch, ELK and New Relic at Masters India, plus Docker, GCP, AWS, Bazel, CI/CD and Kubernetes (literacy only).
  • When to read it: before any "how do you debug production", on-call, reliability or DevOps question.
  • What to memorise: which tool lives where (Datadog is the IA Go edge, LangSmith is Ask Iris, ELK and New Relic are Masters). The Masters numbers: triage down 70% (roughly 30 minutes to under 10, estimated baseline), test coverage from 35% to 82%, and 98% deployment success. And that Kubernetes is literacy, not cluster operations.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. STATED means printed on the resume from the project source. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal.

Say these carefully

  • LangSmith is Ask Iris only. The Keep/Drop batch uses custom JSON telemetry, not LangSmith.
  • Datadog is the IA Go edge. No invented SLA, p99 or uptime number.
  • ELK and New Relic are Masters India. They are both on the current skills line too. Older prep said ELK might be off the skills list. It is on it now.
  • Kubernetes is literacy only. No "I operated clusters". No Terraform production ownership. Do not claim org-wide ownership of Datadog or LangSmith.
  • The 70% triage cut is HISTORICAL. Its 30-minute baseline is ESTIMATED. I claim on-call alerting and faster triage, not a formal pager rotation title.
  • PostHog appeared in older IA prep as product analytics. It is not on the resume. Do not lead with it.

1. Observability in plain English

Observability is how well you can tell what a running system is doing from the outside, using the signals it emits. It answers "what is broken, where, and why" without SSH-ing into boxes and guessing.

The three classic signals:

Signal What it is Analogy Example
Logs Timestamped records of events A ship's logbook {"level":"error","request_id":"r-91","msg":"IRP timeout","client":"c-12"}
Metrics Numbers over time The car dashboard Request rate, error rate, p95 latency, consumer lag
Traces One request's path across services, as timed steps A parcel tracking history API span, then Redis span, then ClickHouse span

More terms you need:

  • Span: one timed step in a trace (an HTTP handler, a database query).
  • Trace id or correlation id: an id carried through every service and log line for one request, so you can stitch them together.
  • APM (Application Performance Monitoring): tools that auto-instrument services to produce traces and latency breakdowns.
  • Structured logs: JSON fields instead of free text, so you can filter by client_id or request_id.
  • SLI, SLO, SLA: an SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a measured signal like p95 latency. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is the target for it. An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a contractual promise. I quote none of these for IA.

2. Datadog at Impact Analytics (bullet C1)

Architected a multi-tenant Go/Gin platform scaling to 10k peak RPS, utilizing Google Wire for compile-time DI. Deployed as a self-protecting HTTP edge without a reverse proxy, guaranteeing high availability through native h2c, nested timeouts, and Datadog distributed tracing.

Datadog is a hosted monitoring platform for metrics, logs and APM traces. Its Go tracer instruments Gin, HTTP clients and database calls, so each request becomes a trace with spans.

Why it matters for this design: with no reverse proxy, there is no proxy access log or proxy dashboard to lean on. The Go process's own traces are the main view into latency. When a pivot is slow, the trace waterfall shows whether the time went to the auth waterfall on a Redis miss, to Postgres role resolution, or to a ClickHouse query.

flowchart LR REQ["Request"] --> S1["Span: Gin handler"] S1 --> S2["Span: Redis auth cache"] S1 --> S3["Span: Postgres roles"] S1 --> S4["Span: ClickHouse query"] S1 --> DD["Datadog APM: one trace id"]

What to notice: one trace id ties every downstream call to the request, so the slowest span is obvious.

Say it: "Datadog distributed tracing on the Go edge, so every request is a trace across Redis, Postgres and ClickHouse." Do NOT add an SLA or a p99.

3. LangSmith on Ask Iris (bullet A4)

LangSmith is the LangChain team's tracing and evaluation platform for LLM apps. Each graph run is a trace tree: nodes, prompts, model responses, token counts, latency and errors.

For Ask Iris it answers questions Datadog can't: which worker did the supervisor route to, why did the evaluator reject the first draft, how many attempts (at most 3) did it take, how many tokens did it cost. See langgraph_mcp_rag.md.

4. Custom JSON telemetry on the Keep/Drop batch (bullet A3)

Engineered a shared orchestration registry to guarantee 88k-article batch runs survive provider failures by implementing hard timeouts, circuit breakers, and durable checkpoints that bypass redundant deterministic scoring. Ensured full observability by stamping every output row with a frozen config hash and custom JSON telemetry tracking tokens, USD cost, step duration, and batch fallbacks.

For a batch job, the questions are different: what did this run cost, how long did each step take, how many batches fell back to deterministic scores, and which configuration produced each row. So each run emits JSON telemetry (tokens, USD cost, step duration, batch fallbacks), and every output row carries config_hash, a SHA-256 of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog.

{"run_id": "kd-2026-09-08-a", "config_hash": "9f2c...", "step": "lenses",
 "items": 88000, "tokens_in": 0, "tokens_out": 0, "usd_cost": 0.0,
 "duration_s": 0, "batches_fallback": 0}

(Field names are illustrative and the values are zeroed on purpose. About $100 per pass is true but off the PDF.)

Why not LangSmith here: we needed per-run cost accounting and fallback counts tied to output rows and to the config hash, inside our own batch CLI. A fallback spike is visible in the telemetry, so fallbacks don't silently hide problems.

5. ELK and New Relic at Masters India (bullet MI3)

Decreased incident triage time by 70% and lowered database read load by 30% by instrumenting ELK and New Relic distributed tracing alongside a Redis caching layer. Hardened the CI/CD release cycle by driving test coverage from 35% to 82%, achieving a 98% deployment success rate across the microservices ecosystem.

5.1 What the tools are

  • ELK is Elasticsearch (search and storage), Logstash (ingest and transform logs) and Kibana (search UI and dashboards). Services ship structured logs, and you search them by any field.
  • New Relic is a hosted APM platform for traces, latency breakdowns, error rates and alerting.

5.2 Before and after

  • Before: SSH into boxes and grep log files, with no way to follow one request across services.
  • After: structured JSON logs carrying a request id shipped to ELK, New Relic APM traces, and alert rules on error rate and latency. One request id follows a transaction across the API, the Kafka consumer and the IRP worker.
  • How the id travels in Spring Boot: a servlet filter (a class that runs before every controller) reads or creates the id and puts it in the MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context), a per-thread map that the JSON log encoder adds to every log line. The producer copies the id into a Kafka header, and the @KafkaListener puts it back into the MDC before doing any work. The New Relic Java agent instruments Spring MVC, JDBC and Kafka calls automatically.
flowchart LR API["Spring Boot services"] --> LOG["JSON logs with request_id"] W["Spring Kafka consumers"] --> LOG LOG --> ELK["ELK: search by request_id"] API --> NR["New Relic APM traces"] W --> NR NR --> AL["Alerts on error rate and latency"] ELK --> TRI["On-call triage"] AL --> TRI

What to notice: the win is correlation. One id joins the logs and traces from every hop.

5.3 The numbers

Number What it measures How derived Tag
70% triage cut Time from alert to knowing which service and request caused it Roughly 30 minutes to under 10 minutes. 30 to 9 is a 70% cut HISTORICAL, baseline ESTIMATED
30% read load cut Read queries hitting PostgreSQL Redis cache-aside layer. It is load, not latency HISTORICAL
From 35% to 82% Test coverage, with JUnit and Mockito tests as a CI gate on money paths first (registration, reconciliation, imports) Coverage reports HISTORICAL
98% Deployments that went out without rollback Release records HISTORICAL

Say it: "Incident triage time fell about 70%, roughly from half an hour to under ten minutes, thanks to ELK and New Relic tracing." Do NOT present the 30-minute baseline as measured, or say "zero downtime" here (that phrase belongs to the FRM stacked Bazel PRs).

6. Docker

Docker packages an application and its dependencies into an image. An image is a layered, read-only filesystem snapshot. A running image is a container. Containers share the host's kernel, so they are much lighter than virtual machines. Analogy: a shipping container. Whatever is inside, the crane and the ship handle it the same way.

Key ideas: layers are cached (put rarely changing steps first), images should be small and pinned to versions, and a container should run one process.

# Teaching sketch.
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]

The sketch above is a Python service such as the IA agent plane. For the Spring Boot services the idea is the same with a JRE base image (for example eclipse-temurin:17-jre) and CMD ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] running the service's single executable JAR.

Where: on the tech line for Impact Analytics, Uber FRM, Uber Menu and Masters India. At Menu it pinned browser and driver versions for the Selenium fleet.

Cloud Where What to say
GCP (Google Cloud Platform) Impact Analytics (with BigQuery on the tech line, and ClickHouse Cloud clusters), Uber Menu Services ran on GCP. Keep product-level detail qualitative unless you are sure
AWS (Amazon Web Services) Masters India Bulk import files landed in object storage (Amazon S3). Secrets used AWS KMS (HISTORICAL framing)

When asked "which services?", name only what you know, and describe patterns instead: object storage for files, managed databases, container deploys, secrets management.

8. Kubernetes (literacy only)

Kubernetes is a system that runs containers across a cluster of machines and keeps them in the desired state. Words to know:

  • Pod: the smallest unit, one or more containers scheduled together.
  • Deployment: declares "run N replicas of this pod" and handles rolling updates.
  • Service: a stable network name and load balancing in front of pods.
  • Ingress: HTTP routing from outside the cluster.
  • HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler): scales replicas on CPU or custom metrics.
  • Liveness and readiness probes: "restart me if dead" and "don't send me traffic yet".

Why it matters for my Go edge: graceful shutdown on SIGTERM is exactly what a rolling deploy on Kubernetes or any orchestrator needs.

Say it: "I understand how Kubernetes deploys and scales services, and I write services that behave well on it, with graceful shutdown, health checks and stateless replicas. I haven't operated clusters, so I don't claim that." No cluster operations claims, no Terraform claims.

9. Bazel (Uber FRM)

Bazel is Google's open-source build system, used in large monorepos. Builds are hermetic (same inputs give the same outputs) and incremental (only rebuild and retest what changed), with explicit dependency graphs in BUILD.bazel files.

At Uber FRM it was the monorepo environment, not a choice. Each layer (entity, repository, service, controller) had a Java test target running JUnit 5 tests, and all had to pass before merge. Stacked PRs are a chain of small dependent pull requests, each reviewable and shippable on its own. They let the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration go out in steps with zero downtime.

10. CI/CD

CI (Continuous Integration) runs automated checks on every change. CD (Continuous Delivery or Deployment) automates releasing it. My CI/CD stories:

Project Gate Number
Masters India JUnit and Mockito coverage as a CI gate, money paths first Coverage from 35% to 82%, 98% deployment success (HISTORICAL)
Uber FRM Bazel test targets per layer (JUnit 5, Mockito, MockMvc), tests required with every PR, stacked PRs 100% module statement coverage (STATED), 1,100+ tests (verbal)
Impact Analytics Offline eval as a promotion gate: at least 80% on the 300-case proxy set 80% gate (MEASURED config). Not live accuracy

11. Debugging end to end: a worked example

"A planner says Ask Iris gave a wrong answer about a dropped article."

  1. Find the Ask Iris run in LangSmith. Which worker did the supervisor choose? What did the evaluator say on each attempt?
  2. Check the data the worker had. If it came from the platform, follow the request into Datadog traces on the Go edge and see the ClickHouse query and its result.
  3. Check the decision itself in the Keep/Drop output. Its config_hash says which prompts and parameters produced it, and the run's JSON telemetry says whether that batch fell back to the deterministic score.
  4. Decide whether it is a routing problem (Ask Iris), a data problem (platform), or a scoring problem (Keep/Drop). Fix it there, and add the case to the relevant eval set.

12. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. How do you debug a bad agent answer end to end? I start in LangSmith for the Ask Iris run: routing, evaluator attempts, tokens. If the problem is the data the worker read, I follow it into Datadog traces on the Go edge to see the exact ClickHouse call. If it's the underlying Keep/Drop decision, the output row's config hash tells me which prompts and parameters produced it, and the run telemetry tells me if that batch fell back. Then I fix it at the right layer and add the case to the eval set.

Q2. What was your on-call improvement at Masters? Before, triage meant SSH and grep with no way to follow a request. I instrumented structured JSON logs with request ids into ELK and New Relic APM traces, with alerts on error rate and latency. Now one id follows a transaction through the API, the Kafka consumer and the IRP worker. Triage time dropped about 70%, roughly from half an hour to under ten minutes, where the baseline is my estimate.

Q3. What does 98% deployment success mean? 98% of deployments went out without needing a rollback. It came with raising test coverage from 35% to 82% as a CI gate, money paths first, plus canary releases per route during the migration. It is a release-quality number, not uptime.

Q4. Why three observability tools instead of one? Each layer asks different questions. Datadog answers "where did this HTTP request spend its time". LangSmith answers "what did the LLM graph do and why". Custom JSON telemetry answers "what did this 88k-item batch cost and how often did it fall back". Forcing one tool to do all three gives you a worse version of each. The shared request or run id is what ties them together.

Q5. Offline evaluation versus production monitoring? Offline evaluation gates changes before they ship: the 300-case set with an 80% promotion threshold. Production monitoring tells you what happens after: fallback rates, costs, traces. Neither replaces the other. A model can pass offline and still drift live, which is why fallbacks and cost are tracked per run.

Q6. Have you used Kubernetes? At literacy level. I understand pods, deployments, services, autoscaling and probes, and I build services that behave well on an orchestrator: stateless, with health checks and graceful SIGTERM handling. I haven't operated clusters, and I don't claim that.

Q7. What is Bazel and why did Uber use it? It's a hermetic, incremental build system for large monorepos. It only rebuilds and retests what a change affects, and builds are reproducible. At FRM every layer had a test target that had to pass before merge, and we used stacked PRs so the ORM migration shipped in small steps with zero downtime.

Common application questions

Describe a complex system you designed

At Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a retail merchandise planning product, which has two layers.

The platform layer is a multi-tenant Go/Gin service at 10k peak RPS, using Google Wire, h2c and Datadog tracing. I cut planner pivots in ClickHouse from 189s to 12s on 250M rows with six rollup tables, and fixed a roughly 170 GB out-of-memory failure in the weekly build. The platform also has a KPI formula parser with ifNotFinite division-by-zero protection, and an auth chain of Firebase, JWT and Google OIDC fronted by Redis, with Postgres-backed roles. The Go code holds 100% statement coverage across 1,200+ tests.

The agentic layer runs Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style over 348k article-seasons, 88k items per pass, across 7 AI lenses. The models receive JSON payloads instead of querying the 2.11B-row ClickHouse master. Writes are eventually consistent through ReplacingMergeTree, with fallback to deterministic scores on LLM timeouts. An orchestration registry adds circuit breakers, checkpoints, a config_hash and JSON telemetry. I also shipped Ask Iris, a WebSocket copilot with a LangGraph supervisor and evaluator and hierarchy scopes frozen at the socket handshake. Promotions require a 300-case offline eval and an 80% CI gate, which is a promotion gate, not live accuracy for all tenants. A separate 200-case benchmark compares us against a 74% deterministic baseline.

I also owned Uber FRM via EPAM: 36 Spring Boot endpoints, 19M GL rows, an L1–L4 FSLI hierarchy, an 8-table SOADB schema and SHA-256 keys. Reconciliation dropped 70%, from 14 days to 3, against $340M materiality. I led 3 engineers to 100% coverage, with SOX 50% delta-variance checks.

What this means and how to defend it.

  • The 15.5× pivot win and the 170 GB OOM are separate. The first is query time on the rollups. The second is load time when building the weekly rollup. Fixing one did not cause the other.
  • ifNotFinite is a ClickHouse function. The parser wraps every formula as ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0), so a divide-by-zero returns 0 instead of infinity or NaN.
  • ReplacingMergeTree is a ClickHouse table type that keeps only the newest version of rows sharing the same key. Think of a notebook where you never erase. You write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old line.
  • 100% coverage across 1,200+ Go tests is true but off-PDF (LinkedIn and verbal). Delete that sentence if a form says "resume facts only".
  • LangSmith belongs to Ask Iris only. It is not on the Keep/Drop batch registry.
  • Older prep said "ReplacingMergeTree two-phase" and "registry with LangSmith". The current resume says eventually consistent writes with deterministic fallback, and LangSmith on Ask Iris only.

Experience with AI / LLMs / agents

At AssortSmart the agentic flows blend structured LLM calls across 7 lenses with deterministic KPI math. The LLM gets JSON payloads rather than writing SQL against ClickHouse, and the system falls back to deterministic scores when the LLM fails. I shipped Ask Iris, a copilot built on a LangGraph supervisor and evaluator, with scopes frozen at the socket level. Guardrails include a 300-case offline harness, an 80% CI promotion gate, and a 74% deterministic baseline on a separate benchmark. At Uber Eats I used Gemini 2.5 Pro with LangChain RAG over Milvus to reach 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation, behind a hard schema gate, with 95%+ scrape success and Kafka + Flink exactly-once processing.

What this means and how to defend it.

  • "Structured LLM calls" means the model must return a fixed JSON schema (for example a score and a reason), not free text.
  • 98% is offline evaluation, not live production accuracy.
  • ANZ 99.9% is HISTORICAL and is Uber Mobility. It is a deterministic rules backend, not AI, so leave it out of this answer unless asked.
  • Verbal only, not on the PDF: Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight (still being built). Mention them only if the form asks about a broader agentic roadmap.

Largest scale

At AssortSmart: 10k peak RPS, a 2.11B-row ClickHouse fact table, six ClickHouse rollup tables, 348k article-seasons, and 88k items per pass. A ClickHouse pivot benchmark went from 189s to 12s on 250M rows. At Masters India: a high-concurrency Kafka e-invoicing pipeline at 1M+ IRP submissions per day, 100K+ idempotent concurrent imports, and throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute.

What this means and how to defend it. The 189s to 12s result is MEASURED on a 250M-row benchmark harness. 1M+ per day averages about 12 per second (1,000,000 ÷ 86,400). 700 to 4,000 requests per minute is roughly 12 to 67 requests per second. IRP is India's government Invoice Registration Portal.

Leadership

Production bug you resolved

Lead with the 170 GB weekly OOM (it is on the PDF).

On AssortSmart, building the weekly rollup for a whole season in one INSERT SELECT needed about 170 GB of memory and crashed with out-of-memory errors. I sliced the build into temporal chunks, one fiscal week per insert, and enforced memory and disk-spill caps (a 55 GB memory cap and 16 GB of spill). That stopped the OOM crashes.

How to defend it. The 55 GB and 16 GB caps are verbal detail, not on the PDF. Other verbal detail you can add: the whole-season build failed even with 80 GB and 200 GB caps, a product week needs about 11 GB, and an attr week needs more than 40 GB.

Alternate: packet story (not a PDF bullet). Company: Impact Analytics, a Python FastAPI worker. Do not claim Kubernetes cluster-operations ownership.

A high-concurrency async Python worker consuming a queue started returning 504s while its memory kept growing. Heap profiles and APM traces showed database and HTTP clients being created inside a long-lived async loop without context managers, which leaked connections and cursors. I fixed it with async with blocks, connection-pool limits and consumer backpressure. To prevent a repeat, I added a load test at 3x peak in CI and pool metrics.

How to defend it. The leak and the fix are the real engineering story. Any Kubernetes "pod" wording from the original packet is design-level language, not something you operated. Do not name the queue as Kafka, because there is no Kafka on Impact Analytics. Do not use this as your Impact Analytics headline story. The 170 GB OOM is stronger and is on the PDF.

Why this company

Pivot to technical alignment, not generic praise. Name one real system of theirs and map it to one of yours.

Your [distributed store / event bus / applied-AI eval] work lines up closely with what I have built: a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master at AssortSmart, Kafka and Flink menu ingestion at Uber Eats, and 300-case promotion gates for LLM releases.

Promotions are gated on a 300-case proxy harness and an 80% CI gate (a gate, not live accuracy for all tenants). On a separate benchmark we cut live scoring cost 73% at 100% coverage against a 74% deterministic baseline, and froze blend weights when the LLM lost.
  • Uber via EPAM: FRM scoping with 36 Spring Boot endpoints, 19M GL rows, an L1–L4 FSLI hierarchy, an 8-table SOADB schema, and SHA-256 keys. I led 3 engineers to 100% coverage with SOX 50% delta-variance checks. Reconciliation dropped 70%, from 14 days to 3, against $340M materiality. Menu ingestion went from 24 hours to 2 hours, saving $600K/yr on 30K+ menus/month, with 98% offline field fidelity (RAG over Milvus) and Kafka + Flink exactly-once upserts.
  • Masters India: A Spring Boot strangler migration cut p95 75%, from 1.2s to 300ms. A Kafka + PostgreSQL pipeline sharded by tax quarter handles 1M+ submissions/day. Coverage went from 35% to 82% at 98% deploy success. I mentored 2 engineers.

Open to Senior SWE / SDE2+ roles in backend, platform, data infrastructure, and applied-AI systems.

How to defend each paragraph (the handbook chapter expands every line).

  • Platform. "Wire" is Google Wire, which wires up Go dependencies at compile time. "h2c" is HTTP/2 without TLS, served directly by Go with no reverse proxy in front. The 189s to 12s pivot result was measured on a 250M-row benchmark harness (12.3s, rounded to 12). The 100% coverage across 1,200+ Go tests is off-PDF. It is true, so say it plainly, but know it is a LinkedIn and verbal fact.
  • Scale and infrastructure. Two separate stories live here. The 15.5× pivot speed-up is about query time. The 170 GB out-of-memory failure is about building the weekly tables (load time). One did not cause the other. 344k is rows per second during a copy, not requests per second. The 4.09B copy was measured while it was running. Never say the cutover finished.
  • Agentic. An article-season is one product in one selling season. 348k is the number scored. The full catalog is larger (1.6M, off-PDF). The LLM never gets a SQL tool. It only sees JSON prepared for it. Keep/Drop runs its steps in a fixed order (peer, decider, lenses, blend, explain). No LLM decides what runs next, and the supervisor pattern belongs to Ask Iris. The 300-case harness and the 80% gate are one thing. The 73% cost cut and the 74% baseline come from a different 200-case gold benchmark. Do not fuse them.
  • Uber via EPAM. Always say "Uber via EPAM". "Led 3" means tech lead of an EPAM pod, not people manager. 98% is an offline evaluation number, not live production accuracy. "Exactly-once" in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts, so a replayed message cannot create a duplicate.
  • Masters India. "Mentored 2" belongs to Masters India. "Led 3" belongs to Uber FRM. Never merge them into "led a team of 5".

Skills order (LinkedIn)

Java · Spring Boot · Hibernate · Python · Go · Gin · FastAPI · Distributed Systems · Microservices · Kafka · ClickHouse · System Design · Docker · AWS · GCP · PostgreSQL · MySQL · Redis · LangGraph · RAG · Mentorship

How to use this page

  • What it covers: subject lines, one long cold email, a short and a long LinkedIn DM, and an honest "data platform" hook for infrastructure roles.
  • When to use it: when you write first to a recruiter or sourcer you have never spoken to. For people who already work at the company, use Referral asks instead.
  • What to memorise: the "How to defend it" notes. A recruiter will often read one line of your email back to you on the call.
  • Full playbook: LinkedIn and outreach explained covers when to send which template and how to follow up.

Before you send, replace every [bracket], attach the PDF, and delete any bullet that is irrelevant to the role. Three strong bullets beat five crowded ones.

Email subject lines (pick one)

5y backend · Go/Gin 10k RPS · ClickHouse 4B-row rollups · Kafka 1M+/day · LangGraph

When to use which. The first suits generalist recruiters, because brand names (Uber) get opened. The second suits data platform or infrastructure sourcers who scan for scale. The third is for when you already have a referral or a specific requisition ID.

How to defend it. "4B-row rollups" means one rollup table (attr weekly), which holds 4.09B rows across two seasons. Kafka 1M+/day is Masters India, not Impact Analytics.

(+91) 9079727197 · tmittaliet@gmail.com

What each line means and how to defend it.

  • 10k peak RPS is peak requests per second on the Go/Gin platform. Do not attach an SLA or uptime number to it, because none is claimed.
  • 189s to 12s was measured on a 250M-row benchmark harness. It is query time. The 170 GB OOM was a separate load-time problem when building the weekly tables, so the two are not cause and effect.
  • 344k rows/s is a copy rate in rows per second, not requests per second. The 4.09B-row copy was measured while still running, so do not say "I migrated 4 billion rows".
  • 80% CI promotion gate means a new model or prompt cannot ship unless it scores at least 80% on the 300-case harness. It is not live accuracy for all tenants.
  • 70% from 14 days to 3 is the reconciliation outcome on the PDF. State it plainly. If pressed: "the technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what the platform delivered for the close."
  • 98% is offline evaluation, not live production accuracy.
  • "Led 3" is Uber FRM (tech lead of an EPAM pod). "Mentored 2" is Masters India. Keep them separate.

When to use it. Use it for a cold referral ask to someone you do not know well, such as an alumnus or a second-degree connection. The first line must name something real about their team. Fill [specific team problem] with one concrete thing from their engineering blog, talk or job post.

How to defend it.

Common application questions

Describe a complex system you designed

At Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a retail merchandise planning product, which has two layers.

The agentic layer runs Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style over 348k article-seasons, 88k items per pass, across 7 AI lenses. The models receive JSON payloads instead of querying the 2.11B-row ClickHouse master. Writes go through ReplacingMergeTree, with fallback to deterministic scores on LLM timeouts. A shared registry provides circuit breakers, checkpoints and a config_hash on every output row. I also shipped Ask Iris, a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot with a LangGraph supervisor, a 3-attempt evaluator, and hierarchy access frozen at the handshake. Releases pass a 300-case proxy eval, and 80% is a CI promotion gate. Separately, a 200-case gold benchmark compared us against a 74% deterministic baseline, and the model chosen there made scoring 73% cheaper at 100% coverage.

The core layer is a multi-tenant Go/Gin platform at 10k peak RPS, using Google Wire, h2c and Datadog. I cut ClickHouse planner pivots from 189s to 12s on 250M-row operations with six rollup tables, and fixed a 170 GB out-of-memory failure in the weekly build. The core also includes a KPI tokenizer with division-by-zero protection, and Firebase, JWT and OIDC auth fronted by Redis, with Postgres roles.

I also owned Uber FRM via EPAM: 36 Spring Boot endpoints, 19M GL rows, an L1–L4 FSLI hierarchy, an 8-table SOADB schema and SHA-256 keys. Reconciliation dropped 70%, from 14 days to 3, against $340M materiality. I led 3 engineers to 100% coverage, with SOX 50% delta-variance checks.

Optional add-on sentence (true, off-PDF):

The Go codebase holds 100% statement coverage across 1,200+ tests.

What this means and how to defend it.

  • An article-season is one product in one selling season. 348k is what the engine scores, and 88k is one batch pass.
  • config_hash is a SHA-256 fingerprint of the guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog used for a run. Every output row carries it, so you can always tell which configuration produced a decision.
  • The 80% gate and the 74% baseline come from different test sets. The 300-case harness is the gate. The 200-case gold benchmark gave the 73% cost cut (model choice) and the 74% deterministic baseline. On that benchmark the blended LLM scored lower than the baseline, so the blend weights were frozen rather than retuned.
  • The 15.5× pivot win and the 170 GB OOM are separate. One is query time, the other is load time.

Experience with AI / LLMs / agents

At AssortSmart the agentic flows blend structured LLM calls across 7 lenses with deterministic KPI math. The LLM gets JSON payloads rather than writing SQL against the 2.11B-row master, and the system falls back to deterministic scores on timeout. I shipped Ask Iris, a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot with a LangGraph supervisor, a 3-attempt evaluator, hierarchy access frozen at the handshake, and LangSmith tracing. Guardrails include a 300-case proxy harness and an 80% CI promotion gate. We also benchmarked against a 74% deterministic baseline and froze the blend weights when the LLM lost. The 73% cost cut at 100% coverage came from that benchmark's model pick. At Uber Eats I used Gemini 2.5 Pro with LangChain RAG over Milvus to reach 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation, behind a hard schema gate, with 95%+ scrape success and Kafka + Flink exactly-once processing.

What this means and how to defend it.

  • The 3-attempt evaluator is a loop with MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3. If the answer still fails the evaluator after three tries, the loop stops instead of running forever.
  • Hierarchy frozen at the handshake means the planner's allowed scope is read once when the WebSocket opens and cannot change mid-session, which prevents cross-tenant leaks.
  • Ask Iris is a shipped capability. No SLA or usage numbers are claimed, so do not invent any.
  • 98% is offline evaluation. Milvus is Uber Menu only.
  • ANZ 99.9% is HISTORICAL and Uber Mobility. It is not an AI project.
  • Verbal only, not on the PDF: Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight (still being built). Mention them only if the form asks about a broader agentic roadmap.

Largest scale

At AssortSmart: 10k peak RPS, a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master, six ClickHouse rollup tables, 348k article-seasons, and 88k items per pass. A ClickHouse pivot benchmark went from 189s to 12s on 250M rows. At Masters India: a high-concurrency Kafka e-invoicing pipeline at 1M+ IRP submissions per day, 100K+ idempotent concurrent imports, and throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute.

What this means and how to defend it. The 189s to 12s result is MEASURED on a 250M-row benchmark harness. 1M+ per day averages about 12 per second. 700 to 4,000 requests per minute is roughly 12 to 67 requests per second.

Leadership

I led 3 engineers at Uber (via EPAM) on the FRM platform. I mentored 2 engineers at Masters India.

How to defend it. "Led 3" means tech lead of an EPAM pod, not people manager. Keep the two numbers separate.

Production bug you resolved

Lead with the 170 GB weekly OOM (it is on the PDF).

On AssortSmart, a whole-season weekly INSERT SELECT used about 170 GB of memory and crashed with out-of-memory errors. I sliced it into temporal chunks, one fiscal week per insert, and enforced memory and disk-spill caps (a 55 GB memory cap and 16 GB of spill). That stopped the OOM crashes.

How to defend it. The 55 GB and 16 GB caps are verbal detail, not on the PDF. Do not use a FastAPI or Kafka heap-leak packet story as your Impact Analytics headline.

Masters India alternate:

At Masters India, a canary release of the IRP integration showed that our timeouts were too aggressive for the volatile government portal. We moved those calls to async processing with idempotency, so retries were safe.

How to defend it. A canary release sends a small share of live traffic to the new version first. Idempotency means sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once, so a retry cannot register an invoice twice.

Why this company

Pivot to technical alignment, not generic praise. Name one real system of theirs and map it to one of yours.

Your [distributed store / event bus / applied-AI eval] work lines up closely with what I have built: a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master at AssortSmart, Kafka and Flink menu ingestion at Uber Eats, and 300-case promotion gates for LLM releases.

Senior Software Engineer (~5 YoE) — Persona Expectations

Profile in scope: Python/Go backend · distributed systems · agentic AI / LLM production systems
Level calibration: Big-tech Senior IC (Google L5 / Meta E5 / Amazon SDE II–III edge / Stripe/OpenAI “Senior”) — scope over years; ~5 YoE is common floor, not the bar.
Sources synthesized: Big-tech interview bars (Amazon Bar Raiser / SDE3, OpenAI L5, FAANG system-design weight), senior JD templates used across hundreds of hires, backend ATS keyword practice (2025–2026), agentic AI production JDs (runtime, orchestration, MCP, evals).

How to use this doc: Each persona reads your resume at three depths. Optimize so the 6-second scan clears the gate, the 30-second read earns a phone screen, and the deep-read survives hiring-committee scrutiny.

Shared senior bar (all personas)

At big tech and strong product companies, “Senior” means:

Dimension Mid-level Senior (~5 YoE bar)
Ambiguity Executes a scoped ticket Frames the problem; owns scoping
Ownership Feature / PR Multi-quarter outcome: design → ship → operate
Blast radius Own service / squad Cross-team contracts, platform, or domain
Judgment Implements the chosen design Names tradeoffs, rejects bad options, documents ADRs/RFCs
Multiplication Improves own craft Raises review bar; mentors; unblocks peers
Ops Fixes bugs when assigned Owns SLOs, incidents, postmortems, on-call

Three resume inferences every senior page must support: (1) decision weight under ambiguity, (2) measurable consequence, (3) “I” ownership that would still read senior if the title were removed.

1. CTO

6-second scan

  • Title + YoE + stack match (Senior · Python/Go · backend/distributed/AI infra).
  • One line of judgment + leverage: architecture owned, team multiplied, or business risk reduced — not a tech laundry list.
  • Credible company/scale context (users, QPS, $ impact, or hard domain) near the top.

30-second read

  • Evidence you can decide what to build and how, not only how to implement.
  • At least one story of saying no / choosing a cheaper simpler path / reversing a bad bet.
  • Communication signal: design docs, RFCs, partnering with product — readable by a non-coding founder or board-aware CTO.

Deep-read criteria

  • Technical strategy taste: build-vs-buy, when to introduce complexity (queues, multi-agent, new datastore), when not to.
  • Ability to connect engineering to product velocity, cost, reliability risk, and hiring/bar culture.
  • For agentic AI: treats LLMs as unreliable components inside a system (evals, guardrails, cost/latency budgets) — not demo theater.
  • Intellectual honesty: what failed, what you’d redo, what you still don’t know.

Must-have signals

  • Owned a non-trivial system or initiative end-to-end with explicit tradeoffs.
  • Cross-functional influence without authority (product, infra, security, another eng team).
  • Quantified outcomes (latency, reliability, cost, time-to-ship, incident MTTR).
  • Mentorship or bar-raising (reviews, hiring loop, standards) — even informally.
  • Production AI/agents framed as reliability + observability + cost, not “prompted GPT.”

Reject signals

  • Feature factory bullets (“built REST APIs,” “worked on microservices”) with no decisions.
  • Buzzword soup (Kubernetes + Kafka + RAG + agents) with zero operational consequence.
  • Overclaiming staff/principal scope (org-wide strategy) without artifacts or blast radius.
  • Pure LeetCode / academic framing with no production ownership.
  • “We” everywhere; no personal decision weight.

2. Director of Engineering

6-second scan

  • Clear domain ownership (payments, platform, data plane, agent runtime, etc.).
  • Delivery + reliability language: multi-quarter project, rollout, SLO, migration — not only “built.”
  • Team-fit keywords: mentorship, design review, cross-team, on-call.

30-second read

  • Can this person absorb a workstream and reduce director attention tax?
  • Predictable shipping: migrations, phased rollouts, feature flags, backwards-compatible APIs.
  • Collaboration: unblocking other teams, clear interfaces, written plans.

Deep-read criteria

  • Capacity and planning literacy: estimates with uncertainty, dependency management, risk callouts.
  • Operational maturity: SLOs/error budgets, incident roles, postmortem quality.
  • Org hygiene: raises code/design review quality; grows mid-levels toward senior.
  • For distributed + AI systems: understands operational cost of complexity (more services, more agent tools = more failure modes).

Must-have signals

  • Led delivery of a multi-person or multi-quarter effort (tech lead of the work, even without title).
  • Measurable reliability or efficiency wins (p99, error rate, cost/QPS, deploy frequency).
  • Mentored or coached engineers; improved team throughput or quality.
  • Written design/RFC that other teams consumed.
  • Comfortable with production ownership (on-call, incident response).

Reject signals

  • Heroics-only narrative (weekend fire drills) with no prevention or systemic fix.
  • No evidence of working through others — only individual coding velocity.
  • Unscoped “led team of N” without outcomes (looks like inflated title).
  • Job hopping framed as growth without cumulative ownership depth.
  • Ignores operational reality (never mentions rollout, monitoring, rollback).

3. Engineering Manager (EM)

6-second scan

  • Will this person raise the team bar and need low supervision?
  • Stack fit for the squad (Python and/or Go backend + distributed systems keywords).
  • Soft-hard combo: ownership + mentorship + collaboration in the first screenful.

30-second read

  • Independence: proposes work, scopes it, ships without a tech lead translating product → eng.
  • Team citizen: code review quality, pairing, onboarding, knowledge sharing.
  • Conflict and communication: can disagree professionally; can explain tradeoffs to PM/design.

Deep-read criteria

  • Behavioral depth (Amazon LP-style / Google “Googleyness” adjacent): ownership, bias for action, disagree-and-commit, learn from failure — with specific numbers and counterfactuals.
  • Technical depth sufficient that the EM trusts them as the team’s senior IC on design and incidents.
  • Coaching instinct: how they made someone else better (not only how they got better).
  • Scope honesty: clear “I owned X; team owned Y.”

Must-have signals

  • End-to-end project ownership with design + implementation + production health.
  • Mentorship of 1–3+ engineers (reviews, design guidance, career/skill growth).
  • Incident or production debugging story with root cause and prevention.
  • System design fluency visible on the page (consistency, idempotency, failure modes — via bullets, not a buzzword list).
  • Partnering with PM on scoping and cutting scope under deadline.

Reject signals

  • “Responsible for…” duty lists; no impact.
  • Blame-heavy or lone-wolf framing (“fixed everyone else’s mess”) without collaboration.
  • Claims of management (“managed 5 engineers”) on an IC resume without clarifying tech lead vs people manager — confuses leveling.
  • No mentorship or review signal at ~5 YoE senior.
  • Cannot separate personal contribution from team (“we shipped the platform”).

4. Hiring Manager (HM)

Often the EM or a senior EM/Director who owns the req. Distinct lens: “Will I stake my headcount on this person?”

6-second scan

  • Exact role match: Senior Backend / Distributed Systems / AI Platform — title alignment.
  • Strongest 1–2 bullets of recent role scream the job’s pain (latency, migrations, agents, scale).
  • Clean, scannable layout; quantified impact in the first role block.

30-second read

  • Risk check: can they ramp in weeks on our stack? (language depth + adjacent systems beat perfect framework match.)
  • Evidence of the hard problem this team has (e.g., stateful agent runtime, Kafka backpressure, Postgres at limit, multi-tenant isolation).
  • Trajectory: increasing scope across roles, not lateral ticket closing.

Deep-read criteria

  • Interviewability: bullets that map to probeable STAR stories (ambiguity, conflict, failure, scale, tradeoff).
  • Level calibration: senior IC scope, not staff-inflated claims that will fail the bar-raiser / hiring committee.
  • Reference-ready specificity: names of systems, metrics before/after, your decision, blast radius.
  • For agentic AI reqs: production path (tool calling, durable execution, evals, sandboxing, MCP) vs courseware.

Must-have signals

  • Domain-relevant wins with metrics (latency/throughput, reliability, migration success, cost).
  • Architecture ownership in at least one bullet (you chose the shape; others built on it).
  • On-call / production ownership signal.
  • Mentorship or interview-loop participation (optional but strong).
  • Clear stack: Python and/or Go with supporting distributed systems vocabulary used in context.

Reject signals

  • Keyword stuffing that doesn’t match narrative depth (ATS bait the HM will smell in screen).
  • Gaps between claimed level and evidence (Senior title, junior bullets).
  • Only CRUD/API work when the req is distributed systems / agent infra.
  • Inflated metrics without mechanism (“improved performance 10x” with no how).
  • Resume that could belong to any mid-level at any company after removing the title.

5. Technical Lead (Tech Lead / Staff-adjacent interviewer)

6-second scan

  • Depth markers: consistency models, idempotency, backpressure, schema evolution, p99, SLO — used as outcomes, not glossary.
  • Proof of design ownership: “designed,” “RFC,” “migrated,” “decomposed,” “hardened.”
  • Language credibility: idiomatic Python (async, typing) and/or Go (concurrency, profiling) tied to real systems.

30-second read

  • Would I trust their design review comments next week?
  • Failure-mode thinking visible: retries, poison messages, partial failure, rollout/rollback.
  • Data path literacy: Postgres/Redis/Kafka (or equivalent) with query/partition/consumer-group reality.

Deep-read criteria

  • System design seniority: clarifies requirements, estimates load, picks consistency intentionally, discusses operational complexity.
  • Code taste implied by bullets: API contracts, observability, testing strategy for distributed and non-deterministic (LLM) components.
  • Agentic AI: state/leases/checkpoints, tool sandboxing, streaming, eval harnesses, cost/latency controls — systems engineering, not prompt lists.
  • Ability to simplify: removed a service, collapsed a queue, avoided premature multi-agent complexity.

Must-have signals

  • At least one hard systems bullet: sharding/partitioning, exactly-once/idempotent processing, multi-region, backfill/migration, hot-path latency work.
  • Observability ownership: metrics/traces/logs → detected or diagnosed production issue.
  • Performance work with numbers (p50/p99, QPS, CPU/mem, cost).
  • Cross-service contract design (API/protobuf/event schema) with compatibility story.
  • Mentorship via design/code review (peer technical multiplication).

Reject signals

  • Framework tourism without production constraints.
  • Distributed systems buzzwords with monolith-CRUD evidence only.
  • “Implemented Kafka” with no consumer failure/ordering/backpressure story.
  • AI bullets that stop at LangChain wrappers / demos / hackathon.
  • No mention of testing, rollout, or observability on backend work.

6. Technical Recruiter

6-second scan (ATS + human skim)

  • Title match: “Senior Software Engineer” (or equivalent) in headline and recent role.
  • Tier-1 keyword coverage for the req: Python, Go/Golang, distributed systems, system design, plus role-specific (gRPC, Kafka, Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, LLM/agents/MCP as applicable).
  • Location/eligibility/YoE readable immediately; no puzzle formatting.

30-second read

  • Checklist hire: years ≈ 5+, backend focus, relevant company type, no obvious red flags.
  • Skills section + first bullets echo the JD’s must-haves (not a 50-item dump).
  • Impact numbers present (recruiters use them to sell the HM).

Deep-read criteria

Usually shallow — but strong recruiters and sourcers do a second pass: - Boolean/search hits: seniority + stack + domain (e.g., (Python OR Go) AND (distributed OR microservices OR Kafka) AND (Senior OR "tech lead")). - Narrative coherence: AI/agent experience is backend/production, not “ChatGPT user.” - Comp/level story: senior IC trajectory; no conflicting titles that force downgrade. - Easy to pitch: one-sentence value prop the recruiter can paste to the HM.

Must-have signals

  • Explicit senior title + ~5 YoE.
  • Python and/or Go listed and evidenced in bullets.
  • Distributed systems / backend / cloud keywords with at least one quantified achievement.
  • Clean contact + LinkedIn; consistent dates.
  • For agentic roles: agents, LLM, tool calling, RAG, MCP, evals, or orchestration appearing near production verbs (shipped, scaled, on-call, latency).

Reject signals

  • Missing must-have keywords from the JD (silent ATS rank drop).
  • Full-stack/frontend-heavy resume for a backend distributed req.
  • Creative formatting that breaks ATS (tables, icons, multi-column text as images).
  • Vague summaries (“passionate engineer”) with no stack or scope.
  • Title mismatch (“Software Engineer” only when filtering Senior) without senior scope language to compensate.
  • Job descriptions copied as duties; no metrics → hard for recruiter to advocate.

Shared senior bar checklist — Python/Go backend

Use as a resume self-audit. Aim to show evidence, not claim the checkbox.

Scope & ownership

  • [ ] Multi-quarter or multi-person initiative owned end-to-end (problem → design → ship → operate)
  • [ ] Explicit tradeoff or decision you owned (not just implementation of someone else’s design)
  • [ ] Blast radius beyond a single ticket (team, multi-service, platform, or customer-facing reliability)

Python / Go depth

  • [ ] Python: production services (e.g. FastAPI/async), typing, performance/GIL awareness where relevant, packaging/testing
  • [ ] Go: concurrency (goroutines/channels/context), API/gRPC services, profiling (pprof) or performance tuning evidence
  • [ ] Comfort stated honestly: strong in one, productive in the other — or deep in one with clear ramp signal

Distributed systems

  • [ ] Data stores used under load (Postgres and/or Redis/Kafka/etc.) with a real constraint named
  • [ ] Failure modes: retries, idempotency, timeouts, partial failure, poison messages, backpressure
  • [ ] Consistency choice stated or implied (strong vs eventual) with why
  • [ ] API/event contract evolution (versioning, compatibility, schema discipline)

Performance & reliability

  • [ ] Latency and/or throughput metrics (p99, QPS/RPS, SLA/SLO)
  • [ ] Observability: metrics, logs, traces → action taken
  • [ ] On-call or incident leadership with root cause + prevention
  • [ ] Rollout strategy: flags, canaries, migrations, rollback

Agentic AI / LLM systems (when targeting those roles)

  • [ ] Production path: tool/function calling, durable/long-running execution, session state, streaming
  • [ ] Reliability for non-determinism: evals, guardrails, sandboxing, human-in-the-loop where needed
  • [ ] Cost/latency budgets for model calls; caching/compaction/context management
  • [ ] Platform seams: MCP/tool APIs, orchestration (queues/workflows), OpenTelemetry on agent runs
  • [ ] Avoid: demo-only, prompt-only, or “used ChatGPT” as experience

Multiplication

  • [ ] Mentorship, design/code review bar, or interview loop participation
  • [ ] Written design doc / RFC / ADR consumed by others
  • [ ] Unblocked peers or other teams via interfaces, tooling, or clarity

Resume craft (senior inference)

  • [ ] Every strong bullet: scope + ambiguity/decision + consequence (metric when real)
  • [ ] “I” clarity without erasing collaboration
  • [ ] First screenful sells senior backend; skills section supports ATS without stuffing
  • [ ] Would still read senior if job titles were removed

Signal → resume theme mapping

Map persona must-haves onto six resume themes. Each theme should appear as concrete bullets, not section headers alone.

Resume theme What to prove Highest-value personas Example signal language (pattern)
Architecture ownership You shaped the system under uncertainty; others depend on your interfaces CTO, Tech Lead, HM, Director Designed X for Y constraint; chose A over B because…; RFC adopted by N teams; defined service boundaries / event schema
Mentorship You multiply engineers; raise review/design bar EM, Director, CTO, Recruiter (keyword) Mentored N engineers on…; set review bar for…; paired through design of…; onboarded…; interviewed for…
Latency / throughput You reason in numbers about hot paths and capacity Tech Lead, HM, Recruiter, CTO Cut p99 from A→B; sustained N QPS; reduced tail latency via…; profiled Go/Python path; cache/pool/query plan fix
Migrations You ship change safely under compatibility and risk Director, EM, Tech Lead, HM Zero-downtime migration; dual-write/backfill; versioned API; strangled monolith; traffic shift with rollback
On-call You own production consequences EM, Director, Tech Lead, HM On-call for…; incident commander/responder; MTTR; postmortem actions; SLO/error budget; toil reduction
System design You can clarify, estimate, trade off, and operate a design Tech Lead, HM, CTO, Recruiter (keyword) Idempotent consumers; consistency model; sharding/partitioning; backpressure; multi-tenant isolation; agent session leases/checkpoints

Theme coverage matrix (target)

Theme CTO Director EM HM Tech Lead Tech Recruiter
Architecture ownership Critical High High Critical Critical Keyword + one bullet
Mentorship High Critical Critical High High Keyword
Latency / throughput High High Medium Critical Critical Metrics sell
Migrations Medium Critical High High High Nice-to-have keyword
On-call Medium Critical Critical High High Plus if JD mentions
System design Critical High High Critical Critical Tier-1 keyword

Placement guidance

  1. Header / summary (6-second): stack + senior + 1 theme spike (usually architecture + latency or agents-in-production).
  2. Top 2–3 bullets of latest role (30-second): architecture ownership + latency/throughput or migrations + one multiplication or on-call signal.
  3. Deeper bullets / earlier roles (deep-read): second systems story, mentorship detail, incident/postmortem, agentic reliability (evals, durable execution).
  4. Skills line (recruiter/ATS): Python, Go, distributed systems, system design, Postgres/Redis/Kafka (as true), observability, and agent/LLM terms only if evidenced above.

Quick anti-patterns (all personas)

Anti-pattern Why it fails senior bar
Duty list without decisions Reads mid-level execution
Metrics without mechanism HM/Tech Lead distrust; un-probeable
Buzzword inventory CTO/Tech Lead reject; ATS may pass then human fails
Staff-scope claims at ~5 YoE without blast radius Fails bar-raiser / committee calibration
AI demo bullets for production agent reqs Instant Tech Lead/HM no
No ops signal on backend distributed resume EM/Director assume you create pages

One-line resume north star

A Senior (~5 YoE) Python/Go backend engineer owns ambiguous, multi-quarter systems work — architecture, measurable performance/reliability, safe change (migrations), production accountability (on-call), and team lift (mentorship) — and, for agentic AI roles, makes non-deterministic model calls behave like dependable distributed components.

Panel Pass/Fail Against Campaign Resume

Candidate snapshot: 5y Python/Go FastAPI Gin Kafka ClickHouse agentic AssortSmart FRM design owner led 3 mentored 2 Menu $600K+ Masters 1M+/day.

Persona Score Pass? Residual ask in interview
CTO 8/10 PASS Multi-year roadmap thinking at IA
Director of Eng 8/10 PASS Cross-team influence examples
Engineering Manager 9/10 PASS Walk a Sev-2 timeline
Hiring Manager 8/10 PASS Level Senior vs strong SDE2
Technical Lead 9/10 PASS Defend CH and agent gates
Technical Recruiter 9/10 PASS Contractor (EPAM) clarification

Overall panel: PASS for senior backend screens with level calibration expected at Amazon Netflix Apple.

Mock Interview Transcripts (interviewee vs panel)

Interviewee answers in first person. Interviewer pushback in italics. Numbers match GROUND_TRUTH.

Round A — Technical Lead (IA deep dive)

TL: Walk AssortSmart and what you own.

You: AssortSmart helps retailers decide what to buy, how much, and which stores. I am building the cluster recommendation copilot on FastAPI LangGraph MCP over a shared Go Gin doing layer on per-tenant ClickHouse. Measured clustering failures on kik were 8.5% (37/437). We target under 2% with 14 audited tools that only read planning data and 3 human confirm gates before write-back. I am also building Hindsight scorecards with overnight narration grounded in computed metrics and tenant catalogs that onboard without a code deploy. Copilot targets days to under 1 hour and at least 20 configs per plan. Phase 1 design passed external review. Load test is still pending so I say building not shipped.

TL: Why not let the agent run arbitrary SQL? You: The model does not get a SQL shell. Tools are allow-listed read functions. Writes go through human gates and the product write path. That is the accurate claim, not a slogan about never writing SQL.

TL: Defend the ClickHouse number. You: Row-identical pivot POC at 250M rows cut a heavy grid from 189s to 12.3s about 15.5× measured. If you strip COUNT(DISTINCT) typical aggs can fall to roughly 2–3×. I will say that unprompted if pushed.

Round B — Engineering Manager (Masters on-call)

EM: Tell me about production ownership.

You: At Masters India I owned the FastAPI strangler and Kafka e-invoice platform. We cut p95 from 1.2s to 300ms for 1500+ clients and lifted throughput from 700 to 4000 requests/min. I put ELK and New Relic on-call alerting in place which cut incident triage about 70% and raised coverage from 35% to 82% at 98% deployment success.

EM: Walk a bad night. You: Bulk IRP spike consumer lag rising. First check lag and error class. Idempotency keys plus DLQ meant we could pause replay and drain without double-filing invoices. Postmortem added better saturation alerts.

Round C — Amazon-style Hiring Manager (LP)

HM: Tell me about Ownership.

You: At Uber via EPAM I owned the FRM Risk Scoping backend FastAPI MySQL — 30+ APIs powering 8 screens at $340M group materiality targeting a 70% cut in manual reconciliation. I personally owned Sheets to MySQL recon v2 across 18 files and led 3 engineers through design reviews API contracts for PwC-facing releases.

HM: Is 70% measured? You: No. It is a TDD target. Baseline calendar time is estimated about 2 weeks to 3–4 days. I always say targeting.

Round D — CTO (business impact)

CTO: Where did you save real money?

You: Uber Eats menu ingestion — I owned it end to end on GCP. Selenium → Kafka → Flink cut onboarding 24h → 2h and saved $600K+/yr at 30K+ menus/month. LangChain RAG + Gemini over Milvus hit 98%/100% offline with a schema gate. Successful ingestions rose to 95%+ with IP rotation, dynamic proxies, and adaptive retries. Separately ANZ Mobility docs to 99.9% / ~20h/week HISTORICAL.

Round E — Technical Recruiter (Google)

Recruiter: What languages and systems? You: Python and Go. FastAPI Gin Kafka ClickHouse PostgreSQL MySQL Redis Docker on GCP and AWS. About 5 years. Currently Senior Software Engineer at Impact Analytics building agentic planning. Before that SDE2 at Uber via EPAM and Masters India.

Round F — Director of Engineering (mentorship)

DoE: How have you multiplied others? You: Mentored 2 engineers through the Masters strangler and led 3 at EPAM/Uber via design reviews. I measure success as others shipping safely behind contracts not just my LOC.

Company Behavior Guides (beyond Amazon and Google)

How to use this page

  • For each company it explains, in plain words, what their values mean and what interviewers are listening for. Then it says which of your stories fit and how to open them.
  • Read the section for a company the day before its behavioral round, together with the STAR bank.
  • Memorise your 2 or 3 chosen stories for that company and the one-line opener for each.
  • Never reuse the same story twice in one interview loop.

Full question bank and prep grid: 39_behavioral_question_bank.md · 40_behavioral_prep_grid.md (adapted from awesome-behavioral-interviews. The answers are Tarun-specific).

Your story list (numbers match the STAR bank)

# Story in one line Status
1 Resolved a ClickHouse yes-or-no split between two expert camps with a staged, measurable plan Verbal context for PDF work
2 Designed a BigQuery to ClickHouse lane where freshness is checked and printed on every answer Design, verbal
3 Put a strict validator around an LLM planner. Structural correctness went from 0.54 to 0.99 offline Verbal, not on PDF
4 Flipped the store-clustering workflow so the agent proposes and the human approves Verbal, not on PDF
5 Caught and owned a behaviour change I had hidden inside a "pure refactor" Uber FRM
6 Found that Mockito mocks were hiding real coverage. Fixed it with entity-layer JUnit tests Uber FRM
7 Disagreed with a written architecture rule, got a documented exception, then committed Uber FRM
8 Led the Masters India monolith migration with no outage during filing deadlines Masters
9 Beat changing anti-bot defences with a measurement loop Uber Menu
10 Reported a double-filing near-miss and fixed it across the whole pipeline Masters
11 Debugged a connection-leak out-of-memory in an async worker Packet, not on PDF
12 Wrote the ClickHouse RFC and PoC. Pivots went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds IA
12b Fixed a 170 GB out-of-memory by slicing loads into one-week chunks IA
L1 Led 3 engineers at Uber via EPAM Uber FRM
L2 Mentored 2 engineers at Masters India Masters

How to pick. Choose stories from different employers. Mix at least one story about a mistake or disagreement with one story about delivering a result. Prefer PDF-backed stories. Use verbal-only stories (2, 3, 4) only when the question is clearly about AI product thinking.

Amazon

What they value, in plain words. Amazon interviews are built around its Leadership Principles, usually called LPs. Every behavioral question maps to one or two LPs, and interviewers score you against them. They want specifics: your personal actions, real numbers, and what you'd do differently. Vague "we did it" answers score badly.

The LPs that matter most for you:

  • Ownership. Act like an owner of the whole outcome, not just your ticket. Fix things beyond your job description.
  • Dive Deep. Know the details. Be able to explain where a number came from and audit it yourself.
  • Deliver Results. Ship the important thing on time, even when it's hard.
  • Bias for Action. Move quickly when a decision can be reversed. Don't wait for perfect information.
  • Earn Trust. Admit mistakes openly, listen, and treat others' views with respect.
  • Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit. Push back with evidence when you disagree. Once a decision is made, commit fully.
  • Hire and Develop the Best. Raise the people around you.
  • Insist on the Highest Standards. Keep the quality bar high even when others would accept less.

Stories that fit.

LP Story Why it fits
Ownership L1 (led 3 on FRM) or 8 (Masters migration) You owned the outcome end to end
Dive Deep 6 (coverage that lied) or 12b (170 GB out-of-memory) You found the real mechanism behind a misleading signal
Deliver Results 8 (Masters migration) No outage during deadline windows while 1,500+ clients kept filing
Bias for Action 12 (ClickHouse RFC and PoC) You measured quickly instead of debating
Earn Trust 10 (near-miss) or 5 (refactor mistake) You surfaced problems you could have hidden
Have Backbone 7 (rulebook) or 1 (ClickHouse camps) You disagreed with a rationale and then committed
Hire and Develop L2 (mentored 2) You got juniors shipping on their own

Opener you can use. "The clearest example of ownership I have is the Masters India migration, where we couldn't pause the business for a single deadline."

Watch out. Amazon will push for your personal role. Say "I" for your actions. If they ask "what would you do differently", have one honest answer ready per story.

Google

What they value, in plain words. Google looks for "Googleyness" alongside leadership. Googleyness is a mix of traits: intellectual humility (you can change your mind when shown better evidence), comfort with ambiguity (you make progress when the problem is fuzzy), collaboration (you work well across teams), bias to action, and doing the right thing for users. They also look for "emergent leadership", which means stepping up to lead when it's needed, even without a title.

Stories that fit.

Signal Story Why it fits
Intellectual humility 1 (ClickHouse camps) You accepted the other side's facts and changed the question
Ambiguity 4 (clustering inversion) or 1 The right answer wasn't obvious and you made it concrete
Problem-first thinking 3 (malformed-plan validator) You wrapped an unreliable LLM in a deterministic contract
Doing the right thing 10 (near-miss) You reported something nobody would have noticed

Opener you can use. "One time I learned the most was when two expert groups disagreed about ClickHouse, and both had real evidence."

Watch out. Stories 3 and 4 are not resume bullets. If you use them, say "this is design and build work beyond my resume" when asked. Google interviewers also like hearing what you'd do differently, so prepare one improvement per story.

Microsoft

What they value, in plain words. Microsoft's culture centres on growth mindset: treating mistakes as learning and staying curious instead of acting like a know-it-all. They also emphasise customer obsession (understanding what the user actually needs), inclusive collaboration (working well with diverse people and teams), and delivering results.

Stories that fit.

Value Story Why it fits
Growth mindset 9 (anti-bot loop) or 6 (coverage) You learned your way through a problem you didn't understand at first
Learning from mistakes 5 (refactor mistake) You owned it and turned it into a team checklist
Collaboration and mentoring L2 (mentored 2) You helped others grow instead of doing it all yourself

Opener you can use. "A good example of learning my way through a problem is the Uber Eats scrapers, where the websites kept changing their bot defences."

Watch out. Don't present yourself as having all the answers. Microsoft responds well to "here's what I got wrong first".

LinkedIn

What they value, in plain words. LinkedIn interviewers tend to probe three themes. The first is transformation: have you changed how a system or team works, not just added features? The second is craft: do you care about doing the work well, with quality and measurement? The third is collaboration: do you build good working relationships and give honest, constructive feedback?

Stories that fit.

Theme Story Why it fits
Transformation 8 (Masters migration) You moved a monolith to services and changed how the team shipped
Scale and data craft 12 (ClickHouse RFC) You chose a database by benchmark and built a summary layer
Quality craft Uber Eats menu pipeline (see story 9 and the menu numbers) 98% field accuracy on an offline evaluation, behind a schema check

Opener you can use. "The project that changed how my team worked the most was the Masters India migration from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices."

Watch out. The 98% is an offline-evaluation number, measured on a fixed set of menus with known correct answers. Say "offline".

Apple

What they value, in plain words. Apple doesn't publish an interview value list the way Amazon does. Interviewers consistently look for quality and attention to detail (sweating small things users would notice), privacy and data protection, and deep ownership. Apple uses the idea of a DRI (directly responsible individual), the one person accountable for a thing.

Stories that fit.

Theme Story Why it fits
Attention to detail 7 (column-aliasing bug) A tiny SQL naming issue silently mapped rows to the wrong id, and you made it impossible
Quality bar 6 (coverage) You refused to accept a misleading metric
Data protection Ask Iris scope lock (see design doc) Each copilot session is locked to the user's allowed data when it connects
Correctness for auditors FRM audit trail Deterministic SHA-256 keys stop duplicate rows across quarters

Opener you can use. "The bug I'm proudest of finding at Uber was invisible: rows silently mapped to the wrong id because two joined tables had the same column names."

Watch out. Older prep mentioned "100% schema" for the menu pipeline. That refers to a schema validation check that rejects malformed output. It is not on the PDF. Lead with the 98% offline field accuracy.

Netflix

What they value, in plain words. Netflix's culture is "freedom and responsibility". You get a lot of autonomy, and in return you're expected to use good judgment without being supervised. "Context, not control" means leaders explain the why and trust you to decide. Candor means giving and receiving direct, honest feedback, including admitting your own mistakes plainly.

Stories that fit.

Value Story Why it fits
High agency 9 (anti-bot loop) You ran your own experiment loop without waiting for instructions
Candor about mistakes 5 (refactor mistake) You called your own foul fast
Owning production 10 (near-miss) or the Masters on-call experience You treated a near-miss as your problem

Opener you can use. "I'll give you one where I was the one who made the mistake, because I think how you handle that says a lot."

Watch out. Netflix values judgment over process. Don't over-explain checklists. Explain the decision and why it was right.

Atlassian

What they value, in plain words. Atlassian's values include "Open company, no bullshit" (be transparent and direct), "Play, as a team" (help others succeed), "Build with heart and balance" (care about the work and the people), "Don't #@!% the customer" (protect the customer), and "Be the change you seek" (improve things yourself instead of complaining).

Stories that fit.

Value Story Why it fits
Play, as a team L1 (led 3) You split ownership and stepped back as people grew
Open company, no bullshit 7 (rulebook disagreement) You disagreed openly in writing and documented the outcome
Be the change 5 (refactor mistake) You added a checklist rule so the team wouldn't repeat it
Don't hurt the customer 10 (near-miss) You protected clients from a compliance error

Opener you can use. "When I led a pod of 3 at Uber via EPAM, the most important thing I did was give each person a clear area to own."

Watch out. "Led 3" was tech-lead work, not people management. Say "tech lead".

Salesforce

What they value, in plain words. Salesforce's core values are Trust (customers trust you with their data, so security and reliability come first), Customer Success, Innovation, Equality and Sustainability. In engineering interviews, Trust and Customer Success come up most.

Stories that fit.

Value Story Why it fits
Trust 10 (idempotency near-miss) You made duplicate government filings impossible
Trust in multi-tenant data Impact Analytics tenant isolation Each tenant sees only its own data across Postgres and ClickHouse
Customer success and audit FRM for Finance and external auditors Every scoping number became reproducible and traceable
Compliance ANZ document checks 99.9% compliance from a deterministic validation backend (historical Uber Mobility work)

Opener you can use. "Trust for me is concrete. At Masters India I found a way our retries could have filed the same invoice twice with the government, and I closed it across the whole pipeline."

Watch out. ANZ is historical Uber Mobility work, not Uber Eats. Tenant isolation is access control, not encryption.

Short mapping cheat sheet

What they're testing Best story Backup
Disagreement 1 7
Ambiguity or product thinking 4 (verbal) 1
Mistake or failure 5 10
Deadline or migration 8 12
Persistence 9 12b
Compliance or trust 10 ANZ
Mentorship L2 (mentored 2) L1 (led 3)
Hardest technical problem 12b 3 (verbal)
