Interview Intros (short and long)

How to use this page

  • It covers every way you introduce yourself: recruiter screen, hiring manager, technical screen opener, the 3-minute career story, why each job switch, and "why this company".
  • Read it the night before any first-round call. Say each intro out loud twice with a timer.
  • Memorise the 30-second recruiter intro word for word. For the longer ones, memorise the order of the beats, not the exact words.
  • Rule of thumb: never say more than three numbers in one answer. Stop after the number and let them ask.

Track: Final Java + AI (IA = Py/Go) (Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf). The resume summary says "Expertise in Java, Python and Go microservices". On this track Uber FRM is Java with Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA and Hibernate, Masters India is Spring Boot microservices, and the Impact Analytics platform APIs are Go with Gin. The AI agent code at Impact Analytics is Python.

Words used below, in one line each:

  • AssortSmart is Impact Analytics' retail planning software. Retailers use it to decide which products to keep, drop or add each season.
  • ClickHouse is a database built for fast analytics. It reads only the columns a report needs, so big summaries come back quickly.
  • Go / Gin is Google's programming language for fast network services. Gin is a small web framework on top of it.
  • Spring Boot is the most common Java framework for building web services. It wires up the web server, database access and configuration for you.
  • FRM (Financial Risk Management) is the Uber Finance team that decides which accounts need audit attention each quarter.
  • Kafka is a durable message queue. Producers drop events in, consumers read them later at their own pace.
  • LangGraph is a Python library for building LLM agents as a graph of steps with explicit loops and exits.

1. Recruiter / HR screen

The recruiter is checking three things: are you senior, does your stack match, and are you a calm communicator. Keep it simple. No jargon unless they use it first.

Short (about 30 seconds)

Hi, I'm Tarun Mittal. I'm a Senior Software Engineer with five years of experience building backend systems in Java, Python and Go. Recently a lot of my work has been production AI, which means LLM features that are measured and tested before they ship. Right now I'm at Impact Analytics, working on a retail planning product. I'm exploring senior backend roles, and [Company] stood out to me because [one specific reason].

Long (60 to 90 seconds)

I'm Tarun, based in Bangalore, with about five years of building production backends.

Right now I'm a Senior Software Engineer at Impact Analytics on AssortSmart. It's software that helps retailers decide which products to keep, drop or add each season. I own two areas. The first is the Go platform that planners use every day. The second is the AI decision engine that scores products. One result I'm proud of: planner reports used to take 189 seconds, and I brought them down to 12 seconds by building a summary layer in ClickHouse, which is a database built for fast analytics.

Before that I was an SDE 2 at Uber, through EPAM. I owned the backend for a Finance risk tool and cut the quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days. I also owned the Uber Eats menu automation pipeline. Before Uber I was at Masters India on GST e-invoicing, and I started my career at GeeksforGeeks.

I'm looking for a senior role where I own a system end to end, from design to production.

Numbers used: 189 to 12 seconds, 14 to 3 days. That is enough. Do not add more here.

Follow-up they may ask: "What does 'through EPAM' mean?" Answer: "EPAM is a services company. I was an EPAM employee working full time inside an Uber team, on Uber's codebase and tools."

2. Hiring manager

The hiring manager wants to know how you work: do you own things, do you measure, can you lead without being told. Lead with ownership, then one proof point per job.

Short (about 30 seconds)

I own backend systems end to end: the APIs, the data model, production support, and the quality gates before release. I'm happy to go deep on any of four systems. The Go platform and AI engine at Impact Analytics, the Finance risk backend at Uber, the Uber Eats menu pipeline, or the GST e-invoicing pipeline at Masters India. Which would be most useful for you?

Long (90 seconds)

I'd describe myself as a strong senior individual contributor who also leads small groups.

At Uber, through EPAM, I owned the design of the FRM scoping backend, which Finance uses to decide which accounts need audit attention. I was tech lead for 3 engineers on a database-layer migration, and the platform cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days.

At Masters India I mentored 2 engineers while we moved a PHP monolith to Spring Boot services piece by piece, and I was on call for the system.

At Impact Analytics I own the platform engineering and the AI decision flows for AssortSmart. On the AI side I care a lot about honest quality gates. For example, we have an automated test that blocks a new model from release unless it clears 80% accuracy on a fixed test set. When the AI scored worse than a simple rule-based baseline, we kept the rule-based weights instead of shipping it anyway.

So the short version is: I own the system, I measure it, and I don't inflate the results.

Say this carefully: "led 3" is Uber FRM. "Mentored 2" is Masters India. Never merge them into "led 5". The 80% is a release gate in CI (continuous integration, the automated checks that run on every code change). It is not "80% accuracy live for every customer".

Off the PDF, only if asked: the Go code at Impact Analytics has 100% statement coverage over 1,200+ tests. That is on LinkedIn, not the PDF. Say "it's on my LinkedIn" if you mention it.

3. Technical screen opener

Use this when the interviewer says "tell me about yourself" at the start of a technical round. Offer a menu so they pick the system you know best.

I can give you a 60-second walk-through of any system you like and then take questions. The options I know deepest are: the AssortSmart Go platform and ClickHouse layer, the AI decision engine and the "Ask Iris" planner copilot, the Uber FRM finance backend, the Uber Eats menu ingestion pipeline with Kafka and Flink, or the Masters India e-invoicing pipeline with Kafka. Which one is closest to what your team does?

Why this works: it shows range, it puts you on home ground, and it hands control back to them. If they say "you choose", pick the one closest to the job description.

4. The 3-minute career story

Use when they say "walk me through your resume". Go oldest to newest. Each job gets one sentence of context, one thing you owned, and one reason you moved.

I graduated in IT from IET Lucknow in 2021.

I started at GeeksforGeeks as an SDE. I moved their doubt-support platform, where students ask coding questions, from PHP to Django so it could survive traffic spikes during live coding contests. I also built an influencer earnings dashboard. That job taught me to ship product features fast.

Then I joined Masters India as an SDE 2. They build GST compliance software. Big Indian companies send us invoices, we validate them and register them with the government's invoice portal. I led the move from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices in Java, mentored 2 engineers, and built the bulk pipeline on Kafka that handled over a million government submissions a day. That was my first time owning a migration end to end.

Next I joined Uber through EPAM as an SDE 2. I owned the Java Spring Boot backend of a Finance risk tool that replaced Google Sheets with a proper MySQL database, and I was tech lead for 3 engineers. I also owned the Uber Eats menu automation pipeline, turning restaurant menus, including messy PDFs, into Uber's catalog format.

Now I'm a Senior Software Engineer at Impact Analytics. I own the Go platform for AssortSmart, the ClickHouse analytics layer, and the AI decision engine that tells retailers which products to keep or drop.

Each move added a layer: product features, then owning a migration, then Uber-scale engineering standards, then data platforms plus production AI. Next I want a role where I own a system for several years.

Numbers used: mentored 2, a million a day, led 3. Keep it at that. Let them ask for the rest.

5. Why each switch (keep each under 45 seconds)

GeeksforGeeks to Masters India (about 1.3 years).

At GFG I was shipping features on a consumer learning platform. Masters India offered ownership of a regulated product and a real platform migration. I wanted to grow from feature delivery into owning a service cutover and mentoring juniors, and that's what I got.

Masters India to Uber via EPAM (about 1.5 years).

I had taken the GST platform through migration and scale. Uber was a jump in engineering bar and systems complexity. I wanted the discipline of a large monorepo with Bazel, which is Google-style build tooling, and work that sat next to Finance and audit.

Uber via EPAM to Impact Analytics (about 1.9 years).

I wanted deeper ownership of data platforms and production AI, not only service APIs. Impact Analytics offered a senior role around ClickHouse analytics and agentic AI for retail planning. That's where I want to go deep.

Why are you exploring after a few months at Impact Analytics?

I joined for a senior charter around analytics and AI. The work itself has been great, and I've shipped real things there. What I'm looking for now is a larger production surface and a stronger design-review culture, where I can own a domain for several years. So I'm talking to fewer companies, more carefully.

If they say "four companies in five years":

Each move added a layer. The longest stretch, at Uber, shows I stay when the scope keeps growing. That's what I'm optimising for again.

Do not: call anyone toxic, lead with compensation, say the current job doesn't count, or apologise as if you failed.

Behavioral / managerial rounds: STAR stories (Final Java + AI (IA = Py/Go))

How to use this page

  • It holds every behavioral story you own, written as first-person answers you can say out loud in 60 to 90 seconds.
  • Read it before any behavioral, managerial or "bar raiser" round. Pick 2 or 3 stories per company using the company guides.
  • Memorise the first sentence and the lesson of each story. The middle can be in your own words.
  • Never tell the same story twice in one interview loop. This bank gives you enough coverage.

Track: Final Java + AI (IA = Py/Go), resume Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf. Uber FRM is Java with Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA and Hibernate. Masters India is Spring Boot microservices. Impact Analytics platform APIs are Go with Gin. The AI agent code is Python.

What STAR means and how to tell one

STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. It is the structure interviewers expect for "tell me about a time when..." questions.

  • Situation (1 to 2 sentences): where you were and what was going wrong.
  • Task (1 sentence): what you personally had to achieve.
  • Action (3 to 4 sentences): what you did. Say "I", not "we", for your part.
  • Result (1 to 2 sentences): what changed, with at most 2 or 3 numbers.
  • Lesson (1 sentence): what you'd carry to the next job.

Most of the time goes to Action. If you notice you're spending a long time on Situation, cut it.

Status tags used below

  • PDF: the story backs a resume bullet. Safe to tell anywhere.
  • Verbal, not on PDF: real work, but not a resume bullet. Tell it only when it fits the question, and say it isn't on the resume if they ask.
  • Design: you designed it. Say "I designed", never "it runs in production".
  • Packet: a prepared story that is not a resume bullet. Tell it as an example, without claiming infrastructure ownership.

1. The ClickHouse disagreement (two expert camps)

Use for: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with your team", "made a decision with incomplete data", "influenced without authority".

Words: ClickHouse is a database built for fast analytics. It is great at reading huge tables but weak at changing individual rows in place. PoC (proof of concept) is a small experiment that proves or disproves an idea before you commit.

Situation. At Impact Analytics the org was split on whether to adopt ClickHouse for the new AI planning product. An audit of the old backend said "no ClickHouse". Senior experts said "yes, move everything to it". Both sides had real evidence, and a wrong call was expensive either way.

Task. I had to produce a recommendation that both camps could commit to, without throwing away either side's evidence.

Action. First I separated facts from conclusions. I accepted every measured fact in the audit. Then I showed that its "no" came from the old system's habit of updating rows in place, which ClickHouse is bad at. It wasn't a property of planning workloads in general. So I designed an insert-only write model, where every change is a new versioned row, which avoids ClickHouse's weakness. Then I proposed a three-gate path: fix what we could inside the current stack first, tighten Postgres second, and run a versioned-write PoC third. Each gate had a measurable pass or fail.

Result. Both camps agreed to the staged path. The PoC held ClickHouse's background mutation queue at zero even at 10 times our expected scale. In July 2026 the org committed to ClickHouse end to end. Nobody "lost", and we didn't spend on infrastructure before the evidence was in.

Lesson. When competent people disagree, it's usually about hidden assumptions, not facts. Make the assumptions explicit and the decision often resolves itself.

Follow-up they may ask: "What did Postgres keep?" Answer: "Postgres kept the thin metadata: users, roles and access rules. ClickHouse took the large analytical reads."

2. The BigQuery to ClickHouse ingestion lane (freshness as a feature)

Status: Design, verbal. This was the read layer designed for the Cluster Recommendation Copilot, which is not a resume bullet. Tell it as a design you're proud of. Do not claim it runs in production. The 500 ms number is a design target.

Words: BigQuery is Google's cloud data warehouse. It's cheap for big batch queries but the same query can take very different times because compute is shared. p95 means the time within which 95% of requests finish. REPLACE PARTITION is a ClickHouse command that swaps a whole slice of a table in one step, so readers see either the old slice or the new one, never half.

Situation. The copilot's AI agent needed fast, predictable reads. But our historical data lives in BigQuery, where the same query can take anywhere from 1 to 20 seconds. The obvious fix was to copy the data into ClickHouse. The trap is that copies go stale silently, and a planner making buying decisions on stale data is worse off than one waiting on a slow query.

Task. Design the lane from BigQuery into ClickHouse so the agent's reads would be fast and provably fresh.

Action. I designed it in three parts. First, nightly exports land in staging tables and get promoted with an atomic partition swap, so nobody reads a half-loaded night. Second, row counts and sums are reconciled per partition against BigQuery, and a mismatch blocks promotion. Third, a freshness stamp, "data as of this date", goes into every agent answer, so staleness is visible in the product instead of found in an incident.

Result. The design targets p95 under 500 milliseconds for agent reads. More importantly, it makes silent staleness structurally impossible: loads are all-or-nothing, mismatches block promotion, and the data date is printed on the answer.

Lesson. When you copy data for speed, freshness and reconciliation are product features, not ops chores. Design them in on day one.

3. Fixing the top LLM-planner failure (malformed plans)

Status: Verbal, not on PDF. Older prep places this in agent-planner work at Impact Analytics. It is not Keep/Drop. Keep/Drop has no LLM planner and runs its steps in a fixed order. The 0.54 and 0.99 scores are offline-evaluation numbers. Confirm which product surface you name before using this story.

Words: an LLM planner is a model that breaks a user's question into a list of steps for other agents to run. A schema is the agreed shape of the data, like a form with required fields.

Situation. We had a multi-agent planner where an LLM turned questions into execution plans. The top failure was malformed plans: plans that named agents that didn't exist, referred to steps that hadn't run yet, or tried to run too many things at once. Structural correctness on our test set was only 0.54.

Task. Make plans safe to run without losing the LLM's flexibility.

Action. I wrote a strict validator that checks every plan before anything executes. It checks agent names, duplicate step ids, how wide each stage is, and references to future steps. If a plan fails, the system gives the LLM one repair attempt, passing back the exact validation errors. I also made every agent's answer function never throw, so one failing agent produces a labelled partial answer instead of crashing the whole response.

Result. Structural correctness went from 0.54 to 0.99 on the offline test set. Failures became visible and recoverable instead of mysterious.

Lesson. With LLMs, don't chase the perfect prompt. Put a deterministic contract around the probabilistic part.

4. Inverting the clustering workflow

Status: Verbal, not on PDF. The Cluster Recommendation Copilot is not a resume bullet. Use it only if they ask about product thinking or an AI roadmap. The baseline numbers (1 configuration tried, 8.5% failed runs, 37 of 437) were measured from audits. The "after" numbers are targets. Say "targeting".

Words: store clustering means grouping a retailer's stores into similar groups, so each group gets a suitable product mix. Silhouette score is a standard measure of how well-separated clusters are.

Situation. Store clustering is the base of every assortment plan, but it was the least-assisted step. The system computed which store attributes mattered and then made people choose from raw score lists. Audits showed users tried exactly one configuration per plan, and 8.5% of runs failed, mostly because of input mistakes.

Task. Define the AI rebuild of this module, with user adoption as the main risk.

Action. I flipped the workflow. The user states only what the system can't work out: which part of the product hierarchy and which reference period. The agent does the rest. It selects features by statistical significance, evaluates a large batch of candidate clusterings and scores them, and presents the top 3 with evidence and plain-English reasons. One of the three is always a baseline that mimics the client's old setup. The human approves at explicit checkpoints. I also kept the old manual wizard available per client, so adoption was a choice, not forced.

Result. The committed target was under an hour to a finished plan instead of days, with far fewer failed runs. Everything the agent chose stays visible to the planner, and results write back into the existing product tables unchanged.

Lesson. The highest-leverage AI feature is often turning the workflow around, not a better model.

5. The "pure refactor" that wasn't (owning a mistake)

Use for: "Tell me about a mistake", "a bug you caused", "your quality standards".

Words: a stacked PR is one of a chain of small pull requests where each builds on the previous one, so reviewers see small, focused changes. A refactor changes how code is organised without changing what it does.

Situation. At Uber, I was shipping a refactor as a stack of 3 PRs. The second PR was supposed to only consolidate constants across 31 files. But a downstream test started failing.

Task. Find out why a test that expected the "component" strategy to be kept was now seeing "aggregate".

Action. I diffed my own PR line by line. I found I'd slipped in a small helper that quietly downgraded the strategy in one case. That was a behaviour change hidden inside a refactor, which is exactly what a refactor must not do. I removed it and restored the pass-through. Then I added a rule to the team's stacked-PR checklist: a pure refactor must cause zero test changes.

Result. It shipped as a true refactor. A few weeks later that checklist rule caught a similar issue in a teammate's PR.

Lesson. Call your own fouls fast and turn them into process. Credibility compounds.

6. Coverage that lied (dive deep)

Use for: "Debugging something non-obvious", "your testing philosophy".

Words: statement coverage is the share of code lines that actually run during tests. A mock is a fake object used in tests so you don't call the real thing. An ORM (object-relational mapper) lets you work with database rows as code objects instead of raw SQL.

Situation. My Uber Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration failed the CI coverage check at 34.6% on new lines, even though I knew those code paths were being tested.

Task. Understand how tested code could show up as "not covered".

Action. I dug into how coverage was measured. The JUnit tests for the data-access layer were mocking the new entity query methods with Mockito. So the entity code itself never actually ran, and coverage was credited to the wrong layer. I wrote 12 direct tests at the entity layer, including the rejection paths like empty updates and unknown columns.

Result. The changed module reached 100% coverage. The rule "test where the code lives, not where it's called" went into the team's testing notes.

Lesson. A metric you don't understand will eventually lie to you.

7. Disagreeing with the architecture rulebook (backbone, then commit)

Use for: "A time you disagreed with a standard", "disagreed with a senior engineer", "conflict with your manager" (frame it upward).

Words: a repository layer is a package of classes whose only job is talking to the database. An entity is the Java class that describes a table (@Entity). A named query (@NamedQuery) is a query declared directly on that entity class.

Situation. Uber's team rules said all database access must live in the repository package. For the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration, I wanted to declare queries on the entity classes instead.

Task. Either follow the rule mechanically, or make the case for an exception.

Action. I wrote down the engineering argument. With queries next to the field mappings, Hibernate validates them when the application starts, so a renamed column fails at startup and in tests instead of quietly at runtime. The repository stays a thin wrapper, and no business logic leaks into entities. I listened to the counter-argument, which was consistency across the codebase. Then I documented the exception explicitly, and I agreed to keep dynamic queries that don't belong to one model as repository functions.

Result. The exception was accepted and written down. The bug that started the migration couldn't come back. In the old raw SQL, joined tables had duplicate column names, so some rows were silently mapped to the wrong id. In one case income-statement rows were read with balance-sheet column lists. Typed entities with explicit column aliases removed that whole class of bug.

Lesson. Disagree with a written rationale, commit visibly, and leave the decision auditable.

8. The migration nobody could pause the business for (deliver results)

Use for: "Delivering under pressure", "leading a project end to end".

Words: a monolith is one big application where everything is deployed together. The strangler pattern means replacing a monolith one endpoint at a time, routing each endpoint to the new service once it's ready, until the old app has nothing left. IRP (Invoice Registration Portal) is the government system that registers each e-invoice.

Situation. At Masters India, our PHP monolith was falling over during monthly GST filing deadlines. Each slow call to the government portal blocked a worker, and the worker pool ran out. Meanwhile more than 1,500 enterprise clients kept filing.

Task. Lead the move to Spring Boot microservices with non-blocking calls to the government portal, with no downtime allowed during deadline windows.

Action. I used the strangler pattern, endpoint by endpoint behind the gateway. We sent shadow traffic to read endpoints first, to compare old and new answers safely. We moved the bulk background paths onto Kafka before touching interactive filing. We kept the data where it was, in PostgreSQL split by tax quarter, so we didn't add a risky data migration on top. We froze cutovers during deadline weeks. And we protected bulk submissions with idempotency keys, retries and a dead-letter queue.

Result. p95 latency went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and we had no outage in a deadline window during the whole migration.

Lesson. Sequencing is the real risk-management tool. The migration plan mattered more than the target architecture.

Follow-up they may ask: "What was throughput?" Answer: "It went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute."

9. The anti-bot arms race (learn and be curious)

Use for: "Working against a moving target", "persistence".

Words: Selenium drives a real web browser from code, so you can load pages that need JavaScript. A proxy pool is a set of different IP addresses you rotate through, so a website doesn't block you for too many requests from one address.

Situation. Our Uber Eats menu scrapers were getting blocked. Success rates dropped as source websites kept changing their bot defences.

Task. Get extraction reliability back up without an unlimited proxy budget.

Action. I treated it as an experiment loop, not a one-off fix. I logged the block signature for each source. I iterated countermeasures: IP rotation, browser fingerprint management and dynamic proxy pools. I set a retry budget per source so retries couldn't run away. And I put block rates on the same dashboards as parse failures, so a new block showed up in minutes.

Result. Successful extraction rose to 95% plus. New defences were spotted and countered in days instead of weeks.

Lesson. Against a moving adversary, the asset is the feedback loop, not any single trick.

10. The double-filing near-miss (earn trust, do the right thing)

Use for: "Integrity", "a time you raised a problem you could have hidden", "a failure".

Words: an idempotency key is a unique id for a request, so if the same request arrives twice the system does the work only once. A dead-letter queue is a holding area for messages that keep failing, so they can be inspected and replayed instead of retried forever.

Situation. At Masters India, a retried bulk import came close to filing duplicate e-invoices with the government portal. For a client, that's a compliance-grade error. It hadn't caused damage yet, and nobody outside the team would have known.

Task. Decide between quietly patching that one retry and treating it as the systemic risk it was.

Action. I flagged it to leadership as a near-miss and wrote the incident review myself. Then I added idempotency keys across the entire bulk pipeline, not just the endpoint that almost failed. The key was built from client, file hash and batch index. I also added a dead-letter replay path.

Result. Zero duplicate filings after rollout. The near-miss review became the template the team used for later incidents.

Lesson. Trust is built in the moments when you could have stayed quiet.

11. Connection-leak out-of-memory (packet story)

Status: Packet, not on the PDF. It's a Python/FastAPI worker story at Impact Analytics. Don't describe it as Kubernetes cluster work, and don't claim cluster operations.

Words: OOM (out of memory) is when a process uses more memory than allowed and gets killed. A 504 is a "gateway timeout" error. Backpressure means slowing down the producer when the consumer can't keep up.

Situation. At peak traffic we saw 504 errors and memory climbing on an async worker.

Task. Find the cause without a local reproduction.

Action. I lined up the APM traces with heap data. APM (application performance monitoring) shows where time and memory go. Database and HTTP clients were being created inside a long-running async loop without being closed. I fixed it with proper context managers (Python's async with, which always closes the resource), added pool limits and timeouts, and added backpressure so the worker couldn't outrun what was downstream.

Result. Memory stabilised and the 504s cleared. As follow-up we added a load test at 3 times peak in CI, plus connection-pool metrics.

Lesson. In async Python, resource lifetime is a correctness bug, not an infrastructure ticket.

12. The ClickHouse RFC and migration (bias for action, technical leadership)

Use for: "Driving a migration", "deciding with incomplete information", "Are Right, A Lot".

Words: an RFC (request for comments) is a written design proposal circulated for review. A pivot here is a planner's grid view that groups sales numbers by product, store and time. A rollup table stores pre-computed totals, so reports read the totals instead of adding up raw rows each time.

Situation. Planner pivots on Postgres were getting slower and slower. On a 250-million-row test, one pivot took 189 seconds.

Task. Write the RFC, prove it with a PoC, and get adoption, without pretending ClickHouse replaces Postgres for everything.

Action. I wrote the RFC comparing a hybrid design with an insert-only store. I ran a PoC where both databases had exactly the same rows. ClickHouse won the large analytical reads, so I built a pre-aggregation layer of six rollup tables for product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly level. Postgres kept users, roles and other small records that change often. And I kept the LLM away from the big master table, serving it prepared JSON instead.

Result. On that 250-million-row test, the pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds. The org committed to ClickHouse for planning analytics.

Lesson. Measure first, choose the write model on purpose, and don't treat a database choice as a religion.

12b. The weekly rollup out-of-memory (hardest technical hurdle)

Use for: "Hardest technical problem", "a failure and how you debugged it", "memory at scale". Full technical pack: 42_clickhouse_rollup_migration.md.

Words: an INSERT SELECT reads from one table, computes, and writes into another in one statement. Disk spill means letting a query write temporary data to disk when memory runs out, instead of crashing.

Situation. Building the weekly rollup for a whole season in one INSERT SELECT needed about 170 GB of memory. It failed with "memory limit exceeded" even when we raised the cap to 200 GB.

Task. Keep the weekly level of detail without crashing the server.

Action. Instead of buying more memory, I shrank the unit of work. I sliced each build into one fiscal week per insert. I set a memory cap and a disk-spill cap, and limited how many weeks ran at once. Then I measured each slice. Even the heaviest weeks fit inside the caps.

Result. The weekly rollups built successfully with predictable memory.

Lesson. Shrink the unit of work before you buy RAM.

Say this carefully: the 170 GB fix is about loading data. The 189 to 12 seconds speed-up is about querying it. One did not cause the other. The exact caps (55 GB memory, 16 GB spill, 8 threads, 4 weeks in flight) are verbal detail, not on the PDF. If they ask for slice sizes: a product week needed about 11 GB and an attribute week went above 40 GB. An 80 GB cap also failed before the 200 GB attempt.

L1. Leading 3 engineers at Uber via EPAM (FRM)

Words: tech lead of an EPAM pod means I set the technical direction and reviewed the work of a small EPAM team inside Uber. I was not their people manager.

Situation. The FRM scoping backend needed a clean layered design and a database migration, while the frontend and Finance kept changing requirements.

Task. Own the service, keep the pod of 3 shipping, and raise test coverage under Bazel, Uber's build system.

Action. I split ownership by layer: request handlers, business logic, and data access. I set PR conventions and reviewed every PR early. I paired on the hardest cutover, the reconciliation move from Sheets to MySQL. Then I stepped back as each person owned their area.

Result. The platform shipped 36 endpoints, the module reached 100% statement coverage, and Finance used it for the quarterly close.

Follow-up they may ask: "How many tests?" Answer: "Over 1,100." That number is verbal, not on the PDF.

L2. Mentoring 2 engineers at Masters India

Situation. Two junior engineers were new to Spring Boot and non-blocking patterns during the monolith migration.

Task. Get them shipping on their own without breaking filing-day traffic.

Action. I pair-programmed the first canary cutover with them. A canary sends a small slice of traffic to the new version first. I wrote the shared retry and idempotency helpers so they didn't have to reinvent them. I reviewed their PRs for input validation (Bean Validation on request DTOs) and logging. Then I let them own full services.

Result. Both shipped services independently, and the platform reached its latency and throughput goals.

Rapid-fire answers (about 30 seconds each)

"Why are you leaving?"

I've built and owned systems end to end: an AI decision platform, streaming pipelines, and a finance-grade audit tool. Now I want a bigger production surface, a stronger design-review culture, and problems where a 1% improvement really matters.

"Biggest weakness?"

I over-invest in written documents, like decision docs and playbooks. I've learned to time-box them and lead with a one-page summary, because a 20-page analysis nobody reads is its own failure.

"Conflict with a manager?" Use story 7, framed as disagreeing upward with a written standard.

"A time you failed?" Story 5 (the refactor regression) or story 10 (the near-miss). Both end in a process fix.

"What are you most proud of?" Story 1. I turned an org-level disagreement into a staged, evidence-based decision that became the committed direction.

Honesty checklist

  • Stories 2, 3 and 4 are not resume bullets. Story 11 is a packet story. Say so if asked.
  • Ask Iris is a shipped capability with no invented usage or uptime numbers.
  • "Led 3" is Uber FRM. "Mentored 2" is Masters India. Never merge them.
  • No Kafka, Flink or Kubernetes operations at Impact Analytics.
  • The 170 GB load fix and the 189-to-12-second query speed-up are separate results.

Why Should We Hire You? / What Work Have You Done?

How to use this page

  • It covers the pitch questions: "why should we hire you", "what work have you done", "why you over someone with more years", "what's your biggest risk", and the objections interviewers raise.
  • Read it before recruiter screens and hiring-manager rounds, and again before the final round.
  • Memorise the 30-second pitch. For everything else, memorise the first sentence and the honest caveat.
  • Each answer uses at most three numbers. The full number list lives in Numbers defense.

Track: Final Java + AI (IA = Py/Go), resume Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf. Uber FRM and Masters India are Java with Spring Boot. Impact Analytics is Go with Gin plus Python agents. Full pitch bank: 38_why_hire_tarun_qa.md. Question bank: 39_behavioral_question_bank.md.

The three things you are selling. Every answer on this page comes back to these:

  1. Ownership. I take a system from design to production and keep it running.
  2. Measurement. I decide with benchmarks, not opinions.
  3. Honesty about AI. I put hard release gates in front of AI features and I don't inflate the results.

Words used below:

  • Release gate (CI gate) is an automated check that blocks a change from shipping unless it passes. CI (continuous integration) runs these checks on every code change.
  • Deterministic baseline is a plain rule-based scorer with no AI. It gives the same answer every time, and AI has to beat it to be worth using.
  • Materiality threshold is the money amount above which an accounting error is big enough to matter to auditors.
  • ClickHouse is a database built for fast analytics on very large tables.

1. Why should we hire you?

Short (30 to 45 seconds)

You should hire me because I own backend systems end to end and I can defend every number I give you. I have five years in Java, Python and Go. At Uber, through EPAM, I owned a Java Spring Boot Finance risk backend that cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days. On Uber Eats, the menu pipeline I architected cut restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours. Now at Impact Analytics I own the Go platform and the AI decision engine for a retail planning product. I bring architecture ownership, production discipline, and honest quality gates on AI.

Numbers used: 14 to 3 days, 24 to 2 hours. Two is enough here.

Long (90 to 120 seconds)

You should hire me if you need a senior backend engineer who owns a system from design through production, and who can connect classic infrastructure with applied AI.

At Uber, through EPAM, I owned the FRM scoping backend. FRM is the Finance team that decides which accounts need audit attention. I moved their process off Google Sheets into a proper MySQL database, designed the schema so many people could edit safely at once, and led 3 engineers through a database-layer migration. The quarterly reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days.

On Uber Eats I owned menu ingestion. That's turning restaurant menus, including messy multilingual PDFs, into Uber's catalog format, using Kafka and Flink for the streaming part and an LLM with retrieval for the PDFs.

At Masters India I led a move from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, one endpoint at a time, and mentored 2 engineers.

At Impact Analytics I own two things: a Go platform that serves retail planners at peak load, and an AI engine that recommends which products to keep or drop. The AI never queries the big database directly. It gets prepared data, and if it times out we fall back to the rule-based score. Every new model must pass an 80% accuracy gate before release. When the AI did worse than our rule-based baseline, we kept the baseline weights instead of shipping it.

So you get ownership, measurement, and someone who won't oversell an AI result.

Numbers used: 14 to 3 days, led 3, 80% gate. The "mentored 2" is a headcount, not a result. Keep it separate from "led 3".

Follow-up they may ask: "Is the 80% live accuracy?" Answer: "No. It's the bar a model has to clear on a fixed 300-case test set before it can be promoted. It's a release gate, not a claim about every customer in production."

2. What work have you done?

Short (one breath per job)

At Impact Analytics I own the Go platform, the ClickHouse analytics layer and the AI decision engine for retail planning. At Uber through EPAM, I owned the Finance risk backend and the Uber Eats menu ingestion pipeline on Kafka and Flink. At Masters India I built the bulk GST e-invoicing pipeline on Kafka and led a PHP-to-Spring Boot migration. At GeeksforGeeks I moved the doubt-support platform from PHP to Django.

Long (walk it chronologically)

Go oldest to newest. For each job give one sentence of context, one thing you owned, and one result. Then end with what you want next.

  1. GeeksforGeeks (SDE). Moved the doubt-support platform to Django so it survived 10x traffic spikes during live coding contests.
  2. Masters India (SDE 2). Led the PHP to Spring Boot migration and built the Kafka pipeline for over a million government submissions a day.
  3. Uber via EPAM (SDE 2). Owned the FRM scoping backend and architected the Uber Eats menu ingestion pipeline.
  4. Impact Analytics (Senior SWE). Owns AssortSmart's Go platform, ClickHouse layer and AI decision engine.
  5. Close: "Next I want a senior backend or platform role, ideally with applied AI at scale, where I own a domain for several years."

3. Why you over someone with more years?

Scope, not years. I've owned a Finance system that auditors relied on against a $340 million materiality threshold. I've run a pipeline doing over a million government submissions a day. And I own a platform with a 2.11-billion-row analytics table behind it. I've also led a small team and mentored juniors. To be clear about my limits: I haven't run a 50-person org and I haven't operated Kubernetes clusters myself. But for owning a system end to end, I've done it at real stakes.

Numbers used: $340M, a million a day, 2.11 billion rows.

4. What's the biggest risk in hiring you?

The honest answer turns a risk into a credibility point.

Probably that some of my AI work is new. "Ask Iris", the planner copilot, is shipped as a capability, but I don't have long-term usage numbers to show you. And the 80% on my resume is a release gate, not proof that every customer sees 80%. Some of my other AI work, like a store-clustering copilot, is design and build work that isn't on the resume. Where I'm strongest is the systems that have run in production for a long time: the Uber Finance backend, the Uber Eats menu pipeline, and the Masters India e-invoicing pipeline.

5. Your differentiators (pick one per answer)

What I can claim Proof Status
Finance-grade backend Uber FRM: 36 Spring Boot endpoints, $340M materiality, led 3, module coverage 100% PDF
Real money saved Uber Eats menu: 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year HISTORICAL
Scale Masters India: 1M+ submissions a day. Impact Analytics: 10k peak requests per second, 2.11B-row table PDF / HISTORICAL
Decisions backed by benchmarks Planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250M-row test MEASURED
Safe AI LLM fed prepared JSON, not database access. 300-case test set, 80% release gate. Weights frozen when AI lost to the 74% baseline PDF
People Led 3 at Uber via EPAM. Mentored 2 at Masters PDF

Tags in this table: MEASURED means there's a benchmark, log or doc behind it. HISTORICAL means it comes from past work records and wasn't re-measured. PDF means it's a resume bullet you can defend as written.

6. Objection handling

Each answer is short on purpose. Say it, then stop.

"Your AI isn't really in production."

Ask Iris is shipped as a capability for planners. The 80% line is a release gate for promoting models. The clustering copilot is separate design and build work, and I don't claim it on the resume.

"No Spark?"

Correct. My streaming work was Kafka and Flink on Uber Eats. Spark isn't on my resume.

"Have you run Kubernetes?"

I've deployed and consumed containerised services. I haven't operated Kubernetes clusters or written the infrastructure code for them.

"Uber through a vendor?"

Yes, I was an EPAM employee embedded full time in an Uber team. I worked in Uber's codebase and owned the FRM scoping backend design.

"Is 70% on reconciliation real?"

Yes. Reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days. The technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what the platform delivered for the close. The value came from automating the financial math and the account hierarchy, which used to be done by hand in Sheets.

"98% on menus, really?"

That's 98% field accuracy on an offline evaluation set, meaning a fixed set of menus with known correct answers.

"10k RPS, what's the latency?"

10k requests per second is the peak load the platform is built for. I don't quote a latency SLA for it.

"You've only been at Impact Analytics a few months."

I joined for the platform and AI ownership, and I shipped real things there. I'm not job-hopping every year. The longest stretch on my resume shows I stay when the scope keeps growing.

"Is 99.9% compliance from Uber Eats?"

No, that was a separate Uber Mobility project in Australia and New Zealand. It automated driver and vehicle document checks. It's historical work.

7. Questions to ask them at the end

  • "How does design review work here before code gets written?"
  • "What's the biggest on-call pain right now?"
  • "What's a technical decision the team would reverse if it could?"
  • "What separates senior from staff here?"
  • "What would a great first six months look like, in measurable terms?"
  • "Where is the team carrying deliberate technical debt?"

8. Delivery rules

  • Lead with the outcome, then explain how.
  • Say "Uber via EPAM" once, early.
  • Uber Eats Kafka and Masters India Kafka are different products. Never blend them.
  • Stop after the number. Let them ask the follow-up.
  • If a number isn't on the PDF (100% Go coverage, 1,200+ Go tests, $100 per run token cost, the 1.6M catalog size), say "that's not on the resume, but" before giving it.

Verbal only, not on PDF: the Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight. Offer them only if they ask about a broader AI roadmap.

What every architecture page contains

Each page below follows the same template. That way, once you have learned one, the others are easy to read, and in an interview you can answer any "draw it" question with the same rhythm.

Architecture: Impact Analytics AssortSmart (Platform and AI)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the full AssortSmart architecture as it appears on the resume. That means the Go/Gin platform, ClickHouse and its rollups, the Python agent plane (Keep/Drop and Ask Iris) and the ClickHouse copier. A separate section at the end covers Hindsight, which is verbal-only.
  • When to read it: before any system design round, and before any "walk me through your current project" question.
  • What to memorise: the main diagram (eight boxes), the planner pivot request and the Keep/Drop batch job step by step, and the split between query-time numbers (15.5×) and load-time numbers (170GB OOM).

Read this first.

  • Hindsight and the Cluster Recommendation Copilot are verbal-only depth. They are not resume bullets. Bring them up only if the interviewer asks what else you are working on, and say "this is in progress, it is not on my resume".
  • Impact Analytics has no Kafka, no Flink, no CDC, no Kubernetes operations, no Milvus and no human review queue (HITL). Kafka and Flink are Uber Menu. Milvus is Uber Menu. The CDC pipeline (pg2ch) was built by a colleague, Ashvin Sharma. Do not claim it.
  • The platform APIs are Go with the Gin framework. The agent plane is Python (FastAPI and LangGraph).
  • LangSmith is on Ask Iris only. The Keep/Drop batch uses custom JSON telemetry, not LangSmith.

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, a doc or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). HISTORICAL means from past work records.

1. The one-paragraph version

AssortSmart is a retail merchandise planning product sold as SaaS (software as a service, meaning many retailers share one hosted product). Merchandise planners at a retailer use it to decide, season by season, which products to keep, which to drop and which to add. Planners look at large pivot tables of sales and inventory, and they also get AI recommendations. I work on two halves. The core platform is a multi-tenant Go/Gin API in front of ClickHouse (a fast analytics database) and PostgreSQL. The agent plane is Python: batch AI pipelines that score every article-season as Keep or Drop, and a chat copilot called Ask Iris that lets planners ask questions about KPIs and AI decisions.

2. Words you need

Read these once. Each one is used later on the page.

  • Article-season. One product (an "article") in one selling season. "Blue linen shirt, Summer 2026" is one article-season. The resume scores 348k of them.
  • Assortment planning. Choosing the range of products a retailer will carry. Think of a shop owner deciding which items stay on the shelf next season.
  • Pivot. A summary table where the planner picks rows (for example product category) and columns (for example store region) and the system sums sales for each cell. Like an Excel pivot table, but over hundreds of millions of rows.
  • Multi-tenant. Many customers (tenants) share the same running system, and each must only ever see its own data. Like flats in one building: shared walls and plumbing, separate locked doors.
  • ClickHouse. A columnar analytics database. "Columnar" means it stores each column separately, so a query that sums one column reads only that column. Think of a library where every book's page 12 is shelved together: if you only need page 12, you grab one shelf.
  • MergeTree. The main ClickHouse table type. Data lands in small sorted chunks called "parts", and ClickHouse merges them in the background, like sorting new mail into an already sorted pile later in the day.
  • ReplacingMergeTree (RMT). A MergeTree variant that keeps only the newest version of rows that share the same key. Think of a notebook where you never erase. You write the new value below the old one, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines. Until the cleaner comes, readers must pick the newest line themselves.
  • Partition. A slice of a table, here one season (PARTITION BY season_code). You can drop or rebuild one partition without touching the others, like replacing one drawer in a filing cabinet.
  • Rollup or pre-aggregation. A table of sums computed ahead of time. Instead of adding up every daily sale when a planner opens a chart, you add them once at load time and store the totals. Like keeping a running monthly total instead of re-adding every receipt.
  • OOM (out of memory). The process needed more RAM than allowed, so the database killed the query.
  • Go and Gin. Go is a compiled, fast language with cheap concurrency. Gin is a lightweight HTTP framework for Go, the layer that maps URLs to handler functions.
  • Google Wire (compile-time dependency injection). Dependency injection means a component receives the things it needs (database client, cache, logger) instead of creating them itself. Wire generates that wiring code at build time, so a missing dependency is a compile error, not a crash at startup. Like a checklist the build system ticks before the plane is allowed to take off.
  • Reverse proxy. A server such as nginx that sits in front of your app and handles timeouts, body limits and HTTP/2. "No reverse proxy" means the Go process does those jobs itself.
  • h2c (HTTP/2 cleartext). HTTP/2 without TLS at the process. It is normally used when TLS is terminated in front of the process (for example by a cloud load balancer), so the app can speak HTTP/2 directly without nginx in between.
  • Nested timeouts. A total deadline for the request, with smaller deadlines inside it for each downstream call (auth, Postgres, ClickHouse). Like a 30-minute meeting where each agenda item also has its own 5-minute limit.
  • Distributed tracing (Datadog). Every request gets a trace ID, and each step records a timed "span" under it, so you can see where time went across services.
  • JWT (JSON Web Token). A signed token that says who the user is. The server checks the signature instead of looking the user up every time, like checking the hologram on an ID card.
  • OIDC (OpenID Connect). A standard login protocol on top of OAuth, used here for Google sign-in.
  • Firebase Admin. Google's server-side SDK that verifies Firebase login tokens.
  • Constant-time comparison. Comparing two secrets in a way that always takes the same time, so an attacker cannot guess an API key one character at a time by measuring response times.
  • UAM (User Access Management). The rules for which part of the product hierarchy (for example which departments or regions) each user may see.
  • LLM (large language model). The AI model (for example a GPT model) that reads text and returns text or structured JSON.
  • Structured invoke. Calling an LLM and forcing the answer into a fixed JSON schema, so code can parse it reliably.
  • Lens. One analytical question the LLM answers about an article, such as "is weekly demand accelerating or dying?". There are 7 active lenses.
  • LangGraph. A Python library for building AI workflows as a graph of steps (nodes) with explicit state and edges. Like a flowchart that the code actually executes.
  • Supervisor. A LangGraph node that decides which step runs next.
  • Evaluator loop. A step that checks a draft answer and sends it back for another try if it fails, here capped at 3 attempts.
  • LangSmith. A tracing and evaluation tool for LLM apps. It records each prompt, tool call, token count and cost.
  • WebSocket. A long-lived two-way connection between browser and server, used for chat. The "handshake" is the first request that opens it.
  • Circuit breaker. A switch that stops calling a failing dependency after too many failures, like a fuse that trips so the whole house does not burn.
  • Checkpoint. A saved progress file so a crashed job can resume where it stopped instead of starting over.
  • config_hash. A SHA-256 fingerprint of the exact guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog used for a run. Stamped on every output row, so you can always tell which configuration produced a decision.
  • CI gate. An automated check in the build pipeline (CI, continuous integration) that blocks a change from being promoted if it fails.

3. The architecture diagram

flowchart LR UI["Planner UI"] EDGE["Go/Gin HTTP edge"] AUTH["Auth waterfall: Redis, Firebase, JWT, OIDC"] PG["PostgreSQL: tenants, roles, UAM"] KPI["KPI formula parser"] CH["ClickHouse: 2.11B-row master and six rollups"] DD["Datadog traces"] REG["Python orchestration registry"] KD["Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style"] LLM["LLM provider"] IRIS["Ask Iris: LangGraph supervisor and evaluator"] LS["LangSmith"] PUMP["Go native-TLS data pump"] CH2["Target ClickHouse Cloud cluster"] UI -->|"REST"| EDGE UI -->|"WebSocket with JWT"| IRIS EDGE --> AUTH AUTH --> PG EDGE --> KPI KPI --> CH EDGE -->|"scoped pivot queries"| CH EDGE -.-> DD REG --> KD CH -->|"fixed SELECTs packed as JSON"| KD KD -->|"structured invokes, no SQL tool"| LLM KD -->|"versioned rows, ReplacingMergeTree"| CH IRIS -->|"reads scoped by plan_scope"| CH IRIS -.-> LS CH --> PUMP PUMP --> CH2

What to notice: the LLM never touches the database. Python code reads ClickHouse with fixed queries and hands the LLM JSON. The platform half (left) and the agent half (right) meet only at ClickHouse.

4. Box-by-box walkthrough

Planner UI

The browser app planners use. It calls the Go/Gin API for grids, pivots and KPI tiles, and opens a WebSocket for Ask Iris chat.

Go/Gin HTTP edge

This is the front door for every platform request, scaling to 10k peak RPS (requests per second). - What it does: routes requests, authenticates them, applies the tenant and hierarchy scope, builds ClickHouse or Postgres queries, and returns JSON. - Why Go/Gin: Go handles many concurrent requests cheaply with goroutines (very light threads), and compiles to one binary. Gin is a thin, fast router. - Why Google Wire: all dependencies (DB pools, Redis client, logger, tracer) are wired at compile time. A missing or mis-typed dependency fails the build instead of failing at 2 a.m. - Why no reverse proxy: the Go process itself enforces timeouts, request body limits and graceful shutdown, and speaks h2c. One fewer hop and one fewer component to configure. The trade-off is that you must implement those protections yourself, carefully. - Nested timeouts: a request deadline wraps smaller deadlines on auth, Postgres and ClickHouse calls. A slow ClickHouse query cannot hold a connection forever. - Datadog tracing: every request carries a trace ID, so a slow pivot shows which span (auth, parse, ClickHouse) took the time.

Auth waterfall (Redis, Firebase Admin, JWT, Google OIDC, API keys)

Different clients log in different ways, so authentication tries a sequence of verifiers. 1. Check Redis for a cached verdict on this token. Redis is an in-memory key-value store, so this is fast and saves repeated cryptographic checks. 2. On a miss, try Firebase Admin token verification. 3. If that does not apply, verify as a JWT or Google OIDC token. 4. Machine clients use API keys, compared in constant time (in Go, subtle.ConstantTimeCompare). 5. Resolve the user's role from PostgreSQL, then compute the UAM hierarchy scope.

Isolation here means "each tenant only reads its own rows and each user only reads their allowed hierarchy". It is not encryption. Do not call it encryption.

PostgreSQL

A normal relational database (row store) for thin, transactional data: tenants, users, roles, UAM rules and metadata. It is not used for the heavy planner grids. Background (verbal): planner pivots used to run on PostgreSQL and were slow. We ran proofs of concept comparing Postgres and ClickHouse, ClickHouse won the large analytical reads, and Postgres kept metadata, UAM and roles.

KPI formula parser

Operators (business users who configure the product) write KPI formulas like units_sold / (units_sold + eop_units) * 100. The parser turns them into safe ClickHouse SQL without a code release. - A Go tokenizer splits the formula into tokens (names, numbers, operators, parentheses). - A parser builds a tree and checks every function against an allowlist. - Logical names (units_sold) map to physical columns. - Division is wrapped as ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0), so divide-by-zero returns 0 instead of infinity or NaN (not a number). - Unknown tokens fail closed, meaning the formula is rejected rather than guessed.

Tiny example (teaching sketch):

Formula typed by operator:   sell_through = units_sold / (units_sold + eop_units) * 100
Tokens:                      IDENT(units_sold) / ( IDENT(units_sold) + IDENT(eop_units) ) * NUM(100)
Generated SQL fragment:      ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(qty) / (sum(qty) + sum(eop_units)) * 100), 0)
Values such as season come in as bound parameters, never pasted into the SQL string.

ClickHouse

The analytics store. Two kinds of data matter here. - The master fact table, 2.11B rows. This is the big table the agent plane reads context from. - Six rollup tables. Product, store and attribute rollups, each at season grain and weekly grain, all PARTITION BY season_code. Planner pivots read these instead of raw daily data.

Grain Product Store Attribute
Season product_season store_season attr_season
Weekly product_weekly store_weekly attr_weekly

The attribute tables are "unpivoted" (one row per attribute and value pair), which is why attr weekly is the largest object.

Python orchestration registry

One shared runner for the three AI pipelines (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style). It gives every pipeline the same safety kit: - Hard timeouts on every LLM call. In the current Keep/Drop config the timeout scales with batch size: min(600, 60 + 8 × articles) seconds, so a 64-article batch gets 572 seconds (verbal depth from the pipeline docs). - Circuit breakers that stop a step after about 5 consecutive failures, or when the failure fraction passes a limit (0.25 in the current config). - Durable checkpoints (det.json, agent_progress.json) and a --resume flag. A resumed run reloads the saved deterministic scores and skips articles the LLM already finished. - config_hash stamped on every output row. - Custom JSON telemetry: tokens, USD cost, step duration and batch fallbacks.

Why not Airflow or Temporal? Those are workflow orchestrators. We needed resume logic tied directly to ClickHouse inserts and to the config hash, inside the app. Adding a whole orchestration platform was not justified for one team's batch jobs.

Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style pipelines

Three batch pipelines that evaluate 348k article-seasons, processing 88k items per pass. Keep/Drop is the one to explain in depth. - No LLM orchestrator. The batch order is fixed in code: peer context, then the decider, then the lenses, then the blend, then the explanation. - Deterministic score (s_det): pure math from sell-through and rate of sale. - Agent score (s_agent): the 7 lenses, each an LLM call that scores the article from 0 to 1, combined by a "decider" into weighted mixes. - Blend: s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent. Keep if s_final ≥ 0.55.

The 7 active lenses are trend velocity, size curve, colour cannibalization, channel divergence, multi-season consistency, discount dependency and margin resilience. A cheap gate runs first, so a lens only runs if the article has the data for it. A one-colour item skips the colour cannibalization lens, for example.

Missed Opportunities and Top Style reuse the same registry and scoring infrastructure. If asked for their internals, keep it qualitative.

LLM provider

The hosted model. It only ever receives JSON context and returns JSON in a fixed schema. It has no SQL tool. "Async" on the resume describes how batches run in parallel, not the LLM querying anything.

Ask Iris (LangGraph supervisor plus evaluator)

A shipped chat copilot for planners to query KPIs and inspect AI decisions. - JWT-secured WebSocket. The JWT is checked at the handshake. - Hierarchy scope frozen at the handshake. The user's plan_scope (which part of the hierarchy they may see) is computed once when the socket opens and attached to the session. Nothing the user types later can widen it. That is what prevents cross-tenant leaks. - Supervisor picks the next step. Evaluator checks the draft answer. If it fails, the graph retries, up to MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3, then stops instead of looping forever. - LangSmith records each run for observability.

Go native-TLS data pump and target cluster

A custom Go program that copied rollup tables between two ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 344k rows per second. Cluster-to-cluster copy was blocked by IP allowlists, so the pump connected to both clusters from an allowlisted machine over ClickHouse's native protocol with TLS (port 9440). Details are in the decisions and numbers sections below.

5. One request, step by step: a planner opens a pivot

Example. A planner at tenant "retailer_a" opens a pivot of revenue by product category (L2) and store region for season 74, weekly grain.

sequenceDiagram participant UI as Planner UI participant E as Go Gin edge participant R as Redis participant P as PostgreSQL participant C as ClickHouse rollups UI->>E: GET pivot for season 74, rows L2, cols region E->>R: cached verdict for this token R-->>E: miss E->>E: verify Firebase or JWT or OIDC token E->>P: load role and UAM hierarchy for user P-->>E: role planner, allowed L1 Womenswear E->>E: build SQL on product_weekly with tenant and hierarchy filters E->>C: parameterized SELECT, partition season 74 only C-->>E: aggregated cells E-->>UI: JSON pivot
  1. The browser sends the request with a token.
  2. The edge starts a request deadline and a Datadog trace.
  3. Redis has no cached verdict, so the edge verifies the token through the waterfall and caches the result.
  4. Postgres says the user is a planner who may only see the Womenswear L1 branch.
  5. The edge builds a query on product_weekly. It adds tenant = retailer_a, l1 = 'Womenswear' and season_code = 74 as bound parameters. Because the table is partitioned by season, ClickHouse only reads partition 74.
  6. ClickHouse sums a pre-aggregated table, not 250M raw rows, so the answer comes back in seconds rather than minutes.
  7. If ClickHouse is slow, the inner timeout fires, the client gets a clean error, and the trace shows exactly where the time went.

Sample SQL shape (teaching sketch):

SELECT l2_name, region, sum(revenue) AS revenue
FROM product_weekly
WHERE season_code = {season:UInt16}
  AND tenant_id = {tenant:String}
  AND l1_name IN {allowed_l1:Array(String)}
GROUP BY l2_name, region

6. One job, step by step: a Keep/Drop batch

Example. A batch of 64 articles from season 74. Follow one article, "A1".

sequenceDiagram participant REG as Registry participant CH as ClickHouse participant DET as Deterministic scorer participant LLM as LLM lenses participant OUT as Output rows REG->>CH: fixed SELECT of KPIs and features for 64 articles CH-->>REG: rows REG->>DET: compute s_det per article DET-->>REG: s_det for A1 is 0.737, saved to det.json REG->>LLM: JSON payload, peer then decider then gated lenses LLM-->>REG: lens scores, mixed into s_agent 0.711 REG->>REG: blend s_final and check 0.55 threshold REG->>OUT: row with outcome keep, config_hash, computed_at REG->>REG: update agent_progress.json and telemetry
  1. Read context. Python code (not the LLM) runs a fixed query and builds one JSON row per article: units sold, revenue, sell-through, rate of sale, number of sizes, colours and channels, and a short weekly sales series.
  2. Deterministic score. For A1, sell-through and rate of sale map onto 0-to-1 ramps and combine into s_det = 0.737. This is saved in the checkpoint so a resumed run never recomputes it.
  3. Lens gate. In this illustrative example A1 has 3 colours, 5 sizes, 2 channels, history in 2 seasons, some discounting and 10 weeks on sale, so all 7 lenses are eligible. A single-colour, single-size sock sold for 2 weeks would only get the margin lens.
  4. LLM calls. The peer step adds context about sibling colours. The decider proposes weighted mixes of lenses. Each lens returns a score, an outcome and reason codes in strict JSON. The mixes are averaged into s_agent = 0.711.
  5. Blend. s_final = 0.4 × 0.737 + 0.6 × 0.711 = 0.295 + 0.427 = 0.721. Since 0.721 is at least 0.55, A1 is Keep.
  6. Write. The output row carries the outcome, the scores, the explanation, the config_hash and a computed_at timestamp.
  7. If the LLM times out for this batch, A1 still gets a usable decision from its deterministic baseline. When the agent score arrives later (for example on --resume), a newer row with the same key is written. ReplacingMergeTree keeps the newest version. That is the "eventually consistent write pattern" on the resume: the right answer settles in over time, and the system is never without an answer.

Sample rows for A1 with the same key (season_code, article):

season_code article computed_at s_final outcome source
74 A1 10:00 0.737 (baseline) keep deterministic fallback
74 A1 10:07 0.721 keep blended

Readers take the latest computed_at per key. Background merges later drop the 10:00 row.

Write-path detail for deep follow-ups: in the current package version, scoring engines write staging files first, and a separate operator command publishes them into ClickHouse. No agent ever holds a write path.

7. Design decisions

Decision 1: Go/Gin edge with no reverse proxy

  • What: the Go process is the HTTP edge. It handles h2c, timeouts, body caps and tracing itself.
  • Why: fewer moving parts, one place to reason about timeouts, and tracing at the exact process that serves traffic.
  • Alternatives: nginx or Envoy in front. They are battle-tested, but they add a hop and a second place where timeouts are configured, which often drift apart.
  • Trade-off: you own every protection a proxy would give you for free. A missed body-size cap is your bug.
  • What I'd do differently: write the edge protections as a small shared middleware package with its own tests from day one, so new services cannot forget them.

Decision 2: ClickHouse for planner reads, PostgreSQL for metadata

  • What: heavy pivots and AI context on ClickHouse. Roles, UAM and metadata on Postgres.
  • Why: pivots read a few columns across hundreds of millions of rows. Columnar storage reads only those columns and processes them in vectorised batches. Postgres reads whole rows.
  • Alternatives: Snowflake or BigQuery. Good warehouses, but interactive pivots need predictable latency and cost on a store we operate. Postgres alone was what we started with, and it was slow.
  • Trade-off: ClickHouse is weak at updating single rows, so writes become insert-new-version (ReplacingMergeTree) rather than UPDATE.
  • What I'd do differently: decide the versioning and dedup strategy for every output table at design time, not after duplicates show up.

Decision 3: serve AI context as JSON, never give the LLM a SQL tool

  • What: Python runs fixed queries and passes JSON to the LLM. The LLM cannot query the 2.11B-row master.
  • Why: an LLM writing SQL can hallucinate a query that scans billions of rows, leaks another tenant's data or writes garbage. Fixed queries are reviewed, scoped and cheap.
  • Alternatives: a read-only SQL tool with guardrails. Still risky for cost and scope, and harder to test.
  • Trade-off: the LLM only sees what we choose to send, so a lens that needs a new field needs a code change.
  • What I'd do differently: add a schema contract test per lens so a missing field fails CI rather than producing a weak score.

Decision 4: blend deterministic math with LLM lenses, and fall back to the baseline

  • What: s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent, keep at 0.55 or above. On LLM timeout, use the deterministic baseline.
  • Why: rules are cheap, explainable and always available. Lenses catch nuance (colour cannibalization, discount dependency). The fallback keeps the product working when the provider is down.
  • Alternatives: LLM-only decisions (unavailable when the provider fails, hard to audit) or rules-only (too coarse).
  • Trade-off: two scoring systems to maintain and evaluate.
  • What I'd do differently: gate on drop recall (catching true drops) from the start, not only on accuracy. See the evals page for why.

Decision 5: app-native orchestration registry instead of Airflow or Temporal

  • What: one Python registry gives every pipeline timeouts, breakers, checkpoints, config hashing and telemetry.
  • Why: resume had to be coupled to ClickHouse inserts and to config_hash. That is easier inside the app.
  • Alternatives: Airflow (task scheduler) or Temporal (durable workflow engine). Both are strong, but they are another platform to run, and they would not remove the need for app-level resume logic.
  • Trade-off: we own the retry and resume code.
  • What I'd do differently: if more teams start running agent batches, revisit Temporal.

Decision 6: pre-aggregated rollups and one-week insert slices

  • What: six rollup tables, and weekly rollups built one fiscal week per INSERT SELECT.
  • Why: pay the aggregation cost once at load time, read cheaply at query time. A whole season at weekly grain needed about 170GB of aggregation memory and crashed.
  • Alternatives: query raw daily data on every request (too slow), or ClickHouse projections (they do not help when queries use FINAL on ReplacingMergeTree).
  • Trade-off: more tables to build, validate and keep in sync.
  • What I'd do differently: run the incremental REPLACE PARTITION design (written, not executed) so rebuilds swap in cleanly for readers.

Decision 7: a custom Go pump to copy across clusters

  • What: a Go program reading from one ClickHouse Cloud cluster and writing to another over native TLS.
  • Why: cross-cluster IP allowlists blocked cluster-to-cluster copy. An allowlisted machine could reach both.
  • Alternatives: INSERT SELECT across clusters (blocked), or exporting to object storage and importing (slower to set up for this one-off).
  • Trade-off: the copy depends on one machine and is not an atomic swap.
  • What I'd do differently: for production cutovers, get the allowlist changed or go through object storage, rather than copying through an operator machine.

8. The numbers on this diagram

Number What it measures Tag
10k peak RPS Peak request rate the Go/Gin edge serves On PDF

88k items per pass Items processed in one batch run On PDF
7 lenses Active LLM lenses per article On PDF
15.5×, 189s to 12s on 250M rows Planner pivot query time before and after rollups MEASURED
170GB Aggregation memory a whole-season weekly build needed before it crashed MEASURED
