15.5× pivot speed-up. It measures how long one planner pivot query took on a 250M-row test harness: 189 seconds on the old path, about 12.3 seconds on the rollup tables. The PDF rounds 12.3 to 12. Arithmetic: 189 divided by 12.3 is about 15.4, and 189 divided by 12 is about 15.75. The reported harness ratio is about 15.5×. If someone checks the arithmetic, say the ratio comes from the measured harness timings, and the headline seconds are rounded. Say it as: "a planner pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, about fifteen and a half times faster." Do not say "sub-second".

170GB OOM. It measures memory, not speed. A whole-season weekly INSERT SELECT needed about 170GB of aggregation state. It failed even with 80GB and 200GB memory caps. The fix was one fiscal week per insert, with a 55GB memory cap, 16GB disk spill, 8 threads and 4 weeks in flight (verbal knobs). One product week peaked around 11GB, one attribute week over 40GB. Say it as: "the weekly build kept crashing out of memory, so I sliced it into one-week inserts with memory and spill caps." This is load time. The 15.5× is query time. One did not cause the other.

~344k rows per second. It measures ingest rate during the copy, not requests per second. Two season streams ran in parallel at roughly 150k to 190k rows per second each, combined about 344k. Say it as "about 344 thousand rows per second", never "344k TPS".

4.09B rows. The attr weekly table for two seasons: 2,779,317,472 plus 1,311,108,195 rows. The copy was measured while running. Do not say the cutover finished.

$100 per pass (off PDF, true). Token spend for one pass. Arithmetic: $100 divided by 88,000 items is about $0.0011, roughly a tenth of a cent per item (ESTIMATED). With 64 articles per LLM batch, one pass is roughly 88,000 / 64 ≈ 1,375 batches (ESTIMATED).

1.6M article-seasons (off PDF). The full product-by-season catalog. It is a different number from the 348k that were scored. Do not mix them.

9. Failure modes and what the system does

What breaks How you notice What happens
LLM provider slow or down Timeouts and fallback counts in JSON telemetry Hard timeout fires. Article keeps its deterministic baseline score. Circuit breaker stops the step after about 5 consecutive failures.
Batch job crashes mid-run Run stops, checkpoint files remain --resume reloads det.json and agent_progress.json, skips finished work, and does not re-run deterministic scoring.
Prompt or config edited New config_hash on new rows Old and new decisions are distinguishable. A change must pass the 80% CI gate before promotion.
Duplicate rows before merges Two rows for the same key Readers pick the latest computed_at. ReplacingMergeTree merges later.
Slow ClickHouse query Datadog span shows ClickHouse time Inner timeout fires, request fails cleanly instead of hanging.
Bad KPI formula from an operator Parser rejects unknown token Fails closed. No SQL is generated.
Divide by zero in a KPI Would produce infinity or NaN ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0) returns 0.
Ask Iris answer keeps failing evaluation Attempt counter Stops after 3 attempts instead of looping.
User tries to see another region in chat Query outside plan_scope Scope was frozen at handshake, so reads stay inside it.
Weekly rollup build out of memory MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED One fiscal week per insert, memory and spill caps.
Half-loaded weekly partition Missing entry in the TSV ledger DROP PARTITION for that season and rebuild.
Copier killed mid-season No .done checkpoint for that table DROP PARTITION then recopy that season. Readers can see a partial season until then. This is not an atomic swap.

10. Observability: what a log line looks like

Every Go and Python service emits structured JSON that Datadog can filter on.

{
  "timestamp": "2026-09-03T03:40:39.123Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "assortsmart-edge",
  "env": "production",
  "trace_id": "4a6f8c9b2e1d3f5a",
  "span_id": "8b2d1c4f5a6e3",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_xyz_99",
  "message": "LLM batch fallback to deterministic score",
  "metadata": { "pipeline": "keep_drop", "batch_id": "b_981273" }
}

Say this carefully: correlate logs with traces through the explicit trace_id field. Do not claim automatic Datadog trace-ID log injection unless you have checked the code does it.

11. Hindsight (verbal-only depth, not on the resume)

Hindsight is not a resume bullet. It is a module I am building against a functional requirements document (FRD v1.2). Say "building", not "shipped". There is no dollar or latency number for Hindsight. Full defense: ../projects/01b_hindsight_defense.md.

Plain English. Hindsight is the first screen of the planning cycle. Before planners buy for next season, they look back at last season: what worked, what did not, which styles to carry forward. It has a scorecard (this year against last year), contribution charts, a store map, an item grid, an attribute heatmap, a carry-forward panel and short AI-written narration.

flowchart LR CAT["Tenant metric catalog, config not code"] METRICS["Computed metrics from ClickHouse"] VIS["Deterministic charts from config"] NARR["Overnight narration batch"] CHECK["Numbers check before save"] TMPL["Template sentence fallback"] UI["Hindsight screen, permission-scoped"] CAT --> METRICS METRICS --> VIS METRICS --> NARR NARR --> CHECK CHECK -->|"pass"| UI CHECK -->|"fail"| TMPL TMPL --> UI VIS --> UI

What to notice: the AI writes sentences, but it never chooses charts and never calculates metrics. Every number in a sentence is checked against the computed value before it is saved.

Key design points: - Overnight batch narration, not live, so filter changes do not trigger LLM cost or latency. - Grounding check: numbers in the narration are compared with computed metrics before save. If they do not match, a templated sentence is used instead. - Charts come from configuration only. The narration agent never picks layout. - One shared metric catalog per tenant, and onboarding config goes live without a code deploy. - Permission-scoped filters: "select all" never leaks outside the user's scope. - Item grid stays fast at 1,000+ items via pagination or virtualized scrolling.

12. Say this, not that

Say this Not this
"The LLM never gets a SQL tool. Python serves it JSON context." "The agents query ClickHouse."
"80% is the CI promotion gate on a 300-case proxy set." "We are at 80% accuracy in production for all tenants."
"15.5× is query time. The 170GB OOM fix is load time." "Fixing the OOM made pivots 15.5× faster."
"About 344 thousand rows per second during the copy." "344k TPS" or "344k requests per second."
"The 4.09B copy was measured in flight." "We finished the 4.09B cutover."
"Partition rollback means DROP PARTITION then recopy that season." "Atomic swap with live readers."
"Ask Iris is a shipped capability." Any usage number or SLA for Ask Iris.
"Kafka and Flink were on Uber Menu." Kafka, Flink, CDC or Kubernetes operations on AssortSmart.
"Isolation means tenant and hierarchy scoping." "Encryption."

13. How to draw it in 3 minutes

Minute 1: the platform spine. Draw the Planner UI on the left, the Go/Gin edge in the middle, and ClickHouse and Postgres on the right. Say: "Planners hit a multi-tenant Go/Gin edge at 10k peak RPS. Wire wires dependencies at compile time, and the process itself handles h2c, nested timeouts and Datadog tracing, with no reverse proxy. Auth is a Redis-fronted waterfall, roles come from Postgres, and every query is scoped by tenant and hierarchy." Add a small KPI parser box between the edge and ClickHouse: "Operator formulas compile to parameterized ClickHouse SQL, with divide-by-zero protection."

Minute 2: the data layer. Inside ClickHouse draw the 2.11B master and a 2×3 grid for the six rollups. Say: "Pivots read pre-aggregated rollups partitioned by season. That took a 250M-row pivot from 189 seconds to 12 seconds. Separately, weekly builds were crashing at around 170GB, so I sliced inserts by fiscal week with memory and spill caps." Draw the Go pump to a second cluster: "I copied rollups across Cloud clusters at about 344k rows a second with a native-TLS Go pump, because allowlists blocked cluster-to-cluster copy."

Minute 3: the agent plane. Draw the Python registry below ClickHouse with an arrow labelled "JSON" into an LLM box. Say: "The decision engine scores 348k article-seasons, 88k per pass, blending deterministic KPI math with 7 LLM lenses. The LLM only sees JSON, never SQL. Output rows go back as versioned rows in ReplacingMergeTree, and if the LLM times out we keep the deterministic baseline. Timeouts, breakers, checkpoints and a config hash on every row come from a shared registry." Finally draw Ask Iris on the WebSocket: "Planners chat through Ask Iris: JWT WebSocket, scope frozen at handshake, LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator, traced in LangSmith. Changes promote only through an 80% CI gate."

Architecture: Uber FRM Scoping Platform (Uber via EPAM)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the FRM (Financial Risk Management) scoping backend I owned at Uber Finance via EPAM. That means the Java Spring Boot service, the MySQL schema, how one edit flows through it, and how the quarterly close runs.
  • When to read it: before system design rounds that touch data modelling, concurrency or correctness, and before any "tell me about Uber" question.
  • What to memorise: the six-box diagram, the PATCH request with the version check, and the three numbers: 70% (from 14 days to 3 days), $340M materiality, 36 endpoints.

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, a doc or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). HISTORICAL means from past work records.

Stack on this track (Java + AI, IA = Py/Go): Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, MySQL, JUnit, Bazel, Docker. Request validation uses Bean Validation. Tests use JUnit 5, Mockito and MockMvc.

1. The one-paragraph version

Every quarter, Uber's finance team must decide which accounts and which legal entities the auditors (PwC) need to test. That decision is called scoping. Before this project it lived in a large Google Sheets workbook with manual formulas, no stable row IDs, no audit trail, and people overwriting each other during the close. I owned the backend that replaced it: a Java Spring Boot service with 36 endpoints on a normalized MySQL schema, migrating 19M raw GL rows off Sheets. It automates the financial math, models a 4-level account hierarchy, and keeps an auditable history. The close-related reconciliation work went from 14 days to 3 days, a 70% cut, against a $340M materiality threshold.

2. Words you need

The finance words

  • FRM (Financial Risk Management). The finance function that decides where the risk of a misstatement in the financial statements is, and therefore what auditors should test.
  • Scoping. Choosing which accounts and entities are "in scope" for audit testing. Like a teacher deciding which chapters will be on the exam.
  • Materiality. The size of error that would matter to someone reading the financial statements. Here it was $340M for the Q4 2025 close. Anything bigger than that cannot be ignored.
  • Residual risk. The part of the balance that is not covered by the in-scope items. On the Q4 2025 close the residual threshold was $170M.
  • GL (general ledger). The master list of every accounting entry, by account and entity. Think of the company's full bank statement for every account.
  • FSLI (Financial Statement Line Item). A line on the balance sheet or income statement, such as "Cash" or "Accounts receivable". FSLIs nest in a hierarchy, here 4 levels, L1 to L4 (for example L1 "Current assets", L2 "Cash and equivalents", down to more detailed lines).
  • HFM (Oracle Hyperion Financial Management). The consolidation system where entity trial balances are loaded, converted to one currency and combined into group numbers.
  • 10-Q. The quarterly report a US public company files with the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission). Its numbers are the publicly attested truth.
  • Reconciliation. Checking that two sources agree, here HFM numbers against the filed 10-Q, line by line. difference = HFM amount − filed amount. Like matching your own budget spreadsheet to your bank statement.
  • SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley). US law that requires companies to have controls over financial reporting. Practically: every change must be traceable and controlled.
  • EMI (Equity Method Investment). A company Uber partly owns and accounts for by its share of profit or loss. It has its own scoping screen.
  • Quarter-annualization. Converting a figure for part of a year into an annual figure so it can be compared with annual thresholds. The general idea: a year-to-date number after two quarters is scaled up to a full-year equivalent. "Dynamic" means the scaling depends on which quarter you are in.

The data and design words

  • SOADB. Uber's standard for service-owned relational databases: MySQL on InnoDB. InnoDB gives ACID transactions (all-or-nothing writes that stay consistent).
  • Normalized schema. Each fact stored once, in its own table, linked by keys, instead of copying the same data into many places. Like keeping one contacts list instead of writing a friend's number in every notebook.
  • Natural key. An ID derived from the data itself rather than a random number. Here, a SHA-256 hash of meaningful fields, so the same question on the same page always gets the same ID.
  • Optimistic row-locking. Each row has a version number. An update only succeeds if the version is still what you read. If someone else saved first, your update affects zero rows and you get a conflict instead of silently overwriting. Like a shared document that warns "this was changed since you opened it".
  • Polymorphic review-status model. One status model reused across many screens. Every screen's rows move through the same states: Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed.
  • FSM (finite state machine). A fixed set of states and allowed transitions. "Draft can go to Review, Review can go to Closed or ReOpen", and nothing else.
  • Bazel. Uber's monorepo build and test system. Stacked PRs are a chain of small pull requests, each building on the previous, so each can be reviewed and shipped safely.
  • Statement coverage. The percentage of code lines executed by tests.

The Java and Spring words

  • Spring Boot. A Java framework that starts a web service with sensible defaults already wired: an embedded web server (Tomcat), JSON handling, database connection pool, configuration and health checks. Think of a furnished flat: you move in and only change what you need.
  • Spring MVC and @RestController. Spring MVC is the web layer inside Spring Boot. A class marked @RestController holds HTTP handlers, and annotations such as @GetMapping and @PatchMapping map a URL and HTTP verb to a Java method. The return value is turned into JSON automatically.
  • Dependency injection and beans. Spring creates the controller, service and repository objects (called beans) and passes each one the others it needs through its constructor. You never write new GroupScopingService(...) yourself. Like a stage manager who hands each actor their props before the scene.
  • Thread-per-request. Spring MVC on Tomcat gives each incoming request its own thread from a pool. Blocking database calls are normal in this model, so there is no event loop to protect.
  • JPA (Jakarta Persistence API). The standard Java API for mapping database rows to Java objects. It is a specification, not a library.
  • Hibernate. The library that implements JPA. It turns object changes into SQL, tracks which objects changed, and writes them at commit. Hibernate is the ORM (object-relational mapper) here.
  • Entity. A Java class marked @Entity that maps to one table. One object is one row.
  • Spring Data JPA repository. An interface such as GroupLineRepository extends JpaRepository<GroupLine, String>. Spring generates the implementation, so findById, save and custom @Query methods work without hand-written data access code.
  • JPQL and native queries. JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language) is SQL-like but written against entity and field names. A native query is plain MySQL SQL run through JPA. Both can return a projection, which is a small read-only shape (an interface or a record) holding only the selected columns.
  • @Version. A JPA annotation on a numeric field. Hibernate adds AND version = ? to every UPDATE and increments the number. If zero rows change, it throws an OptimisticLockException (Spring wraps it as ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException). This is how optimistic row-locking is implemented.
  • @Transactional. Put on a service method, it opens one database transaction when the method starts and commits when it returns. If an exception escapes, everything in the method rolls back. This is how atomic cross-table syncs work.
  • Bean Validation. Annotations such as @NotNull and @NotBlank on request fields. @Valid on the request body makes Spring check them before the method runs. A failed check never reaches the business code.
  • DTO (data transfer object). A plain class or Java record that defines the JSON shape of a request or response, kept separate from the entity so the API does not leak database internals.
  • @RestControllerAdvice. One class that turns exceptions into HTTP responses for the whole service, for example a stale version into a 409 and a validation failure into a 400 with an error body.
  • HikariCP. The database connection pool Spring Boot uses by default. It keeps a fixed number of MySQL connections open and lends one to each request thread for the length of its transaction.
  • JUnit 5, Mockito, MockMvc. JUnit 5 is the Java test runner. Mockito creates fake versions of dependencies so a service can be tested alone. MockMvc sends fake HTTP requests to a controller without starting a real server, so you can assert status codes and JSON.

3. The architecture diagram

flowchart LR UI["React finance screens, 8 pages"] GW["Uber gateway, injects user identity header"] H["Spring Boot REST controllers, 36 endpoints"] S["Service layer: scoping math, FSM gates, @Transactional"] R["Repository layer: Spring Data JPA on Hibernate"] DB["MySQL on SOADB: 8-table normalized schema"] ETL["Shared ETL from Oracle HFM"] TENQ["Filed 10-Q figures"] COL["Separate collaboration service, not mine"] PWC["PwC audit work papers"] UI -->|"HTTPS JSON"| GW GW -->|"request plus user email header"| H H -->|"validated DTO"| S S -->|"entity reads and writes"| R R -->|"SQL over HikariCP pool"| DB ETL -->|"period extracts"| DB TENQ -->|"filed line amounts"| S UI -.->|"comments and alerts"| COL DB -->|"stable row IDs and history"| PWC

What to notice: a classic three-layer service (controller, service, repository) on one transactional database. The ETL from HFM and the collaboration service are shared or separate pieces. I owned the scoping service in the middle.

4. Box-by-box walkthrough

React finance screens (8 pages)

The UI finance managers use. The 8 screens are Reconciliation, Materiality, EMI Scoping, Group Scoping, Threshold Setup, Component Scoping, Residual Risk and Summary. Each screen reads and edits rows through the API. I describe the UI as context; my ownership is the backend.

Uber gateway

Authenticates the user and injects their identity as a header (for example x-auth-params-email). The controller reads it with @RequestHeader, and the service writes that email into created_by and updated_by columns, so every change is attributable. That matters for SOX.

Spring Boot REST controllers (36 endpoints)

The HTTP layer. Each controller method takes a request DTO checked by Bean Validation, calls the service layer, and returns a typed response DTO, including nested trees for the L1 to L4 hierarchy. If asked for the breakdown: about 31 functional routes live in the scoping service controllers, and the comment and notification APIs specified in the technical design doc (TDD) for the collaboration service make up the rest of the 36.

Why Spring Boot. It gives a mature, opinionated stack for a correctness-heavy CRUD service: Spring MVC for the endpoints, Bean Validation at the boundary, Spring Data JPA for data access, declarative transactions, and first-class testing with MockMvc. JPA calls are blocking, and Spring MVC's thread-per-request model handles that naturally, so no extra offloading is needed. Each request thread borrows a MySQL connection from HikariCP for the length of its transaction.

A short controller, so the shape is concrete (teaching sketch, names illustrative):

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/group-scoping/lines")
class GroupScopingController {
    private final GroupScopingService service;

    GroupScopingController(GroupScopingService service) { this.service = service; }

    @PatchMapping("/{uuid}")
    LineResponse updateStatus(@PathVariable String uuid,
                              @Valid @RequestBody StatusUpdateRequest body,
                              @RequestHeader("x-auth-params-email") String email) {
        return service.updateStatus(uuid, body, email);
    }
}

enum ReviewStatus { DRAFT, REVIEW, REOPEN, CLOSED }

record StatusUpdateRequest(@NotNull ReviewStatus status,
                           @NotBlank String conclusionScope,
                           @NotNull Long expectedVersion) {}

Service layer

Where the finance logic lives: - Group scoping: a line is significant if it passes the quantitative test (compared with materiality) or a qualitative test. - Component scoping: drills into entities under each FSLI, using a 5% significance threshold. - Residual risk: computes the balance not covered by in-scope items and compares it with the residual threshold. - Quarter-annualization for comparisons against annual thresholds. - FSM gates: allowed status transitions only, plus a 50% delta-variance check. If a line moves by more than half compared with the prior period, the automatic transition is blocked and the line is flagged. This is a SOX control.

Service methods that change data are marked @Transactional, so every write inside one method commits together or rolls back together. One Spring detail worth knowing: @Transactional works through a proxy (a wrapper object Spring puts around the bean), so calling a transactional method from another method in the same class skips the wrapper. Keep transactional entry points public and call them from the controller.

Repository layer (Spring Data JPA on Hibernate)

All database access goes through Spring Data JPA repositories, with Hibernate underneath. The Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration I led (with 3 engineers) moved this layer to entities, repositories and explicitly aliased JPQL or native projections. That removed a class of column-aliasing bugs (explained below) and brought module statement coverage to 100%.

Reporting SQL allowlists: reporting queries can only run from an approved list, so nobody ships an ad hoc query against financial tables. In practice the approved queries are named repository methods, and nothing else can reach the financial tables.

MySQL on SOADB (8-table normalized schema)

The system of record. The schema stores the hierarchy, the per-quarter balances, the reconciliation leaves, thresholds, questionnaires and assessments. Key properties: - Fiscal period keys on every fact row (fiscal_quarter, fiscal_year) with composite indexes. - The ETL flattens the recursive FSLI tree into a stable level_id in a mapping table, so the API joins facts to a level ID instead of walking a tree in SQL. - Optimistic row-locking through a @Version column checked on every update. - Atomic cross-table syncs: when one edit must change rows in several tables, it happens in one @Transactional method. Either all change or none. - SHA-256 natural keys so re-imported data updates in place instead of duplicating.

If someone has seen the code and asks why there are 11 ORM models (entities): the resume number is the 8-table normalized schema in the bullet. Keep the answer at that level and do not invent a table-by-table mapping.

Shared ETL from Oracle HFM

HFM extracts land in MySQL for each fiscal period. The ETL was a shared pipeline responsibility. Do not claim you built it alone.

Filed 10-Q figures

The reconciliation screen compares HFM amounts with the public 10-Q line amounts, so scoping is built on numbers that match what went to the SEC.

Separate collaboration service

Comments, notifications and Slack alerts live in a separate service. I did not build it. Scope your ownership to the scoping service.

PwC audit work papers

The Summary screen and the stored history feed the auditors. Stable row IDs mean an auditor's comment points at the same line every quarter.

5. One request, step by step: a manager moves a line to Review

Example. A finance manager on the Group Scoping screen marks the "Cash and equivalents" line for Q4 2025 as in scope and moves it from Draft to Review.

sequenceDiagram participant UI as Group Scoping screen participant H as Spring REST controller participant S as Transactional service participant DB as MySQL UI->>H: PATCH group line, status REVIEW, expectedVersion 3 H->>H: Bean Validation checks body, reads user email header H->>S: updateStatus call S->>DB: BEGIN, SELECT line by uuid S->>S: version still 3, FSM allows Draft to Review S->>S: delta check against prior quarter, under 50 percent S->>DB: UPDATE where uuid and version 3, audit columns, COMMIT DB-->>S: 1 row updated, version now 4 S-->>H: response DTO H-->>UI: 200 with new state
  1. The browser sends a PATCH with the new status, the scoping conclusion and the version it last read (3):
{ "status": "REVIEW", "conclusionScope": "In scope", "expectedVersion": 3 }
  1. Bean Validation checks the body before the controller method runs. A missing field fails @NotNull or @NotBlank, and a status that is not one of Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed cannot be read into the enum. Either way the API returns 400 with an error body, and the service is never called:
{ "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED", "message": "expectedVersion must not be null" }
  1. The service loads the line and compares its version with expectedVersion. Then it checks the FSM: Draft to Review is allowed. Closed straight back to Draft would not be.
  2. The service runs the delta-variance check. Illustrative numbers: last quarter $1,000M, this quarter $1,200M, a 20% move. That is under 50%, so the gate passes.
  3. The service sets the new fields on the entity. At flush, Hibernate writes one UPDATE that includes the version check. This is the SQL it generates, in plain form:
UPDATE group_balance_sheet
SET group_status = 'REVIEW', conclusion_scope = 'In scope',
    version = 4, updated_by = :email, updated_at = NOW()
WHERE uuid = :uuid AND version = 3;
  1. One row changed, so it commits. If another manager had saved first, the version would already be 4. Either the version comparison in step 3 catches it, or, if the other save landed between our read and our write, the UPDATE matches zero rows and Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException. Both paths become 409 Conflict instead of silently overwriting.
  2. The UI shows the new state, and the audit columns record who did it.

The entity and the service behind those steps (teaching sketch, names illustrative):

@Entity
@Table(name = "group_balance_sheet")
class GroupLine {
    @Id private String uuid;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) private ReviewStatus groupStatus;
    private String conclusionScope;
    @Version private Long version;
    private String updatedBy;
    private Instant updatedAt;
    // getters and setters omitted
}

@Service
class GroupScopingService {
    private final GroupLineRepository lines;
    private final ScopingGates gates;

    GroupScopingService(GroupLineRepository lines, ScopingGates gates) {
        this.lines = lines;
        this.gates = gates;
    }

    @Transactional
    public LineResponse updateStatus(String uuid, StatusUpdateRequest req, String email) {
        GroupLine line = lines.findById(uuid)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new LineNotFoundException(uuid));
        if (!line.getVersion().equals(req.expectedVersion())) {
            throw new ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException(GroupLine.class, uuid);
        }
        gates.requireAllowedTransition(line.getGroupStatus(), req.status());
        gates.requireDeltaUnderThreshold(line);   // the 50% delta-variance check
        line.setGroupStatus(req.status());
        line.setConclusionScope(req.conclusionScope());
        line.setUpdatedBy(email);
        line.setUpdatedAt(Instant.now());
        return LineResponse.from(lines.saveAndFlush(line));
    }
}

And the one place that maps exceptions to HTTP responses:

@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler({OptimisticLockingFailureException.class, OptimisticLockException.class})
    ResponseEntity<ErrorBody> staleVersion(Exception e) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
            .body(new ErrorBody("STALE_VERSION", "This line changed since you opened it. Reload and retry."));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ErrorBody> invalidBody(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        String msg = e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .map(f -> f.getField() + " " + f.getDefaultMessage())
            .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(new ErrorBody("VALIDATION_FAILED", msg));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(HttpMessageNotReadableException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ErrorBody> unreadableBody(HttpMessageNotReadableException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(new ErrorBody("VALIDATION_FAILED", "Malformed body or unknown status"));
    }
}

record ErrorBody(String code, String message) {}

The quarterly close, as one job

  1. HFM extracts land in MySQL for the fiscal period (shared ETL).
  2. Reconciliation ties HFM to the 10-Q line by line and shows every non-zero difference.
  3. Materiality and thresholds are set: $340M materiality, $170M residual for Q4 2025.
  4. Group scoping marks significant FSLIs. Component scoping drills into entities under each.
  5. Residual risk computes what is still uncovered. EMI scoping handles part-owned investees.
  6. Summary rolls up coverage for PwC.

6. Design decisions

Decision 1: move the close off Google Sheets into a normalized MySQL schema

  • What: an 8-table normalized schema on SOADB replaces the workbook.
  • Why: Sheets has no stable row IDs (so no comments or audit history per line), no concurrency control, and no way to model a recursive hierarchy safely. Versions drift between copies. Finance had ETL lock contention during the close.
  • Alternatives: keep Sheets with Apps Script (no real concurrency control), or use a columnar warehouse (built for scans, not transactional edits).
  • Trade-off: more upfront schema design, and a migration with a parallel run.
  • What I'd do differently: build the parallel-run comparison report as a first-class feature from day one, not as a side script.

Decision 2: optimistic row-locking instead of pessimistic locks

  • What: a JPA @Version column on every editable entity, checked on every update.
  • Why: many managers read and few collide on the same line. Holding row locks while someone thinks in the UI would block others.
  • How: Hibernate adds the version to the UPDATE's WHERE clause. Zero rows changed means OptimisticLockException, and the controller advice turns that into a 409.
  • Alternatives: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (pessimistic, @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) in JPA). Safe, but locks pile up during the close.
  • Trade-off: the UI must handle a conflict response and ask the user to reload.
  • What I'd do differently: return the current row with the 409 so the UI can show a diff.

Decision 3: SHA-256 natural keys

  • What: for example uuid = SHA-256(question_text + normalized page_name) for scoping questions.
  • Why: quarterly re-imports of the same data must update rows, not create duplicates across audit trails.
  • Alternatives: random UUIDs plus a uniqueness constraint on several columns. That works, but the ID is not reproducible from the data.
  • Trade-off: if the source text changes (even a typo fix), the key changes. Normalising the inputs first reduces that.

Tiny example (teaching sketch). MessageDigest is Java's built-in hashing class, and HexFormat turns the bytes into a hex string:

static String questionUuid(String questionText, String pageName) {
    String key = questionText.strip() + "|" + pageName.strip().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
    try {
        byte[] hash = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
            .digest(key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return HexFormat.of().formatHex(hash);
    } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("SHA-256 not available", e);
    }
}

// questionUuid("Is the balance subject to significant estimates?", "Group Scoping")
// gives the same id next quarter, so the upsert updates in place

Decision 4: one polymorphic review-status model across screens

  • What: Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed, shared by every screen. In Java this is one ReviewStatus enum and one set of transition rules that every screen's service calls.
  • Why: one set of FSM rules, one set of tests, one audit format.
  • Alternatives: a separate status column and rules per screen. Faster to start, but rules drift.
  • Trade-off: a screen with special needs has to fit the shared model.

Decision 5: lead a Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration

  • What: move the repository layer to JPA entities and Spring Data repositories, with every multi-table read written as an explicitly aliased JPQL or native projection.
  • Why: a real bug. A raw SQL join returned two columns with the same name. The code built a map from column names, so the second value silently overwrote the first, and some rows were mapped to the wrong uuid.
  • Alternatives: patch each raw query by hand. Fixes today's bug, not the class of bugs.
  • Trade-off: a migration across many modules, which needed tests first. That is why coverage reached 100% for the module.
  • What I'd do differently: add a lint rule that rejects raw SQL with unaliased duplicate column names.

The fix in code (teaching sketch, names illustrative). Every projected column gets its own alias, and Spring Data maps each alias to one getter, so two uuid columns can never collide:

interface LevelBalanceRow {
    String getBalanceUuid();
    String getLevelUuid();
    BigDecimal getAmount();
}

interface GlBalanceRepository extends JpaRepository<GlBalance, String> {
    @Query(value = """
        SELECT b.uuid AS balanceUuid, m.uuid AS levelUuid, b.amount AS amount
        FROM gl_balance b
        JOIN fsli_level_map m ON m.level_id = b.level_id
        WHERE b.fiscal_year = :fy AND b.fiscal_quarter = :fq
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    List<LevelBalanceRow> findQuarterBalances(@Param("fy") int fy, @Param("fq") int fq);
}

The JPQL version works the same way with a constructor expression, for example SELECT new com.example.frm.LevelBalance(b.uuid, m.uuid, b.amount) FROM GlBalance b JOIN b.level m, where each value goes into a named constructor parameter instead of a name-keyed map.

Decision 6: zero-downtime releases through stacked Bazel PRs

  • What: each change is a small PR in a stack. Schema changes ship before code that depends on them.
  • Why: finance cannot have the tool down during the close.
  • Trade-off: more PRs to coordinate and review.

70% (from 14 days to 3 days). It measures how long the quarterly reconciliation took before and after. It mattered because the close is time-boxed, and every day spent on manual tie-outs is a day not spent on analysis. Say it as "we cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days, about 70%". If someone does the arithmetic: 14 to 3 is actually about a 79% cut, because (14 − 3) / 14 ≈ 0.79. The 70% headline is the figure the technical design doc framed, so the resume understates rather than overstates. If pressed on source, say "the technical design doc framed that cut and that is what the platform delivered for the close". Do not walk it back unprompted.

$340M materiality. It is not a volume metric. It is the threshold that drives the scoping rules. Say "against a $340 million materiality threshold".

19M raw GL rows. It is the total migrated off Sheets. Individual quarterly GL extracts were about 38K to 95K rows, about 1.7K to 1.8K accounts and about 400 entities. If asked, say "the value was correctness, hierarchy and auditability, not big-data throughput". Do not invent a breakdown of where 19M comes from beyond "raw GL rows migrated off Sheets".

36 endpoints. About 31 functional routes in the scoping service plus the comment and notification APIs from the TDD. Say "36 Spring Boot endpoints". Older prep said "30+ endpoints, do not say 36". That guidance is obsolete. The current resume says 36.

3 engineers. I was tech lead of an EPAM pod, not a people manager. Never add this to "mentored 2" from Masters India.

8. Failure modes and what the system does

What breaks How you notice What happens
Two managers edit the same line Version mismatch or UPDATE affects 0 rows OptimisticLockException, API returns 409, nobody's change is silently lost.
Request body is missing a field or has an unknown status Bean Validation or JSON parsing fails API returns 400 with an error body. The service never runs.
An edit must touch several tables and one write fails Exception inside the @Transactional method Whole transaction rolls back. No half-applied edit.
Same data re-imported next quarter Same SHA-256 key Upsert updates in place, no duplicates.
Large unexpected swing in a line Delta over 50% FSM gate blocks the automatic transition and flags the line.
Joined raw SQL with duplicate column names Wrong uuid on rows (the real bug) Fixed by the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration: explicitly aliased projections.
HFM and 10-Q do not tie Non-zero difference on Reconciliation Shown and commentable on every line. Managers clear breaks before sign-off. The tool makes breaks visible. Humans do the sign-off.
Ad hoc reporting query Not in allowlist Rejected.
Request threads waiting on the database HikariCP pool exhausted, requests time out waiting for a connection Keep transactions short, never hold one open across a slow call, and size the pool to what the database allows.
Bad release during close Tests and staged PRs Small stacked PRs, 100% module coverage, rollback is one small PR.

9. Verbal depth (not on the PDF, true)

  • Sheets to MySQL reconciliation, v1 to v2. Version 2 endpoints ran in parallel beside version 1. The change touched 18 files, +1,268 lines of code. Stable IDs unlocked per-line comments. Cutover happened after staging parity.
  • The column-aliasing bug. A join of the fact table and the level mapping table returned columns with the same name. The code zipped column names to values, so the last one won, and rows got the wrong uuid. Fix: an explicit AS alias on every projected column, read through a Spring Data projection interface or a JPQL constructor expression, so each value has exactly one named home.
  • Q4 2025 sample: about 55 line items and 14 entities in scope (MEASURED in older prep).
  • Tests: the suite grew past 1,100 tests because every PR had to add or update tests in the matching folder. CI ran five layer targets (database, schema, repository, service, controller). Service tests used JUnit 5 with Mockito fakes for repositories. Controller tests used MockMvc to assert status codes and JSON, including the 400 and 409 paths. As a general practice, repository tests can run against a real MySQL in a throwaway Docker container (Testcontainers).

A MockMvc test for the conflict path, so the testing style is concrete (teaching sketch):

@WebMvcTest(GroupScopingController.class)
class GroupScopingControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean GroupScopingService service;

    @Test
    void staleVersionReturns409() throws Exception {
        when(service.updateStatus(eq("abc"), any(), any()))
            .thenThrow(new ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException(GroupLine.class, "abc"));

        mvc.perform(patch("/group-scoping/lines/abc")
                .header("x-auth-params-email", "manager@example.com")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"status\":\"REVIEW\",\"conclusionScope\":\"In scope\",\"expectedVersion\":3}"))
           .andExpect(status().isConflict())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.code").value("STALE_VERSION"));
    }
}

10. Say this, not that

Say this Not this
"Uber via EPAM." "I worked at Uber" without EPAM.
"I owned the scoping backend." "I built the collaboration and Slack service."
"The HFM ETL was a shared pipeline." "I built the whole data pipeline."
"Led 3 engineers as tech lead of an EPAM pod." "I managed a team" or "led 5".
"36 Spring Boot endpoints." "30+ endpoints" (obsolete prep).
"Value was correctness and auditability." "Big data at 19M rows per quarter."

Say this carefully about optimistic locking. Older prep notes said version-check concurrency lived in the collaboration service. The current resume claims optimistic row-locking in the schema. If pressed, explain the mechanism (a @Version column, the conditional UPDATE Hibernate generates, a 409 on zero rows) and keep the scope to the scoping tables.

11. How to draw it in 3 minutes

Minute 1: the problem and the spine. Write "Google Sheets close, 14 days" on the left and cross it out. Draw UI, gateway, Spring Boot service, MySQL left to right. Say: "Uber's quarterly scoping lived in Sheets: no stable IDs, no audit trail, people overwriting each other. I owned the Spring Boot backend that replaced it, 36 endpoints on MySQL on Uber's SOADB standard, and we migrated 19 million raw GL rows off Sheets."

Minute 2: inside the service. Split the Spring Boot box into controller, service, repository. Say: "Controllers validate request DTOs with Bean Validation and return 400 on bad input. The service holds the finance math: materiality at $340 million, the L1 to L4 FSLI hierarchy, quarter-annualization, and a state machine with a 50% delta-variance gate for SOX. The repository is Spring Data JPA on Hibernate. I led 3 engineers on that migration, which killed a column-aliasing bug and took module coverage to 100%."

Minute 3: the data guarantees. Draw the 8 tables as a stack under MySQL and write three words next to them: "@Version", "@Transactional", "SHA-256". Say: "Every update checks a version, so two managers cannot overwrite each other. A stale save gets a 409. Cross-table edits run in one transaction. Natural keys are SHA-256 of the meaningful fields, so re-imports never duplicate. The result was reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days." Add HFM and 10-Q arrows into reconciliation and a PwC arrow out of Summary to finish.

Architecture: Uber Eats Menu Ingestion and Automation (Uber via EPAM)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the pipeline that turns restaurant menus from partner websites and PDFs into structured Uber Eats catalog entries. That means scraping, Kafka, Flink and the RAG extraction path. A short section covers the separate ANZ document compliance project.
  • When to read it: before streaming, data pipeline or GenAI/RAG system design rounds.
  • What to memorise: the seven-box diagram, one menu traced end to end, the honest meaning of "exactly-once", and the numbers: from 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year, 30K+ menus a month, 98% field fidelity (offline), 95%+ extraction success.

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, a doc or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). HISTORICAL means from past work records.

Tech on this project: Python, Selenium, Kafka, Flink, LangChain, Gemini, RAG, Milvus, GCP, Docker. Not ClickHouse. Not Spark on the PDF.

1. The one-paragraph version

When a restaurant joins Uber Eats, its menu has to be entered into Uber's catalog: every dish, price, section and option, in a strict schema. Menus arrive as messy websites, PDFs and images, often in several languages. Doing that by hand or through a paid third-party tool was slow and expensive. This pipeline automates it. A fleet of Selenium scrapers collects menus, Kafka buffers the events, Flink deduplicates and normalises them, and unstructured PDFs go through a RAG extraction path (LangChain, Milvus and Gemini 2.5 Pro) that produces schema-valid catalog records. Restaurant onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours, saving about $600K a year across 30K+ menus a month.

2. Words you need

  • Menu ingestion. Getting a restaurant's menu from wherever it lives into Uber's catalog database in the right shape.
  • Catalog schema. The strict structure every menu must fit: item name, price, currency, section, modifiers (like "extra cheese"), and so on. Like a form with required fields.
  • Selenium. A tool that drives a real web browser from code. Needed when menus are rendered by JavaScript and there is no clean API. Like a robot that clicks through a website the way a person would.
  • Proxy pool. A set of intermediate IP addresses the scrapers rotate through, so a site does not block one address for too many requests.
  • Adaptive retries. Retrying a failed scrape with backoff and per-site budgets that adjust to how that site behaves.
  • Kafka. A durable, ordered log of events that many consumers can read at their own pace. Think of a conveyor belt that also keeps a recording of everything that passed, so you can rewind and replay.
  • Topic and partition key. A topic is a named stream. The partition key (here the vendor) decides which partition an event goes to, which keeps one vendor's events in order.
  • Consumer lag. How far behind a consumer is from the newest event. The main health signal for a streaming pipeline.
  • Flink (Apache Flink). A stream processing engine that keeps state per key and recovers from crashes using checkpoints. Like a clerk who keeps a folder per restaurant and photocopies all folders every few minutes in case of fire.
  • Keyed state. Data Flink remembers per key, here "the last content hash I saw for this vendor's menu".
  • Content hash. A fingerprint of the menu content. If the hash is the same as last time, nothing changed.
  • Deduplication (dedup). Dropping repeated copies of the same event.
  • Exactly-once. In marketing language, "every event takes effect exactly one time". In practice here: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts. Events may be delivered more than once, but writing the same record twice leaves the catalog unchanged.
  • Idempotent upsert. "Insert or update" keyed by a stable ID, so repeating it has no extra effect. Like pressing a lift button twice: the lift still comes once.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). Before asking the LLM to do a task, you retrieve relevant examples or documents and put them in the prompt. Like giving a new employee three filled-in example forms before asking them to fill in a fourth.
  • Embedding. A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Similar texts have nearby embeddings.
  • Milvus. A vector database that stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones fast.
  • LangChain. A Python framework for chaining LLM steps: load document, retrieve, prompt, parse output.
  • Gemini 2.5 Pro. Google's large language model, used here to read the menu and return structured JSON.
  • Field fidelity. The share of extracted fields that match the correct value on a labelled test set. 98% in offline evaluation.
  • Offline evaluation. Measuring quality on a fixed labelled set before release, not live in production.

3. The architecture diagram

flowchart LR SRC["Partner sites, PDFs, images"] SEL["Selenium fleet on GCP, proxy pools, adaptive retries"] RAW["Object storage for raw files"] KF["Kafka topics keyed by vendor"] FL["Flink: validate, keyed dedupe, normalize, route"] RAG["RAG extraction: Milvus retrieve, Gemini 2.5 Pro"] GATE["Schema gate"] UP["Idempotent catalog upsert"] CAT["Uber Eats catalog"] BAD["Not written: retry or flag"] SRC --> SEL SEL --> RAW SEL --> KF KF --> FL FL -->|"structured items"| UP FL -->|"unstructured PDF or image"| RAG RAG --> GATE GATE -->|"valid"| UP GATE -->|"invalid"| BAD UP --> CAT

What to notice: there are two paths out of Flink. Structured menus go straight to the catalog. Messy PDFs and images take the RAG detour, and nothing reaches the catalog without passing the schema gate.

4. Box-by-box walkthrough

Partner sites, PDFs, images

The raw sources: restaurant websites, third-party menu platforms, uploaded PDFs and photos. Many are rendered by JavaScript, many are multilingual, and many actively block bots.

Selenium fleet on GCP

  • What: Python Selenium workers running in Docker on GCP that load pages like a real browser and emit menu, item and scrape-health events.
  • Why Selenium: many partner pages only render menus with JavaScript, and there was no complete API.
  • Hardening: dynamic proxy pools, adaptive retries with per-source budgets, and rotation so one blocked address does not fail a whole run. That took extraction success to 95%+, up from an estimated 60% to 65%.
  • Alternative: plain HTTP scraping. Faster and cheaper, but it fails on JavaScript-rendered pages.

Object storage for raw files

Raw HTML, PDFs and images are kept so a parser bug can be fixed and the data reprocessed without scraping again.

Kafka topics keyed by vendor

  • What: the ingest bus between scrapers and processing.
  • Why: scrapers are bursty. Kafka absorbs bursts so slow catalog writes never block scraping. Keying by vendor keeps one restaurant's events in order. The log can be replayed after a bad parser deploy, and more than one consumer can read the same topic.
  • Alternative: scrapers call the catalog directly over HTTP. Simple, but a slow catalog stalls the scrapers and there is no replay.

Flink: validate, keyed dedupe, normalise, route

  • What: a stateful stream job reading Kafka.
  • Validate: reject events missing required fields.
  • Keyed dedupe: state keyed by vendor and menu holds the last content hash. Same hash means no change, so the event is dropped.
  • Normalise: map different source formats into one internal shape (currency, price format, section names).
  • Route: structured items go to the catalog upsert. Unstructured PDFs and images go to RAG extraction.
  • Why Flink: real keyed state, event-time handling for late pages, checkpoint recovery and low latency.
  • Alternatives: Spark Structured Streaming (micro-batches, seconds of latency, a fine choice for backfills but weaker for this hot path) or Kafka Streams (could work at this event rate if that were the team standard).

RAG extraction (LangChain, Milvus, Gemini 2.5 Pro)

  1. Extract text from the PDF or image and split it into chunks.
  2. Embed the chunks and retrieve similar, already-labelled menu examples from Milvus.
  3. Build a prompt with the target schema, the retrieved examples and the new menu text.
  4. Gemini 2.5 Pro returns JSON in the catalog schema.

Why RAG instead of a bare prompt: retrieved examples show the model exactly how a similar menu was mapped, which grounds field names and formats and reduces invented fields.

Schema gate

Every extracted record is validated against the catalog schema (required fields, types, price format). Invalid records are not written. They are retried or flagged. Older prep also describes low-confidence results going to manual handling. Keep that qualitative.

Idempotent catalog upsert and the catalog

Writes are keyed by stable IDs (vendor and item, with the content hash), so a replayed event writes the same record again and the catalog does not change. That is what "exactly-once catalog upserts" means on the resume.

5. One menu, step by step

Example (illustrative). A restaurant in Berlin uploads a two-page German PDF. One line reads "Schnitzel Wiener Art mit Pommes … 14,50 €".

sequenceDiagram participant S as Selenium worker participant K as Kafka participant F as Flink participant R as RAG extractor participant G as Schema gate participant C as Catalog S->>K: menu event, key vendor 8812, content hash ab12 K->>F: deliver event F->>F: state for vendor 8812 has hash 77fe, so this is new F->>F: format is PDF, route to RAG path F->>R: menu text R->>R: retrieve 3 similar labelled German menus from Milvus R->>R: Gemini 2.5 Pro returns catalog JSON R->>G: candidate records G->>G: required fields, types, price format all pass G->>C: upsert keyed by vendor and item C-->>G: ok
  1. The scraper downloads the PDF, stores the raw file, and publishes an event keyed by vendor 8812 with content hash ab12.
  2. Flink looks up the state for vendor 8812. The last hash was 77fe, so the menu changed and the event moves on. If the hash had matched, Flink would drop it as a duplicate.
  3. The format is PDF, so Flink routes it to RAG extraction.
  4. The extractor retrieves similar labelled German menus from Milvus and prompts Gemini 2.5 Pro with the schema and examples.
  5. Gemini returns:
{
  "section": "Hauptgerichte",
  "item_name": "Schnitzel Wiener Art mit Pommes",
  "price": 14.50,
  "currency": "EUR",
  "modifiers": []
}
  1. The schema gate checks required fields, the numeric price and the currency code. It passes.
  2. The upsert writes the item keyed by vendor and item. If Kafka redelivers the same event after a crash, the same upsert runs again and nothing changes.

6. Design decisions

Decision 1: Kafka between scrapers and processing

  • What: a durable ingest bus keyed by vendor.
  • Why: absorb bursts, keep per-vendor order, replay after parser bugs, allow several consumers.
  • Alternatives: direct HTTP to the catalog (no replay, scrapers stall), or a simple task queue (deletes messages on acknowledge, so no cheap replay).
  • Trade-off: Kafka is more infrastructure to operate.
  • What I'd do differently: add consumer-lag alerts per source from day one.

Decision 2: Flink for dedupe and normalisation

  • What: a stateful keyed stream job.
  • Why: dedupe needs memory per vendor. Late pages need event-time handling. Crash recovery needs checkpoints.
  • Alternatives: Spark Structured Streaming (micro-batch latency) or Kafka Streams (lighter, could work at this rate). Spark is a verbal backfill option only, not on the PDF.
  • Trade-off: Flink is a separate cluster to understand and tune.

Decision 3: RAG with Gemini for unstructured menus

  • What: retrieval of labelled examples from Milvus, then Gemini 2.5 Pro producing schema JSON.
  • Why: rule-based parsers break on every new PDF layout and language. Retrieved examples ground the model.
  • Alternatives: template parsers per layout (brittle), or a bare LLM prompt with no examples (more invented fields).
  • Trade-off: LLM cost and the need for an offline evaluation set to prove quality.
  • What I'd do differently: grow the labelled evaluation set per language and track fidelity per language, not only overall.

Decision 4: "exactly-once" as at-least-once plus idempotent upserts

  • What: accept duplicate delivery and make writes harmless to repeat.
  • Why: true end-to-end exactly-once across third-party sites, an LLM and an external catalog would need every system to take part in one transaction. That is not possible here.
  • Trade-off: every writer must use stable keys.

7. The numbers on this diagram

Number What it measures Tag
From 24 hours to 2 hours Restaurant onboarding time On PDF
$600K a year Money saved On PDF, conservative floor
30K+ menus a month Menus processed On PDF
98% Field fidelity in offline evaluation On PDF, offline
95%+, from about 60% to 65% Extraction success rate On PDF, baseline ESTIMATED
200 to 500 events a second Peak event rate during fleet runs ESTIMATED, prep-only

From 24 hours to 2 hours. Time from a restaurant's menu arriving to it being live in the catalog. Say "from 24 hours to 2 hours". It mattered because restaurants earn nothing on Uber Eats until their menu is live.

$600K a year. Derivation: about $2 per menu in third-party or manual cost, times 30K menus a month, times 12 months, is $720K. The resume floors that to $600K to stay conservative. Say "about 600 thousand dollars a year, a conservative floor on roughly 720 thousand".

30K+ menus a month. About 1,000 menus a day (30,000 / 30). Each menu produces many item events plus retries and health events, which is why peaks can reach the estimated 200 to 500 events a second. Do not put the events-per-second number on the table unless asked, and call it an estimate.

98% field fidelity. On a labelled offline test set, 98% of extracted fields matched the correct value. Always say "offline evaluation". Older prep also mentioned 100% schema consistency in offline evaluation. The resume number is 98%.

95%+ extraction success. The share of scrape attempts that produced a usable menu. The starting point of about 60% to 65% is an estimate. Say "from roughly 60 to 65 percent to above 95 percent".

8. Failure modes and what the system does

What breaks How you notice What happens
A site blocks the scraper Scrape-health events, success rate drops Proxy rotation, adaptive retries with per-source budgets.
Catalog writes slow down Kafka consumer lag rises Kafka buffers. Scrapers keep running. Flink backpressure slows reading, not scraping.
Parser bug deployed Bad records or schema failures spike Fix, rewind Kafka offsets to before the bad deploy, replay. Raw files allow reprocessing.
Same menu scraped twice Same content hash Flink keyed dedupe drops it.
Event delivered twice after a crash Duplicate in the stream Idempotent upsert, catalog unchanged.
Flink worker crashes Job restarts Restores state from the last checkpoint and continues.
LLM returns malformed or wrong fields Schema gate fails Record not written. Retried or flagged.
Quality drifts on a new language Offline evaluation by language Add labelled examples for that language to Milvus and the test set.

9. ANZ document compliance (separate project, Uber Mobility)

This is a different project, on Uber Mobility (rides), not Uber Eats. It automated verification of driver and vehicle documents in Australia and New Zealand against local authority rules, using a deterministic validation backend. It reached 99.9% regulatory compliance and removed about 20 hours a week of manual effort. Both numbers are HISTORICAL. Do not attach Selenium, Kafka or RAG to this project.

10. Why Kafka here is not the same story as Kafka at Masters India

Interviewers who read the whole resume sometimes ask why Kafka appears twice. Same technology, different reasons. - Menu: Kafka absorbs bursty scrapers, keeps each vendor's events in order, lets us replay after a bad parse, and feeds Flink. - Masters India: Kafka carries GST e-invoice stages to the government portal, with per-taxpayer ordering, replay for compliance disputes, and several consumer groups. There is no Flink at Masters.

11. Say this, not that

Say this Not this
"98% field fidelity in offline evaluation." "98% accurate in production."
"At-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts." "Zero message loss" or "two-phase commit across Gemini".
"Kafka and Flink for ingestion and processing." ClickHouse on Menu.
"Spark would be my backfill option." Spark as something on the resume.
"About $600K a year, floored from about $720K." "$600K+" with no derivation.
"ANZ is Uber Mobility." ANZ as part of the Eats menu pipeline.

12. How to draw it in 3 minutes

Minute 1: sources to Kafka. Draw messy sources on the left, a Selenium box, then a Kafka log. Say: "Restaurant menus live on JavaScript-heavy sites and in multilingual PDFs. A Selenium fleet on GCP with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries took extraction success from roughly 60 to 65 percent to above 95. Events land in Kafka keyed by vendor, so bursts are absorbed and we can replay after a parser bug."

Minute 2: Flink and the two paths. Draw Flink with a small "state per vendor" note, then two arrows out. Say: "Flink validates, deduplicates by vendor and content hash, normalises, and routes. Structured menus go straight to an idempotent catalog upsert. PDFs and images go to a RAG path: retrieve similar labelled menus from Milvus, and Gemini 2.5 Pro fills the catalog schema, with 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation."

Minute 3: correctness and impact. Draw the schema gate and the catalog, and write "at-least-once + idempotent". Say: "Nothing reaches the catalog without passing the schema gate. Exactly-once in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts, so a replay changes nothing. Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours across 30 thousand menus a month, about 600 thousand dollars a year saved."
