Impact Analytics: Core Infrastructure and Pipeline

The product in plain words. AssortSmart helps retailers plan assortments: which products (articles) to keep, drop or add each season. Planners look at big grids of sales numbers, called pivots, and the AI engine recommends decisions. Many retailers (tenants) share the same platform.

flowchart LR UI["Planner UI"] --> EDGE["Go/Gin edge"] IRIS["Ask Iris chat"] --> AGENT["Python agent service"] EDGE --> REDIS["Redis auth cache"] EDGE --> PG["PostgreSQL roles and UAM"] EDGE --> CH["ClickHouse rollups and 2.11B master"] BATCH["Keep/Drop batch engine"] --> JSON["Prepared JSON context"] CH --> JSON BATCH --> CH AGENT --> EDGE

What to notice: the Go edge is the only public door for the planner UI. The AI batch engine reads prepared JSON, not the database, and writes results back through the engine's own insert path.

1. Go/Gin edge with no reverse proxy

What. The planner-facing API is a multi-tenant Go service built on Gin, handling peaks of about 10,000 requests per second. It is wired with Google Wire, serves HTTP/2 directly, uses nested timeouts, and reports Datadog distributed traces. There's no Nginx-style reverse proxy in front doing the protective work.

Words. - A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of your app, like Nginx, and handles things like timeouts and size limits before requests reach you. - Google Wire is a dependency injection tool. Dependency injection means a component is handed what it needs, like a database client, instead of building it itself. Wire generates the wiring code at compile time, so a missing dependency breaks the build instead of a live request. - h2c is HTTP/2 over plain TCP without TLS, used inside a trusted network. HTTP/2 lets many requests share one connection. - Distributed tracing follows one request across services with a shared trace id, so you can see where time went.

Why. At 10k peak RPS, the process that serves traffic should own its own protection. With the timeouts, HTTP/2 handling and tracing in one process, there's one less network hop and one less system to operate. A wiring mistake fails at compile time, not at 2 a.m.

How (illustrative). "Nested timeouts" means an outer limit on the whole connection and inner limits per request and per downstream call. The values below are only examples.

srv := &http.Server{
    Handler:           h2c.NewHandler(router, &http2.Server{}),
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,   // slow clients can't hold sockets
    WriteTimeout:      60 * time.Second,  // outer cap per response
}

func pivotHandler(c *gin.Context) {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(c.Request.Context(), 20*time.Second) // per request
    defer cancel()
    rows, err := chClient.Query(ctx, sql) // the ClickHouse call inherits the deadline
    // ...
}

Alternatives and why not. - Put the Python service at the public edge. Python is fine for the agent plane, but Go handles high concurrency with less memory per request. - Hide it behind Nginx or a cloud load balancer and let them handle protection. That works, but timeouts and limits then live in two places and drift apart. The PDF claim is a self-protecting edge. - Uber Fx or Dig for dependency injection. Those wire things at runtime using reflection, so a wiring error shows up only when the code runs.

Trade-off. You own what a proxy would have given you for free: body-size caps, slow-client protection and graceful shutdown when the process gets a stop signal (SIGTERM). That's more code to own and test.

What I'd do differently. I'd write down the timeout budget per route in one table early, so the outer and inner limits are reviewed together instead of route by route.

Say this carefully. No invented uptime SLA. No claim that you operated Kubernetes clusters for this.

2. ClickHouse plus rollup tables for planner pivots

What. Planner pivots moved from PostgreSQL to ClickHouse, with a pre-aggregation layer of six rollup tables: product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly level, partitioned by season. On a 250-million-row benchmark a pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds (MEASURED). Postgres kept the thin metadata: users, roles, access rules.

Words. - Row store versus column store. Postgres stores each row together, like reading a full index card for every product even if you need one field. ClickHouse stores each column together, so a query that sums "sales" reads only the sales column. - Vectorised execution processes a batch of values at once instead of one at a time. - A rollup is a table of pre-computed totals, like keeping weekly totals instead of re-adding every receipt. - ReplacingMergeTree is a ClickHouse table type that keeps only the newest version of rows with the same key. Think of a notebook where you never erase. You write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines.

Why. Pivots group many columns over hundreds of millions of rows. Postgres had to scan whole rows and slowed down badly. POCs comparing the two on identical data showed ClickHouse winning the large analytical reads.

How (illustrative). A season-level product rollup, and the planner query that reads it:

CREATE TABLE product_season_rollup (
    tenant_id String, season_code String, article_id String,
    sales_units Float64, sales_value Float64, eop_units Float64
) ENGINE = MergeTree
PARTITION BY season_code
ORDER BY (tenant_id, season_code, article_id);

SELECT article_id, sum(sales_units), sum(eop_units)
FROM product_season_rollup
WHERE tenant_id = {tenant:String} AND season_code = 'S26'
GROUP BY article_id;

The pivot reads pre-summed rows instead of the raw fact table.

Alternatives and why not. - Tune Postgres harder. We tried in-stack fixes first. Row storage is the limit for wide analytical GROUP BYs. - BigQuery or Snowflake for the interactive UI. Good for batch analytics, but shared compute means latency varies. BigQuery probes we measured ranged from about 1 to 20 seconds for the same query. That's poor for an interactive screen. - Move everything, including users and roles, to ClickHouse. ClickHouse is weak at updating single rows in place, so small, often-changed records stay in Postgres.

Trade-off. ClickHouse is a poor fit for keyed updates. Writes become insert-only with versioned rows, and you run two databases instead of one.

What I'd do differently. I'd lead the first RFC with the insert-only write model. The debate (see STAR story 1) got stuck on the old update-in-place habit, and that framing would have saved weeks.

3. Slice weekly rollup builds into one-week inserts

What. Building the weekly rollups for a whole season in one INSERT SELECT needed about 170 GB of memory and crashed. Even 80 GB and 200 GB caps failed. I sliced the build into one fiscal week per insert, with memory and disk-spill caps.

Words. INSERT SELECT reads, aggregates and writes in one statement. Disk spill lets a big GROUP BY write temporary data to disk instead of failing when memory runs out. OOM means out of memory.

Why. Shrinking the unit of work is cheaper and more predictable than buying more RAM, and it makes each piece retryable.

How (illustrative). The real caps are verbal detail: 55 GB memory, 16 GB spill, 8 threads, 4 weeks in flight.

INSERT INTO attr_weekly_rollup
SELECT tenant_id, season_code, fiscal_week, attribute_value,
       sum(sales_units), sum(sales_value)
FROM sales_fact
WHERE season_code = 'S26' AND fiscal_week = 202614   -- one week per insert
GROUP BY tenant_id, season_code, fiscal_week, attribute_value
SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 55000000000,
         max_bytes_before_external_group_by = 16000000000,
         max_threads = 8;

With that slicing, a product week needed about 11 GB. An attribute week went above 40 GB but stayed inside the caps.

Alternatives and why not. - Bigger machine. It failed even at a 200 GB cap, and it would just move the cliff. - Drop the weekly level. Planners need weekly detail. - Stream the aggregation with an external system. Kafka or Flink would be new infrastructure for a batch problem. Not used at IA.

Trade-off. More inserts to orchestrate and track, and a longer total build. In return, each week is predictable and can be retried on its own.

What I'd do differently. I'd run a single-week trial and measure its memory before ever attempting a whole-season build.

Say this carefully. This is load time. The pivot speed-up in decision 2 is query time. One did not cause the other.

4. Custom KPI formula parser

What. Operators write KPI formulas, like sell-through, in a simple formula language. A Go tokenizer and parser turn them into parameterised ClickHouse SQL fragments. Only allowlisted functions are accepted. Logical names map to physical columns. Every expression is wrapped to protect against division by zero.

Words. A tokenizer splits text into pieces like names, numbers and operators. A parser checks those pieces follow the grammar and builds a tree. Parameterised SQL means values are passed separately from the SQL text, so they can't change its meaning. Fail closed means anything unknown is rejected, not guessed.

Why. Business teams change KPI definitions often. Without a parser, every change is a code release. And a NaN or infinity from dividing by zero would poison the planner's numbers.

How (illustrative).

Operator writes:   sell_through = sales_units / (sales_units + eop_units)

Parser output:     ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(sls_u) / (sum(sls_u) + sum(eop_u))), 0)

If a product sold nothing and has no stock, the division is 0 / 0. ClickHouse returns NaN, and ifNotFinite(..., 0) turns it into 0. A formula with an unknown token, like DROP or a function not on the allowlist, fails to parse and is rejected.

Alternatives and why not. - Hard-code each KPI in SQL. Every change needs a release. - Let operators type raw SQL. That's a SQL injection and runaway-query risk. - A general expression library. It wouldn't know about our column catalog or the ClickHouse functions we allow.

Trade-off. We own a small language: its grammar, error messages and tests. Operators can only use what the allowlist supports.

What I'd do differently. I'd add a preview step that shows the operator a sample result before a formula is saved.

5. Auth waterfall and tenant isolation

What. Every request is authenticated through a Redis-fronted waterfall: try Firebase Admin first, then JWT or Google OIDC. API keys are compared in constant time. Roles come from Postgres. Every query in Postgres and ClickHouse is scoped to the caller's tenant and their allowed product hierarchy, which is UAM (User Access Management).

Words. A JWT is a signed token that says who you are. OIDC (OpenID Connect) is a standard way to log in with an identity provider like Google. A waterfall tries checks in order until one succeeds. Constant-time comparison takes the same time whether the first character or the last is wrong, so an attacker can't guess a key by timing responses.

Why. In a multi-tenant product, one retailer seeing another's data is a company-ending bug. Different clients arrive with different identity types, so the waterfall accepts each safely. Redis caches verified results so the edge doesn't re-verify every request.

How (illustrative).

if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(given), []byte(stored)) != 1 {
    return errUnauthorized // same cost on every mismatch
}

The tenant id always comes from the verified token, never from the request body.

Alternatives and why not. - Trust a header from the gateway. There's no gateway in front of this edge, and a header is easy to forge. - One identity provider only. Existing clients use different ones.

Trade-off. More code paths to test, and a Redis dependency on the hot path.

What I'd do differently. I'd keep a dedicated suite of cross-tenant negative tests from day one, where tenant A tries to read tenant B and must fail.

Say this carefully. Isolation is access control, not encryption.

6. Custom Go data pump for cluster migration

What. To move rollups between ClickHouse Cloud clusters, I wrote a Go program that reads from one cluster and writes to the other over ClickHouse's native protocol with TLS. It reached about 344k rows per second combined, using 500k-row double-buffered batches, on partitions up to 4.09 billion rows.

Words. IP allowlist means a server only accepts connections from listed addresses. Native protocol is ClickHouse's own fast binary protocol. Double-buffered means reading the next batch while the previous one is being sent.

Why. The clusters' IP allowlists blocked them from connecting to each other directly, so ClickHouse's built-in copy couldn't run. A pump that connects to both from an allowed machine sidesteps that.

How (illustrative).

next := readBatch(src, 500_000)
for next != nil {
    cur := next
    go func() { next = readBatch(src, 500_000) }() // read ahead
    writeBatch(dst, cur)                           // send current
    waitForRead()
}

Alternatives and why not. - ClickHouse's own remote copy. Blocked by the allowlists. - Export to files and re-import. That adds a storage step and doubles the data handling. You can discuss it as an option, but the pump was the direct path.

Trade-off. We own a migration tool, including its retries and ledgers. It ran from one machine, so throughput depended on that machine's network.

What I'd do differently. See decision 7.

Say this carefully. 344k is rows per second, not requests per second. The 4.09B copy was measured in flight. Don't say the cutover finished. Never suggest open-sourcing the copier.

7. Ledgers plus drop-and-recopy against ghost rows

What. A failed insert can still commit some blocks, leaving "ghost rows". To prevent that, the weekly loader records each finished chunk in a TSV ledger and skips it on restart. The copier writes a .done checkpoint file per table. If a season's copy fails, we drop that partition and recopy the season.

Why. "Count greater than zero" doesn't prove a partition is complete. A ledger of finished work does.

How.

migrate-checkpoints/attr_weekly_rollup.done   <- table finished
loader_skip.tsv:  attr_weekly  S26  202614  OK  <- week finished
On failure:  ALTER TABLE attr_weekly_rollup DROP PARTITION 'S26';  then recopy S26

Alternatives and why not. - Atomic swap with REPLACE PARTITION. That's cleaner: load into staging, then swap in one step so readers never see partial data. The incremental REPLACE PARTITION design was written, but not executed. - Trust insert success codes. A failed insert can still leave partial data.

Trade-off. Drop-and-recopy repeats a whole season on failure, and there's a window where that season is missing. It is not an atomic swap with live readers.

What I'd do differently. I'd execute the REPLACE PARTITION design, so a retry swaps in a staged copy instead of recopying in place.

Impact Analytics: Agentic Flows and Orchestration

The AI engine in plain words. For each article-season (one product in one selling season), the engine computes a rule-based score from sales metrics, asks an LLM to judge it from seven angles ("lenses"), blends the two, and writes a keep or drop recommendation with an explanation. It runs as batches of about 88k items per pass, across 348k article-seasons.

flowchart LR DET["Deterministic KPI score"] --> PEER["Peer comparison"] PEER --> DEC["Decider"] DEC --> LENS["7 AI lenses"] LENS --> BLEND["Blend 0.4 det plus 0.6 agent"] BLEND --> EXP["Explanation"] EXP --> OUT["Rows stamped with config_hash"]

What to notice: the order is fixed. There is no LLM deciding which step runs next.

8. Blend rule-based math with LLM lenses

What. A deterministic score s_det comes from sell-through and rate of sale. An AI score s_agent comes from seven lenses combined by a decider. The final score is s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent, and the item is kept if s_final ≥ 0.55.

Words. Sell-through is the share of stock that sold. Rate of sale is units sold per week. A lens is one focused angle of analysis, like one specialist's opinion.

Why. Merchandising decisions have to be explainable to planners and auditable. The math is the anchor. The LLM adds judgment the math can't capture, like context from peers. Neither alone is enough.

How (worked example). s_det = 0.70, s_agent = 0.45. Then s_final = 0.28 + 0.27 = 0.55, which meets the threshold, so it's a keep. If the LLM times out, s_agent is missing and the deterministic baseline is used, so the run continues.

Alternatives and why not. - LLM only. Not auditable, and on our benchmark the LLM blend lost to the rule (decision 12). - Rules only. Misses context and can't explain itself in planner language. - Give the LLM a SQL tool to look things up. See decision 9.

Trade-off. Two scoring systems to maintain, and weights that need evidence before anyone changes them.

What I'd do differently. I'd build the gold benchmark before setting the first blend weights, not after.

Say this carefully. Offline evaluations replaced critic or evaluator agents in Keep/Drop. There's no human review queue, and no LangSmith on this batch (LangSmith is Ask Iris).

9. Keep the LLM away from the 2.11B-row table

What. The scoring LLM never queries the 2.11-billion-row ClickHouse master. The engine prepares context as JSON payloads and sends that in. Results are written by the engine, not the model, into a ReplacingMergeTree table. That makes writes eventually consistent: retries may write a row twice, and the newest version wins. If the LLM times out, the deterministic score is written instead.

Words. Eventually consistent means duplicates or older versions may briefly exist, but reads settle on the right answer. Async here describes how batches run in parallel. It does not mean the LLM queries the database later.

Why. An LLM with database access can generate runaway queries, exhaust connection pools, or be steered by prompt injection. On a table this big, a bad query is expensive and a bad write is very hard to undo.

How (illustrative).

CREATE TABLE kd_decisions (
    tenant_id String, season_code String, article_id String,
    s_det Float64, s_agent Float64, s_final Float64, decision String,
    config_hash String, version UInt64
) ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(version)
ORDER BY (tenant_id, season_code, article_id);

-- read the latest version per article
SELECT * FROM kd_decisions
ORDER BY version DESC
LIMIT 1 BY tenant_id, season_code, article_id;

Alternatives and why not. - A read-only SQL tool for the LLM. It still risks runaway queries and is hard to evaluate. - Plain MergeTree. Retries would leave duplicate decisions. - Two-phase commit for exact-once writes. Heavy, and not needed when the newest version wins.

Trade-off. We decide in advance what context the model sees, so it can't explore. Readers must pick the latest version, because merges happen in the background.

What I'd do differently. I'd version the JSON payload shape explicitly, so prompt changes and context changes are tracked separately.

Say this carefully. No Kafka, Flink or CDC here. CDC work at IA (pg2ch) was a colleague's, not mine.

10. App-native orchestration registry, not Airflow or Temporal

What. One shared registry runs all three pipelines (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style). It provides hard timeouts, circuit breakers, durable checkpoints, a frozen config_hash on every output row, and JSON telemetry for tokens, USD cost, step duration and batch fallbacks.

Words. - A circuit breaker stops calling a failing service for a while after repeated failures, like a home fuse that trips. Ours trips after about 5 consecutive failures or a high fail fraction. - A checkpoint is saved progress, so a restart picks up where it left off. - A config hash is a SHA-256 fingerprint of the guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog used for a run. Two rows with the same hash were produced under identical settings.

Why. A provider error halfway through 88k items must not force a full rerun. And for any output row, we must be able to say exactly which prompts and settings produced it.

How. Deterministic scores are saved first to det.json. As LLM chunks finish, progress is appended to agent_progress.json. Running with --resume reloads both and skips finished work.

config_hash = sha256(json.dumps(
    {"guardrails": g, "params": p, "prompts": prompts, "catalog": cat},
    sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()

Alternatives and why not. - Airflow or Temporal. Both are good workflow engines, but they're extra infrastructure. We needed resume logic tied closely to ClickHouse inserts, config hashing and per-run cost telemetry, inside a batch tool we already owned. - No checkpoints. Every failure would mean recomputing everything.

Trade-off. We own retry, breaker and checkpoint code ourselves, without a workflow UI.

What I'd do differently. If the number of pipelines keeps growing, I'd re-evaluate Temporal, because its durable execution would replace some of our own code.

11. Ask Iris: supervisor, capped evaluator, frozen scope

What. Ask Iris is a shipped chat copilot for planners. It runs over a JWT-secured WebSocket. A LangGraph supervisor routes each question to worker agents. An evaluator checks the answer and retries at most 3 times (MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3). The user's hierarchy access (plan_scope) is frozen at the socket handshake. LangSmith records traces.

Words. - A WebSocket is a connection that stays open for live two-way messages. - LangGraph builds agents as a graph of steps with explicit loops and exits. - A supervisor is the node that decides which worker handles a question. - An evaluator is a node that checks whether an answer is good enough. - LangSmith is a tracing tool that records each step an LLM app took.

Why. Chat is where two things go wrong: agents loop forever, and a clever message tries to read another tenant's data. A capped evaluator stops the first. A scope fixed at connect time stops the second, because no later message can widen it.

How.

1. Client connects: Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
2. Server verifies the JWT, resolves plan_scope = {tenant: T1, hierarchy: Mens/Denim}
3. plan_scope is frozen for this socket. Every tool call inherits it.
4. User: "compare with tenant T2"   ->  tools still run with T1 scope only
5. Evaluator rejects the answer 3 times  ->  graceful "here's what I found" reply

Alternatives and why not. - Check scope per message. Every check is another chance to get it wrong. - No evaluator. Lower quality answers. - Unbounded evaluator. Infinite loops and runaway token cost.

Trade-off. To change scope, the user has to reconnect. Three attempts can sometimes stop just short of a better answer.

What I'd do differently. I'd add usage and answer-quality metrics from day one, so I'd have real numbers to show. Today it's a shipped capability, with no usage or uptime numbers to claim.

12. Evaluation gate and frozen weights

What. A 300-case proxy evaluation set and an 80% accuracy gate in CI block any model or prompt change that scores lower. Separately, a 200-item gold benchmark picked the scoring model. The new model was 73% cheaper and completed 200 of 200 items. The deterministic rule scored 74% on that benchmark. The LLM blend scored about 63%, so the blend weights were frozen instead of retuned.

Words. A proxy evaluation set is a fixed set of cases with known answers that stands in for real decisions. A promotion gate is a CI check that must pass before a change is promoted to production.

Why. The free rule is the bar. If AI can't beat it, it shouldn't drive more of the decision. And retuning weights on a small set to make AI look better would be overfitting.

How. The gate config is gold_min_accuracy: 0.8. On model choice, a "nano" option was slightly cheaper but left items pending, so completion reliability won.

Alternatives and why not. - Ship on demo quality. No protection against regressions. - Retune weights until the AI wins. Overfitting on 200 items. - Pick the cheapest model. It didn't complete every item.

Trade-off. Some AI improvements wait longer to ship. The gold sets need upkeep.

What I'd do differently. I'd grow the gold set so retuning the blend would become statistically safe.

Say this carefully. 80% is a CI gate, not live accuracy for all tenants. 73% and 74% come from the gold-200 benchmark, not the 300-case file. Model names aren't on the PDF.

Verbal only: Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight

These are real design and build work but not resume bullets. Discuss them only if asked about the broader AI roadmap. Details: Hindsight defense and Agent read-tools defense.

Uber via EPAM: FRM Scoping Platform

The product in plain words. Each quarter Uber Finance decides which accounts and entities need audit attention, based on materiality (the money amount above which errors matter to auditors). Before this platform much of it lived in Google Sheets. The platform is a Java service with 36 Spring Boot endpoints, Spring Data JPA and Hibernate over MySQL, and a four-level line-item hierarchy (FSLI L1 to L4). It cut reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days.

13. Sheets to a normalised MySQL schema on SOADB

What. An 8-table normalised MySQL schema on SOADB, Uber's standard service-owned MySQL. It has a polymorphic review-status model, meaning one status model (Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed) reused across all 8 screens. It migrated 19M raw general-ledger rows off Sheets.

Words. Normalised means each fact lives in one place, linked by keys, instead of being copied around. Polymorphic means one structure works for many kinds of things.

Why. Sheets had no stable ids, no safe concurrent editing, and no audit trail tying the finance system's numbers to the filed 10-Q report. ETL jobs locking big tables during close also blocked users. Smaller normalised tables reduce that contention.

How (illustrative).

review_status(entity_type, entity_id, status, version, updated_by, updated_at)
  entity_type = 'materiality' | 'group_scoping' | 'residual_risk' | ...
  status      = Draft -> Review -> Closed  (ReOpen -> Review)

One table and one state machine serve every screen.

Alternatives and why not. - Keep Sheets with scripts. No audit trail or concurrency control. - A status column per screen. Eight copies of the same logic that drift apart. - A document store. Finance data is relational and needs transactions.

Trade-off. Polymorphic rows are harder to enforce with foreign keys. Migration needed a parallel run of the old and new reconciliation (v1 on Sheets, v2 on MySQL).

What I'd do differently. I'd start the parallel run earlier, so differences surfaced before the close deadline.

14. Optimistic locking and SHA-256 natural keys

What. Updates check a version number, so two people editing the same row can't overwrite each other silently. Cross-table syncs happen in one transaction. Rows get deterministic SHA-256 natural keys, for example a hash of the question text plus the normalised page name.

Words. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. Read the version, update only if it hasn't changed, otherwise reload. Pessimistic locking locks the row while you edit. A natural key is an id built from the data itself, so the same item always gets the same id.

Why. Many Finance users edit at once during close. Locking rows would block them. Random ids create duplicates when the same question is loaded again next quarter. Hash-based ids make reloading idempotent.

How (illustrative).

In JPA, a @Version field turns this on. Hibernate adds the version check to every update, and @Transactional makes a cross-table sync commit or roll back as one unit.

@Entity
class ScopingRow {
    @Id String uuid;
    String status;
    @Version long version;   // UPDATE ... WHERE uuid = ? AND version = ?
}

@Transactional
public void submitForReview(String uuid) {
    ScopingRow row = rows.findById(uuid).orElseThrow();
    row.setStatus("Review");
    // stale version on flush -> ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException -> client reloads
}

The SQL Hibernate runs looks like this. Zero rows updated means someone else changed it first.

UPDATE scoping_row SET status = 'Review', version = version + 1
WHERE uuid = :uuid AND version = :seen_version;

String key = questionText + "|" + normalize(pageName);
String uuid = HexFormat.of().formatHex(
    MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)));

Alternatives and why not. - Pessimistic locks. They block users and risk deadlocks during close. - Auto-increment or random ids. They duplicate across quarterly reloads.

Trade-off. Users sometimes see "this changed, please reload". If the normalisation rule for the key changes, the hashes change too, so that rule is frozen.

What I'd do differently. I'd document the key normalisation rule as a contract from the first release.

15. ORM migration with query methods on models

What. I led 3 engineers on a Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration of the data layer. We raised the module's statement coverage to 100%, shipped through stacked Bazel PRs with zero downtime, and kept reporting SQL on an allowlist. Queries are declared on the entity classes, an exception to the team's "repository only" rule.

Words. An ORM maps rows to code objects. Spring Data JPA is the Spring layer that generates repositories over JPA, the Java persistence standard. Hibernate is the JPA implementation that actually writes the SQL. An entity is a Java class mapped to a table with @Entity. Stacked PRs are a chain of small dependent pull requests. Bazel is Uber's build and test system. A reporting SQL allowlist is a fixed list of approved raw queries for reports.

Why. Raw SQL joins had duplicate column names, so some rows silently mapped to the wrong id. That was the column-aliasing bug. Typed entities with explicit aliases remove that bug class. Named queries declared on the entity sit next to the field mappings, and Hibernate validates them when the application starts. So a renamed field fails at startup and in tests, instead of quietly at runtime.

How. Queries tied to one table are @NamedQuery declarations on the entity. Any remaining native SQL uses aliased selects with explicit labels, mapped into a DTO by those labels.

@Entity
@NamedQuery(name = "FsliLine.byQuarter",
    query = "SELECT f FROM FsliLine f WHERE f.quarter = :quarter")
class FsliLine { /* fields */ }

// native report query: every joined uuid gets its own alias
@Query(value = "SELECT a.uuid AS accountUuid, b.uuid AS fsliUuid, a.balance AS balance "
     + "FROM account a JOIN fsli b ON a.fsli_id = b.id", nativeQuery = true)
List<AccountFsliView> accountFsliRows();

Alternatives and why not. - Patch each raw query. The bug class stays. - Strict repository-only layout. Queries end up far from the columns they depend on (see STAR story 7).

Trade-off. A documented exception to the team's rulebook, and a migration in the middle of feature work.

What I'd do differently. I'd do the ORM migration before building more screens on raw SQL.

16. State-machine gates with 50% variance checks

What. Moves between review statuses are automated gates in a finite state machine (FSM). One gate flags any line whose value moved more than 50% against its comparison period, so it can't pass automatically. This supports SOX compliance.

Words. An FSM is a fixed set of states and allowed moves between them. SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley) is the US law that requires controls over financial reporting.

Why. Controls that depend on someone remembering to check are weak controls. Code-enforced gates are reproducible and auditable.

How (illustrative).

BigDecimal delta = current.subtract(comparison).abs()
        .divide(comparison.abs(), 4, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
if (delta.compareTo(new BigDecimal("0.50")) > 0) {
    throw new GateBlockedException("variance above 50%, needs explicit review");
}

Alternatives and why not. Manual checklist. It isn't enforced and isn't auditable.

Trade-off. Legitimate big swings need an extra review step.

What I'd do differently. I'd show the reason for each flag directly in the review screen, so reviewers see why a line was blocked without digging.

Say this carefully. Keep the exact transition rules qualitative in interviews.

Uber via EPAM: Menu Ingestion (Uber Eats)

The product in plain words. Restaurants send menus as websites, PDFs and images, often in several languages. The pipeline turns them into Uber Eats' strict catalog format. It processes 30K+ menus a month and cut onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours.

flowchart LR SEL["Selenium scraper fleet"] --> K["Kafka topics"] K --> F["Flink dedupe and normalise"] F --> CAT["Catalog upsert"] PDF["PDF and image menus"] --> RAG["LangChain RAG over Milvus"] RAG --> GEM["Gemini 2.5 Pro"] GEM --> GATE["Schema check"] GATE --> CAT

What to notice: structured pages go through Kafka and Flink. Messy PDFs go through retrieval plus an LLM, and both paths pass a check before writing to the catalog.

17. Kafka plus Flink for ingestion

What. Scrapers publish to Kafka. Apache Flink deduplicates by key (vendor or menu, plus a content hash), normalises the schema, and upserts into the catalog.

Words. Kafka is a durable log of events that consumers read at their own pace and can replay. Flink is a stream processor that keeps state per key, like "the last content hash I saw for this menu".

Why. Scrapers are bursty and flaky. Kafka absorbs bursts and allows replay after a bad parser release. Flink's keyed state makes deduplication natural as data streams in.

How. Rewinding consumer offsets to before a bad release replays events through the fixed parser.

Alternatives and why not. - Scrapers write straight to the catalog. No buffer, no replay, no dedupe. - Spark micro-batches. Higher latency for catalog freshness. Spark isn't on the PDF. Mention it only as a verbal backfill option.

Trade-off. Two systems to run, and stateful jobs need checkpointing.

What I'd do differently. I'd add per-source lag dashboards from the start, next to block rates.

Backpressure (Menu only). If the catalog sink slows down, Flink's buffers fill and it reads from Kafka more slowly, instead of running out of memory. Events wait in Kafka until the sink catches up.

18. "Exactly-once" as at-least-once plus idempotent upserts

What. The PDF says "exactly-once catalog upserts". In practice, messages may arrive more than once, and the upsert is keyed so applying it twice has the same effect as once.

Why. True exactly-once across third-party systems would need distributed transactions, which aren't realistic here. Idempotency gives the same visible result.

How (illustrative, generic SQL to show the idea).

INSERT INTO catalog_item (menu_key, item_key, content_hash, payload)
VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT (menu_key, item_key) DO UPDATE SET payload = EXCLUDED.payload
WHERE catalog_item.content_hash <> EXCLUDED.content_hash;

Trade-off. Every write needs a stable key and a content hash.

Say this carefully. No claim of zero message loss and no two-phase commit across third parties.

19. RAG over Milvus with Gemini, behind a schema check

What. For unstructured PDFs, LangChain retrieves similar labelled menus from Milvus (a vector database) and gives them to Gemini 2.5 Pro as examples. Gemini then fills in the catalog schema. The output is validated before upsert. Offline field accuracy was 98%.

Words. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means fetching relevant examples or facts and putting them in the prompt. An embedding turns text into a list of numbers, so similar texts end up close together. Milvus stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones quickly.

Why. Menus vary wildly in layout and language. Showing the model similar, correctly labelled menus grounds its output in our schema.

Alternatives and why not. - Template parsers per restaurant. They break on every new layout. - Fine-tuning a model. Not on the PDF, and slower to iterate than retrieval.

Trade-off. Retrieval quality limits output quality, and there's an LLM cost per menu.

What I'd do differently. I'd set up the offline evaluation set before scaling volume, so every prompt change is measured.

Say this carefully. 98% is offline evaluation. Milvus is Uber Menu only, never Impact Analytics.

20. ANZ document compliance: deterministic validation (HISTORICAL)

What. Driver and vehicle document checks for Uber Mobility in Australia and New Zealand were automated against local authority rules with a deterministic validation backend. That gave 99.9% compliance and removed 20 hours a week of manual review.

Why. Regulators need predictable, explainable answers. Rules give the same answer every time.

Alternatives and why not. ML classification. It's harder to explain to regulators.

Say this carefully. This is Uber Mobility, not Uber Eats. No Selenium or RAG here.

Masters India: GST and E-invoicing

The product in plain words. Enterprise clients send invoices. The platform validates them and registers them with the government's IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an invoice reference number and a signed QR code. It serves 1,500+ clients and handles over a million submissions a day.

21. Strangler migration, not a big-bang rewrite

What. A PHP monolith was moved to Spring Boot microservices (Java) one endpoint at a time, with a canary per route. p95 latency went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds.

Words. The strangler pattern routes one endpoint at a time to the new service until the old app has nothing left. A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first and watches for errors.

Why. No downtime was allowed during monthly filing deadlines. One endpoint at a time keeps every step small and reversible.

How. We shadowed read endpoints first, moved bulk async paths before interactive filing, kept the data in place during cutover, and froze cutovers in deadline weeks. Latency came from non-blocking calls to the government portal (Spring WebClient, or a bounded thread pool, so one slow portal call no longer held a request thread), HikariCP connection pooling to PostgreSQL, query and index fixes, and Redis for reads.

Alternatives and why not. Big-bang rewrite. All risk lands on one day.

Trade-off. Two systems run side by side for months, with a shared database during the move.

What I'd do differently. I'd write the contract tests against the old PHP responses even earlier.

22. Kafka with idempotency keys and a dead-letter queue

What. Bulk e-invoicing ran on a Kafka event bus, with exactly-once idempotent processing for 100K+ concurrent imports, bounded retries against the unreliable government portals, and a dead-letter queue.

Words. An idempotency key is a unique id per request, so duplicates are recognised and done once. A dead-letter queue holds messages that keep failing, for inspection and replay. In Spring Kafka, DefaultErrorHandler decides how often to retry, and DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer moves the record to a .DLT (dead-letter topic) when retries run out.

Why. Submitting the same invoice twice to the government is a compliance error. Portals were flaky, so retries were unavoidable. Retries without idempotency are dangerous.

How (illustrative). Each Spring Boot consumer checks the key before calling the portal. Spring Kafka retries a failing record a bounded number of times with a pause between tries, then publishes it to a dead-letter topic.

@KafkaListener(topics = "einvoice-batches")
public void onBatch(InvoiceBatch b) {
    String key = b.clientId() + ":" + b.fileHash() + ":" + b.batchIndex();
    if (results.existsByIdempotencyKey(key)) return;   // retry-safe
    results.save(irpClient.submit(b).withKey(key));
}

@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
    return new DefaultErrorHandler(
        new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template),        // -> einvoice-batches.DLT
        new FixedBackOff(2_000L, 3L));                      // 3 retries, 2 s apart
}

Alternatives and why not. - Synchronous bulk requests. They block workers during peaks. - Unbounded retries. They hammer a failing portal.

Trade-off. A key store to maintain, and DLQ messages need someone to look at them.

What I'd do differently. I'd add idempotency keys from day one, not after a near-miss (STAR story 10).

Say this carefully. This Kafka is a different product from the Uber Menu Kafka. No Flink at Masters.

23. PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, Redis cache-aside

What. Filing data was split across PostgreSQL shards by tax quarter. A Redis cache-aside layer cut database read load by 30%.

Words. Sharding splits a table across separate databases by a key. Cache-aside means the app checks the cache first and only reads the database on a miss, then fills the cache.

Why. Every filing belongs to a tax quarter, so the quarter is a natural split key that keeps each shard smaller. Redis absorbs repeated reads of hot data so they don't hit Postgres every time.

Trade-off. Queries across quarters are harder. A cache can serve stale data until it expires.

GeeksforGeeks

24. PHP to Django, and async scheduled workflows

What. The doubt-support platform moved from PHP to Django, so it could handle 10K+ daily queries and 10x spikes during live coding contests. REST APIs for voting, pinning and locking threads used MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch. Asynchronous scheduled workflows automated video processing, reminders and data cleanup.

Why. Contest spikes overwhelmed the old backend. Manual ops tasks were slow and error-prone.

Trade-off. Four data stores (MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch) to keep consistent, in exchange for using each where it fits best.

Say this carefully. Business lifts (20% premium, 30% course sales) were attributed by the business teams. "I owned the engineering."

Resume Number Catalog / Numbers Defense

How to use this page

  • It explains every number on Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf: what it measures, where it came from, why it mattered to the business, how to say it out loud, and what not to say.
  • Read it before any round where they'll go through your resume line by line. Re-read the "Don't say" lines the morning of the interview.
  • Memorise the spoken form of each number and the one-sentence derivation. If you can say where a number came from in one breath, it sounds credible.
  • A short "off the PDF" list at the end covers numbers you may say out loud but that aren't on the resume.

Sources: canonical IA claims are in docs/ASSORTSMART_TAB_RESUME.md. Cross-links: GROUND_TRUTH.md, 18_resume_number_catalog.md, 09_metrics_derivations.md.

What the tags mean

  • MEASURED means there is a benchmark, log, document or code behind it.
  • TARGET means it was a design goal. Say "targeting".
  • ESTIMATED means it's arithmetic I can show on a whiteboard. Say "roughly, derived from...".
  • HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and wasn't re-measured.
  • PDF means it is on the resume as written and I defend it as written.
  • CI GATE means it is a release check, not a live production result.

Three rules for saying any number

  1. Say it as a change, slowly. "From 189 seconds to 12 seconds" is easier to hear than "15.5x".
  2. Say what it measured. "On a 250-million-row test" or "on a fixed test set".
  3. Stop after the number. Let them ask the follow-up. You have the derivation ready.

Impact Analytics: Agentic Flows and Orchestration

Context in plain words. AssortSmart helps retailers plan assortments: which products to keep, drop or add each season. An article is one product. An article-season is one product in one selling season, like "blue denim jacket, Spring 2026". The AI decision engine scores article-seasons and recommends what to do.

348k article-seasons evaluated (PDF)

  • What it measures. The number of product-in-season combinations the decision engine scored across its pipelines: Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style.
  • How it was derived. It's the count of rows the engine scored, from the AssortSmart run records.
  • Why it mattered. Planners can't review that many items by hand each season. Scoring them all means every item gets a consistent recommendation.
  • Say it. "The engine evaluates about 348 thousand article-seasons, where an article-season is one product in one selling season."
  • Don't say. Don't mix it with 1.6 million. That's the size of the whole catalog, it's off the PDF, and it's a different number. Scored is 348k.

88k items per pass (PDF)

  • What it measures. How many items one batch run of the engine processes.
  • How it was derived. It's the batch size of a single pass in the run records.
  • Why it mattered. It shows the orchestration has to survive long batch runs. A provider failure halfway through 88 thousand items can't mean starting over.
  • Say it. "One pass processes about 88 thousand items."
  • Don't say. Don't claim a specific number of passes unless you know how they split. If someone divides 348k by 88k and gets about 4, say "roughly, depending on the pipeline".

7 AI lenses (PDF)

  • What it measures. The number of separate LLM judgments made per item. A lens is one angle of analysis, like a specialist giving an opinion on one aspect. A decider step combines them.
  • How it was derived. It's a count from the pipeline design.
  • Why it mattered. Splitting the judgment into focused lenses makes each prompt simpler and each output easier to check.
  • Say it. "Each item is looked at through seven AI lenses, and a decider combines them into one AI score."
  • Don't say. Don't say there's an LLM orchestrator choosing which lens to run. Keep/Drop runs in a fixed order: peer comparison, decider, lenses, blend, explanation.

The blend: 0.4, 0.6 and 0.55 (verbal design detail)

  • What it measures. How the final score is built. The deterministic score (from sell-through and rate of sale) gets weight 0.4. The AI score gets weight 0.6. An item is kept if the final score is 0.55 or higher.
  • Worked example. Deterministic score 0.70, AI score 0.45. Final = 0.4 × 0.70 + 0.6 × 0.45 = 0.28 + 0.27 = 0.55. That's exactly the threshold, so the item is kept.
  • Say it. "The final score is 40% rule-based and 60% AI, and we keep the item at 0.55 or above."
  • Don't say. Don't say these weights were retuned after the benchmark. They were frozen (see 74% below).

2.11B-row ClickHouse master (PDF)

  • What it measures. The number of rows in the main ClickHouse fact table, which holds detailed sales and inventory facts.
  • How it was derived. It's the table's row count.
  • Why it mattered. It explains the design choice. A table that large is too risky to let an LLM query directly. A bad generated query could be very slow or expensive, and a bad write would be very hard to undo. So the engine gets prepared JSON context instead.
  • Say it. "The main ClickHouse table has about 2.11 billion rows, so the AI never touches it directly. It gets prepared JSON."
  • Don't say. Don't say "sub-second queries on 2.11 billion rows". That isn't claimed.

300-case evaluation harness and 80% CI gate (PDF, CI GATE)

  • What it measures. The 300 is the number of test cases in a proxy evaluation set. Proxy means it stands in for real decisions with known answers. The 80% is the minimum accuracy a model or prompt change must reach on that set before it can be promoted. In config it's gold_min_accuracy: 0.8.
  • How it was derived. 300 is the count of cases in the evaluation file. 80% is the threshold set in the gate config.
  • Why it mattered. It stops a "looks good in a demo" change from reaching users. A change that makes the AI worse is blocked automatically.
  • Say it. "We have a 300-case evaluation set, and CI blocks any change that scores below 80% on it."
  • Don't say. Never say "the AI is 80% accurate in production" or "all tenants are live at 80%". It's a release gate.

73% lower cost at 100% coverage (PDF, MEASURED)

  • What it measures. In a separate benchmark of 200 gold-labelled items, a newer, cheaper model cost 73% less to run than the previous model. It also completed all 200 items. That's what "100% coverage" means here: every item got a valid answer, none timed out or failed.
  • How it was derived. Comparing the total cost of the two models on the same 200 items. The model names (gpt-5.6-luna versus gpt-5.4-mini) are off the PDF. Use them only if asked.
  • Why it mattered. Lower cost per run, with no loss of completeness, makes it affordable to run the engine regularly.
  • Say it. "On a 200-item benchmark, switching models cut execution cost by 73%, and it still answered all 200."
  • Don't say. Don't say this came from the 300-case file. It's a different set. And "100% coverage" here is not test coverage. It means 200 out of 200 items completed.

74% deterministic baseline, and freezing the weights (PDF, MEASURED)

  • What it measures. The accuracy of the rule-based scorer alone on that same 200-item set, using the production threshold of 0.65.
  • How it was derived. Running the deterministic scorer on the gold-200 set and counting correct decisions.
  • Why it mattered. The blended LLM score came out at about 63%, which is worse than 74%. So we did not retune the blend to make the AI look better. We froze the weights and kept the safer setup.
  • Say it. "The rule-based baseline scored 74% on the benchmark. The AI blend scored lower, so we froze the weights instead of shipping a worse model."
  • Don't say. Don't fuse 73%, 74% and 80% into one story. 80% is the gate on the 300-case file. 73% and 74% come from the 200-item benchmark.

Ask Iris (PDF capability, no numbers)

  • What it is. A copilot that planners chat with over a secure WebSocket (a connection that stays open for live back-and-forth) to ask about KPIs and inspect AI decisions.

Impact Analytics: Core Infrastructure and Pipeline

10k peak RPS (PDF)

  • What it measures. RPS is requests per second. 10k peak means the Go/Gin platform is built for and handles bursts of about 10,000 requests per second.
  • How it was derived. It's the peak figure stated for the platform on the AssortSmart record.
  • Why it mattered. The edge serves many retailers at once and has no reverse proxy in front of it, so it has to protect itself under load. That's why it has nested timeouts and native HTTP/2.

15.5x faster, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, on 250M rows (PDF, MEASURED)

  • What it measures. How long one planner pivot query took. A pivot is the grid view that groups numbers by product, store and time. It went from 189 seconds on Postgres to about 12 seconds on ClickHouse with pre-aggregated rollups.
  • How it was derived. A benchmark harness with 250 million rows, where both databases held identical data. The ClickHouse time was 12.3 seconds, rounded to 12 on the PDF. 189 ÷ 12.3 is about 15.4, and the benchmark doc reports about 15.5x. Either way, say "about fifteen times".
  • Why it mattered. At over three minutes, planners would give up on the screen. At 12 seconds the workflow becomes usable.
  • Say it. "Planner pivots went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250-million-row test, about fifteen times faster."
  • Don't say. Don't say "sub-second". Don't say the 170 GB fix caused this speed-up.

Six rollup tables (PDF)

  • What it measures. The number of pre-aggregated tables. A rollup stores totals in advance, like keeping a running monthly total instead of adding up receipts every time. The six are product, store and attribute, each at season level and at weekly level.
  • Say it. "Six rollup tables: product, store and attribute, each by season and by week."

170 GB out-of-memory prevented (PDF)

  • What it measures. The memory one query would have needed to build a whole season's weekly rollup in one go. OOM means out of memory, where the database kills the query.
  • How it was derived. From the failed runs. The whole-season build needed about 170 GB of working memory and failed even when the cap was raised to 80 GB and then 200 GB.
  • Why it mattered. Without a fix, there was no weekly level of detail at all.
  • The fix in one line. Build one fiscal week per insert, with memory and disk-spill caps. A product week needed about 11 GB. An attribute week went above 40 GB.
  • Say it. "Building a whole season at once needed about 170 GB and crashed. I sliced it into one week per insert, and it fit."
  • Don't say. This is load time, not query time. It is not why pivots got faster. The exact caps (55 GB memory, 16 GB spill, 8 threads, 4 weeks in flight) are verbal detail, not on the PDF.

About 344k rows per second (PDF, MEASURED)

  • What it measures. The combined copy speed of the custom Go data pump while migrating rollups between ClickHouse Cloud clusters.
  • How it was derived. Two season streams ran at the same time, each around 150k to 190k rows per second. Added together that's about 344k rows per second.
  • Why it mattered. Cross-cluster IP allowlists blocked ClickHouse's own cluster-to-cluster copy. The pump made multi-billion-row moves practical anyway.
  • Say it. "The pump copied about 344 thousand rows per second, combined across two streams."
  • Don't say. This is rows per second, an ingest rate. It is not requests per second or transactions per second.

Partitions up to 4.09B rows (PDF, MEASURED)

  • What it measures. The biggest partition group copied: the attribute weekly table across two seasons. A partition is a slice of a table, here one season.
  • How it was derived. 2,779,317,472 rows plus 1,311,108,195 rows equals 4,090,425,667, which is about 4.09 billion.
  • Say it. "The largest table we moved had about 4.09 billion rows across two seasons."
  • Don't say. The 4.09B copy was measured in flight. Don't say the cutover finished.

500k-row double-buffered batches (PDF)

  • What it measures. The batch size the pump reads and writes. Double-buffered means while one batch is being sent, the next one is already being read, so neither side waits.
  • Say it. "It moved 500 thousand rows per batch, reading the next batch while sending the previous one."

Impact Analytics Deep Dive: AssortSmart, Bullet by Bullet

How to use this page

  • What it covers: every Impact Analytics (IA) bullet on the resume, five Agentic bullets (A1 to A5) and five Core bullets (C1 to C5), explained from plain English down to code, plus the older POC and design material that is verbal depth only.
  • When to read it: read sections 1 to 4 the night before any interview. Read the bullet you expect to be grilled on (sections 5 and 6) the morning of. Use section 13 (practice drill) as a self-test.
  • What to memorise: the one-minute version, the Keep/Drop formula (0.4 times deterministic plus 0.6 times agent, keep at 0.55 or above), and the "split these numbers" box below. Everything else you should be able to explain, not recite.
  • Shorter packs: IA interview pack (30 seconds, 2 minutes, mock Q&A) and IA bullet defense. ClickHouse rollup and copier depth: ClickHouse rollup migration.

Role: Senior Software Engineer, Impact Analytics, Bangalore, May 2026 to Present. Individual contributor (no people reports at IA). Project on the resume: AssortSmart, Senior Software Engineer (Platform & AI). Tech line on the resume: Go, Gin, Python, FastAPI, LangGraph, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Redis, PostgreSQL, Datadog, LangSmith, GCP, Docker.

How the honesty tags work on this page. Every number carries a tag so you know how hard you can push it.

  • PDF means it is printed on the resume. Defend it as written.
  • MEASURED means there is a log, a benchmark output, a config file or a design doc behind it.
  • ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show on a whiteboard. Say "roughly, derived from...".
  • TARGET means a design goal that has not been proven. Say "targeting".
  • VERBAL means it is true but deliberately left off the resume. Use it only when asked.

Split these numbers. Never fuse them.

  • 348k article-seasons is the scored Keep/Drop volume (PDF). 1.6M article-seasons is the whole catalog (VERBAL). They are different numbers.
  • 300-case harness and 80% gate are the CI promotion gate. 73% cheaper at 100% coverage and 74% deterministic baseline come from a separate 200-case benchmark. Do not say the 300-case file measured 73%.
  • 80% is a gate a new config must pass. It is not "every tenant runs at 80% accuracy in production".
  • 15.5x (189 seconds to 12 seconds) is query time for planner pivots. 170 GB OOM is load time for weekly rollup builds. Fixing the OOM did not cause the 15.5x.
  • ~344k rows per second is a data copy rate. It is not requests per second or transactions per second.
  • 4.09B rows was measured while the copy was in flight. Do not say the cutover finished.
  • "Atomic partition rollback" means DROP PARTITION, then recopy that season. It is not an atomic swap that live readers never notice.
  • $100 per pass token spend is true but off the PDF.

1. The one-minute version (say this out loud)

30 seconds. "At Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a merchandise planning product that helps retailers decide which products to keep, drop or add each season. I own two areas. On the agentic side, I built a decision engine that scores 348k article-seasons for Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style, blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM calls across seven analytical lenses, behind a 300-case evaluation harness and an 80% CI gate. I also shipped Ask Iris, a WebSocket copilot planners use to question KPIs and AI decisions. On the platform side, I built the multi-tenant Go/Gin edge that peaks at 10k requests per second, and a ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer that took a heavy planner pivot from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250M-row benchmark."

60 seconds (add this). "Two design rules run through all of it. First, the LLM never touches the database. Deterministic code reads ClickHouse, packs the context for each article into JSON, and the model only returns structured scores. If the model times out, we fall back to the deterministic score, so an 88k-item run never stalls. Second, nothing ships on vibes. Every output row carries a frozen config hash, and a new model or prompt has to clear the 80% gate. In one benchmark the blended LLM scored below the free deterministic rule, so we froze the blend weights instead of tuning them on a tiny set. On the data side, the hard problems were memory and movement. Weekly rollups hit about 170 GB of aggregation state and crashed, so I sliced the build to one fiscal week per insert with memory and spill caps. And when cluster-to-cluster copy was blocked by IP allowlists, I wrote a Go data pump on ClickHouse's native TLS protocol that moved rollups at about 344k rows per second."

2. The business in plain English

Who the users are. The users are merchandise planners at retail chains (fashion and general merchandise, for example the tenants called kik and Briscoes in our data). A planner owns a slice of the product range, such as "women's tops" or "kids' footwear", and is accountable for what the stores carry next season.

What they do. Every season a planner builds an assortment plan: which products to carry, in which stores, in what depth. The biggest single decision is Keep or Drop: for each product that sold last season, do we carry it again or cut it? They also want to know what they missed (where demand was left on the table) and what the top styles are (the winners to protect and repeat).

What hurt before. A large retailer has hundreds of thousands of product-season combinations. Planners worked from heavy pivot tables (rows of products, columns of weeks and stores, cells of sales and stock). Those pivots were slow on PostgreSQL, so planners waited minutes for a screen. And the Keep/Drop judgement itself was manual, inconsistent between planners, and hard to explain later.

Why the company paid for this. Assortment is where retailers make or lose margin. Carrying a dead product ties up cash in stock that ends in markdown. Dropping a product that was about to take off loses sales. A system that scores every article-season consistently, explains its reasoning, and lets the planner question it saves planner time and makes decisions auditable. Fast pivots matter because planners will not trust a tool that makes them wait three minutes per click.

A tiny example. Article A1 is a blue cotton T-shirt. In plan season 74 it sold 840 units, with residual stock of 160 units at season end. Its sell-through is 840 / (840 + 160) = 84%. It sold about 1.17 units per store-week where it was on sale. Is that a Keep? The rule layer says "borderline". The lenses look deeper: is demand rising or dying, is the size curve healthy, do sibling colours steal its sales, does it only sell on discount? The engine blends both and returns Keep or Drop with an explanation the planner can read.

3. Words you need

Term Plain meaning
Article One sellable product, for example "blue cotton T-shirt, style 123". Think of it as a row in the product catalog.
Season (plan season) A selling period the retailer plans for, identified by a season_code such as 74 or 76.
Article-season One article in one season. It is the unit the engine scores. The same T-shirt in season 74 and in season 76 is two article-seasons.
Assortment planning Deciding the product range for a season: what to keep, drop and add. Like deciding next term's menu at a restaurant from this term's sales.
Keep / Drop The binary outcome per article-season. There is no third "maybe" outcome in the engine.
Missed Opportunities A pipeline that surfaces demand the plan missed. If asked for its exact rules, keep it qualitative and say it runs on the same harness as Keep/Drop.
Top Style A pipeline that ranks the strongest styles. The related Top Performing card gives Keep articles a short planner-facing tagline.
Product hierarchy (L0 to L4) The tree that groups products, for example division, department, class, subclass. Access control and scoping happen on this tree.
KPI (Key Performance Indicator) A business metric such as sell-through or rate of sale.
Sell-through Units sold divided by units sold plus units left. 84% means 84 of every 100 units available were sold.
Rate of sale (ROS) Units sold per store-week. It tells you how fast an item moves where it is stocked.
Pivot A planner screen that groups and sums data on the fly, like an Excel pivot table over hundreds of millions of rows.
Tenant One retailer customer. Multi-tenant means many retailers share the platform and must never see each other's data.
UAM (User Access Management) Which parts of the hierarchy a given user may see, for example "only kids' footwear in region North".
ClickHouse A column-oriented analytical database. It stores each column separately so a query that needs 5 of 100 columns reads only those 5. Think of reading one column of a spreadsheet instead of every row.
MergeTree The main ClickHouse table engine. Data lands in sorted immutable chunks called parts, and a background process merges parts together.
ReplacingMergeTree (RMT) A MergeTree that keeps only the newest version of rows with the same key, once parts merge. Think of a notebook where you never erase, you just write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines. Until the cleaner runs, readers must pick the latest line themselves.
Partition A physical slice of a table, here one slice per season_code. You can drop or rebuild one season without touching the others.
Rollup / pre-aggregation A table that stores sums that were computed once at load time, so a screen reads 1 row instead of summing 1,000.
OOM (out of memory) A query or process dies because it asked for more RAM than it was allowed.
Disk spill Letting a big GROUP BY write intermediate state to disk instead of holding it all in RAM. Slower, but it finishes.
LLM (Large Language Model) A model like GPT or Claude. Here it returns structured scores, not free text.
Lens One focused LLM analysis of an article, for example "is demand accelerating or dying?" There are 7 active lenses.
Decider The step that chooses which lenses to weigh for each article and how much.
Structured invoke An LLM call whose output must match a strict JSON schema (score, outcome, confidence, reason codes). Bad shape means the call failed.
Circuit breaker A switch that stops calling a failing dependency after repeated failures, like a fuse in a house that trips instead of letting wires burn.
Checkpoint A saved record of finished work, so a restart skips what is already done.
config_hash A SHA-256 fingerprint of the frozen guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog used for a run. It is stamped on every output row.
Gold set Labelled cases with the known right answer, used to grade the engine offline.
Proxy gold Gold labels derived from what actually happened next season, used when planners have not labelled cases by hand.
CI gate (Continuous Integration gate) An automated check that blocks promotion if a quality bar is not met.
LangGraph A Python framework for building LLM workflows as explicit graphs of steps, with state and loop limits.
Supervisor A LangGraph node that routes a user's question to the right worker step.
Evaluator loop A step that checks an answer and asks for a retry if it is not good enough, capped at 3 attempts in Ask Iris.
LangSmith A tracing and evaluation tool for LLM apps. It shows each step, prompt, tool call, tokens and cost. On this resume it belongs to Ask Iris.
WebSocket A long-lived two-way connection between browser and server, good for chat.
JWT (JSON Web Token) A signed token that proves who the user is and carries claims like tenant and role.
OIDC (OpenID Connect) A standard login protocol on top of OAuth. Google OIDC means signing in with Google identity.
Firebase Admin Google's server-side SDK that verifies Firebase-issued user tokens.
Go / Gin Go is a compiled language with cheap concurrency (goroutines). Gin is a fast HTTP router and middleware framework for Go.
Google Wire A Go dependency injection tool that generates the wiring code at compile time. If a dependency is missing, the build fails instead of a request.
h2c HTTP/2 over plain TCP without TLS ("cleartext"). It gives HTTP/2 multiplexing inside a trusted network.
Datadog distributed tracing Each request gets a trace id, and every service and database call it touches is recorded as a timed span under that id.
Native protocol (port 9440) ClickHouse's own binary protocol over TLS, faster than its HTTP interface for bulk data.
IP allowlist A firewall rule that only lets listed IP addresses connect to a cluster.
Double buffering Using two buffers so you can fill the next batch while the previous one is still being sent.
Ghost rows Rows from a failed, partial write that stay in the table and make a broken load look complete.
BigQuery Google's serverless data warehouse. Here it is upstream historical data that feeds ClickHouse.

4. Architecture

flowchart LR UI["Planner UI"] --> EDGE["Go/Gin edge: Wire, h2c, nested timeouts"] UI --> IRIS["Ask Iris: FastAPI WebSocket"] EDGE --> AUTH["Auth waterfall: Redis cache, Firebase Admin, JWT, Google OIDC"] AUTH --> PG["PostgreSQL: tenants, UAM, roles, metadata"] EDGE --> KPI["KPI formula compiler"] KPI --> CH["ClickHouse: 2.11B-row master, six rollup tables"] EDGE --> CH BQ["BigQuery upstream history"] --> CH CH --> DET["Deterministic KPI engine"] DET --> PACK["JSON context payloads"] PACK --> LLM["LLM lenses and decider"] LLM --> BLEND["Blend and explain"] DET --> BLEND BLEND --> STAGE["Staged rows with config_hash"] STAGE --> CH REG["Orchestration registry: timeouts, breaker, checkpoints, telemetry"] --> DET REG --> LLM IRIS --> GRAPH["LangGraph supervisor and 3-attempt evaluator"] GRAPH --> CH GRAPH --> LS["LangSmith traces"] EDGE --> DD["Datadog traces"]

What to notice: there is no arrow from the LLM to ClickHouse. Deterministic code reads the database and the LLM only ever sees JSON.

Walkthrough, box by box.

  1. Planner UI. Planners use web screens (pivots, Keep/Drop grids, KPI views) and the Ask Iris chat panel.
  2. Go/Gin edge. Every normal API call lands on a Go service built with Gin. It is the HTTP edge itself. There is no nginx or Envoy layer we run in front, so the Go process owns HTTP/2 (h2c), request timeouts, body limits and tracing. Google Wire builds the dependency graph at compile time. It peaks at 10k requests per second (PDF).
  3. Auth waterfall. Each request is authenticated through a chain: a Redis cache of already-verified identities first, then Firebase Admin token verification, then JWT or Google OIDC. API keys are compared in constant time. Roles come from PostgreSQL.
  4. PostgreSQL. The small, transactional data: tenants, users, UAM hierarchy scopes, roles, thin metadata. It is the right tool for correct, consistent identity data.
  5. KPI formula compiler. Operators define KPIs as formulas ("units / (units + eop) * 100"). The Go tokenizer and parser compile them into safe, parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragments with division-by-zero protection.
  6. ClickHouse. The big analytical data: a 2.11B-row master fact table and six rollup tables (product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly grain). Planner pivots read rollups, not raw daily facts.
  7. BigQuery. Historical data upstream. It feeds ClickHouse. Interactive screens and agents do not query BigQuery directly.
  8. Deterministic KPI engine (Python). Computes sell-through, rate of sale and the rule score s_det for each article-season, straight from ClickHouse with SQL.
  9. JSON context payloads. For each batch of articles, deterministic code packs the features each lens needs into JSON.
  10. LLM lenses and decider. Structured LLM calls return per-lens scores. The decider weighs lenses per article. Their combination is s_agent.
  11. Blend and explain. s_final = 0.4 x s_det + 0.6 x s_agent. Keep if s_final >= 0.55. Then a planner-facing explanation is written.
  12. Staged rows with config_hash. Results are staged first, then loaded into ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree tables, each row stamped with the run's config_hash.
  13. Orchestration registry. One shared harness for all three pipelines: hard timeouts, circuit breakers, durable checkpoints, and JSON telemetry (tokens, USD cost, step duration, batch fallbacks).
  14. Ask Iris. A FastAPI WebSocket service. The JWT is checked once at the handshake and the user's hierarchy scope (plan_scope) is frozen for the session. A LangGraph supervisor routes questions and a 3-attempt evaluator stops loops. LangSmith traces each run.
  15. Datadog. Distributed traces for the Go edge and its database calls.

4.1 One batch, step by step (Keep/Drop)

sequenceDiagram participant R as Registry participant D as Deterministic engine participant C as ClickHouse participant P as Peer step participant DE as Decider participant L as Lenses participant B as Blend and explain R->>D: start run, freeze config_hash D->>C: SELECT KPIs for the scope C-->>D: sell-through, ROS, features D->>R: write det checkpoint R->>P: batch of up to 64 articles as JSON P-->>DE: sibling and category context DE->>L: lens mixes per article L-->>B: score, outcome, confidence per lens B->>B: s_agent, then s_final = 0.4 s_det + 0.6 s_agent B->>R: staged rows plus agent progress checkpoint

What to notice: the batch order is fixed in code (peer, decider, lenses, blend, explain). There is no LLM orchestrator deciding what runs next.

Concrete walk-through with one article.

  1. The deterministic engine reads article A1, season 74: sell-through 84%, ROS 1.168.
  2. It normalises each KPI to a 0-to-1 score with a ramp (section 5, A1) and computes s_det = 0.65.
  3. The article joins a batch of up to 64 articles. The registry sends the batch as JSON. No SQL is in the payload.
  4. The peer step adds relative context: how A1 compares with its sibling colours and its category.
  5. The decider builds 4 to 5 lens mixes for A1. Lenses with no data are gated out. A1 comes in one colour only, so the colour-cannibalisation lens does not run.
  6. The lenses return scores. Say they combine to s_agent = 0.711.
  7. Blend: 0.4 x 0.65 + 0.6 x 0.711 = 0.687. That is at or above 0.55, so the outcome is Keep.
  8. The explain step writes a planner-facing reason. The row is staged with the run's config_hash, then loaded into ClickHouse.

4.2 One planner pivot request, step by step

  1. The planner opens a "weekly sales by department" pivot for season 74.
  2. The browser calls the Go/Gin API over HTTP/2. Datadog starts a trace.
  3. Auth middleware finds the user's verified identity in Redis (or falls through to Firebase, JWT, OIDC), then loads roles and UAM scope from PostgreSQL.
  4. The handler resolves KPI formulas through the compiler into safe SQL fragments.
  5. It queries the product_weekly rollup with season_code = 74 and the user's hierarchy scope. ClickHouse reads only the season-74 partition and only the needed columns.
  6. The response returns in seconds instead of minutes, because the heavy aggregation was paid once at load time.

5. Agentic Flows & Orchestration (A1 to A5)

A1. Multi-pipeline AI merchandise decision engine

PDF: Architected a multi-pipeline AI merchandise decision engine (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style) evaluating 348k article-seasons. Optimized inference at scale, processing 88k items per pass, by blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM invokes across 7 AI lenses.

In plain words. I built the engine that decides, for every product in every season, whether the retailer should carry it again. It runs three related pipelines (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style). For each article-season it does two things: plain math on the sales numbers, and a set of focused LLM analyses ("lenses"). Then it blends the two into one score and one decision. It is a batch decision engine, not a chatbot.

How it works.

Step 1: the deterministic score s_det. Each KPI is mapped to 0-to-1 with a piecewise ramp that has three knobs: low, target and high.

x <= low              -> 0
low < x < target      -> target_score * (x - low) / (target - low)
target <= x < high    -> target_score + (1 - target_score) * (x - target) / (high - target)
x >= high             -> 1
Signal Weight Low Target High Target score
Sell-through (end of period) 0.55 50 85 98 0.6
Rate of sale 0.45 0.5 1.0 1.5 0.6

Worked example: sell-through 84 gives 0.6 x (84 - 50) / (85 - 50) = 0.583. ROS 1.168 gives 0.6 + 0.4 x (1.168 - 1.0) / 0.5 = 0.734. So s_det = 0.55 x 0.583 + 0.45 x 0.734 = 0.65. Lifecycle staples have a floor (Basics at least 0.85, never-out-of-stock items at least 0.90), so the rule layer never drops a staple on a soft season. The rule layer on its own says Keep at s_det >= 0.65.

Step 2: the agent score s_agent. Seven lenses are active. Each one answers one question:

Lens Question it answers Runs only if
trend_velocity Is weekly demand accelerating or dying? 3 or more weeks on sale
size_curve Is the size distribution healthy or broken? 2 or more sizes
colour_cannibalization Do sibling colours steal this one's demand? 2 or more colours
channel_divergence Does it behave differently online and in store? 2 or more channels
multi_season_consistency Does it perform across seasons or was it a one-off? 2 or more seasons
discount_dependency Does it only sell on markdown? any discount present
margin_resilience How good is the margin? It cannot force a Drop alone. always

A cheap Python gate runs before any LLM call, so a single-colour, single-size sock sold for two weeks only gets the margin lens. No tokens are wasted on lenses with nothing to compare. The decider builds 4 to 5 weighted lens mixes per article: two fixed anchors computed in Python (demand, and risk or cannibalisation) plus two or three adaptive mixes proposed by the LLM. A mix only counts if at least 75% of its planned lens weight actually came back, so a missing lens cannot quietly make a mix look optimistic. s_agent is the mean of the valid mixes.

Step 3: the blend.

s_final = 0.4 * s_det + 0.6 * s_agent      # weights normalised
outcome = "keep" if s_final >= 0.55 else "drop"

Step 4: structured output. Every lens returns the same JSON shape, validated against a schema:

{"article": "A1", "lens": "trend_velocity", "score": 0.72,
 "outcome": "keep", "confidence": 0.64,
 "signal": "rising, peaking near week 9",
 "reason_codes": ["TREND_RISING"]}

Why this design. LLMs are bad at arithmetic and good at pattern judgement. Sell-through and rate of sale must be financially exact and auditable, so they are hard-coded math in one domain/ module that both the SQL generator and the tests call. That means the number a planner sees and the number a test checks cannot drift apart. The lenses do the qualitative work rules cannot: is this trend starting or already peaked, is the size curve broken. The rule layer alone over-keeps, so the agentic layer does most of the real cutting on borderline items.

Alternatives considered and why not. - Let the LLM compute KPIs with a Python or SQL tool. Rejected. At 88k items that is a latency and prompt-injection surface, and math accuracy would depend on the model. - One big prompt per article with every signal. Rejected. Prompts get huge and the model loses focus. Small lens prompts with only the fields they need (and only the last 12 weeks for trend lenses) stay cheap and sharp. - Pure rules. Rejected. Too coarse, and they over-keep. - Let the LLM decide the whole ensemble. Rejected. The fixed anchors are pure Python and add no LLM calls, so one bad LLM response cannot own the decision.

Trade-off. More moving parts than a single model call, and a weights choice (0.4 and 0.6) that has to be governed. That governance is A5.

What I would do differently. Get planner-labelled gold cases earlier. Proxy labels from next-season sales tell you "did demand hold up", which is not quite "was this the right range decision".

The numbers.

Number What it measures Where it comes from How to say it Do not say
348k article-seasons (PDF) Article-season combinations the engine scored Scoring run outputs "We score about 348 thousand article-seasons." "1.6 million." That is the catalog (VERBAL), not the scored set.
88k items per pass (PDF) Size of one batch run of the engine Run configuration and outputs "One pass processes about 88 thousand items." An exact count of passes for 348k unless you know it. The full set takes several passes.
7 AI lenses (PDF) Active lens count in the config decision.json lens list. An eighth lens (spatial variance) exists but is switched off "Seven analytical lenses, gated per article." "Seven LLM calls per article always." The gate skips lenses with no data.
0.4 / 0.6, keep at 0.55 (MEASURED config) Blend weights and final cut line Config, chosen in an architecture benchmark and then frozen (A5) "40% rules, 60% agent, keep at 0.55." That the weights were tuned on production outcomes.
$100 per pass (VERBAL) Token spend for one pass Run telemetry Only if asked about cost: "roughly a hundred dollars of tokens per pass." Put it on the resume line or present it as a monthly bill.

Why the numbers matter to the business: 348k is the scale at which manual Keep/Drop review is impossible, so consistency and explainability are the product.

Questions they will ask.

Q: Why not let the LLM calculate KPIs with tools? I deliberately kept math out of the model. Sell-through and rate of sale are pre-computed in Python and SQL and passed in as JSON. A scoring agent with a code or SQL tool, running over 88k items, is a latency risk and an injection surface, and the math would depend on the model's mood. This way the KPI is identical every run and the LLM only judges patterns. Follow-up they may ask: "Then what does the LLM add?"
