12. Practice drill

  1. What is an article-season? One product in one selling season. It is the unit the engine scores. The same T-shirt in two seasons is two article-seasons.
  2. Give the Keep/Drop formula. s_final = 0.4 x s_det + 0.6 x s_agent. Keep if s_final is 0.55 or more. s_det comes from sell-through and rate of sale. s_agent comes from lens mixes chosen by the decider.
  3. Why does the LLM not query the database? Hallucinated or runaway SQL against a 2.11B-row table risks scans, pool exhaustion and injection. Deterministic code reads ClickHouse and passes JSON. The model only returns structured scores.
  4. What happens on an LLM timeout? The batch falls back to deterministic scores, telemetry records a fallback, and the run continues. Resume can retry those later.
  5. What does the config hash contain? A SHA-256 over frozen guardrails, parameters, prompt text and catalog. It is stamped on every row so any change in output can be traced to a config change or ruled out.
  6. How does resume avoid redundant work? Deterministic results are saved first, LLM progress is appended per article, and a restart reloads both and continues only unfinished articles.
  7. How does Ask Iris prevent tenant leaks? JWT verified at the WebSocket handshake, plan_scope frozen for the session, and every tool call inherits it.
  8. How does Ask Iris stop loops? The evaluator caps retries at 3 attempts, and the graph has a recursion limit. After that it fails closed with a graceful answer.
  9. Is 80% your live accuracy? No. It is the CI promotion gate. 73% and 74% come from a separate 200-case benchmark.
  10. Why did you freeze the blend weights? The blended LLM scored below the 74% deterministic baseline on a small proxy set. Retuning would overfit, and the model had not earned more weight.
  11. Why Wire? Compile-time dependency injection. Wiring errors fail the build, with no runtime reflection.
  12. How is the KPI parser safe? Tokenize, parse, allowlist functions, resolve names through the catalog, bind literals, and wrap in ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0). Unknown tokens fail closed.
  13. Did the OOM fix cause the 15.5x? No. 15.5x is query time on the pivot benchmark. The OOM was load time for weekly rollups.
  14. Is 344k requests per second? No. It is rows per second copied, combined across two season streams.
  15. What does "atomic partition rollback" mean? DROP PARTITION for an incomplete season, then recopy it. Readers can see a partial season during that window. It is not an atomic swap.

13. Three-minute whiteboard script

  1. Draw first (30 seconds): the users and the edge. Planner UI on the left. Arrow to the Go/Gin edge. Write "Wire, h2c, nested timeouts, Datadog, 10k peak RPS". Say: "Every normal API call lands on a Go service that is its own HTTP edge."
  2. Draw second (45 seconds): the two stores. Postgres box ("tenants, UAM, roles") and ClickHouse box ("2.11B master, six rollups, PARTITION BY season"). Redis in front of auth. Say: "Postgres for identity and correctness, ClickHouse for the big reads. Pivots went from 189 seconds to about 12 on a 250M-row benchmark. Weekly rollups are built one fiscal week at a time after a 170 GB OOM."
  3. Draw third (60 seconds): the agent plane. Deterministic engine reads ClickHouse, then a "JSON" arrow to LLM lenses, then blend, then staged rows back into ClickHouse. Cross out any arrow from the LLM to ClickHouse. Write the formula. Say: "348k article-seasons, 88k per pass, 7 lenses. The model never touches the database. Timeouts fall back to the rule score. The registry gives breakers, checkpoints and a config hash on every row."
  4. Draw fourth (30 seconds): Ask Iris. A WebSocket arrow from the UI to a FastAPI box with "supervisor, evaluator x3, frozen plan_scope, LangSmith". Say: "Scope is frozen at the handshake, loops are capped at three attempts."
  5. Close (15 seconds): the gate. Write "300 cases, 80% gate" next to the agent plane. Say: "Nothing is promoted unless it clears the gate, and when the blend lost to the 74% rule on our model benchmark, we froze the weights."
  6. If time remains: draw the copier (source cluster, Go pump on an allowlisted host, target cluster) and say "about 344k rows per second, 500k double-buffered batches, DROP PARTITION and recopy on failure".

Impact Analytics: Interview Pack (AssortSmart, Platform and AI)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: my current role, explained so you can talk about it for 30 seconds, 2 minutes or 45 minutes. It decodes all ten resume bullets, the design decisions, and the questions interviewers ask.
  • When to read it: before every interview. This is the project most interviewers will spend the most time on.
  • What to memorise: the 30-second pitch, the numbers table in section 5, and the "do not say" list at the end.

What is on the resume and what is not.

  • The resume has two Impact Analytics subsections: Agentic Flows and Orchestration (5 bullets) and Core Infrastructure and Pipeline (5 bullets). The canonical wording is in docs/ASSORTSMART_TAB_RESUME.md at the repo root.
  • Verbal-only, not on the PDF: the Cluster Recommendation Copilot (14 tools, the 8.5% failure baseline, its confirm steps), Hindsight, the 63-table / 8-layer ClickHouse DDL design, and the line-plan 12B work. Only bring these up if asked what else you are working on. Hindsight defense: 01b_hindsight_defense.md.
  • True but off the PDF: $100 token spend per pass, the 1.6M article-season catalog, 100% Go statement coverage over 1,200+ tests, the 55GB / 16GB weekly insert caps.
  • Never on Impact Analytics: Kafka, Flink, CDC, Kubernetes operations, Milvus, sub-second ClickHouse, human review queues (HITL).

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, a doc or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). HISTORICAL means from past work records.

Role: Senior Software Engineer, Impact Analytics, May 2026 to present. Individual contributor. Project title on the resume: "AssortSmart — Senior Software Engineer (Platform & AI)". Tech line: Go, Gin, Python, FastAPI, LangGraph, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Redis, PostgreSQL, Datadog, LangSmith, GCP, Docker.

1. The business in plain English

AssortSmart is assortment planning software for retailers. A merchandise planner at a fashion or home retailer has to decide, every season, which products to keep in the range, which to drop and which to add, and how much to buy for which stores. Those decisions are worth a lot of money: keeping a dead product ties up stock and shelf space, and dropping a good one loses sales.

Planners use AssortSmart in two ways. They explore big pivot tables of sales and inventory, sliced by product, store, attribute and week. And they get AI recommendations: should this article be kept or dropped next season, which opportunities did we miss, which styles are top performers. They can also chat with an assistant called Ask Iris to ask about KPIs and about why the AI decided something.

Before my work, pivots on PostgreSQL were slow, KPI changes needed code releases, and AI decisions had no strict guardrails or evaluation. My work sits on both halves: the core platform (Go/Gin on ClickHouse and PostgreSQL) and the agent plane (Python, FastAPI, LangGraph).

2. Say it out loud

30 seconds

"At Impact Analytics I work on AssortSmart, a retail assortment planning SaaS. On the platform side, I own a multi-tenant Go/Gin edge at 10k peak RPS on top of ClickHouse and Postgres. I built the pre-aggregation layer that took a planner pivot from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, a KPI formula compiler, and tenant and hierarchy isolation. On the AI side, I architected a decision engine that scores 348 thousand article-seasons as Keep or Drop by blending deterministic KPI math with seven LLM lenses, with the LLM fed JSON rather than database access. I also shipped Ask Iris, a LangGraph copilot for planners, and an 80% CI gate that every model or prompt change must pass."

2 minutes

"AssortSmart helps retail planners decide what to keep, drop and add each season. I work on both halves of the system.

The platform is a multi-tenant Go/Gin API at 10k peak RPS. It uses Google Wire for compile-time dependency injection, and runs as its own HTTP edge with no reverse proxy, so it handles h2c, nested timeouts and Datadog tracing itself. Auth is a Redis-fronted waterfall of Firebase, JWT and Google OIDC, roles come from Postgres, and every query is scoped by tenant and by the user's hierarchy access. Planner pivots used to be slow, so I built six ClickHouse rollup tables. A 250 million row pivot went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds. Separately, weekly rollup builds were crashing out of memory at around 170 GB, so I sliced inserts into one-week chunks with memory and spill caps. I also wrote a Go pump that copied rollups between ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 344 thousand rows a second.

The AI side is a batch decision engine: Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style, over 348 thousand article-seasons, 88 thousand items per pass. Each article gets a deterministic score and an LLM score from seven lenses, blended 40/60. The LLM never queries the 2.11 billion row ClickHouse master. It gets JSON. If it times out, we fall back to the deterministic score. A shared registry gives every pipeline timeouts, circuit breakers, checkpoints and a config hash on every row. Planners chat through Ask Iris, which I shipped: a JWT WebSocket with a LangGraph supervisor and a 3-attempt evaluator. Nothing gets promoted unless it passes an 80% accuracy gate on a 300-case evaluation set."

3. The architecture in one picture

flowchart LR UI["Planner UI"] --> EDGE["Go/Gin edge, 10k peak RPS"] EDGE --> PG["PostgreSQL: roles, UAM"] EDGE --> CH["ClickHouse: 2.11B master, six rollups"] CH -->|"JSON context"| AG["Python agent plane: 7 lenses"] AG --> LLM["LLM, no SQL tool"] AG -->|"versioned rows"| CH UI -->|"WebSocket"| IRIS["Ask Iris: LangGraph"] IRIS --> CH

What to notice: the LLM sits behind Python code and only sees JSON. Full box-by-box walkthrough, sample request and failure modes are on the architecture page: ../architecture/01_ia_assortsmart_hindsight.md.

4. Each resume bullet decoded

For each bullet: the exact resume line, what it means in plain words, how it works, the numbers, and the question you will get.

A1. The decision engine

Architected a multi-pipeline AI merchandise decision engine (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style) evaluating 348k article-seasons. Optimized inference at scale—processing 88k items per pass—by blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM invokes across 7 AI lenses.

In plain words. Three batch pipelines decide things about products. Keep/Drop is the main one. Each article gets a rules-based score and an AI score, and the two are blended.

How it works. - Deterministic score s_det from sell-through and rate of sale, each mapped onto a 0-to-1 ramp. - Agent score s_agent from 7 lenses (trend velocity, size curve, colour cannibalization, channel divergence, multi-season consistency, discount dependency, margin resilience), combined by a decider. - s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent. Keep if s_final ≥ 0.55. - Worked example: s_det = 0.737, s_agent = 0.711, so s_final = 0.295 + 0.427 = 0.721, which is Keep. - "Structured invoke" means the LLM must answer in a fixed JSON schema. - There is no LLM orchestrator. The batch order is fixed: peer context, decider, lenses, blend, explanation.

The numbers. 348k is the number of article-seasons scored. 88k is the number of items in one pass. 1.6M (off PDF) is the whole catalog, a different number. Do not mix them.

Question they will ask: "Why not let the LLM decide everything?" "Because rules are cheap, explainable and always available, and the LLM is none of those things all the time. The deterministic score anchors the decision and gives reason codes a planner can read. The lenses add judgement on things rules handle badly, like colour cannibalization or discount dependency. Blending them, with the deterministic score as fallback, means a provider outage never leaves a planner without a decision."

A2. Decoupling inference from the database

Decoupled AI inference from a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master by asynchronously serving context via JSON payloads rather than direct database querying. Engineered an eventually consistent write pattern via ReplacingMergeTree that guaranteed system availability by gracefully falling back to deterministic baselines during LLM timeouts.

In plain words. The AI never touches the big database. Code fetches what the AI needs, packs it as JSON and hands it over. Results are written as new versions of rows, and if the AI is slow, the rules-based score stands in.

How it works. - Python runs fixed, reviewed queries and builds one compact JSON row per article. The LLM gets no SQL tool. - "Asynchronously" describes how batches run in parallel. It does not mean the LLM queries anything. - ReplacingMergeTree keeps the newest version of rows with the same key, here (season_code, article), versioned by computed_at. Until background merges run, readers pick the latest row per key. - On an LLM timeout, the article keeps its deterministic baseline. When the agent score arrives later (for example on resume), a newer row replaces it. That is "eventually consistent".

Question they will ask: "What stops the LLM from leaking another tenant's data?" "It never has a query tool. The only data it sees is the JSON our code built for that batch, and that code applies the tenant and season scope. There is no prompt that can make it read something we did not send."

A3. The orchestration registry

Engineered a shared orchestration registry to guarantee 88k-article batch runs survive provider failures by implementing hard timeouts, circuit breakers, and durable checkpoints that bypass redundant deterministic scoring. Ensured full observability by stamping every output row with a frozen config hash and custom JSON telemetry tracking tokens, USD cost, step duration, and batch fallbacks.

In plain words. One shared runner makes every AI pipeline crash-safe, cost-visible and traceable.

How it works. - Hard timeouts on every LLM call. In the current config: min(600, 60 + 8 × articles) seconds, so a 64-article batch gets 572 seconds. - Circuit breakers stop a step after about 5 consecutive failures, or when the failure fraction passes a limit (0.25 in the current config). - Durable checkpoints: det.json holds deterministic scores, agent_progress.json holds which articles the LLM finished. --resume reloads both, so a restart never re-runs deterministic scoring. - config_hash: SHA-256 of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog. Change one word in a prompt and the hash changes, so every decision can be traced to its exact configuration. - JSON telemetry: tokens, USD cost, step duration, batch fallbacks.

Why not Airflow or Temporal: "I needed resume logic tied directly to our ClickHouse inserts and to the config hash, inside the app. A separate orchestration platform would not have removed that need, and it was extra infrastructure one team's batch jobs did not justify."

A4. Ask Iris

Shipped "Ask Iris," a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot enabling planners to interactively query KPIs and inspect AI decisions on a multi-billion-row database. Prevented infinite LLM loops and multi-tenant data leaks by orchestrating a LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator loop, utilizing LangSmith for observability, and strictly freezing hierarchy access on the initial socket handshake.

In plain words. A chat assistant for planners. It is secure by design: who you are and what you may see is fixed the moment you connect, and the AI cannot loop forever.

How it works. - JWT checked at the WebSocket handshake. - The user's plan_scope (their allowed hierarchy) is computed once at the handshake and frozen for the session. Later messages cannot widen it. - A LangGraph supervisor picks the next step. An evaluator checks the draft answer. MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3, then it stops. - LangSmith traces every run (prompts, tool calls, tokens, cost).

Say this carefully: Ask Iris is a shipped capability. There are no usage numbers or SLA to quote. Do not invent any.

Question they will ask: "Why freeze scope at the handshake instead of checking per message?" "Because per-message checks depend on every code path remembering to do them, and a chat prompt is exactly where someone will try 'show me the other region too'. Freezing scope once, at authentication time, means the session physically carries only that scope. It is simpler to reason about and simpler to test."

A5. Evaluation harness and CI gate

Built a 300-case proxy evaluation harness and an 80% accuracy CI gate to enforce strict deployment guardrails. Reduced live execution costs by 73% at 100% coverage by benchmarking models against a 74% deterministic baseline, strategically freezing final decision weights when the LLM underperformed the baseline.

In plain words. Two separate evaluation pieces. A 300-case test set with an 80% pass mark guards every change. A separate 200-case benchmark was used to pick a cheaper model and decide not to retune the blend.

How it works. - The 300-case harness: a "proxy gold" set built from what actually happened next season (150 keeps, 150 drops). The CI gate (gold_min_accuracy = 0.8 in eval.json) blocks promotion below 80%. - The gold-200 benchmark (separate): two models compared on 200 labelled cases, both completing 200 of 200. The chosen one cost 73% less to run at 100% coverage. On the same set, the deterministic baseline (production threshold 0.65) scored 74%. - The blended LLM scored about 63%, below the 74% deterministic baseline. So we froze the blend weights instead of retuning them to chase that one benchmark.

The numbers. 80% is a gate, not live accuracy. 73% and 74% come from the gold-200 benchmark, not the 300-case file. Model names are not on the PDF. Full detail: 01d_agentic_evals_guardrails_flow.md.

Question they will ask: "Your LLM scored worse than the rules. Why ship it?" "Because the gate did its job. The benchmark told us the blend did not beat the deterministic baseline on that set, so we did not pretend it did. We froze the weights rather than overfit them to 200 cases, kept the deterministic fallback, and any future change must pass the 80% gate before promotion. The cost work still stood: the model we picked ran 73% cheaper at full coverage."

C1. The Go/Gin platform

Architected a multi-tenant Go/Gin platform scaling to 10k peak RPS, utilizing Google Wire for compile-time DI. Deployed as a self-protecting HTTP edge without a reverse proxy, guaranteeing high availability through native h2c, nested timeouts, and Datadog distributed tracing.

In plain words. The main API is written in Go. It protects itself instead of relying on nginx, and every request is traced.

How it works. Wire generates dependency wiring at build time, so a missing dependency is a compile error. The process enforces request deadlines with smaller deadlines inside for each downstream call, caps request bodies, speaks h2c (HTTP/2 without TLS at the process, typically behind a TLS-terminating load balancer) and emits Datadog traces.

Say this carefully: no SLA numbers, no Kubernetes cluster operations claim.

C2. KPI configurator and formula parser

Eliminated deployment bottlenecks by architecting a dynamic KPI configurator and custom formula parser. Engineered a real-time compilation layer that tokenizes operator-authored math into parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragments with native division-by-zero protection, decoupling business logic from code releases.

In plain words. Business users type KPI formulas. A Go compiler turns them into safe SQL. New KPIs no longer need a release.

How it works. Tokenizer, then parser, then an allowlist of functions. Logical names map to physical columns. Divisions are wrapped in ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0). Unknown tokens fail closed. Values are bound parameters, never pasted into SQL.

operator types:  margin_pct = margin / revenue * 100
compiles to:     ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(margin) / sum(revenue) * 100), 0)

C3. Multi-tenant isolation and auth

Guaranteed strict multi-tenant data isolation and UAM-scoped hierarchy access control across PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. Redis-fronted Firebase Admin to JWT/Google OIDC waterfall, constant-time API keys, Postgres-backed role resolution.

In plain words. Every request is tied to a tenant and a slice of the product hierarchy, and every query is filtered by both.

How it works. Redis caches token verdicts. On a miss: Firebase Admin, then JWT or Google OIDC. API keys compared in constant time. Roles from Postgres. UAM scope applied to queries in both databases.

Say this carefully: isolation is scoping, not encryption.

C4. Pre-aggregation and the OOM fix

Reduced planner pivot latency by 15.5× (189s to 12s on 250M-row operations) by building a ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer for season and weekly rollups. Prevented 170GB OOM crashes by slicing batch inserts into temporal chunks and enforcing strict distributed memory and disk-spill caps.

In plain words. Two separate wins. Pivots got fast because they read pre-summed tables. Weekly table builds stopped crashing because they were built one week at a time.

How it works. Six MergeTree rollups (product, store, attribute, each at season and weekly grain), all PARTITION BY season_code. Weekly builds use one fiscal week per INSERT SELECT, with verbal knobs of 55GB memory cap, 16GB spill, 8 threads, 4 weeks in flight. A whole-season weekly build needed about 170GB and failed even at 80GB and 200GB caps.

Say this carefully: 15.5× is query time. 170GB is load time. They are not cause and effect. The PDF rounds 12.3 seconds to 12.

C5. Cross-cluster copy with a Go pump

Migrated ClickHouse rollups across Cloud clusters at ~344k rows/s by writing a custom Go native-TLS data pump to bypass strict cross-cluster IP allowlist restrictions. Processed partitions up to 4.09B rows using 500k-row double-buffered batches, and eliminated partial-commit ghost rows using TSV ledgers and atomic partition rollbacks.

In plain words. Two ClickHouse clusters could not talk to each other directly, so I wrote a Go program that read from one and wrote to the other, fast and safely.

How it works. - Native ClickHouse protocol over TLS (port 9440) from an allowlisted machine. - 500k-row columnar batches, double-buffered: read the next batch while the previous one is being sent. - Two season streams of about 150k to 190k rows per second each, about 344k combined. - Ghost rows (rows from a half-finished insert) prevented by a TSV ledger (the weekly loader's skip file) and copier checkpoint files migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done. - "Atomic partition rollback" means DROP PARTITION then recopy that season. It is not an atomic swap with live readers.

Say this carefully: 344k is rows per second, not requests. The 4.09B copy (2,779,317,472 + 1,311,108,195 rows of attr weekly) was measured in flight. Do not say the cutover finished. Never offer to open-source the copier.

6. Design decisions, short form

Each of these has a full What / Why / Alternatives / Trade-off / What I'd do differently write-up on the architecture page.

  • Go/Gin edge without a reverse proxy. Fewer hops, one place for timeouts, tracing at the serving process. Trade-off: I own every protection nginx would give for free.
  • ClickHouse versus PostgreSQL versus Snowflake. Postgres is a row store built for transactions: multi-column pivots read whole rows. ClickHouse reads only the needed columns and processes them in vectorised batches. Snowflake and BigQuery are strong warehouses, but interactive pivots wanted predictable latency and cost on a store we control. Trade-off: ClickHouse is weak at single-row updates, so writes become new versions.
  • JSON context instead of an LLM SQL tool. Safer, cheaper, testable. Trade-off: a lens needing a new field needs a code change.
  • LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator for Ask Iris. Explicit control flow, a hard cap on loops, and a frozen scope. Trade-off: one more framework to learn and maintain.
  • 80% CI gate against a deterministic baseline. A change must beat a free rule, not just "look better". Trade-off: the gate will sometimes block a model. That is the point.
  • Kafka and Flink. These are Uber Menu. Not used on AssortSmart.

7. Mock-interview notes

"Is Ask Iris actually shipped?" "Yes, as a capability: a JWT WebSocket copilot with scope frozen at the handshake and a 3-attempt evaluator loop. I do not have usage or SLA numbers to quote, so I will not make any up."

"Did you build the Postgres-to-ClickHouse CDC pipeline?" "No. That was a colleague, Ashvin Sharma. I can discuss the design pattern, but I did not author it."

"Tell me about an out-of-memory incident." "The one on my resume is the weekly ClickHouse rollup build at around 170 GB, fixed with one-week slices and memory and spill caps." There is also a Python/FastAPI connection-leak OOM story in older prep. That one is a packet story, not a resume bullet. If you tell it, say so, and do not attach Kubernetes cluster operations to it.

"What about the Cluster Recommendation Copilot?" "That is in progress and not on my resume. Happy to talk about its design." Details: 01c_agent_read_tools_defense.md and 01d_agentic_evals_guardrails_flow.md.

"Is 80% your production accuracy?" "No. 80% is the promotion gate on a 300-case proxy set. A change cannot ship unless it clears that bar."

8. Practice drill

  1. What is an article-season? One product in one selling season. We score 348 thousand of them.
  2. What is the blend formula? s_final = 0.4 × s_det + 0.6 × s_agent, keep at 0.55 or above.
  3. Name the seven lenses. Trend velocity, size curve, colour cannibalization, channel divergence, multi-season consistency, discount dependency, margin resilience.
  4. What happens when the LLM times out? The article keeps its deterministic score, and a newer row replaces it when the agent score arrives. ReplacingMergeTree keeps the newest.
  5. What is config_hash? A SHA-256 fingerprint of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog, stamped on every output row so every decision is traceable.
  6. How does resume work? det.json and agent_progress.json checkpoints with --resume. Deterministic scoring is never redone.
  7. Why freeze scope at the WebSocket handshake? So nothing typed later can widen access, which prevents cross-tenant leaks.
  8. Is 80% production accuracy? No. It is the CI promotion gate on a 300-case proxy set.
  9. Where do 73% and 74% come from? A separate gold-200 benchmark, not the 300-case file.
  10. Does 15.5× come from the OOM fix? No. 15.5× is query time on rollups. The 170GB OOM fix is load time.
  11. Is 344k requests per second? No. It is rows per second during the copy.
  12. Did the 4.09B cutover finish? I measured the copy in flight. I do not claim the cutover finished.
  13. What does partition rollback mean? DROP PARTITION then recopy that season. Not an atomic swap.
  14. Why no reverse proxy? Fewer hops and one place for timeouts. I own the protections myself.
  15. Did you use Kafka at Impact Analytics? No. Kafka and Flink were Uber Menu.

9. Do not say

  • "All tenants are live at 80% accuracy."
  • Any throughput beyond the PDF's 10k peak RPS, or any SLA.
  • Spark, Pinot, Kubernetes operations, Terraform, Flink, Kafka or CDC on Impact Analytics.
  • MCP as an Impact Analytics resume skill. It is skills-level.
  • Cluster Copilot or Hindsight as resume bullets.
  • "Sub-second ClickHouse pivots."
  • "LangSmith on the Keep/Drop batch." LangSmith is on Ask Iris.
  • "Human review queue" or "HITL" on Impact Analytics.

Hindsight Module Defense (verbal-only depth)

Verbal-only. Not a resume bullet.

  • Hindsight is not on the PDF. Older prep called this a "resume claim". That is obsolete. The current resume does not mention Hindsight.
  • Use this page only when an interviewer asks "what else are you working on?" or "how do planners use last season's data?". Say "this is in progress and not on my resume".
  • Status: building against a functional requirements document. Do not say shipped or live for all tenants.
  • There is no dollar, latency or adoption number for Hindsight. Do not invent one. Speed numbers stay with the ClickHouse rollup bullet.
  • Defend the live resume from docs/ASSORTSMART_TAB_RESUME.md: 10k RPS, 189s to 12s with six rollup tables, the 170GB OOM fix, Ask Iris shipped, the 300-case / 80% promotion gate.

How to use this page

  • What it covers: what Hindsight is, how it is designed, and the engineering judgement behind it, mapped to the requirement numbers in the source document.
  • When to read it: after you know the main Impact Analytics pack, as extra depth for a long technical round.
  • What to memorise: the 60-second talk track, the four design principles (the AI is not the chart designer, not the calculator, runs overnight, and config beats code), and the honesty lines.

Source: KNOWLEDGE-MATERIAL/Impact-Analytics-work/PRD'S/Hindsight_Module_Functional_Requirements-2.docx (version 1.2).

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, a doc or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). HISTORICAL means from past work records. Most of this page is DESIGN: what the requirements document specifies.

1. What Hindsight is, in plain English

AssortSmart's planning cycle runs in stages: hindsight, then strategy, then clustering, then line plan, then buy. Hindsight is the first stage. Before planners decide what to buy next season, they look back at last season: what sold, what did not, which styles deserve to come back, and which should be dropped.

Without it, planners start next season half blind, piecing together last season from spreadsheets. Hindsight puts that review on one screen, with numbers, charts and short AI-written summaries, all limited to the part of the business each planner is allowed to see.

So the honest pitch is: Hindsight is buying-decision support, not a vanity dashboard. It feeds the decisions that cost real money in the next stages.

2. Words you need

  • FRD (functional requirements document). The product spec that lists what the system must do. Each requirement has a number, like FR-6.1.
  • TY vs LY. This year compared with last year. The scorecard also offers an "Optimised LY" comparison defined in the FRD. If asked for its exact definition, keep it qualitative.
  • Scorecard. A row of headline KPI tiles, such as sales, margin and sell-through, each compared with last year.
  • Contribution chart. Shows how much each category or store contributed to the total.
  • Carry-forward. Styles recommended to bring back next season.
  • Underperformance flag. A marker on items that did worse than a threshold.
  • Keep / Shop / Drop. The recommendation labels on the item grid in the FRD. (The Keep/Drop engine on my resume outputs binary Keep or Drop. See the honesty section.)
  • Narration. Short sentences written by an LLM that describe what happened, for example "Dresses grew 12% while Knitwear fell".
  • Grounding check. Before a narration sentence is saved, every number in it is compared with the computed metric. If they do not match, the sentence is rejected. Like a fact-checker reading a news article before it is printed.
  • Template fallback. A pre-written sentence with blanks filled from computed metrics, used when narration fails the check. Boring but always correct.
  • Template library and metric metadata. A shared set of sentence patterns, chosen based on each metric's description (is higher better, is it a percentage, and so on).
  • Metric catalog. One list per tenant of every metric, its formula and its display rules, shared by every widget.
  • Config vs code. A new metric or chart for a retailer is added as configuration data, not as a software release.
  • Permission scope. The part of the product and store hierarchy a user is allowed to see.
  • Virtualized scrolling. A grid that only renders the rows currently on screen, so 1,000+ items stay smooth. Like a train window: you only see the stretch of track you are passing.

3. What is on the screen (FRD v1.2)

  • A scorecard: this year against last year, or against the "Optimised LY" baseline.
  • Contribution charts.
  • A store performance map.
  • Configurable bar charts.
  • Top performers.
  • A By Item grid with Keep/Shop/Drop recommendations and a per-item note.
  • A By Attribute heatmap (for example colour by size).
  • A Carry-Forward / What Didn't Work panel.
  • Agent narration on the widgets.

4. How it is designed

flowchart LR FILTER["Global filter: product, location, season"] SCOPE["Permission scope check"] CAT["Tenant metric catalog"] CH["ClickHouse planning reads"] MET["Computed metrics"] VIS["Charts from config only"] NARR["Overnight narration batch"] CHECK["Grounding check"] TMPL["Template sentence"] SAVE["Saved narration"] UI["Hindsight screen"] FILTER --> SCOPE SCOPE --> CH CAT --> CH CH --> MET MET --> VIS MET --> NARR NARR --> CHECK CHECK -->|"numbers match"| SAVE CHECK -->|"mismatch"| TMPL TMPL --> SAVE SAVE --> UI VIS --> UI

What to notice: metrics are computed by code. Charts are chosen by configuration. The LLM only writes sentences, overnight, and every sentence is fact-checked against the computed numbers before it is saved.

One narration, step by step (illustrative)

  1. Overnight, the batch computes metrics for each tenant and scope. For example, "Dresses, season 74: sales up 12% against last year, sell-through 81%".
  2. The narration step picks a template family from the metric metadata (a growth metric, higher is better) and asks the LLM for one sentence.
  3. The LLM returns: "Dresses grew 12% year on year with strong sell-through of 81%."
  4. The grounding check extracts 12% and 81% and compares them with the computed values. Both match, so the sentence is saved.
  5. If the LLM had written "grew 15%", the check would fail and the template would be saved instead: "Dresses sales changed by +12% versus last year. Sell-through: 81%."
  6. In the morning, the planner opens Hindsight. Charts render from config, and the narration is read from storage. No LLM call happens on the page.

5. Requirement mapping, explained

What I say FRD reference What it means in practice
"Prior-season decision layer" Overview and pipeline position Hindsight exists so next-season buys are based on evidence.
"Carry-forward and underperformance flags" FR-6.1 The panel shows candidates and underperformers with the metric values beside any narration, never narration alone. The threshold can be personalised by the user within tenant bounds.
"Keep/Shop/Drop recommendations" FR-16.5 The item grid keeps the existing recommendation plus a per-item note, with the same grounding and fallback as other narration.
"Overnight narration checked against computed metrics" FR-2.3, FR-4.3, FR-5.3, FR-8.1 Batch, not live. Shared template library driven by metric metadata. Numbers checked before save. On failure, a templated sentence. No invented KPIs.
"Deterministic visuals" FR-9.1 Chart type, colours and icons come from configuration only. The narration agent never chooses layout.
"Permission-scoped filters" FR-0.1 to FR-0.5 One global product, location and season filter. "Select all" never reaches outside the user's permission scope.
"Shared metric catalog" Section 1.2, FR-1.1 One catalog for scorecard, bars, item grid and attribute heatmap. No per-widget metric lists that drift apart.
"Tenant catalogs without a code deploy" FR-1.3 Onboarding configuration (catalog and chart instances) applies to all tenant users without a code deployment. Changes are versioned with a last-updated stamp.
"Item grid at scale" FR-16.6 Stays fast at 1,000+ items through pagination or virtualized scrolling.

6. Engineering judgement to defend

Principle 1: the LLM is not the chart designer and not the calculator

  • What: charts come from config (FR-9.1). Metrics come from code. The LLM only writes sentences, which are checked.
  • Why: an LLM that picks charts makes every tenant's screen unpredictable. An LLM that computes numbers will sometimes compute them wrong. Both destroy trust.
  • Alternative: let the agent generate the whole dashboard. Impressive in a demo, unreliable in front of a buyer.
  • Trade-off: less "magic". The AI's job is small and boring, which is exactly what makes it safe.

Principle 2: narration runs overnight in batch

  • What: narration is generated once a night (FRD section 13). Live, on-demand narration is Phase 2, for narrow cases only (FR-11.1), with the same grounding check.
  • Why: planners change filters constantly. A live LLM call on every filter change would add seconds of latency and real cost, for sentences that barely change.
  • Trade-off: narration can be up to a day old. For last-season review, that is fine, because last season does not change.

Principle 3: config, not code

  • What: new retailer metrics and charts are data (FR-1.3), versioned.
  • Why: onboarding a retailer should not wait for a release train.
  • Trade-off: configuration needs its own validation, versioning and review, or a bad config breaks a tenant just like bad code.

Principle 4: multi-tenant safety on every widget

  • What: permission scope applies to every widget, including the store map and the item grid.
  • Why: "select all" is the classic leak. It must mean "all that I am allowed to see".
  • Trade-off: every query path must carry the scope, which needs tests per widget.

7. Honesty

  • Status is "building". It is in AssortSmart's Phase 1 posture. Do not claim it is fully shipped to all tenants.
  • Keep/Shop/Drop is existing behaviour that the FRD keeps on the item grid (FR-16.5). I am hardening and shipping it inside the Hindsight surface. I am not claiming a brand-new model.
  • Keep/Shop/Drop versus Keep/Drop. The FRD's item grid uses three labels. The Keep/Drop engine on my resume outputs binary Keep or Drop only. If an interviewer connects the two, say: "the resume engine is binary. The three labels are the item-grid language in the Hindsight spec."
  • No Hindsight numbers. No dollars, latency or adoption figures exist for Hindsight alone. The pivot speed numbers belong to the ClickHouse bullet.
  • No human review queue. Narration falls back to a template automatically. Nothing is queued for a human to approve.

8. 60-second talk track

"Something I am building that is not on my resume is Hindsight. It is how planners learn from last season before they buy for the next one. It is a decision layer: carry-forward and underperformance flags, Keep/Shop/Drop on the item grid, a scorecard and contribution views, all behind permission-scoped filters and a shared tenant metric catalog that goes live without a code deploy. The AI part is deliberately small. Narration runs overnight from a shared template library, and every number in a sentence is checked against the computed metric before it is saved. If it does not match, we save a template sentence instead. Charts are chosen by configuration, so the model can never invent a layout or a KPI."

9. Likely questions

"Does the agent ever invent metrics?" "No. Every number in a narration sentence is checked against the computed value before save, which is FR-2.3. If anything does not match, we fall back to a template sentence built from the computed metrics. It fails closed, so the planner sees a plain but correct sentence rather than a confident wrong one."

"Why overnight and not live?" "Because planners change filters constantly, and last season's data does not change. Generating narration live on every filter change would add latency and cost for nearly identical sentences. Version 1 batches overnight. Live narration is a Phase 2 option for narrow cases, with the same grounding check."

"What is Keep/Shop/Drop?" "It is the per-item recommendation on the By Item grid, with a short note, grounded like the other narration. It guides the planner on what to carry into the next plan. The Keep/Drop engine on my resume is the binary version that scores articles. The three labels are the item-grid language in the Hindsight spec."

"How does this relate to ClickHouse?" "Hindsight reads are scan-heavy, like pivots: sums over many rows sliced by product, store and week. Those reads sit on the ClickHouse planning store and rollups. The FRD is the product contract. ClickHouse is the serving engine. The measured speed numbers belong to the rollup work, not to Hindsight."

"How do you add a new metric for a retailer?" "Through the tenant metric catalog. It is configuration, versioned, and it applies to all of that tenant's users without a code deploy. That is FR-1.3."

"What stops a planner seeing another region?" "The global filter is permission-scoped, FR-0.1 to FR-0.5. Select-all means all within your scope, on every widget including the map and the item grid."

10. Practice drill

  1. Where does Hindsight sit in the planning cycle? First: hindsight, strategy, clustering, line plan, buy.
  2. Is it on your resume? No. It is in progress. I mention it only if asked.
  3. What does the LLM do in Hindsight? Writes short narration sentences overnight. Nothing else.
  4. What happens if a narration number is wrong? The grounding check fails and a template sentence is saved instead.
  5. Who picks the chart type? Configuration. Never the model (FR-9.1).
  6. How does a new tenant get its metrics? Through the versioned metric catalog, without a code deploy (FR-1.3).
  7. How does the item grid stay fast? Pagination or virtualized scrolling at 1,000+ items (FR-16.6).
  8. Is there a Hindsight latency number? No. Do not invent one.
  9. Is there a human approval step? No. Fallback is automatic.
  10. Is Keep/Shop/Drop new? No. It is existing behaviour kept on the item grid.

Agent Tools That Only Read Planning Data (verbal-only depth)

Verbal-only. Not a resume bullet.

  • This page is about the Cluster Recommendation Copilot design at Impact Analytics. It is not on the PDF. Older prep wrote "what the resume means" here. That is obsolete. The current resume does not mention the copilot or its 14 tools.
  • Status: design. The Phase 1 design passed internal and external review. The bring-up load test is pending. Say "designing" or "building", never "shipped".
  • MCP and tool calling are skills-level on my resume. The 14-tool design is something I can explain verbally. It is not an Impact Analytics bullet.
  • Do not call the confirm steps "HITL" or a "human review queue". Impact Analytics has no human review queue in shipped code. The design has planner confirmation clicks, which is a different thing (explained below).
  • Defend the live resume from docs/ASSORTSMART_TAB_RESUME.md: 10k RPS, 189s to 12s with six rollup tables, the 170GB OOM fix, Ask Iris shipped, the 300-case / 80% promotion gate.

How to use this page

  • What it covers: what "the agent's tools only read data" means, why we phrase it that way instead of "the agent never writes SQL", and how the design keeps writes safe.
  • When to read it: before a GenAI or agent-design round, after you know the main Impact Analytics pack.
  • What to memorise: the one-sentence principle ("the LLM proposes and reads, the engine computes, the planner confirms, writes go through product APIs"), the 8.5% (37 of 437) measured baseline, and that under 2% is a target.

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, a doc or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). HISTORICAL means from past work records. DESIGN means it is specified in a design document but not built or measured in production.

1. The problem in plain English

Before planners can decide which products go to which stores, they group stores into clusters: stores that behave alike (similar customers, similar sales patterns) get a similar assortment. Today a planner makes four expert choices more or less blind (attributes, time window, store scope and number of clusters), runs one configuration, and takes what comes out. The system even computes significance scores and then ignores them. On one live tenant's data, 8.5% of runs fail (37 of 437), and most of those failures are avoidable input mistakes. The winning settings are not saved, so a result cannot be reproduced.

The Cluster Recommendation Copilot is the design that fixes this. A planner says what they want in chat. An LLM agent plans the search and calls tools to read data. A deterministic engine (normal code, not the LLM) computes the clusters across many configurations. The planner confirms. Only then is anything saved.

2. Words you need

  • Agent. An LLM in a loop that can decide to call tools, read the results and decide the next step. Like an assistant who can look things up, not just answer from memory.
  • Tool. A function the agent is allowed to call, with a fixed name, typed inputs and typed outputs. The agent never writes the code inside the tool. It only chooses which tool and which arguments.
  • Tool calling. The LLM returns a structured request like {"tool": "get_store_attributes", "args": {...}}. Our code runs the tool and gives back the result.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol). A standard way to describe tools so different LLM clients can call them. In this design it is the tool protocol. On my resume MCP is skills-level.
  • Allowlist. The fixed list of the only tools that exist. If a tool is not on the list, the agent cannot call it.
  • Audited tool. A tool whose code has been reviewed, whose inputs are validated, and whose every call is logged.
  • Read-scoped. The tool can only read data, inside the user's tenant and permission scope.
  • Write path. The only code route allowed to change plans or clusters. Here, the existing product APIs in the Go service.
  • Doing layer. The Go (Gin) services that actually perform product operations: clustering, Hindsight, strategy. The agent asks. The doing layer does.
  • Input boundary. The point where user input enters the system. "Input-boundary mistakes" are things like a wrong season code, a hierarchy node that does not exist, or a store set too small to cluster.
  • Grounding. Checking the agent's understanding against real data before acting, for example confirming the hierarchy node exists in the catalog and the season exists in the fiscal calendar.
  • k. The number of clusters.

3. The claim, stated precisely

"The copilot design exposes 14 audited tools. Those tools only read planning and clustering data. The LLM never gets a raw SQL shell. Any change to plans or clusters happens only after three planner confirmation steps, and then goes through the existing product write path in the Go services, never through model-generated SQL."

The three confirmation steps in the design are: 1. The planner approves the search plan (which attributes, and how many configurations to explore). 2. The planner approves the winning recommendation. 3. Governance sign-off where the tenant requires it.

These are confirm buttons in the product flow, the same way you confirm a bank transfer. They are not a review queue where someone else checks the AI's work. And none of it is shipped yet.

4. The design in one picture

flowchart LR PL["Planner in chat"] AG["FastAPI agent service, LangGraph"] TOOLS["14 audited read-only tools"] ENG["Deterministic clustering engine"] CONF["Planner confirmation steps"] GO["Go/Gin doing layer, product write APIs"] CH["ClickHouse planning store"] PL --> AG AG -->|"choose tool and args"| TOOLS TOOLS -->|"read, scoped"| CH AG -->|"run configs"| ENG ENG --> CH AG --> CONF PL --> CONF CONF -->|"approved config only"| GO GO --> CH

What to notice: there is no arrow from the agent to a write. The only write arrow starts at the Go doing layer, and only after confirmation.

5. One tool call, step by step (illustrative)

Tool names below are illustrative, to show the shape. They are not the real tool registry.

  1. The planner types: "Cluster my Womenswear stores for Summer 2026, I care about size mix."
  2. The agent calls a grounding tool:
{ "tool": "resolve_hierarchy_node", "args": { "text": "Womenswear" } }

The tool looks the name up in the product catalog and returns {"node_id": "L1_204", "found": true}. If it did not exist, the agent would ask the planner instead of guessing. This is exactly the class of input mistake behind most of the 8.5% failures.

  1. The agent calls a read tool for the fiscal calendar to confirm "Summer 2026" maps to a real season code.
  2. The agent calls a read tool that checks sample size: enough stores with enough history to cluster.
  3. The agent proposes a search plan: attributes including size mix, a range of k within the client's minimum and maximum, and a batch of configurations. Confirmation step 1: the planner approves.
  4. The deterministic engine runs the configurations. The LLM does not compute clusters.
  5. The agent presents 3 to 5 distinct scenarios with evidence. Confirmation step 2: the planner picks one.
  6. The approved configuration (recipe, data watermark, seed) is saved, and the Go doing layer writes the clusters through the existing product API.

At no point can the agent issue INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. It has no tool that does.

6. Why we do not say "the agent never writes SQL"

That phrase sounds absolute and confusing. Engineers write SQL all the time, the services write to databases all the time, and an interviewer will poke holes in "never". The accurate claim is about tool permissioning: - Agent tools are read-scoped. - The agent cannot author SQL. It can only call fixed tools with validated arguments. - Writes happen only through the product write path, after confirmation.

That is precise, testable and defensible.

7. How the same principle shows up in shipped code

If an interviewer asks "is any of this real?", anchor on what is shipped, carefully.

  • Keep/Drop (on the resume): the scoring lenses receive JSON context only. The LLM never gets a SQL tool. In the current package, a small peer-context step can call two fixed, batch-level read functions (at most 2 per batch). They are SELECT-only, restricted to an allowlist of tables, have a 15-second query timeout, and any write or DDL statement is rejected. No agent has a write path. Engines write staging files, and an operator command publishes them.
  • The dig-deeper Q&A agent on locked decisions: allow_writes is false and locked. It cannot change a decision.
  • Ask Iris (on the resume): hierarchy scope frozen at the WebSocket handshake, and a 3-attempt evaluator cap.

So the copilot design extends a principle the team already runs: the model reads and proposes, code computes, and writes go through controlled paths.

8. Design decisions

Read-only tools instead of a guarded SQL tool

  • Why: a guarded SQL tool still lets the model write a query that scans billions of rows or slips past a filter. A fixed tool has a known cost and a known scope.
  • Alternative: an LLM SQL tool with a read-only database user. Safer than nothing, but cost and scope are still open-ended, and testing it is hard.
  • Trade-off: every new question the agent should answer needs a new tool, written and reviewed.

Grounding tools before compute

  • Why: over 80% of the measured failures were input-boundary mistakes. Resolving hierarchy, season and sample size first removes that class before the engine runs.
  • Trade-off: a few more tool calls per session.

Deterministic engine for the clusters

  • Why: clustering math must be reproducible and explainable. The LLM chooses what to explore. Code computes.
  • Trade-off: the agent's creativity is limited to the search plan, which is the point.

Confirmation before write-back

  • Why: clusters drive buying decisions worth real money. A planner owns that decision.
  • Trade-off: one or two extra clicks per session.

9. The numbers

Number What it measures Tag
14 Audited read-only tools in the copilot design DESIGN
3 Planner confirmation steps before write-back DESIGN
8.5% (37 of 437) Clustering runs that failed on one live tenant's data MEASURED baseline
Over 80% of those Failures that were input-boundary mistakes MEASURED
~20 seconds Median clustering job time over 370 live runs (engine only, not the full chat) MEASURED
0% Reproducibility, because winning settings were never saved MEASURED baseline
Under 2% Failure rate the design targets TARGET

8.5%. 37 divided by 437 is 0.0847, about 8.5%. Say "on live data, about 8.5 percent of clustering runs failed, 37 out of 437, mostly avoidable input mistakes". Never say "we cut it to under 2%". Say "the design targets under 2%".

10. How to defend it in an interview

"Can your agent write to the database?" "No. In the design, the agent only has 14 audited tools, and they only read planning data within the user's scope. It cannot write SQL at all. It picks a tool and arguments, and our code runs the tool. Any change goes through the existing Go product APIs, and only after the planner confirms the plan and the recommendation."

"What failure rate do you see?" "On one live tenant, about 8.5% of clustering runs failed, 37 out of 437, and more than 80% of those were input-boundary mistakes like a wrong season or a hierarchy node that did not exist. The design adds grounding tools that resolve those before anything runs. Under 2% is the target. I will not claim it until the load test is done."

"Is this shipped?" "No. It is a Phase 1 design that passed review, with the bring-up load test pending. It is not on my resume. The same read-only principle is already shipped in the Keep/Drop engine and in Ask Iris."

"Why not just give the model a read-only SQL user?" "Read-only stops writes, but not a query that scans billions of rows or forgets a tenant filter. Fixed tools give me known cost, known scope and something I can unit test."

11. Say this, not that

Say this Not this
"Tools are read-scoped. Writes go through product APIs after confirmation." "The agent never writes SQL."
"Measured 8.5%, targeting under 2%." "We reduced failures to under 2%."
"Planner confirmation steps in the design." "HITL" or "human review queue".
"Design, load test pending." "Shipped copilot."
"MCP is skills-level for me." MCP as an Impact Analytics resume bullet.

Agentic AssortSmart: Flow, Guardrails, Evals and Benchmarking Honesty

How to use this page

  • What it covers: how the AI side of AssortSmart is kept safe and measured. Part A is resume-backed: the Keep/Drop decision engine and Ask Iris, their guardrails, the 300-case harness, the 80% gate and the gold-200 benchmark. Part B is verbal-only: the Cluster Recommendation Copilot design and its measured baselines and targets.
  • When to read it: before any GenAI, LLM evaluation or "how do you know your AI works?" round.
  • What to memorise: the 80% / 73% / 74% / 63% story and which benchmark each number belongs to, the guardrails list, and the sentence "80% is a promotion gate, not production accuracy".

Never break these.

  • 80% is a CI promotion gate on a 300-case proxy evaluation set. It is not "all tenants live at 80%".
  • 73% lower cost at 100% coverage and the 74% deterministic baseline come from a separate gold-200 benchmark. They do not come from the 300-case file. Never fuse the two.
  • Ask Iris is a shipped capability. No usage numbers, no SLA.
  • LangSmith is on Ask Iris. The Keep/Drop batch uses custom JSON telemetry.
  • No human review queue (HITL) in Impact Analytics code. Offline evals replaced the critic and evaluator agents in Keep/Drop.
  • Part B is verbal-only. The Copilot, its 14 tools, its confirm steps and its 8.5% baseline are not on the resume.

Tags on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, a doc or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). HISTORICAL means from past work records. DESIGN means specified in a design document, not built or measured in production.

Words you need

  • Guardrail. A rule enforced by code that limits what the AI can do or how badly it can fail. Like the rails on a bowling lane for children.
  • Offline evaluation. Testing the system on a fixed labelled set before release, not on live users.
  • Gold set. A set of cases where the right answer is known (the "gold" label).
  • Proxy gold. Labels built from a stand-in for the truth. Here: what actually sold next season, instead of a merchant's judgement.
  • Promotion gate. A CI check that a new config, prompt or model must pass before it replaces the current one.
  • Accuracy. The share of cases where the system's answer matches the gold label.
  • Recall (keep recall, drop recall). Of all the true drops, how many did the system catch? Accuracy can look fine while drop recall is terrible, if most cases are keeps.
  • Over-keep. The failure where the system keeps products that should have been dropped.
  • Coverage. The share of cases that got a complete answer, without timeouts or missing pieces.
  • Deterministic baseline. The rules-only score with no LLM. Free to run and always available, so every LLM change must beat it.
  • Circularity. Grading a system against labels derived from its own inputs. The score looks good whether or not the system is any good.
  • Treatment leakage. When a label encodes a past human decision instead of real demand. For example, a product a planner already dropped sells zero next season because it was not stocked, not because nobody wanted it.

Part A: Resume-backed (Keep/Drop and Ask Iris)

A1. End-to-end flow of a Keep/Drop run

In plain English: a batch job reads sales data, computes a rules-based score for every article, asks the LLM lenses for a second opinion using JSON only, blends the two, and writes versioned results. A shared registry wraps everything with timeouts, breakers and checkpoints. Before any change to prompts, weights or models is promoted, it must pass the 80% gate.

flowchart LR CH["ClickHouse: weekly rollup and 2.11B master"] DET["Deterministic scorer: s_det"] CK["Checkpoints: det.json, agent_progress.json"] JSON["JSON payload per batch"] LENS["Peer, decider, 7 gated lenses"] BLEND["Blend: 0.4 s_det plus 0.6 s_agent"] OUT["Versioned rows with config_hash"] TEL["JSON telemetry: tokens, USD, duration, fallbacks"] EVAL["Offline suite and 80% gate"] CH --> DET DET --> CK CH --> JSON JSON --> LENS CK --> BLEND LENS --> BLEND BLEND --> OUT LENS -.-> TEL OUT --> EVAL

What to notice: the LLM sits in one box, fed by JSON, and its output is blended with a score that exists without it. Evaluation reads the outputs, never the other way round.

The batch order is fixed in code: peer context, then decider, then lenses, then blend, then explanation. There is no LLM orchestrator deciding what runs next.

A2. Ask Iris flow

sequenceDiagram participant P as Planner participant WS as WebSocket handshake participant SUP as LangGraph supervisor participant EV as Evaluator participant LS as LangSmith P->>WS: connect with JWT WS->>WS: verify JWT, compute plan_scope once, freeze it P->>SUP: question about a KPI or an AI decision SUP->>SUP: choose next step, reads limited to plan_scope SUP->>EV: draft answer EV-->>SUP: fail, retry, attempt 2 of 3 SUP->>EV: revised answer EV-->>SUP: pass SUP-->>P: answer SUP-->>LS: trace of prompts, steps, tokens
  1. The JWT is verified when the socket opens.
  2. The user's plan_scope is computed once and frozen for the session. Nothing typed later can widen it.
  3. The supervisor picks steps. The evaluator checks the draft. MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3, then the graph stops instead of looping forever.
  4. LangSmith records the run.

A3. Guardrails (what stops bad decisions and runaway runs)

Layer Mechanism Why it exists
No SQL tool Lenses get JSON built by our code from fixed queries The LLM cannot scan billions of rows, leak a tenant, or write
Read-only helpers The peer-context step may call two fixed batch read functions, at most 2 per batch. SELECT-only, allowlisted tables, 15-second timeout, writes and DDL rejected Peer context without giving the model a query language
Lens gate A lens runs only if the article has the data for it (for example 2+ colours for colour cannibalization) No wasted calls, no confident answers from missing data
Structured output Fixed JSON schema. Unknown lens names dropped, weights renormalised, at most 5 lenses per mix Parseable, bounded output
Coverage rules A mix counts only if at least 75% of its planned weight came back. An article is marked pending if fewer than 75% of mixes are valid Missing answers cannot silently make a score look optimistic
Demand over margin The margin lens can never force a Drop on its own Encodes a business rule the model might ignore
Hard timeouts min(600, 60 + 8 × articles) seconds per LLM call, so 572 seconds for 64 articles A hung provider cannot hold a batch forever
Retries 2 retries per call, then the row is pending Transient errors recover. Persistent ones do not loop
Circuit breaker Stop a step after about 5 consecutive failures, or past a 0.25 failure fraction Stop burning money on a dead provider
Signal-quality abort The deterministic step aborts if a KPI signal is broken (for example almost every article showing 100% sell-through) A broken input cannot dominate scores at full weight
Deterministic fallback On LLM timeout the article keeps its rules-based score Planners always have a decision
Checkpoints det.json, agent_progress.json, --resume A crash costs minutes, not a full re-run
config_hash SHA-256 of guardrails, parameters, prompts and catalog on every row Every decision traceable to its exact configuration
Telemetry Tokens, USD cost, step duration, batch fallbacks as JSON Cost and failure visible per run
Ask Iris scope plan_scope frozen at handshake No cross-tenant leaks through chat
Ask Iris loop cap MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3 No infinite LLM loops

Why no critic or evaluator agent in Keep/Drop? Earlier designs had a critic agent and a batch evaluator agent. In practice they mostly adjusted confidence and almost never changed a Keep or Drop. They cost tokens and added non-determinism. They are disabled, and offline evaluation does that job instead, before promotion, where it is cheaper and repeatable.

A4. Evaluations

The offline suite

Every promotion runs three checks: - Ramp monotonic: editing a scoring ramp must never make a better KPI score lower. - Demand blend guard: a strong deterministic score with a weak agent score must still Keep. For example s_det = 0.9, s_agent = 0.4 gives s_final = 0.36 + 0.24 = 0.60, which is Keep. - Gold outcomes: the pipeline's Keep/Drop must match the gold labels at the gate threshold.

The 300-case proxy harness and the 80% gate

  • What it is: 300 labelled article-seasons, 150 keeps and 150 drops. Season 74 is scored. The labels come only from what happened in season 76.
  • How the labels avoid cheating:
  • Circularity: rate of sale in season 74 is part of the deterministic score, so labelling on it would grade the pipeline against its own input. Labels use only season 76 sell-through and rate of sale.
  • Treatment leakage: an article a planner already dropped sells zero in season 76 because it was not stocked. The builder only keeps articles present in both seasons with enough store-weeks in season 76, so "zero sales" means stocked and still did not sell.
  • Ambiguous cases between the keep and drop bands are skipped on purpose. Placeholder SKUs and negative quantities are filtered out.
  • The gate: gold_min_accuracy = 0.8 in eval.json. Below 80%, the change does not promote.
  • The honest lesson: accuracy alone hides over-keep. The first real proxy run showed the pipeline caught almost every true keep but very few true drops. That is why drop recall matters, and why the config has a drop-recall gate that can be raised.

The gold-200 benchmark (separate)

  • What: 200 labelled cases used to compare two models. Both completed 200 of 200.
  • Result 1: the chosen model cut live execution cost by 73% at 100% coverage.
  • Result 2: on the same 200 cases, the deterministic baseline (production threshold 0.65) scored 74%.
  • Result 3: the blended LLM score came in at about 63%, below the 74% baseline.
  • Decision: freeze the blend weights (0.4 / 0.6) instead of retuning them. Retuning on 200 cases to chase the baseline would overfit one benchmark. The 80% gate still blocks promotion, and the deterministic fallback keeps decisions available.
  • Model names (gpt-5.6-luna and gpt-5.4-mini) are not on the PDF. Mention them only if asked.

Benchmarks that are not quality evidence

A mock architecture benchmark compared aggregation methods and weights on synthetic data, and supported keeping the mean aggregation and the 0.4 / 0.6 weights as defaults. It proves the code behaves as designed. It is not production quality evidence. Say so if you mention it.

A5. How to say the whole evaluation story in 45 seconds

"Every change to prompts, weights or models has to pass an offline suite before promotion. The main gate is 80% accuracy on a 300-case proxy set built from held-out next-season sales, designed so the labels do not leak the pipeline's own inputs. Separately, we benchmarked two models on a 200-case gold set: the one we picked cut execution cost 73% at full coverage. On that same set the rules-only baseline scored 74% and the blend about 63%, so we did not pretend the LLM was winning. We froze the weights rather than overfit them, kept the deterministic fallback, and left the gate to block anything that does not clear 80%."

Part B: Verbal-only (Cluster Recommendation Copilot design)

Not on the resume. Everything in Part B is design or measured baselines for an in-progress module. Status: Phase 1 design passed internal adversarial passes and an external review. The bring-up load test is pending. Say "building", not "shipped". Shipped LangSmith use is Ask Iris only. PostHog appears in the design document but is not on my resume, so do not bring it up unprompted.

B1. Flow

flowchart LR PL["Planner chat"] AG["FastAPI agent service, LangGraph"] TOOLS["14 audited read-only tools"] LLM["LLM plans and selects tools"] GO["Go/Gin doing layer: clustering, Hindsight, strategy APIs"] CH["ClickHouse append-only planning store"] CONF["3 planner confirmation steps"] OBS["Design: LangSmith, Datadog, PostHog joined by trace_id"] PL --> AG AG --> LLM LLM --> TOOLS TOOLS --> CH AG --> GO GO --> CH AG --> CONF CONF -->|"approved config only"| GO AG -.-> OBS

One sentence: the LLM proposes and reads, the deterministic engine computes, the planner confirms, and writes go through product APIs, never through model-generated SQL.

B2. Guardrails in the design

Layer Mechanism Why
Tool allowlist 14 audited tools only No raw SQL shell, no arbitrary code
Read scope Tools only read planning and clustering data Separates exploring from changing
Input grounding Catalog lookup for hierarchy, fiscal calendar for seasons, sample-size guards Removes input-boundary failures, the majority of the 8.5%
k and scenario caps Client minimum and maximum k, a child-cluster cap of about 10, 3 to 5 scenarios in the UI Business limits over pure statistical optimum
Planner confirmations 3 confirm steps before write-back: search plan, recommendation, governance sign-off where required Money decisions stay with the planner. These are confirm clicks, not a review queue
Content-addressed config Save recipe, data watermark and seed, keyed by their hash Reproducibility from 0% toward 100% (TARGET)
Quotas and timeouts Per-tenant concurrency and tool budgets Protect ClickHouse and the Go services from agent storms

Auth and rate-limit depth: ../tech_depth/auth_tenancy_rate_limits.md.

Do not say "the agent never fails" or "we never write SQL". Say: "tools are read-scoped, the planner confirms before write-back, and engineers still write SQL in services".

B3. What is measured and what is a target

Item What it measures Status
8.5% (37 of 437) Clustering run failures on one live tenant. Over 80% were input-boundary mistakes MEASURED baseline
~20 seconds median over 370 runs Clustering engine job time, not the full chat flow MEASURED
0% Reproducibility, because winning config and seed were never saved MEASURED baseline
Tool contract tests Allowlist, schema validators, no write paths on tools DESIGN, CI
LangSmith run replay Prompt version, tool arguments, tokens and cost per agent run DESIGN
Scenario quality rubric Scenarios distinct by lens, time horizon, scope and k, with evidence attached DESIGN
20 to 100 configs explored per run, 3 to 5 shown Search breadth TARGET
Days to under 1 hour Plan turnaround TARGET
8.5% to under 2% Failure rate TARGET

The honest status of production benchmarking

We have not finished a production load test that proves "days to under 1 hour" or "8.5% to under 2%" on the full path from chat to tools to Go to ClickHouse to confirmation to write.

Correct lines: - "The baselines are measured on live clustering runs." - "The targets are design goals we engineer against." - "The Phase 1 design passed review. The load test is pending, so I say building, not shipped." - "LangSmith would be for agent quality and regression. Datadog pages on platform health."

Wrong line: "We benchmarked the agentic flow in production and hit under 2% and under 1 hour."

B4. How I would benchmark it (method, not results)

When asked "how do you benchmark an agent?":

  1. Freeze the baseline. Failure rate, median job time and reproducibility on a named tenant extract. We already have these.
  2. Offline agent suites. Fixed planner prompts with expected tool sequences and expected evidence, run on every change.
  3. Tool latency budgets. p95 per tool against ClickHouse. Reject any tool that can scan unbounded data.
  4. Confirmation funnel. What share of sessions reach each confirmation step, and where planners abandon.
  5. Load test. Concurrent planners times tool fan-out against the Go services and ClickHouse. Pass only when the targets hold under load.
  6. Canary. One tenant first. Compare the failure mix before expanding.

B5. The copilot safety story in 30 seconds

"On live data, about 8.5% of clustering runs failed, 37 out of 437, mostly bad inputs. The design cuts that class with grounding tools and validators, explores many configurations in batch with a deterministic engine, and only writes back through the Go APIs after the planner confirms. Under 2% failures and under 1 hour turnaround are targets until the load test lands. It is not on my resume, it is what I am building next."

Practice drill

  1. Is 80% your production accuracy? No. It is the promotion gate on the 300-case proxy set.
  2. Where does 73% come from? The gold-200 model benchmark: the chosen model cost 73% less at 100% coverage.
  3. What scored 74%? The deterministic baseline on the gold-200 set, at production threshold 0.65.
  4. What scored about 63%? The blended LLM score on the same gold-200 set.
  5. So why freeze the weights? Retuning on 200 cases would overfit. The gate and fallback already protect production.
  6. How were the 300 labels built? From season 76 outcomes for articles scored in season 74, with filters against circularity and treatment leakage.
  7. Why is accuracy not enough? It hides over-keep. Drop recall shows it.
  8. Why disable critic and evaluator agents in Keep/Drop? They rarely changed decisions, cost tokens and added noise. Offline evals do the job better.
  9. What stops an infinite loop in Ask Iris? MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3.
  10. What stops a cross-tenant leak in Ask Iris? plan_scope frozen at the WebSocket handshake.
  11. Is the Copilot shipped? No. Design passed review, load test pending, not on my resume.
  12. Is 8.5% to under 2% a result? No. 8.5% is measured. Under 2% is a target.

How to use this page
