First, every table became an @Entity with typed fields and a @Version column, so optimistic locking is enforced by Hibernate instead of by hand-written WHERE clauses. Second, the joined reads moved from native SQL copied into label-keyed maps to repository @Query methods with an explicit alias on every column, returned as typed interface projections. That is exactly what killed the column-aliasing bug. Third, transactions became declarative: @Transactional on service methods replaced hand-rolled begin, commit and rollback code. So it isn't decoration. Typed entities plus aliased projections are the mechanism behind the correctness fix I'm proudest of.

Q. What does @Transactional actually do, and where does it bite? Spring wraps the bean in a proxy. When an outside caller calls the method, the proxy opens a transaction, runs the method, and commits, or rolls back if a runtime exception escapes. It bites in three places. Checked exceptions don't roll back unless you say rollbackFor. A call from another method in the same class bypasses the proxy, so no transaction starts. And bulk @Modifying queries skip @Version and the in-memory entity state. That's why our rule was: transactional entry points are public service methods called from the controller, and manager edits go through loaded entities.

Q. How do you model a recursive hierarchy in a database with no recursive queries? That sounds contradictory. I resolve recursion once, in the ETL, not on every read. level_mapping holds the flattened path columns level1 to level4 and a stable uuid used as level_id. Every fact row stores that level_id instead of the text, so renaming a parent doesn't rewrite thousands of rows. At read time the service builds the tree in Java and sums children into parents. So the hierarchy is recursive in shape but materialised into stable IDs, which is faster and safer than recursive SQL at this size.

Q. What is level_id, and why join on it plus the period? level_id on a fact row equals level_mapping.uuid. Joins always AND level_id with fiscal_quarter, fiscal_year and the active flags, because the same logical line exists once per period. Joining on the ID alone would fan out across quarters and multiply amounts.

Q. Why DECIMAL(18,2) for money and DECIMAL(5,2) for percentages? Money must be exact, so it's DECIMAL in the database and BigDecimal in Java, with conversion to display strings only at the edge. Percentages fit in (5,2), up to 999.99%. A double would accumulate rounding errors in parent sums, and in finance a one-cent drift is a reconciliation break. The two BigDecimal traps I watch for are equals comparing scale (so I use compareTo) and divide needing an explicit rounding mode.

Finance logic

Q. Explain materiality and FSLI like I don't have a finance degree, then tell me where they live in your system. An FSLI is one line on the balance sheet or income statement, like Cash or Revenue. Materiality is the dollar size of a mistake that would change a reader's decision, usually set as a percentage of a key figure like pre-tax income or revenue. In my system it isn't hard-coded. It's a row in frm_metrics_table with metric_key = "materiality", and on the Q4 2025 close it was $340 million with a $170 million residual threshold. The FSLIs are rows in balance_sheet and income_statement, about 26 and 29 on that close, each with its HFM amount and computed significance.

Q. Walk me through the rule engine. What's the boolean logic that flags an item? Two independent tests and an OR. Quantitative Material is YES if the HFM amount is above materiality. Qualitative Material is a manager's yes or no answer to a scoping question. Overall Significance is Significant if either is YES, and that exact rule is the function conclusion_overall_significance_from_balance_sheet_materials. At component level a second rule applies: Financially Significant if revenue share is over 5% or absolute assets share is over 5%, and those benchmarks are configurable through PUT /update_benchmark_thresholds. It's deterministic and auditable, not a black box.

Q. Residual risk sounds made up. What does it compute? It answers "after everything already in scope, how much uncovered balance is left, and does it still matter?". Per leaf, residual balance is HFM amount minus total in scope, and residual multiple is that divided by materiality. Both are stored on the fact rows. The screen flags lines over 50% of materiality or over a percentage-change threshold, served by GET /residual_risk?fsli_type=bs|is. Scoping isn't just "flag the big lines", it also proves the leftover is small enough to ignore.

Q. What is quarter-annualization and why does it matter? Materiality is an annual concept, but in Q1 to Q3 you only have part of a year of income-statement activity. Annualization scales the part-year figure to a full-year equivalent so comparisons against annual thresholds are fair. For example, half a year of revenue is scaled by four over two. The platform picks the factor dynamically from the fiscal quarter, so the same code works in every close.

Q. Walk me through how HFM numbers get checked against the 10-Q. HFM is the consolidation system: entity balances go in, get currency-translated, intercompany-eliminated and adjusted, and the consolidated group number comes out. The 10-Q is what was filed with the SEC, so it's the publicly attested truth. The recon screen puts them side by side per line, difference = hfm_amount_in_millions - financial_statement_amount_in_millions, and a nonzero difference must be explained before scoping proceeds. In v2 those rows are persisted by quarter and year with stable IDs, so every break is queryable and commentable, which Sheets couldn't do.

Q. If HFM doesn't tie to the 10-Q, does your system block or just display? It surfaces and persists the per-line difference, so a break is explicit, never hidden. Because recon lines have stable IDs, a manager can attach a comment explaining or resolving each break. It doesn't hard-block scoping in that code path. The control is procedural: a manager reviews and clears differences before finalising. The tool enforces visibility and auditability, humans enforce sign-off, and the FSM gates enforce that big swings get attention before a record advances.

Q. What are the 8 screens, and which carry real logic? Reconciliation, Materiality, EMI Scoping, Group Scoping, Threshold Setup, Component Scoping, Residual Risk and Summary. Reconciliation runs the HFM-versus-10-Q tie-out. Group Scoping applies the quantitative-or-qualitative rule with the Draft, Review, ReOpen, Closed status flow. Component Scoping applies the 5% rule, Threshold Setup manages legal-entity significance, Residual Risk computes residual balances and multiples, and EMI handles equity-method stakes. Materiality and Summary are lighter but still write through. I owned the backend for all of them, not the React UI.

Data integrity and concurrency

Q. Multiple managers edit the same close. How do you stop them clobbering each other? Writes are keyed by uuid with explicit column sets, run in a single transaction with rollback on failure, and use optimistic row-locking: the update only succeeds if the row still has the version the editor read. If someone saved first, zero rows match and the second editor reloads instead of silently overwriting. Every mutation records updated_by from the auth header, so it's attributable. What I didn't build is the real-time push to other screens and the notifications. Those were the collaboration service and the frontend.

Q. How do you handle transactions? Declaratively, with @Transactional on the service methods that write. Spring opens the transaction before the method, commits after it, and rolls back if a runtime exception escapes. The connection comes from the HikariCP pool and goes back to it at the end. Multi-step writes happen inside one transactional method so they're atomic. For example, the EMI Total patch mirrors the amount into balance_sheet or income_statement in the same transaction, and an assessment write with sync_required rolls back entirely if the line sync touches zero rows. Updating benchmarks writes both rows and commits once, or throws and rolls back if either is missing.

Q. Idempotency? GETs are naturally idempotent. PATCH and PUT set explicit values by primary key, so replaying the same request gives the same state. Scoping questions use a deterministic SHA-256 ID from question text plus normalized page name and are upserted, so re-posting the same payload updates in place. Assessments are "create once, then update" per line. POST /add_scoping_metrics appends, which is acceptable because metrics are versioned by is_active and timestamp.

Q. What resolved the ETL lock contention? A normalized schema so edits and loads touch different, narrow rows, short transactions, and optimistic locking so no lock is held while a manager is thinking. With pessimistic locks held during an edit, the ETL refresh would wait on every open record. With version checks, nobody waits, and the rare real conflict is caught at save time.

Auth, scale, caching

Q. Your auth is one header. Elegant or a gaping hole? The service reads x-auth-params-email, returns 401 if it's missing, and stores the email as created_by and updated_by. It works because Uber's gateway authenticates the user and only injects the header after that, so the service trusts the edge and captures identity for the audit trail, which a SOX tool needs. The honest limitation is that this is authentication trust plus audit, not fine-grained authorization. That was enforced upstream. Standalone, I'd verify a signed token with Spring Security and add role checks with @PreAuthorize.

Q. How would you scale it? It barely needs scaling, but here's the plan. There's already one HikariCP connection pool, created once at startup and shared by every request, with connection validation so a connection MySQL has silently dropped is discarded before use instead of failing a request. I'd add read-replica routing, since the internal MySQL setup already exposes a read/write split (in Spring that's a routing data source, with @Transactional(readOnly = true) reads sent to the replica), then cache per-period GET responses because a closed period's tree is immutable and expensive to build. And composite indexes on (fiscal_quarter, fiscal_year, level_id). Writes are low volume, so the bottleneck is read fan-out of nested trees, and caching solves that.

Q. Where's your caching and what are your latency numbers? Server-side, the only thing reused across requests in the shipped service is the HikariCP connection pool, and that's connection reuse, not a data cache. There's no Redis, no response cache and no Hibernate second-level cache, so I won't claim one. The design doc has the frontend using TanStack Query for client caching and virtual scrolling, with a sub-second grid target. That's a target, not a latency I measured. If I added caching, it would be a per-period response cache plus composite indexes, and I'd label that as what I would do, not what shipped.

Q. Is this even a hard engineering problem, or a spreadsheet with extra steps? It's deliberately not a throughput problem, and pretending otherwise is how people get caught. We migrated 19 million raw GL rows off Sheets, but a single quarter's extract is tens of thousands of rows. The hard part is correctness, hierarchy and auditability under a close deadline: parent equal to sum of children, running v1 and v2 in parallel, and fixing an identity bug that silently mapped rows to the wrong line. A wrong number here becomes audit evidence for an SEC filing, so trustworthiness is the whole product.

Testing and delivery

Q. How did you test controllers? The scoping controller test class alone has about 112 JUnit 5 tests. They use @WebMvcTest, which starts only the web layer of Spring, plus MockMvc to send fake HTTP requests, with every service replaced by a Mockito mock, so no database is touched. Tests assert status codes, JSON shapes, the 401-on-missing-header path in a dedicated auth test class, the 409 on a version conflict, and the error-to-status mapping in the controller advice. Services are tested the same way one layer down, with mocked repositories.

A representative test:

@WebMvcTest(ScopingController.class)
class ScopingControllerAuthTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean GroupBalanceSheetService groupBsService;   // @MockBean before Spring Boot 3.4

    @Test
    void patchWithoutAuthHeaderReturns401() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(patch("/frm-scoping/group_balance_sheet/abc")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"groupStatus\":\"Review\",\"version\":7}"))
           .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
        verifyNoInteractions(groupBsService);
    }

    @Test
    void staleVersionReturns409() throws Exception {
        when(groupBsService.updateScopeAndStatus(eq("abc"), any(), eq("m@uber.com")))
            .thenThrow(new ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException(BalanceSheet.class, "abc"));
        mvc.perform(patch("/frm-scoping/group_balance_sheet/abc")
                .header("x-auth-params-email", "m@uber.com")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"groupStatus\":\"Review\",\"version\":7}"))
           .andExpect(status().isConflict());
    }
}

For repository queries such as the aliased projections, a test against a real MySQL in a throwaway container (Testcontainers) is the general best practice, because an in-memory database can hide MySQL-specific SQL behaviour.

Q. You claim 1,100+ tests and 100% coverage. Sounds inflated. The resume number is 100% statement coverage on the modules the ORM migration touched, not the whole service. The 1,100+ test count is conservative: a count of @Test methods across about 65 test classes finds roughly 1,288. They're not trivial. The layered design means controllers are tested against mocked services and services against mocked repositories, covering status codes, shapes, auth failures and error mapping.

Q. Bazel for a Java service? Why does CI actually gate anything? Bazel is the Uber monorepo build system, so it's the environment, not a choice. Each package has a BUILD.bazel with java_test targets that run its JUnit 5 tests. CI runs five layer targets, entity, DTO, repository, service and controller, and all must pass to merge. The gate is real because my review rule was that every PR adds or updates tests in the matching folder, and stacked PRs meant each small step was tested on its own.

Q. What are reporting SQL allowlists and why do they matter for SOX? An allowlist means reporting reads can only run approved, parameterized queries. Anything not on the list is rejected. For SOX, that turns "where did this number come from?" into a reviewed, repeatable answer instead of someone's ad hoc SQL. It also shuts the door on injection through report parameters.

Ownership and leadership

Q. Did you build the HFM ETL? No. The service consumes HFM-loaded MySQL tables. I owned the scoping backend, the schema and the recon v2 migration, and the ETL pipeline was a shared responsibility. I can explain how it works: extract balances from HFM, resolve the hierarchy into level_mapping, load period-keyed rows.

Q. "Led 3 engineers" is easy to inflate. What did leading look like? I was tech lead of a 3-engineer EPAM pod, not a people manager. I sliced work along the controller, service, repository and entity boundary so two people could build the same feature without collisions. I set conventions that appear uniformly in the code, like thin controllers, transactions only on service methods, and the updated_by pattern on every write. And I ran the review gate and led the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration as stacked PRs to 100% module coverage.

Q. What was the hardest part? Getting the tree correct and consistent between v1 and v2 while the underlying identity was ambiguous because of the column-aliasing bug, under a hard close deadline, without breaking the live v1 path. The parallel run, explicit column labels and the parent-equals-sum-of-children checks are what made the cutover safe.

Q. What's the single thing most likely to silently produce a wrong scoping result? Aggregation identity errors. Parents are sums of children, so one duplicated or mis-mapped leaf quietly inflates a parent, which is exactly what the aliasing bug could cause. My defences are the parent-equals-sum invariant, labels on every joined column, and active-flag discipline in joins. The remaining risk is upstream data issues, like a malformed currency string parsing to 0.0, which I'd harden with validation and reconciliation alerts.

18. Say this / don't say this

Say this

  • "Uber via EPAM." Tech lead of a 3-engineer pod, not a people manager.
  • "Reconciliation went from 14 days to 3 days, a 70% cut, against a $340M materiality threshold." If pressed: "the technical design doc framed that cut and that's what the platform delivered for the close."
  • "36 Spring Boot endpoints." If asked for the breakdown: about 31 functional scoping routes plus the collaboration-service comment and notification APIs from the design doc.
  • "19M raw GL rows migrated off Sheets." If asked about per-quarter size: tens of thousands of rows per extract, so the value is correctness and auditability.
  • "8-table normalized core schema." If asked about the code: 11 JPA entity classes in the scoping service.
  • "100% statement coverage on the modules the ORM migration touched."
  • "$340M and $170M were the Q4 2025 close values."

Don't say this

  • "I built the HFM ETL." It was a shared pipeline. Say the service consumes HFM-loaded tables.
  • "I built the real-time collaboration / WebSockets / Slack notifications." Those were the separate collaboration service and the frontend.
  • "The whole service is at 100% coverage." It is module statement coverage.
  • Any FRM p95 latency, Redis, response cache or Hibernate second-level cache. Only the HikariCP connection pool is reused across requests.
  • "I built the React screens." You owned the backend that powers them.
  • Materiality as a fixed constant. Qualify it as the Q4 2025 close.
  • "30+ endpoints", "70% was only a target", "don't count 19M". That was older prep. The current resume states 36, 70% and 19M, so defend them.
  • Merging "led 3" (FRM) with "mentored 2" (Masters India). The 35% to 82% coverage figure is Masters India too.
  • Internal hosts or staging URLs.

19. Confidence audit

SOLID means it traces to code, a design doc, or the PDF and you can defend it directly. NEEDS CARE means it needs a qualifier or sits partly outside your direct authorship.

  • F1 backend ownership: SOLID. The screens are product surface powered by your APIs. Do not claim UI ownership.
  • F1 70%, 14 to 3 days, $340M: SOLID as PDF outcome and Q4 2025 materiality. Defend as written, explain the TDD framing only if pressed.
  • F1 36 endpoints: SOLID with the breakdown (about 31 scoping routes plus collaboration APIs). NEEDS CARE only in that you did not build the collaboration service's real-time or Slack parts.
  • F1 19M: SOLID as "raw GL rows migrated off Sheets". NEEDS CARE: do not invent a breakdown.
  • F1 L1 to L4 and quarter-annualization: SOLID. Keep the annualization formula at the general level.
  • F2 8-table schema, polymorphic status, atomic syncs, SHA-256 keys: SOLID. The atomic syncs and natural keys are directly in the code.
  • F2 optimistic row-locking: NEEDS CARE. Defend as the version check on update. Do not extend it into real-time push or WebSocket conflict resolution.
  • F3 led 3, ORM migration, aliasing bugs: SOLID.
  • F3 100%: SOLID as module statement coverage. NEEDS CARE if someone hears "whole service".
  • F3 stacked Bazel PRs, SQL allowlists, 50% delta-variance FSM gates: SOLID as PDF. NEEDS CARE on exact formulas. Explain the mechanism and keep the formula qualitative.
  • Verbal depth (8 screens, ~55 × 14, 11 models, 18-file recon writeup, $170M residual, 1,100+ tests): SOLID as supporting depth, not printed bullets.
  • Caching and latency: NEEDS CARE. Server-side, only the HikariCP connection pool is reused. There is no data cache. Frontend caching and the sub-second grid are design-doc targets.

20. Practice drill

Answer each out loud in 2 to 4 sentences, then check against the sections above.

  1. What is scoping, in one breath? Deciding which financial lines and legal entities are important enough for PwC to test each quarter. Too narrow misses risk, too broad wastes audit hours.
  2. What was materiality on Q4 2025, and where is it stored? $340M, with a $170M residual threshold. It's a row in frm_metrics_table, not a constant.
  3. State the significance rule. Quantitative is HFM amount above materiality. Qualitative is a manager's answer. Significant if either is YES.
  4. State the 5% rule. A component is financially significant if its revenue share is over 5% or its absolute assets share is over 5%. Benchmarks are configurable.
  5. Compute a residual multiple. HFM $900M, in scope $700M, residual $200M, multiple 200 / 340 ≈ 0.59, which is over 50% of materiality, so it's flagged.
  6. What is quarter-annualization? Scaling part-year income-statement figures to a full-year equivalent (for example × 4/2 at Q2) so they compare fairly with annual thresholds.
  7. Why 36 endpoints? About 31 functional scoping routes plus the collaboration-service comment and notification APIs from the design doc.
  8. How does 19M square with tens of thousands per quarter? 19M is the raw GL migrated off Sheets. Per-quarter extracts are 38K to 95K rows. The value was correctness, not throughput.
  9. 14 to 3 days is 79%. Why does the resume say 70%? 70% is the figure the design doc framed for manual reconciliation effort, so it's the conservative number.
  10. Explain optimistic row-locking. Read freely, and at save time update only if the version still matches. Zero rows updated means someone saved first, so reload. No locks held while thinking.
  11. Why SHA-256 natural keys? Same question text and page always give the same ID, so re-running a seed or load upserts instead of duplicating audit rows.
  12. Tell the column-aliasing bug in 30 seconds. A join returned two columns named uuid. Copying the row into a map by column label kept the last one, so rows took the mapping's ID and edits hit the wrong line. Fixed with Spring Data JPA @Query methods that give every column a unique alias and return typed projections.
  13. What does 100% mean exactly? Statement coverage on the modules the ORM migration touched.
  14. What is an FSM gate with a 50% delta-variance check? At a status transition, a line that moved more than 50% against its comparison value can't silently advance. It needs a reviewer's attention.
  15. What did you not build? The HFM ETL (shared), the collaboration service's real-time and Slack parts, and the React UI.

21. Three-minute whiteboard script

First, draw the business (30 seconds). Write "Quarterly close" and three boxes: HFM, the 10-Q, PwC. Say: "Every quarter Finance decides which lines and entities PwC tests. That's scoping. It lived in Google Sheets and took about two weeks."

Second, draw the architecture (60 seconds). Draw HFM → ETL → MySQL on the left. Draw the service as three stacked boxes: controller, service, repository. Draw the screens and the gateway on the right, and the collaboration service off to the side. Say: "I owned the backend: 36 Spring Boot endpoints in a controller, service, repository layering over an 8-table normalized MySQL schema on SOADB. The gateway injects the user's email, and every write records it for audit. 19 million raw GL rows moved off Sheets."

Third, draw the tree and the rules (45 seconds). Draw a small L1 to L4 tree with numbers, and write "HFM > $340M OR qualitative = significant" and "residual = HFM − in scope". Say: "The service builds this tree in Java, sums children into parents, applies materiality, the 5% component rule, residual risk and quarter-annualization. Parent must equal sum of children. That invariant is my main safety net."

Fourth, draw the integrity mechanisms (30 seconds). Draw two managers pointing at one row with "version = 7". Say: "Optimistic row-locking, atomic multi-table writes, SHA-256 natural keys. No locks while people think, no lost edits, no duplicate audit rows. That's what resolved the lock contention with the ETL during close."

Finally, the story and the result (15 seconds). Write "label-keyed map, then explicit aliases". Say: "I led 3 engineers on a Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that removed a silent column-aliasing bug and took module coverage to 100%, shipped as stacked Bazel PRs with SOX gates. Reconciliation went from 14 days to 3."

Uber Eats Menu Ingestion Deep Dive (Uber via EPAM)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the Uber Eats Menu Ingestion and Automation project end to end. That means the business problem, every technology in plain words, the architecture, one menu traced step by step, both resume bullets decoded, the numbers with their arithmetic, failure scenarios, and a practice drill. It also covers the separate ANZ Document Compliance bullet (Uber Mobility), because it sits under the same Uber stint.
  • When to read it: before any Uber-heavy loop, any data or streaming round (Kafka, Flink), and any GenAI round that asks about RAG in production.
  • What to memorise: the one-minute version, the four outcome numbers (from 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year, 30K+ menus a month, 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation), the 95%+ extraction success number with its estimated baseline, the $600K derivation, and the honesty box near the end.
  • Shorter pack: for the quick interviewer pack, start with 23b_uber_interview_packs.md § Menu. Related depth: Flink notes, Kafka and Flink scale defense, Selenium scraping, Menu architecture.

What the tags mean. Numbers on this page carry a tag. MEASURED means there is a log, doc or code behind it. ESTIMATED means it is arithmetic I can show on a whiteboard, so I say "roughly" and give the derivation. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records and earlier resumes. TARGET means a design goal, so I say "targeting". Every number here matches GROUND_TRUTH.md and 09_metrics_derivations.md in the track's prep/ folder.

Current resume bullets (the PDF, word for word in meaning)

  • M1. Accelerated restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saved $600K annually by architecting an automated ingestion pipeline processing 30K+ menus monthly. Converted unstructured, multilingual PDFs into a strict catalog schema at 98% field fidelity using a Gemini 2.5 Pro and LangChain RAG pipeline over Milvus vector embeddings.
  • M2. Scaled menu extraction success to 95%+ by hardening a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries. Designed a large-scale data ingestion and processing pipeline using Kafka and Apache Flink, with stateful keyed deduplication and schema normalization to guarantee exactly-once catalog upserts.
  • Tech line: Python, Selenium, Kafka, Flink, LangChain, Gemini, RAG, Milvus, GCP, Docker.

Not on the PDF: Spark (study-only and verbal backfill option, labeled as such below), peak events per second (an estimate for prep only), Pinot, SFT, and "100% schema consistency" (older prep wording). ANZ Document Compliance is a separate Uber Mobility project, not Uber Eats. Kafka at Masters India is a different product (GST e-invoicing).

1. The one-minute version (say this out loud)

"At Uber, through EPAM, I worked on menu ingestion for Uber Eats. When a new restaurant joins, its menu has to land in Uber's catalog in a strict structured format: items, prices, sections, options. Menus arrive as partner web pages, PDFs and images, often in more than one language. Before this pipeline, a lot of that was manual or done by a paid third-party tool, and onboarding took about a day.

I architected an automated pipeline. A Selenium fleet acquires the menus, hardened with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries, which lifted extraction success to 95% plus. Events go onto Kafka, and Apache Flink does stateful keyed deduplication and schema normalization before an idempotent catalog upsert. For the unstructured PDFs I built a LangChain RAG pipeline with Gemini 2.5 Pro over Milvus embeddings that converts them into the catalog schema at 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation.

The result: onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours, we process 30K plus menus a month, and we saved about $600K a year, which is a conservative floor on roughly $2 per menu of third-party and manual cost."

Follow-up they may ask: "Which part did you own?" Answer: "I architected the pipeline: the acquisition hardening, the Kafka and Flink processing shape, and the RAG extraction path. I'm careful to say 98% is an offline evaluation number."

2. The business in plain English

Who the users are. Restaurants that want to sell on Uber Eats, and the Uber operations teams who onboard them. A restaurant cannot take orders until its menu is in the catalog.

What they do. The restaurant hands over its menu in whatever form it has. That might be a page on its own website, a listing on a partner site, a scanned PDF, or a photo of a printed menu. Uber has to turn that into a clean list of items, each with a name, description, price, section ("Starters", "Mains") and modifiers ("extra cheese +$1").

What hurt before. Menus are messy. Layouts differ for every restaurant. Some are bilingual. Prices hide in tables or footnotes. Vendor websites are JavaScript-heavy and block scrapers. So onboarding leaned on manual data entry and a paid third-party extraction tool. It took about a day per restaurant, cost money on every menu, and a day of delay is a day of lost orders for both the restaurant and Uber.

Why Uber paid for this. Faster onboarding means restaurants start earning sooner, and every menu that no longer goes through manual entry or the paid tool is money saved. At 30K+ menus a month, a couple of dollars per menu adds up to hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.

3. Words you need

Each term gets a plain definition and an everyday analogy. Read this once and the rest of the page will make sense.

Term Plain meaning Analogy
Menu ingestion Getting a restaurant's menu from wherever it lives into Uber's catalog. Moving house: pack everything from an unfamiliar flat into labelled boxes that fit your new shelves.
Catalog schema The strict structure every menu must fit: item, price, section, modifiers, language. A government form with fixed boxes. You cannot write a paragraph where it asks for a number.
Field fidelity The share of extracted fields (name, price, section and so on) that exactly match a human-checked answer. A spelling test marked word by word: 98 of every 100 words correct.
Offline evaluation Measuring quality on a fixed, labelled test set, not on live traffic. A practice exam with an answer key, not the real exam.
Selenium A tool that drives a real web browser from code, so it can load JavaScript-heavy pages like a human would. A robot sitting at a laptop, clicking and scrolling for you.
Headless browser A browser that runs without a visible window, used by Selenium on servers. The same robot, working with the screen switched off.
Proxy pool A rotating set of intermediate IP addresses that requests go through, so one site does not see thousands of hits from one machine. Sending letters from many different post offices instead of one.
Adaptive retries Retrying a failed scrape with smarter timing and a different proxy, within a budget per source. If a shop is busy, come back later and use a different door, but give up after a few tries.
Anti-bot defences Things sites do to block scrapers: rate limits, CAPTCHAs, fingerprinting. A bouncer checking whether you look like a regular customer.
Kafka A durable, ordered log of events. Producers append messages, consumers read at their own pace, and messages can be replayed. A conveyor belt with a CCTV recording, so you can rewind and re-watch what passed.
Topic, partition, key A topic is a named stream. It is split into partitions for parallelism. Messages with the same key always go to the same partition, so they stay in order. A post office with numbered counters. Everyone with the same surname always queues at the same counter.
Offset and consumer lag An offset is a consumer's bookmark in a partition. Lag is how far the bookmark is behind the newest message. Your place in a TV series versus the newest episode. Lag is episodes left to watch.
Apache Flink A stream processing engine that runs continuous jobs over events, with memory (state) per key and recovery on failure. A factory line that never stops, where each worker keeps a notebook about each customer.
Keyed state Data Flink remembers per key, for example "last content hash seen for vendor v_48213". A loyalty card per customer at the till.
Event time and watermark Event time is when something happened (scrape timestamp), not when it arrived. A watermark tells Flink "events older than this have probably all arrived". Sorting postcards by the date written on them, and deciding at some point that late postcards have stopped arriving.
Checkpoint A consistent snapshot of Flink's state and the Kafka offsets it had read, used to resume after a crash. Saving a video game before the boss fight.
RocksDB state backend An embedded on-disk key-value store Flink uses to hold large state. A filing cabinet next to each worker instead of keeping everything in their head.
Deduplication by content hash Hash the normalised menu content. If the hash matches what we stored last time for that vendor, it is a duplicate and we skip it. A fingerprint check: same fingerprint, same person.
Schema normalization Converting different shapes into one standard shape: "Rs. 250", "250.00 INR" and "₹250" all become {amount: 250, currency: "INR"}. Converting every recipe to grams before cooking.
Upsert and idempotent upsert Upsert means insert if new, update if it exists. Idempotent means doing it twice has the same result as doing it once. Setting a thermostat to 21 degrees. Pressing "21" twice still gives 21.
Exactly-once vs at-least-once At-least-once means a message may be processed more than once but never lost. Exactly-once means the effect happens one time. In practice we get exactly-once effect by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes. A courier might ring twice, but you only sign for the parcel once.
Backpressure When a slow downstream step makes upstream steps slow down instead of crashing. Traffic backing up behind a narrow bridge.
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Before asking the language model, retrieve relevant examples or context and include them in the prompt, so the model is grounded. An open-book exam where you first find the right pages, then answer.
Embedding A list of numbers that represents the meaning of text, so similar text has nearby numbers. Coordinates on a map of meaning. "Paneer tikka" and "chicken tikka" live close together.
Milvus A vector database that stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones quickly. A librarian who finds the books most similar to the one in your hand.
LangChain A Python framework for chaining LLM steps: load documents, split, retrieve, prompt, parse output. Plumbing fittings that connect the pipes between your tools and the model.
Gemini 2.5 Pro Google's large multimodal language model, which can read text and images. A very capable reader who can also look at pictures.
Chunking Splitting a long document into pieces small enough to embed and to fit in a prompt. Cutting a long article into paragraphs before filing them.
Spark (study-only) A batch and micro-batch data processing engine. Not on the PDF. I only discuss it as a verbal option for backfills. A huge kitchen that cooks a whole banquet in one go, not one order at a time.

4. Architecture

flowchart LR SRC["Partner sites, PDFs, images"] --> SEL["Selenium fleet on GCP with proxy pools"] SEL --> K["Kafka topics keyed by vendor_id"] K --> FL["Flink job: validate, normalize, dedupe"] FL -->|"structured items"| UP["Idempotent catalog upsert"] FL -->|"unstructured payloads"| RAG["RAG extractor: LangChain + Gemini 2.5 Pro"] RAG --> MV["Milvus: embeddings of labelled menus"] MV --> RAG RAG --> VAL["Schema validation"] VAL --> UP UP --> CAT["Uber Eats catalog"] K -.->|"verbal only: backfill"| SP["Spark batch, study-only"]

What to notice: Kafka sits in the middle so scrapers never wait on slow downstream steps, and both the structured path and the RAG path end in the same idempotent upsert. The dotted Spark box is not on the resume.

Box by box.

  1. Sources. Partner web pages, PDFs and images, in many layouts and languages.
  2. Selenium fleet on GCP. Python Selenium workers in Docker containers load JavaScript-heavy pages through rotating proxies and download files. They emit three kinds of events: menu payloads, item rows, and scrape-health events (success, failure, blocked, retry).
  3. Kafka. Topics keyed by vendor_id. Same key means same partition, so all events for one restaurant stay in order. Kafka also lets us replay after a bad deploy, and lets several consumers read the same log.
  4. Flink job. Reads Kafka, keys the stream by vendor, validates against the schema, normalises fields (prices, currencies, section names), and deduplicates using keyed state that remembers the last content hash per vendor and menu. Structured items go straight to the upsert. Unstructured payloads (scanned PDFs, images) are routed to the RAG extractor.
  5. RAG extractor. Chunks the document, embeds it, retrieves similar already-labelled menus from Milvus as examples, and asks Gemini 2.5 Pro to output items in the catalog schema.
  6. Schema validation. Rejects anything that does not fit the strict schema (missing price, wrong type, unknown currency).
  7. Idempotent catalog upsert. Writes using a deterministic key, so a replayed or duplicated message updates the same row instead of creating a second one.
  8. Spark (dotted, study-only). If asked how I would reprocess months of history after a schema change, I describe a Spark batch job reading from raw storage. It is not a resume claim.

5. One menu, step by step

Here is one illustrative menu traced through the system. The data is made up but realistic.

The input. A bilingual French and English café, "Café Lumière", vendor id v_48213, uploads a scanned two-page PDF. Page 1 has "Entrées / Starters". Page 2 has "Plats / Mains" with prices like "Croque-monsieur ....... 12,50 €".

sequenceDiagram participant S as Selenium worker participant K as Kafka participant F as Flink job participant R as RAG extractor participant M as Milvus participant G as Gemini 2.5 Pro participant C as Catalog S->>K: menu_payload event, key v_48213 K->>F: event read at offset 10452 F->>F: hash content, compare with keyed state F->>R: unstructured PDF, route to RAG R->>M: embed chunks, find similar labelled menus M-->>R: top 3 example menus with gold labels R->>G: prompt with chunks, examples, schema G-->>R: JSON items R->>F: validated items F->>C: idempotent upsert per item F->>F: checkpoint stores state and offset

What to notice: dedupe happens before the expensive LLM call, and the checkpoint at the end is what makes a crash safe to recover from.

Step 1. Acquire. A Selenium worker downloads the PDF through a proxy and emits an event to Kafka:

{
  "event_type": "menu_payload",
  "vendor_id": "v_48213",
  "menu_version_hint": "2025-03",
  "scraped_at": "2025-03-14T09:12:44Z",
  "content_type": "application/pdf",
  "blob_uri": "gs://menus-raw/v_48213/menu.pdf",
  "languages_detected": ["fr", "en"]
}

Step 2. Dedupe. Flink computes a hash of the normalised content. Keyed state for v_48213 says the last hash was different, so this is a new version and it proceeds. If the same PDF had been scraped twice in an hour, the hash would match and Flink would drop the second copy before any LLM cost is spent.

Step 3. Route. It is a scanned PDF, not structured HTML, so Flink routes it to the RAG path.

Step 4. Retrieve. The extractor splits the PDF into chunks (roughly one menu section each), embeds them, and asks Milvus for the most similar labelled menus. Milvus returns three bilingual French café menus whose correct catalog output is already known.

Step 5. Generate. Gemini 2.5 Pro gets the chunks, the three examples, and the target schema, and returns JSON:

{
  "vendor_id": "v_48213",
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": {"fr": "Plats", "en": "Mains"},
      "items": [
        {"name": {"fr": "Croque-monsieur", "en": "Croque-monsieur"},
         "price": {"amount": 12.50, "currency": "EUR"},
         "modifiers": []}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Step 6. Validate. The output is checked against the schema. "12,50 €" became 12.50 with currency EUR, which is exactly the normalisation we want. A missing price or an unknown currency would fail validation.

Step 7. Upsert. Each item is written with a deterministic key, for example a hash of vendor id, section and normalised item name. If Kafka redelivers the event after a crash, the same keys are written again and nothing duplicates.

Step 8. Checkpoint. Flink snapshots its keyed state and the Kafka offset (10452). If the job crashes later, it resumes from here.

6. Bullet M1 decoded: onboarding, money, and the RAG extractor

Accelerated restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and saved $600K annually by architecting an automated ingestion pipeline processing 30K+ menus monthly. Converted unstructured, multilingual PDFs into a strict catalog schema at 98% field fidelity utilizing a Gemini 2.5 Pro and LangChain RAG pipeline over Milvus vector embeddings.

In plain words

I built the automated pipeline that turns a restaurant's messy menu into clean catalog data. It made onboarding take 2 hours instead of a day, it handles more than 30,000 menus a month, and it replaced enough manual work and paid-tool usage to save about $600K a year. For the hardest inputs, the scanned and multilingual PDFs, I used an LLM with retrieval so the output fits the catalog schema almost perfectly.

How it works

The RAG extractor has five steps.

  1. Load and chunk. Read the PDF or image and split it into section-sized chunks.
  2. Embed and retrieve. Turn each chunk into an embedding and ask Milvus for the nearest labelled menus. These act as worked examples ("here is a similar menu and its correct output").
  3. Prompt. Give Gemini 2.5 Pro the chunks, the retrieved examples, and the exact target schema, and ask for JSON only.
  4. Parse and validate. Parse the JSON with a strict schema. Anything that does not fit is rejected.
  5. Hand back. Valid items go to the idempotent catalog upsert.

An illustrative sketch (not the production code) of how the chain fits together in LangChain:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

class Price(BaseModel):
    amount: float
    currency: str

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: dict[str, str]          # language code -> text
    price: Price
    modifiers: list[str] = []

class Section(BaseModel):
    name: dict[str, str]
    items: list[Item]

class Menu(BaseModel):
    vendor_id: str
    sections: list[Section]

retriever = milvus_store.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 3})
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
    "Convert this menu into the schema.\nExamples:\n{examples}\nMenu:\n{chunk}"
)
chain = prompt | gemini_25_pro.with_structured_output(Menu)

examples = retriever.invoke(chunk_text)
menu = chain.invoke({"examples": examples, "chunk": chunk_text})

The key idea is that the schema is enforced twice: once by asking the model for structured output, and again by validation before anything touches the catalog.

Why this design

  • Why an LLM at all? Layouts vary endlessly. Hand-written templates or regex per restaurant do not scale to 30K+ menus a month in many languages.
  • Why RAG and not just a prompt? Retrieved examples of similar, already-labelled menus show the model what a correct answer looks like for that style of menu. That grounds the output and improves field accuracy, especially for prices and section names.
  • Why Milvus? It is a purpose-built vector database for fast nearest-neighbour search over many embeddings.
  • Why Gemini 2.5 Pro? It is multimodal, so it can read scanned PDFs and images, and it handles multilingual text well. It was also a natural fit on GCP.
  • Why LangChain? It gives ready building blocks for loading, splitting, retrieval, prompting and structured output, so the team writes glue, not plumbing.

Alternatives and why not

Alternative Why not
OCR plus regex or per-restaurant templates Breaks on every new layout. Too much maintenance at this volume.
Keep the paid third-party extraction tool Costs about $2 per menu and was part of the slow onboarding path.
Fully manual data entry Slow (the day-long onboarding) and expensive.
LLM prompt with no retrieval Less grounded. More format drift and mistakes on prices and sections.
A different vector store (for example pgvector) Workable at small scale. Milvus was the dedicated vector store on this project. pgvector is only skills-level for me.

Trade-off and what I'd do differently

The trade-off is cost and nondeterminism. Every LLM call costs money and the model can occasionally produce a wrong field. That is why dedupe runs before the LLM and validation runs after it. If I did it again I would add a small gold set per language and track field fidelity per language over time, so a drop in one language shows up early. (This is a reflection, not a claim that it already existed.)

The numbers

From 24 hours to 2 hours (HISTORICAL). - What it measures: the onboarding cycle time for a restaurant menu, from receiving the menu to it being usable in the catalog. - Derivation: before and after cycle time from my work records. 22 of 24 hours saved is about a 92% cut. Older notes rounded this to "90%". - Why it mattered: a restaurant cannot take orders until its menu is live. Same-day onboarding means revenue starts the same day. - Say it: "We took restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours." - Don't say: "Menus go live in real time" or "sub-minute".

30K+ menus a month (HISTORICAL). - What it measures: the volume the pipeline processes. - Derivation: 30,000 menus a month is about 1,000 a day (30,000 divided by 30), or roughly 40 an hour if spread evenly. Real traffic is bursty because scrape runs happen in fleet windows. - Say it: "It processes more than 30,000 menus a month."

$600K a year (HISTORICAL, conservative floor). - What it measures: annual cost avoided by replacing the third-party tool and manual work. - Derivation: about $2 per menu of third-party and manual cost, times 30,000 menus a month, times 12 months, is $720,000 list. I floor it to $600K to stay conservative.

$2 per menu  x  30,000 menus per month  x  12 months  =  $720,000 per year (list)
Resume figure: $600K (conservative floor, below the list value)
  • Say it: "Roughly $2 a menu at 30,000 a month is about $720K a year. I quote $600K as the conservative number."
  • Don't say: an exact dollar figure from a finance report. It is arithmetic, not an audited savings statement.

98% field fidelity (offline evaluation). - What it measures: the share of extracted fields that match a human-labelled answer on a held-out evaluation set. - Derivation: offline evaluation against labelled menus. If asked for the size of the evaluation set, keep it qualitative. I do not have a number to quote. - Why it mattered: the catalog schema is strict, so wrong fields mean wrong prices for customers. 98% is what made automation trustworthy. - Say it: "98% field fidelity in offline evaluation." - Don't say: "98% accuracy in production" or "98% of live menus are perfect".

Older prep vs current resume

Older prep described this path as "RAG plus Gemini plus SFT, 98% fidelity, 100% schema consistency", with low-confidence results going to human review. The current PDF claims only 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation with Gemini 2.5 Pro, LangChain RAG and Milvus. Do not volunteer SFT or "100% schema consistency". If asked what happens to low-confidence extractions, you can say older notes describe routing them to a review step, and keep it at that level.

Questions they will ask

Q: Why RAG instead of fine-tuning? "RAG let us improve quality by adding labelled examples to Milvus, without retraining a model every time a new menu style showed up. The retrieved examples show Gemini what a correct output looks like for that style. It is faster to iterate and cheaper to maintain. Fine-tuning can be layered on later, but it is not what the resume claims."

Q: What does 98% field fidelity actually mean? "It is field-level agreement with a human-labelled answer key, measured offline. If a menu has 100 fields across items, prices and sections, about 98 match. It is not a live production accuracy number, and I always say offline."

Q: How do you stop the LLM from inventing items? "Three ways. The prompt includes the actual chunks and real retrieved examples, so the model is grounded. The output must fit a strict schema, so free text cannot sneak in. And validation rejects anything missing a required field like price." Follow-up they may ask: "What about a hallucinated item that fits the schema?" "That is exactly what the offline evaluation set catches, because it compares against labelled menus."

Q: How did you get to $600K? "About $2 per menu of third-party and manual cost, times 30,000 menus a month, times 12, is $720K. I floor it to $600K to be conservative."

7. Bullet M2 decoded: Selenium hardening, Kafka, Flink, exactly-once

Scaled menu extraction success to 95%+ by hardening a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries. Designed a large-scale data ingestion and processing pipeline using Kafka and Apache Flink, with stateful keyed deduplication and schema normalization to guarantee exactly-once catalog upserts.

In plain words

Two things. First, I made the scrapers much more reliable, so 95%+ of menu extractions now succeed. Second, I designed the streaming backbone behind them: Kafka to buffer and replay events, and Flink to clean, standardise and deduplicate them so each menu item lands in the catalog exactly once in effect.

How it works: Selenium hardening

  • Dynamic proxy pools. Requests rotate through a pool of IP addresses. Blocked or slow proxies are taken out of rotation.
  • User-agent rotation (spoofing). Each session presents a realistic, varied browser identity.
  • Adaptive retries with per-source budgets. A failure is retried with backoff and a fresh proxy, but each source has a retry budget so one hostile site cannot eat the fleet.
  • Scrape-health events. Every attempt emits success, blocked or failed to Kafka, so success rate per source is visible.

Illustrative sketch of the retry loop:

def scrape(vendor, max_attempts=4):
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        proxy = proxy_pool.pick(exclude=vendor.recent_bad_proxies)
        try:
            page = fetch_with_selenium(vendor.url, proxy=proxy, user_agent=random_ua())
            emit("scrape_health", vendor.id, status="ok", attempt=attempt)
            return page
        except (Blocked, Timeout) as e:
            proxy_pool.penalize(proxy)
            emit("scrape_health", vendor.id, status=type(e).__name__, attempt=attempt)
            sleep(backoff_with_jitter(attempt))
    emit("scrape_health", vendor.id, status="gave_up")

How it works: Kafka

Topics are keyed by vendor_id, so all events for one restaurant land on the same partition and stay in order. Kafka gives three things the scrapers need: a buffer so scrapers never block on slow downstream writes, replay so we can reprocess after a bad parser deploy, and fan-out so several consumers (the Flink job, audit, any reprocessing job) read the same log. The main health signal is consumer lag: if lag climbs, something downstream is slow.

How it works: Flink keyed dedupe and normalisation

The Flink job keys the stream by vendor (and menu), keeps the last content hash in keyed state (backed by RocksDB), uses event time from the scrape timestamp with watermarks for late pages, and checkpoints state plus Kafka offsets together.

Illustrative PyFlink-style sketch:

class DedupeAndNormalize(KeyedProcessFunction):
    def open(self, ctx):
        self.last_hash = ctx.get_state(ValueStateDescriptor("last_hash", Types.STRING()))

    def process_element(self, event, ctx):
        normalized = normalize(event)          # prices, currency, section names, languages
        h = sha256(canonical_json(normalized))
        if self.last_hash.value() == h:
            return                              # duplicate: same vendor, same content
        self.last_hash.update(h)
        if normalized.is_structured:
            yield ("upsert", normalized)
        else:
            yield ("rag", normalized)

stream.key_by(lambda e: (e.vendor_id, e.menu_id)).process(DedupeAndNormalize())

How it works: "exactly-once" catalog upserts

Say this carefully. Across Selenium, Kafka, Flink and an external catalog, what you really get is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts. Kafka and Flink can redeliver after a crash. The upsert uses a deterministic key, so writing the same item twice leaves one row. The effect is exactly-once. I do not claim zero message loss, and I do not claim two-phase commit across Gemini or third-party sites.

-- Illustrative: deterministic key makes the write idempotent
INSERT INTO catalog_items (item_key, vendor_id, section, name, price_amount, currency, content_hash)
VALUES (:item_key, :vendor_id, :section, :name, :price, :currency, :hash)
ON CONFLICT (item_key) DO UPDATE
SET price_amount = EXCLUDED.price_amount,
    currency     = EXCLUDED.currency,
    content_hash = EXCLUDED.content_hash
WHERE catalog_items.content_hash IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED.content_hash;

The catalog's real storage is not something I quote. The SQL is a teaching sketch of the idempotent pattern.

Why this design

Why Kafka and not direct HTTP from scrapers to the catalog? Scrapers must not block on slow catalog writes. We need replay after a bad parser deploy. And several consumers share one log. Direct HTTP gives none of that.

Why Flink for the online path? Scrapes are bursty. We need keyed state for per-vendor dedupe, event-time ordering when late pages arrive, and low latency so catalog freshness stays at minutes, not hours.

Why keyed by vendor? Ordering per restaurant matters (an old version must not overwrite a newer one), and per-key state is exactly what dedupe needs.

Alternatives and why not

Alternative Why not here
Direct HTTP writes from scrapers No buffer, no replay, scrapers stall on slow writes.
Kafka Streams A valid option for lighter transforms. Flink was chosen for richer event-time handling, larger keyed state, and a clearer ops story for a dedicated processing cluster. I admit Kafka Streams could work at this event rate if the team standard were Streams only.
Spark Structured Streaming (study-only) Micro-batch latency (seconds) is weaker for live catalog freshness under scrape bursts. Not on the resume.
A plain Python Kafka consumer Fine for volume this size, but you hand-build state, checkpoints and event time. Flink gives these out of the box.
Two-phase commit for true exactly-once The external catalog and Gemini do not participate in transactions. Idempotent upserts give the same effect with far less complexity.

Trade-off and what I'd do differently

Flink is more infrastructure to operate than a simple consumer. At 30K menus a month the volume is moderate, so the argument for Flink is the shape of the problem (stateful dedupe, event time, replay), not raw throughput. If the team had no Flink platform, I would start with a plain consumer plus a dedupe table and move to Flink only when state and event-time needs grew.

The numbers

95%+ extraction success (HISTORICAL outcome, ESTIMATED baseline). - What it measures: the share of scrape attempts that end in a usable menu. - Derivation: the outcome is from my work records. The starting point was roughly 60 to 65%, which is an estimate, not a logged figure. - Why it mattered: every failed scrape becomes manual work or a delayed onboarding. - Say it: "We took extraction success to 95% plus, from what I'd estimate was around 60 to 65%." - Don't say: "+95%" or "improved by 95%". Older prep wrote "+95% success", which sounds like a 95% increase. The resume says success reached 95%+.

Peak events per second (ESTIMATED, prep only, not on the PDF). - Roughly 200 to 500 events per second at peak during fleet runs. - Derivation: 30K menus a month is about 1,000 menus a day. Each menu emits many item events, plus retries and health events. Fleet runs compress that into short windows, so peaks reach hundreds of events per second. Steady state is much lower. - Say it only if asked: "Order of a few hundred events per second at peak. That's an estimate, not a dashboard number."

Questions they will ask

Q: Is it really exactly-once? "In effect, yes, but I'm precise about how. Delivery is at-least-once, because Kafka and Flink can replay after a failure. The catalog upsert is idempotent on a deterministic item key, so replays don't create duplicates. I don't claim two-phase commit across Gemini or third-party sites, and I don't claim zero message loss."

Q: Why not Kafka Streams? "Kafka Streams is a good choice for lighter transforms. We chose Flink for richer event-time handling and bigger keyed state, and a clearer operating model for a dedicated processing cluster. Honestly, at this event rate Streams could have worked if that were the team standard."

Q: Why key by vendor_id? "Two reasons. Ordering per restaurant, so an older menu version can't overwrite a newer one. And dedupe state is per vendor and menu, so keying by vendor puts the state right next to the events that need it."

Q: How did you get extraction success up? "Dynamic proxy pools that drop bad IPs, rotating user agents, and adaptive retries with backoff and a per-source budget. Every attempt emits a health event, so we could see which sources were failing and why. That took success from an estimated 60 to 65% to 95% plus."

8. Flink deep dive (must-know for streaming rounds)

Flink is the piece interviewers probe hardest. Know these seven ideas.

Topic What to say
API DataStream (or Table API), keyed by vendor_id.
Time Event time from the scrape timestamp. Watermarks with bounded out-of-orderness handle late pages.
State Keyed dedupe state (last content hash or menu version) in the RocksDB state backend.
Fault tolerance Checkpoint barriers flow through the job. On a TaskManager loss, the job restores from the last successful checkpoint.
Delivery Kafka source is at-least-once (or exactly-once with a transactional sink if required). The catalog sink is idempotent either way.
Backpressure A slow catalog fills Flink's network buffers, Flink reads Kafka more slowly, and consumer lag rises. Rising lag is the alert.
Failure mode A bad normalizer deploy is fixed by rewinding Kafka offsets to before the bad window and reprocessing.

How checkpoints work, in plain words. Every so often Flink injects a "barrier" marker into the stream. When each operator sees the barrier it saves its state. When all operators have saved, Flink records the checkpoint together with the Kafka offsets it had read. After a crash it reloads that state and rewinds Kafka to those offsets. Events after the checkpoint are processed again, which is why the sink must be idempotent.

Official Flink references - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/stateful-stream-processing/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/deployment/ha/overview/

12. Hard problems and failure scenarios

These are the scenarios interviewers push on. They come from my prep answers. Present them as "here is what happens and how we handle it". Do not dress them up as specific dated incidents.

Anti-bot blocks dragging success down. What breaks: sites rate-limit or fingerprint the fleet, and success drops. How you see it: scrape-health events show blocked rates rising per source. Fix: dynamic proxy pools that penalise bad IPs, rotating user agents, backoff with jitter, and per-source retry budgets. Lesson: make every attempt observable, or you cannot tell a hostile site from a broken parser.

A bad normalizer deploy writes wrong data. What breaks: a parser change mangles prices for some vendors. How you see it: validation failures spike or downstream checks flag bad values. Fix: roll back the job, rewind Kafka offsets to before the bad window, and reprocess. Idempotent upserts mean the reprocess overwrites cleanly. Lesson: this is exactly why Kafka's replay matters. (For a very large window, a batch backfill would be the study-only answer.)

A Flink checkpoint fails mid-fleet run. What happens: the job restores from the last successful checkpoint, Kafka offsets rewind to the checkpointed positions, events are reprocessed, idempotent upserts prevent duplicates, and the lag alert fires until the job catches up.

Late pages arrive out of order. What breaks: page 2 of a menu arrives after a newer version's page 1. Fix: event time from the scrape timestamp, watermarks with bounded out-of-orderness, and dedupe by content hash and version so an older version never overwrites a newer one.

The catalog slows down. What happens: backpressure. Flink's buffers fill, it reads Kafka more slowly, and consumer lag rises. Nothing crashes. Lag is the alert, and scrapers keep producing into Kafka.

Hot vendors with huge menus. One giant menu can overload a single partition or key. Mitigation in the streaming path is to key by vendor plus menu. The salting and whale-isolation ideas belong to the study-only Spark discussion.

13. Document Compliance (Uber Mobility ANZ): the separate bullet

Achieved 99.9% regulatory compliance for Uber Mobility ANZ by automating driver and vehicle document verification workflows against local authority requirements. Eliminated 20 hours of manual operational overhead per week by replacing manual review queues with a deterministic validation backend.

In plain words. This is Uber Mobility (rides), not Uber Eats. In Australia and New Zealand (ANZ), drivers and their vehicles must hold valid documents (licences, registrations, inspections) that meet local authority rules. I automated checking those documents with a deterministic rules backend, replacing a manual review queue.

Words you need. Deterministic validation means fixed rules that always give the same answer for the same input, with no model guessing. Analogy: a checklist at airport security, not a guard's hunch. Manual review queue means people opening each document and ticking boxes by hand.

The numbers (HISTORICAL). 99.9% regulatory compliance, and 20 hours a week of manual effort eliminated. Both come from my past work records and earlier resumes. They were not re-measured from logs for this prep.

Say this carefully. - Say "Uber Mobility ANZ", never "Uber Eats" and never "main app". - Do not invent Selenium, RAG or LLMs for this project. It is a deterministic validation backend. - If asked for implementation detail beyond "rules checked against local authority requirements", keep it qualitative.

Q: How do you get to 99.9% compliance? "Because the validation is deterministic. Every document is checked against the same encoded local-authority rules, every time, instead of depending on a reviewer's attention on a busy day. That's where both the compliance number and the 20 hours a week of saved manual review came from. Both numbers are from my work records at the time."

17. Practice drill

  1. What problem did Menu Ingestion solve? Restaurants couldn't sell on Uber Eats until their messy menus were in the strict catalog schema. Onboarding was slow and partly manual or paid-tool based. The pipeline automated it, from 24 hours to 2 hours.
  2. Walk me through the architecture. Selenium fleet on GCP with proxy pools, Kafka keyed by vendor, a Flink job that validates, normalises and dedupes, then an idempotent catalog upsert. Unstructured PDFs detour through a RAG extractor using LangChain, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Milvus.
  3. Derive $600K. About $2 per menu × 30,000 a month × 12 is $720K. I floor it to $600K to be conservative.
  4. What is 98% field fidelity? Field-level match against a labelled answer key in offline evaluation. Not a live production accuracy number.
  5. Why RAG? Retrieved, already-labelled similar menus ground the model, so prices and sections come out right more often. Adding examples is cheaper than retraining.
  6. What does Milvus do here? Stores embeddings of labelled menus and returns the nearest ones as examples for the prompt.
  7. How did you raise extraction success? Dynamic proxy pools, rotating user agents, adaptive retries with backoff and per-source budgets, plus health events per attempt. From an estimated 60 to 65% to 95%+.
  8. Why Kafka? Buffer bursts so scrapers never block, replay after bad deploys, and multiple consumers on one log.
  9. Why Flink? Keyed state for per-vendor dedupe, event-time handling for late pages, and checkpointed recovery. The shape of the problem, not raw volume.
  10. Is it really exactly-once? Exactly-once in effect: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts on a deterministic key. No two-phase commit across third parties.
  11. What happens when the catalog is slow? Backpressure. Flink slows its reads, Kafka lag rises, and lag is the alert. Nothing is lost because Kafka holds the events.
  12. What about Spark? Not on my resume. For a large historical reprocess I'd design a Spark batch job, but I present it as a design answer only.
  13. Is ANZ part of Menu? No. It's Uber Mobility in Australia and New Zealand: deterministic validation of driver and vehicle documents, 99.9% compliance and 20 hours a week saved, from my work records.
  14. What would you improve? Per-language field fidelity tracking on a gold set, so quality drops in one language show up early.
