Part E. Practice drill

  1. What does Masters India do? GST e-invoicing for Indian enterprises: we validate invoices and register them with the government IRP, which returns a signed IRN and QR.
  2. Why migrate off PHP? Synchronous workers blocked on slow IRP calls, deploys were all-or-nothing, and deadline spikes caused timeouts.
  3. How did the migration avoid risk? Strangler with per-route Nginx canaries, shared database during cutover, contract tests pinning PHP responses, rollback by config.
  4. What actually cut p95? Taking IRP calls off request threads (Kafka consumers with WebClient timeouts), HikariCP connection pooling, N+1 and index fixes. Redis helped the median.
  5. Derive the 75%. From 1,200 ms to 300 ms saves 900, and 900 ÷ 1,200 is 75%.
  6. Convert 700 and 4,000 requests per minute. About 12 and 67 requests a second.
  7. Why Kafka? Per-GSTIN ordering, replay for disputes, and independent consumer groups on one log.
  8. Why shard by tax quarter? GST is quarter-scoped. Hot writes in the current quarter, small indexes, clean archiving.
  9. What's the idempotency key? Client plus file hash plus batch index, with a unique constraint, checked before calling the IRP.
  10. Is it truly exactly-once? In effect: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes.
  11. What does the DLQ do? Parks poison batches after bounded retries so the rest of the import continues, for operator replay.
  12. Where does 70% triage come from? Request IDs across services, ELK and New Relic. Roughly 30 minutes to under 10, baseline estimated.
  13. Why did Redis cut reads 30%? Every row of a bulk import hit the same config and GSTIN lookups.
  14. GFG: why Django? In 2021 a CMS-style product benefits from Django's admin, auth and ORM.
  15. GFG: how are votes idempotent? Unique user and content constraint. Redis counters reconcile to MySQL.

Part F. 3-minute whiteboard script (Masters India)

First (30 seconds): the problem. Write "Invoice in, signed IRN out". Say: "Enterprises must register B2B invoices with the government IRP. We had 1,500+ clients, a synchronous PHP monolith, and deadline spikes that caused timeouts."

Second (90 seconds): draw the system. Client ERP, then Nginx gateway with a split arrow to "PHP (old)" and "Spring Boot (new)". From Spring Boot draw Redis, PostgreSQL by quarter, S3, and Kafka. From Kafka draw Workers (Kafka consumers and Spring Batch), then IRP. Add a DLQ box off Workers and ELK and New Relic underneath. Say: "Strangler with per-route canaries took p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds and throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests a minute. Bulk imports go S3, Kafka keyed by GSTIN, workers with bounded concurrency to the IRP. Idempotency key client plus file hash plus batch index means a retry never double-registers. Poison batches go to the DLQ. Over a million submissions a day."

Third (60 seconds): numbers and caveats. Write "12/s avg, 8–10x peak (est.)", "triage −70%", "reads −30%", "coverage 35→82%, 98% deploys". Say: "Freeing request threads from IRP waits, pooling and query fixes moved p95, Redis moved the median. Exactly-once means at-least-once plus idempotency. I mentored two engineers through the migration."

GFG in 30 seconds if asked: draw Django in the middle with MySQL, Redis, MongoDB and Elasticsearch around it. Say: "PHP to Django for reliability at 10K+ daily queries and 10x contest spikes. Votes idempotent by unique constraint, Redis counters reconciled to MySQL. 20% premium lift attributed by growth."

Authentication, authorization, tenancy and rate limits (API level and AI level)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: how identity, permissions, tenant isolation and throttling worked on each resume project. Most depth goes to Impact Analytics (the Go auth waterfall, UAM hierarchy scope, Ask Iris handshake freeze, AI-level budgets). Uber FRM, Masters India, Uber Menu and GeeksforGeeks are covered more briefly. It also teaches the general concepts: JWT, OIDC, RBAC, constant-time comparison, token buckets, noisy neighbours.
  • When to read it: before any security, multi-tenant SaaS, API design or "how do you stop the agent leaking data?" question.
  • What to memorise: the IA waterfall order (Redis, then Firebase Admin, then JWT or Google OIDC, constant-time API keys, Postgres roles). Tenant and hierarchy come from the token, never the request body. Ask Iris freezes plan_scope at the WebSocket handshake. The Keep/Drop LLM has no SQL tool. And isolation is access control, not encryption.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal. DESIGN or verbal means a mechanism I can describe but that is not a resume bullet; say "the design was..." and do not quote numbers.

Say these carefully

  • Do not invent quota numbers ("50 requests per minute per tenant"). Describe the mechanism.
  • Do not claim org-wide IAM ownership (Okta, corporate identity provider). I built service-level auth.
  • Isolation is not encryption. C3 is access control and data scoping.
  • No human review queues (HITL) at Impact Analytics. Older prep described "3 human confirm gates before write-back". That belongs to the Cluster Recommendation Copilot design, which is verbal only, not to shipped IA systems. In shipped Keep/Drop, offline evals replaced critic agents, and the LLM never writes directly.
  • LangSmith is Ask Iris only, not the Keep/Drop batch.
  • Uber FRM: authorization was enforced upstream by Uber's gateway. Say so before the interviewer does.

1. The concepts in plain English

1.1 Authentication versus authorization

  • Authentication (AuthN) answers "who are you?" Think of showing your ID at a building's front desk.
  • Authorization (AuthZ) answers "what are you allowed to do?" Your badge opens floors 3 and 4 but not the server room.

A failed AuthN is HTTP 401 Unauthorized (we don't know who you are). A failed AuthZ is 403 Forbidden (we know who you are, and you can't do this). Too many requests is 429 Too Many Requests.

1.2 JWT

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed, compact token that carries claims such as user id, tenant id, roles and expiry. The server verifies the signature with a key, so it can trust the claims without a database lookup. Analogy: a wristband at a festival. Security checks the stamp, not a guest list. Two warnings: a JWT is signed, not encrypted (anyone can read the claims), and you cannot easily revoke one before it expires, so keep them short-lived.

header.payload.signature
payload example: {"sub": "u_123", "tenant_id": "t_acme", "roles": ["planner"], "exp": 1760000000}

1.3 OIDC and Firebase

  • OAuth 2.0 is a standard for delegated access. OIDC (OpenID Connect) adds identity on top of it: after you sign in with Google, Google issues an ID token (a JWT) saying who you are. The service verifies it against Google's published public keys.
  • Firebase Authentication is Google's hosted sign-in product. The Firebase Admin SDK lets a backend verify Firebase-issued ID tokens.

1.4 API keys and constant-time comparison

An API key is a long secret string for machine callers. Compare it in constant time: a normal string compare stops at the first wrong character, so a wrong first character returns slightly faster than a wrong last character. An attacker can measure that and guess the key one character at a time. That is a timing attack. Constant-time compare always takes the same time.

1.5 RBAC and hierarchy scope

  • RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) gives permissions to roles (planner, admin, read-only) and roles to users.
  • Hierarchy scope goes further. A planner may only see part of the merchandise hierarchy, for example "Womenswear, Tops, all regions". At IA this is UAM (User Access Management) scoping.

1.6 Multi-tenancy

A tenant is one customer company sharing the SaaS. Common isolation models:

Model Isolation Cost
Database or cluster per tenant Strongest, smallest blast radius Most expensive to run
Schema per tenant Strong Many schemas to migrate
Shared tables with a tenant_id column Weakest, depends on every query filtering Cheapest

Whatever the model, the golden rule is that the tenant comes from the verified token, never from the request body or URL alone.

A noisy neighbour is one tenant whose heavy usage slows everyone else.

1.7 Rate limiting algorithms

  • Token bucket: a bucket refills at R tokens per second up to a capacity B. Each request takes one token. That allows bursts up to B and an average of R. This is the most common algorithm.
  • Leaky bucket: requests drain at a fixed rate, which smooths bursts.
  • Fixed window: count requests per minute. Simple, but it allows double bursts at window edges.
  • Sliding window: a smoother count over the last N seconds.
# Teaching sketch: token bucket.
def allow(bucket, now):
    bucket.tokens = min(bucket.capacity, bucket.tokens + (now - bucket.last) * bucket.rate)
    bucket.last = now
    if bucket.tokens >= 1:
        bucket.tokens -= 1
        return True
    return False   # caller returns HTTP 429

3. Impact Analytics in depth

3.1 Bullet C3

Guaranteed strict multi-tenant data isolation and UAM-scoped hierarchy access control across PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. Secured system entry by implementing a Redis-fronted Firebase Admin to JWT/Google OIDC verification waterfall, constant-time API keys, and Postgres-backed role resolution.

In plain words: every request into the Go platform proves who it is, and we work out which tenant and which part of the merchandise hierarchy it may see. Then every query to Postgres and ClickHouse is limited to that scope. Redis caches verification results so most requests don't repeat expensive checks.

3.2 The authentication waterfall

A waterfall here means "try verifiers in a fixed order until one succeeds". Different callers carry different credentials: browser users with Firebase tokens, others with Google OIDC tokens or service JWTs, machines with API keys.

sequenceDiagram participant C as Caller participant G as Go/Gin auth middleware participant R as Redis cache participant F as Firebase Admin participant O as JWT or Google OIDC verify participant P as PostgreSQL roles and UAM C->>G: Request with token or API key G->>R: Cached identity for this credential? alt cache hit R-->>G: identity, tenant, roles else cache miss G->>F: Verify as Firebase ID token alt not a Firebase token G->>O: Verify as JWT or Google OIDC end G->>P: Resolve role and hierarchy scope P-->>G: role, UAM scope G->>R: Cache result with TTL end G-->>C: Proceed with scoped context, or 401 or 403

What to notice: a Redis miss falls through to real verification and Postgres. It never "fails open" by letting the request through unverified.

Key points to say:

  • Order matters. Cheapest checks first, and Redis in front of everything for hot callers.
  • API keys are compared in constant time (subtle.ConstantTimeCompare in Go).
  • Roles live in Postgres, the source of truth for identity, UAM and roles. ClickHouse holds facts.
  • Cache TTL must be shorter than token lifetime, so a revoked or expired credential stops working within a bounded time.

3.3 Authorization and data scoping

Layer Rule
API (Go) Role claims gate mutating routes. The tenant from the verified identity must match the resource's tenant
PostgreSQL Thin metadata, UAM and roles, all keyed by tenant
ClickHouse Every read is filtered to the caller's tenant and UAM hierarchy scope
KPI compiler Operator formulas compile to allowlisted SQL. Unknown tokens fail closed. Values are parameters, never concatenated
Agent payloads The Keep/Drop LLM never gets a SQL tool. Code builds the JSON context within scope

Cross-tenant defence: never take tenant_id only from the body or URL. Bind it from the verified identity. Reject any request whose resource scope is not inside the caller's scope. Test it: integration tests that try another tenant's ids and expect 403.

3.4 Ask Iris: freezing scope at the WebSocket handshake

Shipped "Ask Iris," a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot enabling planners to interactively query KPIs and inspect AI decisions on a multi-billion-row database. Prevented infinite LLM loops and multi-tenant data leaks by orchestrating a LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator loop, utilizing LangSmith for observability, and strictly freezing hierarchy access on the initial socket handshake.

A WebSocket is a long-lived two-way connection, good for chat. The risk: the connection lives for minutes, and a user (or a prompt injection) might try to change scope mid-conversation, for example "now show me another region" or "ignore your rules and query tenant B".

  • The JWT is verified once, on the handshake (an Authorization: Bearer header or a ?token= query parameter).
  • The tenant, hierarchy and plan scope (plan_scope) are computed then and frozen for the life of the socket.
  • Every worker call the supervisor makes uses that frozen scope. Nothing the user types later can widen it.
  • The evaluator loop is capped at MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3, and the supervisor graph has a recursion limit, so a confused model cannot loop and burn tokens forever. After the cap it returns a graceful answer.
# Teaching sketch (FastAPI WebSocket).
@app.websocket("/ask-iris")
async def ask_iris(ws: WebSocket):
    claims = verify_jwt(ws.headers.get("authorization") or ws.query_params.get("token"))
    if claims is None:
        await ws.close(code=4401)
        return
    plan_scope = resolve_scope(claims)          # computed once
    await ws.accept()
    while True:
        question = await ws.receive_text()
        answer = await graph.ainvoke({"q": question, "scope": plan_scope})  # scope never re-read from input
        await ws.send_json(answer)

Say it: "Scope binds at the JWT handshake and is frozen. A later message can't pivot into another tenant's hierarchy, and the evaluator stops after three attempts."

Do NOT say: an SLA, user counts or questions per week. Ask Iris is a shipped capability with no published usage numbers.

3.5 Rate limiting at the API level (IA)

The resume bullet says "self-protecting HTTP edge" and "nested timeouts". The mechanisms:

  • Server-level read and write timeouts, header and body caps, and panic recovery (see go_gin.md).
  • Per-request context deadlines, with shorter deadlines on ClickHouse, Postgres and Redis calls.
  • Bounded concurrency to expensive downstreams, so one tenant's heavy pivot cannot exhaust ClickHouse connections or goroutines.

Older prep also described per-route request and burst limits on interactive APIs, with stricter quotas on bulk saves than on reads. Present that as the mechanism I would apply. There is no numeric quota on the resume, so do not invent one.

3.6 Budgets at the AI level (IA)

An HTTP 429 cannot stop an LLM job that is already running. AI work needs its own limits.

Control Where What it stops
Hard timeouts per LLM call Keep/Drop orchestration registry (A3) A hung provider call stalling an 88k-item pass
Circuit breakers Registry. Trips after about 5 consecutive failures or a failure fraction (verbal) Hammering a failing provider
Deterministic fallback A2. Timeout means the deterministic baseline score is written The run stalling or leaving gaps
Durable checkpoints and --resume Registry. det.json, agent_progress.json Paying again for work already done after a crash
Token, USD cost, step duration and fallback telemetry Custom JSON telemetry on every run (A3) Cost surprises. About $100 per pass is true but off the PDF
config_hash on every output row SHA-256 of guardrails, params, prompts and catalog Not knowing which config produced a decision
Evaluator cap of 3 attempts and a recursion limit Ask Iris (A4) Infinite LLM loops
No SQL tool for the model A2 Runaway or hallucinated queries against a 2.11B-row master

Say: "AI limits are product budgets, not just an Nginx limit_req. The dangerous amplifier is fan-out times retries, so the budgets are timeouts, breakers, attempt caps and cost telemetry."

3.7 Noisy neighbours (IA)

  1. Scope everything by tenant in Postgres and ClickHouse, which limits the blast radius of a bug.
  2. Onboarding is configuration, not a code fork. The KPI configurator lets a tenant's formulas change without a release.
  3. Bounded concurrency and deadlines at the Go edge, so one tenant's heavy pivot cannot starve others' interactive reads.
  4. Traces carry request context, so a slow tenant-specific path is visible in Datadog.

Verbal only: Cluster Recommendation Copilot design (not a resume bullet)

Use this only if an interviewer asks how I would design tool access and budgets for an agent that can propose write-backs. It is design depth. Say "the design was...", and say "building", not "shipped".

  • 14 audited tools, all read-only over planning data. No free-form SQL from the LLM.
  • 3 confirm gates in the design before any write-back through normal product APIs. This is a confirmation flow in a design, not a shipped human review queue.
  • Budgets in the design: tool calls per session, parallel clustering jobs per tenant, token and cost caps, per-tool timeouts, scenario caps (3 to 5 in the UI, 20 to 100 in batch explore), and child-cluster caps (about 10 by default, client min and max k).
  • Hindsight tenant metric catalogs were designed as configuration that goes live without a code deploy, still behind admin authorization.
  • A measured clustering failure rate of 8.5% (37 out of 437) with a TARGET under 2%.
  • Older prep also mentioned keeping "the ~0.4 ms interactive edit path" protected from batch explore. I cannot source that figure, so do not quote it.

4. Uber FRM: trusting the gateway, capturing identity for audit

flowchart LR U["Finance user"] --> GW["Uber gateway: authenticates user"] GW --> API["FRM Spring Boot service"] API --> CHK{"x-auth-params-email present?"} CHK -->|"no"| E401["401"] CHK -->|"yes"| W["Write path stores created_by and updated_by"] W --> DB["MySQL on SOADB"]

What to notice: the service does not check passwords. It trusts the header the gateway injects and records it on every write.

  • In the service: every write endpoint reads the x-auth-params-email header with @RequestHeader, returns 401 if it is missing, and stores the email as created_by / updated_by. That is identity capture for a SOX-adjacent audit trail. SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley) is the US law requiring auditable controls over financial reporting.
  • Not in the service: fine-grained "who may edit Materiality" decisions. Those were enforced upstream.
  • Why it is acceptable: inside Uber's mesh, only the gateway can inject that header. It would not be acceptable on the public internet.
  • If I hardened it standalone: verify a signed token instead of a plain header, using Spring Security as an OAuth2 resource server (a filter that validates the JWT before any controller runs), and add role checks with @PreAuthorize on mutating methods.
// Teaching sketch. The header is required for writes, and its value goes into the audit columns.
@PatchMapping("/thresholds/{uuid}")
public ThresholdDto update(@PathVariable String uuid,
                           @Valid @RequestBody ThresholdUpdate body,
                           @RequestHeader(value = "x-auth-params-email", required = false) String email) {
    if (email == null || email.isBlank()) {
        throw new UnauthorizedException();        // mapped to 401 by @RestControllerAdvice
    }
    return service.update(uuid, body, email);     // service sets updated_by = email
}

What to notice: @Valid runs Bean Validation on the request body (for example @NotNull, @Positive on its fields) before the method body runs, and the identity check is the first line.

There is no retail-style multi-tenancy here. The data is Uber Finance's, scoped by fiscal period.

5. Masters India: JWT, RBAC and compliance data

Control How
Authentication Short-lived JWT access tokens plus refresh tokens, over TLS
Authorization RBAC on mutating e-invoice and reconciliation APIs
Audit Who, what, when, and before and after values on mutations
Enterprise IP allowlisting for some clients
Secrets AWS KMS (HISTORICAL framing)
Cache Redis for IRP auth tokens (TTL shorter than the token's life) and client config
Throughput Gateway and service capacity (from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute). A fixed number of Spring Kafka consumer threads caps concurrent IRP calls. Kafka absorbs bulk (100K+ concurrent imports), so the HTTP tier is not the bulk meter
Per client Config and feature flags. GSTIN-keyed Kafka partitions for ordering. Not separate databases per tenant

Two Masters specifics worth explaining:

  • Outbound rate limiting. The government IRP is the fragile party. We used bounded concurrency and exponential backoff with jitter on calls to it, so our retries did not make its bad day worse.
  • Caching IRP auth tokens. The IRP issues a session token. Caching it in Redis with a TTL safely under its lifetime avoids re-authenticating on every invoice.

6. Uber Menu: service identity and the reverse rate-limit problem

  • Jobs run under service accounts, not end-user JWTs.
  • Here "rate limiting" is about us being limited by others. Vendor sites block bots, so we used IP rotation, dynamic proxy pools and adaptive backoff. That drove extraction success to 95%+. This protects against external blocks. It is not multi-tenant fairness.
  • Downstream, Kafka consumer lag is the backpressure signal, and Flink parallelism is bounded by partitions.

Do not mix up Menu proxy backoff with IA tenant budgets. They are opposite problems.

7. GeeksforGeeks, briefly

Django's built-in session authentication and permission system. Voting, pinning and locking threads are permission-checked actions. Locking or pinning is a moderator-style permission. Vote APIs are idempotent through a unique (user, content) constraint, so double-submitting a vote does nothing.

8. API level versus AI level: cheat sheet

Concern API level (Gin, FastAPI, Spring Boot) AI level (LangGraph, LLM calls)
Identity JWT, OIDC, Firebase, API key, gateway header Same identity propagated into the agent's context, frozen at handshake
Authorization Route plus role plus tenant match Frozen scope. No SQL tool. Only code-built JSON payloads
Abuse Request floods, slow clients, oversized bodies Loops, prompt injection, cost blow-ups

One sentence to say: "APIs authenticate who you are and throttle requests. The agent stack freezes what you can see and budgets how much non-determinism you can burn."

9. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. How do you stop cross-tenant data leaks? The tenant and hierarchy scope come from the verified identity, never from the request body. Every Postgres and ClickHouse read applies that scope. For Ask Iris, the scope is frozen at the WebSocket handshake, so nothing typed later can widen it. And the Keep/Drop model never gets a SQL tool. Code builds its context. I'd also test it: integration tests that try another tenant's ids and expect a 403.

Q2. Walk me through your auth waterfall. The Go middleware first checks Redis for a cached identity for this credential. On a miss, it tries Firebase Admin verification, and if the token isn't a Firebase token it verifies it as a JWT or Google OIDC token. API keys are compared in constant time. Then it resolves role and UAM hierarchy scope from Postgres and caches the result with a TTL shorter than the token's life. A cache miss falls through to real verification. It never fails open.

Q3. Why constant-time comparison for API keys? A normal comparison returns as soon as one character differs, so response time leaks how many leading characters were right. With enough requests an attacker can guess a key character by character. Constant-time comparison always does the same work. In Go that is subtle.ConstantTimeCompare.

Q4. How do you rate-limit the agent differently from the API? An HTTP limit can't stop an LLM job that has already started, so AI work needs its own budgets. On the Keep/Drop batch: hard timeouts per call, circuit breakers that trip after about five consecutive failures, a deterministic fallback on timeout, and token and USD telemetry on every run. On Ask Iris, the evaluator is capped at three attempts with a recursion limit. The API side is classic: timeouts, body caps and bounded concurrency at the Go edge.

Q5. What if the LLM ignores a "read-only" instruction? Instructions are not the control. The control is what the model can physically do. In Keep/Drop the model only receives JSON and returns a structured score, and code validates it and writes it. In Ask Iris the scope is frozen in code, outside the model's reach. A prompt injection can make the model say something wrong, but it cannot make it read another tenant's data or write to the database.

Q6. Per-tenant limits: give me the numbers. I won't invent a quota figure that isn't documented. The mechanism is tenant-scoped data access, bounded concurrency and deadlines at the Go edge, and, on the AI side, attempt caps, timeouts, breakers and cost telemetry. Onboarding is configuration, through the KPI configurator, not code. If you want a concrete design, I'd use a token bucket per tenant and route class, with bulk routes on a smaller bucket than interactive reads.

Q7. At Uber FRM you trusted a header. Isn't that insecure? Inside Uber's network only the gateway can inject that header, after it authenticates the user, so the service's job was identity capture for the audit trail. It returns 401 if the header is missing and stores the email on every write. The honest limitation is that authorization was upstream, not in my service. If it ever faced the internet, I'd verify a signed token and add role checks in a dependency.

Q8. At Masters, JWT or sessions? Stateless short-lived JWT access tokens with refresh tokens, because there were many microservices behind a gateway and we didn't want a shared session store on every call. RBAC protected the mutating money paths, and every mutation was audited with before and after values for GST compliance. Some enterprise clients also had IP allowlists.

10. Thirty-second story (IA)

"AssortSmart is multi-tenant. At the Go edge, a Redis-fronted waterfall verifies Firebase, JWT or Google OIDC tokens, compares API keys in constant time, and resolves roles and hierarchy scope from Postgres. Every Postgres and ClickHouse read is scoped to that. In the AI layer, Ask Iris freezes scope at the WebSocket handshake and caps its evaluator at three attempts. The Keep/Drop batch model never gets a SQL tool, and it is budgeted with timeouts, breakers and cost telemetry."

ClickHouse

How to use this page

  • What it covers: what ClickHouse is, how MergeTree tables, partitions and ReplacingMergeTree work, and exactly how I used it at Impact Analytics (AssortSmart). That includes the rollup layer, the 170GB OOM fix, the Go copier and the 2.11B-row agentic master.
  • When to read it: before any IA deep dive, any data-platform or analytics round, or any "hardest technical problem" question.
  • What to memorise: from 189 seconds to 12 seconds (15.5x) on a 250M-row harness, 170GB OOM fixed by one-week inserts, about 344k rows per second, partitions up to 4.09B rows, the 2.11B-row master. Also memorise the two traps: 15.5x is query time and 170GB is load time, and 344k is rows per second, not requests.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal (say "targeting"). "Verbal" means true and safe to say if asked, but not printed on the resume.

Say these carefully

  • 15.5x is query time (planner pivots). 170GB OOM is load time (weekly rollup builds). One did not cause the other.
  • 344k is rows per second of copy throughput. It is not requests per second or transactions per second.
  • 4.09B was measured in flight. Say "measured on a partition set of up to 4.09B rows". Do not say "I finished migrating 4.09B rows".
  • "Atomic partition rollback" means DROP PARTITION, then recopy that season. It is not an atomic swap with live readers. The REPLACE PARTITION incremental design was written but not executed.
  • ClickHouse is an Impact Analytics story only. No Kafka, Flink or CDC on IA. The CDC pipeline (pg2ch) was written by a colleague, Ashvin Sharma. Do not claim it.
  • No sub-second ClickHouse claims. The number is 12 seconds.

1. What ClickHouse is, in plain English

ClickHouse is an open-source database built for analytics. It answers questions like "total sales by store and week for this season" over hundreds of millions or billions of rows. It is not built for "update this one customer's email address". It is called an OLAP database (Online Analytical Processing), which means it is tuned for big reads that scan, filter and aggregate many rows. The opposite is OLTP (Online Transaction Processing), like PostgreSQL or MySQL, which is tuned for many small reads and writes of single rows.

Columnar storage is the core idea. A normal database stores a row together: product, store, date, units, revenue, all side by side. ClickHouse stores each column separately. Think of a filing cabinet where each drawer holds one column for every record. If you want total revenue, you open only the revenue drawer and the date drawer. You never touch the 100 other columns. That is why a column store can scan billions of values per second on one machine. Values in one column also look alike, so they compress very well.

Who uses it: product analytics teams, observability platforms, ad-tech, and in my case a retail planning SaaS where merchandise planners pivot sales data on screen.

Where it sits in my work

Where What ClickHouse did Resume bullet
Impact Analytics, Core Six rollup tables that cut planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds C4
Impact Analytics, Core Weekly rollup builds that stopped hitting a 170GB OOM C4
Impact Analytics, Core A Go native-TLS copier that moved rollups between ClickHouse Cloud clusters at about 344k rows per second C5
Impact Analytics, Core Tenant-scoped analytics store next to PostgreSQL metadata C3
Impact Analytics, Core Target of the KPI formula compiler (ifNotFinite wrapped SQL) C2
Impact Analytics, Agentic The 2.11B-row master that the LLM is never allowed to query, and the ReplacingMergeTree that stores scores A2

Nowhere else. Uber Menu used Kafka and Flink into a catalog, not ClickHouse. Masters India used PostgreSQL.

2. How ClickHouse works: the ideas interviewers probe

2.1 MergeTree: the default table engine

A table engine in ClickHouse decides how data is stored on disk. MergeTree is the main family.

  • Every INSERT writes a new immutable chunk called a part. The rows inside a part are sorted by the table's ORDER BY key.
  • In the background, ClickHouse merges small parts into bigger sorted parts. Think of sorting index cards in small piles as they arrive, then a clerk later merges the small sorted piles into one big sorted pile.
  • Because parts never change in place, updates and deletes are expensive. ClickHouse prefers you to insert new rows rather than edit old ones.
-- Teaching sketch. Column names are illustrative, not the production schema.
CREATE TABLE product_season
(
    tenant_id     String,
    season_code   String,
    product_id    String,
    store_count   UInt32,
    sales_units   Float64,
    sales_revenue Float64
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
PARTITION BY season_code
ORDER BY (tenant_id, product_id);

2.2 The sparse primary index

The ORDER BY key doubles as a sparse primary index. ClickHouse does not index every row. By default it keeps one index entry (a "mark") for every 8,192 rows. When you filter on the leading columns of the key, it uses the marks to skip whole blocks it knows cannot match. Analogy: a phone book with only the first name on each page printed in the corner. You can jump to the right page quickly without an entry for every person.

Lesson for design: put the columns you filter on most at the front of ORDER BY.

2.3 Partitions

PARTITION BY season_code splits the table into separate folders, one per season. Two big benefits:

  1. Pruning. A query for season 7 only opens the season-7 folder.
  2. Operations by unit. You can DROP PARTITION '7' and reload just that season. That was the basis of our recovery story for the copier and the weekly loader.

Do not over-partition. Thousands of tiny partitions create too many parts and slow merges. Season is a coarse, natural unit for retail planning.

2.4 ReplacingMergeTree

ReplacingMergeTree is a MergeTree variant that keeps only the newest version of rows that share the same ORDER BY key. Think of a notebook where you never erase. You write the new value on a new line, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines with the same key.

-- Teaching sketch.
CREATE TABLE article_scores
(
    tenant_id   String,
    article_id  String,
    season_code String,
    s_final     Float64,
    source      String,     -- e.g. 'blend' or 'det_fallback'
    config_hash String,
    updated_at  DateTime
)
ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(updated_at)
ORDER BY (tenant_id, season_code, article_id);

Two things interviewers check:

  • Deduplication happens at merge time, not at insert time. Until a merge runs, a query can see two versions of the same key. That is why we call it eventually consistent: it becomes correct after the background merge.
  • To read only the latest version right now, you either add FINAL to the query (slower, and older prep notes it does not use projections) or use an aggregate such as argMax(s_final, updated_at) grouped by the key.

2.5 Aggregate functions that matter in my story

  • any(x) keeps some value of x for the group. It is cheap and is used for "carry this attribute along" columns.
  • argMax(value, time) returns the value that has the largest time. It is used for "latest attribute wins".
  • ARRAY JOIN turns one row with an array into many rows. We used it to unpivot attribute pairs, which is why the attribute rollup is so much bigger than the product rollup.

2.6 Memory and spill settings

A GROUP BY keeps one in-memory state per group. With many groups and many any() / argMax states on wide strings, memory explodes. ClickHouse gives you knobs:

Setting What it does
max_memory_usage Hard cap on memory for one query. Over the cap, the query fails with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED.
max_bytes_before_external_group_by When the GROUP BY state passes this size, spill partial results to disk instead of failing.
max_threads How many threads one query may use. More threads means more parallel state in memory.

3. Bullet C4: the rollup layer and the 15.5x pivot win

Reduced planner pivot latency by 15.5x (189s to 12s on 250M-row operations) by building a ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer for season and weekly rollups. Prevented 170GB OOM crashes by slicing batch inserts into temporal chunks and enforcing strict distributed memory and disk-spill caps.

3.1 In plain words

Planners look at sales grids (pivots) such as "units by product by store for this season". A pivot is the spreadsheet-like grid: rows by product hierarchy, columns by week or store, cells aggregated. On PostgreSQL the heavy pivot grid took 189 seconds on a 250M-row benchmark harness. On ClickHouse the same query on the same 250M rows took about 12 seconds (12.3 seconds, rounded on the resume). That engine comparison is where 15.5x comes from. In production, the grids are served from a pre-aggregation layer: six rollup tables, so most of the summing happens once at load time and the screen reads small summarised tables.

Say this carefully: the 189-to-12 measurement is PostgreSQL versus ClickHouse on the same heavy query. The rollup layer is how production serves those grids on ClickHouse. If an interviewer asks "was 189 seconds the daily table and 12 seconds the rollup?", the honest answer is no. It was the engine comparison that justified moving the grids to ClickHouse, and the rollups are the production design built on that decision.

3.2 How it works

flowchart LR RAW["Daily facts: SKU x store x date"] --> BUILD["Rollup build job: INSERT SELECT with GROUP BY"] BUILD --> PS["product_season"] BUILD --> SS["store_season"] BUILD --> AS["attr_season"] BUILD --> PW["product_weekly"] BUILD --> SW["store_weekly"] BUILD --> AW["attr_weekly"] PS --> API["Go/Gin planner API"] SW --> API AW --> API API --> UI["Planner pivot grid"]

What to notice: all the heavy GROUP BY work moves to the left (load time). The planner screen on the right only reads small tables.

Six MergeTree tables, all PARTITION BY season_code:

Grain Product (keeps SKU dimensions) Store (no SKU) Attribute (unpivoted with ARRAY JOIN)
Season product_season store_season attr_season
Weekly product_weekly store_weekly attr_weekly

A worked example. Suppose the daily table has these rows for one product in one store:

product store date units
P1 S1 2026-03-02 4
P1 S1 2026-03-03 6
P1 S1 2026-03-09 5

The weekly rollup stores two rows (week 10: 10 units, week 11: 5 units). The season rollup stores one row (15 units). Multiply this by every day of a season and every store, and the planner reads a table that is orders of magnitude smaller.

-- Teaching sketch of a season rollup build.
INSERT INTO product_season
SELECT tenant_id, season_code, product_id,
       uniqExact(store_id)   AS store_count,
       sum(units)            AS sales_units,
       sum(revenue)          AS sales_revenue
FROM daily_facts
WHERE season_code = '7'
GROUP BY tenant_id, season_code, product_id;

Two design details worth saying:

  • Store and attribute totals must match the SKU totals. Older prep describes two-pass weighted sums with re-weighting, then validating sum(product) against sum(store) against sum(attr) at the same filters. Earlier season-grain parity checks showed 0% difference on revenue across seasons 1 to 7 (verbal).
  • The attribute table is an unpivot. One product with several attribute pairs becomes several rows. That is why attr weekly is roughly 5 times the size of product weekly on the same seasons (verbal).

3.3 Why this design

  • What: pay once at load, read cheap at query time.
  • Why: planners click through grids all day. Waiting minutes per pivot kills the product. A GROUP BY over a wide daily table with many any() / argMax states is the wrong thing to run per click.
  • How: six rollup tables, partitioned by season, generated load SQL, build order product then store then attribute per grain.
  • Alternatives considered:
  • Stay on PostgreSQL. Planner pivots were slow on PostgreSQL. We ran POCs comparing Postgres and ClickHouse at 5M, 50M and 250M rows. ClickHouse won the heavy grid at every size (13.8x at 5M, 13.0x at 50M, 15.5x at 250M), and Postgres also spilled about 42 GB of sort files to disk on the 250M run. The harness was not tilted toward ClickHouse: Postgres ran natively on a 48 GB host with 8 parallel workers, while ClickHouse ran in a 10-CPU, 3.3 GB Docker VM. The same POCs showed Postgres much faster for single-cell write-back (POC history, verbal only), which is why the verdict was hybrid. Postgres stays for thin metadata, UAM (User Access Management), roles and writes.
  • Query BigQuery directly. BigQuery is on the IA tech line. Older Copilot design notes compared against BigQuery's variable interactive latency (roughly 1 to 20+ seconds). That comparison is verbal only. The simple point is that a serverless warehouse billed per bytes scanned is a poor fit for a click-heavy grid.
  • Snowflake. Older prep lists cost and latency for this interactive UI as the reasons against.
  • Materialized views in ClickHouse. They update on insert, which is great for simple sums. Our rollups carry many attribute states and need controlled rebuilds, so explicit build jobs were easier to reason about and to recover.
  • Trade-off: data in rollups is only as fresh as the last build. Rollups also take disk and build time. And rollups do not help every query shape (see the caveat below).
  • What I'd do differently: design the incremental path (only rebuild changed partitions, with REPLACE PARTITION from scratch tables) from day one. That design exists on paper. It was not executed.

3.4 The numbers

Number What it measures How derived Tag
189s to 12s Wall time of the heavy pivot grid query (group-by plus contribution percent plus option count) on PostgreSQL, then on ClickHouse Benchmark harness: Postgres 189,408 ms, ClickHouse 12,256 ms on the same query and the same 250M rows. 12.3s rounds to 12s MEASURED
15.5x Speed ratio of the two 189,408 / 12,256 is about 15.45, which rounds to 15.5x MEASURED
250M rows Size of the benchmark dataset Built at 5M, 50M and 250M. The largest client was around 5M at the time, so 250M tested growth. It is not the production table size (the master is 2.11B) MEASURED

Why it mattered: at 189 seconds the grid is unusable, because planners wait three minutes per click. At about 12 seconds it becomes workable.

Say it out loud: "Planner pivots got about fifteen and a half times faster, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on 250 million rows. We benchmarked at 250 million so the decision would survive growth."

Do NOT say: "sub-second", "every query is 15x faster", "our production table is 250M rows", or "the OOM fix made it 15x faster".

Caveat to keep in your pocket: 15.5x is the heavy grid query. The benchmark's own adversarial review said typical aggregates are closer to 2 to 3 times faster. If asked whether every query got 15x faster, say no and give that number.

4. Bullet C4 continued: the 170GB OOM on weekly builds

This is my best "hardest technical problem" story. OOM means out of memory: the database killed the query because it needed more RAM than it was allowed.

4.1 What broke

Weekly rollups need about 110 any() states plus argMax / argMin over wide string columns. A whole-season weekly INSERT SELECT was estimated at around 170GB of aggregation state. It failed with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED even at an 80GB cap, and again at a 200GB cap. The replica had about 59 cores and about 234 to 236 GiB of RAM (verbal).

4.2 How I fixed it

The unit of work became one fiscal week per INSERT, not one season. Then I capped each insert.

Knob (verbal, off PDF) Value
Memory cap per insert 55 GB
Disk spill threshold 16 GB
Threads per insert 8
Weeks in flight at once 4
Observed peak, product week about 11 GB
Observed peak, attribute week over 40 GB (a 40GB cap was too low) 
-- Teaching sketch: one fiscal week per insert, with caps.
INSERT INTO attr_weekly
SELECT ...
FROM daily_facts
WHERE season_code = '7' AND fiscal_year_week = 202611
GROUP BY ...
SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 55000000000,
         max_bytes_before_external_group_by = 16000000000,
         max_threads = 8;
flowchart LR S["Whole season weekly insert"] --> F["About 170GB of state. Fails at 80GB and 200GB caps"] W["One fiscal week per insert"] --> C["Caps: 55GB memory, 16GB spill, 8 threads"] C --> P["4 weeks in flight. Product week about 11GB. Attr week over 40GB"] P --> OK["Weekly grain builds succeed"]

What to notice: I made the work unit smaller before I touched the memory limit. Raising RAM had already failed twice.

4.3 Lessons to say

  • Profile by grain first. Attribute weeks were the memory hog.
  • Shrink the unit before raising the cap.
  • Do not raise season parallelism and week parallelism together on the same box, because caps are per query and they add up.

4.4 Ghost rows on the weekly loader

A ghost row here means rows left behind by a half-finished load that look like a complete load. A failed HTTP INSERT in ClickHouse can still commit some blocks. Once, a half-loaded partition of 64.1M rows passed a naive "skip this season if the partition already has rows" check (verbal). The fix:

  • Keep a TSV ledger (a simple tab-separated file) of finished (kind, season_code) pairs. Resume only skips entries in the ledger.
  • If a season is not in the ledger, DROP PARTITION for that season and rebuild it.
  • Treat an insert as finished only when system.query_log shows it completed (QueryFinish for that query id), not when the HTTP client exits.

5. Bullet C5: the Go native-TLS copier

Migrated ClickHouse rollups across Cloud clusters at ~344k rows/s by writing a custom Go native-TLS data pump to bypass strict cross-cluster IP allowlist restrictions. Processed partitions up to 4.09B rows using 500k-row double-buffered batches, and eliminated partial-commit ghost rows using TSV ledgers and atomic partition rollbacks.

5.1 In plain words

We had to move rollup tables from one ClickHouse Cloud cluster to another. The normal approach is to have the target cluster pull from the source directly. That was blocked: each cluster only accepted connections from an IP allowlist (a list of approved network addresses), and cluster-to-cluster pulls were not on it. An operator machine was allowlisted on both sides. So I wrote a Go program that reads from the source and writes to the target over ClickHouse's native protocol with TLS (port 9440), streaming columnar batches through that machine.

5.2 How it works

source ClickHouse Cloud  --native TLS-->  Go copier  --native TLS-->  target ClickHouse Cloud
        SELECT stream                     buffer A fills              INSERT Send() of buffer B
        500k rows, columnar               while B sends               checkpoint per season

What to notice: reading the next batch overlaps with sending the previous one. That overlap is "double buffering".

  • Native protocol, not HTTP. It sends data in columnar blocks, which is cheaper than text formats. Older prep notes HTTP SELECT streams also hit "unexpected EOF" while sitting idle during a long INSERT.
  • Columnar 500k batches. batchSize = 500_000. Values go into typed slices per column (batch.Column(i).Append), then Send(). No per-row reflection.
  • Double buffering. Two buffer sets. While batch N is being sent, batch N+1 is being read.
  • Partition unit is season_code. -workers N copies N seasons in parallel, each with its own source and target connections.
  • Checkpoints. A finished season is recorded in migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done. A per-table file lock stops two terminals copying the same table.
  • Failure handling. On SIGINT the copier finishes the in-flight batch but does not mark that season done. Never retry Send() on a spent batch, because that risks duplicates. An incomplete season gets DROP PARTITION, then a recopy.
// Teaching sketch of double buffering. Not the production code.
next := make(chan *Batch, 1)
go func() {
    for rows.Next() {
        b := readBatch(rows, 500_000) // fill buffer while the other one sends
        next <- b
    }
    close(next)
}()
for b := range next {
    if err := b.Send(ctx); err != nil {
        return err // do not retry a spent batch; season is not checkpointed
    }
}
markDone(table, season) // writes migrate-checkpoints/<table>.done

5.3 Why this design and alternatives

  • Why: the allowlists made the simple path impossible. The pump is a workaround for a network constraint, not an architecture goal.
  • Alternatives:
  • Use ClickHouse's built-in cluster-to-cluster copy (INSERT SELECT with the remoteSecure table function). This is the right answer when the clusters can reach each other. The allowlists blocked it.
  • Export to object storage and re-import. This is a valid approach for frozen data. It adds a staging hop and storage cost.
  • Write CSV over HTTP. Slower, and it hit the EOF problem.
  • Trade-off: copying through one operator machine means its network and CPU are the ceiling, and a connection reset crashes the run. Checkpointing only finished seasons limits the blast radius.
  • What I'd do differently: for production cutovers, push for the allowlist change or an object-storage freeze, and run the REPLACE PARTITION design so readers never see a partial season.

5.4 The numbers

Number What it measures How derived Tag
~344k rows/s Combined copy throughput of two season streams Each stream sends a 500k-row batch about 0.3 to 0.4 times a second, so 0.3 x 500,000 = 150k and 0.4 x 500,000 = 200k rows per second per stream. Observed about 150k to 190k each at a live snapshot about 34 minutes in. Two streams combined gave about 344k MEASURED snapshot
4.09B Largest object copied: attr weekly, two seasons 2,779,317,472 + 1,311,108,195 MEASURED, copy in flight
500k Rows per batch Code constant MEASURED

Say it out loud: "The copier ran two season streams at about 150 to 190 thousand rows a second each, so about 344 thousand rows a second combined. I measured that on the largest object, an attribute weekly table of about 4.09 billion rows across two seasons."

For scale only: 4.09B rows at 344k rows per second would take roughly 11,900 seconds, a bit over 3 hours, and 4.09B / 500k is about 8,180 batches. That is arithmetic, not a measured duration.

Do NOT say "344k RPS", "344k TPS", or "migrated 4.09 billion rows" as if it finished. If asked "did it finish?", say: "At the snapshot, some tables were done and attr weekly was still in flight. So I say measured on, not migrated."

6. Bullet A2: the 2.11B-row master and why the LLM never queries it

Decoupled AI inference from a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master by asynchronously serving context via JSON payloads rather than direct database querying. Engineered an eventually consistent write pattern via ReplacingMergeTree that guaranteed system availability by gracefully falling back to deterministic baselines during LLM timeouts.

In plain words: the Keep/Drop engine needs facts about each article-season (an article-season is one product in one selling season). Instead of giving the LLM a database tool, our code queries ClickHouse, builds a small JSON payload of the facts for each item, and sends that to the LLM. The LLM returns a structured score. Our code writes the result back as a new row version into a ReplacingMergeTree table. If the LLM times out, we write the deterministic baseline score instead, so every item still gets a decision.

sequenceDiagram participant Batch as Python batch participant CH as ClickHouse 2.11B master participant LLM as LLM lens call participant RMT as ReplacingMergeTree scores Batch->>CH: SQL written by our code CH-->>Batch: Facts for 88k items Batch->>LLM: JSON payload per item, no SQL tool alt LLM answers in time LLM-->>Batch: Structured score Batch->>RMT: INSERT blended score with config_hash else LLM timeout Batch->>RMT: INSERT deterministic baseline score end

What to notice: the LLM only ever sees JSON. It has no way to run a query against 2.11 billion rows.

  • Why: a 2.11B-row master cannot take hallucinated queries, and the model must never write. "Async" describes how batches run. The isolation rule is that the model has no SQL tool.
  • Why ReplacingMergeTree: a re-run or a fallback simply inserts a newer version. No UPDATE statements on a column store. Readers converge on the latest version after merges.
  • Trade-off: an extra hop to build payloads, and readers may briefly see two versions until a merge, unless they read with argMax or FINAL.
  • Different table: the 2.11B master is the agentic fact table. It is not the 4.09B attr weekly rollup and not the 250M harness. Keep the three numbers apart.

7. Tenancy and the KPI compiler (bullets C2 and C3), briefly

  • C3: every ClickHouse read is scoped to the caller's tenant and their UAM hierarchy. The same tenant id lives in PostgreSQL (identity, UAM, roles) and in ClickHouse (facts). Isolation is access control, not encryption. Details: auth_tenancy_rate_limits.md.
  • C2: operators write KPI formulas such as sales_units / (sales_units + eoh_units). A Go tokenizer and parser turn them into parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragments with allowlisted functions, map logical names to physical columns, and wrap the result in ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0). A divide by zero produces 0 instead of inf or nan, so bad values never reach the planner's JSON. Unknown tokens fail closed. Details: go_gin.md.
-- Illustrative output of the KPI compiler for "sell-through".
ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(sales_units) / (sum(sales_units) + sum(eoh_units))), 0) AS sell_through

8. Verbal-only ClickHouse material (not on the resume)

Use only if the interviewer goes deeper and you are comfortable.

  • Older prep described a per-tenant planning-store DDL design of 63 tables across 8 layers, insert-only, with partition swaps, and an agent connection set to readonly=1. That belongs to the Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight designs, which are verbal only and not resume bullets. Present it as design work, not as shipped tables.
  • Older prep also said not to quote a "624 columns" figure. Leave it out.
  • The catalog is about 1.6M article-seasons (off PDF). That is different from the 348k article-seasons scored by the Keep/Drop engine.
  • Product weekly for seasons 6 and 7 is about 839M rows (569.4M + 269.8M). This is verbal scale context.
  • Older prep quoted "2.4B weekly rollups". The current resume uses 4.09B (attr weekly, two seasons). Do not quote 2.4B.
  • POC history behind the hybrid verdict ("Order Batching 60x", "Postgres single-cell edit about 82x faster") is background, not a resume claim.

9. ClickHouse versus the alternatives

Option Best at Why not for planner pivots
PostgreSQL Transactions, joins, row updates, metadata Row store. The heavy grid took 189 seconds at 250M rows in our benchmark
BigQuery Serverless warehouse, ad hoc analysis Variable interactive latency, cost per bytes scanned
Snowflake Managed warehouse Cost and latency for a click-heavy UI (older prep)
Apache Druid / Pinot Real-time OLAP from streams Not used. More moving parts. Do not claim
ClickHouse Fast columnar scans and aggregation, cheap compression Painful updates and deletes, eventual dedupe, needs care with memory

When I would pick something else: if the workload is mostly single-row updates with strict transactions, PostgreSQL. If the team has no ops capacity and queries are ad hoc and rare, a managed warehouse.

10. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. Why ClickHouse and not PostgreSQL for everything? Postgres is a row store built for transactions. Planner pivots scan and aggregate hundreds of millions of rows, which is a columnar workload. We benchmarked both at 5M, 50M and 250M rows, and on the heavy grid ClickHouse took about 12 seconds where Postgres took 189 seconds at 250M. Postgres was still better at single-cell write-back, so the answer was hybrid: Postgres keeps thin metadata, UAM, roles and writes, and ClickHouse serves the facts and rollups. Follow-up they may ask: "How do you keep the two consistent?" The same tenant id and hierarchy keys exist in both, and the access layer applies scope to both. Postgres is not replicating facts into ClickHouse in my story.

Q2. Explain MergeTree and partitions. Every insert writes an immutable sorted part, and background merges combine parts. The ORDER BY key is also a sparse index, one mark per block of rows, so filters on the key skip whole blocks. Partitions split the table by a coarse key. We used season, so queries prune to one season and we can drop and reload a single season. That made recovery simple: if a season load was incomplete, drop that partition and rebuild it.

Q3. Tell me about the 170GB OOM. Weekly rollups carry about 110 any() states plus argMax over wide strings. A whole-season weekly insert needed about 170GB of aggregation state, and it failed even at 80GB and 200GB caps. I changed the unit of work to one fiscal week per insert, capped each insert at 55GB with a 16GB disk spill and 8 threads, and ran 4 weeks in flight. A product week peaked around 11GB and an attribute week over 40GB, and the weekly grain built cleanly. Follow-up: "Did that cause the 15.5x?" No. The OOM was load time. 15.5x is query time on a separate harness.

Q4. How did you get about 344k rows per second? It is copy throughput, not request rate. Two season streams over the native protocol with TLS, each about 150 to 190 thousand rows a second. The copier uses 500k-row columnar batches with typed buffers and double buffering, so the read of the next batch overlaps the send of the previous one. I measured it on the largest object, about 4.09 billion rows of attribute weekly data, while that copy was in flight.

Q5. How did you make billion-row copies safe to restart? The unit is one season partition. A season is marked done in a checkpoint file only after every batch is sent. If a run dies mid-season, I drop that partition on the target and recopy it. I never retry a spent batch, because that is how you get duplicates. I am careful to say this is not an atomic swap: readers can see a partial season until the recopy finishes. The REPLACE PARTITION design that fixes that was written but not run.

Q6. What is ReplacingMergeTree and why use it for AI scores? It keeps the latest version of rows with the same key, using a version column, and it deduplicates during background merges. For scores, that means a re-run or a fallback just inserts a newer version, with no UPDATE on a column store. If the LLM times out, we insert the deterministic baseline so every article still has a decision. The trade-off is that until a merge runs, a reader can see two versions, so reads use argMax or FINAL when they need exactly one.

Q7. Why did you not let the LLM query ClickHouse directly? Because a hallucinated query against a 2.11-billion-row master is a cost and safety risk, and the model must never write. Our code runs known SQL, builds a JSON payload per item and sends that to the model. The model returns a structured score that our code validates and inserts. It is one extra hop, and it is the isolation guarantee.

Q8. What are ClickHouse's weaknesses? Updates and deletes are expensive mutations. Deduplication is eventual. Joins on very large right-hand tables need care. And memory blows up on high-cardinality GROUP BYs, which is exactly what bit us on weekly builds. I design around those by inserting new versions instead of updating, partitioning by a coarse unit, and slicing heavy builds.

Apache Flink (Uber Menu hot path), with Spark as a verbal backfill option

How to use this page

  • What it covers: what Apache Flink is, the ideas interviewers probe (keyed state, event time, watermarks, checkpoints, backpressure, exactly-once), and how the Flink job sat in the Uber Menu ingestion pipeline. It also covers Spark, but only as a verbal "how I would backfill" answer.
  • When to read it: before the Uber Menu deep dive, any streaming design round, or a "why Flink and not Spark" question.
  • What to memorise: Flink did keyed deduplication (by vendor and content hash), schema validation and normalization, and routing between the structured path and the RAG path. Exactly-once catalog upserts in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts. Flink is Menu only.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal.

Say these carefully

  • Flink is Uber Menu only. Never Masters India (that was Kafka plus Spring Kafka consumers). Never Impact Analytics (that was ClickHouse plus a Python batch pipeline).
  • Spark is not on the resume. Treat it as "how I would do backfills", a verbal option. Do not claim Spark ownership.
  • Do not claim a measured Flink peak throughput. The about 200 to 500 events per second figure is an ESTIMATE used in prep only.
  • Exactly-once on the resume means the catalog ends up with each change once. Mechanically that is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts. No zero-message-loss claims and no two-phase commit across Gemini or third-party sites.
  • The menu pipeline wrote to a catalog, not ClickHouse.

1. What Flink is, in plain English

Apache Flink is a stream processor: a framework for running long-lived programs that read an endless stream of events, keep some memory about what they have seen, and emit results continuously. Think of a sorting clerk at a post office who never goes home. Letters (events) arrive all day. The clerk remembers which letters each address already got, throws away exact duplicates, fixes badly written addresses, and drops each letter into the right outgoing bin. The clerk also takes a photo of the desk every few minutes, so if they faint, a replacement can pick up exactly from the last photo.

The "memory" is what makes Flink different from a simple Kafka consumer. Flink manages state for you, keeps it fault tolerant, and lets you reason about when events happened rather than when they arrived.

Who uses it: companies with real-time pipelines for fraud detection, metrics, enrichment, deduplication and stream joins.

2. How Flink works: the ideas interviewers probe

2.1 Jobs, operators and parallelism

A Flink job is a graph of operators, for example source, then map, then keyed process, then sink. Each operator runs as several parallel copies called subtasks. When reading from Kafka, a source subtask reads one or more partitions, so useful source parallelism is roughly the Kafka partition count.

2.2 keyBy and keyed state

keyBy(vendor_id) routes every event with the same key to the same subtask. That subtask can keep keyed state: a small value per key, such as "the last content hash I saw for this vendor's menu". Flink stores it, scales it across machines, and restores it after a crash. For large state, a disk-backed state backend such as RocksDB is used (older prep names RocksDB for this job).

# Teaching sketch in PyFlink style. Not production code.
class DedupeMenu(KeyedProcessFunction):
    def open(self, ctx):
        self.last_hash = ctx.get_state(ValueStateDescriptor("last_hash", Types.STRING()))

    def process_element(self, event, ctx):
        h = event["content_hash"]
        if self.last_hash.value() == h:
            return                      # exact duplicate page or retry: drop it
        self.last_hash.update(h)
        yield normalize(event)          # schema normalization, then route downstream

stream.key_by(lambda e: e["vendor_id"]).process(DedupeMenu())

What to notice: dedupe is a per-vendor memory of "what did I last see", which is exactly what keyed state is for.

A worked example. Vendor 42's menu page is scraped three times because of anti-bot retries:

Arrival vendor_id content_hash Action
1 42 a1f9 New hash: normalize and send to catalog upsert
2 42 a1f9 Same hash: drop
3 42 c77e Menu actually changed: normalize and upsert the new version

2.3 Event time and watermarks

  • Processing time is when Flink sees the event.
  • Event time is when the event really happened, here the scrape timestamp carried in the event.

Scrapes arrive out of order because of retries and slow pages. If you decide "latest menu wins" by arrival order, a late, older page can overwrite a newer one. Flink lets you work in event time.

A watermark is Flink's running statement that "I believe I have now seen everything up to time T". With bounded out-of-orderness of, say, a few minutes (illustrative), Flink waits that long before closing windows or treating a key as settled. Events that arrive later than the watermark are late events and can be dropped, sent to a side output, or used to update state, depending on the design.

Analogy: a teacher collecting homework says "anything dated before Monday counts if it reaches me by Wednesday". Wednesday is the watermark.

Older prep describes the Menu rule as event-time last-write-wins: the version with the newest scrape timestamp wins, not the one that arrived last.

2.4 Checkpoints and recovery

Flink periodically takes a checkpoint, a consistent snapshot of all operator state plus the Kafka offsets that produced it. It does this by sending checkpoint barriers through the stream, like a marker dropped into a conveyor belt. When every operator has seen the marker, the snapshot is complete. If a machine dies, Flink restarts the job from the last checkpoint: state goes back to the snapshot, and Kafka is re-read from the matching offsets.

The consequence: after a crash, some events after the checkpoint are processed again. That is fine if the sink is idempotent, and it is why the catalog upsert had to be idempotent.

2.5 Exactly-once, honestly

  • Inside Flink, checkpoints give exactly-once state: each event affects Flink's state once.
  • Into Kafka, a transactional sink can give exactly-once output.
  • Into an external catalog, you need the catalog write to be idempotent or transactional. We used idempotent upserts keyed by vendor, menu and version or content hash.

So the resume's "exactly-once catalog upserts" means the catalog shows each change once. Mechanically it is at-least-once plus idempotent upserts.

2.6 Backpressure

If the sink (catalog or the RAG path) slows down, Flink's network buffers fill up and its credit-based flow control slows the upstream operators, which in turn read Kafka more slowly. The visible symptom is rising Kafka consumer lag, which is the right alert. The system slows down instead of running out of memory.

3. Where Flink sat in Uber Menu

Scaled menu extraction success to 95%+ by hardening a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries. Designed a large-scale data ingestion and processing pipeline using Kafka and Apache Flink, with stateful keyed deduplication and schema normalization to guarantee exactly-once catalog upserts.

flowchart LR SEL["Selenium scrapers"] --> K["Kafka keyed by vendor_id"] K --> V["Flink: schema validate"] V --> D["Flink: keyed dedupe by content hash, event-time latest wins"] D --> N["Flink: normalize to catalog schema"] N --> R{"Structured enough?"} R -->|"yes"| CAT["Idempotent catalog upsert"] R -->|"no, PDF or image or low confidence"| RAG["LangChain RAG plus Gemini 2.5 Pro over Milvus"] RAG --> CAT

What to notice: one Flink job does validate, dedupe, normalize and route, before anything touches the catalog or the expensive LLM path.

Step by step for one menu:

  1. A scraper fetches vendor 42's menu page and publishes an event with vendor_id, scrape timestamp, raw payload reference and content hash.
  2. Kafka stores it in vendor 42's partition.
  3. Flink validates the event shape and drops malformed events to a side path.
  4. Keyed dedupe: if the content hash equals the last one seen for vendor 42, drop it. If it is newer in event time, keep it.
  5. Normalization maps fields to the catalog schema (names, prices, currency, modifiers).
  6. Routing: clean structured menus go straight to the catalog upsert. Unstructured inputs (multilingual PDFs, images) go to the RAG extraction path, then back through schema validation to the catalog.
  7. The catalog upsert is keyed, so a re-delivery after a checkpoint restore changes nothing.

Why we needed Flink at Menu scale

30K+ menus a month is about 1,000 a day. That is not a "huge TPS" problem, and I say so. The drivers were the shape of the data:

  1. Bursts and retries from the Selenium fleet and anti-bot backoff. You need continuous processing, not a nightly batch.
  2. Keyed dedupe. The same vendor emits duplicate and late pages. Keyed state drops duplicates cheaply.
  3. Event time. Scrape timestamps arrive out of order. Watermarks bound how long to wait.
  4. Freshness. Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours. Waiting for batch windows would eat into that.
  5. Fan-out routing. One job validates and then splits structured and unstructured paths.

4. Design decisions

Flink on the hot path

  • What: a stateful Flink job between Kafka and the catalog.
  • Why: keyed dedupe, event-time ordering and routing in one place, with checkpointed state.
  • Alternatives considered:
  • Plain Kafka consumers in Python. Fine for stateless transforms. You end up re-implementing keyed state, checkpoints and late-event handling yourself.
  • Kafka Streams. A real option for lighter transforms, and I admit it could have worked at this event rate. Flink was preferred for richer event-time support, larger keyed state and a clearer operational model for a dedicated processing cluster.
  • Spark Structured Streaming. Micro-batches add seconds of delay and keyed state is more awkward. Better for batch-shaped work.
  • Dedupe in the catalog database only. Possible with unique keys, but every duplicate still costs a write and possibly an LLM call. Dropping duplicates before the RAG path saves money.
  • Trade-off: Flink is another cluster to run, and state can grow large if key cardinality explodes.
  • What I'd do differently: add state TTL (time-to-live) from the start so dedupe state for vendors that went quiet expires automatically, and version the parse modules so a bad parser can be rolled back without touching the job graph.

Flink versus Spark

Need Flink Spark
Keyed state per vendor or menu Native More awkward
Event time and late pages Watermarks Possible, with micro-batch delay
Catalog freshness in minutes Better fit Heavier
Huge historical reprocess (for example 90 days) Possible Better fit

Spark as a verbal backfill answer (not on the resume)

If asked "how would you reprocess 90 days after a schema change?", the answer is a batch job, and Spark is a natural tool: read raw payloads from object storage, transform with DataFrames, write idempotent upserts. Older prep estimated about 1 to 2 million item rows for a typical multi-day reprocess window. Treat that as ESTIMATED and verbal only. Watch for skew: very large vendors can be salted or isolated. Do not claim Spark kernel or Delta Lake work.

5. Failure modes and recovery

Failure What happens Recovery
TaskManager (worker) dies Job restarts from the last checkpoint State and Kafka offsets roll back together. Idempotent catalog upserts absorb re-processed events. Lag alert fires until caught up
Bad parser or normalizer deploy Wrong data goes to the catalog Stop the job, fix, rewind Kafka offsets to before the bad deploy (restore from a savepoint or checkpoint from before it), reprocess. Batch backfill for larger gaps
State blowup Key cardinality explodes, checkpoints get slow State TTL, tighter keys, RocksDB backend
Idle partitions stall watermarks A quiet Kafka partition holds back event time for everyone Idleness detection on the source so idle partitions do not block the watermark
Brittle HTML or PDF parsing inside the job Exceptions on certain vendors Route failures to a side output, version parse modules, keep the job alive

6. The numbers tied to Flink

Number What it measures How derived Tag
30K+ menus a month Volume through the pipeline Work records. About 1,000 a day HISTORICAL
From 24 hours to 2 hours Onboarding time Work records. 24 / 2 = 12 times faster, about a 92% cut HISTORICAL
95%+ extraction success Usable scrapes From an estimated 60 to 65% HISTORICAL, baseline ESTIMATED
About 200 to 500 events per second peak Kafka and Flink event rate during fleet runs About 1,000 menus a day, each emitting many item, retry and health events, concentrated into short fleet windows ESTIMATED, prep only

Say it out loud: "Volume was about 30 thousand menus a month. The pipeline is justified by burstiness, duplicates and replay, not raw throughput."

Do NOT say: "We ran Flink at millions of events per second", or anything that ties Flink to ClickHouse.

7. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. Why Flink and not just Kafka consumers? Plain consumers are fine for stateless work. We needed per-vendor keyed state for dedupe, event-time ordering because scrapes arrive late and out of order, and one job that validates, dedupes, normalizes and routes before anything hits the catalog or the LLM. Flink gives that state with checkpoints, so I am not hand-building fault-tolerant state in a consumer. For example, a retried scrape with the same content hash is dropped in Flink and never costs a Gemini call.

Q2. Why Flink and not Spark? For the hot path, freshness and keyed state matter, and Flink is built for true streaming with native keyed state and watermarks. Spark Structured Streaming works in micro-batches, which adds delay and makes per-key state clumsier. Spark is the better tool for big historical reprocessing, so that is where I would use it, but it is not on my resume and I describe it as an option.

Q3. How do you handle late events? We use event time from the scrape timestamp, with a watermark that allows bounded out-of-orderness. Within that bound, a late but newer-in-event-time page still wins. Anything later than the watermark goes to a side output instead of silently overwriting newer data. The rule is that the newest scrape timestamp wins, not the last arrival.

Q4. What is in your dedupe key? The key is the vendor id, which is also the Kafka partition key, so ordering and state line up. The state is the last content hash or menu version seen for that vendor. A duplicate hash is dropped. A changed hash is a real update and flows on. The catalog upsert is keyed the same way, so even if Flink replays after a restore, the catalog sees no duplicate.

Q5. A checkpoint fails mid-fleet. What happens? The job restarts from the last successful checkpoint. State goes back to that snapshot and Kafka offsets rewind to the positions recorded with it. Events after that point are processed again, and the idempotent upserts absorb them. Consumer lag rises and alerts until the job catches up. If a whole window was corrupted by bad code, we rewind further or run a batch backfill.

Q6. Is 30K menus a month enough to justify Flink? Not if you only look at the average. About 1,000 menus a day is modest. The justification is the shape: bursty scraper waves, retries that create duplicates, out-of-order pages, a need to replay after bad deploys, and a split into structured and RAG paths. At this event rate Kafka Streams or a careful consumer could also work, and I would say that openly. Flink gave us managed keyed state and checkpoints for those properties.

Q7. How did you get exactly-once catalog upserts? Flink checkpoints give exactly-once state inside the job, but the catalog is an external system. So the catalog write is an idempotent upsert keyed by vendor, menu and version. Delivery is at-least-once, and replays are no-ops. I do not claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across Gemini or third-party sites.

Q8. How do you roll back a bad parser? Stop the job, fix or revert the parser, and restart from a checkpoint or savepoint taken before the bad deploy, which rewinds Kafka offsets with it. Then reprocess. Because upserts are idempotent and latest event time wins, the corrected output overwrites the bad output. For gaps bigger than Kafka retention, a batch backfill from the stored raw payloads is the tool.

Resume placement

  • Skills line: Apache Flink under Data and Streaming.
  • Menu bullet and Menu tech line: Kafka plus Flink.
  • Masters: Kafka only. IA: neither.
