Go and Gin (Impact Analytics platform)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: what Go and the Gin framework are, the Go ideas interviewers probe (goroutines, context, middleware, timeouts, HTTP/2, dependency injection), and exactly how I used Go at Impact Analytics. That means the 10k-peak-RPS Gin platform with Google Wire, h2c, nested timeouts and Datadog, the KPI formula compiler, the auth middleware and the ClickHouse copier.
  • When to read it: before any Go round, any backend or platform system design round, and the IA Core Infrastructure deep dive.
  • What to memorise: "self-protecting HTTP edge without a reverse proxy" means the Go process itself owns timeouts, limits, HTTP/2 and tracing. Also memorise what Wire, h2c and ifNotFinite each do in one sentence, and that 10k peak RPS is the stated peak with no SLA attached.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. STATED means it is printed on the resume from the project's own source, with no extra arithmetic in prep; if asked how it was measured, keep it qualitative. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. TARGET means a design goal. Verbal means true but off the resume.

Say these carefully

  • IA platform APIs are Go/Gin. The IA agent plane (Keep/Drop batch, Ask Iris) is Python with FastAPI and LangGraph.
  • 10k peak RPS is the stated peak of the Go edge. Do not add a latency SLA, a p99, a tenant count or any other IA throughput number.
  • No Kubernetes cluster operations claim. Kubernetes is skills-level literacy only.
  • Snippets on this page are teaching sketches with illustrative values. They show the mechanism. They are not copies of company code.
  • 100% Go statement coverage and 1,200+ Go tests are true but off the resume (LinkedIn and verbal).

1. What Go and Gin are, in plain English

Go (also called Golang) is a programming language from Google. It compiles to a single native binary, has static types, a garbage collector, and very cheap concurrency built into the language. It is popular for network services, infrastructure tools and APIs because it gives predictable latency and low memory use without the complexity of C++.

Gin is a lightweight web framework for Go. It sits on top of Go's standard net/http server and adds a fast router, middleware chaining, request binding and validation, and JSON helpers. Think of net/http as the engine and Gin as the dashboard and steering wheel.

Who uses them: cloud infrastructure companies, fintech backends, and API platforms that need many concurrent connections per machine.

Where Go sits in my work

Where What Go did Resume bullet
IA Core Multi-tenant Go/Gin platform, 10k peak RPS, Wire, h2c, nested timeouts, Datadog tracing C1
IA Core KPI configurator: Go tokenizer and parser that compiles formulas to ClickHouse SQL C2
IA Core Auth waterfall middleware (Redis, Firebase Admin, JWT and Google OIDC, API keys, Postgres roles) C3
IA Core Native-TLS ClickHouse copier at about 344k rows per second C5

Go appears only at Impact Analytics. Uber FRM and Masters India were Java with Spring Boot. Uber Menu was Python. GeeksforGeeks was Django.

2. How Go works: the ideas interviewers probe

2.1 Goroutines and the scheduler

A goroutine is a very lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime. It starts with a few kilobytes of stack, so a server can run tens of thousands of them. Go's net/http server starts one goroutine per connection or request. The runtime scheduler multiplexes many goroutines onto a few OS threads. When a goroutine waits on network I/O, the scheduler parks it and runs another one. Analogy: a restaurant with a few cooks (OS threads) and hundreds of order tickets (goroutines). A cook never stands still waiting for an oven; they pick up the next ticket.

2.2 Channels and sync

Channels pass values between goroutines safely ("share memory by communicating"). The sync package gives mutexes and wait groups, and errgroup runs several goroutines and returns the first error. My copier's double buffering is a goroutine reading batches into a channel while the main loop sends the previous batch.

2.3 context.Context: deadlines and cancellation

A context.Context is passed down every call. It carries a deadline and a cancel signal. If the client disconnects or the deadline passes, every downstream call that respects the context (database query, HTTP call) stops. This is how Go services avoid doing work nobody is waiting for. It is the foundation of nested timeouts (section 3.3).

2.4 Middleware

Middleware is a function that wraps a handler, doing something before and after it: auth, logging, tracing, panic recovery, timeouts. Gin chains them in order.

// Teaching sketch.
r := gin.New()
r.Use(gin.Recovery())        // turn panics into 500s instead of crashing the process
r.Use(tracing())              // Datadog span per request
r.Use(authWaterfall(deps))    // who is calling, which tenant, which hierarchy
r.GET("/v1/plans/:id/pivot", pivotHandler)

2.5 Errors and panics

Go returns errors as values (val, err := f()), so failure handling is explicit at each step. A panic is a crash of the current goroutine. In a server, an unrecovered panic in a handler would kill the process, which is why recovery middleware is the first thing in the chain.

2.6 Garbage collection

Go's garbage collector is concurrent and tuned for low pause times. For high-throughput code, the lesson is to avoid allocating per row or per request where you can. My copier reuses typed column buffers instead of reflecting per row for exactly this reason.

3. Bullet C1: the Go/Gin platform

Architected a multi-tenant Go/Gin platform scaling to 10k peak RPS, utilizing Google Wire for compile-time DI. Deployed as a self-protecting HTTP edge without a reverse proxy, guaranteeing high availability through native h2c, nested timeouts, and Datadog distributed tracing.

3.1 In plain words

AssortSmart's planner screens and services call one Go/Gin platform for plan data, KPIs and pivots. It handles up to about 10 thousand requests per second at peak. Usually a web service sits behind a reverse proxy such as Nginx or Envoy, which handles slow clients, timeouts, body limits and protocol details. We deployed the Go service without one, so the Go process itself had to protect itself. It does that with careful server timeouts, per-request deadlines, HTTP/2 support in plain text (h2c), and tracing for every request.

flowchart LR UI["Planner UI and services"] --> EDGE["Go/Gin edge: h2c, server timeouts, limits"] EDGE --> MW["Middleware: recovery, Datadog trace, auth waterfall"] MW --> H["Handlers built by Wire"] H --> R["Redis"] H --> PG["PostgreSQL: UAM and roles"] H --> CH["ClickHouse: rollups and facts"] EDGE --> DD["Datadog traces"]

What to notice: there is no Nginx or Envoy box. Everything a proxy would do for safety lives inside the Go edge.

3.2 Google Wire: compile-time dependency injection

Dependency injection (DI) means a component receives the things it needs (database client, cache, config) instead of creating them itself. That makes code testable, because tests can pass fakes. Many DI frameworks do this at runtime with reflection. Google Wire does it at compile time: you declare provider functions, Wire generates plain Go code that wires them together, and if a dependency is missing the build fails. Analogy: instead of a stage manager running around during the show to find props, the props list is checked and laid out before the curtain goes up.

// Teaching sketch.
// providers.go
func NewClickHouse(cfg Config) (*ch.Conn, error) { /* ... */ }
func NewRedis(cfg Config) *redis.Client          { /* ... */ }
func NewPivotService(c *ch.Conn, r *redis.Client) *PivotService { /* ... */ }
func NewServer(p *PivotService) *gin.Engine      { /* ... */ }

// wire.go (build tag: wireinject)
func InitializeServer(cfg Config) (*gin.Engine, error) {
    wire.Build(NewClickHouse, NewRedis, NewPivotService, NewServer)
    return nil, nil
}
// `wire` generates wire_gen.go with the real constructor calls in order.
  • Why Wire: no runtime reflection, no startup surprises, errors at build time, and the generated code is readable.
  • Alternatives: manual wiring in main.go (fine for small services, gets messy), Uber's fx or dig (runtime DI with lifecycle hooks, more magic).
  • Trade-off: one more code generation step to keep in sync.

3.3 Nested timeouts

Nested timeouts means each layer has a deadline, and inner deadlines are shorter than outer ones, so the innermost work gives up first and the outer layer still has time to return a clean error.

Server level      ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout
  Request level     context deadline for this route
    Downstream        ClickHouse query timeout  <  request deadline
                      Redis / Postgres call timeout  <  request deadline

// Teaching sketch. Values are illustrative, not production settings.
srv := &http.Server{
    Addr:              ":8080",
    Handler:           h2c.NewHandler(router, &http2.Server{}),
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,  // stops slow-header (slowloris) clients
    ReadTimeout:       30 * time.Second,
    WriteTimeout:      60 * time.Second,
    IdleTimeout:       120 * time.Second,
    MaxHeaderBytes:    1 << 20,
}

func pivotHandler(c *gin.Context) {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(c.Request.Context(), 25*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    rows, err := pivots.Query(ctx, req) // ClickHouse call honours ctx
    // ...
}

Why this matters without a proxy: a single slow client or a stuck query must not hold a goroutine and a database connection forever. With nested deadlines, the stuck work is cancelled, the client gets an error, and resources are freed.

3.4 Other self-protection the process owns

Older prep summarises the trade-off as "you own the caps and SIGTERM". The general list of what a proxy normally provides, and what a self-protecting Go edge must therefore handle itself:

  • Header and body size caps (MaxHeaderBytes, http.MaxBytesReader on request bodies).
  • Slow client protection (ReadHeaderTimeout).
  • Panic recovery so one bad request does not crash the process.
  • Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests finish within a deadline, then exit. This matters for rolling deploys.
  • Bounded concurrency to expensive downstreams, so one tenant's heavy pivot cannot exhaust ClickHouse connections.

Keep this as "how the edge protects itself". Do not quote numeric limits.

3.5 h2c: HTTP/2 in cleartext

HTTP/2 sends many requests over one TCP connection at once (multiplexing), with compressed headers. Normally HTTP/2 runs inside TLS. h2c is HTTP/2 without TLS, in "cleartext". It is used when something in front (typically a managed load balancer or platform front door) terminates TLS and forwards traffic to the service over a private network. Go's standard server only speaks HTTP/2 over TLS by default, so you wrap the handler with h2c.NewHandler to accept HTTP/2 in plain text.

  • Why: without a proxy translating protocols, the service itself must speak HTTP/2 to get multiplexing from the front door. Fewer connections, less head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.
  • Trade-off: h2c must only be exposed on a trusted network. Never on the public internet.
  • If asked exactly what terminates TLS in front, keep it general unless you are sure of the product name.

3.6 Datadog distributed tracing

Distributed tracing follows one request across services. Each unit of work is a span (for example "HTTP GET /pivot", "ClickHouse query", "Redis GET"), and spans share a trace id. Datadog shows them as a waterfall, so you can see that a slow request spent 90% of its time in one ClickHouse query.

// Teaching sketch using Datadog's Go tracer.
import gintrace "gopkg.in/DataDog/dd-trace-go.v1/contrib/gin-gonic/gin"

tracer.Start(tracer.WithService("assortsmart-api"))
defer tracer.Stop()
r.Use(gintrace.Middleware("assortsmart-api"))

More on Datadog versus LangSmith in observability_cloud.md.

3.7 Why this design, alternatives and trade-offs

  • What: a single Go/Gin edge, no reverse proxy, with protection built into the process.
  • Why: fewer hops and moving parts, and one place to reason about timeouts and traces. Go gives predictable latency and cheap concurrency at 10k peak RPS.
  • Alternatives considered:
  • Nginx or Envoy in front. Battle-tested protection and TLS. It is an extra hop and an extra config surface, and timeouts then live in two places.
  • A Python (FastAPI) platform. Great for the LLM ecosystem and fast to write. For a high-RPS, CPU-and-I/O-mixed edge, Go's concurrency and memory profile are more predictable. The agent plane stays in Python, where the LLM libraries are.
  • A Java Spring Boot platform. If asked "you know Spring, why Go here?": Spring Boot is excellent for large business services with many entities and transactions, which is how I used it at Uber FRM and Masters India. A thin, high-RPS edge over Redis, Postgres and ClickHouse benefits more from Go's small memory footprint per instance, fast startup and goroutine-per-request model. Never describe the IA platform as Spring Boot.
  • Runtime DI (fx, dig, or Spring's container). More magic, and wiring errors show up at startup instead of build time. Wire generates plain Go constructor calls, so a missing dependency fails the compile.
  • Trade-off: we own every safety knob a proxy would have given us. A missing timeout is our bug.
  • What I'd do differently: write the timeout and limit budget down per route as a table in the repo, so new routes inherit sane defaults instead of copying them.

3.8 The number

Number What it measures How derived Tag
10k peak RPS Peak HTTP requests per second handled by the Go/Gin platform Stated on the AssortSmart tab. No separate arithmetic in prep STATED

Why it mattered: it is the load the edge has to absorb without a reverse proxy, which is why timeouts, h2c and tracing live inside the process.

Say it: "The Go platform scales to about 10 thousand requests per second at peak."

Do NOT say: "99.9% availability", "p99 under X ms", "N tenants", or that you operated the Kubernetes cluster it runs on. If pressed for the measurement source, say it is the stated peak for the edge and keep the rest qualitative.

4. Bullet C2: the KPI formula compiler in Go

Eliminated deployment bottlenecks by architecting a dynamic KPI configurator and custom formula parser. Engineered a real-time compilation layer that tokenizes operator-authored math into parameterized ClickHouse SQL fragments with native division-by-zero protection, decoupling business logic from code releases.

4.1 In plain words

Retailers define KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) differently. "Sell-through" at one retailer is units sold divided by units sold plus ending inventory. Before this, each new KPI meant a code change and a release. Now an operator types the formula in a configurator, and Go compiles it into a safe SQL fragment for ClickHouse.

4.2 How it works

  1. Tokenize. Break the text into tokens: names, numbers, operators, parentheses, function names.
  2. Parse. Build a tree that respects operator precedence (multiplication before addition), for example with a recursive-descent parser.
  3. Validate. Every function must be on an allowlist. Every logical name (such as sales_units) must map to a known physical column. Unknown tokens fail closed: the formula is rejected, never passed through.
  4. Emit SQL. Walk the tree and produce a SQL fragment with values passed as parameters, not string-concatenated.
  5. Protect. Wrap the result in ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0). If a division by zero produces infinity or NaN (not a number), the KPI becomes 0 instead of breaking the planner's JSON.
Operator types:   sell_through = sales_units / (sales_units + eoh_units)

Tokens:           IDENT(sales_units) SLASH LPAREN IDENT(sales_units) PLUS IDENT(eoh_units) RPAREN

Tree:                    (/)
                        /   \
             sales_units     (+)
                            /   \
                   sales_units   eoh_units

Emitted SQL (illustrative column names):
  ifNotFinite(toFloat64(sum(sls_u) / (sum(sls_u) + sum(eoh_u))), 0) AS sell_through

What to notice: logical names on the left become physical columns on the right, and the whole expression is wrapped so a zero denominator gives 0.

// Teaching sketch of fail-closed identifier mapping.
var columns = map[string]string{"sales_units": "sls_u", "eoh_units": "eoh_u"}
var allowedFuncs = map[string]bool{"sum": true, "avg": true, "min": true, "max": true}

func (p *parser) ident(tok Token) (Node, error) {
    col, ok := columns[tok.Text]
    if !ok {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown identifier %q", tok.Text) // fail closed
    }
    return Column{Name: col}, nil
}

4.3 Why this design

  • Why a parser and not "let operators write SQL": raw SQL from users is an injection and cost risk. An allowlisted grammar only allows math on known columns.
  • Alternatives: hard-code KPIs in Go (safe but needs a release per KPI), a general expression library (more power than we wanted, harder to restrict), or store SQL snippets in config (injection risk).
  • Trade-off: the grammar is deliberately small, so exotic formulas need a new allowed function and a code change.
  • What I'd do differently: add a "dry run" that shows operators the generated SQL and a sample result before saving.

5. Bullet C3 in Go: the auth waterfall middleware (summary)

The Go edge resolves identity in a fixed order. It checks Redis first for a cached result. On a miss it tries Firebase Admin token verification, then JWT or Google OIDC verification. It compares API keys in constant time. Then it resolves the caller's role and UAM-scoped hierarchy from PostgreSQL. A cache miss falls through to Postgres; it does not "fail open". Full walk-through: auth_tenancy_rate_limits.md.

// Teaching sketch: constant-time API key comparison.
if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(presented), []byte(expected)) != 1 {
    c.AbortWithStatus(http.StatusUnauthorized)
    return
}

Constant-time comparison takes the same time whether the first character or the last character is wrong. Without it, an attacker can measure response times and guess a key one character at a time (a timing attack).

6. Bullet C5 in Go: the copier (summary)

The ClickHouse copier is also Go: native protocol over TLS on port 9440, 500k-row columnar batches, double buffering with a goroutine and a channel, per-season checkpoint files, and per-table file locks. About 344k rows per second combined across two season streams, measured on partitions up to 4.09B rows while that copy was in flight. Full story: clickhouse.md.

7. Failure modes to talk about

These are general risks of a Go platform shared by UI and agent callers. Older prep listed them for a Python-plus-Go design. Use them as "what I watch for", not as incidents.

Risk Why it happens Guard
Missing tenant or scope check on a new route Someone adds a handler and forgets the scoping helper Scope applied in middleware, plus tests that try cross-tenant ids and expect 403
Divergent auth between Python and Go services Two code paths verify identity differently One identity contract, same claims, same tenant binding
Lost trace context across services A caller does not forward the trace id Tracing middleware on both sides. Trace id in JSON logs
A stuck downstream holds goroutines No deadline on a ClickHouse or Redis call Nested timeouts, context everywhere
LLM logic creeping into the Go edge Convenience Keep LLM orchestration in the Python agent plane. Go stays deterministic

8. Verbal-only Go material (not on the resume)

  • Older prep called the Go service the shared "doing layer" for the Hindsight clustering strategy, where both the manual UI and agent tool calls would hit the same Go engines so authorization and business rules stay in one place. Hindsight and the Cluster Recommendation Copilot are verbal-only designs, not resume bullets. Use this only as "how I would let agents call platform logic safely": the agent plans in Python, then calls audited Go endpoints with the same identity, rather than duplicating business rules.
  • Tool contract drift (an agent's tool schema getting out of sync with the Go API) is the main risk in that design. Version the contracts and test them.
  • 100% Go statement coverage and 1,200+ Go tests are on LinkedIn and verbal, not the PDF.

9. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. Why Go for the platform when the agent plane is Python? Different jobs. The platform is a high-concurrency HTTP edge that talks to Redis, Postgres and ClickHouse at up to about 10 thousand requests per second at peak. Go gives cheap goroutines, predictable latency and low memory for that. The agent plane needs the LLM ecosystem (LangGraph, provider SDKs), which is strongest in Python. Keeping the deterministic platform in Go and the non-deterministic LLM work in Python also keeps the blast radius of each clear.

Q2. What does "self-protecting HTTP edge without a reverse proxy" mean? It means we did not put Nginx or Envoy in front, so the Go process does the protective work a proxy would. That includes server timeouts for slow clients, per-request context deadlines, header and body size caps, panic recovery, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, and native h2c so it speaks HTTP/2 to the front door. The benefit is one fewer hop and one place to reason about timeouts. The cost is that every safety knob is our responsibility.

Q3. Explain nested timeouts. Every layer has a deadline, and inner ones are shorter. The server has read and write timeouts, each route sets a context deadline, and each downstream call like a ClickHouse query gets a deadline shorter than the route's. So if ClickHouse is stuck, the query is cancelled first, the handler still has time to return a clean error, and the goroutine and connection are freed. Without that, one slow dependency slowly eats all your connections.

Q4. What is Google Wire and why use it? Wire is compile-time dependency injection. I declare provider functions for things like the ClickHouse client, Redis client and services, and Wire generates the Go code that constructs them in the right order. If something is missing, the build fails instead of the service crashing at startup. Compared with runtime DI like fx, or the Spring container I used in the Java services at Uber FRM and Masters India, there is no reflection and the generated code is just readable Go.

Q5. What is h2c and when is it safe? h2c is HTTP/2 over plain TCP without TLS. You use it when TLS is terminated in front of the service and traffic to the service is on a trusted private network. Go's server needs the h2c handler wrapper to accept it. It gives HTTP/2 multiplexing without the service doing TLS. It is not safe to expose h2c on the public internet.

Q6. How does your KPI parser stay safe? It is a small grammar, not a SQL passthrough. The tokenizer and parser only accept numbers, operators, parentheses, allowlisted functions and known logical names, which are mapped to physical columns. Anything unknown fails closed. Values are passed as parameters, and the result is wrapped in ifNotFinite(toFloat64(expr), 0), so a divide by zero produces 0 rather than infinity in the planner's JSON. That let business users add KPIs without a code release.

Q7. How do goroutines differ from threads? Goroutines are managed by the Go runtime and start with a tiny stack, so you can run tens of thousands cheaply. The scheduler maps them onto a small number of OS threads and parks a goroutine when it blocks on I/O. OS threads are heavier and are scheduled by the kernel. That is why Go's one-goroutine-per-request model scales well for I/O-heavy servers.

Q8. How would you debug a latency spike on the Go edge? Start with Datadog traces for the slow route and look at which span dominates: usually a ClickHouse query, sometimes the auth path on a Redis miss. Then check saturation, meaning goroutine count, connection pool usage and ClickHouse concurrency. If it is one tenant's heavy pivot, bounded concurrency and deadlines contain it. Then fix the root cause, for example a query that is not hitting a rollup.

Kafka and Flink: where they are used, why at these numbers, and how to defend them

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the attack-and-defense sheet for Kafka and Flink. It shows where each technology sits on my resume, the numbers behind each project, the arithmetic, and speakable answers to the hard pushback ("30K a month is tiny", "prove you needed Flink", "what was your peak TPS?").
  • When to read it: right after kafka_streaming.md and flink.md, and again the night before any streaming or system design round.
  • What to memorise: the map (Menu has Kafka and Flink, Masters has Kafka only, IA has neither), the four rate derivations in section 4, and the line "we chose Kafka and Flink for burst, replay and keyed state, not for vanity throughput".

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show; say "roughly, derived from...". HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records; state it plainly as the outcome. TARGET means a design goal. STUDY means study-only or verbal, not a resume claim.

Say these carefully

  • Do not invent a throughput number you never measured. Menu peak events per second and Masters peak per second are ESTIMATED.
  • No Kafka or Flink at Impact Analytics. Older versions of this sheet said IA used Kafka for async embedding jobs. The current resume says no. IA's data story is ClickHouse.
  • Masters Kafka is a different product from Menu Kafka. No Flink at Masters.
  • Spark and Pinot are not on the resume. Study only.
  • "Exactly-once" means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes. No zero-loss claims.

2. Uber Menu: why not "just call the catalog API from the scraper"?

Pressure Number or shape Why synchronous HTTP breaks Why Kafka helps Why Flink helps
Volume 30K+ menus a month, about 1,000 a day, with spikes when vendors refresh Scrapers block on slow catalog writes Buffers and allows several consumers Processes continuously without waiting for batch windows
Latency goal Onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours Retry storms amplify delay Decouples scrape success from catalog success Stateful dedupe avoids redoing work
Burstiness Scrape waves, anti-bot backoff, retries Thread pools melt down The partitioned log absorbs spikes Backpressure shows as Kafka lag, not scraper crashes

The rate arithmetic, done correctly

30,000 menus a month divided by about 2,592,000 seconds in a 30-day month is about 0.012 menus per second, or one menu every 80 to 90 seconds on average. That is tiny, and I say so.

But the bus does not carry one event per menu. Each menu emits many item-level events, plus retries, page chunks and health events, and fleet runs concentrate work into short windows. Older prep estimates the peak bus rate at about 200 to 500 events per second during fleet runs (ESTIMATED, prep only). Steady state is much lower.

Older versions of this sheet said "about 0.4 to 1 event per second average if one event per menu". That arithmetic was wrong. One event per menu is about 0.012 per second. Use the corrected figure.

Say it: "On average it's about a thousand menus a day, which is modest. The design driver was bursts, retries, duplicates and replay, not average throughput."

Bulk import 100K+ concurrent imports Memory pressure and request timeouts Chunk the file, publish chunks, let consumers process them
API throughput From 700 to 4,000 requests per minute (about 12 to 67 per second) The monolith scaled as one unit Microservices plus an async bulk path

Why no Flink at Masters: Spring Kafka consumers (@KafkaListener methods with a bounded retry and dead-letter handler) and idempotent database writes were enough. Each message is processed independently, with an idempotency check. There was no stateful windowing or dedupe-by-event-time requirement like Menu's late scrape pages. Adding Flink would duplicate the pipeline for no gain.

5. Attack and answer (memorise these)

"Kafka and Flink for only 30K menus a month? Isn't that overkill?" Average rate was not the design driver, and I agree the average is small: about a thousand menus a day. Scrapers are bursty and flaky because of anti-bot blocks and retries, and the catalog and RAG extraction have very different latency. Kafka lets a scrape succeed even when downstream is slow, and lets us replay after a bad parser. Flink owns keyed dedupe and routing, so we never double-apply the same vendor's menu when late or retried pages arrive. With only synchronous chains, a bad deploy meant re-scraping instead of rewinding the log.

"Prove you needed Flink and not just Kafka consumers." Plain consumers are fine for fire-and-forget transforms. We needed keyed state per vendor, event-time handling for late pages, and a single job that validates, dedupes, normalizes and routes before the catalog or the RAG path. That is Flink's core strength, and it gives checkpointed state so I am not hand-building fault tolerance. I will also say that Kafka Streams or a careful consumer could have worked at this event rate. Flink was the stronger fit for state and event time.

"What was your peak events per second on Menu?" I don't claim a measured Flink peak. What I can state is the outcome: 30K+ menus a month, onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours, and 95%+ extraction success. If you want an order of magnitude, my estimate is a few hundred events per second during fleet runs, because each menu fans out into many item, retry and health events. That is an estimate, not a dashboard number.

"Masters 1M+ a day: was that Kafka or the API?" Both, and they are different paths. The interactive API went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute after the strangler migration from the PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices. Bulk submissions, 1M+ a day and 100K+ concurrent imports, went through Kafka so deadline spikes did not melt Postgres or overload the IRP. Idempotency keys stopped double filing on replay.

"How do you get exactly-once?" End-to-end exactly-once delivery is a slogan. The practical recipe is at-least-once from Kafka plus an idempotent sink. At Menu the catalog upsert is keyed by vendor, menu and version. At Masters the key is client plus file hash plus batch index. Flink can write transactionally into Kafka, but the external catalog still needs idempotent writes. Poison messages go to a DLQ, never infinite retry.

"A bad Flink or parser deploy shipped. How do you recover?" Stop the job, fix it, and restart from a checkpoint or savepoint from before the bad deploy, which rewinds Kafka offsets too. Then reprocess, and idempotent upserts make the re-run safe. If the gap is longer than Kafka retention, a batch backfill from stored raw payloads repairs it. Spark would be my tool for that, as a verbal option. We do not re-hit the open web for every repair if the raw payload is still stored.

"Why Kafka and not RabbitMQ, SQS or just background jobs?" We needed a replayable, partitioned, multi-consumer log with per-key ordering. A task queue or in-process @Async jobs are good for "run this and retry it", but weak for "reprocess last Tuesday's events", and an in-memory task dies with the pod. SQS deletes on acknowledgement and does not give the same ordered multi-subscriber replay. RabbitMQ could have handled Masters' task dispatch at our scale, and I say that honestly. Kafka matched Menu's fan-out and Masters' replay needs.

"Why not put Kafka at Impact Analytics too?" There was no streaming requirement in my scope there. The IA work is interactive analytics on ClickHouse rollups and batch AI scoring with checkpoints. Adding a bus would add infrastructure without a problem to solve. I also don't claim the CDC pipeline there, because a colleague built it.

6. Twenty-second stories

Menu: "Scrapers are bursty. Kafka is the replayable bus. Flink does keyed dedupe and normalization and routes structured menus straight to the catalog and messy PDFs to the RAG path. That pipeline is how 30K+ menus a month went from 24-hour to 2-hour onboarding."

Masters: "Filing deadlines spike IRP traffic. Kafka plus idempotent consumers and quarter-sharded Postgres handled 1M+ submissions a day without double filing on replay, and the API went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute. No Flink, because Spring Kafka consumers were enough."

Kafka and event-driven paths (Uber Menu and Masters India)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: what Apache Kafka is, the five or six ideas every interviewer probes (topics, partitions, keys, offsets, consumer groups, delivery guarantees), and how I used it on two different products: Uber Menu ingestion and Masters India e-invoicing.
  • When to read it: before any streaming, event-driven or "design a pipeline" round, and before the Menu or Masters deep dives.
  • What to memorise: Kafka is a replayable, partitioned log. Menu keys by vendor, Python services produce, and Kafka feeds Flink. Masters keys by client GSTIN, with Spring Kafka consumers (@KafkaListener, DefaultErrorHandler plus DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer), idempotent processing and no Flink. "Exactly-once" in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes.
  • Hard pushback on scale ("isn't 30K a month tiny for Kafka?") lives in kafka_flink_scale_defense.md.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal.

Say these carefully

  • Kafka is on the resume at Uber Menu (with Flink) and at Masters India (without Flink). These are two different products with different Kafka setups. Do not merge them.
  • No Kafka at Impact Analytics. Older prep said IA used Kafka for async embedding jobs. The current resume has no Kafka, Flink or CDC at IA. If asked, say ClickHouse and the Python batch pipeline are the IA data story.
  • Do not claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across third parties. Say "at-least-once delivery with idempotent upserts".
  • Menu peak event rate (about 200 to 500 events per second) is an ESTIMATE used only in prep. It is not on the resume. Masters peak rate is also ESTIMATED.

1. What Kafka is, in plain English

Apache Kafka is a system for moving streams of events between services. An event is a small record that says "something happened", such as "menu page scraped for vendor 123" or "invoice batch 7 of file X accepted". Producers write events into Kafka. Consumers read them later at their own pace.

The key difference from a normal queue: Kafka keeps the events after they are read. It is an append-only log, like a ledger book where every new line is written at the bottom and nothing is torn out when someone reads it. Each reader keeps a bookmark. If a reader has a bug, you fix it and move its bookmark back to re-read old pages. That ability is called replay, and it is the main reason I used Kafka in both projects.

Who uses it: almost every large company with event-driven services, for activity tracking, order pipelines, log shipping, change streams and so on.

2. How Kafka works: the ideas interviewers probe

2.1 Topics, partitions and offsets

  • A topic is a named stream, for example menu.scrape.events (illustrative name).
  • A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on a broker (a Kafka server). Partitions are how Kafka scales: more partitions means more parallel readers.
  • Each event in a partition gets an increasing number called its offset. Offset 0, 1, 2, and so on.
topic: menu.scrape.events
  partition 0:  [o0 vendor=12] [o1 vendor=40] [o2 vendor=12] ...
  partition 1:  [o0 vendor=7]  [o1 vendor=7]  [o2 vendor=91] ...
  partition 2:  [o0 vendor=55] ...

What to notice: all events for vendor 12 are in partition 0, in order. Different vendors can be processed in parallel on different partitions.

2.2 Keys decide ordering

When a producer sends an event with a key, Kafka hashes the key to choose the partition. Same key, same partition, so events for one key stay in order. Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition, not across the whole topic.

  • Uber Menu keyed by vendor_id, so one restaurant's menu updates are processed in order.
  • Masters India keyed by the client's GSTIN (GST Identification Number, the tax id of a business), sometimes GSTIN plus document type, so one taxpayer's invoice submit, IRN callback and webhook stay in order.
// Teaching sketch (Spring Kafka producer). Not production code.
// KafkaTemplate is Spring's Kafka producer. The second argument is the message key.
kafkaTemplate.send("irp.submit.jobs",
        clientGstin,                          // same taxpayer, same partition, ordered
        new ImportChunk(fileHash, 7));        // value, serialized to JSON

Watch out for hot keys: if one vendor or one client produces most of the traffic, its partition becomes the bottleneck. Mitigations include splitting the key (GSTIN plus document type) or isolating very large tenants.

2.3 Consumer groups

A consumer group is a set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Kafka gives each partition to exactly one consumer in the group. If you have 12 partitions and 4 consumers, each consumer reads 3 partitions. Add a fifth consumer and Kafka rebalances, moving partitions between them.

The big benefit: different groups read the same topic independently. At Masters, IRP submit consumers, an audit projector and a metrics consumer could all read the same events without the producer knowing about any of them. At Menu, Flink was the main online consumer, and health or audit readers could attach separately.

Rule of thumb: maximum parallelism in a group equals the partition count. A sixth consumer on a 5-partition topic sits idle.

2.4 Offsets, commits and replay

Each consumer group stores its committed offset per partition, which is its bookmark. Two important behaviours:

  • Commit after processing, not before. If you crash after processing but before committing, you will re-read that event. That is at-least-once delivery. Duplicates are possible, so the processing must be safe to repeat.
  • Replay means resetting a group's offsets to an earlier point and reprocessing. For example: a parser bug shipped on Tuesday, so after the fix we rewind to before the deploy and re-run. This is only possible if retention (how long Kafka keeps data) covers that window.

2.5 Durability: replication and acks

Each partition is copied to several brokers (the replication factor, typically 3). One copy is the leader. With acks=all, a write is acknowledged only after the in-sync replicas have it, so a single broker failure does not lose acknowledged data. This is general Kafka behaviour. I do not claim specific broker configurations for either project.

2.6 Delivery guarantees in one table

Guarantee Meaning How you get it
At-most-once May lose events, never duplicates Commit before processing
At-least-once Never loses committed events, may duplicate Commit after processing
Exactly-once (inside Kafka) Each event affects Kafka state once Idempotent producer plus Kafka transactions, read-process-write within Kafka
"Exactly-once" end to end The external store shows each change once At-least-once plus an idempotent sink. This is what I built in both projects

An idempotent operation has the same effect whether you do it once or five times, like pressing a lift button twice. An upsert inserts a row or updates it if the key already exists.

2.7 Dead-letter queues and retries

A poison message is an event that will always fail, such as a malformed payload. If a consumer retries it forever, the whole partition stalls behind it. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a side topic or table where such events are parked after a bounded number of retries, so the rest keeps flowing and an operator can inspect and replay them later.

Bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter means: wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s, with a little randomness so thousands of retries do not all fire at the same instant, and stop after N tries.

2.8 Consumer lag and backpressure

Consumer lag is how far a consumer group is behind the newest offset. It is the single most useful Kafka health metric. Rising lag means the consumer cannot keep up, or the downstream it writes to is slow. Backpressure is the system slowing intake when downstream is slow. With Kafka in the middle, slow downstream shows up as growing lag rather than producers crashing, because Kafka simply holds the events.

3. Where I used Kafka

3.1 Uber Menu Ingestion (Uber via EPAM)

Scaled menu extraction success to 95%+ by hardening a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries. Designed a large-scale data ingestion and processing pipeline using Kafka and Apache Flink, with stateful keyed deduplication and schema normalization to guarantee exactly-once catalog upserts.

flowchart LR SEL["Selenium scrapers on GCP"] --> K["Kafka topics keyed by vendor_id"] K --> FL["Flink job: validate, dedupe, normalize, route"] FL --> CAT["Catalog upsert, idempotent"] FL --> RAG["Unstructured path: LangChain RAG plus Gemini"] RAG --> CAT K --> OPS["Other consumers: health or audit"]

What to notice: scrapers only have to get the event into Kafka. They never wait for the catalog or the LLM path.

What Kafka did here

  • Decoupling. Scrapers are bursty and flaky (anti-bot blocks, retries). The catalog write and the RAG extraction are slower and have different latency. Kafka lets a scrape "succeed" as soon as its event is stored.
  • Per-vendor order. Keyed by vendor_id, so updates for one restaurant are applied in order.
  • Replay. After a bad parser deploy, rewind the consumer and reprocess from the log instead of re-scraping the internet.
  • Fan-out. Flink reads it for the hot path, and other consumers can read the same events.

3.2 Masters India GST e-invoicing

Architected a high-concurrency bulk e-invoicing pipeline processing 1M+ daily government submissions by orchestrating a Kafka event bus and a PostgreSQL database horizontally sharded by tax quarter. Enforced exactly-once, idempotent processing for 100K+ concurrent imports with fault-tolerant state management via dead-letter queues and bounded retries against volatile state IRP portals.

Plain words: enterprise clients upload invoice files. Each invoice must be registered with the government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal), which returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number) and a signed QR code. The IRP is slow and flaky around filing deadlines. Registering the same invoice twice is a compliance problem, not just a data bug.

flowchart LR UP["Client uploads invoice file"] --> API["Spring Boot upload service"] API --> OBJ["File stored in object storage"] API --> K["Kafka: import chunks keyed by client GSTIN"] K --> W["Spring Kafka consumers: validate, call IRP with bounded concurrency"] W --> IRP["Government IRP"] W --> PG["PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter"] W --> DLQ["Dead-letter topic for poison batches"] K --> AUD["Audit and metrics consumers"]

What to notice: the HTTP request returns quickly. The slow, risky IRP calls happen in consumers that can retry safely.

What Kafka did here

  • Load levelling. Deadline spikes are absorbed by the log, so Postgres and the IRP see a controlled rate.
  • Ordering per taxpayer. Keyed by client GSTIN.
  • Safe retries. Every chunk carries an idempotency key like client + fileHash + batchIndex. Before registering, the consumer checks whether that key is already done. Re-delivery from Kafka becomes a no-op.
  • DLQ and bounded retries. Poison batches park for operator replay instead of blocking a whole 100K-row import.
  • Multiple consumers. IRP submit consumers, audit and metrics read the same events independently.
  • Side work that needs no replayable log (PDF generation, emails) ran as @Async tasks and scheduled jobs inside the Spring Boot services, and chunked bulk imports follow the Spring Batch pattern. Kafka was the event bus between stages.

3.3 The Masters client view: Spring Kafka

Spring Kafka is Spring's Kafka integration. It wraps the plain Kafka client so you write a normal Java method and Spring handles polling, threads, offset commits, retries and dead-lettering. Three pieces matter:

  • @KafkaListener marks a method that Spring calls for every record a consumer group receives. groupId names the group, and concurrency is how many consumer threads run in this instance. Because the thread count is fixed, it also caps how many IRP calls run at once, so a slow IRP can never eat every thread in the service.
  • DefaultErrorHandler catches an exception thrown by the listener, waits according to a back-off schedule, and redelivers the same record. Errors you mark as not retryable (for example an invalid GSTIN) skip the retries.
  • DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer runs when retries are exhausted. It publishes the record to a dead-letter topic with the error in its headers, and the consumer moves on to the next record.

Offsets are committed by the listener container after the method returns normally, which gives at-least-once delivery. The idempotency claim makes the repeat harmless.

// Teaching sketch. Topic names, counts and delays are illustrative, not remembered production values.
@KafkaListener(topics = "irp.submit.jobs", groupId = "irp-submit", concurrency = "8")
public void onChunk(ImportChunk chunk) {
    if (!batches.claim(chunk.idemKey(), chunk.clientId())) {
        return;                                   // already processed: duplicate delivery is a no-op
    }
    irpClient.register(chunk);                    // WebClient call with a strict timeout
    batches.markDone(chunk.idemKey());
}

@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler irpErrorHandler(KafkaTemplate<String, Object> template) {
    var toDlq = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
            (record, ex) -> new TopicPartition("irp.submit.jobs.dlq", record.partition()));
    var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);   // bounded retries
    backOff.setInitialInterval(1_000);
    backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
    var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(toDlq, backOff);
    handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(InvalidGstinException.class);  // straight to the DLQ
    return handler;
}

What to notice: the listener just does the work and throws on failure. Retries, back-off and dead-lettering are configuration, not hand-written loops.

Why Spring Kafka and not the raw client: consumer groups, retries with back-off and DLQ publishing come built in, so every service handles failures the same way. The trade-off is less control over the poll loop, which we did not need.

At Uber Menu the producers were Python services next to the Selenium fleet, and Flink was the main consumer. Section 3.1 covers that side.

Numbers

Number Meaning Tag
1M+ submissions a day IRP submissions HISTORICAL
About 12 per second average 1,000,000 / 86,400 is about 11.6 ESTIMATED
Peaks 8 to 10 times average Roughly 90 to 120 per second around filing deadlines ESTIMATED
100K+ concurrent imports Bulk imports processed idempotently HISTORICAL
From 700 to 4,000 requests per minute API throughput, about 12 to 67 per second HISTORICAL, per-second ESTIMATED

The 700 to 4,000 requests per minute is the interactive API path. The 1M+ a day is the bulk submission path through Kafka. They are complementary numbers, not the same measurement.

3.4 Why Menu had Flink and Masters did not

Masters needed ordered, replayable, retry-safe job delivery. Spring Kafka consumers and idempotent database writes were enough. Menu needed stateful stream logic: dedupe by vendor and content hash with keyed state, event-time handling for late pages, and in-stream routing between the structured and RAG paths. That is Flink's job. See flink.md.

4. Design decisions

Why Kafka at all (both projects)

  • What: a durable, partitioned log between producers (scrapers, upload API) and consumers (Flink at Menu, Spring Kafka consumers at Masters).
  • Why: bursts, slow downstreams, and the need to replay after bugs.
  • How: keyed topics, consumer groups, commit after processing, idempotent sinks, DLQ.
  • Alternatives considered:
  • Synchronous HTTP calls from scraper to catalog, or from upload to IRP. A slow downstream blocks threads, and there is no replay.
  • RabbitMQ. A good broker for task dispatch. At Masters' scale it could have worked, and I say that honestly. Kafka won on cheap replay for GST disputes and multiple independent consumer groups.
  • Amazon SQS. Messages are deleted on acknowledgement, so there is no cheap multi-consumer replay. SQS FIFO also limits throughput per message group.
  • A plain task queue or in-process jobs (Celery in Python, @Async tasks in Spring). Great for "run this job and retry it", but a weak audit and replay bus for "reprocess last Tuesday". An @Async task also lives only in memory, so a pod restart loses it.
  • Google Pub/Sub (Menu was on GCP). It is a reasonable managed choice. I have no story where we evaluated it, so if asked, say it is a valid alternative with different replay and ordering semantics.
  • Trade-off: Kafka is operationally heavier: partitions, retention, rebalances and lag monitoring. You also have to design for duplicates.
  • What I'd do differently: define the event schema and versioning (a schema registry) up front, and put DLQ replay tooling in place before the first incident rather than after.

5. Failure modes and how we handled them

Failure What it looks like Mitigation
Duplicate delivery Same invoice or menu processed twice after a crash or rebalance Idempotency keys and upserts. Commit offsets after processing
Poison message One partition stops moving, lag grows on one partition only Bounded retries, then DLQ
Bad deploy of a consumer Wrong data written for an hour Fix, rewind offsets to before the deploy, reprocess. Idempotent sink makes the re-run safe
Slow downstream (IRP, catalog) Lag rises across all partitions Bounded concurrency, backoff, alert on lag. Kafka buffers in the meantime
Hot key One partition far behind the others Better key choice (GSTIN plus document type), isolate whale tenants
Dual writes without idempotency Database and Kafka disagree Write state once with an idempotent key. Never "write DB, then publish" without a recovery story

6. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. What is Kafka and why is it different from a queue? Kafka is a partitioned, append-only log. Consumers track their own offsets, and events stay after being read, so I can replay them and several consumer groups can read the same stream independently. A classic queue deletes a message once it is acknowledged. I used Kafka at Uber Menu and at Masters India mainly for replay and decoupling. For example, after a bad parser deploy at Menu we could rewind and reprocess instead of re-scraping.

Q2. How does Kafka guarantee ordering? Only within a partition. The producer's key is hashed to pick a partition, so all events with the same key land in order on one partition. At Menu the key was the vendor id. At Masters it was the client GSTIN, sometimes GSTIN plus document type. If you need global ordering you need one partition, which kills parallelism, so you design the key around what actually needs ordering.

Q3. How did you get exactly-once? End to end, I got exactly-once effects, not exactly-once delivery. Kafka gave at-least-once delivery because we committed offsets after processing. The sink was idempotent: catalog upserts keyed by vendor, menu and content hash at Menu, and an idempotency key like client plus file hash plus batch index at Masters. So a duplicate delivery becomes a no-op. I do not claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across the government portal. Follow-up they may ask: "What about Kafka transactions?" They give exactly-once for read-process-write inside Kafka. The moment you write to an external system, you still need idempotency there.

Q4. What is a DLQ and when do you use one? A dead-letter queue is where a message goes after a bounded number of failed retries, so it does not block the partition behind it. At Masters, a malformed batch in a 100K-row import would otherwise stall every later batch for that client. We retried with exponential backoff and jitter against the IRP, and after the limit the batch parked in the DLQ for an operator to inspect and replay. In Spring Kafka terms, that is a DefaultErrorHandler with a bounded back-off and a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, with permanent errors like an invalid GSTIN marked not-retryable so they go straight to the DLQ.

Q5. How do you size partitions? Partitions cap consumer parallelism in a group, so I size for the peak consumer count I expect, with headroom, because adding partitions later reshuffles key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering during the change. I also check key skew, since a hot key can make one partition the bottleneck no matter how many partitions exist. I do not quote exact partition counts from either project.

Q6. Consumer lag is growing. What do you do? First, check whether lag is growing on all partitions or one. One partition usually means a poison message or a hot key. All partitions means the consumer or its downstream is slow. Then look at the downstream: at Masters that was usually the IRP slowing near a deadline, at Menu the catalog or the RAG path. Mitigations are scaling consumers up to the partition count, bounded concurrency to the slow dependency, and DLQ for poison messages. Kafka buffering is the reason this is an alert and not an outage.

Q7. Why not RabbitMQ or SQS at Masters? We needed per-taxpayer ordering, cheap replay for GST disputes and audit reprocessing, and multiple consumer groups on the same events. SQS deletes on acknowledgement and FIFO limits throughput per group. RabbitMQ could honestly have worked at our scale for task dispatch. Kafka won on replay and independent consumers, and the trade-off was more operational work.

Q8. Why did Menu need Flink but Masters did not? Masters' processing was stateless per message plus an idempotency check in the database, so plain Spring Kafka consumers were enough. Menu needed keyed state to dedupe repeated or late pages per vendor, event-time handling, and in-stream routing to the structured or RAG path. That is what a stream processor like Flink is for. Adding Flink at Masters would have duplicated the pipeline without a stateful requirement.

Q9. How did your Masters consumers work in Spring? Each consumer was a @KafkaListener method with its own consumer group, so IRP submission, persistence and audit read the same events independently. The listener first claimed the chunk's idempotency key in Postgres, then called the IRP through WebClient with a strict timeout. If it threw, Spring Kafka's DefaultErrorHandler retried with back-off, and after the last attempt the DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer moved the record to a dead-letter topic. The fixed consumer thread count doubled as a cap on concurrent IRP calls. Follow-up they may ask: "When are offsets committed?" After the listener returns normally, so a crash mid-processing means redelivery, which the idempotency claim makes safe.

PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis and Spring Data JPA / Hibernate (plus MongoDB and Elasticsearch, briefly)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the relational databases and cache on my resume, taught from scratch: transactions, indexes, locking, sharding, cache-aside and stampedes. It also covers the Java data layer (Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, JdbcTemplate, HikariCP, Spring Data Redis) and where I used each one: Uber FRM on MySQL, Masters India on sharded PostgreSQL with Redis, Impact Analytics' thin Postgres plus a Redis-fronted auth path, and GeeksforGeeks on MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch.
  • When to read it: before any database, data modelling or "design the schema" round, and before the FRM and Masters deep dives.
  • What to memorise: FRM is an 8-table normalized MySQL schema on SOADB, with SHA-256 natural keys, optimistic row-locking through a JPA @Version field, and @Transactional cross-table syncs. The column-aliasing bug story and its fix (a JPQL query with an explicit, unique alias on every column, mapped into a typed projection). Masters is PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, reached through Hibernate and JdbcTemplate over HikariCP pools, with Redis cache-aside cutting read load 30%. At IA, Postgres keeps thin metadata, UAM and roles while ClickHouse holds the facts.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. STATED means printed on the resume from the project source. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. Verbal means true but off the resume.

Say these carefully

  • FRM schema is 8 tables on the resume. 11 is the ORM entity count in code (verbal). Older prep said "11-table schema". Use 8.
  • 100% is module statement coverage for the FRM migration. It is not all of Uber Finance.
  • Led 3 engineers is Uber FRM (tech lead of an EPAM pod, not people manager). Mentored 2 is Masters India. Do not merge them.
  • 30% is database read load, not latency.
  • The FRM real-time collaboration and Slack notification service was a separate service I did not build.
  • Snippets are teaching sketches. Column, table and class names are illustrative unless stated.

1. Relational database ideas interviewers probe

A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns, links tables with keys, and guarantees transactions. PostgreSQL and MySQL are the two most common open-source ones. Both are OLTP databases (Online Transaction Processing): many small, correct reads and writes. ClickHouse, by contrast, is built for big analytical scans (see clickhouse.md).

1.1 Transactions and ACID

A transaction groups statements so they all happen or none do. ACID stands for:

  • Atomic: all or nothing. A bank transfer debits and credits together.
  • Consistent: constraints hold before and after.
  • Isolated: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work.
  • Durable: once committed, it survives a crash.

Isolation levels trade safety for concurrency: Read Committed (Postgres default), Repeatable Read (MySQL InnoDB default), Serializable (strictest).

1.2 Indexes

An index is a sorted lookup structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the table. It is like the index at the back of a book. A composite index on (client_id, invoice_date) serves queries that filter by client and then by date range, but not queries that filter by date alone (the leftmost-prefix rule). Indexes speed reads and slow writes. Use EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see whether the planner uses them.

1.3 The N+1 query problem

Loading 100 invoices, then running one extra query per invoice for its client, is 1 + 100 queries. The fix is a join or a batched IN (...) query. ORMs make this easy to do by accident. In Hibernate the classic cause is a lazily loaded association touched inside a loop. The usual fix is a join fetch in the JPQL query or an entity graph.

1.4 Locking: pessimistic versus optimistic

  • Pessimistic locking locks the row while you work on it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). It is safe, but others wait, and long locks cause contention.
  • Optimistic locking does not lock. Each row has a version column. You update only if the version is still what you read, and bump it. If someone else changed it first, your update affects 0 rows and you retry or tell the user. Analogy: editing a shared document that warns "this was changed since you opened it".
-- Optimistic row-locking, the SQL underneath. Teaching sketch.
UPDATE scoping_assessment
SET status = 'Review', version = version + 1, updated_by = :email
WHERE uuid = :uuid AND version = :version_read;
-- 0 rows affected means someone else won: reload and retry.

In Java with JPA you rarely write that SQL by hand. Section 2.7 shows how a @Version field makes Hibernate write it for you.

1.5 Connection pooling

Opening a database connection is expensive (TCP, TLS, auth). A pool keeps a set of open connections and lends them out per request. Without pooling, a traffic spike becomes a connection storm. HikariCP is the connection pool Spring Boot uses by default: you set a maximum pool size and a connection timeout, and each request borrows a connection and returns it when done. At Masters, per-service HikariCP pools replaced PHP-FPM's per-request connections and were one of the causes of the latency win.

1.6 Partitioning versus sharding

  • Partitioning splits one table into pieces inside one database (Postgres declarative PARTITION BY RANGE).
  • Sharding splits data across separate tables, schemas or servers, with routing logic choosing where each row goes.

Both let you prune what a query touches and archive old data cheaply. Sharding also spreads write load, at the cost of routing complexity.

1.7 Natural keys versus surrogate keys

A surrogate key is an arbitrary id (auto-increment, random UUID). A natural key comes from the data itself. A deterministic hashed natural key computes the id from the identifying fields, so the same logical record always gets the same id, and re-imports cannot create duplicates.

2. MySQL at Uber FRM (Uber via EPAM)

2.1 The bullets

Owned the Financial Risk Management scoping backend, reducing quarterly reconciliation time by 70% (from 14 days to 3 days) against a $340M materiality threshold. Engineered the Sheets-to-MySQL migration across 19M raw GL rows, shipping 36 Spring Boot endpoints to automate custom financial math and a nested 4-level FSLI (L1-L4) hierarchy with dynamic quarter-annualization.

Resolved ETL pipeline lock contention during financial close by designing an 8-table normalized MySQL schema on Uber's SOADB featuring a polymorphic review-status model. Guaranteed real-time, multi-user collaboration integrity by implementing optimistic row-locking, atomic cross-table syncs, and deterministic SHA-256 natural-key hashing to eliminate data duplication across quarterly audit trails.

Led 3 engineers in a core Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that eliminated latent column-aliasing bugs and raised module statement coverage to 100%. Orchestrated zero-downtime releases via stacked Bazel PRs, embedding reporting SQL allowlists and automated FSM gates with 50% delta-variance checks to enforce SOX compliance.

2.2 In plain words

Uber Finance used Google Sheets to decide each quarter which financial line items and entities were material enough to need audit testing. FRM is Financial Risk Management. A GL (general ledger) is the master record of accounting entries. An FSLI (Financial Statement Line Item) is one line on the balance sheet or income statement, organised in four levels, L1 (broadest) to L4 (most detailed). SOADB is Uber's service-owned MySQL standard. We moved the data and the math from Sheets into MySQL behind a Java Spring Boot service.

2.3 How the schema solved lock contention

During financial close, an ETL load and several analysts were writing at the same time. With wide, denormalised tables, the load and the analysts' edits fought over the same rows and locks. An 8-table normalized schema separated the fact data (balance sheet and income statement rows) from mappings, assessments, thresholds and review status, so loads and edits touch different rows and tables.

Facts about the schema (verbal depth):

  • Every table carries a fiscal period key (fiscal_quarter, fiscal_year) and audit columns (created_at/by, updated_at/by).
  • Relationships are logical joins on level_id plus fiscal period, not database-level foreign keys. That matters for the bug story below.
  • There are 11 JPA entity classes in code. The resume number is 8 tables.
flowchart LR ETL["HFM ETL load"] --> FACT["Fact tables: balance_sheet, income_statement"] MAP["level_mapping: L1 to L4"] --> SVC["FRM Spring Boot service"] FACT --> SVC SVC --> ASM["Assessments and thresholds"] SVC --> REV["Polymorphic review status"] U["Finance analysts"] --> SVC

What to notice: the ETL writes facts while analysts mostly write assessments and review status, so the two stop fighting over the same rows.

2.4 The polymorphic review-status model

One review-status model is reused across all eight screens (Reconciliation, Materiality, EMI Scoping, Group Scoping, Threshold Setup, Component Scoping, Residual Risk, Summary) instead of a status column per screen. The statuses are Draft, Review, ReOpen and Closed. The allowed moves between them form a finite state machine (FSM), with automated gates such as the 50% delta-variance check: a period-over-period change of 50% or more is flagged at a gate, supporting SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley) controls.

Draft --submit--> Review --approve--> Closed
                    |                   |
                    +--reject--> Draft  +--reopen--> ReOpen --submit--> Review
(illustrative transitions)

In Java the statuses are a single enum shared by every entity that can be reviewed, stored as a string column with @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING), and the service checks each transition against the allowed moves before saving.

2.5 Atomic cross-table syncs

Some edits must update two tables together. For example, patching an EMI "Total" also mirrors the amount into balance_sheet / income_statement, and updating benchmark metrics touches two benchmark tables. These run inside one @Transactional service method. @Transactional is a Spring annotation that means "run this whole method as one database transaction": Spring opens a transaction when the method starts, commits when it returns, and rolls back if it throws an unchecked exception. If the dependent sync affects zero rows, the method throws and the whole thing rolls back. No half-updated audit trail.

// Teaching sketch.
@Transactional
public void patchEmiTotal(String uuid, BigDecimal amount, String email) {
    EmiLine line = emiRepo.findById(uuid).orElseThrow(NotFoundException::new);
    line.setTotal(amount);
    line.setUpdatedBy(email);                       // written at commit (dirty checking)
    int synced = balanceSheetRepo.mirrorAmount(line.getLevelId(), amount, email);
    if (synced == 0) {
        throw new SyncFailedException(uuid);        // unchecked, so Spring rolls back both writes
    }
}

What to notice: both writes commit together or not at all. Dirty checking means Hibernate notices which loaded entities changed and writes them at commit, so there is no explicit save call for line.

2.6 SHA-256 natural keys

Each quarter's import must not duplicate rows from the previous one. The uuid is computed deterministically, for example uuid = SHA-256(question_text + normalized page_name). SHA-256 turns any input into a fixed 64-character fingerprint, and the same input always gives the same fingerprint. Importing the same logical record twice gives the same key, and the upsert becomes a no-op.

// Teaching sketch.
static String naturalKey(String questionText, String pageName) {
    String norm = pageName.strip().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
    try {
        byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
                .digest((questionText + "|" + norm).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest);
    } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) {
        throw new IllegalStateException(e);   // SHA-256 is always present in the JDK
    }
}

2.7 Optimistic row-locking with @Version

Several analysts can edit during close. Optimistic locking (section 1.4) means nobody holds long locks, and a stale edit is rejected rather than silently overwriting a colleague's change.

In JPA (the Java Persistence API, the standard for mapping Java classes to tables) you get this by adding a @Version field to the entity. Hibernate then adds AND version = ? and version = version + 1 to every UPDATE it generates. If the row changed since you loaded it, zero rows match and Hibernate throws an optimistic-locking exception, which the API maps to 409 Conflict so the user reloads.

// Teaching sketch.
@Entity
@Table(name = "scoping_assessment")
public class ScopingAssessment {
    @Id
    private String uuid;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private ReviewStatus status;
    private String updatedBy;
    @Version
    private long version;          // Hibernate checks and bumps this on every update
    // getters and setters omitted
}

@Transactional
public AssessmentDto submit(String uuid, long versionFromClient, String email) {
    ScopingAssessment a = repo.findById(uuid).orElseThrow(NotFoundException::new);
    if (a.getVersion() != versionFromClient) {
        throw new StaleVersionException(uuid);      // mapped to 409
    }
    a.setStatus(ReviewStatus.REVIEW);
    a.setUpdatedBy(email);
    return AssessmentDto.from(a);   // at commit: UPDATE ... WHERE uuid = ? AND version = ?
}

What to notice: the service compares the version the browser saw with the one it loaded. Hibernate's own check at commit catches the race where someone else writes in between.

Say this carefully if pressed on the real-time side: the real-time collaboration and notification service was a separate service I did not build. Older prep notes that the version-check layer for real-time sync lives partly in that collaboration service and the client, so keep your detailed claims to the scoping service's transactional, per-uuid writes.

2.8 The numbers

Number Meaning Tag
70%, from 14 days to 3 days Quarterly reconciliation time STATED. The technical design doc framed that cut and the platform delivered it for the close. (14 - 3) / 14 is about 79%, so 70% is the conservative figure
$340M Group materiality threshold on the Q4 2025 close. It is a threshold, not a volume MEASURED (config row)
19M Raw GL rows migrated off Sheets STATED. Per-quarter extracts were about 38K to 95K rows. The value was correctness, hierarchy and auditability, not big-data throughput
