3. Spring Data JPA, Hibernate and the column-aliasing bug

3.1 What these are

  • JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) is the Java standard for mapping classes to tables. It is a specification, a set of annotations and interfaces, not a library you run.
  • Hibernate is the most widely used JPA implementation. It turns entity changes into SQL, tracks which loaded objects changed (dirty checking), and handles @Version checks. An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) like Hibernate lets you work with objects instead of raw SQL strings. Analogy: a translator who speaks both Java and SQL, so you talk in objects and it writes the SQL.
  • Spring Data JPA sits on top. You declare a repository interface, and Spring generates the implementation: findById, save, and query methods derived from names like findByFiscalQuarterAndFiscalYear. For anything more complex you write JPQL, a SQL-like language that talks about entities and fields instead of tables and columns.
  • An entity is a class marked @Entity that maps to a table. A projection is a query that returns only some columns into a small typed result instead of whole entities. Spring Data maps each result column to a projection getter by its alias, which is why aliases matter in the bug story.
// Teaching sketch.
@Entity
@Table(name = "level_mapping")
public class LevelMapping {
    @Id
    private String uuid;
    private String levelId;
    private String fiscalQuarter;
    private int fiscalYear;
}

public interface LevelMappingRepository extends JpaRepository<LevelMapping, String> {
    List<LevelMapping> findByFiscalQuarterAndFiscalYear(String quarter, int year);
}

What to notice: the repository is just an interface. Spring writes the query from the method name.

3.2 The bug (tell this precisely)

The legacy read path ran raw SQL through JDBC and built each result row into a map keyed by column label. That is only safe when column names are unique. The component aggregate joined the fact table to level_mapping, and both had columns named uuid, level_id, fiscal_quarter and fiscal_year. The result had two columns literally labelled uuid. The loop walked columns by position, and Map.put with a key that already exists replaces the old value, so each row silently kept the last one: the level_mapping uuid instead of the fact uuid.

Symptom: rows looked right on screen, but a PATCH by uuid or a comment pointed at the wrong line. It surfaced when editing one reconciliation line appeared to change a different line.

// Before: silent collision. Two columns labelled "uuid", the last one wins.
for (int c = 1; c <= meta.getColumnCount(); c++) {
    row.put(meta.getColumnLabel(c), rs.getObject(c));
}

// After: JPQL with an explicit, unique alias on every column, mapped to a typed projection.
public interface ComponentRow {
    String getFsliId();
    String getLevelMappingUuid();
    String getFactQuarter();
}

@Query("""
    select min(i.uuid)          as fsliId,
           max(lm.uuid)         as levelMappingUuid,
           max(i.fiscalQuarter) as factQuarter
    from ComponentEntity i
    join LevelMapping lm on lm.levelId = i.levelId and lm.fiscalQuarter = i.fiscalQuarter
    where i.fiscalQuarter = :quarter and i.fiscalYear = :year
    group by lm.level1
    """)
List<ComponentRow> findComponentRows(@Param("quarter") String quarter, @Param("year") int year);

What to notice: with explicit aliases, no two result columns can share a name, and each value lands in its own typed getter.

3.3 Leading the migration

  • Led 3 engineers as tech lead of the EPAM pod. Work was sliced along controller, service, repository and entity layers, so two people could build one feature without merge collisions.
  • Transaction discipline: @Transactional on service methods replaced hand-written commit and rollback code in every repository. Short, single-purpose transactions also kept locks short during close.
  • Thread model: Spring Boot's servlet stack serves each request on its own thread from a pool, so blocking JDBC calls are normal and need no special offloading.
  • Stacked Bazel PRs: small dependent PRs, each passing Bazel test targets per layer (JUnit 5 with Mockito, and MockMvc for controllers), so the migration shipped in steps with zero downtime.
  • Reporting SQL allowlists: only known, reviewed reporting queries may run.
  • Defences against double-counting: a parent-equals-sum-of-children invariant in the test plan, an explicit alias on every projected column, and active-flag filters so stale rows drop out.

3.4 Alternatives and trade-offs

  • Keep raw SQL and just fix the one query. Fixes the symptom, not the class of bug.
  • MyBatis or jOOQ. More direct control over SQL, but no built-in @Version checks or dirty checking, and the platform's Spring conventions already pointed at JPA.
  • Trade-off: migrating every query is slow work, and an ORM can hide what SQL runs. That is why coverage had to reach 100% on the module, to prove nothing regressed, and why we kept explicit aliases even inside JPQL.

4. PostgreSQL at Masters India: sharded by tax quarter

Architected a high-concurrency bulk e-invoicing pipeline processing 1M+ daily government submissions by orchestrating a Kafka event bus and a PostgreSQL database horizontally sharded by tax quarter. Enforced exactly-once, idempotent processing for 100K+ concurrent imports with fault-tolerant state management via dead-letter queues and bounded retries against volatile state IRP portals.

4.1 Why shard by tax quarter

Indian GST (Goods and Services Tax) reporting is quarter-scoped and deadline-driven. Writes concentrate in the current quarter. Older quarters are mostly read for reconciliation and audits. Separate per-quarter tables or schemas:

  • keep the hot write set and its indexes small,
  • let us archive or prune a whole cold quarter without touching the hot one,
  • give clear runbooks ("Q3 is frozen").
flowchart LR API["Invoice API in Spring Boot"] --> ROUTE["Quarter router: derive quarter from invoice date"] ROUTE --> Q1["Shard: FY Q1"] ROUTE --> Q2["Shard: FY Q2"] ROUTE --> Q3["Shard: current quarter, hot writes"] Q1 --> ARCH["Archive cold quarters"]

What to notice: routing happens in application code, from the invoice date, before any write.

  • Trade-off versus native partitioning: we owned routing in application code, which is more moving parts than Postgres declarative partitions, in exchange for explicit control over archiving whole quarters.
  • The main risk: a write going to the wrong quarter. We derived the quarter from the invoice date at the API boundary and rejected mismatches.
  • In Spring terms: if quarters are separate tables, the repository picks the table name from the derived quarter. If they are separate schemas, Spring's AbstractRoutingDataSource does the same job one level down: the service sets the quarter for the current call and the routing data source hands Hibernate a connection to that quarter's schema. Either shape is an illustration of "routing in application code".

4.2 How the services talked to PostgreSQL

  • Hibernate entities for normal reads and writes of invoices, clients and import batches.
  • JdbcTemplate for hot paths that are one SQL statement, such as the idempotency claim below and bulk inserts. JdbcTemplate (and NamedParameterJdbcTemplate) is Spring's thin helper for running plain SQL with parameters, without loading entities.
  • HikariCP pools per service, so no request pays for opening a connection.

4.3 Idempotency in the database

Each import chunk carries an idempotency key like client + fileHash + batchIndex. A unique constraint on it means a re-delivered Kafka message cannot create a second registration. Duplicate registration with the government is a compliance problem, not just a data bug.

// Teaching sketch. Returns true only for the first delivery of this chunk.
boolean claim(String idemKey, long clientId) {
    int inserted = jdbc.update("""
        INSERT INTO import_batches (idem_key, client_id, status)
        VALUES (:k, :client, 'processing')
        ON CONFLICT (idem_key) DO NOTHING
        """, Map.of("k", idemKey, "client", clientId));
    return inserted == 1;          // 0 means already seen: skip
}

What to notice: the database's unique constraint is the referee. Two consumers racing on the same chunk cannot both win.

4.4 Where the latency win came from

p95 went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds (HISTORICAL) across 1,500+ clients during the PHP-to-Spring Boot migration. The database-related causes: per-service HikariCP connection pooling, composite indexes such as (client_id, invoice_date), removing N+1 list queries, and pagination. Moving slow IRP calls off the request path into Kafka consumers and Redis for reads were the other causes.

5. PostgreSQL at Impact Analytics: thin metadata

Planner pivots were slow on PostgreSQL, and POCs showed ClickHouse winning large analytical reads. Postgres stayed for what it is good at: thin metadata, UAM (User Access Management), roles, and single-row writes. The Go auth waterfall resolves roles and hierarchy scope from Postgres (see auth_tenancy_rate_limits.md). The same tenant id exists in both stores.

6. Redis

6.1 What Redis is

Redis is an in-memory key-value store. Reads and writes take well under a millisecond because data lives in RAM. It has rich data types (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets), TTLs (keys that expire automatically) and atomic operations such as INCR and SET NX. It is used for caching, counters, rate limiting, sessions and locks.

6.2 Cache-aside

Cache-aside means the application checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result with a TTL, and returns it. On a write, it updates the database and deletes the cache key.

At Masters this ran through Spring Data Redis, Spring's Redis integration. StringRedisTemplate is its ready-made client for string keys and values.

// Teaching sketch. TTL values are illustrative.
public ClientConfig get(long clientId) {
    String key = "cfg:" + clientId;
    String hit = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
    if (hit != null) {
        return json.readValue(hit, ClientConfig.class);
    }
    ClientConfig cfg = db.findClientConfig(clientId);
    long ttl = 300 + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(61);     // TTL with jitter
    redis.opsForValue().set(key, json.writeValueAsString(cfg), Duration.ofSeconds(ttl));
    return cfg;
}

@Transactional
public void update(long clientId, ClientConfig cfg) {
    db.saveClientConfig(clientId, cfg);
    redis.delete("cfg:" + clientId);                              // invalidate on write
}

For slow-changing reference data such as tax-rate masters, Spring's cache annotations are simpler. @Cacheable means "look in the cache first and only run this method on a miss". Backed by a Redis cache manager with a TTL, it is cache-aside in one line:

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "taxRates", key = "#hsnCode")
public TaxRate rateFor(String hsnCode) {
    return taxRateRepo.findByHsnCode(hsnCode);
}

6.3 Cache stampede

A stampede (thundering herd) is when a hot key expires and hundreds of requests miss at once and all hit the database. Guards:

  • TTL jitter, so keys don't all expire together.
  • A short lock (SET key:lock 1 NX EX 5), so one worker recomputes while others wait briefly or serve slightly stale data. In Spring Data Redis that is setIfAbsent(lockKey, "1", Duration.ofSeconds(5)).

6.4 Where I used Redis

Project Use Number
Masters India Cache-aside through Spring Data Redis for client config, feature flags, GSTIN master lookups, tax-rate masters, and IRP auth tokens (TTL under the token's life). Invalidate on write for config. TTL with jitter for slow-changing masters Database read load down 30% (HISTORICAL)
Impact Analytics Front cache of the Go auth waterfall, so verified identities are not re-verified on every request. A miss falls through to real verification No number on the resume
GeeksforGeeks Vote counters and unread counts for display, reconciled to MySQL asynchronously to avoid hot-row contention Part of the 10K+ daily queries story

Why 30% fewer reads is plausible at Masters: the same client config and GSTIN validation ran for every invoice in a bulk import. Caching those across a 100K-row import removes a huge amount of duplicate reading. Caching mostly helped p50 and read-heavy endpoints. Moving IRP calls off the request path and query fixes drove the p95 tail.

6.5 Alternatives

  • Memcached: simpler and very fast, but no rich types, persistence options or atomic data structures.
  • An in-process cache (for example Caffeine in Java): fastest, but each instance has its own copy and invalidation across instances is hard.
  • No cache, just more database replicas: moves the load around without removing duplicate reads.

7. MongoDB and Elasticsearch, briefly

  • MongoDB is a document database that stores flexible JSON-like documents. At Masters it held invoice payload snapshots and signed IRP responses, whose shape varied. At GeeksforGeeks it held doubt bodies and attachments with varying structure.
  • Elasticsearch is a search engine built on inverted indexes (a map from each word to the documents containing it). At Masters it powered invoice search and was the storage of the ELK logging stack. At GeeksforGeeks it powered search across doubts and content.

More depth: ../../../prep/02_mongodb_elasticsearch.md.

8. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. Walk me through your FRM schema design. It was an 8-table normalized MySQL schema on SOADB, Uber's service-owned MySQL standard. Fact tables hold the balance sheet and income statement lines, separate from level mappings, assessments, thresholds and review status. Every table carries the fiscal period and audit columns. Normalizing meant the close-time ETL load and analysts' edits stopped fighting over the same rows, which is how it resolved lock contention. SHA-256 natural keys stopped duplicates across quarters, and one polymorphic review-status model served all eight screens.

Q2. Tell me about the column-aliasing bug. The legacy code ran raw SQL through JDBC and built each row into a map keyed by column label. A join between the fact table and level_mapping returned two columns both labelled uuid, and the map kept the last one. So rows silently carried the mapping's uuid instead of the fact's. It surfaced when editing one reconciliation line seemed to change another. The fix was moving reads to Spring Data JPA queries with an explicit, unique alias on every column, mapped into typed projections, so values can't collide. We raised the module's statement coverage to 100% to prove nothing else regressed.

Q3. Optimistic or pessimistic locking, and why? Optimistic, for analyst edits during close. Edits are short and conflicts are rare, so holding locks would only create contention with the ETL. With a JPA @Version field, Hibernate only updates the row if the version still matches, so a stale edit is rejected with a 409 instead of silently overwriting a colleague's work. Pessimistic locking makes sense when conflicts are frequent and retries are expensive. Follow-up they may ask: "What does @Transactional do if you call the method from inside the same class?" Nothing. Spring applies it through a proxy around the bean, and a call from inside the same object skips the proxy. So transactional methods live on the service and are called from the controller.

Q4. Why shard Postgres by tax quarter? GST work is quarter-scoped. Writes land in the current quarter, while old quarters are mostly read for reconciliation and audits. Per-quarter shards keep the hot write set and its indexes small and let us archive a whole cold quarter safely. The trade-off is that routing lived in our code, so the risk was a write going to the wrong quarter. We derived the quarter from the invoice date at the API boundary and rejected mismatches.

Q5. How did Redis cut read load 30% at Masters? Cache-aside through Spring Data Redis on hot, repeated reads: client config, feature flags, GSTIN masters, tax rates and IRP auth tokens. In a 100K-row import the same lookups ran for every invoice, so caching them removed most of the duplicates. Config keys were invalidated on write, and slow-changing masters used TTL with jitter or @Cacheable. A short SET NX lock prevented stampedes.

Q6. How do you invalidate a cache correctly? Write to the database first, then delete the key, so the next read refills it from the truth. Don't update the cache in place, because racing writers can leave stale values. Add TTLs as a safety net, and jitter them. For data where staleness is dangerous, such as credentials, use short TTLs that stay below the real lifetime.

Q7. How do you find a slow query? Start from the slow endpoint in tracing, find the query, and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Look for sequential scans on big tables, bad row estimates and sorts spilling to disk. In a Hibernate service, also turn on SQL logging for that path to catch N+1 patterns from lazy loading. Common fixes from my work: a composite index matching the filter order, a join or IN batch instead of N+1, and pagination on list endpoints.

Q8. PostgreSQL or MySQL? Both are solid OLTP databases, and the choice is usually the platform standard. At Uber it was MySQL because SOADB is the service-owned standard. At Masters it was Postgres. Postgres has richer SQL features, extensions like pgvector, and native declarative partitioning. MySQL InnoDB is very well understood for high-volume simple OLTP. I design for transactions, indexes and keys either way, and JPA keeps the Java code largely the same on both.

Q9. Why Spring Data JPA and Hibernate at FRM instead of plain JDBC? Plain JDBC with maps keyed by column name is what caused the aliasing bug. With entities and typed projections, each value lands in a named, typed field. @Version gave optimistic locking without hand-written SQL, and @Transactional gave one consistent way to make cross-table writes atomic. The cost is that an ORM can hide the SQL it runs, so we kept explicit aliases, reviewed reporting queries against an allowlist, and tested every layer.

Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, asyncio, Celery (and Django)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: Python as a backend language (the GIL, async versus threads), how FastAPI and Pydantic work, Celery and asyncio as skills, and Django briefly. Then where I used Python on this resume: the Impact Analytics agent plane (the Ask Iris WebSocket and the Keep/Drop batch pipeline), Uber Menu's Python services, and GeeksforGeeks on Django.
  • When to read it: before any Python backend or AI-engineering round, and before the IA Agentic deep dive.
  • What to memorise: at IA the platform is Go and the agent plane is Python. Ask Iris is a FastAPI WebSocket that verifies a JWT on the handshake, freezes plan_scope, and runs a LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator. Uber Menu's scrapers and RAG extraction were Python. GeeksforGeeks moved from PHP to Django. Uber FRM and Masters India are Java and Spring Boot services on this resume (section 4 points to that material).

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. STATED means printed on the resume from the project source. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. Verbal means true but off the resume.

Say these carefully

  • IA platform APIs are Go/Gin. Python at IA is the agent plane: the Keep/Drop batch pipeline and Ask Iris (FastAPI WebSocket plus LangGraph). Older prep said "FastAPI hosts LangGraph/MCP agent chat endpoints". Drop "MCP", which is skills-level.
  • FastAPI on this resume means Impact Analytics' agent plane. Uber FRM (36 Spring Boot endpoints) and Masters India (PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices) are Java services. Do not describe them as FastAPI.
  • Celery and asyncio are skills-line items. No resume bullet names them. Explain them well, but don't attach them to a project outcome.
  • Ask Iris is a shipped capability with no SLA or usage numbers. Don't invent any.
  • Snippets are teaching sketches, not company code.

1. Python for backends, in plain English

Python is a high-level, dynamically typed language with a huge ecosystem. For backends its strengths are speed of development, readable code, and the best libraries for data and AI work. Its weakness is raw CPU speed and the GIL.

1.1 The GIL

The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) in CPython means only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time inside one process. Think of a kitchen with one knife: several cooks can be in the kitchen, but only one can chop at a time.

  • For I/O-bound work (waiting on databases, HTTP calls, LLM APIs), the GIL is released while waiting, so threads and async work well.
  • For CPU-bound work (heavy number crunching in pure Python), threads don't help. You use multiple processes, native libraries (NumPy) or another language.

That is part of why IA's high-RPS platform is Go while the LLM-heavy agent plane is Python. The agent plane mostly waits on model APIs.

1.2 asyncio

asyncio is Python's built-in framework for cooperative concurrency. An async def function can await a slow operation, and while it waits the event loop runs other tasks. One thread can juggle thousands of waiting network calls. Analogy: a waiter who takes an order, hands it to the kitchen, and serves other tables instead of standing at the kitchen door.

The main rule: never block the event loop. A synchronous database call or time.sleep inside an async def freezes every other request on that worker. Offload blocking work with await asyncio.to_thread(fn) or use an async driver.

# Teaching sketch, generic.
async def fetch_all(client, urls, store):
    pages = await asyncio.gather(*(client.get(u, timeout=10) for u in urls))  # concurrent I/O
    await asyncio.to_thread(store.save_many, pages)   # sync DB call off the event loop
    return pages

What to notice: gather runs the waits side by side, and to_thread keeps the one blocking call from freezing the loop.

1.3 Typing

Python type hints (def f(x: int) -> str) are not enforced at runtime by Python itself, but tools such as mypy check them, and frameworks such as Pydantic and FastAPI use them at runtime to validate data.

2. FastAPI and Pydantic

2.1 What they are

FastAPI is a modern Python web framework built on Starlette (the async web toolkit) and Pydantic (data validation). It runs on an ASGI server such as Uvicorn. ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is the async successor to WSGI and supports async handlers and WebSockets.

Pydantic turns type-annotated classes into validators. Incoming JSON is parsed into a typed object or rejected with a clear 422 error. The same idea validates LLM output: you describe the shape you expect, and anything else is rejected.

2.2 The ideas interviewers probe

# Teaching sketch of a FastAPI route. Names are generic.
class ScenarioRequest(BaseModel):
    season_code: str = Field(min_length=1)
    max_items: int = Field(gt=0, le=1000)

def get_claims(request: Request) -> dict:
    claims = verify_jwt(request.headers.get("authorization"))
    if claims is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
    return claims

@router.post("/scenarios", response_model=ScenarioOut)
async def create_scenario(body: ScenarioRequest,
                          claims: dict = Depends(get_claims),
                          svc: ScenarioService = Depends(get_service)):
    return await svc.create(body, tenant=claims["tenant_id"])
  • Validation from types. ScenarioRequest rejects an empty season or a negative item count before your code runs.
  • Dependency injection with Depends. Auth, database sessions and services are injected per request, and tests can override them with app.dependency_overrides.
  • Automatic OpenAPI docs. Every route's schema is published at /docs.
  • async def versus def. FastAPI runs async def handlers on the event loop and plain def handlers in a thread pool. Mixing them wrongly (sync I/O inside async def) is the most common performance bug.
  • WebSockets are first-class, which is how Ask Iris is served.

2.3 Layering I use in any service

flowchart LR H["Handler: HTTP, auth, validation, error mapping"] --> S["Service: business logic"] S --> R["Repository: all SQL and session lifecycle"] R --> M["Models: typed table classes"] M --> DB["Database"]

What to notice: dependencies point one way, so each layer can be unit tested with the layer below mocked.

  • Handlers stay thin: HTTP, auth, parameter validation, mapping errors to status codes.
  • Services own orchestration and business rules.
  • Repositories own every query and the session: open, commit on success, roll back on any exception, close at the end.
  • Models hold column definitions.

This is framework-neutral. The Uber FRM service used the same shape in Spring Boot (controller, service, repository, entity). See section 4.

3. Where I used Python and FastAPI

3.1 Impact Analytics: the Python agent plane

Shipped "Ask Iris," a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot enabling planners to interactively query KPIs and inspect AI decisions on a multi-billion-row database. Prevented infinite LLM loops and multi-tenant data leaks by orchestrating a LangGraph supervisor with a 3-attempt evaluator loop, utilizing LangSmith for observability, and strictly freezing hierarchy access on the initial socket handshake.

In plain words: Impact Analytics has two halves. The platform is a Go/Gin API that serves planner screens at up to 10k peak RPS. The agent plane is Python, because the LLM libraries (LangGraph, provider SDKs, Pydantic schemas for structured output) are strongest there and the work mostly waits on model APIs.

  • Ask Iris is a FastAPI WebSocket endpoint. A WebSocket is a long-lived, two-way connection, which suits a chat copilot. The handler verifies the JWT on the handshake, computes plan_scope once and freezes it for the life of the socket, then runs a LangGraph supervisor whose evaluator loop stops after 3 attempts (MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3). LangSmith traces each run.
  • Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities and Top Style run as a Python batch pipeline: deterministic KPI math, structured LLM lens calls validated against schemas, blending, durable checkpoints (det.json, agent_progress.json, --resume) and JSON telemetry. The step order is fixed, with no LLM orchestrator. See langgraph_mcp_rag.md.
# Teaching sketch (FastAPI WebSocket).
@app.websocket("/ask-iris")
async def ask_iris(ws: WebSocket):
    claims = verify_jwt(ws.headers.get("authorization") or ws.query_params.get("token"))
    if claims is None:
        await ws.close(code=4401)
        return
    plan_scope = resolve_scope(claims)          # computed once, frozen
    await ws.accept()
    while True:
        question = await ws.receive_text()
        answer = await graph.ainvoke({"q": question, "scope": plan_scope})
        await ws.send_json(answer)

What to notice: the scope is read once from the verified token. Nothing the user types later is used to widen it.

Why FastAPI here: WebSockets are built in, handlers are async (one worker can hold many idle chat sockets), and it is the same language as LangGraph, so there is no extra hop between the socket and the graph.

3.2 Uber Menu: Python services (Uber via EPAM)

The Selenium scrapers and the LangChain RAG extraction with Gemini 2.5 Pro over Milvus were Python services on GCP. Python was the natural choice because Selenium's richest bindings, LangChain and the Gemini SDK all live there. See selenium_scraping.md and langgraph_mcp_rag.md.

3.3 GeeksforGeeks: Django

Stabilized the doubt-support platform to handle 10K+ daily queries and 10x traffic spikes during live coding contests by migrating the backend to Django. Engineered high-throughput REST APIs for voting, pinning, and locking threads utilizing MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, and Elasticsearch, driving a 20% lift in premium subscriptions.

Django is a "batteries included" Python web framework: ORM, admin, auth, forms and migrations out of the box. Django REST Framework (DRF) adds API tooling. We rebuilt the PHP doubt platform incrementally, page by page, behind the same URLs. Reliability came from ORM-managed transactions, request validation and separating reads from writes. Votes used a unique (user, content) constraint, so double-submitting is idempotent, with Redis counters for display.

10K+ a day averages about 0.1 per second, so the engineering challenge was the 10x contest spikes, not the average.

Why Django at GFG and FastAPI for Ask Iris? In 2021 GFG was a CMS-style product that benefited from Django's admin, auth and ORM. Ask Iris is a small async service whose main job is holding WebSockets and calling a LangGraph graph, which FastAPI does natively with almost no framework weight.

3.4 Celery and asyncio: skills-level

Both are on my skills line. Neither is named in a resume bullet, so I explain them as skills, not as project outcomes.

Celery is a Python distributed task queue. Your code enqueues a task onto a broker (such as Redis or RabbitMQ), and worker processes pick it up and run it, with retries, rate limits and scheduling. Think of a ticket rail in a kitchen: the waiter clips tickets, cooks take them in turn.

# Teaching sketch, generic.
@app.task(bind=True, max_retries=5, rate_limit="50/s")   # illustrative values
def send_report(self, idem_key, payload):
    if already_done(idem_key):
        return
    try:
        mailer.send(payload)
    except TemporaryError as exc:
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=2 ** self.request.retries)

What to notice: the idempotency check makes a retried task safe, and the countdown doubles on each retry (exponential backoff).

Celery or Kafka? Celery is for "run this job, retry it, rate-limit it". Kafka is for "keep this ordered stream, let several consumers read it, replay it later". See kafka_streaming.md for Kafka on this resume.

The GeeksforGeeks bullet mentions "asynchronous scheduled workflows" for video processing, reminders and cleanup. The resume does not name the tool behind them, so if asked, describe the pattern (scheduled background jobs with retries) and only name a tool you are sure of.

4. On this resume, the Java services

Two projects on this resume are Java and Spring Boot, not Python. Their depth lives on other pages. Here is the short map so you don't mix them up.

Spring Boot in one paragraph. Spring is the most widely used Java framework for backend services. Its core is a container that creates your objects (called beans) and passes each one the other objects it needs, which is dependency injection. Spring Boot is Spring with sensible defaults and an embedded web server, so a service starts with one main method. A controller class marked @RestController turns methods into HTTP endpoints. Analogy: Spring is a stage manager who builds the set and hands every actor their props before the curtain rises, so actors (your classes) never fetch props themselves.

Project What it is on this resume Where to read
Uber FRM (Uber via EPAM) 36 Spring Boot endpoints over an 8-table MySQL schema on SOADB. Led 3 engineers on a Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that removed column-aliasing bugs and reached 100% module statement coverage postgres_mysql_redis.md, ../../../handbook/05_uber_frm.md
Masters India PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices. p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, mentored 2 engineers. Spring Kafka consumers for the 1M+ a day IRP pipeline kafka_streaming.md, postgres_mysql_redis.md, ../../../handbook/07_masters_india.md

Remember for Masters: the latency win came from moving slow IRP calls off the request path into Kafka consumers, HikariCP connection pooling, query and index fixes, and Redis cache-aside for reads. It was not "the framework is fast".

Python idea and its Spring counterpart (useful when an interviewer compares them):

Python / FastAPI Spring Boot equivalent
Pydantic request model DTO class with Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotNull)
Depends(...) injection Constructor injection by the Spring container
Router function with @router.patch @RestController method with @PatchMapping
SQLAlchemy session and commit Spring Data JPA repository plus @Transactional service method
async def on an event loop Thread-per-request servlet model, or WebClient for non-blocking HTTP
Celery task Kafka consumer (@KafkaListener), @Async method, @Scheduled job or Spring Batch step
pytest with TestClient JUnit 5 with Mockito and MockMvc

Per-technology entries for Java, Spring Boot, Spring MVC, Spring Security, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, Spring Batch, Spring Kafka, Maven and JUnit are in ../../../handbook/09_tech_glossary.md.

5. Design decisions

Python for the agent plane, Go for the platform (IA)

  • What: the Go/Gin platform serves planner screens and APIs. The Python agent plane runs Keep/Drop batches and Ask Iris.
  • Why: the LLM ecosystem is strongest in Python, and agent work waits on model APIs, so the GIL barely matters. The platform needs predictable latency at 10k peak RPS, where Go's goroutines and memory profile shine.
  • Alternatives and why not:
  • Everything in Python. Simpler stack, but a high-RPS analytical edge is where Python's per-request overhead and the GIL show up.
  • Everything in Go. Go LLM libraries are thinner, so we would rebuild what LangGraph and the provider SDKs give for free.
  • Trade-off: two languages and two identity code paths to keep consistent. The fix is one identity contract (same claims, same tenant binding) in both.
  • What I'd do differently: write that identity contract down as a shared spec with tests on both sides from day one.

FastAPI for Ask Iris

  • Why: native WebSockets, async handlers that hold many idle sockets cheaply, Pydantic validation, and no language hop to LangGraph.
  • Alternatives and why not: Django Channels brings Django's weight for a service that needs none of its batteries. A Go WebSocket server calling a Python graph adds a network hop and a second deployment for no gain at this point.
  • Trade-off: you must be disciplined about blocking calls inside async code.

When I'd pick Spring Boot, FastAPI or Go for a new service

  • Spring Boot: a large, long-lived business service with many entities, transactions and integrations, and a team that values strong typing and a standard structure. That is the FRM and Masters profile.
  • FastAPI: an AI or data service that lives next to Python libraries, or a small async service.
  • Go: a hot, latency-critical edge at high RPS with stable, deterministic logic.

6. Failure modes

Failure Symptom Guard
Blocking call inside async def Latency spikes for every request or socket on the worker Async drivers or asyncio.to_thread. Lint for it in review
Fat handlers Business logic untestable without HTTP Handler, service and repository layering
Pydantic models drifting from the real data 500s or silent field loss Response models, contract tests, schema changes reviewed together
LLM call hangs or provider fails A batch stalls or burns money Hard timeouts, circuit breakers, deterministic fallback score (IA A2 and A3)
Agent loops forever Token cost climbs, user waits Evaluator capped at 3 attempts plus a graph recursion limit (Ask Iris)
Scope changes mid-conversation Cross-tenant leak risk Freeze plan_scope at the WebSocket handshake
Unbounded retries Retry storms against a fragile dependency Bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter

7. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. Why is the IA agent plane Python when the platform is Go? Different jobs. The platform is a high-concurrency HTTP edge at up to 10k requests per second at peak, where Go gives cheap goroutines and predictable latency. The agent plane mostly waits on LLM APIs and needs LangGraph and the provider SDKs, which are strongest in Python. Keeping deterministic platform logic in Go and non-deterministic LLM work in Python also keeps each blast radius clear.

Q2. How is Ask Iris served? It's a FastAPI WebSocket endpoint. On the handshake it verifies the JWT, computes the planner's hierarchy scope and freezes it for the life of the socket. Each question runs through a LangGraph supervisor with an evaluator that stops after three attempts, and LangSmith traces every run. Because the scope is frozen, nothing typed later can widen access to another tenant's data. Follow-up they may ask: "What usage does it get?" It's a shipped capability. I don't quote usage or latency numbers for it.

Q3. async def or def for a FastAPI route? Use async def when everything inside is non-blocking, for example async HTTP clients and async drivers. Use plain def when the code is synchronous, and FastAPI will run it in a thread pool. The bug to avoid is synchronous I/O inside async def, which freezes the event loop for every other request. If one blocking call is unavoidable, offload it with asyncio.to_thread.

Q4. What is the GIL and when does it matter? It's a lock in CPython that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time per process. For I/O-bound services it barely matters, because the lock is released while waiting on the network. For CPU-bound work you need processes, native libraries or another language. That's one reason our high-RPS platform at IA is Go, while the agent plane, which mostly waits on model APIs, is Python.

Q5. How do you structure a Python service? Thin handlers that only do HTTP, auth and error mapping. Services that own business logic. Repositories that own every query and the session lifecycle. Typed models underneath. Dependencies point one way, so I can test a handler with a mocked service and a service with a mocked repository. It's the same layering I used in Spring Boot at Uber FRM, just with different framework names.

Q6. Why Django at GeeksforGeeks? It was a content-heavy product that benefited from Django's admin, auth, ORM and migrations. We moved the doubt platform off PHP page by page behind the same URLs. Votes were idempotent through a unique user-and-content constraint, with Redis counters for display. The hard part was the 10x spikes during live contests, not the 10K+ daily average.

Q7. Celery versus Kafka? Different tools. Celery is a task queue: run this job, retry it, rate-limit it, schedule it. Kafka is a durable, ordered log that many consumers can read and replay. I know Celery well as a skill, but my production queue story on this resume is Kafka, at Masters India with Spring Kafka consumers and at Uber Menu feeding Flink.

Q8. You've shipped both Spring Boot and FastAPI. How do they compare? Spring Boot gives a standard structure for large business services: dependency injection, @Transactional boundaries, JPA repositories, Bean Validation and mature testing with JUnit and MockMvc. That fit FRM's finance rules and Masters' many services. FastAPI is lighter and async-native and sits next to the Python AI libraries, which is why Ask Iris uses it. I pick by the service's job and the team's ecosystem, not by habit.

Q9. How would you test a FastAPI service? Use TestClient and override dependencies with app.dependency_overrides, so auth and services are fakes and no database is needed. Assert status codes, response shapes, the 401 path and error mapping. For LLM code, test the deterministic parts directly and gate model changes with an offline eval set, which at IA is the 300-case proxy set with an 80% promotion gate.

Selenium and anti-bot scraping (Uber Menu)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: what Selenium is, how browser automation works (WebDriver, locators, waits), why scrapers fail (bot detection, layout changes, rate limits), and how I hardened the Uber Menu Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries to reach 95%+ extraction success.
  • When to read it: before the Uber Menu deep dive, and before any "design a web crawler" or "how do you make a flaky dependency reliable" question.
  • What to memorise: extraction success went from an estimated 60 to 65% to 95%+. The tools were dynamic proxy pools, IP rotation and adaptive retries with backoff. Scrapers only publish events to Kafka and never write to the catalog directly. Selenium is Uber Menu only, never ANZ Document Compliance.

Labels used on this page. MEASURED means we have a log, doc or code for it. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal.

Say these carefully

  • The 60 to 65% baseline is ESTIMATED. The 95%+ outcome is HISTORICAL. Say "from roughly 60 to 65% to over 95%".
  • Selenium is Uber Menu. Do not add Selenium or RAG to the Uber Mobility ANZ document compliance story. That was a deterministic validation backend.
  • $600K a year is the resume figure (about $2 per menu x 30,000 x 12 = $720K list, floored). Older prep wrote "$600K+". Use $600K.
  • On the resume, I architected the ingestion pipeline and hardened the Selenium fleet. Older prep said "owned Eats menu ingestion end to end". Stick to the resume wording.
  • Anti-bot work is about getting through external limits. It is not the same as multi-tenant rate limiting at Impact Analytics.

1. What Selenium is, in plain English

Selenium is a tool for controlling a real web browser from code. Your program tells Chrome (or Firefox) to open a page, wait for it to load, click a button, scroll, and read what is on screen, exactly as a person would. It was built for automated testing of websites and is also widely used for scraping sites that need JavaScript to render.

Analogy: a robot sitting at a computer, following a script. "Open this restaurant's page. Wait until the menu section appears. Click 'Download menu'. Save the PDF."

Why a real browser and not a simple HTTP request? Many modern sites build the page with JavaScript after it loads. A plain HTTP request just gets an empty shell. A browser runs the JavaScript and sees the real content.

Where I used it

Scaled menu extraction success to 95%+ by hardening a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries. Designed a large-scale data ingestion and processing pipeline using Kafka and Apache Flink, with stateful keyed deduplication and schema normalization to guarantee exactly-once catalog upserts.

Uber Eats needs restaurant menus in a strict catalog schema. Many menus live on restaurant or partner web pages, often JavaScript-heavy, or as PDFs and images linked from them. A fleet of Selenium browsers on GCP fetched them. The fleet's output fed Kafka, then Flink, then the catalog or the RAG extraction path.

2. How Selenium works: the ideas interviewers probe

2.1 WebDriver

WebDriver is a W3C standard protocol for controlling browsers. Your code (the Selenium client library) sends commands such as "navigate to URL" or "find element" to a driver (ChromeDriver), which controls the browser. Headless mode runs the browser without a visible window, which is what you want on servers.

2.2 Locators

You find elements by locators: CSS selectors, XPath, id or link text. Brittle locators (div:nth-child(7) > span) break on any layout change. Robust ones target stable attributes or text.

2.3 Waits

Pages load asynchronously. Implicit waits apply a global timeout to all lookups. Explicit waits wait for a specific condition, such as "the menu section is visible". Explicit waits are the reliable choice. time.sleep is the classic anti-pattern: too short and it fails, too long and it wastes time.

# Teaching sketch. Selectors and URLs are illustrative.
opts = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
opts.add_argument("--headless=new")
opts.add_argument(f"--proxy-server={proxy.url}")      # one proxy per session
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=opts)
try:
    driver.get(vendor.menu_url)
    WebDriverWait(driver, 20).until(
        EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, "[data-section='menu']"))
    )
    html = driver.page_source
    pdf_links = [a.get_attribute("href") for a in driver.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "a[href$='.pdf']")]
finally:
    driver.quit()

2.4 Why scrapers fail

Cause What it looks like
Bot detection CAPTCHAs, 403 or 429 responses, empty pages, "access denied" interstitials
IP reputation and rate limits One IP making many requests gets throttled or blocked
Browser fingerprinting Sites detect automation from headers, user agent, navigator.webdriver and similar signals
Layout changes A selector that worked yesterday finds nothing today
Slow or flaky pages Timeouts, half-loaded content
Resource leaks Browsers not closed, so memory fills up and nodes crash

3. How I hardened the fleet

3.1 The mechanisms

  • Dynamic proxy pools and IP rotation. A proxy is an intermediate server your request goes through, so the site sees the proxy's IP instead of yours. A pool is many proxies. "Dynamic" means the pool is managed at runtime: proxies that get blocked or slow are rested or removed, and healthy ones get more traffic. Each browser session uses one proxy.
  • User-agent rotation. Older prep also mentions varying the browser identity string (UA spoofing) so the fleet does not look like one machine.
  • Adaptive retries. On a failure, retry with exponential backoff and jitter (wait 2s, 4s, 8s plus randomness), on a different proxy, within a per-source retry budget. "Adaptive" means the retry policy reacts to the failure type: a block means switch proxy and slow down for that source, a timeout means retry soon, a "page not found" means do not retry.
  • Health events. Each attempt publishes a scrape-health event (success, failure type, source, proxy) to Kafka, so failure patterns per source are visible and the proxy pool can react.
flowchart LR JOB["Scrape job for vendor"] --> PICK["Pick healthy proxy from pool"] PICK --> BR["Headless browser session"] BR --> RES{"Result"} RES -->|"success"| K["Publish menu event to Kafka"] RES -->|"blocked"| BAN["Rest that proxy, slow this source"] RES -->|"timeout"| RETRY["Backoff with jitter, new proxy"] BAN --> RETRY RETRY --> BUD{"Retry budget left?"} BUD -->|"yes"| PICK BUD -->|"no"| FAIL["Publish failure health event"] RES --> H["Publish health event"]

What to notice: a failure changes the proxy and the pace, not just "try again". Every attempt leaves a health signal.

# Teaching sketch of adaptive retry.
def scrape_with_retries(vendor, pool, budget=4):
    for attempt in range(budget):
        proxy = pool.pick(source=vendor.source)
        outcome = scrape_once(vendor, proxy)
        publish_health(vendor, proxy, outcome)
        if outcome.ok:
            return outcome
        if outcome.kind == "blocked":
            pool.rest(proxy); pool.slow_down(vendor.source)
        elif outcome.kind == "not_found":
            return outcome                      # retrying will not help
        time.sleep(min(60, 2 ** attempt) + random.random())
    return outcome

3.2 Why scrapers publish to Kafka and never write the catalog

Scrapers are the flakiest part of the system. If each scraper also called the catalog and the RAG path synchronously, slow downstreams would hold browsers open, and a scraper crash would lose work. Publishing to Kafka means a scrape is done once its event is stored. Downstream can be slow, fail or replay without touching the fleet. See kafka_streaming.md and flink.md.

3.3 Running a fleet

  • Docker images with pinned browser and driver versions, so a Chrome auto-update does not silently break the fleet.
  • One browser per job, always closed in finally, to avoid memory leaks.
  • Bounded concurrency per source, so we do not hammer one site.
  • Monitoring success rate per source, so a layout change on one site is noticed as "source X dropped from 97% to 20%" rather than buried in a global average.

4. Design decisions

  • What: a Selenium fleet with dynamic proxy pools, adaptive retries and health events, publishing to Kafka.
  • Why: many menu sources are JavaScript-heavy and have no API, and blocks were the main cause of failed extractions.
  • Alternatives considered:
  • Partner APIs or direct menu uploads. Best when available, and always preferred. Coverage was incomplete, which is why scraping existed.
  • Plain HTTP plus an HTML parser (requests and BeautifulSoup). Much cheaper per page, but fails on JavaScript-rendered pages. A good first try per source.
  • Playwright or Puppeteer. Modern browser automation with better auto-waiting and network interception. A reasonable alternative. If asked, say I would evaluate Playwright for a new build.
  • A third-party scraping or menu-processing vendor. That is part of what the pipeline replaced. The $600K a year saving is derived from about $2 per menu in third-party or manual cost.
  • Trade-off: browsers are heavy (CPU and memory per session) and brittle to layout changes. Proxy pools cost money.
  • What I'd do differently: try plain HTTP first per source and only escalate to a browser when needed, and add automatic selector health checks on a sample of sources every day.

5. The numbers

Number What it measures How derived Tag
95%+ Share of scrape attempts that produced a usable menu Work records HISTORICAL
About 60 to 65% Success rate before hardening Estimate from before proxy pools and adaptive retries ESTIMATED
30K+ menus a month Volume through the pipeline. About 1,000 a day Work records HISTORICAL
From 24 hours to 2 hours Restaurant onboarding time, about 92% faster Work records HISTORICAL
$600K a year About $2 per menu x 30,000 x 12 = $720K list, floored to $600K Arithmetic on HISTORICAL inputs ESTIMATED

Why it mattered: every failed scrape is a manual fallback, and a restaurant that is not live is not earning.

Say it: "Extraction success went to over 95%, from roughly 60 to 65% before, by adding dynamic proxy pools and adaptive retries to the Selenium fleet."

Do NOT say: the baseline as measured, "100% success", or "$720K saved".

6. Interview questions with speakable answers

Q1. Why scrape at all instead of using APIs? We used partner feeds and uploads wherever they existed, but coverage was incomplete. Many restaurants only had menus on JavaScript-heavy pages or as linked PDFs. Without automation those went to a manual or third-party process that cost about $2 a menu and took about a day. Scraping plus RAG extraction closed that gap, and onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours.

Q2. How did you get from about 60% to 95%+ success? Most failures were blocks and timeouts, not bad parsing. We added dynamic proxy pools, so each session used a healthy proxy and blocked ones were rested. We added adaptive retries: exponential backoff with jitter on a different proxy, within a per-source budget, and no retry on errors that won't change. Every attempt published a health event, so we could see which sources and proxies were failing.

Q3. How do you detect that a site changed its layout? Track success per source, not just globally, so one site dropping sharply stands out. Downstream schema validation also catches pages that load but parse into nonsense. A sudden spike of "selector not found" or empty extractions for one source is the alert. Then you fix the selector, and Kafka replay lets you reprocess the stored raw payloads without re-scraping.

Q4. How does backoff with jitter work and why the jitter? After each failure you wait longer, for example 2, 4, then 8 seconds, up to a cap. Jitter adds randomness to each wait. Without jitter, thousands of failed jobs retry at exactly the same moments and hit the site in synchronized waves, which looks even more like a bot and makes blocks worse. With jitter, retries spread out.

Q5. What about the ethics and legality of scraping? Respect the site's terms and robots rules where they apply, keep request rates polite with per-source concurrency limits, and prefer official feeds or partner uploads whenever they exist. Business and legal decisions about which sources to use were not mine to make, and I would say that plainly. My job was to make the approved sources reliable and gentle on the sites.

Q6. Selenium or Playwright today? For a new build I'd evaluate Playwright first. It has better auto-waiting, network interception and multi-browser support in one API. Selenium is a mature W3C WebDriver standard with a huge ecosystem, which is why fleets built on it are common. The reliability techniques I used, proxy pools, adaptive retries and health signals, apply to either.

Q7. How do you keep a browser fleet from leaking memory? One browser per job, always quit in a finally block, with a hard timeout per job. Pin browser and driver versions in the Docker image so updates are deliberate. Recycle workers periodically, and alert on node memory. Most "fleet falls over" incidents are orphaned browser processes.

Assort Keep/Drop flow (assort_kd_flow) — Deep End‑to‑End Pipeline Reference

Hybrid Keep / Drop decisioning at article × plan‑season grain, combining a deterministic rule score (s_det) with an agentic LLM score (s_agent) into a final blended score (s_final). Outcomes are binary: keep or drop (no "shop").

This document explains every stage: what it does, why it exists, the SQL it runs, the maths, the config it reads, the agents involved, prompts, guardrails, timeouts/retries, evals, and how to run it in production — with worked examples.

Package note. assort_kd_flow is the only Keep/Drop package in this repo (former assortment/ / assortment_v2 names retired). It is self-contained for config, prompts, agents, engines, and CH clients (shared only: repo .env + ClickHouse). It has a pure domain/ math layer, offline evals/, ops/ helpers, a prompt registry, and Critic/Evaluator disabled. All engines write staging CSVs only. Ops loads bake via python -m assort_kd_flow.ops.load_csv_to_ch --target bake, then promotes with python -m assort_kd_flow.ops.migrate_bake. Config source.*_table defaults point at *_bake for mid-run reads; *_table_main names are for promote. Evals grade whatever source.final_table names (bake by default).

0. Mental model in one paragraph

For each article in a season we compute a rule score from sell‑through and rate of sale (s_det), and an LLM score from a set of analytical "lenses" combined by a per‑article "decider" (s_agent). We blend them: s_final = 0.4·s_det + 0.6·s_agent. Keep if s_final ≥ 0.55. Everything is config‑driven; formulas live in domain/; LLM behaviour is bounded by guardrails; quality is checked offline by evals/.

1. Architecture layers

assort_kd_flow/
  config/decision.json     # weights, ramps, lenses, agents, guardrails  (the knobs)
  config/eval.json         # promotion gates
  domain/                  # PURE math + rules (no I/O, no LLM)
    kpis.py                #   KPI formulas + SQL exprs (single source of truth)
    scoring.py             #   ramps, s_det, s_final, confidence, mixes
    rules.py               #   binary outcome, demand>margin, cutover matrix
  context/                 # what each agent is allowed to see (ranked fields)
  prompts/registry.py      # prompt id -> path
  prompts/md/              # base + lens + decider + explain + topN + peer prompts
  lenses/
    features.py            # feature SQL from reco_article_store_week
    gate.py                # cheap prefilter: which lenses apply to an article
  agents/
    tool_agent.py          # LangGraph ToolNode loop (bounded)
    peer.py                # PeerBenchmark agent (relative context)
    critic.py, evaluator.py# DISABLED in v2 (replaced by offline evals)
  engines/
    deterministic.py       # s_det SQL engine
    decider.py             # per-article lens mixes
    agentic.py             # orchestration: scopes, parallelism, resume
    agentic_batch.py       # per-batch: peer -> decider -> lenses -> blend -> explanations
    ensemble.py            # re-exports domain.scoring (compat)
    confidence.py          # re-exports domain.scoring (compat)
    explain.py             # planner-facing Keep/Drop explanation JSON
    topn_explain.py        # short Top Performing card tagline for Keeps
    run_ensemble.py        # patch s_det/s_final only (no LLM)
  fill/
    article_store_week.py  # master_input → week bake CSV (SELECT only)
    detect_new.py          # watermark: which l1×l2×week changed
  ch/, tools/, settings/, llm.py
  evals/                   # offline gold suite + post-run report
  ops/                     # load_csv_to_ch, migrate_bake, promote_config, run_controller
  logs/                    # run ledgers only (<run_id>/events.jsonl + summary.json)
  run_pipeline.py          # CLI

No LLM orchestrator. Batch order is fixed in engines/agentic_batch.py (peer → decider → lenses → blend → explain → topN explain). Run-level oversight is deterministic ops/run_controller.py (ledger, circuit breaker, signal-quality abort) — not an agent.

Design rule: KPI/ramp/ensemble/confidence maths exist once in domain/. SQL generators and Python tests both call the same functions, so the number a planner sees and the number a test checks can never silently diverge.

2. Tables (ClickHouse, database kik_dev)

Table Grain Written by Purpose
master_input_imputed_assort_* article × store × date upstream (read‑only) raw sales + inventory
reco_article_store_week_bake article × store × fiscal_year_week load_csv_to_ch (from fill CSV) bake week rollup (approved)
reco_deterministic_score_bake article × plan‑season load_csv_to_ch (from det CSV) bake s_det + approved
reco_agentic_score_bake article × plan‑season load_csv_to_ch (from agentic CSV) bake s_agent + approved + l0–l4
reco_final_score_bake article × plan‑season load_csv_to_ch (from final CSV) bake finals + approved
reco_article_store_week / reco_deterministic_score / reco_agentic_score / reco_final_score same grains migrate_bake main tables after promote

| global.fiscal_date_mapping, global.season_master | calendar | upstream | maps fiscal_year_week → plan_season_code |

Since output.mode = csv, all engines write staging CSVs only (exact table columns + staging-only ch_load_status). Publish path:

  1. ops.load_csv_to_ch --target bake (default) → *_bake
  2. ops.migrate_bake → main (approved=1 on bake)

Operator order for a fresh season: fill CSV → load week bake → det CSV → load det bake → agentic CSV → load agentic/final bake → migrate when ready. output.mode clickhouse/dual requires ops --dangerous-write-ch — agents never get that flag. Host resource_budget caps workers and pool size. Staging lives under assort_kd_flow/staging/<run_id>/. Fill resume is checkpoint JSON by year×l1×l2. Critical calendar note: season_code has one meaning across the week, deterministic, agentic, and final tables: the Kik plan season (e.g. 74/76). The fill maps it once from fiscal_year_week via global.fiscal_date_mapping → global.season_master; scoring propagates that stored key directly. The source product-fashion value (0–4) is retained only as reco_article_store_week.product_season_code.

Provenance columns. Every reco_* row carries config_hash (SHA‑256 of the config JSON and all referenced prompt files) and computed_at. Uniqueness / resume is by (season_code, article) (latest computed_at), not a run UUID. reco_deterministic_score also stores matched_terms + reason_codes + det_reason; reco_agentic_score stores per‑lens lens_results and agent_status (ok/pending/error); reco_final_score stores outcome, Keep/Drop explanation, Top Performing explanation_topN, and explanation_json. Score tables also carry the product hierarchy l0_name…l4_name (denormalized from the week table; one article → one path). Store hierarchy (s0/s1/region) stays on the week table only — score grain is article×season, not store. Because config_hash folds in prompt text, editing any prompt changes the hash — you can always tell which config+prompts produced a row.

3. Prerequisites before a run

  1. ClickHouse access via .env (CLICKHOUSE_HOST, _PORT, _USER, _PASSWORD, _DATABASE, _SECURE). App is SELECT/INSERT only — never DDL. Schema (reco_* tables, incl. explanation_json) is applied out‑of‑band by a privileged user.
  2. LLM access via .env (OpenAI/Azure/Anthropic/etc.); assort_kd_flow/llm.py builds a model per call (no global singleton).
  3. Source populated: master_input_imputed_assort_* for the target fiscal years, containing units_sold, revenue, margin, cost, msrp, discount_percentage, oh, oh_cost, eop_inv, bop_inv, receipts_quantity, ….
  4. Calendar populated: global.fiscal_date_mapping + global.season_master covering those weeks (so plan seasons resolve).
  5. Config chosen: assort_kd_flow/config/decision.json (weights, ramps, active lenses, guardrails). Its config_hash is stamped on every output row.

Data reality that shaped v2: in the Kik feed eop_inv/bop_inv are all zero, but daily on‑hand oh is populated ~71%. So sell‑through uses ending on‑hand as residual stock, clamped ≥ 0. See §6.

4. End‑to‑end flow

flowchart TD A[master_input_imputed_assort_*] -->|fill SELECT rollup
checkpoint resume| Wcsv[staging/.../reco_article_store_week_bake/*.csv] Wcsv -->|OPERATOR load_csv_to_ch bake| Wbake[reco_article_store_week_bake] Wbake -->|det SELECT KPI + ramps| Dcsv[staging/.../reco_deterministic_score_bake/*.csv] Dcsv -->|OPERATOR load_csv_to_ch bake| Dbake[reco_deterministic_score_bake] Wbake -->|agentic feature SQL| Dfeat[features per article] Dbake -->|s_det join| E Dfeat --> E subgraph E [Per-batch agentic - LLM, NO DB writes] P[PeerBenchmark agent] --> DEC[Decider: lens mixes] DEC --> L[Lenses run in parallel] L --> MIX[score mixes -> s_agent] MIX --> BL[blend s_det+s_agent -> s_final] BL --> CONF[confidence] BL --> EXP[Explain + TopN taglines] end E --> F[staging/.../reco_agentic_score_bake/*.csv] E --> G[staging/.../reco_final_score_bake/*.csv] F -->|OPERATOR load_csv_to_ch bake| Abake[reco_agentic_score_bake] G -->|OPERATOR load_csv_to_ch bake| Fbake[reco_final_score_bake] Wbake -->|OPERATOR migrate_bake| Wmain[reco_article_store_week] Dbake -->|OPERATOR migrate_bake| Dmain[reco_deterministic_score] Abake -->|OPERATOR migrate_bake| Amain[reco_agentic_score] Fbake -->|OPERATOR migrate_bake| Fmain[reco_final_score]

Fixed order: fill → deterministic → agentic → (ensemble optional) → evals. --steps auto|all expands to fill, deterministic, agentic, evals.

Write model (who writes ClickHouse):

Stage Writes CH? Artifact Resume mechanism
fill No (CSV only) reco_article_store_week_bake/*.csv checkpoint JSON (year×l1×l2)
deterministic No (CSV only; optional --dangerous-write-ch) reco_deterministic_score_bake/*.csv staging ch_load_status
