Masters India and GeeksforGeeks: MongoDB and Elasticsearch

How to use this page

  • What it covers: why MongoDB and Elasticsearch appear on the Masters India and GeeksforGeeks tech lines, what each one is, how it works, where I used it, and how to defend the choice against "why not just PostgreSQL or MySQL?".
  • When to read it: when a job asks for NoSQL or search experience, or when an interviewer points at those two words on the resume.
  • What to memorise: the one-line split ("relational database for correctness, Mongo where the document shape varied, Elasticsearch for search and, at Masters, the log plane"), the inverted-index explanation, and the honesty rule about schemas.

Companion docs: full project context in 12_masters_gfg_deep_dive.md and the speakable packs in 23c_masters_gfg_interview_packs.md.

Both technologies were added to the resume's Tech line for these two roles because I worked with them there. They are supporting stores, not the system of record. PostgreSQL (Masters India) and MySQL (GeeksforGeeks) held the transactional truth.

Honesty rule. The example documents and queries below are illustrative shapes to teach the idea. They are not the real production schemas. If asked which collections or indexes you touched, describe the purpose (payload snapshots, flexible doubt bodies, log search) and do not invent field-level schemas you cannot draw from memory.

1. The one-line split (say this first)

"PostgreSQL or MySQL for transactional correctness, MongoDB where the document shape varied, and Elasticsearch for search and, at Masters India, the log plane in ELK."

flowchart LR APP["Application services"] --> SQL["PostgreSQL or MySQL: source of truth"] APP --> MG["MongoDB: variable-shape documents"] APP --> ES["Elasticsearch: full-text search"] LOGS["Service logs with request IDs"] --> LS["Logstash or log shipper"] LS --> ES ES --> KB["Kibana: search and dashboards"]

What to notice: the relational database is the truth. MongoDB and Elasticsearch each do one job the relational database does poorly. At Masters India, Elasticsearch also receives logs as part of ELK.

2. MongoDB in plain English

What it is. MongoDB is a document database. Instead of rows in fixed-column tables, it stores documents: JSON-like records (stored internally as BSON, a binary form of JSON) grouped into collections. Two documents in the same collection can have different fields. Think of a relational table as a spreadsheet where every row must fill the same columns, and a MongoDB collection as a folder of forms where each form can have extra pages.

The ideas that matter in interviews.

  1. Flexible schema. You can store nested objects and arrays directly, and new fields need no migration. That is great for payloads whose shape you do not control, and risky if you need strict consistency across records.
  2. Indexes still matter. MongoDB scans the whole collection without an index, just like SQL. You create indexes on the fields you query, including compound indexes such as {client_id: 1, created_at: -1}.
  3. One document is the unit of atomicity. An update to a single document is atomic. Multi-document transactions exist in modern MongoDB but cost more. So you model data to keep things that change together in one document.
  4. Replica sets and write concern. Production MongoDB runs as a replica set (one primary and copies). Write concern (for example w: "majority") controls how many copies must confirm a write before it counts.
  5. Sharding. MongoDB can split a collection across servers by a shard key. That is a capability, not something I claim to have operated.

Where I used MongoDB

Masters India. MongoDB held snapshots of flexible, semi-structured payloads alongside PostgreSQL as the system of record for invoices and returns. The main use was the raw invoice payload as received and the IRP's signed response, whose shapes varied by document type and changed over time. Older notes also mention client config blobs, import job metadata and other non-relational side collections. In the Kafka pipeline, one stage persisted the signed IRP response to a MongoDB snapshot.

An illustrative snapshot document:

{
  "_id": "42:INV-2024-000917",
  "client_id": 42,
  "seller_gstin": "29ABCDE1234F1Z5",
  "request_id": "7f3c9a1e",
  "received_payload": { "doc_type": "INV", "doc_no": "INV-2024-000917", "items": [ "..." ] },
  "irp_response": { "irn": "<64-char hash>", "ack_no": "...", "signed_qr": "..." },
  "created_at": "2024-01-18T10:42:09Z"
}

// Illustrative index for "show me this client's recent snapshots"
db.irp_snapshots.createIndex({ client_id: 1, created_at: -1 })

GeeksforGeeks. MongoDB held flexible documents for community and content shapes that did not fit cleanly in MySQL, such as doubt bodies and attachments that varied in structure. Older notes also mention dual-write or dual-read paths during the PHP to Django migration. MySQL remained the primary relational store for threads, permissions and votes.

Why MongoDB there, and the alternatives

Why. The payloads were documents by nature. An invoice payload or IRP response is a nested JSON object whose fields differ by document type and change when the government updates its schema. Storing it whole, as received, is simple and preserves an exact audit copy.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. - PostgreSQL JSONB. A JSON column inside PostgreSQL, with indexing. Today I would seriously consider this for Masters India, because it keeps one database to operate and lets you join snapshots to invoice rows. MongoDB wins when document volume is large, the documents are the main access pattern, and you want to scale that store independently. - Object storage (S3). Cheapest for raw blobs you rarely query. The trade-off is that you cannot query inside them easily. - Columns in MySQL or PostgreSQL. Correct and strict, but every shape change needs a migration.

Trade-off. Two databases mean two things to back up, monitor and keep consistent. MongoDB is not the place for anything that needs a cross-record transaction or a unique business constraint. That stayed in the relational database.

3. Elasticsearch in plain English

What it is. Elasticsearch is a distributed search engine built on Apache Lucene. You send it JSON documents, and it indexes every word so you can search text fast, rank results by relevance and run aggregations (counts, histograms). Think of it as the index at the back of a book, built automatically for millions of documents at once.

The ideas that matter in interviews.

  1. Inverted index. The core structure. It maps each term to the list of documents that contain it. Searching "kafka timeout" looks up two short lists and intersects them, instead of reading every document.
  2. Analyzers. Before indexing, text passes through an analyzer that splits it into tokens, lowercases it, and can remove stop words or reduce words to their stem. "Timeouts" and "timeout" can then match. The same analyzer runs on the search query.
  3. Mappings. The schema of an index. text fields are analyzed for full-text search. keyword fields are stored exactly, for filters and aggregations such as request_id or client_id.
  4. Shards and replicas. An index is split into shards spread across nodes, and each shard can have replicas for availability and read throughput.
  5. Near real time. New documents become searchable after a short refresh interval (about one second by default), not instantly. It is not a transactional database.
  6. Relevance scoring. Results are ranked by a scoring formula (BM25 by default) that rewards rare terms and term frequency.

A tiny inverted-index example:

doc 1: "IRP timeout on bulk import"
doc 2: "bulk import finished"
doc 3: "IRP returned duplicate IRN"

term       -> documents
"irp"      -> 1, 3
"timeout"  -> 1
"bulk"     -> 1, 2
"import"   -> 1, 2
"duplicate"-> 3

query "irp bulk" -> docs containing both: 1

What ELK is

ELK is Elasticsearch, Logstash and Kibana used together for logs. Services write structured JSON log lines. Logstash (or a lightweight shipper) collects and parses them. Elasticsearch stores and indexes them. Kibana is the screen where you search and build dashboards. It is a searchable library of every log line from every service.

Where I used Elasticsearch

Masters India: the log plane, plus invoice search. Elasticsearch was the "E" in ELK. Every log line was structured JSON with a request ID (a correlation ID), so a single Kibana search showed a request's whole journey through the API, the Kafka consumer and the IRP worker. That is the core of the "incident triage down 70%" bullet, together with New Relic tracing. Older notes also say Elasticsearch powered invoice search.

An illustrative Kibana query (KQL, Kibana Query Language) during an incident:

request_id:"7f3c9a1e"

and a broader one:

service:"irp-worker" and level:"ERROR" and event:"irp_timeout" and client_id:42

An illustrative log index mapping:

{
  "mappings": {
    "properties": {
      "ts":         { "type": "date" },
      "service":    { "type": "keyword" },
      "level":      { "type": "keyword" },
      "request_id": { "type": "keyword" },
      "client_id":  { "type": "long" },
      "message":    { "type": "text" }
    }
  }
}

request_id is a keyword because you want an exact match, not word splitting.

GeeksforGeeks: product search. Elasticsearch powered full-text search and feed retrieval over doubts, posts and content. This is a different use from Masters India's logging, so distinguish them if asked.

An illustrative doubt search:

GET doubts/_search
{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must":   [{ "match": { "body": "segmentation fault in recursion" } }],
      "filter": [{ "term": { "course_id": 118 } }, { "term": { "is_locked": false } }]
    }
  },
  "size": 10
}

match is analyzed full-text search and is scored for relevance. term filters are exact and unscored, which makes them cheap and cacheable.

Why Elasticsearch there, and the alternatives

Why at Masters India. Logs from many services needed one searchable place with fast filtering by request ID, client and error type. ELK is the standard self-managed answer for that, and it pairs with New Relic for traces.

Why at GeeksforGeeks. Learners search doubts and content in free text with typos, plurals and partial matches. Relevance ranking and analyzers are what a search engine does well and what LIKE '%...%' in MySQL does badly.

Alternatives and when I'd pick them. - PostgreSQL or MySQL full-text search (tsvector in PostgreSQL, FULLTEXT in MySQL). Good enough for small, simple search without another cluster. I'd pick it for a small catalogue. - OpenSearch. The open-source fork of Elasticsearch, offered as a managed service on AWS. It has the same model and is a reasonable choice on AWS. - CloudWatch Logs (for the logging use case on AWS). Less to run, but weaker search and dashboards for heavy incident work.

Trade-off. Elasticsearch is not a source of truth. It is near real time, and data in it can be rebuilt from the primary store. It also costs memory and disk, and log retention needs a policy or storage grows forever.

4. MongoDB vs Elasticsearch vs the relational database

Question Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) MongoDB Elasticsearch
Best at Transactions, constraints, joins Variable-shape documents Full-text search, log search, aggregations
Source of truth? Yes Sometimes, for its own documents No, rebuildable
Schema Strict, migrations Flexible Mapping per index
Where I used it Masters invoices and job state, GFG threads and votes Masters payload snapshots, GFG flexible doubt bodies Masters ELK logs and invoice search, GFG doubt search

The rule behind the table: keep anything that needs a unique constraint or a transaction in the relational database. That is why idempotency keys at Masters India and the one-vote-per-user rule at GeeksforGeeks lived in PostgreSQL and MySQL, not in MongoDB.

5. Interview questions with speakable answers

"Why did you need MongoDB if you had PostgreSQL?" PostgreSQL was the system of record for invoices and job state, and MongoDB held the documents whose shape we did not control. The raw invoice payloads and the government's signed responses are nested JSON that varies by document type and changes when the schema changes. Storing them whole in MongoDB gave us an exact audit copy without a migration for every change. Anything that needed a constraint, like the idempotency key, stayed in PostgreSQL. If I built it again today, I would also consider PostgreSQL JSONB to run one fewer database.

"How does Elasticsearch search so fast?" It builds an inverted index, a map from every term to the documents that contain it, much like the index at the back of a book. A query looks up a few short lists and intersects them instead of scanning every document. Analyzers normalise text first, lowercasing it and splitting tokens, so "Timeouts" can match "timeout". Results are then ranked by relevance.

"Is the Elasticsearch on your Masters line the same as on your GeeksforGeeks line?" No, they were different uses. At Masters India it was mainly the log plane in ELK: structured logs with request IDs, searched in Kibana during incidents, which drove the triage improvement. Older notes also say it powered invoice search there. At GeeksforGeeks it was product search over doubts and content for learners.

"Can Elasticsearch be your primary database?" I would not use it that way. It is near real time rather than transactional, it lacks the constraints and transactions you need for business truth, and you should be able to rebuild it from the primary store. We treated it as a derived index in both jobs.

"How do you index MongoDB?" The same way you think about SQL indexes: index the fields you filter and sort on, in query order. For "this client's latest snapshots", a compound index on client ID ascending and created-at descending serves both the filter and the sort. Without an index, MongoDB scans the whole collection.

Follow-up they may ask: "Which collections did you design?" Say what they were for (payload and response snapshots at Masters, flexible doubt bodies at GeeksforGeeks), and do not invent field-level schemas.

6. Say this / don't say this

Say this

  • "Relational database for correctness, Mongo where the document shape varied, Elasticsearch for search and, at Masters, the log plane."
  • "At Masters, ELK plus request IDs is what made triage fast."
  • "At GeeksforGeeks, Elasticsearch was product search, a different use from Masters logging."

Don't say this

  • That MongoDB or Elasticsearch was the system of record for invoices or votes.
  • Detailed collection schemas or cluster sizes you cannot draw from memory.
  • That you operated MongoDB sharding or large Elasticsearch clusters. Keep it to how you used them.

Uber Menu: Streaming Numbers Explained

How to use this page

  • What it covers: every number connected to the Uber Eats Menu pipeline (Kafka, Flink, the RAG path and the scraping fleet), what each one measures, how it is derived, and how to say it out loud.
  • When to read it: right before an interview, as a five-minute numbers drill. For the full architecture, read the Menu deep dive.
  • What to memorise: from 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year (from $720K list), 30K+ menus a month (about 1,000 a day), 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation, 95%+ extraction success from an estimated 60 to 65%. Know that 200 to 500 events a second is an estimate for prep only.

This page is a numbers companion. It does not repeat the full design. For that, go to:

  1. Menu deep dive: architecture, Kafka and Flink explained from scratch, RAG over Milvus, mock questions.
  2. Uber interview packs, Menu section: one-minute versions and speakable answers.
  3. Metrics derivations, section 3: the source table for these numbers.
  4. Optional older cross-track material, which also discusses Spark and Pinot (not on this PDF): Menu ingestion project notes and Tech deep dives.

Tags on this page

  • MEASURED: there is a log, a document or code behind it.
  • TARGET: a design goal. Say "targeting".
  • ESTIMATED: arithmetic I can show. Say "roughly, derived from...".
  • HISTORICAL: from my past work records and resume, not re-measured from logs in this repo.

A thirty-second refresher on the pipeline

Restaurant menus come in as websites, PDFs and photos. A Selenium fleet fetches them through dynamic proxy pools with adaptive retries. Each fetched menu becomes an event on Kafka, a durable log that keeps messages in order per key and lets you replay them. The key is vendor and menu, so one restaurant's events stay in order. Flink, a stream processor, reads the events, remembers the last content hash per key (keyed state) to drop duplicates, normalizes fields to the catalog schema, and upserts to the catalog. The upsert is idempotent, meaning running it twice leaves the same result. Unstructured PDFs go through a LangChain RAG path: retrieve similar labelled menus from Milvus (a vector database), prompt Gemini 2.5 Pro, and validate the output against the schema before writing.

flowchart LR A["Selenium fleet: 95%+ success"] --> B["Kafka: peak 200-500 events per sec, estimated"] B --> C["Flink: keyed dedupe and normalize"] C --> D["Catalog upsert: 30K+ menus a month"] C --> E["RAG over Milvus plus Gemini: 98% offline"] E --> D D --> F["Onboarding: 24 hours to 2 hours, $600K a year"]

What to notice: each box carries the number that belongs to it. The throughput number on Kafka is the only one that is an estimate and not on the PDF.

The resume numbers, one by one

From 24 hours to 2 hours (onboarding time)

  • What it measures: how long a restaurant's menu takes to go from submitted to ready in the catalog.
  • How it is derived: before and after cycle time, from records (HISTORICAL). 22 of 24 hours saved is about a 92% cut, or twelve times faster.
  • Why it mattered: a restaurant can go live and start taking orders the same day instead of the next day.
  • Say it like this: "Onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours."
  • Don't say: a precise percentage like "91.7%". Keep it to the hours.

$600K a year (savings)

  • What it measures: annual cost removed by replacing a third-party or manual menu conversion step.
  • How it is derived: about $2 per menu, times 30,000 menus a month, is $60,000 a month. Times 12 months is $720,000 a year list. I floor it to $600K so I am not quoting the best case.
$2 per menu x 30,000 menus/month = $60,000/month
$60,000/month x 12 months        = $720,000/year (list)
Resume figure (conservative)     = $600,000/year
  • Why it mattered: it is a direct, recurring saving at Uber Eats volume.
  • Say it like this: "About $600K a year. The vendor tool was roughly $2 a menu, at 30K menus a month that's $720K list, and I quote the conservative $600K."
  • Don't say: "$720K saved". The list figure is the ceiling, not the claim.

30K+ menus a month (volume)

  • What it measures: menus processed by the pipeline each month (HISTORICAL).
  • How to picture it: 30,000 divided by 30 days is about 1,000 menus a day. That is a steady daily workload with bursts during fleet runs, not a firehose.
  • Why it mattered: at this volume, a per-menu vendor cost adds up fast, and manual work does not scale.
  • Say it like this: "30K-plus menus a month, roughly a thousand a day."
  • Don't say: "millions of events a day" or "hundreds of millions of transactions".

98% field fidelity (offline evaluation)

  • What it measures: on a hand-labelled test set of menus, the share of extracted fields (item name, price, category and so on) that match the correct answer.
  • A toy example to explain the metric: a test menu with 10 items and 4 fields per item has 40 fields. If 39 match the labels, that menu scores 97.5%. The 98% is the result across the evaluation set.
  • Why offline matters: offline evaluation runs on a fixed set, so it is repeatable and lets you compare versions. It is not the same as a live production quality measurement.
  • Say it like this: "98% field fidelity in offline evaluation."
  • Don't say: "98% accuracy in production" or present it as an SLA. Older prep also quoted "100% schema consistency". That is not on the current PDF. If asked, say the schema gate rejects anything malformed, so everything that lands is schema-valid by construction.

95%+ extraction success (from an estimated 60 to 65%)

  • What it measures: the share of scrape or extraction attempts that produce a usable menu.
  • How it is derived: 95%+ is the end point after hardening (HISTORICAL). The 60 to 65% starting point is ESTIMATED.
  • What moved it: dynamic proxy pools (swap out blocked IP addresses), IP rotation, and adaptive retries with per-source budgets.
  • Why it mattered: every failed scrape is a restaurant waiting or a manual fallback.
  • Say it like this: "To 95%-plus, from roughly 60 to 65% before hardening. That starting point is an estimate."
  • Don't say: "from 60% to 95%" as if the baseline were measured.

The prep-only throughput estimate

About 200 to 500 events a second at peak (ESTIMATED, not on the PDF)

  • What it measures: messages per second flowing through Kafka during a fleet run.
  • How it is derived: about 1,000 menus a day. Each menu produces many events, not one: item-level events, plus retry and scrape-health events. Fleet runs bunch work into windows instead of spreading it evenly over 24 hours. Put those together and the peak lands in the hundreds per second. Steady state is much lower.
  • Why it matters in an interview: it shows you can size a system from business volume. It also shows why Kafka helps. Bursts are absorbed by the log, and Flink catches up.
  • Say it like this (only if asked): "Order of magnitude, a few hundred events a second at peak during fleet runs, much lower at steady state. That's an estimate from the menu volume, not a dashboard number."
  • Don't say: it as a measured fact, or put it next to 30K menus a month on a resume. The two look inconsistent without the explanation.

Component table

The table maps each component to the reason it exists and the number tied to it. Rows marked "study only" are not resume claims.

Component What it is Why it is here Number
Kafka Durable, partitioned log Absorbs scrape bursts, replay after a bad deploy, keeps per-vendor order About 200 to 500 peak events a second (ESTIMATED, prep only)
Flink Stateful stream processor Keyed dedupe by content hash, event-time ordering, checkpointed recovery Same peak. Healthy state means consumer lag near zero at steady state.
Selenium fleet with proxy pools Browser automation plus rotating IP addresses JavaScript-heavy sites, anti-bot defenses 95%+ success (from an estimated 60 to 65%)
RAG over Milvus with Gemini 2.5 Pro Retrieval-grounded LLM extraction Multilingual PDFs with no stable structure 98% field fidelity, offline evaluation
Spark (study only, NOT on PDF) Distributed batch engine Would be an option for large historical backfills About 1 to 2 million item rows per typical 90-day window (ESTIMATED, study only)
Pinot (study only, NOT on PDF) Real-time analytics database Older prep used it for an operational health dashboard idea Older prep said sub-second queries and detection from hours to minutes. Not a claim. Do not raise it.

Words in the table, in one line each.

  • Consumer lag: how far behind the newest Kafka message the consumer is. It is the main health signal. Rising lag means processing cannot keep up.
  • Keyed dedupe: Flink keeps a memory per vendor and menu of the last content hash, and drops exact repeats.
  • Event time: ordering by when the scrape happened, not when the event arrived, so a late old page cannot overwrite a newer one.
  • Checkpoint: a periodic snapshot of Flink's state plus Kafka positions, used to recover after a crash.
  • Exactly-once catalog upserts: in practice, at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes. Replays are harmless. Never say zero message loss.

Quick drill

  1. "What does 30K menus a month mean per day?" About 1,000 a day.
  2. "Walk me through the $600K." $2 times 30,000 is $60K a month, times 12 is $720K list, floored to $600K.
  3. "Is 98% live?" No, offline evaluation on a labelled set.
  4. "What was extraction success before?" Roughly 60 to 65%, and that is an estimate.
  5. "What's your peak throughput?" A few hundred events a second at peak, estimated, not measured.
  6. "Did you use Spark?" Not on my resume. I'd consider it for a large historical backfill, but the live pipeline is Kafka and Flink.

Tech deep dives: every skill on the Java + Python + Go resume

PDF: Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf · Summary line: "Expertise in Java, Python and Go microservices"

How to use this page

  • What it covers: every technology on this track's Skills line, in plain English: what it is, where I used it, why it was chosen there, what the alternatives were, and one interview question with a short answer.
  • When to read it: the night before a technical screen, or when a job description lists a tool and you want to know how honestly you can claim it.
  • What to memorise: the "where I used it" line for each tech, especially which ones are skills-level (literacy, no production claim), and the "what not to say" list at the end.

Labels on this page. Production means a resume bullet or tech line backs it. Skills-level means I understand it and can discuss it, but I do not claim production ownership. Number tags: MEASURED means a log, document or code. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records.

For longer entries see the tech glossary. For project context see IA core platform, IA agentic AI, Uber FRM, Uber Menu, Masters India and GeeksforGeeks.

1. Where each technology lives

flowchart LR IA["Impact Analytics"] -->|platform| IAG["Go, Gin, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Redis, Datadog"] IA -->|agents| IAP["Python, FastAPI, LangGraph, LangSmith"] FRM["Uber FRM"] -->|service| FRMJ["Java, Spring Boot, JPA, Hibernate, MySQL, JUnit, Bazel"] MENU["Uber Menu"] -->|pipeline| MENUP["Python, Selenium, Kafka, Flink, Gemini, RAG, Milvus"] MI["Masters India"] -->|services| MIJ["Java, Spring Boot, Hibernate, Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, ELK"] GFG["GeeksforGeeks"] -->|backend| GFGD["Python, Django, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch"]

What to notice: Java lives at Uber FRM and Masters India. Go and the Python agent plane live at Impact Analytics, which is never Spring Boot. Kafka appears twice, at Masters and at Menu, and never at Impact Analytics. Flink and Milvus are Menu only.

2. Java and the Spring family

Java

What it is. A statically typed language that compiles to bytecode and runs on the JVM (Java Virtual Machine), with automatic garbage collection. Think of it as a strict, well-tooled language where the compiler catches many mistakes before production.

Ideas that matter in interviews. The heap and garbage collectors (G1 by default, ZGC for very low pauses). Thread pools through ExecutorService with a bounded queue and a rejection policy. CompletableFuture for fan-out. Virtual threads (Java 21) for cheap blocking concurrency. ConcurrentHashMap instead of HashMap across threads. The equals and hashCode contract.

Where I used it. Production: Uber FRM (36 Spring Boot endpoints) and Masters India (Spring Boot microservices). Why there: typed services with a mature ecosystem for web, data, security and Kafka. Alternative: Python web stacks, which I use at Impact Analytics for agents and used at GeeksforGeeks.

Q: Why should a thread pool have a bounded queue? A: An unbounded queue hides overload. Requests pile up in memory until latency explodes or the process runs out of memory. A bounded queue with a rejection policy fails fast, so the caller can retry or shed load.

Spring Boot

What it is. A framework on top of Spring that gives you sensible defaults: auto-configuration, "starter" dependency bundles, an embedded web server and health endpoints (Actuator). Like a furnished flat for Java services.

Ideas that matter. Dependency injection through constructors. Configuration in application.yml with profiles and @ConfigurationProperties. @Transactional works through a proxy, so calling a transactional method from the same class skips the transaction (the self-invocation trap).

Where I used it. Production: Uber FRM and Masters India (PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices). Why there: fast, standard path to REST microservices with JPA, validation and Kafka support built in. Alternative: FastAPI or Django in Python, Gin in Go.

Q: Why might @Transactional silently not apply? A: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy. If a method in the same class calls the annotated method directly, the call bypasses the proxy and no transaction starts. Move the method to another bean or call it through the proxy.

Spring MVC

What it is. Spring's web layer for the servlet model, where each request gets a thread. A request flows through filters, then the DispatcherServlet, which finds the right @RestController method, and Jackson converts JSON to Java objects and back. @ControllerAdvice maps exceptions to status codes in one place.

Where I used it. Skills-line item. It is the web layer under the FRM controllers (@GetMapping, @PatchMapping, a 409 for stale versions) and the Masters services. Why there: thread-per-request is simple and fits short database calls. Alternative: Spring WebFlux (reactive), which pays off when requests wait on slow I/O at very high concurrency.

Q: MVC or WebFlux for a service that calls a slow government API? A: First move the slow call off the request path, for example into a Kafka consumer, and return 202. Then MVC is fine. That is what we did at Masters. WebFlux is worth its complexity only if requests must wait on slow I/O at high concurrency.

Spring Security

What it is. A chain of servlet filters that authenticates the caller and authorizes the request before your controller runs. For APIs it usually validates a JWT (a signed token carrying who the caller is) and runs statelessly.

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.requestMatchers("/health").permitAll()
                                     .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}

Where I used it. Skills-level. It is where identity handling fits in Java services: at FRM the gateway injects the caller's email header and the service records it on every write, and at Masters there was an auth service among the extracted services. I do not claim a Spring Security outcome. Alternative: custom filters, or a gateway that does all auth.

Q: What do you validate on a JWT? A: The signature, expiry, issuer (iss) and audience (aud). Then map claims to roles and check them per method with @PreAuthorize.

Spring Data JPA and Hibernate

What they are. JPA is Java's standard for mapping rows to objects. Hibernate is the engine that implements it, with a persistence context (a per-transaction cache of loaded entities) and dirty checking (it writes changed fields at commit). Spring Data JPA generates repositories from interfaces like JpaRepository<Line, String>.

Ideas that matter. @Version for optimistic locking. N+1 queries from lazy loading, fixed with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph. Typed projections into records. Keep "open session in view" off in APIs.

Where I used it. Production: Uber FRM (led 3 engineers on the Spring Data JPA and Hibernate migration that removed column-aliasing bugs and reached 100% module statement coverage) and Masters India (Hibernate on the tech line, where N+1 fixes helped the p95 drop). Why there: @Version, @Transactional and typed projections gave correctness by default. Alternative: jOOQ or MyBatis for SQL-first teams, or plain JDBC.

Q: How do you find and fix N+1? A: Turn on SQL logging or watch query counts in APM. If a list of 50 invoices fires 51 queries, fetch the children in one go with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph or a batch size.

Spring Batch

What it is. A framework for chunked batch jobs. A Job has Steps, and a chunk step reads N items, processes them, writes them, and commits, with a job repository that remembers progress so a failed job restarts from the last committed chunk.

@Bean
Step validateInvoices(JobRepository repo, PlatformTransactionManager tx,
                      ItemReader<InvoiceRow> reader,
                      ItemProcessor<InvoiceRow, Invoice> validator,
                      ItemWriter<Invoice> writer) {
    return new StepBuilder("validateInvoices", repo)
            .<InvoiceRow, Invoice>chunk(500, tx)
            .reader(reader).processor(validator).writer(writer)
            .faultTolerant().skip(ValidationException.class).skipLimit(100)
            .build();
}

Chunk size and skip limit are illustrative. Where I used it. Skills-level. It fits the chunked bulk-import validation at Masters India. I do not claim a Spring Batch outcome. Alternative: Kafka consumers for stage-to-stage events, which is what the Masters pipeline is built on.

Q: Spring Batch or Kafka? A: Spring Batch for a bounded file with restart-from-chunk semantics. Kafka when several consumers need a durable, replayable stream.

Maven

What it is. Java's standard build tool. A pom.xml declares dependencies and plugins, and the Spring Boot parent pins compatible versions.

Where I used it. Skills-level. The FRM build was Bazel because Uber uses a monorepo, so I do not claim Maven on FRM. Alternative: Gradle (faster incremental builds), Bazel (monorepos).

Q: Why use the Spring Boot parent or BOM? A: It pins versions of dozens of libraries that are tested together, so you avoid dependency conflicts.

JUnit (with Mockito and MockMvc)

What it is. JUnit 5 is Java's test framework. Mockito creates fake collaborators. MockMvc calls controllers without a real server. Slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) load only part of the app.

Where I used it. Production: Uber FRM (JUnit on the tech line, 100% module statement coverage, 1,100+ tests is verbal depth) and Masters India (coverage from 35% to 82%, 98% deployment success). Why there: layer-by-layer tests with mocks need no database and run fast in CI. Alternative: integration tests only, with Testcontainers for real databases, which are slower but closer to production.

Q: What does 100% statement coverage not prove? A: That the assertions are meaningful or that every branch combination was tested. It proves every line ran at least once.

asyncio Python's event loop for concurrent I/O How IA LLM batches run concurrently Threads

gRPC Binary RPC over HTTP/2 with generated clients Skills-level REST

Go: why Go for the IA platform? Goroutines handle thousands of concurrent requests cheaply, a single static binary deploys easily, and Google Wire wires dependencies at compile time, so a missing dependency fails the build instead of production. h2c is HTTP/2 without TLS, used because the edge runs with no reverse proxy in front.

One question each.

  • Python. Q: What is the GIL and when does it matter? A: A lock that lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time. It hurts CPU-bound threads, not I/O-bound work, so for LLM calls async I/O works well.
  • Go. Q: How do you stop a goroutine leak? A: Pass a context.Context with a deadline and have every goroutine return when it is cancelled.
  • Gin. Q: What are nested timeouts? A: An outer request deadline with tighter deadlines for each downstream call inside it, so one slow dependency cannot use the whole budget.
  • FastAPI. Q: What happens if you call blocking code in an async endpoint? A: It blocks the event loop for every request. Use async libraries or run it in a thread pool.
  • Pydantic. Q: Why validate LLM output with a schema? A: Models sometimes return malformed or extra fields. A schema rejects them before they reach storage.
  • asyncio. Q: How do you cap concurrent LLM calls? A: An asyncio.Semaphore around each call, plus a timeout.
  • Celery. Q: Celery or Kafka? A: Celery for fire-and-forget tasks. Kafka when you need ordering, replay and many independent readers.
  • Django. Q: Why Django at GFG? A: Admin, auth, ORM and migrations out of the box for a content product.
  • REST. Q: Is PATCH idempotent? A: Not by definition, but you can make it so with a version check or by setting absolute values.
  • gRPC. Q: When pick gRPC over REST? A: Internal service-to-service calls that need strict contracts, streaming or low overhead.
  • SQL. Q: How do you stop SQL injection? A: Bound parameters and allowlists, never string concatenation.
  • C, C++. Q: Stack vs heap? A: Stack is automatic, fast and scoped to a function. Heap is manual or garbage-collected and lives until freed.

Tech What it is Where I used it

LangChain Library for chaining loaders, retrievers, prompts and parsers Production: Uber Menu RAG. LangChain Academy certificate
RAG Retrieve examples or facts, then generate Production: Uber Menu, 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation

pgvector Vector search inside PostgreSQL Skills-level
LLM agents (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude) Programs where an LLM decides or scores within guardrails Production: IA 7 AI lenses and Ask Iris, Menu Gemini 2.5 Pro
Tool calling The model asks the app to run a named function with JSON arguments Skills-level. IA tool design is verbal depth only

LangSmith Tracing and debugging for LangChain and LangGraph runs Production: Ask Iris only

Key facts to keep straight. Keep/Drop scores 348k article-seasons, 88k items per pass, blending deterministic KPI math with structured LLM calls across 7 lenses. The LLM never queries the database. Context arrives as JSON from a 2.11B-row ClickHouse master. Keep/Drop has no LLM orchestrator, its order is fixed in code. The 80% is a CI promotion gate on the 300-case harness. The 73% lower live cost at 100% coverage and the 74% deterministic baseline come from a separate gold-200 benchmark. Do not fuse them.

One question each.

  • LangGraph. Q: How do you stop an agent looping forever? A: A hard cap. Ask Iris has a 3-attempt evaluator loop, then it returns the best answer or a clear failure.
  • LangChain. Q: What does it add over raw API calls? A: Reusable pieces for loading, splitting, retrieving and parsing, so the pipeline is easy to rearrange.
  • RAG. Q: RAG or fine-tuning for menus? A: RAG. A newly labelled menu helps the next extraction immediately, with no retraining when the schema changes.
  • Milvus. Q: What does a vector index trade off? A: Approximate nearest-neighbour search gives speed in exchange for occasionally missing the exact best match.
  • pgvector. Q: When is pgvector enough? A: When vectors fit comfortably in one PostgreSQL instance and you want them next to relational data.
  • LLM agents. Q: What if the model times out? A: Fall back to the deterministic baseline score, which is what Keep/Drop does.
  • Tool calling. Q: Why does Keep/Drop give the LLM no SQL tool? A: Safety and cost. Context is prepared as JSON, so the model cannot run arbitrary queries on a 2.11B-row table.
  • MCP. Q: How does MCP relate to tool calling? A: Tool calling is the model asking for a function. MCP standardises how tools are described and served so any client can use them.
  • Prompt engineering. Q: How do you get reliable JSON? A: Give the schema, show examples, ask for JSON only, then validate and reject failures.
  • LangSmith. Q: What do you look at in a trace? A: Each node's inputs and outputs, tokens, latency and where retries happened.
  • Offline evaluation. Q: What did you do when the LLM lost to the baseline? A: The blended score was about 63% against a 74% deterministic baseline, so we froze the blend weights instead of retuning to chase the benchmark.

5. Data and streaming

Tech What it is Where I used it Alternative
Apache Kafka Durable, partitioned, replayable message log Production: Masters India (Spring Kafka consumers), Uber Menu (Python pipeline). Not IA RabbitMQ, SQS
Apache Flink Stateful stream processor with event time Production: Uber Menu only Kafka Streams
ClickHouse Columnar analytics database Production: IA 2.11B-row master, six rollup tables, cross-cluster copy BigQuery, Druid, Pinot
BigQuery Google's serverless data warehouse On the IA tech line as the upstream warehouse. Keep claims qualitative ClickHouse
ETL pipelines Extract, transform, load jobs IA rollup builds, Masters bulk imports, Menu ingestion. FRM consumes a shared ETL Ad hoc scripts

ClickHouse facts to keep straight. Planner pivots went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds (15.5×) on a 250M-row harness through six pre-aggregated MergeTree rollups. Separately, weekly rollup builds hit a 170GB out-of-memory failure, fixed by inserting one fiscal week at a time with memory and disk-spill caps. 15.5× is query time and 170GB is load time. They are not cause and effect. The cross-cluster migration ran at about 344k rows per second (ingest rate, not requests per second) with a custom Go native-TLS pump, partitions up to 4.09B rows (measured in flight, not a finished cutover). Rollback meant DROP PARTITION then recopy, not an atomic swap. ReplacingMergeTree keeps only the newest version of rows with the same key, eventually, like a notebook where you write new values below and a cleaner later crosses out old lines.

One question each.

  • Kafka. Q: How do you keep one customer's events in order? A: Use the customer ID as the message key, so all their events land on one partition. Masters used the GSTIN, Menu used vendor_id.
  • Spring Kafka (Masters). Q: When do you commit offsets? A: After processing succeeds. Committing first can lose work on a crash. Committing after can duplicate it, so processing must be idempotent.
  • Flink. Q: What is a watermark? A: Flink's estimate that all events up to time T have arrived, so it can finish a window while tolerating bounded lateness.
  • ClickHouse. Q: Why not just add indexes in PostgreSQL? A: Pivots scan and aggregate hundreds of millions of rows. Columnar storage reads only the needed columns, compressed, and rollups pre-compute the common shapes.
  • BigQuery. Q: Why not serve pivots from BigQuery? A: Interactive, repeated pivots need predictable latency and no per-scan cost, which pre-aggregated ClickHouse rollups gave us.
  • ETL. Q: How do you make a load safe to re-run? A: Deterministic keys, checkpoint or ledger files, and partition-level replace or drop-and-recopy.

6. Databases and storage

Tech What it is Where I used it
PostgreSQL Relational database with strong transactions Production: IA metadata, UAM and roles, Masters India sharded by tax quarter
MySQL Popular relational database Production: Uber FRM on SOADB (8-table schema), GeeksforGeeks
Redis In-memory key-value store Production: IA auth front, Masters cache-aside (30% fewer reads), GFG counters
MongoDB Document database for varying JSON shapes Production: Masters signed IRP responses, GFG doubt bodies
Elasticsearch Search engine over an inverted index Production: Masters (ELK logs), GFG search
DynamoDB AWS managed key-value and document store Skills-level
Amazon S3 AWS object storage Masters ran on AWS and my design notes put bulk upload files in S3. No bullet names it

One question each.

  • PostgreSQL. Q: App-routed quarter shards or native partitioning? A: Today I would start with native range partitioning. It gives pruning and clean detach with less custom code.
  • MySQL. Q: How does optimistic locking work? A: A version column in the WHERE clause. Zero rows updated means someone else saved first.
  • Redis. Q: How do you prevent a cache stampede? A: TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, plus a short SET NX lock so only one worker rebuilds a hot key.
  • MongoDB. Q: Why not put signed responses in PostgreSQL? A: Their shape varies and they are stored for audits, so a document store avoids constant schema changes.
  • Elasticsearch. Q: Why is it fast for text search? A: An inverted index maps each word to the documents containing it, like a textbook's back index.
  • DynamoDB. Q: What drives DynamoDB design? A: Access patterns first. You choose partition and sort keys for the queries you will run.
  • Amazon S3. Q: Why land uploads in object storage first? A: The upload returns fast, and the file stays available for retries and replays.

9. Cross-cutting interview questions

"Why do you use three languages?"
Each fits its job. Java with Spring Boot for transactional business services at Uber FRM and Masters India, Go for the high-concurrency platform edge at Impact Analytics, and Python wherever AI and data libraries matter, the IA agent plane and the Uber Menu pipeline. I pick by the problem and the team's standard, not by habit.

"Kafka at Masters and Kafka at Menu. Same thing?"
Same technology, different products. At Masters, Spring Boot consumers carried e-invoice stages keyed by GSTIN with dead-letter topics. At Menu, Kafka fed an Apache Flink job keyed by vendor. Flink was only at Menu.

"What does exactly-once mean in your systems?"
At-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes, which gives an exactly-once effect. At Masters the key was client plus file hash plus batch index. At Menu the upsert was keyed by vendor, menu version and item key. I never claim zero message loss.

"Hibernate or plain SQL?"
Hibernate with typed projections for transactional services, because @Version and @Transactional give correctness by default. Explicit SQL for heavy reporting or analytics. At FRM, moving untyped native queries to typed projections is what removed the column-aliasing bug.

"How do you decide between PostgreSQL and ClickHouse?"
PostgreSQL for many small transactional reads and writes, ClickHouse for large scans and aggregations. At Impact Analytics, POCs showed ClickHouse winning large analytical reads, so planning facts moved there and PostgreSQL kept thin metadata, access control and roles.

"Which items on your Skills line are not production claims?"
C and C++, pgvector, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, gRPC, MCP, tool calling, Celery on this track, Maven, Spring Security and Spring Batch. I can discuss each one and I am clear that they are skills-level.

Behavioral and managerial rounds: my STAR stories

How to use this page

  • This is my bank of 13 behavioral stories (numbered 1 to 12, plus 12b), written the way I would actually say them out loud.
  • Read it the night before any behavioral, hiring-manager or "culture" round. Pick 2 or 3 stories per loop and never tell the same story twice to the same company.
  • Memorise the numbers in bold and the "Say this carefully" notes. Everything else I can say in my own words.
  • To find the right story for a question fast, use the prep grid.

Before you start

What a STAR story is. STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. Interviewers use it to check that I did something real, that I know why I did it, and that I can measure what happened. I add a fifth part, What I learned, because senior interviewers almost always ask for it.

How long. Aim for 60 to 90 seconds. That is one or two sentences of Situation, one sentence of Task, three or four concrete Actions, a Result with a number, and one sentence of learning. Then stop and let them ask follow-ups. The follow-ups are where the real interview happens.

Amazon Leadership Principles (LPs) are the 16 values Amazon interviewers score against, such as Ownership, Dive Deep and Earn Trust. Googliness is Google's word for how I work with people: intellectual humility, bias to action, collaboration, comfort with ambiguity, and doing the right thing. Most other companies ask the same kinds of questions with different labels, so this mapping works everywhere.

What the tags mean. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind the number. TARGET means a design goal, so I say "targeting". ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. "On the PDF" means it is a bullet on my current resume (Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf). "Verbal only" means I can talk about it if asked, but it is not a resume bullet.

Stack wording on this track. On this resume, Uber FRM uses Java with Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA and Hibernate, and Masters India uses Spring Boot microservices. At Impact Analytics, the platform APIs are written in Go with the Gin web framework, and the AI agent side is Python (FastAPI and LangGraph). Never say Spring Boot for Impact Analytics.

What is on the Impact Analytics PDF. Two groups of bullets: Core Infrastructure and Pipeline, and Agentic Flows and Orchestration (Keep/Drop, Missed Opportunities, Top Style, Ask Iris, the 300-case harness and the 80% gate). The Cluster Recommendation Copilot and Hindsight are verbal only. The source of truth for the Impact Analytics wording is docs/ASSORTSMART_TAB_RESUME.md.

Company names. I always say "Uber via EPAM" once per story, because I was employed by EPAM Systems and worked on Uber's teams.
