Stories 1 and 12 cover the same ClickHouse decision from two angles. Story 1 is about the disagreement. Story 12 is about leading the work. Use only one of them per loop.

1. The ClickHouse decision between two expert camps

Status: Impact Analytics. This is the background to my ClickHouse bullets. The details of the two camps come from my own notes, not the PDF.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with your team." "Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete data." "How do you influence people when you have no authority over them?" "What are you most proud of?"

Words to know. ClickHouse is a database built for analytics. It stores data by column, so it can scan and sum billions of rows quickly, a bit like reading one column of a huge spreadsheet instead of every row. Its weak spot is editing existing rows in place, because each edit (called a "mutation") rewrites whole chunks of data in the background. OLAP means analytical processing: big read queries that summarise lots of rows.

Situation. When I joined Impact Analytics in May 2026, our planners' pivot screens were slow on PostgreSQL. A pivot is the grid where a planner slices sales by product, store and week. The organisation was split on whether to adopt ClickHouse for the new AI planning product. One group had run a live audit of the legacy backend and concluded "no ClickHouse". Senior subject-matter experts were pushing "yes, one unified analytics store". Both sides had real evidence, and a wrong call would be expensive either way.

Task. My job was to produce a recommendation the whole organisation could commit to, without throwing away either side's evidence.

Action. - I separated facts from conclusions. I accepted every measured fact in the audit. - Then I showed that the audit's "no" came from the legacy system's write pattern, which edited rows in place. That is exactly what ClickHouse is bad at. It was not a property of planning workloads themselves. - I designed an insert-only, versioned write model. Instead of editing a row, you write a new version, and the database keeps only the newest one. That sidesteps ClickHouse's weak spot. - I proposed a path with three gates, each one measurable. First, fix what we could inside the existing BigQuery stack. Second, tighten how we used Postgres. Third, run a proof of concept (PoC) of the versioned write model in ClickHouse.

Result. Both camps agreed to the staged path. In the PoC, the mutation queue (the backlog of pending background rewrites) stayed at zero at 10 times our scale. In July 2026 the organisation committed to ClickHouse end to end. We spent no money on infrastructure before we had evidence, and neither camp "lost".

What I learned. When two competent groups disagree, they usually disagree about a hidden assumption, not about the facts. If you make the assumption explicit, the decision often resolves itself.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "What was in the audit?" "It measured how the legacy backend behaved, and I accepted all of it. Where I differed was the conclusion. Its pain came from editing rows in place, and the new design didn't do that." If they push for specifics, keep it qualitative. - "What would you have done if the PoC failed?" "That was the point of the gates. If the third gate failed, we would have kept the improvements from gates one and two and stayed on BigQuery and Postgres. Nobody would have spent money on a migration that didn't work." - "What stayed in Postgres?" "Thin metadata, user access management (who can see which part of the product hierarchy) and roles. ClickHouse took the large analytical reads." - "You'd only been there two months. How did you get people to listen?" "I didn't ask anyone to trust me. I wrote it down, accepted their facts, and proposed gates that anyone could check. The evidence carried the decision."

Say this carefully. The "10 times scale" and the July 2026 commitment come from my notes, not the PDF. The PDF numbers that came later (from 189 seconds to 12 seconds) are a separate measurement. That story is in Story 12.

2. The BigQuery to ClickHouse ingestion lane (freshness as a feature)

Status: Impact Analytics, verbal only. This is a design I wrote, not something that was executed. It was meant for the Cluster Recommendation Copilot, which is also verbal only. The p95 under 500 ms and the 0.1% tolerance are TARGETS in the design, not measured results.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about a design decision you're proud of." "How do you handle failure modes nobody else is thinking about?" "Tell me about a time you raised the bar."

Words to know. BigQuery is Google's cloud data warehouse. Its compute is shared across users, so the same query can take 1 second one minute and 20 seconds the next. p95 latency means 95 out of 100 requests finish faster than that time. A partition is a slice of a table, for example one season of data. REPLACE PARTITION is a ClickHouse command that swaps a whole slice in from a staging table in one step, so readers see either the old slice or the new one, never half of each. Reconciliation means comparing row counts and totals between the source and the copy.

Situation. The copilot's design had agents asking many small data questions ("probes") while a planner waited, so they needed fast, predictable answers. The design target was p95 under 500 milliseconds. But our historical data lives in BigQuery, where the same query can take anywhere from 1 to 20 seconds. The obvious fix is to copy the data into ClickHouse. That has a known trap: copies go stale silently. A planner making buying decisions on stale data is worse off than one waiting for a slow query.

Task. Design the ingestion lane from BigQuery into ClickHouse so the agents' read path is both fast and provably fresh.

Action. I designed it in three parts. - Atomic loads. Scheduled exports land in ClickHouse staging tables first. They get promoted to the live table with REPLACE PARTITION, so nobody ever reads a half-loaded night. - Reconciliation that blocks. Before promotion, each partition's row count and sums are compared with the BigQuery source. If they differ by more than 0.1%, promotion is blocked. - Freshness on the answer. A "freshness sentinel" stamps the data-as-of date onto every agent recommendation. If data is stale, the planner sees it in the product instead of us discovering it in an incident.

I also added a nightly precompute of attribute significance (which store attributes actually explain sales differences) for product hierarchies with active plans. That way most copilot sessions would start with that work already done.

Result. The design was written but not executed. What I can honestly claim is the design's property: silent staleness is structurally hard. Loads are atomic, mismatches block promotion, and the as-of date is printed on every answer. The latency number is a target, not a measurement.

What I learned. When you copy data for speed, freshness and reconciliation are product features, not operations chores. Design them in on day one.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Why not just query BigQuery directly?" "Because shared compute makes its latency unpredictable, from 1 to 20 seconds for the same query. An agent making many small probes would feel that every time." - "Did this ship?" "No. I wrote the design and it wasn't executed. What we actually ran for ClickHouse migrations was simpler. If a season's copy went wrong, we dropped that partition and recopied it." - "Why 0.1%?" "It was the tolerance in the design, tight enough to catch a broken load but loose enough to ignore rounding. I'd tune it with real data."

Say this carefully. Never say "the read plane serves p95 under 500 ms". Say "the design targeted p95 under 500 ms". Never say REPLACE PARTITION ran in production. The rollback we actually used was DROP PARTITION, then recopy that season. That is not an atomic swap with live readers.

3. Fixing the top failure in an LLM planner (malformed plans)

Status: Verbal only, not on the PDF. Older prep does not name which system this was. Confirm the project in my own records before using this story. Never attach it to Keep/Drop, because Keep/Drop has no LLM orchestrator. Its batch order is fixed. The 0.54 and 0.99 numbers come from an offline evaluation in my prep notes.

Questions this answers: "What's the hardest technical problem you've solved?" "How do you keep quality high with non-deterministic systems like LLMs?"

Words to know. An LLM (large language model) planner is a setup where the model breaks a user's question into a list of steps, called an execution plan, that other agents then run. A validator is ordinary code that checks the plan before anything runs. A forward reference is when step 2 tries to use the result of step 4, which hasn't happened yet.

Situation. We had a multi-agent planner where an LLM broke questions into execution plans. Malformed plans were our top failure class. They called agents that didn't exist, they had forward references, or a stage tried to run too many things at once. On our evaluation set, only 0.54 of plans were structurally correct.

Task. Make plans safe to execute without giving up the flexibility of the LLM.

Action. - I wrote a strict structural validator over the plan's schema. It checked for unknown agent names, duplicate step ids, stages that were too wide, and forward references. It runs before anything executes. - If validation fails, the system does one self-repair pass. It sends the LLM the specific errors and asks for a fixed plan. - I made every agent's answer() function non-throwing. If one agent fails, the user gets a clearly labelled partial answer instead of a crash.

Result. Structural correctness went from 0.54 to 0.99 on the offline evaluation. Failures became explicit and recoverable instead of mysterious.

What I learned. With LLMs, don't chase a perfect prompt. Put a deterministic contract around a probabilistic component.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Why only one repair pass?" "To keep cost and latency bounded. If the model can't fix a plan when it's told exactly what's wrong, a second or third try rarely helps, and an endless loop is worse than a clear failure." - "What does 0.99 mean exactly?" "99 out of 100 plans in the evaluation set passed the structural validator. It's structure, not whether the final answer was right."

4. Inverting the clustering workflow

Status: Impact Analytics, verbal only, not on the PDF. This is the Cluster Recommendation Copilot. Use it only if they ask about product thinking or a clustering roadmap. The "before" numbers came from live audits in my notes. The "after" numbers are TARGETS, not results.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about a time you challenged the status quo." "Show me some product thinking." "How do you handle ambiguity?"

Words to know. Store clustering means grouping stores that behave alike, so each group gets an assortment that fits it. For example, small urban stores in one group and large suburban stores in another. "k" is the number of groups. A silhouette score measures how cleanly separated the groups are. Higher is better.

Situation. Store clustering is the foundation of every assortment plan, but it was the least-assisted step. The system computed which store attributes mattered and then made people choose from raw score lists. Our live audits showed users tried exactly 1 configuration per plan, out of a huge search space (12 algorithms, k from 3 to 10, and any subset of attributes). 8.5% of runs failed (37 out of 437), and more than 80% of those failures were input mistakes. Nothing was reproducible.

Task. Define how to rebuild the module with an AI agent, with adoption risk as the main constraint.

Action. - I inverted the workflow. The user states only what the system can't work out alone: the product hierarchy and the reference time period. - The agent turns that into concrete scopes and picks features by statistical significance. It evaluates about 100 candidate clusterings in a batch and scores them on silhouette. - It shows the top 3 with evidence and a plain-English rationale. One of the three is always a baseline that mimics the client's old configuration, so the planner can compare against what they know. - The planner confirms the choice at clear checkpoints before anything is written back. - I kept the old manual wizard alive per client, so adoption is opt-in, not forced.

Result. The design committed to these targets: under 1 hour to a finalised plan, down from days. Top 3 of about 100 evaluated candidates, up from 1 configuration ever tried. Failures under 2%. Features and k fully visible to the planner. Results write back into the existing product tables unchanged.

What I learned. The highest-leverage AI feature is often turning the workflow around, not a better model.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Did this ship?" "No, it's a design with committed targets, and it isn't a resume bullet. I can walk you through the design and the audit numbers that motivated it." - "Why keep the old wizard?" "Because adoption was the biggest risk. Planners trust what they know. Letting each client opt in costs a bit of maintenance, but it means nobody gets forced onto a tool they don't trust yet."

Say this carefully. These are targets, so say "targeting under 1 hour", not "cut it to under 1 hour". Don't describe the checkpoints as a human review queue or a "human-in-the-loop system". My resume makes no human-in-the-loop claim. One more thing: another prep doc phrases the candidate target as "at least 20 configurations". This story says "about 100". Check my design notes and use one number consistently.

5. The "pure refactor" that wasn't (owning a mistake)

Status: Uber via EPAM, FRM (Financial Risk Management) scoping platform. Supports the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration bullet.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about a mistake you made." "Tell me about a bug you caused." "How do you hold your own quality bar?" "Tell me about a time you failed."

Words to know. A refactor is a change that tidies code without changing what it does. Stacked PRs are a chain of small pull requests, each one built on the one before, so reviewers see one small step at a time. In this codebase, a scoping "strategy" decides whether scoping is done at the component level (COMPONENT) or rolled up (AGGREGATE).

Situation. At Uber via EPAM, I was running a 3-PR stacked refactor. PR 2 was supposed to be constants only: moving repeated fixed values into one place across 31 files. A downstream test started failing.

Task. Find out why a test that asserts "keep the COMPONENT strategy when the selection is empty" was now getting AGGREGATE.

Action. - I diffed my own PR line by line, assuming the bug was mine until proven otherwise. - I found it. I had slipped in a small resolveStrategy helper that silently downgraded the strategy. That was a behaviour change hidden inside a refactor. - I removed it and restored the simple pass-through. - I added a rule to the team's stacked-PR checklist: "a pure refactor means zero test changes". That way this kind of mistake gets caught by process, not by someone happening to notice.

Result. The PR shipped as a true refactor. A few weeks later the checklist caught a similar issue in a teammate's PR.

What I learned. Call your own fouls fast and turn them into process. Credibility compounds.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Why did you add the helper in the first place?" "It felt like a harmless clean-up while I was in the file. That's exactly the trap. Any behaviour change, however small, belongs in its own PR with its own tests." - "How did you tell the team?" "I raised it myself, with the fix and the checklist item ready at the same time, so the conversation was about prevention, not blame."

6. Coverage that lied (dive deep)

Status: Uber via EPAM, FRM. Supports the bullet on raising module statement coverage to 100%.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about debugging something non-obvious." "What's your testing philosophy?"

Words to know. Statement coverage is the percentage of code lines that actually run during tests. Mocking means replacing a real piece of code with a fake one in a test, so you can test the caller in isolation. In Java the usual mocking library is Mockito, and the tests themselves run on JUnit 5.

Situation. My Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration at Uber via EPAM failed the CI (continuous integration) coverage check at 34.6% on new lines, even though I knew those code paths were being exercised by tests.

Task. Understand how tested code could show up as "uncovered".

Action. - I dug into how coverage was being measured. - The repository-layer tests were replacing the new entity methods with Mockito mocks. So the entity code never actually ran during tests. The mocks had moved coverage to the wrong layer. - I wrote 12 direct JUnit tests at the entity layer, including the rejection paths: empty updates and unknown column names.

Result. The changed module reached 100% statement coverage. The pattern "test where the code lives, not where it's called" went into the team's testing notes.

What I learned. A metric you don't understand is a metric that will lie to you.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Is 100% coverage worth it?" "On a small, critical module that handles financial data, yes. Here the point wasn't the number. The number was hiding the fact that the real code never ran." - "How many tests overall?" "The platform had over 1,100 tests." (This is verbal, not on the PDF.)

7. Disagreeing with the architecture rulebook (backbone, then commit)

Status: Uber via EPAM, FRM. Supports the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration bullet.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a standard." "Tell me about a disagreement with a senior engineer or manager." "Tell me about a conflict with your manager." For the manager version, frame it upward: I made the case to the people who owned the rules.

Words to know. An ORM (object-relational mapper, here Hibernate used through Spring Data JPA) lets code work with database rows as Java objects called entities. A repository layer is a folder of code whose only job is talking to the database. A @NamedQuery is a JPQL query declared on the entity class itself, right next to the fields that define the table's columns.

Situation. The team's architecture rules said all data access lives in the repository/ folder. For the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration, I put the query definitions on the entity classes instead.

Task. Either follow the rule mechanically or make an honest case for the exception.

Action. - I made the engineering case in writing. With the queries next to the field definitions, renaming a field breaks immediately, because Hibernate validates named queries when the application starts, instead of failing at runtime on a real request. The repository stays a thin Spring Data interface. No business logic leaks into the entity. - I listened to the counter-argument, which was consistency of the rulebook, and took it seriously. - I documented the deviation explicitly. I also committed to using plain repository methods for dynamic queries that don't belong to one entity.

Result. The exception was accepted and documented. The latent column-aliasing bug that had motivated the migration could no longer recur. That bug was raw SQL that joined tables with duplicate column names, so rows got silently mapped to the wrong id. In one case, income-statement rows were read with the balance-sheet column list.

What I learned. Disagree with a written rationale, commit visibly, and leave the decision auditable.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "What if they had said no?" "I would have followed the rule and kept the queries in the repository. I'd still have used explicit, aliased column names to kill the bug. The disagreement was about where code lives, not about whether to fix the bug." - "How did you fix the aliasing bug itself?" "Aliased selects with explicit labels, so every column has one unambiguous name, and then the JPA entity mappings, so column lists come from the entity, not hand-typed SQL."

8. The migration nobody could pause the business for (deliver results)

Status: Masters India. On the PDF.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about delivering under pressure." "Tell me about leading a project end to end." "Tell me about a disagreement over sequencing or priorities."

Words to know. Masters India sells GST (India's Goods and Services Tax) compliance software. Businesses send us invoices, and we register them with the government's IRP (Invoice Registration Portal). A monolith is one big application. The strangler pattern means replacing it one route at a time behind the same front door, until the old system can be switched off. Shadow traffic means copying real requests to the new service and comparing answers, without showing users the new answer yet. A DLQ (dead-letter queue) is a holding area for messages that keep failing, so they can be inspected and replayed later.

Situation. Masters India's PHP monolith was struggling during the monthly GST filing peaks. Its worker pools ran out because they sat blocked, waiting on slow government portal calls. Meanwhile, 1,500+ enterprise clients kept filing.

Task. Lead the migration to Spring Boot microservices, with non-blocking calls to the government portal, with zero tolerance for downtime during filing deadlines. I was also mentoring two engineers through it.

Action. - I used the strangler pattern, moving one endpoint at a time behind the gateway. - I sent shadow traffic to read paths first, so we could compare answers safely. - I moved the bulk, Kafka-driven background paths before the interactive filing paths. Kafka is a message queue that lets work be processed in the background. - I kept the data where it was, in PostgreSQL sharded by tax quarter, to avoid a risky data migration during cutover. - I froze cutovers during deadline weeks. - I hardened bulk submissions to the IRP with idempotency keys, bounded retries and a DLQ. An idempotency key is a unique id per job, so a retry can never file the same invoice twice.

Result. - p95 latency went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, a 75% cut. - The system handles 1M+ government submissions a day and 100K+ concurrent imports. - Throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute, roughly 12 to 67 per second. - We had no outage in a deadline window during the migration.

What I learned. Sequencing is the risk-management tool. The migration plan mattered more than the target architecture.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Where did the latency win actually come from?" "Mostly non-blocking calls to the government portal, using Spring WebClient and bounded thread pools, so request threads weren't blocked waiting. Then HikariCP connection pooling, query and index fixes, and Redis for frequent reads." - "What was your role versus the two engineers?" "I led the migration and mentored them. I paired on the first cutover, wrote the shared retry and idempotency helpers, and then let them own full services." - "Why not migrate the data too?" "It would have added a second risky change at the same time. Keeping data in place meant each cutover was only a code change, which we could roll back by routing traffic back."

Say this carefully. 1M+ a day averages about 12 per second (1,000,000 divided by 86,400 seconds). Peaks around filing deadlines were roughly 8 to 10 times that, which is ESTIMATED. I "mentored 2" here. Don't mix that with "led 3" at Uber.

9. The anti-bot arms race (learn and be curious)

Status: Uber via EPAM, Uber Eats menu ingestion. On the PDF (95%+ extraction success).

Questions this answers: "Tell me about working against a moving target." "Tell me about a time you had to persist." "Tell me about an early failure you turned around."

Words to know. The pipeline used Selenium, a tool that drives a real web browser automatically, to collect restaurant menus from source platforms. Those platforms run bot defences that block automated traffic. A proxy pool is a set of different network addresses to send requests from. A retry budget is a cap on how many times you retry a source before you stop.

Situation. At Uber via EPAM, our menu scrapers were getting blocked. Success rates kept dropping as the source platforms rotated their bot defences. Before my work, success was an estimated 60 to 65%.

Task. Get ingestion reliability up without an unbounded proxy budget.

Action. - I treated it as an experiment loop, not a one-off fix. - I instrumented each source's block signatures, meaning what a block looks like for that site. - I iterated on countermeasures: IP rotation, browser fingerprint and user-agent management, and dynamic proxy pools. - I set adaptive retry budgets per source, so a hostile source couldn't burn the whole budget. - I put block-rate metrics on the same dashboards as parse failures, so regressions showed up in minutes.

Result. Successful extractions rose to 95%+, from an estimated 60 to 65%. Because of the measurement loop, we detected and countered new defences in days instead of weeks.

What I learned. Against an adversarial, moving target, the asset is the feedback loop, not any single countermeasure.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "What happened after a menu was scraped?" "It went into a Kafka and Apache Flink pipeline. Flink is a stream-processing engine. It removed duplicates per vendor and menu using a content hash, normalised the schema, and did idempotent upserts into the catalog." - "How did this connect to the business result?" "It fed the bigger outcome. Restaurant onboarding went from 24 hours to 2 hours, saving about $600K a year across 30K+ menus a month."

Say this carefully. 60 to 65% is an estimate. The "exactly-once" catalog upserts are really at-least-once delivery plus idempotent writes. Don't claim zero message loss.

10. The double-filing near-miss (earn trust, do the right thing)

Status: Masters India. Supports the idempotency and dead-letter-queue bullet.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about your integrity." "Tell me about a problem you raised that you could have hidden." "Tell me about a time you failed."

Words to know. An e-invoice registered with the government gets a unique IRN (Invoice Reference Number). Filing the same invoice twice is a compliance error for the client. A retry is an automatic second attempt after a failure.

Situation. At Masters India, a retried bulk import came close to filing duplicate e-invoices with the government portal. It hadn't hurt any customer yet, and nobody outside the team would have known.

Task. Decide between quietly patching that one retry and treating it as the systemic risk it really was.

Action. - I flagged it to leadership as a near-miss. - I wrote the incident review myself. - I retrofitted idempotency keys across the whole bulk pipeline, not just the endpoint that almost failed. Each key was built from client, file hash and batch index, so a retried batch is recognised as the same batch. - I added a dead-letter replay path, so failed batches could be fixed and replayed safely.

Result. We had zero duplicate filings after the rollout. The near-miss review became the template the team used for later incidents.

What I learned. Trust is built in the moments where you could have stayed quiet.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Why build the key from client, file hash and batch index?" "That combination uniquely identifies a piece of work. The same client re-uploading the same file gets the same keys, so the system knows it already processed those batches." - "Wasn't it embarrassing to raise it?" "A little, but a duplicate filing would have been far worse for the client. Raising it early was cheap compared to that."

11. The connection leak that caused out-of-memory errors

Status: Impact Analytics, Python/FastAPI worker. Not a resume bullet. It is a prep ("packet") story. If it comes up in a Kubernetes context, say the service ran in containers. Do not claim I operated clusters.

Questions this answers: "Tell me about a production bug." "Tell me about a cascading failure." "Tell me about diving deep into a problem you couldn't reproduce."

Words to know. A 504 is the error a gateway returns when the service behind it takes too long. APM (application performance monitoring) is tooling that shows where time and memory go in a live service. The heap is the memory a program allocates as it runs. In Python, async with is a context manager: it guarantees a connection gets closed when the block ends, even after an error. Backpressure means slowing down intake when the downstream system can't keep up.

Situation. During peak traffic, an async ingestion and agent worker started returning 504s, and its memory kept climbing.

Task. Diagnose it without being able to reproduce it locally.

Action. - I lined up the APM traces against heap snapshots. - The cause was database and HTTP clients and cursors being created inside a long-lived async loop without context managers. They were never released. - I fixed it with async with blocks, pool limits and timeouts. I added consumer backpressure so the worker could not outrun the systems downstream of it.

Result. Memory stabilised and the 504s cleared. As follow-ups, I added a load test at 3 times peak to CI and added connection-pool metrics.

What I learned. In async Python, how long a resource lives is a correctness bug, not an infrastructure ticket.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Why didn't it show up in testing?" "Tests ran short loops, so leaked connections never piled up. Only a long-running worker under peak load accumulated enough to matter. That's why I added the 3-times-peak load test."

12. Leading the ClickHouse RFC and migration (bias for action, technical leadership)

Status: Impact Analytics. On the PDF: 15.5 times faster pivots (from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250M-row harness), the KPI formula parser, versioned writes with ReplacingMergeTree, keeping the LLM away from the 2.11B-row table, and the 170GB out-of-memory story (Story 12b).

Questions this answers: "Tell me about driving a migration." "Tell me about acting on incomplete information." "Tell me about a time you were right when others doubted." "Tell me about technical leadership."

Words to know. An RFC (request for comments) is a written design proposal that others review before work starts. A row-identical PoC means loading exactly the same rows into both databases, so the comparison is fair. A rollup table is a pre-summarised table, like a monthly total kept ready so you don't add up every daily row each time. ReplacingMergeTree is a ClickHouse table type that keeps only the newest version of a row with the same key. Think of a notebook where you never erase: you write the new value below, and a cleaner later crosses out the old lines.

Situation. Planner pivots on Postgres were blowing past 30 seconds. On our 250M-row test harness, one heavy pivot took 189 seconds.

Task. Write the RFC, run a proof of concept, and drive adoption, without pretending ClickHouse is a general replacement for Postgres.

Action. - I wrote the RFC. It compared a hybrid store with an insert-only store for the agent workloads. - I ran a row-identical PoC comparing Postgres and ClickHouse. - I chose ClickHouse for analytical reads and built a pre-aggregation layer of six rollup tables (product, store and attribute, each at season and weekly level). - I kept Postgres for roles and transactional edits. - I kept the LLM away from the 2.11B-row fact table entirely. It gets context as JSON payloads and never a database query tool.

Result. The organisation committed to ClickHouse for planning analytics. Pivots went from 189 seconds to 12 seconds (12.3, rounded), which is 15.5 times faster, on the 250M-row harness. Several related pieces are now on my resume: the KPI formula parser, the versioned writes with ReplacingMergeTree, the six rollup tables, and the Go data pump that copied rollups between ClickHouse clusters.

What I learned. Measure first. Separate how you write data from how you read it. Don't choose a database out of loyalty.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Why not just tune Postgres?" "Postgres stores data by row. A pivot across many columns and hundreds of millions of rows makes it read far more than it needs. Tightening Postgres was one of the gates, but the row-identical benchmark showed the gap was structural." - "Why keep the LLM away from the database?" "Safety and predictability. A model writing its own SQL against 2.11 billion rows can run something huge or wrong. Giving it a prepared JSON context means it reasons over exactly what we chose to show it."

Say this carefully. 15.5 times is query time on a benchmark harness. The 170GB out-of-memory fix was about load time for weekly builds. They are separate. One did not cause the other.

12b. The weekly rollup out-of-memory problem (hardest technical hurdle)

Status: Impact Analytics. On the PDF (prevented a 170GB out-of-memory failure on weekly rollup builds). Full technical pack: 42_clickhouse_rollup_migration.md.

Questions this answers: "What's the hardest technical hurdle you've faced?" "Tell me about a failure." "How do you debug memory problems at scale?"

Words to know. INSERT SELECT builds a table by running a query and inserting its results. While aggregating, ClickHouse keeps running totals per group in memory. That is the "aggregator state". Spilling means writing overflow to disk when memory runs out. OOM means out of memory.

Situation. Building the weekly rollup for a whole season in one INSERT SELECT needed about 170GB of aggregator state. It failed with a memory-limit error even when we set the cap to 80GB, and again at 200GB.

Task. Keep the weekly level of detail, without overwhelming a replica with about 59 cores and 236 GiB of memory.

Action. - I sliced the work into one fiscal week per insert instead of a whole season. - I set explicit caps: 55GB of memory, 16GB of spill to disk, 8 threads, and at most 4 weeks in flight at once. - I measured the slices. An attribute-level week peaked above 40GB. A product-level week was around 11GB. Both fit under the cap.

Result. The weekly rollups build reliably at full weekly detail.

What I learned. Shrink the unit of work before you buy more RAM.

Follow-ups they may ask. - "Why not just get a bigger machine?" "It failed even at a 200GB cap, and season sizes grow. Slicing by week makes memory use bounded and predictable no matter how big the season gets." - "Did this make the pivots faster?" "No, that's a separate result. This fixed how we load the rollups. The 15.5 times speed-up was about query time on the benchmark."

Rapid-fire answers (about 30 seconds each)

"Why are you leaving? Why big tech?" "I've built and owned systems end to end: an AI decision platform, a streaming ingestion pipeline and a finance-grade audit tool. Now I want bigger problems. I'm after harder distributed-systems work, a deeper bench of peers to learn from, and infrastructure where a 1% improvement really matters." For the full answer on why I'm moving after joining Impact Analytics in May 2026, see why switch.

"What's your biggest weakness?" "I over-invest in written artifacts like decision docs and playbooks. I've learned to time-box them and lead with a one-page summary, because a 20-page analysis nobody reads is a failure too." This works because it's real, specific and shows I've corrected it.

"Tell me about a conflict with a manager." Use Story 7 (the rulebook disagreement), framed upward.

"Tell me about a time you failed." Use Story 5 (the refactor regression) or Story 10 (the near-miss). Both end in a process fix.

"What are you most proud of?" Use Story 1. I turned an organisation-level disagreement into a gated, evidence-based decision that became the committed direction.

Also study: 39_behavioral_question_bank.md maps about 43 common questions to stories. 40_behavioral_prep_grid.md is the one-page drill sheet of question types by project. 13_behavioral_why_switch.md has intros and why-switch answers.

Role targeting + rapid-fire (Java + Python + Go track)

How to use this page

  • Part 1 tells you which project story to lead with for each kind of job, and why. Read it while you tailor an application or before a recruiter call.
  • Part 2 is rapid-fire: the tricky one-line questions where a careless answer over-claims. Read it the night before any screen.
  • Memorise the 15-second lead for your target role and the first sentence of every rapid-fire answer.

Use this page when applying with this track's PDF, final_java_pygo_ia/artifacts/Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf (summary line: "Expertise in Java, Python and Go microservices"). On this track, Uber FRM is Java and Spring Boot with Spring Data JPA and Hibernate, Masters India is Spring Boot microservices, and Impact Analytics platform APIs are Go/Gin with a Python agent plane.

Which roles this track suits. Send this PDF to JVM and Spring-heavy backend roles, where the Uber FRM and Masters India work in Java is the direct match. It also works for AI and data roles, because the Impact Analytics Go platform, ClickHouse work and Python agents are the same on every track.

Tags used here. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind the number. TARGET means a design goal, so say "targeting". ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records.

Part 1. Which story fits which role

The idea in plain English

Recruiters skim. In the first 15 seconds of a call they decide whether you "are" the role they are hiring for. You have six projects, and each one proves something different. So the trick is not to tell all six. Lead with the one project whose problem looks most like their problem, back it with one more, and keep the rest for follow-ups.

A good fit has three parts. The problem shape matches (for example, "make analytics queries fast" or "make a pipeline never double-process"). The stack overlaps with their job post. And the seniority signal matches, such as leading people, owning design, or setting quality gates.

Role families at a glance

Why each pairing works

Java and Spring backend roles lead with Uber FRM. It is the clearest proof that I own a Spring Boot service end to end. The scoping backend has 36 Spring Boot endpoints, an 8-table MySQL schema mapped with Spring Data JPA and Hibernate, optimistic locking through a @Version field, and atomic cross-table syncs in one @Transactional method. I led 3 engineers on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that removed latent column-aliasing bugs and raised module coverage to 100% with JUnit. Masters India backs it up with a second Java story: a PHP monolith moved to Spring Boot microservices, with p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds.

Backend / platform roles lead with Impact Analytics Core. It is my current work and the most direct proof of platform ownership. The Go/Gin service handles 10k peak RPS, uses Google Wire (a tool that wires up dependencies at compile time, so a missing dependency is a build error rather than a crash at startup), and protects itself without a reverse proxy, using nested timeouts and Datadog tracing. Masters India backs it up with a classic migration story, from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, with a measurable latency win.

Data infrastructure roles lead with ClickHouse. ClickHouse is a column-oriented analytics database. It stores each column separately, so a query that sums one column over millions of rows reads only that column. My story has a query-time win (planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds through six rollup tables), a load-time fix (the 170GB out-of-memory failure solved by inserting one fiscal week at a time with memory and spill caps) and a data-movement tool (a Go pump copying about 344k rows per second between clusters). Uber Menu's Kafka and Flink pipeline adds the streaming side.

Applied AI roles lead with Impact Analytics Agentic. Most AI candidates can describe a demo. My story shows production discipline: the LLM never touches the database, every output row carries a config_hash (a fingerprint of the exact prompts and settings that produced it), a timeout falls back to a deterministic score, and nothing is promoted without passing an 80% CI gate. Uber Menu then shows RAG on real documents with a measured 98% offline field fidelity.

Streaming roles lead with Uber Menu. Kafka is a durable message log that many services can read at their own pace. Flink is a stream processor that keeps state per key, for example "the last content hash I saw for this vendor". Together they gave keyed deduplication and idempotent catalog upserts. Masters India is the second Kafka story, in a different product, with dead-letter queues and retries against a flaky government portal.

Fintech and compliance roles lead with Uber FRM. The problem is correctness under audit, not speed. The story covers moving 19M general ledger rows off Google Sheets, an 8-table normalized MySQL schema, optimistic locking (each row carries a version number, and an update succeeds only if the version has not changed since you read it), SHA-256 natural keys to stop duplicates, and finite-state-machine gates with 50% delta-variance checks for SOX (the US Sarbanes-Oxley law on financial controls). Masters India's GST work and the ANZ compliance automation reinforce it.

High-throughput roles lead with Masters India. It has the cleanest traffic numbers: 1M+ government submissions a day, 1,500+ clients, p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and throughput from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute. p95 latency is the response time that 95% of requests beat, so it reflects what slow users actually feel.

Senior and tech-lead roles lead with leadership facts, kept separate. I led 3 engineers on the Uber FRM Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration as tech lead of an EPAM pod, not as a people manager. At Masters India I mentored 2 engineers. Never merge these into "led 5".

Product-minded roles can open with GeeksforGeeks. It shows user-facing features (voting, pinning and locking doubt threads), handling 10x traffic spikes during live contests, and an influencer earnings dashboard tied to a 30% course sales lift that the business team attributed.

Part 2. Rapid-fire: tricky questions and safe answers

Each answer starts with the direct answer. Keep it to two or three sentences unless they push.

Numbers that are easy to over-claim

"So your agent is 80% accurate in production?" No. 80% is the CI promotion gate: a change to the agent is blocked unless it scores at least 80% on our 300-case evaluation harness. It is how we refuse a bad agent, not a claim that every tenant runs at 80% live. Follow-up they may ask: "Then what is the 73%?" That is a cost cut. On a separate 200-case benchmark, switching models cut live execution cost by 73% while still completing all 200 cases. The deterministic baseline scored 74% on that same benchmark.

"Did the LLM beat the deterministic baseline?" Not on the blend. On the 200-case benchmark the blended LLM score came in around 63%, below the 74% deterministic baseline. So we froze the blend weights instead of retuning them until the numbers looked good. I think that is the honest way to run an AI system.

"Did the ClickHouse rollups also fix the out-of-memory problem?" No, those are two separate wins. The 15.5x speedup, from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, is query time for planner pivots. The 170GB out-of-memory failure was load time, when building weekly rollups, and I fixed it by inserting one fiscal week at a time with memory and disk-spill caps.

"344k requests per second?" No, 344k is rows per second, a data copy rate. It was the combined rate of two season streams when my Go pump copied rollups between ClickHouse Cloud clusters. API traffic is a separate number: 10k peak RPS on the Go/Gin platform.

"Did the 4.09B-row migration finish?" Say this carefully. The 4.09B-row partition set was measured while the copy was in flight. I do not claim the cutover finished. What I can describe is how restarts were made safe: checkpoint files, a ledger of completed weeks, and rollback by dropping a partition and recopying that season.

"Is the partition rollback an atomic swap?" No. It is DROP PARTITION followed by a recopy of that season. It is not a live swap that readers never notice. I also wrote an incremental design using REPLACE PARTITION, which would allow a swap, but that design was written, not executed.

"Is the 70% reconciliation cut real?" Yes. The platform cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days for the close. If they press on how it was measured, say the technical design doc framed that cut and that is what the platform delivered. Do not walk it back unprompted.

"Thirty-six endpoints? What are they?" About 31 functional routes in the scoping service controllers, plus the collaboration-service APIs for comments and notifications described in the technical design doc. Together that makes 36. I did not build the collaboration service itself.

"Nineteen million rows sounds big. Was this big data?" No, and I don't pitch it that way. 19M is the count of raw general ledger rows migrated off Sheets. Individual quarterly extracts were smaller, roughly 38K to 95K rows. The value was correctness, the four-level hierarchy and auditability, not raw throughput.

"A million submissions a day. What's that per second?" About 12 per second on average, because 1,000,000 divided by 86,400 seconds is roughly 11.6. Peaks around tax filing deadlines were roughly 8 to 10 times higher, which is an estimate. That is why the pipeline had queues, idempotency and dead-letter handling.

"700 to 4,000 requests per minute. In RPS?" Roughly 12 to 67 requests per second. The latency win, p95 from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, came from non-blocking calls to the government portal (Spring WebClient and bounded thread pools), HikariCP connection pooling, query and index fixes, and a Redis read cache.

"How did you get $600K?" About $2 per menu of manual and third-party cost, times 30K menus a month, times 12 months, is $720K. I round down to $600K to be conservative. The 98% is field fidelity on an offline evaluation set, not live production accuracy.

Wording traps

"Your resume says lock contention. What locks?" That is Uber FRM. During financial close, the ETL loads were running into lock contention on the old data model. I fixed it with an 8-table normalized MySQL schema on SOADB (Uber's standard for service-owned MySQL), optimistic row-locking with a version check on update, and one-transaction cross-table syncs. On Impact Analytics the related idea is different: ReplacingMergeTree writes are insert-only, so there are no row locks or ClickHouse mutations to contend on, and reads resolve the newest version.

"BigQuery is on your skills. What did you do with it?" BigQuery is on the Impact Analytics tech line as an upstream historical data source that feeds ClickHouse. I don't claim BigQuery warehouse optimisation as my work. If they want depth, steer to ClickHouse, where my measured work is.

"Is Kafka part of Impact Analytics?" No. Kafka on my resume is Uber Eats Menu (with Flink) and Masters India (the IRP pipeline). Impact Analytics uses Go/Gin, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Redis and Python for the AI layer. The Postgres-to-ClickHouse CDC pipeline there was a colleague's work.

"Did you run the Kubernetes cluster?" No. Kubernetes is on my skills line as working literacy. I don't claim cluster operations. The same goes for Terraform, Spark and multi-region setups: study-level only.

"Are you an Uber employee?" I worked on Uber projects through EPAM Systems, from July 2024 to May 2026. Always say "Uber via EPAM".

"How many people did you lead?" Two separate facts. I led 3 engineers on the Uber FRM Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration as tech lead of an EPAM pod, not as their manager. At Masters India I mentored 2 engineers during the Spring Boot migration.

"What's your FRM stack on this resume?" Java, Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, MySQL, JUnit, Bazel and Docker. The ORM migration was to Spring Data JPA / Hibernate, and it removed latent column-aliasing bugs, where duplicate column names in joined SQL silently mapped rows to the wrong ID.

"Is Ask Iris used by every customer? What's its SLA?" Ask Iris is a shipped capability: a JWT-secured WebSocket copilot planners use to query KPIs and inspect AI decisions. I don't quote usage numbers or an SLA, because I don't have ones I can defend.

"Do you use human review queues in the AI pipeline?" Not on Impact Analytics. In Keep/Drop, offline evaluations replaced critic and evaluator agents, and the batch runs a fixed step order with no LLM orchestrator. The evaluator loop I talk about is in Ask Iris, capped at 3 attempts.

"Have you used MCP or Milvus at Impact Analytics?" No. MCP and tool calling are skills-level for me. I can talk through a tool design for a clustering copilot, but that is verbal design depth, not a resume bullet. Milvus was Uber Eats Menu only.

"Why are MongoDB and Elasticsearch on your skills?" They come from Masters India and GeeksforGeeks, where both are on the tech lines. gRPC, pgvector, DynamoDB, C and C++ are literacy-level. Cassandra, DuckDB and Rust are not on this resume because I can't point to a bullet that uses them in production.

"Under one hour?" (only if they ask about clustering) That is the Cluster Recommendation Copilot, which is verbal design work, not a resume bullet. Under one hour is a TARGET from the design. The measured baseline was about 8.5% run failures (37 of 437 runs), and I don't claim production results for it yet.

For the full arithmetic behind every number, see 09_metrics_derivations.md and 18_resume_number_catalog.md. For the locked facts, see GROUND_TRUTH.md.

Behavioral: introductions and why I switched jobs

How to use this page

  • It covers my self-introduction, why I made each job move, why I'm exploring now, short leadership stories, and a value-to-story mapping.
  • Read it before every recruiter screen and hiring-manager round. These questions come up in almost every loop, usually in the first five minutes.
  • Memorise the 60-second intro and the "why now" answer. Practise them out loud until they sound like talking, not reciting.
  • Full behavioral stories are in the STAR stories page.

What the tags mean. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind the number. TARGET means a design goal. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means it comes from past work records. "Verbal only" means I can talk about it if asked, but it is not on my resume.

Ground rules for this whole page. Stay positive about every employer. Lead with what I'm moving toward, not what I'm leaving. Say "Uber via EPAM", because EPAM Systems employed me and I worked on Uber's teams. On this track, Uber FRM is Java with Spring Boot, Spring Data JPA and Hibernate, Masters India is Spring Boot microservices, and Impact Analytics platform APIs are Go with the Gin framework.

The 60-second introduction

Say this in your own words. The structure matters more than the exact sentences: current role first, then one line per earlier job, then what I want next.

I'm a Senior Software Engineer with five years of building backend and data platforms in Java, Python and Go. Right now I'm at Impact Analytics on AssortSmart, a merchandise planning product that helps retailers decide which products to keep, drop or add each season. I work on the multi-tenant Go platform, the ClickHouse analytics layer that made planner pivots 15.5 times faster, and an AI decision engine that scores 348k article-seasons. I also shipped Ask Iris, a copilot planners use to ask questions about their KPIs.

Before that, at Uber via EPAM, I owned the backend of the Financial Risk Management scoping platform for Uber Finance. It cut quarterly reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days. I also worked on Uber Eats menu ingestion, which processes over 30,000 menus a month.

Earlier, at Masters India, I led the migration of a GST compliance platform from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices and mentored two engineers. I started at GeeksforGeeks, moving PHP services to Django.

I'm looking for a senior backend or platform role where I can own systems end to end for the next several years.

A 30-second version for recruiter screens:

I'm a Senior Software Engineer with five years in Java, Python and Go backends. Today I build the Go platform and the AI decision engine for a retail planning product at Impact Analytics. Before that I owned Uber Finance's risk-scoping backend via EPAM, and led a monolith-to-microservices migration at Masters India. I want a senior role where I own systems end to end for the long run.

Say this carefully. Don't lead with the Cluster Recommendation Copilot. It is verbal only and not a resume bullet. Older prep led with it. The current resume leads with the Go platform, the ClickHouse layer and the AI decision engine.

Why I made each move (keep each under 45 seconds)

The pattern across all of these: each move added a new layer of ownership. Say that once, and every individual answer sounds like part of one story instead of four separate exits.

GeeksforGeeks to Masters India (after about 15 months)

At GeeksforGeeks I was shipping features on a consumer learning platform, and I learned a lot there. Masters India offered something I hadn't had yet: ownership of a regulated financial product and a real platform migration. I wanted to grow from delivering features to owning a service cutover and mentoring others. That's what happened. I led the PHP to Spring Boot migration and mentored two engineers.

Masters India to Uber via EPAM (after about 18 months)

I had taken the GST platform through its migration and through scale. Uber via EPAM was a step up in engineering bar, in product reach and in systems complexity. I wanted to learn Bazel monorepo discipline (Bazel is the build system Uber uses for one giant shared codebase), Uber-scale engineering practices, and work that sits next to Finance and audit. That's where I owned the FRM scoping backend and the reconciliation migration from Google Sheets to MySQL.

Uber via EPAM to Impact Analytics (after about 22 months)

I wanted deeper ownership of data platforms and AI systems, not only service APIs. Impact Analytics offered a senior role building a ClickHouse analytics platform and agentic AI decision systems for retail planning. That was exactly where I wanted to go deep, and I've delivered there: a multi-tenant Go platform, planner pivots 15.5 times faster, and an AI decision engine with a CI quality gate.

Say this carefully. Older prep described the Impact Analytics charter as "CQRS analytics offload" and "the agentic clustering product". Don't use either phrase. The Postgres-to-ClickHouse CDC (change data capture) pipeline was built by a colleague, and the clustering copilot is verbal only.

Why I'm exploring now (joined Impact Analytics in May 2026)

This is the hardest question on the page, because I joined recently, about five months ago as of October 2026. The answer must be honest, positive and short. Never badmouth anyone.

The main answer:

I joined Impact Analytics in May 2026 and I'm proud of what I've built there. That includes the Go platform, the ClickHouse pre-aggregation layer and Ask Iris. I'm still delivering on that work. What I want next is a role where I can own a system for several years and keep building on it. As the role took shape, I realised the mix of scope and team structure wasn't quite the long, multi-year ownership I was looking for. So rather than drift, I'm being deliberate. I'm talking to a small number of teams, yours included, because I want the next move to be one I stay in.

If they ask "Only five months?"

Yes, and I take that seriously, which is why I'm being selective. I'm not leaving because something went wrong. I'm moving toward a specific kind of role, and I'd rather be clear about that early than stay in a fit that isn't quite right.

If they ask about four companies in five years:

Each move added a layer. At GeeksforGeeks it was product features, at Masters India a SaaS migration and mentoring, at Uber via EPAM platform work at Uber scale, and at Impact Analytics data and AI systems. My longest recent stretch was nearly two years at Uber, which shows that I stay when the scope keeps growing. That's what I'm optimising for now.

Avoid: - Calling any team or manager toxic, or blaming anyone. - Leading with compensation. - Saying the current role "doesn't count" or leaving it off. - Apologising as if I failed. - Saying I've already left or "closed out" my work. My resume shows Impact Analytics as my current role. (Older prep said "I closed my open work professionally". Replace it with "I'm still delivering on my current work".)

Leadership stories in STAR form (use the real headcounts)

Two different leadership roles. Never merge them: I led 3 at Uber via EPAM and mentored 2 at Masters India.

Leading 3 engineers at Uber via EPAM (FRM)

What this is. FRM (Financial Risk Management) scoping is how Uber Finance decides which accounts and entities are material enough to need audit controls each quarter. I was the tech lead of an EPAM pod of three engineers, not their people manager.

  • Situation. The FRM scoping backend needed a clean layered architecture. It also needed a migration of the reconciliation step from Google Sheets to MySQL, while the frontend team and Finance stakeholders kept changing requirements.
  • Task. Own the service, keep the pod shipping, and raise test coverage inside Uber's Bazel build system.
  • Action. I split ownership by layer: controllers (the Spring Boot API entry points), services (the business logic) and repositories (Spring Data JPA database access). I set PR conventions that came out of the backend team sync. I paired on the cutover of reconciliation version 2. I reviewed every PR early on, then stepped back as each engineer took real ownership.
  • Result. The platform grew to 8 screens and 36 endpoints, with over 1,100 unit tests. Reconciliation moved to MySQL, and Finance uses the tool for quarterly close. Quarterly reconciliation time dropped 70%, from 14 days to 3 days, against a $340M materiality threshold. I also led the three engineers on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration that raised module statement coverage to 100%.

Say this carefully. Older prep said "30 plus endpoints". The resume says 36. If asked for a breakdown: about 31 functional routes in the scoping service, plus the collaboration-service APIs for comments and notifications, make 36. The 1,100+ test count is verbal, not on the PDF.

Mentoring 2 engineers at Masters India

  • Situation. Two junior engineers were new to Spring Boot and to non-blocking calls against slow third-party APIs during the move from the monolith to microservices.
  • Task. Get them shipping independently without breaking filing-day traffic.
  • Action. I pair-programmed the first canary cutover with them. A canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new service first. I wrote the shared retry and idempotency helpers, so a retried request never files an invoice twice. I reviewed their PRs for input validation at service boundaries and for observability (logs and traces). Then I let them own full services.
  • Result. Both shipped services on their own. The platform's p95 latency went from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute.

Amazon Leadership Principles: which story to use

Amazon interviewers score answers against their Leadership Principles. Other companies use similar values under different names. This table points each value to a real example.

Leadership Principle Story to use
Ownership The FRM reconciliation version 2 migration and owning its schema
Dive Deep The column-aliasing bug at Uber FRM (Story 7). Also the ClickHouse update-strategy bake-off (see note below)
Deliver Results Menu pipeline: onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours and about $600K a year saved. Masters India: from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute
Hire and Develop the Best Led a pod of 3 at Uber via EPAM. Mentored 2 at Masters India
Insist on the Highest Standards Masters India test coverage from 35% to 82%. Over 1,100 FRM tests
Bias for Action The Go data pump at Impact Analytics (see below)

The ClickHouse update-strategy bake-off. In the PoC, handling 10K row updates on a roughly 29M-row table went from about 39 seconds with full-table merges to about 7 seconds with partition-scoped merges. That was MEASURED, but it came from an older resume version and is not on the current PDF. Use it only if asked for more ClickHouse depth.

The Go data pump, for Bias for Action. We needed to move ClickHouse rollup tables between ClickHouse Cloud clusters, but IP allowlists between the clusters blocked a direct copy. Instead of waiting on a network change, I wrote a custom Go data pump over ClickHouse's native TLS protocol. It moved data at about 344k rows per second combined, using double-buffered batches of 500k rows. Say "rows per second", not "requests per second". The largest copy (4.09B rows) was measured while in flight, so don't say the cutover finished.

Older prep mapped Bias for Action to "early exit from a short tenure rather than coasting". Don't use that. It frames the current job negatively and implies I've already left.

Netflix-style culture one-liners

Netflix and similar culture-heavy interviews ask about judgment, candor and ownership. One sentence each, then be ready to expand.

  • Judgment. "I prefer one source of truth over writing the same data to two databases, because dual writes drift apart silently. At Impact Analytics I also kept the LLM away from our 2.11-billion-row table and gave it prepared JSON context instead of a database tool." (The CDC pipeline at Impact Analytics was a colleague's work. Don't claim it.)
  • Candor. "I'm precise about what my numbers mean. For example, our 80% accuracy is a CI promotion gate that a model must pass before release, not a claim that every customer sees 80% live."
  • Ownership. "The FRM reconciliation version 2 branch was mine end to end, from design to cutover."

Say this carefully about the 70%. Older prep told me to call the FRM 70% cut "a design-doc target, not a measured KPI". That guidance is obsolete. The resume states 70%, from 14 days to 3 days, as the outcome. Don't walk it back unprompted. If pressed: "The technical design doc framed that cut, and that's what the platform delivered for the close."

Recruiter gut-check (applies to both variants)

6-second scan test

What stands out first 1. Header title: Senior Software Engineer + Bangalore 2. Brand names: Uber, then Impact Analytics, Masters India, GeeksforGeeks 3. Dense metrics: 60x ClickHouse POC, $600K+, 1M+ daily invoices, 30K+ menus/month 4. Skills row: either Python/Go/Kafka/ClickHouse or Java/Spring Boot/Kafka

What a recruiter notices next (seconds 3-6) - Uber is via EPAM (contractor / vendor staffing, not Uber FTE) - Current SSE role started May 2026 (~2 months as of this review) - Prior titles were SDE2 / SDE, not Senior, until IA - One page is packed; metrics read strong but some lines feel target-heavy (“targeting…”)

Title alignment

“Senior Software Engineer” at Impact Analytics since May 2026 is credibly stretch, not fraud, for ~5 YoE India market titles. For FAANG L5 / Amazon Sr SDE / Airbnb Senior / Netflix L5 screens, it is optimistic:

  • Scope at Uber (led 3, design reviews, CI gates) supports SDE2 / mid-senior.
  • Two months in title does not yet prove senior ownership at the new company.
  • Safer external framing in outreach: “SDE2 / Senior-track backend (~5 YoE)” while keeping resume title if IA HR letter matches.

Inflation / AI-sounding risk

Signal Recruiter read
Precise CH numbers (3.86s, 5.9M rows/sec, 60x) Strong if defendable; looks measured, not fluff
“targeting a 70% cut”, “designed to cut… to under 2%” Honest hedging; good. Do not upgrade to past-tense in interviews
“Defeated anti bot defenses…” Slightly marketing; prefer “handled anti-bot via IP rotation…”
Dense SaaS + Agentic + RAG + migrations in one page Can read as keyword-maxed; keep one crisp ownership story per role
Java variant: Spring Boot on Uber FRM / Masters / GFG ATS win for Java shops. Integrity risk if interviewer expects Java code ownership at Uber Finance (position as architecture + outcomes; clarify stack in interview)

SSE title + 2 months Medium Ask why leave so soon; prepare “comp/level/stack fit” story

Top 10 changes ranked by impact

(Wording/keyword only. Do not invent experience. No .tex/.pdf edits made in this task.)

  1. Split targeting: Use Java variant for Airbnb / Amazon / Netflix / Databricks Java pods; Py/Go for PlanetScale / Microsoft AI-agent / Google Go teams. Biggest screen lift with zero new skills.
  2. Fix Amazon architecture years claim: Summary line that states years leading design/architecture honestly (e.g. 2-3+) plus reliability/scaling, instead of implying 5 years of leading design.
  3. Promote Go on Py/Go resume into summary (PlanetScale / Google / Rubrik-adjacent): production Gin, worker pools, not only skills row.
  4. Add explicit on-call / incident / live-site bullet (Microsoft, Netflix, Amazon, Google).
  5. Verbatim SaaS + SOA/microservices at scale in summary (Databricks, Airbnb, Microsoft).
  6. Strengthen Kubernetes beyond skills list only if true: “deployed/operated services on Kubernetes” with one production proof point (PlanetScale, Databricks, Rubrik future).
  7. EPAM framing: Keep “Uber (via EPAM)” for honesty, but lead with Uber product org / Finance / Eats ownership so ATS brand match survives human discount.
  8. Tone down AI-marketing verbs (“Defeated anti bot…”) to neutral eng voice; reduces inflated/AI-written skim risk.
  9. Add “design patterns, reliability, and scaling” phrase near FRM/Masters leadership bullets (Amazon ATS).
  10. Do not chase Roku 8+ / Rubrik 9+ with keyword stuffing; retarget 5y-bar postings at those companies if any exist, or revisit later.

Final recruiter note

Both one-pagers are above average for a ~5 YoE Bangalore backend candidate: real metrics, migration ownership, mentorship, and a modern agentic stack. They are not yet default FAANG Senior / L5 auto-passes. The limiting factors are years at senior ownership, vendor tenure at Uber, brand-new SSE title, and company-specific language stacks (Go vs Java), not a missing laundry list of buzzwords.

Best near-term screen strategy: Microsoft + Databricks backend + Airbnb (Java) + Google (language-matched) + PlanetScale (Py/Go only). Treat Amazon Sr SDE and Netflix L5 as referral / borderline campaigns. Park Rubrik Enterprise AI and Roku Backend-and-Data until YoE and infra depth catch up.

Senior Systems Deep Dive (Ownership, Reliability, Data Infra)

How to use this page

  • What it covers: the "senior systems" topics that big-tech screens love: ownership, on-call and SLOs, fault tolerance, multi-region, Kubernetes, Terraform, Spark, Flink, design patterns. Each topic is taught from zero, then mapped to what I can honestly claim.
  • When to read it: the week before an infra-heavy or senior backend loop, and again the night before any round with "reliability", "platform" or "data infrastructure" in the title.
  • What to memorise: the status table in the next section (which topics are RESUME-SAFE and which are STUDY ONLY), plus the "How to talk about it honestly" paragraph under each STUDY ONLY topic.

The STUDY ONLY rule. Any section marked STUDY ONLY - NOT RESUME EXPERIENCE is study material for interview fluency. I must not present it as production ownership. Multi-region, Kubernetes cluster operations, Terraform and Spark are study-only for me. I can explain how they work and how I would design with them. I do not say "I operated clusters", "I owned our Terraform" or "I ran Spark in production".

What the tags mean on this page. MEASURED means there is a log, doc or code behind the number. ESTIMATED means it is arithmetic I can show on a whiteboard, so I say "roughly, derived from...". HISTORICAL means it comes from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal, so I say "targeting". RESUME-SAFE means a resume bullet backs it. STUDY ONLY means I can teach it but I did not own it in production.

1. Ownership and software design / architecture (RESUME-SAFE)

Plain English first

When a recruiter says "end-to-end ownership", they mean you were the person who could answer every hard question about a system, not just the person who wrote some of its code. Think of the difference between renting a room and owning a house. A renter fixes what is in their room. An owner knows where the water main is, who to call when the roof leaks, and what it costs to rebuild the kitchen. Interviewers probe ownership because seniors are hired to own outcomes, not tickets.

How it works: the five questions that prove ownership

An owner can answer all five of these about a system:

  1. Who wrote the design doc? You can explain the problem, the options considered and why one won.
  2. Who set the API contracts? You froze request and response shapes before the UI team started building, so two teams could work in parallel.
  3. Who owned the cutover? You planned how traffic or data moved from old to new.
  4. Who owned the rollback? You knew exactly what you would do if the cutover went wrong, before it went wrong.
  5. Who owned the post-incident fix? When something broke, you found the root cause and closed the gap.

A tiny example from my own work: on Uber FRM, the reconciliation screen moved from Google Sheets (v1) to MySQL (v2). I owned that migration branch. The design was a parallel run: v1 and v2 endpoints served side by side, the numbers were compared, and v1 stayed alive until the MySQL path was trusted. That covers questions 1, 3 and 4 in one story.

Map to my work

Pattern My evidence How I say it
Owned a platform Uber FRM Risk Scoping (via EPAM): 8 screens, 36 Spring Boot endpoints "I owned the FRM scoping backend and the recon v2 migration, and I enforced layer boundaries across the pod."
Software design and architecture FRM controller, service, repository, JPA entity layering "Controllers stay thin. Services own the business rules. Repositories own the SQL."
Led design reviews Led 3 engineers on the FRM pod (EPAM tech lead, not people manager) "I sliced work by layer and reviewed PRs for API contracts and test gates."
Strangler migration ownership Masters India PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices, mentored 2 engineers "Per-endpoint canary, shared database first, no dual-write source of truth."
Platform architecture Impact Analytics Go/Gin platform at 10k peak RPS, shared orchestration registry "I designed the Go/Gin edge and the orchestration registry that every AI pipeline runs through."

Keep "led 3" (Uber FRM) and "mentored 2" (Masters India) as two separate facts. Never merge them into "led 5".

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: What does "owned design and architecture" mean for you day to day? Me: It means I am the person who can explain every non-obvious trade-off on the critical path. Concretely, I ran the design review agenda, froze API contracts before the UI started, wrote the migration plan with its rollback, and set the CI quality gates. On Uber FRM that looked like freezing the scoping endpoints, then running recon v1 and v2 side by side until the MySQL numbers matched. Follow-up they may ask: "What did you do when someone disagreed with the design?" Answer with the trade-off you wrote down and how the review settled it.

Interviewer: Amazon asks for years of leading design. How do you answer without lying? Me: I do not say five years of leading design. I say roughly three years of leading design reviews and architecture decisions, across Masters India (about 1.5 years) and Uber FRM via EPAM (about 1.9 years), plus individual-contributor architecture ownership at Impact Analytics since May 2026. That is honest arithmetic from my dates, and it still shows a pattern of owning design.

Interviewer: Give me an example of a decision you owned that you would make differently now. Me: At Impact Analytics I chose an app-native orchestration registry over Airflow or Temporal, because I needed resume behaviour tightly coupled to ClickHouse inserts and config hashing. That was right for one team and a handful of pipelines. If the number of pipelines grew a lot, I would revisit a managed workflow engine, because the registry's custom code becomes something we must maintain forever.
