2. On-call, incident response, SLOs (PARTIAL RESUME-SAFE)

Plain English first

SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) is Google's name for treating operations as an engineering problem. Instead of "keep the servers up at all costs", you agree on how reliable a service must be, measure it, and spend the leftover unreliability on shipping features. Think of a monthly phone data plan. You know your limit, you check how fast you are using it, and you slow down when you are close to the cap.

Words you need

  • SLI (Service Level Indicator): the thing you measure. Example: the share of requests that finish under 300 ms.
  • SLO (Service Level Objective): the target for that measurement. Example: 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days.
  • SLA (Service Level Agreement): a contract with a customer, usually with money attached if you miss it. The SLA is normally looser than the internal SLO.
  • Error budget: 100% minus the SLO. It is the amount of failure you are allowed.
  • Burn rate: how fast you are using the error budget compared to the normal pace.
  • Postmortem: a blameless write-up after an incident: timeline, root cause, blast radius, action items with owners.
  • p95 latency: the time under which 95% of requests finish. It shows what slow users feel, which an average hides.

How it works, with a worked example

Say the SLO is 99.9% availability over 30 days.

30 days x 24 hours x 60 minutes = 43,200 minutes
Error budget = 0.1% of 43,200 = 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime per month

If the service is burning budget at 14.4 times the normal rate, the whole month's budget is gone in about 30 / 14.4, which is roughly 2 days. That is why good alerts fire on burn rate, not on single blips. A fast burn pages a human now. A slow burn opens a ticket.

Three ideas interviewers want to hear:

  1. Alert on symptoms users feel, like error rate or p95 latency, not on every CPU spike.
  2. Mitigate first, then diagnose. Roll back, open a circuit breaker or shed load before you hunt the root cause.
  3. Correlation IDs are the fastest triage tool. One request ID that appears in every log line across API, queue consumer and worker lets you follow a single failed request end to end.

Resume-safe wording

  • Masters India: I set up ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana, a log search stack) and New Relic tracing, and incident triage time fell about 70%. The 70% is HISTORICAL. The baseline of roughly 30 minutes down to under 10 minutes is ESTIMATED. Test coverage went from 35% to 82%, and deployment success was 98%.
  • Impact Analytics: the Go/Gin platform uses Datadog distributed tracing, and the AI pipelines emit custom JSON telemetry (tokens, USD cost, step duration, batch fallbacks). That is observability I built. It is not a pager-rotation title.

Do not claim

A pager rotation that I owned, an incident commander or "SEV commander" title, Netflix-scale error budgets, or Uber Menu dashboards as proof of on-call work.

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: Walk me through an incident from alert to close. Me: First the alert fires on an error-rate or p95 spike, and it carries request IDs. I search those IDs in ELK and follow one request across the API, the worker and the third-party call. I mitigate before I diagnose, so I roll back, open the circuit or shed load. Then I write an incident note with the cause and follow-up actions with owners. At Masters India the big triage win was correlation IDs across API, Kafka consumer and IRP worker. I do not claim a formal pager rotation I cannot prove.

Interviewer: How would you pick an SLO for a new service? Me: I start from what users feel, usually success rate and p95 latency on the main user path. I look at current performance and pick a target slightly better than today, not a heroic number. Then I compute the error budget and agree with product what happens when it runs out, for example a feature freeze. An SLO nobody acts on is just a dashboard.

Interviewer: Why alert on p95 and not average latency? Me: An average hides the slow tail. If 5% of requests take 10 seconds, the average can still look fine. p95 shows the experience of the unhappy users, which is what drives complaints. At Masters our latency headline was p95, from 1.2 seconds to 300 ms.

Official references

  • Google SRE: Service Level Objectives
  • Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs
  • Monitoring distributed systems

3. Fault tolerance (RESUME-SAFE at Masters, IA and Menu)

Plain English first

Fault tolerance means the system keeps doing the right thing when a part of it fails. In real systems the failing part is usually something you do not control: a government portal, a third-party website, an LLM provider. A good analogy is a careful courier. If the recipient is not home, the courier tries again later, never delivers the same parcel twice, and after a few failed tries puts the parcel in a "needs attention" pile instead of driving around forever.

Words you need, with tiny examples

Idempotency key. A unique label for an operation, so doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Like a cheque number: the bank will not cash cheque #1042 twice. At Masters India the key looked like client + fileHash + batchIndex.

String key = clientId + ":" + fileHash + ":" + batchIndex;
Optional<IrpResult> previous = store.find(key);
if (previous.isPresent()) {
    return previous.get();              // already done, return the old result
}
IrpResult result = irp.submit(batch);
store.save(key, result);
return result;

Exponential backoff with jitter. After each failure, wait longer before retrying, plus a small random amount so a thousand clients do not all retry at the same moment.

for (int attempt = 0; attempt < MAX_RETRIES; attempt++) {
    try {
        return callPortal();
    } catch (TransientPortalException e) {
        long waitMs = (1000L << attempt) + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1000);
        Thread.sleep(waitMs);
    }
}
throw new GiveUpException();   // bounded: we stop and park the work

Dead-letter queue (DLQ). A side queue where messages that keep failing are parked so an operator can inspect and replay them. It is the "needs attention" pile.

Circuit breaker. A switch that stops calling a dependency after repeated failures, so you stop hammering something that is already down. Like a household fuse. At Impact Analytics the orchestration registry trips after about 5 consecutive failures or a high failure fraction.

Cache-aside. The app checks Redis first. On a miss it reads the database and writes the result into Redis. Adding a small random spread to expiry times (TTL jitter) and a lock (Redis SETNX) stops many requests rebuilding the same key at once, which is called a cache stampede.

Graceful fallback. When the smart path fails, return a safe, simpler answer. At Impact Analytics, if the LLM times out, the Keep/Drop engine falls back to the deterministic baseline score.

Checkpoint and resume. Save progress to disk so a crashed job continues where it stopped. At Impact Analytics that is det.json, agent_progress.json and a --resume flag, which skips redundant deterministic scoring.

Resume-safe wording

At Masters India I built fault-tolerant bulk paths with idempotency keys, bounded retries and DLQ replay, plus a Redis cache-aside layer that cut database read load by 30%. At Impact Analytics I built a shared orchestration registry with hard timeouts, circuit breakers, durable checkpoints and fallback to deterministic scores on LLM timeouts. On Uber Menu (via EPAM), "exactly-once catalog upserts" means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts.

Patterns I can defend

Pattern Why it exists My example
Idempotency key Retries must not double-register invoices with the government IRP (Invoice Registration Portal) Masters: client + fileHash + batchIndex
Exponential backoff + jitter The government portal is flaky, especially near filing deadlines Masters: bounded concurrency and retries on IRP submit
Dead-letter queue Park poison batches for operator replay Masters bulk import DLQ
Circuit breaker Stop hammering a dead dependency IA registry trips after about 5 consecutive failures. Masters IRP breaker is a prep narrative, not a PDF bullet
Hard and nested timeouts A slow call must not hold a thread or a batch forever IA registry timeouts, IA Go/Gin nested timeouts
Graceful fallback Ship a safe answer when the smart path fails IA: deterministic baseline on LLM timeout
Checkpoint and resume Crashes must not redo expensive work IA: det.json, agent_progress.json, --resume
Cache-aside + TTL jitter + SETNX Stampede protection Masters Redis masters and config cache

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: Why not exactly-once end to end? Me: Because the government portal is outside my transaction boundary. True exactly-once needs a sink that can join one shared transaction with my queue, and the IRP cannot. So I do at-least-once delivery plus idempotency, which gives the same visible result: each invoice is registered once even if a message is processed twice. The same logic applies to Menu, where "exactly-once catalog upserts" really means at-least-once plus idempotent upserts.

Interviewer: How do you stop retries from making an outage worse? Me: I bound them. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter so clients spread out. There is a maximum attempt count, after which the work goes to a dead-letter queue. A circuit breaker stops calls entirely after repeated failures, and checks again later. At Impact Analytics the registry breaker trips after about 5 consecutive failures, and the batch falls back to deterministic scores instead of waiting.

Interviewer: What is the difference between a timeout and a circuit breaker? Me: A timeout protects one call: it gives up on a single slow request. A circuit breaker protects the whole system: after enough failures it stops sending any requests for a while. You usually need both. Timeouts alone still send every request into a dead dependency and wait the full timeout each time.

Official references

  • AWS Reliability: Fault isolation
  • Google SRE: Handling overload

4. Multi-region / HA / DR (STUDY ONLY - NOT RESUME EXPERIENCE)

Why it is off the resume

There is no personal multi-region ownership in my source material. Some Impact Analytics CDC (change data capture) docs mention active-active and disaster-recovery goals, but that tool was authored by a colleague, Ashvin Sharma, and I do not claim it. I never say I built multi-region HA.

One subtle point: my Impact Analytics C1 bullet says the Go/Gin edge guarantees high availability through native h2c, nested timeouts and Datadog tracing. That "high availability" is about a single service protecting itself under load. It is not geo-failover across regions. Do not let an interviewer blur the two.

Plain English first

A region is a geographic area where a cloud provider runs data centres, like "Mumbai" or "Iowa". An availability zone (AZ) is one or more separate data centres inside a region, with independent power and cooling. Multi-region design means your service survives the loss of an entire region. Think of a bank that keeps copies of its records in two cities, so a flood in one city does not close the bank.

  • HA (High Availability): the service stays up through component failures.
  • DR (Disaster Recovery): how you get back after a big failure, like losing a region.
  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data you are allowed to lose, measured in time. "RPO of 5 seconds" means you may lose the last 5 seconds of writes.
  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long you are allowed to be down while recovering.
  • Replication: copying data from one database to another. Synchronous waits for the copy before confirming a write (safe, slower). Asynchronous confirms first and copies later (fast, may lose recent writes).
  • GSLB (Global Server Load Balancing) or DNS failover: the traffic switch that sends users to the healthy region.

How it works

Client
  |
  +-- Region A (active) ---- DB primary + replicas
  |
  +-- Region B (passive or active) ---- replica or second primary
         |
         +-- DNS / GSLB failover + data replication lag budget

What to notice: the replication arrow between regions is where the trade-offs live. Its lag sets your RPO, and the DNS switch sets most of your RTO.

flowchart LR U["Users"] --> G["DNS or GSLB"] G --> A["Region A active"] G -.->|"failover"| B["Region B standby"] A --> DA["Primary DB"] B --> DB2["Replica DB"] DA -->|"async replication"| DB2

What to notice: in active-passive, Region B only takes traffic after failover, so there is one writer and no conflicts.

Active-passive vs active-active.

Model How it works Strength Cost
Active-passive One region serves, the other waits with a replica Simple consistency, one writer Longer failover, idle capacity
Active-active Both regions serve and accept writes Lower RTO, users served nearby Write conflicts need resolution rules

Worked example. With async replication and a typical lag of 5 seconds, a sudden loss of Region A can lose up to about 5 seconds of writes, so the RPO is about 5 seconds. If DNS failover plus warming the standby takes 10 minutes, the RTO is about 10 minutes. To get RPO near zero you need synchronous replication, which adds cross-region round-trip time to every write.

Trade-offs to recite:

  • Active-passive gives simpler consistency but longer failover.
  • Active-active gives lower RTO but harder conflict resolution.
  • RPO is data you can lose. RTO is time to recover.
  • Multi-AZ is not multi-region. An AZ failure is not a region failure.
  • A failover you have never tested is a hope, not a plan. Run game days.

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: Have you operated multi-region production? Me: No. My production reliability work has been single-region SaaS with fault-tolerant bulk paths and strong observability. I can design for multi-region: I would define RPO and RTO with the business, choose async or sync replication based on that, decide active-passive or active-active, and test failover on a schedule.

Interviewer: How would you resolve write conflicts in active-active? Me: First I would try to avoid them by routing each user or tenant to a home region, so each record has one writer. Where that is impossible, I would pick a rule per data type: last-writer-wins with timestamps for low-value fields, or merge logic and CRDTs (data types designed to merge safely) for counters and sets. For money, I would keep a single writer region and accept a higher RTO.

Interviewer: Multi-AZ or multi-region for a new SaaS? Me: Usually multi-AZ first. It handles the common failures, a data centre or a rack, at much lower cost and complexity. Multi-region is justified when the business needs to survive a full-region loss or has data-residency rules.

How to talk about it honestly given my experience

"I have not run multi-region production. What I have done is design single-region systems to fail gracefully: idempotent retries and DLQs at Masters India, circuit breakers and checkpoint-resume at Impact Analytics. I understand RPO, RTO and replication trade-offs and can whiteboard an active-passive design, but I would be learning the operational side on the job."

Official references

  • Kubernetes multiple zones
  • AKS multi-region models
  • GCP Architecture Framework: Reliability

5. Kubernetes operational depth (STUDY ONLY beyond the skills keyword)

Resume boundary

Kubernetes appears on my skills line as literacy. There is no kubectl, Helm or operator production narrative in my material, and Impact Analytics has no Kubernetes operations claim. I do not say "operated production clusters". Docker is real: my services were containerised.

Plain English first

A container is a packaged app with everything it needs to run, like a shipping container that fits on any ship. Kubernetes (often "K8s") is the port authority. You tell it "I want 3 copies of this container running, each with this much memory", and it finds machines, starts them, restarts them when they crash, and routes traffic to the healthy ones. You declare the desired state and Kubernetes keeps reality matching it.

Words you need

  • Cluster: a set of machines (nodes) managed by Kubernetes. The control plane is the brain. etcd is the key-value database where the control plane stores cluster state.
  • Pod: the smallest unit Kubernetes runs, one or more containers sharing a network address.
  • Deployment: says "keep N copies of this pod running at this version" and handles rolling updates.
  • Service: a stable internal address that load-balances across pods, because pods come and go.
  • Ingress: the front door that routes outside HTTP traffic to services.
  • ConfigMap and Secret: configuration and sensitive values injected into pods. Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, not encrypted, unless you enable encryption at rest.
  • Requests and limits: requests are what the scheduler reserves for a pod. Limits are the ceiling. Exceed the memory limit and the pod is killed (OOMKilled).
  • HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler): adds or removes pods based on CPU or custom metrics.
  • PDB (Pod Disruption Budget): "never take more than one of my pods down at a time during maintenance".
  • Readiness probe: "is this pod ready for traffic?" If it fails, the pod is removed from the Service but not restarted.
  • Liveness probe: "is this pod stuck?" If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container.

A tiny example

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: example/api:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }
            limits:   { memory: "512Mi" }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }

What to notice: three replicas, a memory ceiling, and two different probes. Readiness gates traffic. Liveness triggers restarts.

Rollouts and failure modes

  • Rolling update: replace pods a few at a time. Default for Deployments.
  • Blue/green: run the new version beside the old one and switch all traffic at once.
  • Canary: send a small share of traffic to the new version first. This is the same idea as my Masters India per-route canary, just done at the cluster layer.
  • CrashLoopBackOff: the container keeps crashing on start, and Kubernetes waits longer between restarts. Check logs from the previous run and the startup config.
  • OOMKilled: the container passed its memory limit. Fix the leak or raise the limit with evidence.
  • ImagePullBackOff: Kubernetes cannot fetch the image, usually a wrong tag or missing registry credentials.
  • Network policy blocks: pods cannot talk because a policy denies the traffic.

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: How deep is your Kubernetes experience? Me: Honestly, it is literacy rather than operations. I have built containerised services with Docker and I list Kubernetes as familiarity. I have not owned cluster upgrades, operators or the control plane. What I can defend from production is the service side: health checks, timeouts, deploy gates and canary rollouts, like the per-route canary in the Masters India migration.

Interviewer: Readiness vs liveness, what is the difference? Me: Readiness decides whether a pod gets traffic. Liveness decides whether a pod gets restarted. A pod that is warming a cache should fail readiness, not liveness, otherwise Kubernetes will kill it in a loop. A common bug is pointing liveness at a check that depends on the database, so a database blip restarts every pod at once.

Interviewer: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What do you do? Me: I look at the logs of the previous crashed run, then describe the pod to see events and the exit code. Exit code 137 usually means OOMKilled. Otherwise it is often a bad config value, a missing secret or a failing startup dependency. I fix the cause and roll back the Deployment if the new version is the trigger.

Interviewer: How do you scale pods automatically? Me: With the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, on CPU or a custom metric like queue depth or requests per second. It only works well if requests are set honestly, because utilisation is measured against them. For bursty work I prefer queue depth, since CPU reacts late.

How to talk about it honestly given my experience

"Kubernetes is on my skills line as literacy. I understand the objects, probes, autoscaling and rollout strategies, and I have designed services that behave well inside a cluster. I have not operated clusters in production, so for a role with heavy cluster ownership I would be ramping on the operations side."

Official references

  • kubeadm HA
  • Kubernetes production best practices

6. Terraform / IaC (STUDY ONLY - NOT RESUME EXPERIENCE)

Why it is off the resume

There are no Terraform modules, state files or IaC ownership in my material.

Plain English first

IaC (Infrastructure as Code) means describing your cloud resources in text files that live in Git, instead of clicking around a console. Terraform is the most common IaC tool. Think of an architect's blueprint. You edit the blueprint, Terraform compares it with the building that exists, shows you exactly what will change, and then makes only those changes.

How it works: the ideas that matter in interviews

  1. Providers are plugins that talk to a cloud (AWS, GCP and others). Resources are the things you create, like a bucket or a cluster.
  2. State is Terraform's record of what it created and the real IDs. Teams keep it in remote state (for example a cloud bucket) with locking, so two people cannot apply at the same time.
  3. Plan then apply. terraform plan shows the diff. terraform apply executes it. Reviewing the plan in a PR is the main safety gate.
  4. Drift is when reality changes outside Terraform, for example someone edits a firewall rule by hand. The next plan shows it. Import brings an existing hand-made resource under Terraform.
  5. Modules are reusable bundles of resources. Workspaces keep separate state for environments.
  6. Secrets in state: state can contain sensitive values in plain text, so lock down the state bucket and pull secrets from a secret manager.

A tiny example

resource "google_storage_bucket" "exports" {
  name                        = "example-exports-bucket"
  location                    = "US"
  uniform_bucket_level_access = true
  lifecycle_rule {
    condition { age = 30 }
    action    { type = "Delete" }
  }
}

What to notice: this is desired state. Running apply twice changes nothing the second time, which is what "idempotent infrastructure" means. Compare that with a "snowflake server" that someone configured by hand and nobody can rebuild.

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: Did you manage infrastructure with Terraform? Me: No, I have no production Terraform ownership. I owned application deploy quality instead: CI gates, test coverage from 35% to 82% and 98% deployment success at Masters India, and stacked Bazel PRs for zero-downtime releases on Uber FRM. I can explain plan and apply, remote state and drift, and I would be comfortable learning a team's modules.

Interviewer: Two engineers run apply at the same time. What happens? Me: With remote state and locking, the second run waits or fails to get the lock, so state is not corrupted. Without locking, both can write state and you can end up with resources Terraform no longer knows about. That is why remote state with locking is the first thing a team sets up.

Interviewer: Someone changed a resource by hand. How do you handle it? Me: The next plan shows the drift. I decide whether the manual change was right. If yes, I update the code to match. If no, I apply to put it back. Then I close the gap that allowed console edits, for example by restricting write permissions.

How to talk about it honestly given my experience

"I have not owned Terraform. My deploy-side ownership is CI gates, tests and safe rollouts. I understand the plan, apply and state model well enough to read and review modules, and I would ramp on writing them."

Official references

  • Terraform language
  • AWS EKS Terraform resource
  • GKE Terraform resource

7. Spark (STUDY ONLY - not on the PDF)

Resume boundary

Spark is not on the current PDF. Older prep listed Spark as a Uber Menu resume claim for batch backfills and reprocessing after the Selenium, Kafka and Flink online path. That is obsolete. Spark is now a verbal backfill option only: if someone asks "how would you reprocess a year of scraped menus?", Spark is a reasonable answer, but I do not say I ran it. Older prep also estimated about 1 to 2 million item rows per reprocess window. Because Spark is off the PDF, do not quote that number. See 14_uber_menu_deep_dive.md for the Menu pipeline that is on the PDF.

Plain English first

Apache Spark is an engine for processing large datasets by splitting the work across many machines. Think of counting every word in a library. One person would take years. Spark hands each shelf to a different helper, each helper counts their shelf, and then the counts are combined. It is mostly used for batch ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) jobs and machine-learning feature generation over files in object storage.

How it works: the ideas that matter in interviews

  1. Driver and executors. The driver is the coordinator that plans the job. Executors are worker processes that do the actual work on chunks of data.
  2. Partitions. Data is split into partitions. One task processes one partition. More partitions means more parallelism, up to a point.
  3. Lazy evaluation. Transformations like filter and groupBy only build a plan. Nothing runs until an action like write or count.
  4. Shuffle. Operations like groupBy and join must move rows with the same key to the same executor. Shuffles go over the network and are the usual bottleneck.
  5. Skew. If one key has far more rows than others, one task runs forever while the rest sit idle. Fixes include salting the key or AQE.
  6. AQE (Adaptive Query Execution). Spark re-plans at runtime using real statistics, for example splitting skewed partitions or switching join strategies.
  7. Structured Streaming processes streams as a series of small batches (micro-batches). Flink processes event by event. On my resume, Flink owns the online Menu path.

A tiny example

df = spark.read.parquet("gs://example-bucket/menus/2025/")
latest = (
    df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
        Window.partitionBy("vendor_id", "menu_id").orderBy(F.desc("scraped_at"))))
      .filter("rn = 1")      # keep newest version per menu
      .drop("rn")
)
latest.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("gs://example-bucket/menus_dedup/2025/")

What to notice: the window function forces a shuffle by vendor_id, menu_id. If one giant vendor dominates, that partition becomes skewed.

Spark vs Flink vs ClickHouse

Tool Best at Not great at
Spark Large offline ETL, backfills, ML features over object storage Low-latency per-event processing, interactive dashboards
Flink Continuous per-event stream processing with state Ad-hoc analytics
ClickHouse Interactive analytical queries on huge tables Heavy multi-stage ETL with many joins and custom code

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: Have you used Spark in production? Me: No, Spark is study-level for me and it is not on my resume. My production streaming work was Kafka plus Flink on Uber Menu, and my analytics work was ClickHouse at Impact Analytics. I understand Spark's model, driver and executors, partitions, shuffles and skew, and on Menu I would pick it for a large historical backfill.

Interviewer: A Spark job has one task running much longer than the others. Why? Me: Almost always data skew. One key, say one huge vendor, has far more rows, so its partition is much bigger. I would check task-level metrics, then enable AQE skew-join handling or salt the hot key by adding a random suffix, aggregating, then combining.

Interviewer: Spark or ClickHouse for planner analytics like AssortSmart? Me: ClickHouse, for the interactive part. Planners need pivots on demand, and at Impact Analytics I cut planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds on a 250M-row harness with ClickHouse pre-aggregation rollups. Spark fits large offline ETL and ML feature generation across object storage. I own the ClickHouse path. Spark remains study-only for me.

How to talk about it honestly given my experience

"Spark is not something I have run in production. Menu's online path was Kafka and Flink, and at Impact Analytics the interactive analytics are ClickHouse. If you asked me to design a backfill over a year of scraped data, Spark is what I would reach for, and I can explain why and where it would hurt."

Official references

  • https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/cluster-overview.html
  • https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/structured-streaming-programming-guide.html

8. Flink (RESUME on Uber Menu, study extras below)

Resume claim

On Uber Menu (via EPAM), the PDF says I built a large-scale Kafka plus Apache Flink ingestion and processing pipeline with stateful keyed deduplication, schema normalization and exactly-once catalog upserts. The deduplication is keyed by vendor and menu with a content hash. "Exactly-once catalog upserts" means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent upserts in practice. I do not claim zero message loss or two-phase commit across third parties. Peak of roughly 200 to 500 events per second is an ESTIMATE for prep only, not a PDF number. Flink is not part of Masters India or Impact Analytics. See 14_uber_menu_deep_dive.md and 03_uber_menu_streaming_numbers.md.

Plain English first

Kafka is a durable log of events, like a conveyor belt that remembers every parcel it carried. Flink is the sorting machine standing next to the belt. It reads each event as it arrives, remembers things about what it has seen (state), and emits clean results. Unlike Spark batch jobs, it never "finishes". It runs continuously.

How it works: the ideas that matter in interviews

  1. Event time vs processing time. Event time is when the thing happened. Processing time is when Flink saw it. Late or out-of-order events make these differ.
  2. Watermarks. A watermark is Flink's statement "I believe I have seen everything up to time T". It lets windows close even when events arrive late.
  3. Keyed state. Flink splits the stream by a key (for Menu, vendor and menu) and keeps small state per key, for example "the last content hash I saw".
  4. Checkpoints and savepoints. Flink periodically snapshots all state plus the Kafka offsets. After a crash it restores both, so state and input position stay consistent. Savepoints are manual snapshots for upgrades.
  5. Exactly-once. Inside Flink, checkpoints give exactly-once state. End to end, you also need a transactional or idempotent sink. Menu used idempotent upserts.
  6. Backpressure. If a downstream step is slow, Flink slows the upstream reads rather than dropping data.

A tiny example (keyed dedupe in pseudocode)

class DedupeByContent(KeyedProcessFunction):     # key = (vendor_id, menu_id)
    def process_element(self, menu, ctx):
        h = sha256(menu.normalized_payload)
        if self.last_hash.value() == h:
            return                                # same content, drop it
        self.last_hash.update(h)
        yield menu                                # changed, send to upsert

What to notice: a re-scrape that produced identical content is dropped. Because the catalog write is an upsert on a stable key, a replay after a crash writes the same row again harmlessly.

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: Why Flink and not just Kafka consumers in Python? Me: Because we needed state per vendor and menu, the last content hash, kept consistent with Kafka offsets across restarts. Flink's keyed state and checkpoints give that out of the box. Hand-rolled consumers would need their own state store and offset bookkeeping, which is exactly where duplicate and lost updates come from.

Interviewer: You say exactly-once. Prove it. Me: I say exactly-once catalog upserts, and I mean it carefully. Delivery is at-least-once, so a message can be processed twice after a failure. The catalog write is an idempotent upsert keyed by vendor and menu, so the second write produces the same row. The visible effect is once. I do not claim zero message loss or a distributed transaction across third-party sites.

Interviewer: Flink vs Kafka Streams vs Spark Structured Streaming? Me: Kafka Streams is a library inside your app, great when everything is in Kafka and the logic is simple. Spark Structured Streaming uses micro-batches, so latency is higher but it shares code with batch jobs. Flink is a dedicated per-event engine with strong state and event-time support, which fit Menu's keyed dedupe.

Bridge line

"Masters India Kafka was asynchronous e-invoice processing with no Flink. Uber Menu is where Flink sits. Impact Analytics has no Kafka or Flink."

Official references

  • https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/
  • https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/deployment/ha/overview/
  • https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/stateful-stream-processing/

9. Design patterns (verbal depth, not a skills keyword)

Plain English first

A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a common design problem. Naming patterns lets engineers talk quickly: saying "strangler migration" replaces ten minutes of explanation. Design Patterns is no longer a keyword on my skills line, but interviewers still ask for examples, so I keep these ready.

Patterns I can name from my projects

Pattern What it is in one line Where I used it
Strangler Fig Replace an old system route by route, like a vine slowly replacing a tree Masters India PHP monolith to Spring Boot, canary per route
Layered / Repository Each layer has one job: controller, service, repository Uber FRM controller, service, Spring Data JPA repository, Hibernate entities
Parallel run / expand-contract Run old and new side by side, compare, then remove the old Uber FRM recon v1 (Sheets) and v2 (MySQL)
Cache-aside Check cache, on miss read DB and fill cache Masters Redis
Idempotent consumer Processing a message twice has the same effect as once Masters bulk IRP, Menu catalog upserts
Circuit breaker Stop calling a failing dependency for a while Impact Analytics orchestration registry
Checkpoint / resume Save progress so restarts skip finished work Impact Analytics Keep/Drop batches
Split read and write stores (CQRS-like, verbal only) Different stores for different access patterns Impact Analytics: PostgreSQL keeps thin metadata, UAM and roles. ClickHouse serves large analytical reads

On the last row, say this carefully. It is a verbal example, not a resume bullet, and I would not call it formal CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation). Older prep cited an Impact Analytics "Order Batching" POC for this row. The safer, current framing is the PostgreSQL versus ClickHouse split above.

Typical interview questions with answers

Interviewer: Give me one design pattern and its trade-off. Me: Strangler versus a full rewrite. At Masters India we moved route by route from the PHP monolith to Spring Boot, with a canary per route. Strangler kept filing day safe because any route could roll back on its own, at the cost of running two stacks and a more complex gateway for a while. A rewrite is cleaner in the long run but was unacceptable for compliance deadlines.

Interviewer: Why a repository layer? Isn't it just boilerplate? Me: It keeps SQL in one place. On Uber FRM, a latent column-aliasing bug in joined raw SQL silently mapped rows to the wrong identity. Because SQL lived in repositories, the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration could fix it in one layer with aliased selects and explicit labels, and the services did not change.

10. Mock interviewer loop (hardest combined questions)

Q1: Sell me on your ownership in 60 seconds without buzzwords. A: At Uber, via EPAM, I owned the FRM scoping backend and the recon v2 migration end to end: schema, repository, service, controllers, tests, and the cutover off Google Sheets. I led 3 engineers on the core Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration. At Masters India I owned the strangler migration plan from the PHP monolith, mentored two engineers through canaries, and owned the bulk e-invoicing path that handles over 1 million government submissions a day. At Impact Analytics I designed the Go/Gin platform and the orchestration registry the AI pipelines run on.

Q2: Where is fault tolerance in your stack, with numbers? A: The clearest example is Masters bulk e-invoicing: over 1 million daily submissions, which is about 12 per second on average (1,000,000 divided by 86,400). Peaks around filing deadlines were roughly 8 to 10 times that, which is an estimate. Throughput went from 700 to 4,000 requests per minute. Idempotency keys stop double registration with the IRP across 100K+ concurrent imports, bounded retries with backoff absorb portal flakes, a DLQ holds poison batches, and Redis cut database read load by 30%. At Impact Analytics, circuit breakers, hard timeouts and deterministic fallback keep batches finishing when the LLM fails.

Q3: Why should PlanetScale or Netflix care if you lack multi-region and Terraform? A: Because I can show production ownership of data correctness, sharding, throughput, latency and observability. Multi-region and Terraform are study-ready, and I will not invent cluster or IaC ownership. My closest HA story is fault-tolerant bulk processing and observability, not geo-failover.

Q4: Spark vs ClickHouse for AssortSmart analytics? A: ClickHouse for the interactive planner metrics. On a 250M-row harness, ClickHouse pre-aggregation rollups took planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds, about 15.5 times faster. An earlier PostgreSQL versus ClickHouse POC showed ClickHouse winning large analytical reads, while PostgreSQL stayed for thin metadata, UAM and roles. Spark fits large offline ETL and ML features over object storage. I own the ClickHouse path. Spark remains study-only for me. Say this carefully: do not say "sub-second" for ClickHouse. If they ask for the POC numbers, use 19_ia_ch_pg_poc_source.md with its hardware caveat, and say they are POC numbers, not resume numbers.

Q5: How do you answer Kubernetes depth without failing the screen? A: I give the honest scope first: Dockerised services, Kubernetes listed as familiarity, no claim of operating control planes. Then I show that I understand the model, probes, autoscaling and rollouts, and pivot to deploy-quality stories I own: CI gates, health checks, canary cutovers and rollback plans.

Q6: Design a multi-region version of your Masters India e-invoicing pipeline. A: I would start by asking the business for RPO and RTO. Because invoice registration is money and compliance, I would keep one writer region per tax quarter shard and make the second region a warm standby with async replication, so active-passive. Idempotency keys already make replays safe, so after failover we can safely re-drive anything in flight. I would be clear that this is a design answer. I did not run it multi-region.

Q7: What happens if your Flink job dies mid-stream? A: It restarts from the last checkpoint, restoring both keyed state and Kafka offsets. Events after the checkpoint are replayed, so some catalog upserts happen twice, but they are idempotent, so the catalog ends up the same. That is why I describe it as at-least-once delivery with idempotent upserts.

Units reminder. RPS means requests per second (Impact Analytics 10k peak RPS). TPS means transactions per second (Masters about 12 TPS average). Rows per second is an ingest rate (the ClickHouse migration pump at about 344k rows per second), not RPS. Never mix them.

ASSORTMENT PLANNING · DATA PLATFORM · ENGINE EVALUATION

ClickHouse vs PostgreSQL — POC Report

A consolidation of the controlled benchmark POCs and live-data decisions run to answer one question: should the Assortment-Planning read/write surfaces move from PostgreSQL to ClickHouse? Every figure below was executed on row-identical data and verified adversarially — magnitudes are corrected down from first-pass, not headline-inflated.

Verdict: HYBRID, per surface — not a wholesale swap · Prepared from executed harnesses (pivot-poc, lineplan) + live BQ/PG evidence · v1.0

§ 0 Executive summary

Across four POCs — two controlled engine benchmarks and two live-data architecture decisions — the answer is consistent: use both engines, one per surface. PostgreSQL owns interactive edits and system-of-record writes; ClickHouse owns large analytical reads. Neither replaces the other, and the biggest lever is not the engine at all — it is the schema.

HEADLINE VERDICT

Writes / interactive cell edits → PostgreSQL. Sub-millisecond keyed UPDATE, scale-flat. ClickHouse has a ~5 ms floor (HTTP round-trip) and is part-creation bound; it is append-first, not edit-first.

Large analytical / full-grid reads at scale → ClickHouse. ~2–3× faster typically, up to ~13–15× when the grid needs COUNT(DISTINCT) (option counts) that spills to disk on Postgres.

The schema is the real lever. Redesigning flat → aggregate + distribution profile + explode/derive-on-demand is a 100–450× win — larger than any engine swap. Don't materialize combinatorial explosions.

Honest, adversarially-corrected magnitudes

First-pass numbers overstated ClickHouse's edge. After tuning both engines fairly and using high-entropy (non-synthetic) data, the directions all held but the magnitudes came down:

PG was given every hardware advantage (48 GB host); CH ran constrained (10 CPU / 3.3 GB Docker VM). The corrections make the case against the constrained engine — i.e. conservative.

WHERE EACH POC LANDED

PG Pivot benchmark — hybrid per surface; writes to PG, grid reads to CH; use-case 1.1.1 runs better on PG today.

PG Line-planning benchmark — don't materialize the 12B store-week; store the small editable aggregate on PG, derive on demand; CH for cross-plan rollups.

PG mtp-assort (existing app) — No to ClickHouse now; the real cost drivers are cheaper to fix inside BigQuery.

CH Agentic clustering (new module) — ClickHouse chosen for the runtime read surface; writes still land in PG. This is where CH earns its place.

§ 1 Test harness & methodology

Both benchmarks used the same controlled rig, deliberately biased toward PostgreSQL so any ClickHouse advantage is a floor, not a ceiling.

Row-identical data across engines — aggregate fingerprints match; at 250M the float-derived sums reconcile to 2e-12.

Real-schema anchor — data modeled on the live assort_smart.line_plan_choice_launch_ia layout, not toy tables.

Adversarial verification — every headline magnitude was attacked and re-measured; overstatements were corrected downward before publication.

Reproducible harnesses live in POC/pivot-poc/ (SQL, generators, benchmark scripts, an 11-endpoint FastAPI service) and POC/pivot-poc/lineplan/.

§ 2 POC 1 — Assortment pivot engine benchmark

The dominant Assortment-Planning surface is the pivot grid (choice × cluster × fiscal-week, measures joined to product dims). We benchmarked reads, writes and storage at 5M / 50M / 250M rows.

Reads (warm median wall-clock, ms)

R1 CH advantage ~13–15× (option-count spills PG). R2 flips: PG wins at 5M (1.8×), CH wins at 250M (18.5×). R3/R4 widen from ~2.5× to ~10× with scale.

Writes

PG single-cell is scale-independent (0.35→0.94 ms). The raw ~82–216× gap shrinks to ~14× against a tuned CH (~16 ms). CH batch-append instead widens with scale (12× → 2,520×). CH also carries a FINAL read-tax (~4× with multiple parts).

Storage & modeling

The 54–138× is synthetic-favorable. Real-world anchor (briscoes PG ~5.3 GB vs arhaus CH ~112 MB, ~5M rows) ≈ 47×; high-entropy data collapses this to ~1.6–2.6×. JSONB modeling penalty = 2.06× (fact_flat 2,779 ms vs fact_json 5,719 ms); the live briscoes pivot at 11,298 ms is mostly modeling, not PG's ceiling. Bulk reload (5M): PG 19.3 s vs CH 6.0 s = 3.2×.

POC 1 VERDICT

Hybrid, per surface. ClickHouse for grid/aggregate reads at scale; PostgreSQL for interactive cell write-back. The advantage is real but not a landslide — CH reads ~2–3× typical (~13× on distinct-counts); PG writes ~14× vs a tuned CH.

§ 3 POC 2 — Pivot POC (wireframe views 1.1.1 / 1.1.2 / 1.1.3)

To validate the benchmark against real product interactions, we built a working POC — schema h111, 5.76M rows, an 11-endpoint FastAPI service (hindsight_api.py on :8090) serving all three wireframe views with live read grids + Wp write-back. Full artifact in POC/pivot-poc/.

CROSS-VIEW FINDING

Writes (Wp cells, thresholds) → PostgreSQL at every scale (sub-ms, scale-flat). Full-grid reads → ClickHouse at every scale (widening to 13–15×). Selective reads → PostgreSQL while small, flipping to ClickHouse as they grow. So 1.1.1 — today's dominant surface — runs better on Postgres; the ClickHouse case is the cross-cutting analytical views plus catalog growth.

§ 4 POC 3 — Line-planning benchmark (store-week explosion)

The Line-Planning module's line_arch_store_week explodes to ~12B rows per plan for KiK (4,800 stores) — and ~50 plans exist. We benchmarked month-view reads + cell/choice edits, PG vs CH and flat-table vs a redesigned schema.

THE KEY INSIGHT — PARTITION OF UNITY

Store-week is a deterministic explosion of the choice aggregate: store_week = choice × flow_cluster_perc × cluster_store_perc × store_week_perc, where the percents sum to 1. So SUM(store-week) ≡ choice aggregate (reconciled to the cent at 10M/100M/1B on both engines). The editable truth is choice × cluster × week — ~25M rows for a 12B-flat plan, ~427× smaller. Store-week is derived on demand (~25 ms to explode one choice) and never materialized for editing. Users already edit at cluster × choice × delivery; there is no store-level edit path — finer edits are sparse per-week/per-store overrides.

Reads, edits & storage — flat vs aggregate

Aggregate is ~140–457× faster to read than flat. 12B-flat is infeasible on PG (~2–4 TB/plan); flat editing is bad on both engines (PG bulk UPDATE of 249,600 rows; CH part-rewrite mutation). @50 plans: flat PG ~70 TB / CH ~1.1 TB vs aggregate PG ~155 GB / CH ~940 MB.

ClickHouse technique deep-dive (@1B granular)

Multi-plan & sparse overrides

Multi-plan is a storage-at-rest problem, not a per-op one. Users edit one plan at a time → single-plan read is constant regardless of N (partition-pruned: PG 725 ms / CH 33 ms). Must PARTITION BY plan_code.

Clone-plan: aggregate PG 67.7 s / CH 0.85 s vs flat ~12 min/plan. Cross-plan portfolio rollup (rare, no pruning): PG 13.3 s / CH 0.19 s.

Sparse overrides (per-week/per-store exceptions, 0.008–0.4% of a 12B plan): point-upsert WRITE PG 0.15 ms flat / CH ~2 ms. Correction rollup grows on PG (98 ms → 15.5 s at 50M) but deltas are additive → pre-aggregate with SummingMergeTree/AggregatingMergeTree. Table stays MB-scale — the 12B is never materialized.

POC 3 VERDICT

The schema (flat → aggregate + distribution profile + explode-on-demand, plus base + sparse-override) is the 100–450× lever, not the engine. Writes → Postgres (sub-ms keyed UPDATE, scale-flat). Big rollup reads → ClickHouse (or PG at the aggregate's ~25M size, already sub-second). For an editable aggregate in CH use ReplacingMergeTree(version) — never AggregatingMergeTree (it sums states, wrong for set-a-cell), never heavyweight mutation, and not lightweight UPDATE (unreliable in 26.5).

§ 5 POC 4 — mtp-assort (existing app): should we move to ClickHouse?

Beyond the synthetic benchmarks, we evaluated the live existing application against real BigQuery + Postgres evidence (briscoes-01082024, australia-southeast1). The question: does the shipping mtp-assort backend belong on ClickHouse?

The edit model is fundamentally OLTP-mutable — keyed UPDATE, JSONB merge (||), scoped delete-where-plan_code + reinsert, upsert, soft-delete. ClickHouse (append-first, non-keyed async mutations) cannot replace this.

The analytical scans are ClickHouse-shaped, but the real cost drivers — SELECT * / LIMIT with no date filter (one job billed 38.8 TiB), recurring full-category rollups re-scanning ~2.9 TiB — are cheaper to fix inside BigQuery.

ClickHouse would become a third engine (BigQuery + CH + PG + sync + dialect translation), replacing neither.

POC 4 VERDICT — NO, NOT NOW

Fix it in BigQuery instead, in three tiers: (1) kill SELECT * and force a date filter (require_partition_filter=TRUE); (2) point heavy reads at the already-clustered _assort table (~3× cheaper, free win); (3) materialize one store × category × fiscal-week rollup → MB instead of 2.9 TiB (~284× less). ClickHouse only makes sense later if a high-concurrency, sub-second interactive BI product emerges.

§ 6 POC 5 — Agentic clustering (new module): where ClickHouse wins

For the greenfield Agentic Assort clustering module, the calculus is different — and this is where ClickHouse earns its place. The decision (2026-07-06) was to serve the entire runtime read surface (including clustering-job feature pulls) from a new dedicated ClickHouse instance.

Rationale = slot-determinism. BigQuery's shared STANDARD-edition slots make latency depend on org-wide load; a dedicated ClickHouse gives deterministic response and near-zero marginal probe cost — exactly what an interactive, agentic copilot needs.

Writes still land in PostgreSQL. Cluster results must join the strategy-flow tables, so the system of record stays PG; ClickHouse is the read/analytics plane only.

Greenfield schema, new instance, reusing an existing BQ→CH ingestion pipeline. This is a new build with an analytical read plane, not a swap of a transactional system.

POC 5 VERDICT — YES, FOR THE READ PLANE

The same hybrid principle, applied forward: ClickHouse for the analytical/interactive read surface of a new module where determinism matters; PostgreSQL remains the system of record for edits. This is the natural conclusion of the benchmark arc — CH is adopted exactly where the POCs said it belongs.

§ 7 Consolidated recommendations

DESIGN RULES THAT OUTRANK THE ENGINE CHOICE

  1. Schema first. Flat → aggregate + distribution profile + explode/derive-on-demand is 100–450×. Never materialize a combinatorial explosion (store-week, full grids) for editing.

  2. Base + sparse override. Store the derived base as a formula; persist only the exceptions; effective = COALESCE(override, derived). Keeps 12B-row plans at MB scale.

  3. If you do put an editable layer in ClickHouse: ReplacingMergeTree(version) for set-a-cell edits; AggregatingMergeTree/SummingMergeTree only for additive rollups & override-deltas; EmbeddedRocksDB for a PG-like KV path; Projection/AMT for read rollups; never heavyweight ALTER UPDATE; avoid lightweight UPDATE until read-after-write is reliable.

Bottom line: the engine debate is real but secondary. Run PostgreSQL and ClickHouse side by side, each on the surface it wins — and invest first in the schema, which pays more than either engine ever could.

RECOMMENDATION

Don't store the explosion. Store the aggregate + a distribution profile.

The store-week value is a deterministic partition-of-unity explosion of the choice aggregate: store_week = choice × flow_cluster_perc × cluster_store_perc × store_week_perc, and those percentages sum to 1 — so SUM(store-week) ≡ choice aggregate (verified to the cent at every scale). The editable truth lives at choice × cluster × week (~25M for a 12B-flat plan); per-store-week is derived on demand, never materialized for editing.

Engine split (under the good schema): Postgres owns the interactive edit (in-place keyed UPDATE, sub-ms, transactional); ClickHouse owns the big rollup reads and can even scan the flat 12B if you ever must. The flat materialization is the enemy — not the engine choice.

THE TWO OPERATIONS THAT HURT

Flat vs Aggregate, across scale

Same logical plan, two storage models. "Month view" = SUM to final_level × fiscal_month. "Edit a choice" = rescale one choice's plan (the backend's SCALE_LINE_ARCH path). Medians, ms.

At 100M the flat design already needs ~3 s to render a month and ~1.5 s to edit one choice; the aggregate does both in single-digit ms (~140–200× faster). The gap grows linearly with rows — at 12B the flat path is minutes-per-operation, the aggregate is unchanged.

WHY IT'S SAFE TO NOT MATERIALIZE

The explosion is lossless & reversible

The backend builds store-week by chaining four percentages onto the choice aggregate (verbatim from SCALE_LINE_ARCH_FROM_CHOICE_LAUNCH):

Each percentage is a partition of unity (sums to 1 over its dimension), so summing store-week back up returns the choice aggregate exactly. We verified SUM(flat)==SUM(agg) to the cent at 10M / 100M / 1B, on both engines.

So the aggregate loses nothing

You can always rebuild any store-week cell as aggregate × stored percentages. Store:

• choice_agg — plan × final_level × choice × cluster × week (the editable layer; ~25M for a 12B plan)

• store_dist — store → cluster + cluster_store_perc (4,800 rows)

• (week/delivery percentages — small profiles)

Explode to store-week only when a downstream truly needs it (allocation export), for one slice — ~25 ms/choice.

WHAT USERS ACTUALLY EDIT · FROM THE CODEBASE

It's all overrides — never a dense store-week grid

The backend confirms it: the edit endpoint (update_line_arch_store_week_cluster_data) writes at cluster × choice × delivery, and line_arch_store_week is 100% re-derived from the cluster×choice aggregate via the exact percentage chain we hypothesized:

Finer edits are per-week or per-store overrides — sparse manual exceptions, not a full grid. So the model is base + sparse override: the derived base (aggregate × percentages) is never stored; only the cells a human actually overrode are. The effective value is COALESCE(override, derived); a rollup is aggregate_rollup + Σ(override deltas) — so you never scan 12B, even with overrides.

Override layer benchmark — sparse overrides at 1M / 10M / 50M (0.008%–0.4% of a 12B plan)

Override write is sub-millisecond on Postgres at every density (0.15 ms keyed upsert, flat from 1M→50M) — this is the interactive path, and it never touches the 12B grid. The override-aware rollup correction is a scan of only the sparse overrides: fine on Postgres at realistic volumes (~98 ms at 1M) but it grows with override count (985 ms at 10M, 15 s at 50M), while ClickHouse stays in ms (5→52 ms).

The fix for high override volumes — and where AggregatingMergeTree finally fits

Override deltas are additive (unlike the base "set cell = X" edit). So the correction rollup can be pre-aggregated incrementally with a SummingMergeTree / AggregatingMergeTree MV (or a small PG rollup) → instant regardless of override count. This is the correct use of AMT in this system: RMT for the editable base, AMT for the additive override-delta rollup. In practice override counts are thousands–low-millions per plan (human-made), where Postgres alone is already sub-100 ms.

RECOMMENDED SCHEMA

Concrete design, per engine

Why not AggregatingMergeTree for the editable layer?

AMT/SummingMergeTree merge by summing states — built for additive accumulation, not "set this cell = X". A planner edit is a SET; modelling it as AMT means inserting compensating deltas (fragile). Use ReplacingMergeTree(version) for edits; reserve AMT for the read rollup if on-the-fly GROUP BY ever proves too slow.

STORAGE

Footprint at scale

Postgres cannot realistically store the 12B flat table (~2–4 TB + indexes); ClickHouse can (columnar, ~100–250 GB) and scan it — but neither should, because the aggregate is ~427× smaller (measured: 115 GB flat vs 276 MB agg at 1B) and lossless. CH numbers ≥1B are projected from the real 10M/100M points: when we tried to ingest 998M flat rows into ClickHouse on the constrained 3.3 GB VM it OOM-killed the container — a fitting reminder that even columnar engines pay to materialize an explosion you never needed.

CLICKHOUSE TECHNIQUE DEEP-DIVE · MEASURED AT 1B

AggregatingMergeTree, or something better?

We loaded the full 998.4M-row granular store-week into ClickHouse (1.87 GiB on disk; the same data is 115 GB in Postgres) and benchmarked every realistic technique for the two jobs: roll up to a month view, and edit a value.

Read — month rollup over 1B granular

Both AggregatingMergeTree and Projection turn the 2-second scan into a ~2–4 ms read (~1,000×). They're the right tools if you keep the 1B granular as source-of-truth and must roll it up.

Edit — mutation techniques compared (point edit + immediate read-after-write)

"Is there a better mutation technique?" — we benchmarked all of ClickHouse 26.5's options for a single-cell edit the user must see immediately.

Better CH mutation technique? Yes — and no. The clearly worse options are heavyweight mutations (1.6 s, rewrites parts) and — surprisingly — the new lightweight UPDATE (fast to issue but read-after-write is unreliable in 26.5, so a planner wouldn't see their own edit). The two good CH options are ReplacingMergeTree (append+argMax) and EmbeddedRocksDB (point upsert+get) — both ~5 ms and immediately consistent. EmbeddedRocksDB is the most PG-like (keyed upsert, no parts, no FINAL) and is the best CH-native home for the editable/override layer; pair it with a MergeTree for analytics. But none beats Postgres's ~0.2 ms — the ~5 ms CH floor is mostly the HTTP round-trip. So: keep interactive edits in Postgres (or EmbeddedRocksDB if you want it CH-native); for the read rollup use Projection/AMT; for the editable base never use heavyweight mutation or AMT.

And the deeper point still holds: if you store the 2M aggregate (not the 1B flat), a plain GROUP BY over it is already ~17 ms and edits are point ops — you don't need AMT or projections at all. They only earn their keep when the 1B granular store-week must remain the system of record.

MULTI-PLAN · ~50 PLANS

12B is per plan — and there are ~50

A planner opens and edits one plan at a time, so multi-plan is a storage-at-rest problem, not a per-operation one: with the table partitioned by plan_code, an individual plan's read/edit is isolated and stays constant no matter how many plans exist. We verified all of it with 10 plans (250M aggregate) resident.

Storage at rest — the real multi-plan cost

The multi-plan verdict: performance per planner is unchanged by plan count (partition by plan_code); the only thing that scales with N is footprint — and the flat design becomes a ~70 TB Postgres table at 50 plans (infeasible), versus a ~155 GB aggregate (or ~940 MB in ClickHouse). Plus the one true multi-plan op — clone-a-plan — is seconds on the aggregate and ~12 min+ on the flat. Both reinforce the same conclusion: store the aggregate, not the explosion.

UNBIASED HYPOTHESIS — CONFIRMED

The honest read

The schema, not the engine, is the 10–100× lever. Flat→aggregate is ~140–200× on both read and edit at 100M, and the gap grows linearly with stores/rows. Fix the schema first.

Writes belong to Postgres — aggregate cell edit is sub-ms, transactional, scale-flat. ClickHouse's editable-aggregate path (ReplacingMergeTree append) is ~60–70 ms/edit (tunable) — fine for occasional saves, not for rapid cell-by-cell typing.

Big rollup reads favor ClickHouse, but at the aggregate's modest size (~25M) Postgres is already sub-second — so a PG-only aggregate stack is viable for KiK today; ClickHouse earns its place as the read/rollup accelerator as plans/tenants multiply.

Flat editing is bad on both engines — Postgres bulk-UPDATEs hundreds of thousands of rows; ClickHouse mutations rewrite parts (even slower). Don't edit the flat table on either.

12B is a storage/write problem, not a read problem — ClickHouse can scan it; nobody can edit it interactively. The aggregate sidesteps it entirely.

Bottom line: re-model line_arch_store_week as aggregate + distribution profile + explode-on-demand. Keep edits in Postgres (sub-ms), serve big rollups from ClickHouse (or PG at today's size), and treat the flat 12B as a derived export, never the system of record. This turns a multi-minute, multi-TB plan into a millisecond, few-GB one.

All figures are real measurements on row-identical synthetic data modeled on assort_smart.line_arch_store_week (KiK-test schema; partition-of-unity reconciled). 12B rows shown as projection where local materialization is infeasible. Postgres native (full host RAM); ClickHouse in a 3.3 GB Docker VM — engine wins are conservative for ClickHouse.

AggregatingMergeTree as the editable layer | — | — | ✗ wrong tool: AMT merges by summing states (models "add", not "set = X")

Table 11

MULTI-PLAN OPERATION | POSTGRES | CLICKHOUSE | NOTE

Single-plan month read (10 plans resident) | 725 ms | 33 ms | = the 1-plan number → constant with N (partition-pruned)

Single cell edit in one plan | sub-ms | ~6 ms | unaffected by other plans

Copy / clone a plan (aggregate, 25M) | 67.7 s | 0.85 s | spawn a new plan from an existing one

Copy / clone a plan (flat, 12B) | infeasible | ~12 min | CH anchor: 1B copy = 60 s → ×12

Cross-plan / portfolio rollup (rare) | 13.3 s | 0.19 s | no partition pruning → CH columnar wins

Table 12

MODEL | PER PLAN | 10 PLANS (MEASURED) | ~50 PLANS (PROJ)

FLAT — Postgres | ~1.4 TB | ~14 TB | ~70 TB ✗

FLAT — ClickHouse | ~22 GB | ~220 GB | ~1.1 TB

AGGREGATE — Postgres | ~3.1 GB | 31 GB | ~155 GB ✅

AGGREGATE — ClickHouse | ~19 MB | 188 MB | ~940 MB ✅

Project Interview Packs (canonical)

How to use this page

  • This is the front door to the per-project interview packs. Each pack plays a tough interviewer against you, project by project.
  • Read this page first to pick the right pack for the role, then open the pack.
  • Memorise the one-line pitch and the "current PDF bullets" for each project below. They are the version to trust if a pack's older headings disagree.

Every project on the current PDF (Tarun_Mittal_SSE_5yr_Java_PyGo_AI.pdf, Java + Python + Go track) has a pack. A pack is a coaching file with a 30-second and 2-minute explanation, an architecture sketch, the design decisions, a bullet-by-bullet defence, a mock interview, and a "do not say" list. The packs were first generated in July 2026 by pairing an interviewer agent with a candidate agent for each project, and they have been partly re-synced since.

Tags used here. MEASURED means there is a log, document or code behind the number. ESTIMATED means arithmetic I can show. HISTORICAL means from my past work records. TARGET means a design goal, so say "targeting".

One-line pitch per project

Say these out loud until they feel natural. Each is the opener you use before diving into a pack.

  • Impact Analytics (AssortSmart). "I own the Go/Gin platform and the AI decision layer of a retail planning product. The platform handles 10k peak RPS, I cut planner pivots from 189 seconds to 12 seconds with ClickHouse rollups, and I shipped the Ask Iris copilot behind an 80% CI gate."
  • Uber FRM. "At Uber via EPAM I owned the backend that moved Finance's quarterly risk scoping off Google Sheets into MySQL, cutting reconciliation from 14 days to 3 days against a $340M materiality threshold, and I led 3 engineers on the Spring Data JPA / Hibernate migration."
  • Uber Eats Menu. "I worked on menu ingestion that turns multilingual PDF menus into catalog data with Gemini and RAG, at 98% field fidelity in offline evaluation, cutting restaurant onboarding from 24 hours to 2 hours."
  • Uber Mobility ANZ. "I automated driver and vehicle document checks against local authority rules with a deterministic validation backend, reaching 99.9% compliance and removing about 20 hours a week of manual work." (HISTORICAL.)
  • Masters India. "I led the move from a PHP monolith to Spring Boot microservices for a GST e-invoicing product, cutting p95 latency from 1.2 seconds to 300 milliseconds, and worked on a Kafka pipeline handling over a million government submissions a day."
  • GeeksforGeeks. "I migrated the doubt-support backend from PHP to Django so it handled 10K+ daily queries and 10x spikes during live contests, and built the influencer earnings dashboard."

The two questions every pack will throw at you

"What exactly did you own versus the team?" Start with the direct answer: name the bullets you owned. Then name what you did not own. At Uber FRM, the HFM extract pipeline was shared and the real-time collaboration and Slack notification service was built by others. At Impact Analytics, the Postgres-to-ClickHouse CDC pipeline was a colleague's work. Saying what you did not own makes everything else you say more believable.

"How do you know that number is real?" Give the measurement source in one sentence, then the arithmetic. For example: "The 15.5x is 189 seconds divided by about 12.3 seconds on a 250-million-row benchmark harness." Or: "The $600K is about $2 per menu times 30K menus times 12 months, which is $720K, and I round down to $600K to be conservative." The full derivations live in 09_metrics_derivations.md and 18_resume_number_catalog.md.

Study order

  1. GROUND_TRUTH.md: the locked facts for this track.
  2. 31_resume_deep_explain_map.md: every bullet explained.
  3. The pack for the role you are interviewing for (table above).
  4. The deep dive for that project: 10_impact_analytics_deep_dive.md, 11_uber_frm_deep_dive.md, 12_masters_gfg_deep_dive.md or 14_uber_menu_deep_dive.md.
  5. STAR stories: 07_behavioral_star_stories.md.

Stack note for this track

On this track (Java, Python and Go), Uber FRM is Java and Spring Boot with Spring Data JPA and Hibernate on MySQL, and Masters India is Spring Boot microservices with Hibernate. Impact Analytics platform APIs are Go/Gin, the IA agent plane is Python (FastAPI, LangGraph), Uber Menu is Python, and GeeksforGeeks is Django. Always say Spring Boot and Spring Data JPA / Hibernate for FRM, and Spring Boot for Masters India.

EPAM / Uber scope validation

Date: 2026-07-27
Sources: GROUND_TRUTH.md, FRM code dump + TDD, 11_uber_frm_deep_dive.md, 23b_uber_interview_packs.md, Menu HISTORICAL ops
Purpose: Answer CTO/EM red flag — “via EPAM = fake Uber ownership?”

Verdict

Claim Validated? Confidence How to say it
Employed by EPAM, embedded on Uber Finance / Menu products YES High “SDE2 at Uber via EPAM (staff aug)”
Uber FTE / people manager NO High Never claim Uber employee or perf reviews
Tech lead of 3-engineer EPAM pod YES (user-confirmed + code conventions) High Design reviews, API contracts, design reviews
Owned FRM scoping service design + recon v2 migration YES (code + branch + migration doc) High Personal branch tmitta1/recon-income-api-migration
Owned HFM ETL end-to-end NO High “Service consumes HFM-loaded MySQL; ETL was shared”
Owned frm-collaboration-service (Slack/collab) NO High Separate service — don’t claim
70% recon cut measured NO — TARGET only High “Targeting 70%…”
Menu $600K / 24h→2h / 98% fidelity HISTORICAL (past resume + ops) Medium Defend as Menu work on same employment; offline eval honesty
Menu Kafka/Flink peak TPS measured NO High Burst/replay/keyed dedupe defense; ESTIMATED peaks

Panel answer: Scope is real IC ownership inside Uber product + monorepo, with employer = EPAM. Not inflated “Uber Staff.” Not ticket-only if you can walk FRM code (layers, recon migration, 1,100+ tests).

Employment facts (canonical)

Field Truth
Employer EPAM Systems
Client / product Uber (Finance FRM + Uber Eats Menu)
Title Software Engineer A2 / SDE2
Dates Jul 2024 – May 2026 (~1.9y)
Location Bangalore
Resume line UBER (via EPAM Systems) — keep this; do not hide EPAM

What was actually owned (FRM) — evidence-backed

Area Evidence Ownership level
Platform: FastAPI + MySQL (Fusion.js), 8 screens, 30+ REST APIs Code: ~32 routes incl. health; TDD Primary backend owner of scoping service
11-table SQLAlchemy 2.0 schema database/models/ Design + implementation
Layered handler → service → repository Uniform across codebase Set/enforced conventions for pod
Recon v1 Sheets → v2 MySQL RECON_API_MIGRATION.md; 18 files, +1,268 LOC; branch under your id Personally owned migration
Auth via gateway x-auth-params-email Middleware pattern in code Implemented in service
Tests 1,100+ (grep ~1,288 def test_) Bazel uber_py_test Grew suite + CI gate
Materiality $340M / residual $170M Q4 2025 sample CSVs MEASURED sample, not eternal constants
Feeds PwC work papers Product purpose / TDD Platform output; you didn’t “work at PwC”
Led 3 engineers User-confirmed EPAM pod Tech lead, not manager

Explicit non-ownership (say out loud if probed)

  1. HFM ETL pipeline — shared; you consume loaded tables.
  2. Collaboration / Slack service — separate repo.
  3. Uber org design review board as FTE — you worked in EPAM+Uber stakeholder cadence (PM/Finance); don’t invent ARB membership.
  4. People management — no Uber/EPAM perf reviews of the 3 as “my reports” in HR sense.
  5. Measured 70% time save — TDD target only.

What “led 3” means (validated framing)

Safe one-liner:
“I was tech lead of a 3-engineer EPAM pod on Uber Finance FRM — not a people manager. I sliced work by layer, enforced API/ORM conventions from backend syncs, and gated merges on Bazel tests.”

Concrete actions (prep-backed):

  • Task split along handler / service / repository / model so two people could ship one feature without merge wars (recon migration is the example).
  • Conventions: thin handlers; services own trees; repos own sessions; updated_by from auth header; asyncio.to_thread for blocking DB.
  • Review gate: tests + uber_py_test before merge → suite to 1,100+.

Fail answer: “I managed three Uber engineers and owned the Finance org roadmap.”

Menu (same employment) — scope honesty

Claim Tag Interview rule
Same EPAM→Uber engagement HISTORICAL role OK to discuss as second Uber product
30K+ menus/mo, 24h→2h, $600K+/yr, 95%+ ingest HISTORICAL ops Keep; don’t invent new TPS
RAG + Gemini + Milvus schema gate 98% / 100% Offline eval Say offline, not online A/B; no SFT on PDF
Kafka + Flink on PDF (post-Flink update) HISTORICAL / ESTIMATED rates Defend burst, replay, keyed dedupe — not vanity TPS

How recruiters / CTO should hear it

Bad packaging Good packaging
“I worked at Uber” (implies FTE) “SDE2 on Uber FRM via EPAM”
“Led Uber’s Finance eng team” “Tech-led EPAM pod of 3 on FRM”
“Built Uber’s entire audit stack” “Owned FRM scoping service + recon migration; feeds PwC work papers”
Hide EPAM Lead with product problem + ownership, EPAM as employment vehicle

Amazon recruiter guidance already matches this: EPAM secondary; product + owned design primary.

Reference-check questions (what would validate)

Ask an EPAM lead / Uber PM peer:

  1. Who owned the recon Sheets→MySQL migration and the SQLAlchemy schema?
  2. Did Tarun set review/CI standards for the pod?
  3. Was he presenting progress to Uber Finance stakeholders or only EPAM internal?

If answers align with migration doc + backend sync notes → scope validated. If “he only took tickets under Uber Staff design” → downgrade “owned design” language.

Score: EPAM risk after validation

Dimension Score Note
Honesty of employment framing 9/10 “via EPAM” on resume is correct
Hands-on FRM depth 8/10 Code + migration doc strong
Leadership claim accuracy 7/10 Solid if “pod TL”; fails if “manager”
Outcome metrics honesty 8/10 70% TARGET correctly worded on good resumes
Inflated Uber brand risk Mitigated If verbal matches this doc

CTO condition still stands: advance to rounds; offer only after EPAM-scope story holds in interview (and IA exit narrative is clean). Scope itself is defensible, not fabricated — if you stay inside the guardrails above.
